articles.text: During the June 12 Piedmont School Board meeting True North Research presented survey findings showing that Piedmont residents were likely to support an increase to Measure H to fund schools. The poll results show strong support for tax-based financial support for faculty in the school district. The school board is set to vote tonight for the increase to be on the November ballot. The tax aims to generate more revenue to fund teacher salaries, and the 2025-26 raise of 4.5% for teachers is contingent upon its passing. The survey was conducted in April by email, text and telephone with 282 responses. The district is proposing to increase the tax on residents from 25 cents per square foot of home to 50 cents. An initial ballot test, which uses a sample 75 word ballot statement, showed 77% of survey takers would pass the increase to Measure H, and two-thirds of the vote is needed. “I think obviously the answer is yes. These are not muddy results; these are results that other districts would dream of having,” said True North president Tim McClarney. articles.text: Egg Drop on final day the highlight Piedmont Cub Scouts enjoyed a wide range of arts and crafts, learned valuable Scout skills, and participated in STEM-related activities at the Piedmont Council’s annual Cub Scout Day Camp. A tradition for more than 55 years, the day camp welcomes first through fifth graders for five afternoons of activities in Dracena Park. The highlight each year is an egg drop facilitated by the Fire Department and its 75-foot extension ladder This year’s camp ran from Monday to Friday, June 10-14. “For a lot of our kids it’s a tradition; many attend for all five years,” said Eris Turner, Program Manager with the Piedmont Council. “We had several campers who were sad they had to leave early on certain days because of other commitments.” Nearly 20 Cub Scouts were repeat attendees. Each day the campers cycled through six stations – cooking, crafts, Den time, Scout skills, sports and STEM activities, each with unique daily activities inspired by this year’s camp theme, “Outdoor Adventure.” Some of these activities included making decorative sun catchers out of recycled water bottles, designing Den flags, creating cheers, learning how to do a flag ceremony, playing “Ranger Says” (an activity similar to “Simon Says”), making a homemade battery by using with dirt and making homemade ice cream. The Day Camp also presents leadership opportunities for older Scouts. This year’s camp had 15 Scout volunteers of various ranks from every troop in the Council. “Most of the volunteers oversee the activities and even develop the station programs for the kids,” explained Kate Benson, Scout Executive for the Piedmont Council. “It takes a lot of preparation in advance, but it’s a cool leadership opportunity for those interested in taking advantage of it.” One such volunteer was One ingenious egg drop design used popcorn, boba straws and a grocery bag parachute to great success. (Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on June 29, 2022.) KATHY KELLEHER, Daughter of Parade Founder It was when I was six years old and on my first float, which was a crepe paper American flag. I waved to people, and felt very proud. We had Betsy Ross and Uncle Sam in a pickup truck leading our float. The plague of catalytic converter thefts Editor The following letter was sent to Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. Dear Chief Bowers, I am writing this as an open letter to you because I believe many Piedmont residents have a similar concern. A few weeks ago, the catalytic converter on my Prius was stolen ... for the second time. The CAT was cut out despite my having installed a protective plate. “That happens a lot,” the responding police officer told me, “The thieves know how to cut around those protective plates, it just takes them a few minutes longer.” I don’t fault the Piedmont Police for not being able to catch the thieves in the act; they are in and out of Piedmont very quickly. But I do wonder what our police department is doing, and can do, to stem this rampant crime. Here are two suggestions. I’d like to know Piedmont’s reaction. 1) This is a regional problem. It must be solved with cooperative effort of all the police departments in Alameda County, the County sheriff, and probably all the counties in the Bay Area. CAT thieves should not be safe from apprehension simply by crossing jurisdictional lines. 2) A joint-agency force must investigate and apprehend the criminals at the top of the money chain. Low-level thieves cut out the CATs, and then take them to some kind of chop shop where the valuable platinum elements are removed. Then the platinum is sent to some kind of refinery where it is molded into a high-priced, saleable resource. The money for this enterprise flows down the chain: from the refiner to the chop shop to the street thief. This plague of thefts can only be stopped by identifying and apprehending the perpetrators at the top of the money chain. What is Piedmont doing, in collaboration with other law enforcement agencies, to stop these CAT thefts at the source of the problem? I have spent money on a new CAT and a new blocking plate, knowing that this just makes it slightly more difficult for the CAT thieves. What else can a Piedmont resident do besides call on our Police Chief to participate in, or establish if necessary, a region-wide effort to stop the CAT thieves’ money source? –Bruce Joffe Piedmont resident ROLAND LAZZAROTTO, Parade Starter I liked the time we had horses and a guy assigned to walk behind the horses to clean up after them. He had a wheelbarrow painted blue with white stars, and he was given a golden shovel. CAROLYN BRUCK, Parade Committee Thinking back through all the years, the creative neighborhood floats were always a highlight for me. The ones from Bellevue Ave. – the Gruber family & neighbors – always showed such imagination and creativity. One year they had the White House, and another the Statue of Liberty. JOHN MORRISON, Parade Car Organizer I had a ‘54 Corvette for several years. My favorite times were driving it in the parade around 20 years ago. I have since sold the car and miss it. CARLA BETTS, Parade Committee Chair Every year for the past 22 years the parade has been a wonderful memory for me. articles.text: Photo by Greg Slatoff The Piedmont Community Band marches in last year’s 4th of July Parade with its large banner. celebrate its 40th anniversary at this year’s 4th of July parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – who can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led each year by Ken Kawaichi dressed as Emperor Norton, that time-honored resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Emperor of the United States” in 1859, despite having no formal political power. Kawaichi has the distinction of being the only person to march the length of the parade route backwards. Piedmont Community Band was established in 1984 by then-student Jane Reed with the assistance of PHS Music Director Alan Harvey. “The first thing Mr. Harvey told me was ‘We have no marching equipment,’” she laughed. It was a beginning strongly reminiscent of the Meredith Willson musical, The Music Man, except the band to be created was to include adults and schoolkids. Undaunted, Reed knew she could count on the community for help. Daughters of the American Revolution donated $100 to help buy straps for the instruments and donations came in little by little, year after year. The Piedmont Recreation Department donated a banner in subsequent years. “It was a community effort,” Reed explained. The band’s “one rehearsal, one performance” mantra evolved out of necessity. “I was trying to get other high school kids, who are typically very busy, to set aside one evening to practice before we played in the parade. So, we just did one practice, hoping that enough students would come and that we would look okay on the parade day,” recalled Reed. The Community Band’s first performance was in the parade in 1984. “That first year was a little bit difficult because none of these kids had marched and played at the same time. So they were learning to do that,” she said. Greg Slatoff, a longtime member of the band, stepped forward this year as one of its directors, picking up the reins of Ray Per- 4th of July Parade man, who led the band until his death in 2017. Slatoff is best known for organizing the Piedmont Jazz Festival each year. He said he joined the band for the wonderful, near romantic feeling it gives him. “It just reminds you of everything right with America. It’s a time when you’re marching down Highland and you’re blowing your horn with your friends and neighbors around you,” he said. “I mean, that’s just as good as it gets.” The band is also known for its loose structure and hierarchy. Musicians who show up for the annual rehearsal are welcomed into the lineup with open arms. “It’s kind of ‘ragged, but right’ in that sense,” explained Slatoff. “We have some ringers. We’ve got people that are from the USC band who really know what they’re doing, And then they have bozos like me that sort of play the tenor saxophone and sort of fumble their way through it,” he joked. “We love doing it because we love seeing it,” added Reed, also a saxophone player. “We love seeing the band every year. I really feel it’s important to have music in the parade,” said Reed. Keeping with tradition, the band meets once a year on the evening of July 2 on Dracena Avenue for a one-block street. The band typically plays three standard pieces of music, anchored by the University of Wisconsin fight song, “On Wisconsin.” All musicians – adults and older students – with an interest in being part of the band aencouraged to contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com. New band members will be sent copies of all music to be played before the parade.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Band celebrates 40th anniversary

articles.text: Book is a celebration and description of what makes great cartoons great The book Funny Stuff: How Great Cartoonists Make Great Cartoons, co-authored by Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner, will be released nationally in hard cover next month on July 16. The book is a 135-page exploration of comics and cartoons with a particular emphasis on the art form of the single-panel cartoon. The pages contain over 100 cartoons which the authors use to spark discussions about process, inspiration, art and diversity in the world of cartooning. The book is now available for pre-order on Amazon and has already received endorsements from well-known cartoonists. Witte’s single panel cartoon FLIP appears weekly in the Piedmont Post. “Funny Stuff is a must-read for cartoon fans who wonder about the strange process of turning life inside-out, twisting and combining unrelated topics and creating a mental story that makes us laugh at ourselves,” said Dan Piraro, creator of the Bizarro comic strip which appeared for years in the San Francisco Chronicle. “If you only buy Funny Stuff for the 100 great cartoons, you’d be getting your money’s worth. But the real bang for the yuck comes from what cartoonist Phil Witte and cartoon afficionado Rex Hesner have to say about them,” said Bob Mankoff, former cartoon editor of the New Yorker, who suggested the idea for the book to Witte and Hesner. Witte and Hesner were the creators of Cartoon Companion, Photo by Phil Witte Long-time Piedmont residents Phil Witte and Rex Hesner met in the early 2000s but didn’t begin collaborating until 2016. articles.text: Meet KP, a lively and loveable, 9-month-old at-risk pup. Weighing in at 59 pounds, KP is full of life and ready to find his forever home. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers describe KP as social with dogs and people. He enjoys interacting with people and giving them affection. He also enjoys wrestling with other dogs during playgroups and may do well in a multi-dog home with other social dogs who could show him the ropes. A strong boy, he would benefit from continued training on loose leash walking. KP is motivated by treats. He currently knows sit and down. Staff at the shelter say he would do best in a home with children over 12 years old due to his energy level. The book is a 135-page exploration of comics and cartoons with a particular emphasis on the art form of the single-panel cartoon. The pages contain over 100 cartoons which the authors use to spark discussions about process, inspiration, art and diversity in the world of cartooning. But the real bang for the yuck comes from what cartoonist Phil Witte and cartoon afficionado Rex Hesner have to say about them,” said Bob Mankoff, former cartoon editor of the New Yorker, who suggested the idea for the book to Witte and Hesner. articles.text: School districts in California must present a Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP) every three years for their school board and county boards to approve. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich delivered a comprehensive initial public hearing during the June 12 school board meeting, and the LCAP for 2024-27 stands to be approved in tonight’s, June 26, meeting. “This was a heavy lift. There were so many different things about it and this was a three-year LCAP. We were aligning with the strategic plan,” said Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen of the 87-page report. Goal #1: Creating an Environment to Thrive Goal #2: Investing in Outstanding Academics Goal #3: Partnering Beyond the Classroom Goal #4: Building for Operational Excellence Next year, for the first time, Piedmont will offer Independent Study on a third-party platform, with Irma Munoz Daniels as liaison. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn added her excitement about Independent Study, which can be hybrid as well. “[Independent Study] is a program gap in our district, which could build our enrollment, and it could offer an alternative option for students who need it,” said Hawn. The broadest direction for the district is its Strategic Plan. The LCAP functions within the strategic plan. For individual concerns or needs the district looks specifically to the Single Plan for Student Achievement (SPSA). In tonight’s school board meeting the LCAP will receive further consideration and is subject to further public comment before board approval.
articles.title: LCAP delivers three-year vision for Piedmont schools

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, June 26, 2024 Summer Thoughts By Randall Grayson Are you the parent of a schoolaged child? This is for you. Why did you decide to have children? What brings you joy in parenting now? And most importantly, how can you make the most of this precious time? Is it their laughter, their curiosity, or watching them grow and learn? Perhaps it is the way they see the world with fresh eyes? These are the moments that make parenthood so rewarding. A look at the stats • 75% of the time we spend with our kids in our lifetime will be spent by age 12. • During an average school week, parents spend less than an hour a day truly engaged with their children—playing games, taking walks, or sharing distraction-free meals. • Parents spend about 20 more minutes a day with children in the summer than during the school year. • Pondering: how much time do you spend, and would you like to spend? • With 2 hours a day during the summer weekdays, and 6 hours each day over the weekend, a 10-week summer could offer an extra 220 hours of quality time – that’s equivalent to over 9 full days. “Quality time” isn’t just about being in the same room; it’s about full engagement – playing, talking, sharing meals without screens, or simply being present. It’s not about elaborate plans or expensive outings; it’s about connection. Below are some broad, varied ideas to get your juices flowing. Outdoor Activities • Outdoor Adventures: Hike, camp, or explore local parks. Nature provides endless opportunities for bonding and learning. • Gardening: Plant and tend to a garden together, teaching patience and responsibility. • Picnics: Pack some food and a blanket and head to the nearest park. As the Senior Patrol Leader, I was able to connect with both adults and kids who participated in the camp, which, in itself, was a reward.” As is tradition, the day camp culminated in its much-anticipated egg drop contest, where Scouts put their creative minds to the test by finding the best way to drop a raw egg from a height of seven stories without the egg breaking. Members of the Piedmont Fire Department assisted by dropping the eggs, one by one, in homemade protective enclosures from the engine’s 75-foot extension ladder. The contest is unique in that Scouts are given very little restrictions on how to achieve their goal. All that is required is the container’s dimension must measure less than 8” x 8” x 8”, the egg must be raw and campers may not affix anything to the egg itself. Other than that, “anything goes,” according to organizers. Designs this year included an egg-holding box with a parachute to slow its descent and a box of loose crash pads made from popcorn and packing peanuts. Everyone whose egg survived the fall received a free icee at Mulberry’s Market. Staffer Ciaran Gallagher helps a young camper put the finishing touches on his foam rocket. One of the craft activities involved building a maze for a plant to grow through.

articles.text: Preview of this year’s course and favorite riders Photos courtesy of CyclingWeekly.com Tadej Pogačar looks to win his third Tour de France General Classification standings. This year’s Tour de France marks the 111th edition of La Grande Boucle, starting on Saturday, June 29 in Florence, Italy and, for the first time ever, finishes on July 21 in Nice, France, not Paris due to preparations for the Olympic Games this summer. Another intriguing item is that the Grand Finale, the last race day, will be an individual time trial, and could decide the fate of this year’s Yellow Jersey. The start in Florence marks the first time the tour will begin in Italy. The country will host the first four stages, beginning with 206 km and 200 km hilly stages to Bologna. Following a flat stage on July 3, the tour turns up for its first mountain classification on Stage 4 as they leave Italy from Pinerolo 138 km to Valloire, France. It will feature three steep climbs, including a 23 km climb up Col du Galibier before the descent to the finish. Stages 5-6 provides a collective 376 km of flat riding, which should be good days for the sprinters with both stages including individual intermediate sprints. Stage 7 is another good day for speed with a 25.3 km individual time trial from France’s Nuits-Saint-Georges to Gevrey-Chambertin. Stage 8 continues the sprinting on a 183.4 km flat stage from Semur-en-Auxois to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises, which will feature relentless up-and-down movement with five different categorized climbs. Stage 9 in Troyes is a 199-km hilly stage with more ascents, including four categorized mountains. It will include 14 gravel-road sections called “White Roads,” which leaves riders susceptible to crashes. July 9’s Stage 10 is a 187.3 km flat course from Photos courtesy of CyclingWeekly.com Jonas Vingegaard is hoping to win his third straight Yellow Jersey. Orléans to Saint-Amand-Montrond, including one intermediate sprint. Stage 11 is a difficult 211 km mountain course from Évaux-lesBains to Le Lioran, including six categorized mountains and a grueling 4,350 meters of elevation gain—making it a critical day for the climbers. Stages 12-13 are both flat courses with respective days of 204 km and 171 km, taking the tour through the Pyrenees to Pau. Stages 14-15 then provide 350 km of mountain riding. Stage 14 has three steep climbs, including 19 km up Col du Tourmalet which will have a pair of 9% gradient climbs. Stage 15 comes on Bastille Day, July 14 and has five mountain climbs and a 15.8km summit finish up Plateau de Beille. Stage 16 is a 188.6 km flat course but will include a lot of Photo courtesy of LeTour.com Map of this year’s Tour de France – 3,492 km kilometers (2,170 miles) from Florence, Italy to Nice, France. It marks the first time the race will start in Italy and end in a major city other than Paris.

articles.text: Preview: Track’s sprinting events Photo courtesy of Outsports Sha’Carri Richardson is favored to win 100 and 200 meters at the Olympics. The 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris are quickly approaching and will take place from July 24 to August 11. We’ll be doing a rundown of the most popular events in the weeks leading of to the summer games. This week, we’ll start with a preview of sprinting events in track. The United States has dominated track and field since the first modern-era Olympic Games in 1896, claiming 828 total medals. England is the next closest nation with 211. United States Track & Field is currently in the middle of its U.S. Olympic Trials ending on June 30. Here are some events and names to keep an eye on next month. All events will be streamed on NBC’s app, Peacock. Women’s 100 & 200 meter dash Sha’Carri Richardson recently won the United States’ 100 meter qualifier on Saturday, June 22 with a time of 10.71. She is also expected to compete in the 200 meter dash and will look to qualify on Thursday, June 27. articles.text: With only so many of our end-of-year awards to go around, some of the mighty contributions made throughout the year tend to get lost on the shuffle. In this article, we reflect on three athletes at the school who were either entering their first year as a starter or getting time in a featured role for the first time in their PHS athletic career. Three who made a huge impact in the largest role of their time at Piedmont included twosport athlete Friedie Schickedanz, John Olsen of baseball, and Lindsey Wirgler of basketball. John Olsen graduates from Piedmont High after helping baseball win the WACC’s regular season title and reach the finals in NCS and CIF NorCal tournaments. 15 appearances, totaling 57.2 innings pitched, three complete games, and two shutout victories. He logged 51 strikeouts, carrying an ERA of 2.32. Olsen earned first-team AllLeague honors. LINDSEY WIRGLER Basketball Staff Photos Friedie Schickedanz was an offensive leader in lacrosse and lined up at quarterback on the flag football team. FRIEDIE SCHICKEDANZ Flag Football & Lacrosse Friedie Schickedanz just finished her junior year at PHS and is a two-sport athlete in flag football and lacrosse. She lined up at quarterback in Piedmont’s inaugural flag football season and was an attacker in the spring on the lacrosse team. In lacrosse she was a marquee ball handler who helped PHS win its first WACC championship since 2019 in an 8-7 victory over Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont answered a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, quickly responded with goals by Schickedanz and two Ruby Guzdar. She earned first-team All-League honors. In the fall, Schickedanz was a quarterback for the flag football team, rotating with Mia Leggett. She helped the team for 4-6 in its first year of action, throwing the first touchdown in school history on a game-winning connection to Malea Hartford on 4th-and-goal in a 12-6 win over Mt. Eden. Lindsey Wirgler, Class of 2024, emerged as a starter in her first year of eligibility after missing her junior year after transferring to Piedmont. She proved to be a vital player as the team’s second-leading scorer behind Natalia Martinez. The girls’ basketball team finished with a 20-8 overall record and was co-WACC Champions alongside Bishop O’Dowd, marking the school’s second consecutive WACC banner. They received the No. 6 seed in the NCS Open Division, the upper echelon of the section, losing in the first round No. 3 Carondelet. They qualified to the CIF State Tournament, receiving the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 bracket, falling 53-41 to No. 8 Whitney in Rocklin. Wirgler’s top performances included scoring 23 points in a 54-48 win over Alameda and 23 points in a 69-50 loss to O’Dowd. She also hit five 3-pointers and scored 20 points in a 73-27 win over Berkeley. She earned first-team AllLeague honors. JOHN OLSEN Baseball John Olsen,a. recent graduate, emerged as the baseball team’s starting pitcher. He helped Piedmont go 19-10 on their way to the WACC Regular Season title. Baseball reached the D4 NCS Championship and D4 CIF State NorCal Championship. Olsen nearly doubled his stats from the previous year. He went 6-4 as a starting pitcher, to go along with two saves in relief. He led the Highlanders with Lindsey Wirgler emerged as a critical 3-point shooter as a senior.

articles.text: With the new school year quickly approaching, the Class of 2025 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them. ENZO BERNALES Soccer Enzo Bernales is a key player in coach Todd Sullivan’s system as a central attacking midfielder, often leading the front line of Piedmont’s attack. The Highlanders’ boys soccer team finished 12-3-3 overall, reaching the Division 3 North Coast Section postseason. As the No. 2 seed, PHS bashed No. 15 Novato 6-1 in the opening round, but was upset 3-1 by No. 7 Archie Williams in the quarterfinals. On January 23, PHS defeated Berkeley 1-0 for the first time since joining the Western Alameda County Conference in 2012. Bernales scored the game-winning goal in the 24th minute and PHS closed out the following 56 minutes of regulation without allowing a goal. He was our Sophomore of the Year in 2023 after helping lead PHS to the Division 4 NCS championship, earning them a promotion to Div. 3. Bernales earned first-team All-League honors in 2024. TOMMY ASHTON Football Tommy Ashton is a bruising running back and linebacker on coach Jordan Seiden’s football team. The Highlanders went 7-4 last fall on its way to winning the WACC Shoreline Division in a 29-26 battle over Newark Memorial. It was the school’s first league title since 2015. They were given the No. 5 seed in the D5 NCS playoffs and lost to No. 4 Alhambra in the first round. Ashton led the team with 882 rushing yards on 143 carries for 6.2 yards per carry and seven Soccer player Enzo Bernales enters his senior year. Staff Photos He was the Pos’s 2023 Sophomore of the Year. touchdowns as a bruiser-style running back—lower his shoulder to put the boom on defenders. He was a key player in setting the tone against Newark Memorial, recording 67 rushing yards including several key first-down runs where he bowled over defenders. Other big performances include 83 yards and a touchdown in a 36-8 win over Arroyo, 74 yards and a score in a 41-3 win over Encinal, he scored twice in a 46-7 win over Mt. Eden. He also put up 134 rushing yards in a 16-13 loss to Alameda. He earned first-team AllLeague honors. Ashton also plays pm a club rugby team. Tommy Ashton is football’s lead running back and middle linebacker. Miya Fujimoto is a key player in softball and flag football. MIYA FUJIMOTO Softball, Flag Football Miya Fujimoto enters her fourth year as a starter on the softball team. She emerged as a leader in flag football’s inaugural season last fall. She often lined up as a receiver and utilized her speed as a running back, PHS finished its first season fourth in the WACC after opening with a nail-biting 13-12 loss to top-seed Berkeley. In 2025, NCS will debut postseason playoffs in flag football. Next spring she will be captain of the softball team as an infielder and pitcher. The team finished 10-8 overall and reached the D4 NCS postseason, losing in the quarterfinals as the No. 5 seed to No. 4 Fortuna, 7-1. Fujimoto batted for a sterling .467 average, including a team-leading three doubles, two triples, and two home runs. She also led the squad with 25 RBIs and 29 runs scored. On the mound, Fujimoto was Piedmont’s marquee starter with 62.2 inning of work for 90 strikeouts and an ERA of 3.01. articles.text: Next up: Panama on Thursday, Uruguay on Monday The CONMEBOL Copa América is rolling through its first of three Group Stage matches. The United States Men’s National Team opened with an expected 2-0 win over Bolivia on Sunday, June 23 at AT&T Stadium in Dallas. They are now set to face No. 45 Panama tomorrow, June 27, and close against No. 15 Uruguay on Monday, July 1 in a match that will likely determine the fate of Group C. For No. 11 ranked USA, avoiding any upsets against No. 85 Bolivia was needed to get out of Group C into the knockout stages at the bare minimum. Against Bolivia, the U.S. dominated possession with 61 percent of the ball and reeled off 20 shots with eight on target. AC Milan winger and U.S. captain Christian Pulisic was surgical with a goal in the third minute, where he curved a right-footed shot into the net. The Stars and Stripes made it 2-0 with a goal in the 44th minute by Monaco 22-year-old striker Folarin Balogun. Bolivia entered the tournament as the worst-ranked overall team in the tournament, so getting two by the Bolivians doesn’t come as much Christian Pulisic buried a beautiful arcing shot in the third minute in the United States’ 2-nil win over Bolivia. of a surprise. In fact, they’ll need to play at a much higher level if they want a chance at winning the group. The United States looks ahead Panama, which is coming off of a 3-1 loss to Uruguay. USMNT will be the hands-down favorites, meaning the U.S. must avoid any letdowns once again. If the United States drops points against Uruguay poses the largest threat to the U.S. in Group C. Panama, it’ll undoubtedly leave the door wide open for Uruguay to take the group. Given Uruguay will be heavy-favorites over Bolivia; it’s all shaping up for a tantalizing July 1 match with the U.S. for Group C’s crown. Group C’s winner will face the second seed out of Group D: No. 5 Brazil, No. 12 Colombia, No. 52 Costa Rica, and No. 56 Paraguay. If the United States finishes with the second-seed, they’ll face the winner of Group D. Colombia currently leads after one match with a 2-1 win over Paraguay, while Brazil was lackluster in a 0-0 draw against Costa Rica. Brazil plays Paraguay on Friday, while Colombia faces Costa Rica earlier in the day. Elsewhere in the tournament, Ecuador was my favorite to win Group B and dropped its opening match against Venezuela with a 2-1 loss and drew a red card on the nation’s top scorer, Enner Velencia. Will the Ecuadorian’s collapse despite having one of the highest valued rosters in the tournament? The United States looks ahead to Panama on Thursday.

articles.text: Kronos Quartet: Violinists David Harrington and John Sherba (left), Hank Dutt (viola) and Paul Wiancko (cello) Even after 50 years, the unique Kronos Quartet is still plunging headlong into new music with its San Francisco festival last weekend, adding uncommon extras, summed up as partly concert, partly quintet, partly historical interview, partly an exhumed Cantonese opera recording. The unorthodox concert tribute entailed a talk on Chinese-American history leading into a rousing quintet of Kronos plus Wu Man – the East meeting West squarely and amicably, pentatonic and tonality blended – in Dai Wei’s Through the Narrow Gate. Wu Man’s accomplished play plucking the strings of a Chinese pipa is extraordinary, whether blending nimbly with the four Kronos string players or doing dulcet accompaniments to an interview with former Piedmonter, historian and legal scholar David Lei – arguably the most heterogeneous interplay yet attempted at the SFJazz Center’s Miner Auditorium. Wu Man’s deft play can make cherry trees bloom. And as background for Through the Narrow Gate came, snatches of an early-20th-century Edison-cylinder recording of Cantonese opera found in an archive blended with composer Dai Wei’s own voice. Another Kronos marker was that most of the program featured women composers, including Marvel Jem Roth, Haeon Lee, Dai Wei and Aleksandra Vrebalov, with the latter winning the sought-after Gravemeyer Prize for composition this year. Here, in Gold Came from Space, Vrebalov has created a work destined to win wide acceptance, settling down after a whirlwind of tremolos to a fetching, song-like viola solo, beautifully rendered by Hank Dutt. The fearless Kronos players bite off one challenge after another, even delving into the spikiest music of recent times. These entailed on June 20 – in addition to a Sun Ra/Terry Riley adaptation – Sahba Aminikia’s Four Seasons excerpt, Zachary Watkins’ Black Body Radiance, and an arrangement of a Philip Glass piano etude – the latter the only score all night written prior to last year. Works were amplified, with several prerecorded segments, keeping sound engineer Scott Fraser on the move. The fearless Kronos players, still in lightning-fast form, included the longest tenured players David Harrington, John Sherba, Hank Dutt, and at cello newcomer Paul Wiancko. These concerts will entail a farewell to both Sherba and Dutt, two stalwarts with 35-plus years of service here. Under longtime executive director Janet Cowperthwaite, who is also stepping aside this year, Kronos is San Francisco-based. Kronos Festival, the quartet featured in the first of the June 20-23 concerts. Nightly new rep. Miner Auditorium, S.F. Jazz Center. For Kronos info: www. kronosquartet.org or call (415) 788-7353. 196 Moraga Way • Orinda • (625) 254-3714 Open Wednesday – Sunday

articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s Phoenix Kingdoms exhibition, based on recent archaeological discoveries, is on view now through July 22. The exhibition highlights two kingdoms that flourished during China’s Bronze Age, the Zeng and Chu states, encompassing over 2,000 years of imperial history. Phoenix Kingdoms marries art and history while describing one of the most sophisticated, but forgotten, points of Chinese art and culture. The Zeng and Chu states reflect a shamanistic spirituality, rife with belief in human-animal communication, fascination with river and mountain deities, rituals filled with bell and drum music, and a proliferation of magical phoenix totems. “Drawing on the vibrant talent of its artisans and taking advantage of technological advances, the painting, sculpture, calligraphy, and music of this culturally fertile land were developed to an exceptionally high degree,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “It was in Chu that a distinctive religious and philosophical tradition evolved and matured into Daoism, a rival to Confucianism that emerged largely in northern China.” “We have no record that speaks of China’s unification from the perspective of the defeated Chu people,” said Jay Xu, Museum Director and CEO. “Because they were never told by the victor, the stories of Phoenix Kingdoms have remained hidden until now.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org.
articles.title: Phoenix Kingdoms exhibit at Asian Art Museum open through July 22

articles.text: 30th annual event on view through August 11 The 30th annual Sculpture in the Garden is underway at Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek, exhibiting a range of returning local artists and newcomers. Sculpture in the Garden is the annual art exhibit and sale that celebrates sculptural art with the natural, arid beauty of the garden. This unique exhibit features art installations and sculptures by local craftspeople, ranging in design and materials used. The event also serves as a fundraiser for Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery. All artwork is available to purchase, and proceeds from this exhibit go back into the Garden to help protect the plant collection, promote education and support preservation. Sculpture in the Garden is on view through August 11 and is open to the public during regular garden hours. The event is free with regular Garden admission. The nursery is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek. For more information, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/2024-sculpture-in-thegarden/. This year’s event will feature over a dozen local artists

articles.text: When Kathleen Crandall saw a need in the Berkeley arts community, she took the initiative to address it. Crandall, a member of the Berkeley Symphony Board of Directors and a newly appointed member of the Berkeley Civic Arts Commission, noticed that many of the city’s arts organizations recently had appointed new leaders — but they hadn’t yet had a chance to speak to one another. “I wanted to create an opportunity for them to convene, discuss common goals, and envision collaborative opportunities,” Crandall said. “It is a challenging time for arts organizations as they rebuild their communities in the post-pandemic era. I wanted these leaders to know that they are not alone: they have each other, and they have tremendous support among business and civic leaders.” More than a dozen arts leaders attended the meeting, which took place on the campuses of Freight & Salvage and the California Jazz Conservatory in downtown Berkeley. They enjoyed a lunch catered by ACT Catering and coffee provided by the Berkeley Jazzcaffè. The event included performances by musicians from the California Jazz Conservatory, the Berkeley Symphony, and Berkeley Symphony Board member James Parrish Smith. Jen Lovvorn of the Berkeley Civic Arts Commission said, “It was just what was needed with all the new arts leaders in Berkeley – a perfect event to introduce the new directors to those who’ve been here for a while.” Clayton Shelvin, Managing Director of Freight & Salvage, agreed: “We have amazing leaders in this community and it was exciting to see what happens when we all put our minds together.” The summit concluded with a champagne reception for community leaders sponsored by The Grubb Co and Panoramic Interests and Berkeley Symphony board member Shariq Yosufzai. “The Berkeley Symphony was proud to co-host the 2024 Music & Art Summit, along with our neighbor organization Freight & Salvage,” said Marion Atherton, Berkeley Symphony Executive Director. “We really felt the outpouring of support from the community, and I am very grateful to have played a part in this event.”
articles.title: Berkeley Arts supported by Berkeley Symphony

articles.text: Launching tributes to the Fathers The Father of Our Country had intoned, This newborn nation needs its horses, wagons, Muskets, shock troops tough as dragons. Farmers, turned to Minute Men, now standing firm! Forgetting crops to serve their freedom term! Facing all adversity, even drown On crossing River Delaware to thwart the red-coats of the Crown! Most of all, we need Our fathers standing tall, With weapons meeting every onslaught, every call, Till victory is ours on Yorktown’s mall! And when we win, we’ll designate a day To honor them, in June or May, Which then perpetually will be the Fathers’ Day! –George Washington’s long-lost address to fighting men, unearthed just now in a musty West Coast den, inscribed with parchment, ink, and ballpoint pen. Longtime Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy is the city’s Poet Laureate.
articles.title: GW’S long-lost exhortation to his ragtag army

articles.text: With your kind permission, I’d like to look into the future of education. First, let me assert my firm belief that three subjects should be required throughout life. These three subjects are music, foreign language and sports. Put them in any order you like. Education has been a vexing problem since the beginning of education itself. The Talmud addresses the problem directly. In a loose translation, the Talmud says: “educators are self-serving bureaucrats.” When we look further into the Talmud’s comments we find that these self-serving bureaucrats are noted for having a political agenda contrary to the progress of education. It is interesting to note that the Talmud, as a text, was begun in approximately the year 200 CE. Deep thinkers have added to its content for more than 1000 years. In my opinion, education continues on a line of mediocrity. The reason for this mediocrity is simple. The bureaucrat identifies the “problem” and solves it. The real “problem” is that education bureaucrats are replaced by other bureaucrats. All of them have simplistic solutions which continue to fail, and yet they hope for a different result. Who would do such a thing? My proposal is that three subjects should be in the constant repertoire of every student. Every kid should learn to speak another language. By doing so, we learn to think in a completely different way. Mark Twain devoted an entire chapter to this type of thinking in his book “The Bible, according to Mark Twain.” He is credited for stating “For every problem there is a solution that is simple, neat—and wrong.” The second important subject is the participation in sports or physical education in general. As everyone knows, there is great concern about the problem of obesity in our society. What would help is for physical education to be a requirement, not an elective. I advocate that physical education is the participation in sports… not with the intent that we should become professional athletes. It is for the simple reason that physical education teaches us good sportsmanship. There are many other reasons which you probably know. Music should also be a required subject. Singing is certainly the easiest. The marvel of singing is that you can continue it long after you leave school. There are choruses all over the place looking for new members. It hardly matters what your outlook on life is. You can find a chorus that will welcome you. Music education is a subject which is important. When I taught classroom music, my students would often ask me to teach them pop music. I always replied that they listen to pop music regularly. It was my job to teach them something new. It was my job to present this “different music” in an interesting way. Even though it was a challenge, the results were very encouraging. The listening spectrum of the students became wider. Every kid learned to sing a variety of songs from different countries and different ethnicities. They learned to recognize all of the instruments of the orchestra and the band by sight and by sound. Also, they learned to read music proficiently and learned to play the recorder. And finally, instrumental music should be offered to any student who is interested. The schools should have musical instruments available. It is my opinion that things should be made easy for students to learn music. If they need an instrument, the school should provide

Who would do such a thing? My proposal is that three subjects should be in the constant repertoire of every student. Every kid should learn to speak another language. By doing so, we learn to think in a completely different way. Mark Twain devoted an entire chapter to this type of thinking in his book “The Bible, according to Mark Twain.” He is credited for stating “For every problem there is a solution that is simple, neat—and wrong.” The second important subject is the participation in sports or physical education in general. As everyone knows, there is great concern about the problem of obesity in our society. What would help is for physical education to be a requirement, not an elective. I advocate that physical education is the participation in sports… not with the intent that we should become professional athletes. It is for the simple reason that physical education teaches us good sportsmanship. There are many other reasons which you probably know. Music should also be a required subject. Singing is certainly the easiest. The marvel of singing is that you can continue it long after you leave school. There are choruses all over the place looking for new members. It hardly matters what your outlook on life is. You can find a chorus that will welcome you. Music education is a subject which is important. When I taught classroom music, my students would often ask me to teach them pop music. I always replied that they listen to pop music regularly. It was my job to teach them something new. It was my job to present this “different music” in an interesting way. Even though it was a challenge, the results were very encouraging. The listening spectrum of the students became wider. Every kid learned to sing a variety of songs from different countries and different ethnicities. They learned to recognize all of the instruments of the orchestra and the band by sight and by sound. Also, they learned to read music proficiently and learned to play the recorder. And finally, instrumental music should be offered to any student who is interested. The schools should have musical instruments available. It is my opinion that things should be made easy for students to learn music. If they need an instrument, the school should provide Margaret Mead it. The cost is minimal. If the instruments are kept in good working order, they will last for many generations. When students learn music, they learn many things at the same time. They learn history. By the very nature of music, it is the history of the entire world. The teacher might present one aspect, but the implication is that the student should delve into all of the other aspects. Music also teaches individual thought as well as how to follow directions both from the instructor and from the composer. Along the way, we learn to interpret what we see on the page. The latitude is very great. Music is a vast science, and arithmetic is part of that science. We learn to appreciate music from every country. I have always found it fascinating to appreciate musical instruments throughout history and from every part of the world. The longer I live, the more appreciation I acquire. Please understand that my “big three” subjects do not preclude the learning of other subjects. For obvious reasons, those subjects are important also. What I am proposing is to acquire a broad spectrum of appreciation for education in general. In the early 1930s, my father engaged in an argument with Margaret Mead (1901-1978), the American cultural anthropologist known throughout the world. My father’s stance was that all children should be taught to think analytically. Mead countered that it was sufficient to teach them to read. After much discussion, Mead agreed that my father’s philosophy was better than hers. Please voice your opinion. You can be sure the bureaucrats are listening. Keep in mind that the education of our kids is at stake. GW’S long-lost exhortation to his ragtag army Launching tributes to the Fathers By Paul Hertelendy The Father of Our Country had intoned, This newborn nation needs its horses, wagons, Muskets, shock troops tough as dragons. Farmers, turned to Minute Men, now standing firm! Forgetting crops to serve their freedom term! Facing all adversity, even drown On crossing River Delaware to thwart the red-coats of the Crown! Most of all, we need Our fathers standing tall, With weapons meeting every onslaught, every call, Till victory is ours on Yorktown’s mall! And when we win, we’ll designate a day To honor them, in June or May, Which then perpetually will be the Fathers’ Day! –George Washington’s long-lost address to fighting men, unearthed just now in a musty West Coast den, inscribed with parchment, ink, and ballpoint pen. Longtime Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy is the city’s Poet Laureate.

articles.text: British film with superb performances Rachel Weisz, Rachel McAdams and Alessandro Nivola in Disobedience reach for one another. It is more than they can bear. Disobedience is both beautiful and devastating, a powerful narrative which is, from the first scene, quietly unrelenting. The film is set in the North of London and opens with Rav Krushka, a much loved leader of an orthodox Jewish community, speaking to his congregation about that ambivalent place in life that is book-ended by spirituality and goodness. The contrast is with aspects of the human heart that can be dark beyond comprehension. God, the Rav explains, has given man the power of free will, meaning the ability to choose and thereby disobey. It’s a moving and compelling sermon. And when he unexpectedly dies, his daughter, Ronit (Rachel Weisz), a photographer living in New York, is notified. She flies to London, the community where she grew up, just in time for the funeral preparations. She has been gone for some time and those still remembering her are noticeably surprised to see her. Ronit discovers that her two childhood friends, Dovid (Allesandro Nivola) and Esti (Rachel McAdams), are married. Dovid asks her to stay with them in their home. What has been part of the past for Ronit and Esti becomes part of the present and the reason for Ronit’s exile slowly is revealed. What has been an attraction long buried is slowly and intensely resurrected. Their desire for one another, their heat, is palpable; however, it is also a taboo, forbidden in this cloistered community. The dilemma they face comes raging to the fore, repressed, denied and yet overpowering. Their torment is relentlessly present, most often conveyed by a look, a glance, their eyes averted while they It is a shattering line they are helpless not to cross. And symbolizing the emotional chasm between their need for one another and the judgment of the community is Dovid, angry but decent, deeply conflicted and yet trapped by his love for Esti. Disobedience is a love story, first and foremost. But it is also about the inherent consequences, intended and unintended, that await the women. Their attraction is riven with potential ostracism from a people who have the power based upon religious belief and mores of tightly wound steel. And so Ronit and Esti are faced with that moment, spoken of at the outset by Rav Krushka, regarding free will. The only question, and the source of their anguish and hesitation, is can they summon the strength necessary to be who they are and accept that they must separate from those they have known and obeyed all of their lives. As well as, of course, Esti’s husband, Dovid. This is a wonderfully told film, powerful in its muted conversations in grey tones and the coldness of deep winter. It is also a narrative about all that is forbidden, yet impossible to deny, which ultimately is about one’s identity. The sense of crushing repression and fervency are made starkly clear by the stunning performances of Weisz and McAdams, to include a superb supporting cast in a film that is gripping, ruinous and deeply human. Disobedience. Directed by Sebastian Lelio. Starring Rachel Weisz, Rachel McAdams, Allesandra Nivera. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. Streaming on VUDUF/Netflix/Prime/ Apple tv

articles.text: A scene from Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit Kids will love Wallace & Gromit, an Oscar-winning franchise of 30-minute shorts, plus one feature. The first short was A Grand Day, followed by The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave, and A Matter of Loaf and Death. The Curse of the Were-Rabbit was the Aardman studio’s first Claymation feature film. The stars of the franchise are, of course, Wallace (Peter Sallis), a suburban Brit with a pearshaped head and wide, ear-to-ear smile, and his faithful, industrious, ever-silent Beagle (graduate of the Dogwart Academy). They live together in a house filled with labor saving inventions and Rube Goldberg-like contraptions, invented by Wallace, whose day jobs include window cleaner and baker. In Were-Rabbit, he is the owner of the Anti-Pesto Services, a pest control company. His current responsibility is to keep the village gardens free of vegetable-eating rabbits. He, of course, has an invention just for this purpose, a vacuum that sucks up the rabbits, which he keeps in his basement. All of this is in preparation for the Town’s annual vegetable growing competition, the winning prize being a golden carrot. One evening, using his invention, Wallace captures a rabbit who is eating Lady Tottington’s (Helena Bonham Carter) veggies. Unfortunately, his contraption has a miscalculation, and he creates a gigantic Were-Rabbit that is ravenous for vegetables, and is chomping its way through garden after village garden, something that will surely upset the coming veggie-growing contest. Hearing of this garden emergency, Lord Victor Quartermaine (Ralph Fiennes) volunteers to hunt down the culprit with his rifle and shoot it; however lady Tottington objects, and convinces the town folk to allow Wallace and his Anti-Pesto Services to take care of the problem. The mystery that Wallace must solve is, who or what is this Were-Rabbit? It’s a puzzle that takes Wallace and Gromit on an adventure. Wallace even discovers giant muddy footprints that lead into his house. What is going on, Wallace wonders? And even Gromit, who is highly intelligent, can’t figure out the source of the footprints. There are lots of surprises and chases, even threats by Quartermaine to kill the Were-Rabbit with a golden bullet. Things get more than a bit chaotic, involving at one point an airborne dogfight between Gromit and Q.’s dog Phillip. There’s a bit of light romance thrown in (Wallace and Lady T. have some chemistry). Mostly, it’s all daffy fun, wonderfully creative and involves lots of pratfalls and puns. Youngsters will be smitten. And adults will howl over the puns. Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. Claymation by Aardman Animations. Directed by Nick Park. With voices of Peter Sallis, Ralph Fiennes, Helena Bonham-Carter. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated G. Released 2015. Streaming on Peacock/Fandango/prime/apple tv. articles.text: New releases for June The New York Times (NYT) has compiled two long lists of fiction and non-fiction books for reading enjoyment this summer. The Piedmont Post presents the following books with June 2024 release dates from NYT’s Wilson Wong’s non-fiction list and Kate Dwyer’s fiction list. Both lists were originally printed in the NY Times on June 14 at Nytimes.com/2024/06/14/ books/new-summer-fiction.html and Nytimes.com/2024/06/14/ books/nonfiction-summer-books. html Farewell, Amethystine Books The latest in this best-selling mystery series about Easy Rawlins centers on a missing-persons case that takes the beloved private detective deep into his own past. Easy’s lost love asks for help finding her ex-husband – a forensic accountant who got mixed up in trouble – prompting a torrent of memories. Fire Exit This novel, from the author of “Night of the Living Rez,” is told from the perspective of a man who was expelled from Maine’s Penobscot Reservation when he was a young adult, and must decide how much of his history to reveal to his daughter. Godwin This globe-trotting romp from the author of Netherland chronicles a man’s quest to find a mysterious soccer prodigy in West Africa and the unraveling of his workplace back in Pittsburgh. tasy. The final installment in her Between Earth and Sky series, this novel follows the ultimate fates of the people of Meridian. The Road to the Country Set during Nigeria’s civil war, this novel follows a man who is conscripted to fight for the Biafran army after embarking on a search for his missing brother. Swift River Schuster Diamond Newberry is the only Black person in Swift River, a New England mill town in decline. When her mother decides to start filing the paperwork to declare her missing father officially dead, Diamond uncovers a lineage of Black women she didn’t know existed. Horror Movie Morrow Alternating between the ’90s, the present day and scenes from a screenplay, Tremblay’s latest follows the Hollywood remake of “Horror Movie,” a cult-favorite art house film with a cursed history. Tragedy struck the original shoot, and just a handful of scenes ever made it to the public, yet the only surviving cast member is hellbent on reliving his very dark past. One of Our Kind The promise of Liberty, Calif., is a Black utopia, but when Jasmyn and King move their young family there, they discover a place whose citizens are more interested in luxury wellness than social justice. the people closest to Artie – move to the West Coast. After an accident, Artie unexpectedly finds a group of kindred spirits at a local L.G.B.T.Q. senior center. ligence officers. As the world careens toward global conflict, Daniel works to keep his loved ones safe. The Glassmaker From the author of Girl With a Pearl Earring, this is a new historical novel with an artistic bent, following a family of Murano glassblowers starting in 1400s Venice. Little Rot Emezi’s novel takes readers into the underworld of Lagos, where sex, power and corruption intersect. After Kalu breaks up with his longtime partner, he crosses paths with two sex workers at a party hosted by his best friend, turning all of their lives upside down. Same As It Ever Was After decades of instability, Julia Ames finally feels in control of her life. But after she bumps into an estranged friend at the grocery store, her 20-something son announces plans to marry his pregnant girlfriend and her teenage daughter starts acting out in increasingly worrisome ways, Julia reflects upon her life’s pivotal moments, including her own mother’s ambivalence and its ripple effects. Sandwich Rocky is middle-aged, grappling with the intensities of perimenopause and “sandwiched” between her young adult children and ailing parents. Each chapter of this novel covers a day at her idyllic but aging house on Cape Cod, tracing her family’s revelations during a moment of transition. Bear Two sisters work service jobs on a wealthy tourist island off the coast of Washington. When a bear swims across the channel and arrives in their backyard, the sisters take it as a sign to change their lives. lyn, to advising every president since Ronald Reagan (as well as millions of Americans) through modern-day scourges like AIDS, Ebola and SARS. Night Flyer A historian turns her eye to the future face of the $20 bill: Harriet Tubman. Though broad strokes of Tubman’s story are widely known, Miles probes deeper, examining her inner life, faith and relationships with other enslaved Black women to paint a deeper, more vibrant portrait of a historical figure whose mythic status can sometimes overshadow her humanity. We Were Illegal Goudeau’s 2020 book, After the Last Border, offered a searing indictment of this country’s response to humanitarian crises through the stories of two refugees in Austin, Texas. Now, she broadens the lens on her home state, mapping pivotal moments in Texan history through multiple generations of her family, She draws parallels with issues of displacement, migration, mass violence and civil rights that continue to ripple through the United States. Mirrored Heavens Saga Press Roanhorse is one of several Indigenous writers reshaping American science fiction and fanSwan Song Brown The final novel in Hilderbrand’s beloved Nantucket series is here. The Richardsons caused a stir on the island when they purchased a $22-million beach house, started hosting Gatsby-ish parties and campaigned to join the oldmoney Field & Oar club. But when the couple’s home burns down and their personal assistant disappears, the police chief Ed Kapenash must put his retirement plans on hold and find the missing girl. Four Squares Sons Shifting between 1992 and 2022, Finger chronicles the life of Artie, a gay copywriter who meets his partner, Abe, at the height of the AIDS crisis. Thirty years later, Abe has passed away, and his ex-wife and daughter – Shanghai In the mid-1930s, many Jewish refugees fled Germany for Shanghai, where they didn’t need an entry visa. One of them, Daniel Lohr, reconnects there with his uncle Nathan, a gangster who works in nightlife. Now embroiled in some murky business dealings, Daniel finds Leah — a fellow émigré with whom he had an affair — involved with one of the lawless city’s top intelCue the Sun! House The New Yorker staff writer traces the history of the divisive and influential phenomenon that is reality television. From “America’s Funniest Home Videos” to “The Real World,” “Survivor” and “The Bachelor,” the Pulitzer-winning critic investigates how this genre reveals as much about our country as it does ourselves. Do Something Trebay, a New York Times journalist, maps his young adult years in a landscape of emerging artists, filmmakers and other creative types in 1970s Manhattan. It’s a fun and fascinating glimpse into the many artistic tribes that thrived in a city then on the skids. The Garden Against Time A garden is nominally a nurturing place for plants, but it is also fertile ground for generating ideas and exploring history. Inspired after restoring her own green space in 2020, the English cultural critic takes an anthropological approach to gardens both imagined and real, surveying them as both sites of “larger patterns of privilege and exclusion” and places of “rebel outposts and dreams of a communal paradise.”

articles.text: The Friday Afternoon Club Judy Garland, Sean Connery, Carrie Fisher: Celebrities abound in the actor’s new memoir. Dunne’s book is engaging as much for his fame-adjacent vignettes as for his frank exploration of his famous family’s complicated history. His sister, Dominique Dunne, was a rising star in Hollywood whose career was cut short when she was killed by her ex-boyfriend. His account of her death and the subsequent infamous trial is an illuminating perspective. Roctogenarians Greenberg, Simon & Schuster Worried that you’re past your prime? Fret not. Rocca and Greenberg make the case that our most remarkable years come later in life. The authors weave their argument from stories about the artist Henri Matisse, the actor Morgan Freeman and even Mr. Pickles, a tortoise who became a first-time father at 90 years old. Mirrored Heavens By Rebecca Roanhorse, S & S/ Saga Press Roanhorse is one of several Indigenous writers reshaping American science fiction and fanSwan Song By Elin Hilderbrand, Little, Brown The final novel in Hilderbrand’s beloved Nantucket series is here. The Richardsons caused a stir on the island when they purchased a $22-million beach house, started hosting Gatsby-ish parties and campaigned to join the oldmoney Field & Oar club. But when the couple’s home burns down and their personal assistant disappears, the police chief Ed Kapenash must put his retirement plans on hold and find the missing girl. Four Squares By Bobby Finger, G.P. Putnam’s Sons Shifting between 1992 and 2022, Finger chronicles the life of Artie, a gay copywriter who meets his partner, Abe, at the height of the AIDS crisis. Thirty years later, Abe has passed away, and his ex-wife and daughter – Shanghai By Joseph Kanon, Scribner In the mid-1930s, many Jewish refugees fled Germany for Shanghai, where they didn’t need an entry visa. One of them, Daniel Lohr, reconnects there with his uncle Nathan, a gangster who works in nightlife. Now embroiled in some murky business dealings, Daniel finds Leah — a fellow émigré with whom he had an affair — involved with one of the lawless city’s top intelOn Call By Anthony Fauci, Viking Fauci was thrown into the national spotlight after becoming the de facto face of the United States’s fight against the Covid-19 pandemic. Nearly two years after retiring from his five-decade career in the public health sector, Fauci returns with a memoir that traces his path from growing up as a young boy in BrookCue the Sun! By Emily Nussbaum, Random House The New Yorker staff writer traces the history of the divisive and influential phenomenon that is reality television. From “America’s Funniest Home Videos” to “The Real World,” “Survivor” and “The Bachelor,” the Pulitzer-winning critic investigates how this genre reveals as much about our country as it does ourselves. Do Something By Guy Trebay, Knopf Trebay, a New York Times journalist, maps his young adult years in a landscape of emerging artists, filmmakers and other creative types in 1970s Manhattan. It’s a fun and fascinating glimpse into the many artistic tribes that thrived in a city then on the skids. The Garden Against Time By Olivia Laing, Norton A garden is nominally a nurturing place for plants, but it is also fertile ground for generating ideas and exploring history. Inspired after restoring her own green space in 2020, the English cultural critic takes an anthropological approach to gardens both imagined and real, surveying them as both sites of “larger patterns of privilege and exclusion” and places of “rebel outposts and dreams of a communal paradise.”

Witte and Hesner produced “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for nearly four years. When the two began looking for new projects, Mankoff asked them during a Zoom call, “Why don’t you guys do a book?” They were stunned – but inspired. Funny Stuff is the fruit of Witte and Hesner’s latest partnership together. Despite their philosophical approach to the business of cartoons, Hesner insisted that they didn’t want to write a book that took away the joy of their favorite art form. “These cartoonists have given us all sorts of private insights into what they do, how they do it, how they get their ideas, their neuroses, their parents, all sorts of stuff. So, it’s not just like, it’s not just a dry kind of analysis. It really delves into the whole world of cartoonists and the twisted minds that create them,” Hesner said. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 26, 2024 Piedmont Park’s History Trail Markers Part 1: Faux Bois Benches The map of the city’s 10 markers on the Piedmont Park History Trail is located outside the Veterans’ Building at Highland and Vista Avenue. By Jay Russell For the City of Piedmont’s centennial anniversary in January 2007, the City installed 10 historic land markers to create the Piedmont Park History Trail. These markers shine a light on the wonders that were in the park not so long ago. The map of the history trail outlining all the markers can be found in front of the Veterans’ Hall on the corner of Highland and Vista Avenue. The first marker is on the patio in front of City Hall. Stop by and stoke up on your Piedmont history on your next essential dog walk. Marker 1: Faux Bois Benches Frank C. Havens developed Piedmont Park between 1898 and 1920. Using eucalyptus saplings and branch stickwork, he had 3,000 rustic wood benches constructed and placed throughout the park. An article in the Oakland Tribune dated May 5, 1898 described the park at the time. “[Seating accommodations] have been admirably supplied by the scattering in every direction The original benches were made out of eucalyptus and installed throughout Piedmont Park at the turn of the 20th century. Marker #1 of the Piedmont Park History Trail is on the patio in front of City Hall and describes the origin of the faux bois benches. of 3,000 settees made of eucalyptus. They throng the walks near the music stand, grace the side of the streamlet, cluster about trees and in some places muster in such forces as to be intended for the use of picnic parties,” the article stated. But the wooded benches proved to be prone to falling apart. Because of the homespun frontier look, people liked them so much in the 1920’s the city made some faux bois (fake wood) replica park benches out of concrete. The park had faux bois benches through the early part of the 20th Century. The only remaining bench was kept at the Corporation Yard, and in 2001 in attempting to restore it, the bench collapsed. During the city’s 100th anniversary in January 2007, a new concrete bench was created and lowered into place on the patio in front of City Hall. Given its weight and girth, it is the one public bench that doesn’t need to be bolted to the ground. The decision to build the original benches with eucalyptus is a clue to a larger story about the development of California. Frank C. Havens owned a eucalyptus nursery in the Lakeshore area. In his lifetime the hills surrounding Piedmont were largely bare due to the clear-cutting of pine, cedar and redwood to rebuild houses in San Francisco destroyed by the fire following the 1906 earthquake. Havens imported and planted millions of eucalyptus saplings on a 14-mile strip of the hills for a hardwood forest, knowing that eucalyptus was a fast-growing tree. At the time he was unaware that it was used in other locations primarily as pulp for paper or firewood, but not building materials. As a pioneer in introducing eucalyptus to the region, Havens is partially responsible for today’s vast prevalence of non-native Eucalyptus trees in the Oakland and Berkeley hills. Eucalyptus tends to take over areas, sending roots horizontally and growing quickly. Eucalyptus rapidly drinks up water and nutrients in the soil. Native trees can’t compete, and grass can’t grow under the dense canopy and oily leaf cover. Eucalyptus trees are not without fans however for their beauty, useful oil and as koala food. The faux bois benches serve as a gateway seat to our past. There are history lessons all around us. articles.text: Men’s 100 & 200 meter dash In the 100 and 200 meter sprint events, Noah Lyles walks in as a favorite from the United States. He just clocked a 9.92 at the Olympic Trials on Saturday and will also look to qualify in the 200 on Thursday. Christian Coleman also ran a 9.99 at the U.S. trials. Some of the States’ top competition in the 100 is Italy’s Marcell Jacobs, who is the defending Olympic champion. Canada’s Andre De Grasse also won the 200 meter at the 2020 Olympics. The men’s prelims in the 100 are on August 3 with the semifinals and finals the next day. The 200 starts August 5 with the prelims, semifinals the next day, and finals on August 7. Women’s 4x100 Relay Richardson will be accompanied by Thomas, Jenna Prandini, and Teahna Daniels. Their top competition as usual will be Jamaica with its defending champion cast of Thompson-Herah, Fraser-Pryce, Jackson, and Briana Williams. The women’s 4x100 heats are set for August 8 with the finals set for August 9. Men’s 4x100 Relay Lyles will be joined by Fred Kerley, Trayvon Bromell, and Coleman. Yet again, Jamaica is the country to keep an eye on for the Gold Medal. Its team consists of Yohan Blake, Oblique Seville, Julian Forte, and Rasheed Dwyer. The defending champions Italy will likely have Jacobs, Filippo Tortu, Lorenzo Patta, and Fausto Desalu. The men’s 4x100 opens on August 8 with the finals the following day.

Walkers By Jim Kellogg and Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group had another special walk last week on June 19. Architect and walker Jim Kellogg researched and presented an architectural history tour for the group’s weekly walk. A strong turnout of 54 walkers and two K-9 best friends were on hand for the outing. Before they got started, it was recognized and appreciated that it was the Juneteenth holiday. The home of James Ballentine who built this house at 241 Hillside Avenue. The second story was added in 1937. government arrived in Galveston, Walking on WednesdayOn this day in 1865, the federal Texas, to declare that all enslaved people must be freed. The enslaved people in Texas were the last ones in the Confederacy to learn they were freed. June 19, now known as Juneteenth, has become the symbolic holiday to celebrate Black history, culture and unity. It was also noted that the Wednesday walkers will be an entry in this year’s Piedmont 4th of July parade. The focus of Jim Kellogg’s tour was the distinctive architectural character of early Piedmont, beginning in 1907 when Piedmont was incorporated. At that time, Piedmont was thought of as “The Queen of the Hills.” Piedmont was a beautiful place to live and included homes with exceptional architectural character that are still appreciated today. The city’s character was influenced by many families from around the country who moved to Piedmont in early 1900 and wanted their new homes to recall the architectural style from their childhood. On last week’s walk, the city center provided the opportunity to see examples of more than a half dozen architectural styles: French Colonial, Victorian, English Tutor, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, Bungalow and Craftsman. The walk was a little less than two miles and focused on the historic central area of the city, including Vista, Hillside and Bonita Avenues. The walkers stopped at 225 Hillside to talk about the beautiful Queen Anne Shingle Style house and then gathered for a group photo. As they were getting ready to move on, the homeowner, Alissa Welch, came out and graciously told the group about her family’s work on the house. Further down Hillside, the walkers noted one of the last remaining original street lamps in Piedmont and studied homes designed by well-known Bay Area architects at that time, including: Albert Farr, Charles Dickey, and the firm Bakewell and Brown. Interesting stories about the people who shaped the character of early Piedmont were shared with the walkers. The famous architect Albert Farr’s favorite carpenter was known as “One-Nail” MacGregor because as a Scotsman he was known to have said “Build homes quickly and efficiently, and don’t use two nails when one nail will do.” All of the homes were beautiful and appreciated by the walkers. So was Jim’s preparation and the knowledge he shared with the group. He will come back soon for another tour with the group. People who want to learn more about the early history and architecture of Piedmont were encouraged to purchase a copy of “Cottages and Castles: The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont”, by Ann Swift. This was published in 2007 and a limited number of copies are still available at Piedmont City Hall for $30. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: How do I figure out the proper fix? Dear Jim: I have noticed over the last few years that my foundation and drainage problems are getting worse. I have cracks in my living room, water in my crawlspace, and my foundation doesn’t look great. I have talked to a bunch of Contractors and they all tell me something different. Why this disparity in solutions? And how do I figure out what my house really needs? Unfortunately, this is the same story I hear every day. “What Long term drainage issues ruined this foundation. Plastic covering the soil and plywood for seismic did not help with the real problem. Improper repairs can often lead to structural issues. These patched together supports under the front landing eventually made things worse. should I do?” The good news is that there is likely one best answer to your structural woes. You just have to talk to the right person. The “Why” Behind the Confusion In simplest terms, most General Contractors lack the background and insight to provide you with the best solution. These problems are often wholistic, involving multiple structural components that are all interacting- drainage, foundation, framing and structure, seismic, etc. It takes a lot of experience, specifically with residential structural work and drainage, to be able to find the best solution in the short window of an initial meeting. And the problem may be very different from what you suspect- most commonly that your foundation issues and cracks are mostly related to faulty drainage that also needs to be addressed. Timing is also a big issue. Structural problems are sometimes fast developing, but most often have been brewing for decades. Everyone wants to know “when” these repairs need to be made, and whether or not they are serious issues. The Reality You Need to Consider Fou ndation and d rainage issues cannot typically be “fixed”. Older foundations in poor condition generally need to be replaced. Most drainage issues occur because you have no real drainage system when you need one. Short term repairs can make your problems worse. Proper solutions can be expensive work that most aren’t looking forward to. And often drainage, foundation, and seismic repairs are best done all together. The bottom line is that you need to do what is best long term for your home and avoid short-term fixes unless you have an immediate problem. It shouldn’t need to be a question of what- just a question of when. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim and Lisa Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. A long-time Piedmont resident, he has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983.
