articles.text: If you’ve retired, you may have thought you closed the book on one chapter of your life. But what happens if you need to “reverse” your retirement? Due to higher inflation and rising interest rates, many retirees are taking out more money from their retirement accounts than they had originally anticipated. As a result, some are headed back to the workforce. If you’re thinking of joining them, you’ll need to consider some factors that may affect your finances. First, if you’ve been taking Social Security, be aware that you could lose some of your benefits if you earn over a certain level, at least until you reach your full retirement age, which is likely between 66 and 67. Specifically, if you are under your full retirement age for the entire year, Social Security will deduct $1 from your benefit payments for every $2 you earn above the annual limit, which, in 2024, is $22,320. In the year you reach your full retirement age, Social Security will deduct $1 in benefits for every $3 you earn above a different limit, which, in 2024, is $59,520. Social Security will only count your earnings up to the month before you reach your full retirement age, at which point your earnings will no longer reduce your benefits, regardless of how much you earn. Also, Social Security will recalculate your benefit amounts to credit you for the months your payments were reduced due to your excess earnings. Social Security also allows you to pay back early benefits received if you withdraw your application within 12 months of starting benefits. This move could help you receive substantially higher benefits at full retirement age. Your Social Security isn’t the only benefit that could be affected by your earnings. Your Medicare Part B and Part D premiums are based on your income, so they could rise if you start earning more money. Also, your extra income could push you into a higher tax bracket. Nonetheless, you can certainly gain some benefits by returning to the working world. Obviously, you’ll be making money that can help you boost your daily cash flow and possibly reduce some debts. But depending on where you work, you might also be able to contribute to a 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. And regardless of where you work, you’ll be eligible to contribute to an IRA. By putting more money into these accounts, you may well be able to strengthen your financial position during your retirement years. You might also be able to receive some employee benefits, such as group health insurance – which could be particularly valuable if you haven’t yet started receiving Medicare. In addition to the potential financial advantages of going back to work, you might get some social benefits, too. Many people enjoy the interactions with fellow workers and miss these exchanges when they retire, so a return to the workforce, even if it’s on a part-time basis, may give you an emotional boost. In the final analysis, you’ll want to weigh the potential costs of going back to work against the possible benefits. There’s no one right answer for everyone, but by looking at all the variables, you should be able to reach a decision that works for you. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a financial advisor with the Piedmont office of Edward Jones at 370 Highland Ave., Suite 201/. Tel: 510-547-4589.

articles.text: Roti tissue sprinkled with sugar Sweat trickled down my back. Why did I choose to wear my sweatshirt in Malaysia’s 80°F heat? After a grueling 30 hours of non-stop travel (during which I admittedly watched more movies than slept), my parents decided the best way to cope with the jet lag was to stay awake for even longer. Unfortunately, that meant pushing through all of that jetlag and an air-conditioned government office. The only reprise available was the ice-cold glass of 100 plus sitting in front of me, along with the sliced pork atop perfectly yellow rice – an iconic Malaysian dish. The first thing after more than a full day of airplane food, the dish warmed and comforted me. These two principles are some of the most fundamental building blocks of Asian cuisine, especially in Malaysia, one of the most diverse places in Southeast Asia. It blends Indian, Chinese, native Malay, and many other ethnic groups’ distinct flavors to create incredibly unique dishes. Roti Roti canai (named second best food in the world by Taste Asia), roti tissue, thossia tissue, and many others are just a few of the plentiful variations of this flatbread of indian roots which is often served with curry or daal - an adapted curry with a more soupy consistency and split pulses. A staple on breakfast tables all over Malaysia, roti canai is actually a unique blend of paratha and naan, originally Thossia tissue with daal and curry Ais kacang after enduring the Malaysian heat created by South Indian indentured laborers who were brought to Malaysia by British colonists. Over time it has woven itself into the fabric of Malaysia. Satay A quintessentially Malay dish, satay consists of meat (usually chicken) grilled on a skewer and Chendol with extra green rice flour jelly served with a spiced sauce. A fixture at the famous outdoor food stalls (hawker stands), satay is a food that expresses comfort for many Malaysians. Recently, I stopped by to visit a family member in the dead of night. I passed my time by zoning out at a floor tile (courtesy of the language barrier) until my second cousin arrived with satay, chicken wings, and tofu pudding. Food not only nourishes our bodies but also our souls, serving as a connection with power beyond words. Char Kuey Teow A popular South Asian dish, char kuey teow, consists of stirfried rice noodles often with cockerels or shrimp, eggs, bean sprouts, and doused in soy sauce. pages.text: Wednesday, June 26, 2024 29 Roti tissue sprinkled with sugar Malaysia and the cultural importance of food By Daisy R. Seymour Sweat trickled down my back. Why did I choose to wear my sweatshirt in Malaysia’s 80°F heat? After a grueling 30 hours of non-stop travel (during which I admittedly watched more movies than slept), my parents decided the best way to cope with the jet lag was to stay awake for even longer. Unfortunately, that meant pushing through all of that jetlag and an air-conditioned government office. The only reprise available was the ice-cold glass of 100 plus sitting in front of me, along with the sliced pork atop perfectly yellow rice – an iconic Malaysian dish. The first thing after more than a full day of airplane food, the dish warmed and comforted me. These two principles are some of the most fundamental building blocks of Asian cuisine, especially in Malaysia, one of the most diverse places in Southeast Asia. It blends Indian, Chinese, native Malay, and many other ethnic groups’ distinct flavors to create incredibly unique dishes. Roti Roti canai (named second best food in the world by Taste Asia), roti tissue, thossia tissue, and many others are just a few of the plentiful variations of this flatbread of indian roots which is often served with curry or daal - an adapted curry with a more soupy consistency and split pulses. A staple on breakfast tables all over Malaysia, roti canai is actually a unique blend of paratha and naan, originally Thossia tissue with daal and curry Ais kacang after enduring the Malaysian heat created by South Indian indentured laborers who were brought to Malaysia by British colonists. Over time it has woven itself into the fabric of Malaysia. Satay A quintessentially Malay dish, satay consists of meat (usually chicken) grilled on a skewer and Chendol with extra green rice flour jelly served with a spiced sauce. A fixture at the famous outdoor food stalls (hawker stands), satay is a food that expresses comfort for many Malaysians. Recently, I stopped by to visit a family member in the dead of night. I passed my time by zoning out at a floor tile (courtesy of the language barrier) until my second cousin arrived with satay, chicken wings, and tofu pudding. Food not only nourishes our bodies but also our souls, serving as a connection with power beyond words. articles.text: Douglas Sekimura, a 2003 graduate of Piedmont High School and the son of Gerry and Joy Sekimura, and Monica Fernandez, the daughter of Jacqueline Santo Domingo, were married on October 1, 2022. The wedding was held in downtown Los Angeles with close family and friends and was officiated by Doug’s uncle, Ben Hashiba. The couple met while working together at Beats Electronics in Santa Monica in 2013. The bride, an Aeronautical and Astronautical Engineering graduate of Purdue University, works as a Systems Engineering Manager at Northrop Grumman in Redondo Beach. The groom completed his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Engineering at UCLA and works at Apple as a Reliability Engineering Manager in Culver City. The couple resides with their dog Jimi in West Los Angeles. Douglas Sekimura and wife Monica Fernandez.

articles.text: Construction crews working on the city’s new swimming pool facility are using the school summer break to do more extensive construction, particularly along Magnolia Avenue. Contractors plan on removing and rebuilding the curb and sidewalk on the pool side of the street as well as repaving the full width of the roadway on Magnolia Avenue. Construction is expected to last approximately three weeks through July 3, just in time for pedestrians and vehicles to use during the fourth of July. Magnolia Avenue will remain open to car traffic during construction, save for two to three days when the roadway is being repaved near the end of construction, currently scheduled for July 1–3. On June 13, workers started removing significant portions of the sidewalk and asphalt along the Magnolia side of the construction site. Street trees had lifted the concrete sidewalks in the past and contributed to its instable safety. “The asphalt and sidewalk were already in poor shape and would have been slated for replacement eventually,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Photo by Staff Photos Behind the fences on Magnolia Avenue, the sidewalk and asphalt are being removed as part of construction on the community pool. Construction is expected to finish before July 4.

articles.text: Piedmont’s school board officially ratified teacher contract at the June 12 meeting. Piedmont School District and the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) are now in agreement with teacher salary raises in place for the current school year and the next two years. “I’m going to be short on comments, but very large on regard for our APT members. This, as we know, is a year in the making, and we have finally arrived,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Board members were also brief with their comments, two and half hours into the penultimate meeting of the school year. No public comment was made and no comments were made by teacher union representatives. “The three year agreement means that we can really focus on all the things that we want to come together and collaborate on for the next few years. So a huge thanks to the negotiating teams. This is exciting,” said Board Vice President Lindsay Thomasson. Board member Cory Smegal eagerly jumped at the chance to present a motion for the agenda item, setting the stage for the unanimous 5-0 vote approving the agreement. Teachers secured a 3% retroactive raise to salaries for this past year, 4% next year and 4.5% in 2025-26. The final year’s raise would only be 3% if the increase to Measure H, one of two school parcel taxes, does not pass in the upcoming November election. Piedmont teachers, shown at graduation, wore many hats this year as educators, coaches, mentors and negotiators.
articles.title: Teacher contract finalized

articles.text: A suspect has been arrested by the Piedmont Police Department in a sexual assault case. On Friday, May 31, two women on Bonita Avenue independently reported having their buttocks groped by a stranger around 9:24 a.m. before the perpetrator fled the scene in a black Toyota Prius. Using a video recorded by a nearby resident’s front door camera, police were able to track the car through the city’s camera system, which monitors traffic and photographs the rear of all passing vehicles. On Wednesday, June 5, the suspect voluntarily reported to the police department at the request of detectives. During an interview, he confessed to being involved in the assaults. The suspect was subsequently arrested for sexual battery and booked into Santa Rita Jail without incident. The PPD announced the man’s arrest via their Instagram page on Wednesday, June 12. He has been described by police as a 27-yearold Hispanic adult with scars on his neck. The first victim, a 44-yearold woman, was walking along Bonita Avenue when the suspect approached her from behind and grabbed her buttocks. A debate that needs to end By Pastor Jim Hopkins Every once in a while I need to explain to someone that yes, I serve a Baptist congregation, that yes we are proud of that identity, and yes we are quite different from the largest Baptist, and largest Protestant denomination in the United States, the Southern Baptist Convention. The Baptist tradition in the United States has always been quite diverse in terms of theology, culture, worship style, racial/ethnic identity, emphasis in ministry, etc. (The first Baptist Church in the colonies was the First Baptist Church in America, founded by Roger Williams in Providence, Rhode Island in 1638. That congregation is still active.) What defined the Baptist tradition was an emphasis on what historian Walter Shurden calls the four fragile freedoms: Soul Freedom, Bible Freedom, Church Freedom and Religious Freedom. The Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 when it separated from other Baptists over the issue of slavery. It included the American Baptist Home Mission Society, the precursor of the American Baptist Churches USA to which the congregation I serve belongs. Most precisely the Baptist Foreign Mission Board denied a request by the Alabama Convention that enslavers be eligible to become missionaries. The Southern Baptist Convention was formed in protest. Currently, the Southern Baptist Convention is frequently in the news over its refusal to support women as ordained ministers. Many of its congregations have been forced out for ordaining, hiring and supporting women in pastoral roles. In May, one of the founding churches of the convention, the First Baptist Church of Richmond, Virginia, voted to sever ties with the SBC rather than fire a female pastor. While no congregation, including Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, can claim that it has supported women in ministry without failure or fault, we were one of the first American Baptist congregations to ordain (1972) and hire women. While there are scattered verses in the Bible that can be marshalled against women in pastoral roles, there are many verses and examples that are supportive of the same. Some of the most important are: 1. articles.text: Move signals decline of camphor trees in Piedmont Citing its ill health and declining state, the Piedmont Public Works Department removed a “prominent” camphor (cinnamomum campora) street tree near the corner of Guilford and Highland Avenues on Tuesday, June 11. Though popular, most of the city’s camphor trees are in different stages of decline, according to the Public Works Department. The removal of this tree is part of the city’s plans to move away from using camphor trees in the near future. “It is sad because it is a really prominent tree,” said Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent at a Park Commission meeting earlier this month. Camphor trees are commonly seen on Piedmont’s streets. A total of 90 are maintained by the City of Piedmont on Ronada Avenue, Ramona Avenue, York Drive, Grand Avenue, Cambridge Way, Highland and Indian Avenue. Though prominent, this camphor tree on Highland Avenue had been in poor health for a decade. In her presentation at the Park Commission Meeting on June 5, Kent described the tree as “totally dead,” and used a series of Google Earth images to show that it had been slowly deteriorating since 2020. Resident Richard Nagler, who lives near Hazel Lane, confirmed her reports. “It was a tree that was clearly dead. I’d been kind of watching that tree for months and months and months, waiting to see what was going to happen,” said Nagler. He recalled that he and his wife would often have conversations about it, wondering if a branch would fall or if the tree itself might fall someday. In general, if a tree is in decline but safe, the City will usually leave it in place until there are signs of structural concerns. At the Park Commission Meeting, Kent explained that on the whole, camphor trees in Piedmont are in a state of decline. “They are at the height of their mature level and at various levels of [...] fair to poor condition,” she explained. Of the total 90 camphor trees, she reported that 36 were in “good” condition, 47 were “fair,” six were “poor,” and one was in “critical.” “We’re going to have to start replacing a lot of the camphors in the city, and we will not be replanting with camphors,” she declared. “There are a lot of issues with them [...] over time, these camphors are going to leave our urban forest.” Park Commission member David Johnson acknowledged that the tree is one many cities in California have started to transition away from, but urged the City to “think of keeping some in parks or open spaces where they have lots of room to grow.” Nagler witnessed the tree’s removal on Tuesday, June 11, as he was walking down Highland Avenue. “It was just three guys from Public Works working very quietly, meticulously, taking down this big tree. One guy up in the tree, two guys on the ground guiding him. It’s pretty extraordinary that our Public Works department could handle a project that big. It was very impressive to see how carefully and thoroughly they were working,” he said. Nagler suggested that this particular space on Highland Avenue could do without a tree for now. “Maybe it’ll give the cars going in and out of Guilford a little bit more visibility.” For more information about street trees and the city’s future plans, please contact Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager, by phone at (510) 420-3064 or by email at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. Photo by Richard Nagler A camphor tree in decline on Highland Avenue was removed by the City on Tuesday, June 11. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: Hello Piedmont & Oakland Friends and Neighbors. As many of you know, I’ve been deeply committed to improving public safety in the Piedmont and Oakland communities. Recently, I ran for County Supervisor on a platform focused on public safety. Now, I’m dedicating 100% of my time and energy to enhancing public safety in Oakland, as it is the most crucial priority for our combined communities. The first vital step in this effort is to support new leadership in Oakland. Specifically, we need to elect LeRonne Armstrong to the At-Large (all districts) City Council seat. Winning this seat is of paramount importance, and I cannot stress enough how critical your support is in this endeavor. STEP #1: I’m excited to invite you to a special event in support of former Oakland Police Chief LeRonne Armstrong’s City Councilmember At-Large campaign. Armstrong’s dedication to public service, commitment to community safety and vision for a thriving Oakland make him the ideal candidate to represent the City of Oakland. Tuesday, June 18 at 5:30pm - 7pm, 431 Pacific Ave., Piedmont This November the stakes are very high and we are going to bring change to Oakland. Your support and contributions are crucial to elect experienced leaders LeRonne Armstrong and to change the trajectory of Oakland. If you are unable to attend but would still like to support Chief Armstrong’s campaign, please visit https://secure.actblue.com/ donate/chrismoore6.18 to make a contribution. There’s a big fundraising deadline on June 30th and your support would send a strong message that there is time for change in City Hall. I hope you will chip in. Thank you for your support and please reach out if you have any questions. –Chris Moore Piedmont resident

articles.text: Miss Dinah came to Oakland Animal Services with a broken hip. She has made a full recovery while at a foster’s home and her foster family says she has been an excellent patient. Check out her Instagram account @adopt.dinah to see her in action. Her foster family report she has been a wonderful addition to their house due to her friendly and gentle nature. She’s smart, making her easy to train. To date she’s mastered ‘sit’ and ‘wait;’ she’s working on ‘shake’ and ‘spin’. Completely housetrained and crate-trained, 7- year-old Dinah happily sleeps through the night in her crate. She’s also content to nap in there during the day. At sixty pounds, she walks nicely on the leash and rarely pulls. Her fosters are working with her on feeling more comfortable being left alone. If interested in meeting Dinah, fill out an application online at Oakland Animal Services and her foster parents will arrange a time for you to meet her. articles.text: Staff photo Piedmont Community Service Crew members Asha Byers (left), Jessica Liu and Simran Titan serve pancakes, sausages and fruit to attendees of the annual pancake breakfast on July 4. Piedmont’s annual Pancake Breakfast will return to the Veterans Hall this year as part of the city’s Fourth of July Parade festivities. The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a coed Piedmont Scout Venturing unit, will serve a nourishing breakfast from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. with pancakes, sausages, fresh fruit and coffee. “It is a longstanding Piedmont tradition that old-timers and sometimes newcomers look forward to,” said Ken Li, crew advisor for the PCSC. “It’s got great community spirit and PCSC has been fortunate to take it over.” The Pancake Breakfast is one of the city’s most anticipated events of the year. The Piedmont-Montclair Rotary Club operated it for many years after inheriting it from the Fire Department. The Piedmont Recreation Department operated it for some years, then handed it over the tradition to the PCSC in 2015, which has carried it on ever since. This will be the PCSC’s sixth year in charge of the event. In addition to its popularity, the Pancake Breakfast is one of the PCSC’s largest fundraising events. Every year, crew members sign up to volunteer at the breakfast, set up the dining area, cook, prep-cook (including slicing fruit and making pancake batter), serve food and drinks, keep the dining area clean during operations and finally store the organization’s kitchen supplies until the following year. “Every year there’s a classic marketing question,” said Li. Will the attendance or the community support be smaller or bigger than last year?” The event typically attracts about 400 people, but Li expects that number will be even higher this year. “One of the things I challenged our crew members on was to do more marketing and see if that can push up our attendance,” he said. “The money we raise is not for the crew members. It’s for the philanthropy that we do – building tiny houses, cooking for the food insecure. That’s where you can see our funding at work,” he explained. The Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-led venturing crew under the auspices of Piedmont Scout Council, inspiring teenagers to actively uplift the broader community through service projects. For more information and to learn how you can help or join, visit pcservicecrew. org/new-member and contact crew advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@ sbcglobal.net. The Pancake Breakfast will take place at Veteran’s Hall on Thursday, July 4 from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. Tickets to the pancake breakfast are $15 per person. They will accept both cash and PayPal as payment.
articles.title: PCSC to host annual Pancake Breakfast on July 4

articles.text: The Barrelhouse Jazz Band has been playing traditional (Dixieland) jazz in the Bay Area since 1972. Like the earliest traditions of jazz music, the Barrelhouse boys sprang from a church. More than 50 years ago, a small group of musicians at Montclair Presbyterian Church formed a traditional jazz band. The band’s focus remains the West Coast brand of New Orleans-style jazz developed by San Francisco musician Lu Watters using a two-trumpet sound. The band loves to see people dancing to its music, something that brings out the best in the Barrelhouse musicians. The band often plays for church services in several denominations in the Bay Area, providing much joy among the parishioners. In addition to playing swing music and fox-trots for dance music, the band plays struts, stomps, blues and rags. The current band members are director Al Flood (clarinet & sax), Virginia Tichenor (piano), Jim Klippert (trombone), Bruce Stangeland (banjo), Art Wood (trumpet), David Auerbach (tuba) and Scott Wild (drums). articles.text: Photo by Rob Peterson Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team put girls’ sports on center stage on September 30, 2022 by hosting the school’s Homecoming game for the first time in a year when the football game was canceled. In the photo Bauer Peterson sets Bree DeYoung (3) for a spike. It was a time to celebrate another Piedmont sports achievement at the school board meeting on June 12. Piedmont’s Title IX Task Force celebrated not a win, but a tie, with the announcement that Piedmont High School had an equal number of boys and girls playing on sports teams. A participation gap by gender was formally first addressed by conducting an interest survey in Spring 2022 among 8th-12th graders. This led to the offer of girls’ beach volleyball in 2022-23. The survey also showed that girls would enjoy playing flag football if offered as a varsity team. The State added flag football as a varsity sport for girls the following year, and PHS athletes responded with 41 girls signing up this past fall, requiring two teams. Title IX coordinator, and district Director of Instructional Technology, Stephanie Griffin, who not incidentally was the high school’s first Girl’s Athletic Director, reported to the board on the year end progress of gender equity in sports. “We’re a model when it comes to Title IX. It’s something for our community to be proud of,” said Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. The Title IX Task Force officially was created by former PHS Principal Adam Littlefield in the Spring of 2022. Two experts also helped support the task force, Dr. Donna Lopiano, CEO of Women’s Sports Foundation for 15 years, and former Alameda County Deputy District Attorney Kim Hunter, a Piedmont resident. Parents Molly Lloyd and Kim DeYoung repeatedly spoke at the board meetings, gathered data on their own and advocated publicly for the participation of more sports for girls. “Prior to [the taskforce] there was a huge amount of effort by parents in the district trying to get the attention of administration to actually do this work,” said school board member Cory Smegal. In addition to the participation gap, Griffin and Dolowich spoke about specific issues the Title 9 effort has faced affecting the qualitative experience of athletes. “Over the last couple of years we have observed several disparities in those experiences along gender lines- maybe in competition, in uniforms and equipment, practice times, etc. Addressing these sorts of issue is very operational it’s in the trenches with the director of athletics and the school administration,” said Griffin. Newly hired Athletic Director Tyler Small was on hand at the meeting to show support for the effort of the Task Force. “This is like a present, gift wrapped for your desk [as you arrive],” said School Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen to Small. The task force also looked at the intangibles from participating in sports and did so with the methodology of Lopiano. When the task force was formed in 2022, 15 of 48 categories were determined to be an advantage for boys, only one for girls. Two years later, there are now 11 areas of benefits advantaged towards girls sports. “Obviously we are not done; we have an action plan and Tyler’s got some more work to do. He’s ready and fired up for that. But you guys have laid the groundwork for how we are going to measure this,” said Smegal.
articles.title: Title IX Task Force celebrates equal number of boys, girls in sports

articles.text: A complete transformation of the NASA Ames Visitor Center at Chabot Space & Science Center will be celebrated this weekend, June 22-23, from 10 a.m.- 4:00 p.m. The public is invited to the reopening, called NASA Fest, with new sights and exhibits, and special NASA guest speakers. Significant changes will create a fully reimagined 360-degree experience, featuring new models and exhibits. The weekend of astronomical fun for the whole family, will be highlighted with talks from NASA scientists Parul Agrawal, Brian Barrientez, and Spyros Kasapis. At the new NASA Ames Visitor Center, visitors will enter a space of constant discovery, where new exhibits have been designed to continuously evolve. Here, visitors will step into the shoes of a NASA engineer as they explore the cutting-edge research and technology conducted at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View through interactive exhibits and models. The event offers the chance to gain exclusive insights from individuals at the forefront of missions like Artemis, while exploring exciting artifacts, and learning about the latest space developments. Visit Chabotspace.org to learn more and purchase tickets. NASA Fest tickets are $30 for adults, $25 for youth (ages 3-12) and seniors, $15 for members, and free for member youth. The exhibition is part of a larger partnership between NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and Chabot Space & Science Center to re-envision STEM learning in Oakland. Together, the organizations are modeling innovative education approaches in museum experience, community engagement, and workforce development that have direct impacts and outcomes on Oakland youth.
articles.title: NASA Fest At Chabot Space & Science Center this weekend

articles.text: You can turn a gathering around the campfire into a perfect summer science lesson with this activity. We are putting a twist on the classic s’mores snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore, acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science. Materials: • Waffle cones • Mini marshmallows • Chocolate • Graham crackers • Your choice of toppings, chopped into small pieces - Chocolate candies, candy bars, nuts, sprinkles, popcorn, Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. • • • peanut butter cups, coconut, fresh fruit, etc. Foil Camp fire or oven Bowls for toppings Procedure: 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice! 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using the oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d. How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. Finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! Find more activities and at-home exper i ment s on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your observations with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills.
articles.title: Did you ever hear of S’more Science?

We are putting a twist on the classic s’mores snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore, acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science. Materials: • Waffle cones • Mini marshmallows • Chocolate • Graham crackers • Your choice of toppings, chopped into small pieces - Chocolate candies, candy bars, nuts, sprinkles, popcorn, Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. • • • peanut butter cups, coconut, fresh fruit, etc. Foil Camp fire or oven Bowls for toppings Procedure: 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice! 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using the oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d. How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. Finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! Find more activities and at-home exper i ment s on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your observations with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills.

articles.text: Hip Wah, a Chinese cultural summer program, returns to Beach School for four weeks starting June 17. This year Hip Wah will host over 140 campers, led by Vitalis Obidi and supported by a dedicated team of teachers, staff, camp aides, and At Hip Wah, campers learn about Chinese holidays, traditions, mythology, Chinese-American immigration history, and more through art, cooking, music, language, and history projects. The community is invited to an Open House on the evening of July 2 at Beach Elementary Hip Wah was founded in 1984 by parents Kalei Inn Lam and the late Shirlaine Kee Baldwin who wanted to create a summer enrichment program that encouraged strong self-image and identity through Chinese and Chinese-American cultural studies. Hip Wah is known for introducing and deepening its students’ connection to Chinese culture and the Chinese-American experience, although they do not have to be Chinese to attend. The program, now in its 40th year, started with one class in the Berkeley Chinese Community Church. Today, there are seven classes with campers ranging from age six to 13. Hip Wah has grown on the campuses of St. Paul’s Episcopal School and Redwood Day School in Oakland and spent one summer each at Beach Elementary and Wildwood Elementary schools. Campers come from throughout the East Bay, and more than 90% return summer after summer. Hip Wah board president Li Zhu and registrar Esther Cheung Hill have volunteered many hours for the organization. Photo by Eric Londgren Photography Hip Wah site director Vitalis Obidi, teaches middle school math during the regular school year. In the book Summer at Squee, Newbery Honor-Winning Author Andrea Wang tells the story of a young Chinese-American camper who returns each year to a program where she experiences “summertime Chinese culture, wellness, and enrichment.” Wang refers to Hip Wah in her Author’s Notes, recognizing the Hip Wah Summer Program as one of the few Chinese heritage camps in the United States. The Hip Wah Board includes Piedmonters Elizabeth Shook, Christine Chou, and Esther Cheung Hill. The Board is planning a Music Festival on July 13 at the Alan Harvey Theater followed by a celebratory luncheon. For more information, contact registrar@hipwah.org.

articles.text: serves the homeless and unsheltered population of Southern Oregon. Rogue Retreat offers a broad array of services including temporary housing, recovery programs for unhoused people with past trauma and substance abuse issues and community food programs that make reintegrating into the community easier for unhoused people. PCSC also partnered with Rogue Retreat last year. During their trip, volunteers from PCSC were tasked with repairing and improving homes in Rogue Retreat’s 150-person tiny house village. In specific, the team was tasked with building entry stairs for 19 of the site’s duplex homes as well as repainting them. When they weren’t working on the houses, the crew was serving food to its inhabitants at the site’s kitchen. “While we were working, we could see the residents coming and going, and some of them would talk to us,” said Li. He described the experience as “insightful” and “heartwarming” for many of the volunteers. Volunteer Bryson Cheney agreed. “We got to interact a lot more with the people we were helping, see our work come together and have an impact day by day. With a lot of other projects, we don’t often see the full impact of our work or get to meet those that we help. That was a nice change and motivator,” he recalled. At night, the crew stayed with local host family David Nilson (a professional colleague and friend of Ken Li), Leslie Nilson (David’s wife) and Julie Madiarmid (David’s sister). Between serving local communities, the crew also made some time for some fun excursions into Oregon and Northern California. The students went whitewater rafting on the Smith River, hiked through Redwoods in the Ashland area and visited Rogue Creamery, a cheesemaker whose claim to fame involves serving its cheese to French President Emmanuel Macron in 2022. Harry McNulty and Shou Presley greet one of the Billy goats at WillowWitt farm. One of the crew’s weekend excursions was a hike along in the mountains above Ashland, Oregon with stunning views of redwoods and expansive vistas.

articles.text: Qatar Airways is one of the most awarded and prestigious airways in the world. With over 18,000 “excellent” ratings on Trip Advisor and proud winner of the Travelers Choice award from 2017-2020. It turned out to be one of the worst flight experiences for my family. We took two flights – a 15-hour flight from SFO to Doha and another one clocking in at approximately five hours to Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia. Qatar Air had come highly recommended to us from my uncle, who frequently flew with them and often raved about it. I’m sure anyone who has ever sat in economy will tell you how uncomfortable the chairs are, how little legroom there is or the strange mush of substance the airline calls ‘food’. The oxblood colored seats were almost entirely devoid of cushioning, and all three meals tasted off. Overall, it was an extremely disappointing experience. On top of this, chairs were packed together tighter than any other airline I’ve flown. Why would my uncle not stop bragging about this airline when my family swore to never fly it again? For starters my uncle, recently retired, flew mostly for business, sitting in business and occasionally first class. Qatar Airways is constantly celebrated for its decadent business class along with the luxurious cabins, spacious bathrooms and gourmet meals that come with shelling out up to ten times more on a seat. While our flight was uncomfortable and led to irritation, it was, overall, a rather small thing in the grand scheme of it all. But it’s not a small thing. The portrayal of Qatar as a first-class airline and often overlooking portrayal of economy class in advertisements is harmful to many. Qatar isn’t the only airline or service or product to do this. In fact, portraying the best parts of something is the goal for marketers alike whether it’s for an air fryer or trendy restaurant. By adapting more transparency as a marketing norm, companies can build and foster trust between themselves and their customers. My family didn’t book economy class then walk on the plane and expect a gourmet filet mignon and fully reclining seats. We did, however, hold Qatar to a higher standard, excited to see why it was so highly praised. Qatar Airways is not alone in the struggle of preferential marketing. It’s universal and has existed since probably the Dark Ages. This is precisely why it needs to be changed. By embracing transparency, companies can bridge the gap of customer expectations to build lasting trust and loyalty. While it is important to showcase the strengths of a corporation and its goods, it is equally important to show a diverse, inclusive range. My experience is an opportunity to call for improvement. Industries must reflect on their image and communication to spot flaws and strive for truthful portrayals of their services. Until this notion has been accepted as a norm, we cannot achieve truly beneficial consumer-producer relationships. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen who frequently writes for The Post.
articles.title: Qatar Airways and preferential marketing

Qatar Airways is constantly celebrated for its decadent business class along with the luxurious cabins, spacious bathrooms and gourmet meals that come with shelling out up to ten times more on a seat. While our flight was uncomfortable and led to irritation, it was, overall, a rather small thing in the grand scheme of it all. But it’s not a small thing. The portrayal of Qatar as a first-class airline and often overlooking portrayal of economy class in advertisements is harmful to many. Qatar isn’t the only airline or service or product to do this. In fact, portraying the best parts of something is the goal for marketers alike whether it’s for an air fryer or trendy restaurant. By adapting more transparency as a marketing norm, companies can build and foster trust between themselves and their customers. My family didn’t book economy class then walk on the plane and expect a gourmet filet mignon and fully reclining seats. We did, however, hold Qatar to a higher standard, excited to see why it was so highly praised. Qatar Airways is not alone in the struggle of preferential marketing. It’s universal and has existed since probably the Dark Ages. This is precisely why it needs to be changed. By embracing transparency, companies can bridge the gap of customer expectations to build lasting trust and loyalty. While it is important to showcase the strengths of a corporation and its goods, it is equally important to show a diverse, inclusive range. My experience is an opportunity to call for improvement. Industries must reflect on their image and communication to spot flaws and strive for truthful portrayals of their services. Until this notion has been accepted as a norm, we cannot achieve truly beneficial consumer-producer relationships. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen who frequently writes for The Post. articles.text: Oakland Strokes continued its prowess as one of the top rowing programs in the country. It had a club record of 69 athletes, with nine boats competing in the finals at the U.S. Rowing Youth National Championships in Sarasota, Florida from Thursday through Sunday, June 6-9. Of the Strokes total, 15 were from Piedmont. The National Championship includes over 8,000 athletes from 224 clubs across the United States. Oakland Strokes’ Women’s Youth 8+ boat. Jackson Violich (second from right) helped the Strokes’ Youth 8+ boat finish third at the Youth Nationals in competition with 29 other boats. The Strokes claiming its 24th national title with the men’s Youth 4 boat, which included Piedmont senior Zachary Feldstein and Graham Young, a senior at Bentley School. They posted a winning time of 6:29.90 in a field of 30 boats. Men’s coach Jovan Jovanovich had high praise for Feldstein and Young’s accomplishment in the Youth 4 boat. “This victory is a testament to our athletes’ hard work and dedication. I couldn’t be more proud of them,” Jovanovich said. The men’s Youth 8+ boat also reached the podium, finishing third overall with recent graduate Jackson Violich. His boat finished with a time of 2:59.01 in the finals in a field of 30. Piedmont sophomore Connor Cross was a member of the U16 8+ boat, which finished ninth of 17 with a time of 6:39.14. Oakland Strokes had two rowers from Piedmont in its National Championship winning Youth 4 boat, featuring Piedmont High Class of 2024 graduate Zachary Feldstein (third from right) and Graham Young (third from left), who just graduated from Bentley School. PHS had three rowers on Strokes’ women’s the U17 8+ boat that finished sixth of 25 boats: juniors Geneva Johnson (back left) and Laurel Minor (second from left), and sophomore Sophia Brenner (fourth from left). Jackson Violich, a member of the Men’s Youth 8 boat. PHS also had three rowers in the Strokes’ Youth 8+ boat that placed 11th of 31: Ali Gallacher (second from left), Claire Von Metszch (third from right), and Cleo Tahawi (second from right).
articles.title: Oakland Strokes sends 15 Piedmonters to National Championships

articles.text: Tournament bracket for Copa America 2024 soccer tournament Summer soccer is here! Copa América officially returns this week with Argentina and Canada getting things started on tomorrow, June 20 at 5:00 p.m. Provided is how each group shapes up, each team’s FIFA ranking, and our final predictions of how the tournament plays out. We’ll start with the United States’ Group C and go from there. Group C: No. 11 USA, No. 15 Uruguay, No. 45 Panama, No. 85 Bolivia The United States walks into Group C in an inconsistent run of form, giving fans some uneasiness entering Copa America. They recently lost to Colombia 5-1 on June 8 but tied 1-1 with tournament favorites Brazil on June 12. Regardless, they should be the favorites to take the group, which would make their lives easier given C’s runner-up will face Group D’s top team, which will likely be Brazil. No. 45 Panama and No. 85 Bolivia shouldn’t pose much of a problem for the U.S. or No. 15 Uruguay. The United States opens competition against Bolivia on June 23 and faces Panama on June 27 before squaring off with Uruguay—which will likely determine the fate of the group. Uruguay is coming off of a mighty 4-nil win over Mexico on June 5 and possess a cast that could pose problems for the U.S., like Liverpool striker Darwin Núñez, Manchester United winger Facundo Pellistri, Tottenham midfielder Rodrigo Betancur, former Bracelona and Liverpool striker Luis Suárez, and world-class manager Marcelo Bielsa who loves to play on the attack. If I’m going off current run of form and quality of manager, it’s difficult to choose USA over Uruguay. I’m taking La Celeste to take Photo courtesy of CopaAmerica.com Can the U.S. win Group C? They face tough competition from a surging Uruguay group. 1C and USA as 2C, which should be a huge indictment against U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter. Group A: No. 1 Argentina, No. 32 Peru, No. 42 Chile, No. 49 Canada Aside from defending World Cup champions Argentina winning the group, this is an extra-difficult batch to predict. Each team has players that can provide a huge impact, like Peru with veteran forward André Carrillo, Chile with Inter Milan forward Alexis Sánchez, and Canada with Bayern Munich winger Alphonso Davies and Lille striker Jonathan David. In the end, I’m taking the Canadians’ star-power. Argentina takes 1B, Canada with 2B. Group B: No. 14 Mexico, No. 31 Ecuador, No. 54 Venezuela, No. 55 Jamaica Mexico enters its first tournament in years without veteran goalkeeper Memo Ochoa, but are still the favorites in the group with players like West Ham midfielder Edson Álvarez and shifty forward Alexis Vega. Jamaica brings talented players like West Ham striker Michail Antonio and Aston Villa winger Leon Bailey, but I’m leaning toward Ecuador’s talented cast of Bayern Leverkusen def’ender Piero Hincapié, Chelsea midfielder Moisés Caicedo, and the country’s All-Time top goalscorer, Enner Valencia. In the end, I’m taking Ecuador to take 1B and Mexico as runners up. Group D: No. 5 Brazil, No. 12 Colombia, No. 52 Costa Rica, No. 56 Paraguay This should be an easy prediction with a lot of disparity in the group; Brazil as 1D and Colombia as 2D. Quarterfinals predictions (1A) Argentina beats (2B) Mexico; (1B) Ecuador beats (2A) Canada; (1C) Uruguay beats (2D) Colombia; (1D) Brazil beats (2C) United States. Photo courtesy of The Japan Times Lionel Messi and Argentina enter with FIFA’s No. 1 ranking. Can the defending World Cup champions get it done in Copa América?

articles.text: The school year is has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post lists our favorite 10 moments of the year. 1. Boys’ Water Polo’s NCS Championship Our top moment came before New Year on November 11 when Piedmont’s No. 4 seeded boys’ water polo team made history by winning the Division 2 North Coast Section title with a 10-8 win over No. 3 Alameda. Piedmont won the Western Alameda County Conference title in 2021 and 2022, but fell in the NCS semifinals in the two previous years against Marin Academy, finally getting over the hump with a 13-9 semis victory over the No. 1 ranked Wildcats. It marked the school’s first NCS title. 2. Baseball’s NCS & CIF run It was a historic 2024 season for Piedmont High’s baseball team. They won the WACC regular season first-place banner and reached the finals of the North Coast Section and the State NorCal tournaments. After falling as the No. 2 seed in the NCS postseason to No. 4 Justin-Siena on May 25, Piedmont battled to the CIF NorCal Championship as the No. 1 seed with a 13-1 win over No. 8 Capuchino on May 28, shutout No. 4 Colusa 5-0 in the semifinals on May 30, but lost 6-0 to Bradshaw Christian on June 1. 3. Football team wins Shoreline title On November 3, Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Division title in a stress-inducing 29-26 win over Newark Memorial. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015, which was also the last time they won the Shoreline title. 2023 marked the return of the school’s 100 year-old varsity football program after it was shut down the previous year due to a lack of players. Going into 2024, the Highlanders were promoted to the Mission Division—the second tier of the WACC’s football pyramid. 4. Girls’ Lacrosse wins WACC title over Bishop O’Dowd The girls’ lacrosse team won its first WACC title since 2019 by beating rival Bishop O’Dowd 8-7 on April 26. Piedmont responded to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but quickly answered with goals by Friedie Schickedanz and two by Ruby Guzdar. Holding an 8-7 lead in the fourth quarter, the Highlanders killed over three minutes of clock to win the game. It was a big performance by goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter, recording 12 saves. 5. Natalia Martinez’s historic career 2023-24 was a historic season for senior guard Natalia Martinez, who graduates and is set to attend San Diego State. She concluded her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia went perfect 10/10 for 3-pointers, also creating a school record for hitting 100 percent beyond the arc for double-digit attempts. She is the Post’s first back-toback Athlete of the Year award winner. A top moment in sports includes the boys’ water polo team’s first North Coast Section championship on November 11. Pictured are Finn Burke helping to dunk coach Rik Krumins in the pool to celebrate. On November 3 Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Championship against Newark Memorial. The baseball team advanced to the North Coast Section and the State regional playoffs and also played a game on March 23 at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. 6. Sebastien Swain, the frosh phenom Freshman distance runner Sebastien Swain was a story, becoming our Freshman of the Year after qualifying for the State cross country meet in the fall and reaching the finals of the North Coast Section Meet of Champions in the spring track season. Swain was Piedmont’s only cross-country runner to qualify for the State meet on November 25 in Woodward Park. He finished 67th of 201 runners with a time of 16:41.3, earning him a selection on the 2023 All-State Freshman Team at the Division 4 level by Prep CalTrack. 7. Boys Basketball reaches NCS Finals The boys’ basketball team made it to the NCS Finals against No. 1 University where it lost 65-55 as the No. 3 seed. It marked the school’s first NCS Finals appearance since its D4 championship win in 2020. Reaching the championship meant Piedmont qualified for the CIF State Tournament as the No. 14 seed in the D3 bracket, falling to No. 3 Valley Christian in the opening round. Piedmont’s arrival in the State tournament marked a moment of triumph for the basketball program, which reachws the semifinals each year since winning the The girls’ lacrosse team won this year’s WACC Championship with a heated 8-7 win over Bishop O’Dowd on April 26. Natalia Martinez stands with basketball coach Bryan Gardere after surpassing g 2,000 career points. She set the school’s single-game record for points with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28.

Football team wins Shoreline title On November 3, Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Division title in a stress-inducing 29-26 win over Top sports moments from 2023-24 school year Newark Memorial. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015, which was also the last time they won the Shoreline title. 2023 marked the return of the school’s 100 year-old varsity football program after it was shut down the previous year due to a lack of players. Going into 2024, the Highlanders were promoted to the Mission Division—the second tier of the WACC’s football pyramid. 4. Girls’ Lacrosse wins WACC title over Bishop O’Dowd The girls’ lacrosse team won its first WACC title since 2019 by beating rival Bishop O’Dowd 8-7 on April 26. Piedmont responded to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but quickly answered with goals by Friedie Schickedanz and two by Ruby Guzdar. Holding an 8-7 lead in the fourth quarter, the Highlanders killed over three minutes of clock to win the game. It was a big performance by goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter, recording 12 saves. 5. Natalia Martinez’s historic career 2023-24 was a historic season for senior guard Natalia Martinez, who graduates and is set to attend San Diego State. She concluded her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Scripps Ranch on December 28. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia went perfect 10/10 for 3-pointers, also creating a school record for hitting 100 percent beyond the arc for double-digit attempts. She is the Post’s first back-toback Athlete of the Year award winner. Staff Photos A top moment in sports includes the boys’ water polo team’s first North Coast Section championship on November 11. Pictured are Finn Burke helping to dunk coach Rik Krumins in the pool to celebrate. On November 3 Piedmont’s football team won the WACC Shoreline Championship against Newark Memorial. The baseball team advanced to the North Coast Section and the State regional playoffs and also played a game on March 23 at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. 6. Sebastien Swain, the frosh phenom Freshman distance runner Sebastien Swain was a story, becoming our Freshman of the Year after qualifying for the State cross country meet in the fall and reaching the finals of the North Coast Section Meet of Champions in the spring track season. Swain was Piedmont’s only cross-country runner to qualify for the State meet on November 25 in Woodward Park. He finished 67th of 201 runners with a time of 16:41.3, earning him a selection on the 2023 All-State Freshman Team at the Division 4 level by Prep CalTrack. 7. Boys Basketball reaches NCS Finals The boys’ basketball team made it to the NCS Finals against No. 1 University where it lost 65-55 as the No. 3 seed. It marked the school’s first NCS Finals appearance since its D4 championship win in 2020. Reaching the championship meant Piedmont qualified for the CIF State Tournament as the No. 14 seed in the D3 bracket, falling to No. 3 Valley Christian in the opening round. Piedmont’s arrival in the State tournament marked a moment of triumph for the basketball program, which reachws the semifinals each year since winning the D4 section banner in 2022 and 2023. 8. Diver Nina Schwab reaches State finals On May 11 Nina Schwab competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming Diving Championship in the one-meter dive on May 11 at Clovis West High School, becoming Piedmont’s only diver to do so. She finished 16th of 28 athletes with a score of 429.55. To get there, Nina finished fourth of 16 at the NCS Championships with a final score of 423.35. 9. Baseball team plays at Oracle Park The baseball team makes a second appearance on this list due to the sheer uniqueness of March 23 against University. Playing in the Dante Benedetti Classic, the Highlanders defeated the Red Devils 8-1 while playing at Oracle Park of the San Francisco Giants. As a Giants’ fan watching Barry Bonds hit homers in the stadium’s original name, Pac Bell Park, it was an incredible moment. articles.text: Violinist Jascha Heifetz Throughout history, great teachers have influenced public opinion. Sometimes they paid with their lives- Socrates, for example. We probably should include Jesus also. In America, we need to include Abraham Lincoln and Martin Luther King. This evening a friend treated us to a gondola ride on Lake Merritt, which gave me the opportunity to write this column. There were six musicians aboard making it the perfect opportunity to ask some probing questions. The noted pianist Gerald Robbins has been in town for a week. He has been regarded as an outstanding pianist for more than 60 years. What is particularly interesting is that he combines being an important soloist with being an important piano accompanist. Imagine being the pianist to the likes of Jascha Heifetz, Gregor Piatigorsky, Nathan Milstein, Rugierro Ricci and Aaron Rosand. All were the top echelon for the entire 20th century. What did Gerry learn from them? That’s what I asked him while we were gliding on the water at Lake Merritt. It turns out that Robbins was attuned to the highest levels of musical artistry from the beginning. Some people just know the secrets innately. In his case, he did learn a lot rubbing shoulders with genius and listening attentively. Here are some of the secrets of the masters which performers should know. It might be a good idea if listeners know some of the secrets also. 1) Always be prepared. Be sure to take the advice of those who have experience. 2) Always be diplomatic. You will get more gigs if people like you. 3) Be sure to position yourself in the best place when you perform. The truth is that it really does matter. We are fortunate to have videos that show where to position yourself. String players always ask themselves if they should have a really expensive instrument (such as a Stradivarius.) Yes, a Strad does help. But if you control the volume of your piano accompanist, you will always sound better. These are just a few of the secrets of the masters. Along the way it helps to be observant. Be an inspired performer. Inspiration gives us the ability to rise above the mundane problems of life. By doing so we can transport the listener to another world. Listeners should never accept mundane performances. Sometimes it’s a good idea to voice our opinion. Standing ovations are warranted when a performance is particularly good. Unfortunately, we yell “bravo!” for mediocrity. Jascha Heifetz was always very critical of his own playing. One time, he was not happy with his performance. The audience was standing up and yelling “bravo!” Heifetz said to himself “Please don’t give me a standing ovation. I didn’t play very well. I deserve to be booed.” Honesty like this is certainly rare. articles.text: Stern Grove Festival, the country’s oldest nonprofit and free music festival, kicks off this Sunday, June 23. The amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove in San Francisco will host ten weeks of admission-free concerts beginning June 23 and running through August 25. Reservation is required and is given on a first-come, first-serve basis. Last year’s festival drew 90,000 attendees over the course of two months. The festival, now in its 87th season, opens June 23 with performances by King Isis, a queer Oakland-based multi-genre artist and the pop duo of siblings Tegan and Sara. San Francisco Symphony will perform a special concert on July 7 with Jessica Vosk, who performed as Elphaba in the Broadway musical Wicked. Sibling pop-duo Tegan and Sara perform at Stern Grove this Sunday. The SFJAZZ Collective, an allstar ensemble, will partner with the legendary Herbie Hancock on August 11. The Big Picnic Weekend, the festival’s annual fundraiser, is expanding this year to two days. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites.The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater and music. of summer performances. Visit https://www.sterngrove.org to reserve tickets.

articles.text: Three popular art exhibitions at the Fine Arts museums of San Francisco will continue to be on view this summer. Irving Penn exhibit at de Young An exhibition featuring the work of widely-recognized photographer Irving Penn is on view at the de Young museum in San Francisco through July 21. Penn is Vogue Magazine’s longest-standing contributor, and he became the most influential fashion photographer in the postwar era. Known for his use of neutral backgrounds, he emphasized models’ personalities through their gestures and expressions. The exhibition includes 175 photographs, spanning every period of Penn’s nearly 70-year career and ranging from early documentary scenes, celebrity portraits, and workers with the tools of their trades to abstract nudes and fashion studies. This presentation also features a special section of photographs made during Penn’s 1967 trip to San Francisco, where Penn captures the iconic “Summer of Love.” Included are his portraits of bona fide hippies, members of the Hells Angels Motorcycle Club, and local rock bands the Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company. To learn more, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.famsf.org/ exhibitions/irving-penn?mc_ cid=20 ab 0f 52d7& a mp;mc _ eid=573801a180. Fashion exhibit at de Young Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style features iconic collections of 20th and 21stcentury women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture, and is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Fashioning San Francisco is on display through August. Visit https://www.famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more. Japanese prints exhibit at Legion of Honor Legion of Honor in San Francisco’s newest exhibition Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World is on view through August 18. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of feudal military rule in the Asian country. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked both pre and postMeiji era. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. A patron views Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style at de Young Museum. Museum goers at the Legion of Honor exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World

articles.text: Sat. & Sun., June 22-23, 10 a.m.– 5 p.m. Nor Cal Glass Festival The Glass Alliance of Northern California (GLANC) is hosting the Nor Cal Glass Festival, an inaugural exhibition of glass art. Fifteen artists will be featured in the gallery spaces at the Center. The artworks are executed using a broad range of methods for working with glass including blown, kiln fired, cold- and flame-worked techniques. Visitors will be able to meet the artists. To learn more about the Glass Alliance of Northern California, go to www. glancinfo.org. Free! Saturday, June 29, 7 p.m. Diluvian String Quartet Concert The public is invited to Strings & Serenades: A Summer Quartet Concert. The program will include Glazunov’s 5 Novelettes, Beethoven’s Quartet No.1 in F major, and works by Price and Turina. The musicians are Elizabeth Castro Greenberg and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. Doors will open at 6:45 p.m. and tickets will be available at the door; music program begins at 7 to be followed by a dessert reception. Advance tickets, $20 general, under 12 free, may be purchased at https://www.eventbrite.com/e/915646050987. Sunday, July 21, 3 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Sextet In a lovely homage to early summer, a skilled sextet of Piedmont Chamber Orchestra musicians will present a concert called Concentric Circles with music for winds and piano spanning three-quarters of a century. Mostly French and French-inspired, the program includes works by Rimsky-Korsakov, Koechlin, Villa-Lobos, Poulenc, and Milhaud, performed by Martha Stoddard, flute; Jan Davis, oboe; Marcelo Meira, clarinet; Adam Williams, bassoon; Alex Stepans, horn; and Stanley Wolfersberger, piano. The concert is free; donations are welcome. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations.

articles.text: A few backstory comments: Going in Style was first made in 1979 and starred George Burns, Art Carney and Lee Strasberg. It was well received then, as was the 1993 “Grumpy Old Men,” starring the incomparable Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon. Cantankerous old men at loose ends, seated on a generic park bench sharing their mildly cynical commentary on life as it passes them by, is a theme that Hollywood has often visited and revisited. In the current incarnation, Going in Style has an A-list trio of actors – Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Alan Arkin – in what proves to be a familiar yet satisfactory story about three geezers, Willie (Freeman), Joe (Caine) and Albert (Arkin), who are all facing their end-game while exigent circumstances bear down, forcing them to transcend old age and retirement with more than a sigh and a shrug of the shoulders. As they soon learn, the company they spent 30 years serving has just been outsourced and in doing so cancelled their pensions. Willie is also suffering from renal failure, a fact he is keeping to himself. It is a truism that when you’re living what will likely be the last full decade of your life, you are reminded daily that your body will offer one small (or large) betrayal after the next. When Albert is reminded that life is short, he says something akin to, “tell me something I don’t know.” As well, Joe has just learned his house is in foreclosure (no pension means no house). While in the bank, asking the manager what that exactly that will mean, the place is held up. The robbers abscond with serious cash and, Joe notices the holdup guys pull off the job with essentially no harm no foul (well, there is the question of 2 million bucks now missing). It’s at this point when Going in Style could have been the movie it should have been. At least in act one and perhaps part of act two. The park bench conversations could have dealt with the reality of what it means to live in a culture where oldsters are pretty much assigned to the cheap seats. Ours is a culture where if you are in your 80s, life is happening on the field of play, observable, at times a bit confusing or disconcerting, especially since it seems to be moving with the speed of a double play or someone trying to steal home plate. And it can often feel just a bit (or a lot) out of reach. Their halcyon days are now recalled while looking in the rearview mirror. What the dynamic trio does, instead of mulling over their existential plight, is decide to plan a bank caper, inspired by Joe after observing his own bank being held up. So the three old guys, who are each a delight to watch as they keep this average story moving right along, work out their own heist (same bank), right down to a gnats eyebrow. The only question left to answer has nothing to do with their geezer-hood, but the how of planning a crime that will allow them to later enjoy the spoils of the robbery. Of course, going to jail at 80 is the equivalent of a life sentence and to be avoided at all cost. That proves to be their challenge. Anyway, there are three reasons to see Going in Style, and they are Freeman, Caine and Arkin. They are treasures and, to use a cliché, could read the menu at their favorite movie diner (where they are loathe to tip) and make it sound interesting. Going in Style. Directed by Zach Braft. articles.text: Film contains top talent of actors Pedro Almodovar: two Oscars, six BAFTAs (British), nine Goyas (Spanish), honorary doctorates from Harvard and Oxford, and 40 years of working at the craft of filmmaking, his chosen a medium which has allowed him to repeatedly examine the richness of the human condition. In his most recent film, Pain and Glory, he has created a spare narrative, never stark, never confused by vanity, but one that is close-to-the-bone subtle and nuanced, offered as auto-fiction and written and directed by Almodovar, who is now in his 70s. The lead character, Salvador Mallo, is a world-famous writer and filmmaker named Salvador Mallo, superbly portrayed by Antonio Banderas who is a ringer for Almodovar, down to the clothes he wears, his graying beard and spiky hair. The setting, almost exclusively, is Mallo’s Madrid apartment (recreated from Almodovar’s own apartment, with his personal art on the walls). Mallo is a man who is aging badly and feels betrayed by his body. And just to be clear about the vagaries of that betrayal, at the outset of the film, using animation, Mallo, in voice over, lists the afflictions that plague him: sciatica, depression, tinnitus, migraines, insomnia, a fused back, a throat that abruptly closes causing uncontrollable coughing, all buffered by alcohol and meds. Professionally, he refuses to write because physically he cannot direct what he might create. He wonders if he will ever work again, a voiced lament to a longago collaborator, actor Alberto Crespo (Asier Etxeandia), a man he has not seen for some 30 years, and with whom he smokes, for the first time, heroin; anything to relieve the pain. And it is when he falls into a heroin-induced reverie and dreams about his childhood and his mother, Jacinta (Penelope Cruz), he remembers an apartment-like cave they lived in when the family left their village and the underground home being filled with his mother’s love. In truth, Pain and Glory is a kind of reverie, often dream-like when Mallo, who lives like a hermit, and is only visited or rescued by loyal women who satellite his life while caring for him. In is a series of revelations, often steeped in regret, his story now a soft lament. Keep in mind that this film is told by an unreliable narrator (Mallo/Almodovar), and is framed by a spectrum of startling primary colors that belie Mallo’s condition and viewpoint. Deep reds enter almost every scene, often coordinated with his shirts and the window coverings; rainbows of colors are everywhere, in his flashbacks and in his daily life, a seeming contradiction. The exposition, in an unexpected way, is uplifting, for Mallo still refuses to yield. He even writes as if that very act is one of self-deception, yet the words are his own. Pain and Glory is, to be sure, a quiet meditation on aging and the physical betrayal that accompanies that experience. For Mallo, his physical pain is a reminder of a reality from which he can find no exit. He acknowledges that he is in the autumn of his life, heading toward winter. His dreams – his mother, of her washing clothes by a river, singing with the other village women – are of spring. This is his life, wistfully told, tenderly offered, a nexus of pain and glory while he hopes that still there is work ahead. A fact that is demonstrated so eloquently in this film. Pain and Glory. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. In Spanish with subtitles. Starring Antonio Banderas, Penelope Cruz and Asier Etxeandia.1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Released in 2019, Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime. Antonio Banderas and Julieta Serrano in Pain and Glory
