articles.text: Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of tweens and newbie teens. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Fransokyo, where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro, who graduated from high school at the age of 14, spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s night-time antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. They hope to influence the young prodigy to give up his underground exploits, and come to the realization that there is a world beyond his own niche of homegrown high tech stuff. A scene from Big Hero 6 As it turns out, the visit to the university proves a success. Hiro, captivated, meets kindred spirits, sees advanced labs, and meets the distinguished Professor Callaghan (James Cromwell), head of robotics, and the inventor of a medical bot, Baymax (Scott Adsit), programed to care for his charge. It eventually becomes Hiro’s sidekick of sorts. Of course, there is a sudden turn of events, which impacts Hiro and his buds, and they soon discover that as a result, their lives have been turned upside down. What occurs? Well, they unexpectedly discover an ominous, dangerous plot that pulls the gang into a harrowing adventure that is brimming with fun, action, and imaginative science (an example being a swarm of buzzing microbots). Older kids, tweens and teens will find Big Hero 6 a compelling watch, and Hiro an interesting role model. The world of high tech/A.I. is upon us. Hiro is already there. Big Hero 6. Directed by Don Hall, Chris Williams. Disney Studios animation. Voiced by Ryan Potter, Scott Adsit, T.J. Miller. Released 2014. Rated PG. 1hr 24min. Streaming on Disney+/ prime/Fandango

articles.text: I found Gifted engaging and watchable. The cast – a wonderful ensemble – is excellent, especially the performance of McKenna Grace as Mary, a 7-year-old math prodigy. She is a small powerhouse of emotion and a perfect contrast to Chris Evans as her laconic uncle Frank. As it is quickly revealed, Frank has raised Mary since infancy (her mother committed suicide) and the two have formed an unshakable bond. He has accomplished this while living in a shack in Florida, supporting the two of them by repairing boats. He also has the help of a neighbor, Roberta, played perfectly by Octavia Spencer. Their nicely balanced lives are abruptly disrupted when Frank decides that Mary should attend first grade at the nearest school. His thought is that she needs to learn to live among other kids. Mary votes for continued homeschooling. As does Roberta. What Mary’s teacher, Bonnie (Jenny Slate), is not prepared for is that Mary is a math genius and bored to distraction (and crankiness) by the simple rote learning. At a young age Mary is already doing quadratic equations. Frank is called in for a parent-teacher conference with Bonnie and school administrators who argue that Mary belongs in a gifted school where she will be challenged. Frank, wanting her to experience the world as it is, disagrees. And it’s then that Frank’s estranged mother, Evelyn (Lindsay Duncan), a wealthy Bostonian, enters their lives, bringing her high-priced attorney and a suit for custody. She has decided that Mary needs a far different environment than the one provided by Frank. It becomes clear that Gifted is a child custody story where both Mary and Frank are put under the court’s microscope while Evelyn is relentless. Throughout the film the interactions between Mary and Frank are priceless. And the courtroom drama is filled with tension as Mary’s fate hangs in the balance. What is agreed to, is not what you might expect, and it all has to do with Mary’s one-eyed cat named Fred. Gifted is simple and direct, with enough emotional horsepower to bring a tear or two. This may be Chris Evans’ best movie to date. And McKenna Grace delivers a tour de force performance as Mary and carries the film from the first scene. Gifted. Directed by Marc Webb. Starring Chris Evans, McKenna Grace and Jenny Slate. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Mckenna Grace in Gifted

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 19, 2024 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore city’s cul-de-sacs By Dick Carter It was another lovely morning on June 12 for the Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. A strong turnout of 47 walkers and two K-9 best friends were on hand. One of the enjoyable aspects of the group is going to seldom traveled roadways and paths. These are streets, back alleys, hidden paths and cul-de-sacs that most people don’t know about. There are a set of them on the southwest side of town, so that was the groups destination last week. Lois Price and Sherry Jacobs reminded the group that the Wednesday walkers will be marching in Piedmont’s 4th of July parade (Thursday, July 4, 11 a.m. on Highland Avenue). The group intended to go through Piedmont Park to get to Wildwood Avenue, but part of the park was closed for tree work. A quick change in the route plan was made, and the walkers went up a path to Guilford Road. They took a hidden path on Guilford to Hazel and then down Requa Road to Wildwood Avenue. The walkers took the lower portion of Wildwood opposite Wildwood School. This is a seldom traveled roadway because the upper portion of Wildwood gets almost all the traffic. The lower section is a delightful, seldom seen street with lovely front gardens. Near the street’s end is a path that leads to an alley providing access to garages on Ranleigh Way and Winsor Avenue. The alley was a surprise for the group because it feels like walking in a secluded park with large pines, redwoods and palm trees in the backyards. The group followed the alley to Harvard Road, crossed the Oakland city line and continued on to Lakeshore Avenue where they saw a surprising number of large, old palms lining the street, a carryover from developer Frank C. Havens’ grand entrance to his Piedmont Park attraction. The walkers went up Boulevard Way and back into Piedmont. On Boulevard, there was another path to the top of Sylvan Way. There was still the challenge of going down a very steep hill to Wildwood Avenue. Walkers went arm-in-arm down it to be safe. Wildwood quickly ran into Palm Drive, named for the palm trees Havens planted over a hundred years ago as the entrance to Piedmont Park. The group found another hidden path on Palm that took them to Magnolia Avenue for the climb back to the Exedra. For a little rest break, they went to seldom visited Larmer Court which runs off Magnolia above Witter Field. The cul-de-sac has only three homes. Continuing up Magnolia, they came to one last seldom walked street: Hillside Court, a cul-de-sac with only four homes located next to Piedmont Middle School. The walkers checked out the construction progress on the Piedmont pool and were back at the Exedra slightly before noon. It had been a fun three-mile walk in less than 90 minutes, filled with seldom seen streets, hidden paths, a back alley, cul-de-sacs,and lots of good conversations with new and old Wednesday walking friends. articles.text: Oakland Zoo hosted its third annual Bear Camp event to celebrate National Black Bear Day on Saturday, June 1. Guests watched the Zoo’s black bears destroy a demonstration campsite set up inside the habitat, and learned how to be beware while in bear country. U.S. Forest Service Rangers and Smokey the Bear joined in to watch the bears explore a tent and picnic table. As guests said hello to Smokey and wished him a happy 80th birthday, they got to talk with the Rangers and learn about fire safety, just in time for summer. In June 2017, when they were just cubs, this family of bears entered an older woman’s home, and the mother bear injured the homeowner who was trying to chase them out. After this incident, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife moved the bear family to Oakland Zoo. Not all human-wildlife conflict situations have this positive outcome. The Zoo urges the public to join them in Taking Action for Wildlife to minimize these conflicts. The most common humanbear conflicts involve unsecured garbage and food. For more information on how to stay bear-safe, see: Oaklandzoo.org/blog/how-to-bearware-in-black-bear-country Table for One? articles.text: If you are like me, the differences between all those buildings with prominent columns on them has always been a little unclear. Maybe today we can begin to sort it out. First, we go back to the Greeks. Their architecture was simpler, characterized by closely spaced columns because their era did not have the spanning capability of the arch. Along came the Romans, who in addition to borrowing heavily from the Greeks, were beneficiaries of the invention of concrete which allowed vaults, domes and arches, leading to a different, more developed architecture. Although the Greek and Roman civilizations were about 1000 years apart at their peaks, in our era the architecture they produced has been conventionally lumped together as Classical Architecture. This Classical Architecture was, and indeed is, pretty amazing. Well thought out with mathematically calculated proportions that are pleasing to the eye and mind, they seem to form a natural part of the universal order. Certainly they have endured over the centuries, having been “revived” numerous times. As this country was being formed in the late 1700’s, most of the new construction was strongly influenced by settlers from Europe, especially from England, to which we were attached as colonies. At that time there was a Classical Revival in vogue in Europe. It appeared on this side of the pond as well, and was the start of our Colonial Architecture style. Fast forward 100 years of style preference upswings and downswings to the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 in Chicago – America’s first World’s Fair. With 10 million visitors viewing the pervasive Classical style architecture of the fair developed principally by the architect Daniel Burnham, America was exposed and reawakPhots and Sketches by Will Adams The classical orders are the various sub-styles of Classical Architecture that evolved over the centuries. They are most easily identified by the column capitals, but include the whole of the building – proportions, profiles, and detailing. This seemingly timeless aesthetic still remains a source for various design styles (including some contemporary styles) in the 21st century. On the spectrum of revival styles, these impressive Piedmont homes tend towards Classical Revival (or Neoclassical). That is because they utilize the classical characteristics of large porticos (covered, columned entries), tall columns and classical orders (note the Ionic and Corinthian columns). They also tend towards formality because of their symmetry – the entry in the center of the building mass with the same balanced facades on each side.

articles.text: High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk-producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Lombardi High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” By 1885, the mulberry grove was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. A sketch of the Silk Farm building published in the San Francisco Call in 1894. Seven of the eight rooms were devoted to raising silkworms. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s, silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. After six years, the Piedmont silk station failed to make a profit despite federal aid. articles.text: tories in the mid-1600s. At the onset of the Glorious Revolution in 1688, England’s king fled to France, never to return. Possibly Salvator Mundi was gifted – or snatched up in the chaos – by the king’s mistress, Catherine Sedley, Countess of Dorchester. Once the painting left the royal house and fell into private hands, it was lost for 200 years. The painting surfaced in 1900, badly damaged from aggressive cleaning and overpainting. Sotheby’s sold it for £120 to the Cook Collection in London. In 1958 Sotheby’s handled the Cook Collection sale, including Salvator Mundi, to a couple in Baton Rouge, Louisiana for £45. Prior to the family placing it for auction, Salvator Mundi had hung for decades in a nondescript staircase. The family had it appraised at $750; but the New Orleans auctioneer valuation was between $1,200 and $1,800. Its catalog blurb played up “the fine antique gilt frame.” Gallery owner Robert Simon of New York City was tipped off by an associate Alexander Parish, an art-picker whose expertise is scouring the internet for potential finds, shared the hope of connecting the work to a Leonardo disciple. When Simon examined the work in person, he deemed it a wreck with “wormy panel, cradled [lattice support backing], badly overpainted, and scraped with a sharp tool.” That said, he recognized the oil-on-panel looked to be of Renaissance vintage and noted that parts were skillfully done, such as the figure’s left-side curls, the orb, and right hand in blessing: also “it was dirty, dark, and gloomy.” They were stunned to win the bid at $1,000. The Salvator Mundi controversy The art-dealer consortium turned to Dianne Modestini, a New York University research professor and renowned restorer. Dianne’s first reaction was that Christ’s face looked like a “clown mask” and she recommended a junior restorer, but after a few sample-test cleanings, she changed her mind. They engaged a Madrid specialist, Monica Griesbach, who disengaged the painting’s backing, and “the entire painting came apart in her hands breaking into seven pieces.” She spent six months reassembling the painting – mending with adhesive and tiny wood slivers. The restoration was slow and painstaking and took six years, while Simon researched for authentication. Once they concluded it was Leonardo’s work, the job was to build consensus among art historians. Opinions were far from unanimous. The big breakthrough happened in 2011 when the National Gallery in London accepted Salvator Mundi in the Leonardo da Vinci: from Milan show. The art dealers were ecstatic: the National Gallery would show Salvator Mundi as an autograph da Vinci – meaning not a collaboration, not a partial Leonardo – but a Leonardo da Vinci original. Carmen Bambach, a trusted Renaissance art historian wrote, “it’s a severely damaged original painting exhibiting large portions” of extensive restoration “with passages done by Leonardo himself”, meaning she Leonardo da Vinci was a man of dignity, grace, and elegant bearing; attired fastidiously and always with an abundant beard. He made about 18 self-portraits. Previosly printed in the Piedmont Post on May 12, 2021. Among European art extravaganzas, perhaps the most popular was Leonardo da Vinci at the Louvre, a retrospective celebrating 500 years since the artist’s death and showing off the artist’s remarkable works. Bu, one late entry that sold for an eye-popping $450 million missed the show. A fascinating debate is still ongoing that challenges the authenticity of da Vinci’s painting, Salvator Mundi, while asking what the next move will be by the secretive Saudi prince who may or may not have buyer’s remorse. Twice the painting’s unveilings were abruptly canceled without explanation. Paintings by the enigmatic Leonardo are among the rarest of Old Masters. Except for two in private hands – most are owned by museums. The Louvre owns five, including Mona Lisa. Italy owns three, counting the ruined Last Supper. The U.S. has one. How many Leonardo paintings exist remains in dispute, but the number is believed to be fewer than 20. Though unquestionably one of the greatest painters known to the world, based upon the time invested in the paintings, he was not prolific. He frequently abandoned works when his interest waned or was diverted. His painting was slow, and he clung to works to reach perfection. Consider the Mona Lisa (La Joconde in French), a painting he carted around Italy and France to his dying day. Leonardo’s philosophy was that money in abundance does not end well. Renaissance Man Born in the Florence countryside in 1452, Leonardo’s gifts manifested early. By age 14, he was apprenticed to Andrea del Verrocchio’s workshop, where his formal schooling trailed off and self-study bloomed. He became immersed in languages, natural sciences, history, philosophy, and mathematics – disciplines that substantially informed his art. Much of what is known about his polymathic genius is in his notebooks – thousands of pages of densely inscribed notes and drawings that have survived and were displayed at the Louvre. Leonardo’s longest patronage was with Duke Ludovico Sforza of Milan – where he especially thrived, not just as painter and sculptor. He was an engineer and architect, especially for military charting and weaponry. As First Painter, he designed theatre and opera sets. It was there he completed The Last Supper and Virgin of the Rock. Wherever work was offered, Leonardo packed up shop and went – to Florence, Milan, Rome, and late in life, to France. In his 60s, Leonardo faced dwindling patronage and was unable to attract any work from Pope Leo X who favored more reliable painters, including Raphael and Michelangelo. When the new French King Francois the First – a devoted patron of the arts – beckoned with an exceptional offer of generous pension, a chateau in Amboise, and the post of Court Painter, Architect, and Engineer – Leonardo quickly accepted, forging a close friendship with the king during his final years of life and work. Where the painting has been Old Masters typically have a spotty provenance, and Salvator Mundi, especially so. The art work disappeared for centuries. Christie’s auction house assembled the provenance, beginning with French King Louis XII who possibly commissioned Salvator Mundi in 1500, then passing in descendant to Princess Henrietta Maria in 1625 when she married England’s King Charles 1st. It then was in the hands of both her sons who each ascended to the throne. The painting is documented in England’s royal inven- 1515: Invited by King Francois 1st, Leonardo moved to the Château de Close Lucé on a hillside overlooking the Loire River. Today the period-era home and gardens are a museum open to the public. 1650: England’s royal collection inventory includes etchings by Wenceslas Hollar. Another inventory in 1666 confirms ‘Salvator Mundi’ in England. 1913: The Cook Collection’s catalog includes this sketch of ‘Salvator Mundi’ acquired in 1900.

Dealbreaker for Mohammed bin Salman No one is doubting that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) bought Salvator Mundi via proxy. Its unveiling was expected at Louvre Abu Dhabi’s inaugural in 2018 but canceled. The exhibit Leonardo da Vinci at the Louvre the following year was expected to feature the rediscovered painting, but also was abruptly cancelled. By all accounts, Salvator Mundi hasn’t appeared in public since the November 2017 auction. Rumor has it was spotted on display on bin Salman’s luxury yacht the Serene or possibly stored on the yacht pending completion of a luxe museum in Medina, northwest Saudi Arabia. Or, possibly, it is in storage in Geneva. No one, especially MBS, has any comment. A documentary film, The Savior for Sale, has the art world buzzing about why Salvator Mundi is in hiding. It describes an insider story insisting that the Louvre refused to commit to authenticating the painting as wholly Leonardo’s. The multiple restorations, it claims, make it impossible to discern how much of the original remains – though it’s probably from da Vinci’s workshop and Leonardo did some portions of the work. Was the Louvre’s refusal to MBS’s two top demands the dealbreaker? Apparently so. The Crown Prince demanded that Salvator Mundi be paired with the Mona Lisa, but a side-by-side display was physically impossible in the heavily safeguarded gallery. MBS demanded that the Louvre fully authenticate Salvator Mundi as painted wholly by the hand of Leonardo da Vinci. It wasn’t an easy decision, but the Louvre refused. Their strict policy to not comment on any work of art examined by their own experts and not displayed at the museum – has resulted in no comment. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and now bide their time until the pandemic is tamped down, and Paris will be Paris again. Swiss art-broker Yves Bouvier of Singapore was interested but declined to pay the desired $150 million, and the exhausted dealers accepted $80 million. The next day, Bouvier flipped the painting to Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev for $127.5 million. Details of the deal gone awry leaked, and all parties were unhappy and filed lawsuits – still active three years later when Rybolovlev hired Christie’s to resell Salvator Mundi. Prior to 2005, two Leonardo da Vinci paintings remained unaccounted for, Leda and the Swan, a large-scale mythological allegory, and the Salvator Mundi (Savior of the World), which depicted Christ’s benediction. It was favored by private devotees and became wildly popular in this period. Disciples and followers of da Vinci created their own versions, and about 30 paintings exist today. Those attributed to da Vinci’s workshops in Florence and Milan are highly valued. The Salvador Mundi slated for exhibition – and withdrawn – is believed to be the original of this genre: an oil-on-walnutpanel of Christ, larger than life size wearing a blue robe with a golden leathery embroidered sash: he makes a sign of the cross with his right hand and cradles a quartz-crystal orb in his left hand symbolizing the world. Three detailed sketches and Windsor Castle’s red-chalk drawing of the folds of Christ’s robe are evidence of da Vinci’s work. Whether he painted it entirely – or collaborated is a question worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The most recent restorer vehemently disagrees that restoration excessively altered Salvator Mundi or affected its attribution to Leonardo. Others are not so sure. their handling of the sale was sure to come under fire. articles.text: ened to the architecture of antiquity and its colonial past, which we knew principally through our Colonial Architecture. Colonial Revival was born, and was immensely popular, flourishing for decades throughout the country, including California. So, Classical and Colonial Revival styles are stylistically These beautiful Piedmont homes are of the Colonial Revival style. Less monumental, they are asymmetrical and exhibit many classical motifs including the balustrades (fancy guardrails) and dentils (the small repetitive protrusions at the cornice). The Colonial Revival giveaway is the use of paired columns, not employed in earlier eras, something I think adds an incredible richness to the design. The arches (but not the solar panels) are a Roman contribution. A variant of the Colonial Revival is the Georgian style from England. It is restrained in classical ornamentation but wonderfully proportioned and balanced over the entire symmetrical facade. The Gambrel (double sloped) roof with dormers, and curved eave on this fine home is a characteristic of the Dutch influence, another subcategory of the Colonial Revival genre.

Colonial Revival was born, and was immensely popular, flourishing for decades throughout the country, including California. So, Classical and Colonial Revival styles are stylistically linked, although there are many variants out there. Generally, the “purer” Classical Revival (or Neoclassical) style is more formal and monumental, occurring in larger institutional and civic buildings such as city and state capitals. The White House and U.S. Capitol These beautiful Piedmont homes are of the Colonial Revival style. Less monumental, they are asymmetrical and exhibit many classical motifs including the balustrades (fancy guardrails) and dentils (the small repetitive protrusions at the cornice). The Colonial Revival giveaway is the use of paired columns, not employed in earlier eras, something I think adds an incredible richness to the design. The arches (but not the solar panels) are a Roman contribution. A variant of the Colonial Revival is the Georgian style from England. It is restrained in classical ornamentation but wonderfully proportioned and balanced over the entire symmetrical facade. buildings are certainly the most famous Neoclassical buildings in this country. Colonial Revival used the classical characteristics on more modest sized buildings, especially homes. This style is more eclectic (derived from a range of styles or subtypes) and I think generally richer and more interesting as a result. Colonial Revival is the architectural style of a number of beautiful homes in Piedmont, all with their own particular personalities. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: Third major residential fire this year A significant house fire took place at an under-construction home on St. James Drive early morning on Tuesday, May 21, around 1:00 a.m. No one was hurt or injured, although damage to the property included significant damage to the room where the fire was located and smoke damage throughout the structure. It is the third major house fire this year in Piedmont, a city that averages one fire every two to three years. The cause of the fire is currently under investigation. Piedmont Police Department Officer Jason Germano was on night patrol when he smelled smoke in the air. A cursory investigation of the area revealed a fire had started at 140 St. James Drive. Germano immediately had the dispatch center notify the Fire Department. Firefighters arrived at the home to find a fire burning on the main floor. Captain Justin McNulty was the incident commander and Lt. Zach Heliker was the first person to make entry into the building. pages.text: Wednesday, June 12, 2024 3 More than 50 years ago, KNBR disc jockeys Mike Cleary of Piedmont and Frank Dill challenged their Bay Area listeners to put on a parade, and Pleasanton was selected. It became the KNBR Good Times Parade, and anyone with a little red wagon could enter. A Mariners group at the Pleasanton Presbyterian Church entered with a Viking ship the first year, then came up with the idea of tubby sailors carrying mops. The group quickly became a popular comic marching group. Though many of the men were veterans of various branches of the military, there was a belief that slavish obedience to commands was counterproductive, so the Balloon Platoon was born. Invitations soon came to participate in other communities’ parades. In 22 years, the group has trooped in several bowl games, appeared at the Indianapolis 500 Balloon Platoon returns for 4th of July Parade and marched in the Christmas parade in London. Though not bearing bagpipes the Platoon went to Edinburgh in 2000 to participate in the Millennium Pipe Festival. One spring the Balloon Platoon appeared in the National Cherry Blossom Festival parade in Washington, D.C. The group meets only to decide which parade invitations to accept. “We usually reject offers that are strict forward-motion parades,” explained leader Hal Strunk. “The Marine Corps band does that really well – we do not.” The age of Platoon members ranges from 21 to 80, and all are associated with the church in Pleasanton. As the Balloon Platoon passes by on the 4th of July, look for its special routines: Shake-nBake, pirouettes, carousels, big pinwheels, the Manual of Mops and its famous 21-Mop Salute. The Balloon Platoon, based in Pleasanton, has been a staple of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade for more than 13 years. articles.text: A fire on Wednesday, June 5, totally destroyed the vehicle of a local worker. At around 2 p.m., a domestic worker on Selborne Drive started his car to go home for the day when something malfunctioned and the vehicle caught fire. “Because this was in the middle of the day, and it was a car where the body panels are largely plastic, it created a really large black plume of smoke,” said Dave Brannigan, Chief of the Piedmont Fire Department. “So, we got lots of calls from concerned residents about a fire.” The fire spread quickly and damage to the vehicle was severe. “It was fully engulfed [in flames] by the time we arrived,” said Brannigan. The property on Selborne has a steep driveway which prevented fire engine access to the fire. Firefighters carried their hoses up the driveway by hand to reach the fire. “We had a crew member pretty close to the area, and we got water on it within 10 minutes,” said Brannigan. “The property owners did a great job of having a clear driveway. There was no vegetation hanging down blocking us, nor cars in the driveway, which helps with fire safety, but it also helps us access your property. So, putting your cars in the garage or parking spots and not blocking your driveway is something everybody can do to keep themselves a little bit safer every day,” he said.” For more information, contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 or email FireInfo@ piedmont.ca.gov. The first major fire of the year occurred on March 6 in the 200 block of Sea View Avenue. The second major fire took place on April 9 in the 600 block of Blair Avenue and threatened to spread to adjacent homes by the time firefighters arrived. “We investigate every fire thoroughly. Marshall, a young lab-Pittie mix Car on Selborne Drive totaled by fire By Matt Simons A fire on Wednesday, June 5, totally destroyed the vehicle of a local worker. At around 2 p.m., a domestic worker on Selborne Drive started his car to go home for the day when something malfunctioned and the vehicle caught fire. “Because this was in the middle of the day, and it was a car where the body panels are largely plastic, it created a really large black plume of smoke,” said Dave Brannigan, Chief of the Piedmont Fire Department. “So, we got lots of calls from concerned residents about a fire.” The fire spread quickly and damage to the vehicle was severe. “It was fully engulfed [in flames] by the time we arrived,” said Brannigan. The property on Selborne has a steep driveway which prevented fire engine access to the fire. Firefighters carried their hoses up the driveway by hand to reach the fire. “We had a crew member pretty close to the area, and we got water on it within 10 minutes,” said Brannigan. “The property owners did a great job of having a clear driveway. There was no vegetation hanging down blocking us, nor cars in the driveway, which helps with fire safety, but it also helps us access your property. So, putting your cars in the garage or parking spots and not blocking your driveway is something everybody can do to keep themselves a little bit safer every day,” he said.” For more information, contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 or email FireInfo@ piedmont.ca.gov. Housefire Continued from page 1 and were able to extinguish the fire before it spread through the house. In a stroke of luck, the firefighters had run a training exercise of the same situation earlier in the day, said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. A homeowner called the fire department for an inspection of the vegetation management of their property, “which had a long, winding, and complicated” driveway. Brannigan asked if he could run a training exercise on the property. “I got the owner’s permission, and we brought the whole shift over and walked through what we would do if we had a fire at the far end of the property,” he recalled. The exercise paid off almost immediately. “We were able to take that experience and translate it directly to the actual fire we had later that night in a completely different neighborhood,” said Brannigan. The house under construction is U-shaped and the most affected parts of the fire were near the center of the structure, outside of the public eye. The first major fire of the year occurred on March 6 in the 200 block of Sea View Avenue. The second major fire took place on April 9 in the 600 block of Blair Avenue and threatened to spread to adjacent homes by the time firefighters arrived. “We investigate every fire thoroughly. We look for suspicion, we look for common threads and we work with the police department to determine if there’s anything that we need to be concerned about. So far, we are not able to tie anything to these three different fires other than just bad luck and coincidental timing. [...] We’ve looked at it and haven’t determined that there’s any connection,” said Brannigan. In addition to other fire safety guidelines, Chief Brannigan urged homeowners with long driveways to keep them clear and accessible in case of an emergency. “The property owners did a great job of having a clear driveway. There was no vegetation hanging down blocking us, nor cars in the driveway, which helps with fire safety, but it also helps us access your property. So, putting your cars in the garage or in parking spots and not blocking your driveway is something everybody can do to keep themselves a little bit safer every day,” he said. The Fire Department can help Piedmont residents with fire safety tips and examinations. For more information, call the fire station at 420-3030 or email FireInfo@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: California Assemblymember Mia Bonta recently named Children’s Fairyland in Oakland as the 2024 California Non-Profit of the Year. This year marks the ninth year of the California Non-profit of the Year initiative, a state-wide effort honoring nonprofit organizations’ critical role in California. Bonta highlighted Children’s Fairyland’s contributions to young lives in Oakland and across the Bay Area at a ceremony in Sacramento on Wednesday, June 5. Founded on the shores of Oakland’s Lake Merritt in 1950, Children’s Fairyland has served as Oakland’s Storybook Theme Park for over 70 years. The park inspired other cities to open similar storybook parks for children and even inspired Walt Disney’s development of Disneyland. “Children’s Fairyland has long been a center of joy for the East Bay’s youngest residents and an iconic staple of Oakland,” said Bonta. “Annually, the park waives admission costs for over 4,000 low-income children to ensure everyone can experience its attractions. I’m incredibly proud to have this wonderland in my district. It has brought my family’s little ones and so many others a space for their creativity and imagination to thrive. Children’s Fairyland has operated as a non-profit for the past 30 years, and I’m honored to name them Non-Profit of the Year for Assembly District 18 for the continued enjoyment and learning they provide our community.” “We are honored to be recognized as the 2024 California Nonprofit of the Year by Assemblymember Mia Bonta for the magic we have woven into the fabric of Oakland and the Bay Area,” said Kymberly Miller, the executive director at Children’s Fairyland. “Through the unwavering support from our community, we will continue to serve families across the region and keep the tradition of fostering creativity, imagination, storytelling, and a love for learning alive for the next 75 years.” Nearly all of California’s 120 state legislators select their own Non-Profit of the Year as part of California Nonprofits Day. Now in its ninth year, the program seeks to highlight local nonprofits across the state. Since its inception, more than 774 different nonprofit organizations have been selected. Bonta represents California’s 18th Assembly District which includes Oakland, Alameda, Piedmont, and Emeryville. She also chairs the Assembly Health Committee. For more information, contact Bonta’s Sacramento office at (916) 319-2018 or her district office in Oakland at 286-1670. articles.text: Two fourth grade classes from Beach school collected 101 pounds of trash during their 4th-grade community service field trip on May 24. Students in small groups with parent leaders walked around the neighborhoods of Piedmont and Oakland and collected 6,638 pieces of trash in two hours. The students from the classes of Ben Spencer and Alicia Martinez cataloged every item and then weighed their bags on campus. Last year’s totals, 5,276 pieces and 85 pounds, were significantly outpaced by the students this year. Does this mean they worked harder, or that there is more litter around, students pondered? “Students have been learning about organisms and biomes in science for the last seven weeks,” said Spencer. “Earlier this year we also took a field trip to the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. They learned about the impact humans have on our oceans and marine life.” Beach dad Justin Laubach checks the white board and the results of trash collection by each group. Alicia Martinez and Ben Spencer’s 4th grade classes at Beach School show 101 pounds of trash they collected in the school neighborhood. The nine- and ten-year old students were determined to make sure that the trash in their community stays out of storm drains and out of the Bay and the ocean. The field trip engaged students’ minds and bodies by giving them the privilege of getting to be off campus. Parent chaperones took groups to different nearby areas to pick up trash, including the Rose Garden, Piedmont Avenue, Grand Avenue and Dracena Park. Armed with gloves, tongs, and safety goggles the students racked up tally marks on their worksheets showing what’s hiding in bushes and what otherwise would be eventually careening into waterways. One group, in just a couple of hours, collected a dozen medical masks, 50 cigarette butts and hundreds of plastic bottles and plastic pieces. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, June 12, 2024 Beach 4th graders collect over 100 pounds of trash By Jay Russell Two fourth grade classes from Beach school collected 101 pounds of trash during their 4th-grade community service field trip on May 24. Students in small groups with parent leaders walked around the neighborhoods of Piedmont and Oakland and collected 6,638 pieces of trash in two hours. The students from the classes of Ben Spencer and Alicia Martinez cataloged every item and then weighed their bags on campus. Last year’s totals, 5,276 pieces and 85 pounds, were significantly outpaced by the students this year. Does this mean they worked harder, or that there is more litter around, students pondered? “Students have been learning about organisms and biomes in science for the last seven weeks,” said Spencer. “Earlier this year we also took a field trip to the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. articles.text: Our systems are designed to experience the world through a multi-sensory experience. But, in our current crazy world, our ancient minds don’t actually know how to understand what is happening. My favorite example of this is that if you are wearing a VR headset and a lion comes at you and roars, your nervous system is going to react as if that lion is actually there, raising our cortisol levels and activating our flight/fight/freeze systems. So, even though you are not actually smelling the smells of the lion den or feeling the warmth of the Sub-Saharan African breeze, our sense of sight overrides all the other senses and we believe the threat is real. So, as we move into summer, I am really focusing for myself and with my kids on experiencing the world in its full sensory experience–not on screens, not inside– but, instead with smells and textures and sounds and taste. How can every day be an explosion of senses? Here are some questions that you can explore with your family: • Sight: What does the sun look like at 6am, 12pm and 8pm? • Smell: How does the air smell near the ocean? In the forest? In the middle of the city? • Taste: What does a fresh picked piece of fruit taste like? How long does the taste of chocolate last on your tongue if you let it melt? • Texture: Can you find something prickly? What about something as soft as a baby bunny? What does it feel like when you touch ice and then something warm? • Hearing: How many different bird calls can you hear first thing in the morning? What is the sound of the washing machine in the spin cycle? Can you hear the variations between the barks of different dogs in your neighborhood? you and your family to lift eyes out of screens and reset your nervous system to real life. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Our senses connect us to IRL

articles.text: Dads from Havens, Wildwood and Beach elementary schools battled for bragging rights at Coaches Field on Saturday, June 1, in the annual Buzz Redford Tri-School Softball Tournament. The Wildwood Wild Things took home top honors in the end-ofthe-year round-robin tournament by shutting out both the Havens Dads and the Beach Padres, 4-0, in two seven-inning games. Havens topped Beach 6-2 in the Consolation game, and a team of Alumni tied an all-star team of current players, 7-7. Wild Things manager Alexander Shartsis, a Piedmont native, said the win was big. The last time Wildwood won the tournament was 15 years ago in 2009. That year, the Wildwood pitchers combined for a no-hitter against Beach. The last time Wildwood won a single game in the end of year tournament was 2017 against Havens, when Shartsis was in his rookie year managing the team. The 2024 Wildwood Wild Things brought their gloves and got to work early on Saturday. No runner reached beyond second base in either game. “On defense, John Labrum threw 14 scoreless innings. Randy Wells made at least 12 outs in left field including a slide into the fence on a foul ball that you probably saw on SportsCenter,” said Shartsis. The Wildwood Dads Wild Things team won the Piedmont elementary dads clubs’ end-of-year softball tournament by defeating the Havens and Beach dads clubs by identical 4-0 scores. articles.text: Honorable Mention: Hailey Marshburn, Breah Bell, Declan Linnane, Peter Krumins Another school year has come and gone. This past year, 2023- 24, Piedmont High earned one North Coast Section title, six league championships, earned 132 All-League honors, and three Western Alameda County Conference Player of the Year awards. The Post has named Natalia Martinez and Markos Lagios as our Athletes of the Year, with Breah Bell, Peter Krumins, Declan Linnane, and Hailey Marshburn as honorable mentions. and Sophomore of the Year recipients. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Natalia Martinez becomes the Post’s first person to receive back-to-back Athlete of the Year awards. She received our end-ofyear awards in each year of her high school career; we named her our 2021 Freshman of the Year, 2022 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Athlete of the Year as a junior. Martinez led the Highlanders to a 20-8 overall record and 7-1 league record to split this year’s WACC title with Bishop O’Dowd, marking Piedmont’s second consecutive league banner. PHS received the No. 6 seed in the NCS Open Division, losing to Carondelet 83-53 in the first round. They automatically qualified for the D1 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed, losing to No. 8 Whitney 53-41 in the first round. This year she won the WACC Player of the Year award for the second consecutive year, and named for a second time to the SF Chronicle’s All-Metro firstteam. CalHiSports named her to the second-team in the Open Division. It was an illustrious scoring year for Martinez, putting up record numbers throughout the season. She concludes her high school career with 2,272 total points, including the school-record for most points in a single game with 52 in a 75-58 win over Staff Photos Natalia Martinez earns our second consecutive Athlete of the Year award after an historic scoring season. Scripps Ranch on December 28. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia went perfect 10/10 for 3-pointers, also creating a school record for hitting 100 percent of her shots beyond the arc for double-digit figures. Martinez becomes one of Piedmont’s highest scorers of all time alongside Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. She concluded her high school career as a four-year starter and never missed a single game since coming to Piedmont in 2020. articles.text: BOYS’ WATER POLO Just reaching the 2023 NCS Finals was a major accomplishment for Piedmont High. The school had never reached the finals according to records dating back to 1995, and after backto-back semifinals appearances, any onlooker could tell this year’s team was made of championship quality as they went on long scoring runs against No. 1 Marin Academy 13-9 in the semifinals and No. 3 Alameda 10-8 on their way to the title on November 11. As the clock struck zero against the Alameda Hornets, Finn Burke dragged coach Rik Krumins into the pool, while members of PHS’ student section jumped in the water to celebrate with their classmates. Piedmont won the WACC title in 2021 and 2022, but had to get over the pesky NCS postseason hump after losing to Marin Academy the previous two years. It marked a peak to PHS’ Golden Age of water polo. FLAG FOOTBALL PHS wrapped up its first girls’ flag football season, proving to be a highly-competitive and well-structured program. They were the largest team within the league by a considerable margin, showing how high the interest in football is for girls at the small-enrollment school. Piedmont fought to the end, but finished fourth in the first WACC Tournament at Hayward High on October 28 after entering as the fourth seeded school. They opened with a nail-biting one-point 13-12 loss to top-seed Berkeley, while they fell 22-6 to third-seed San Leandro in the battle for third place. In the previous round against Berkeley, the Highlanders rallied from a 13-0 deficit to make it 13-12 with 36 seconds left in the game, but fell short on its 1-point conversion. FOOTBALL Piedmont’s win over Newark Memorial on November 3 marked mission accomplished for the football team, which captured the WACC Shoreline Division title by defeating the Cougars in a heated 29-26 battle. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015, which was also the last time they won the Shoreline. After trailing 14-7 going into halftime, but Piedmont’s defense responded to the call, forcing a monumental six turnovers in the second half including four in the fourth quarter. Piedmont gained its 29-26 lead with an 80-yard touchdown pass from a hobbled Markos Lagios to Sam Shelby with 5:27 left in the game. Lagios suffered a knee injury with six minutes left, but never missed a play. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco is currently showing Corrine Smith: Silene Capensis in its series of emerging artists. The exhibit is on view now through June 21. Oakland-based artist Smith, who also goes by Critty Smitty, named the exhibition after the Silene capensis root, also known as “African dream.” Her vivid paintings, illustrations, risographs and animations hauntingly capture the artist’s experience with sleep paralysis and night terrors. Smith’s artwork blends the line between reality and fantasy, while displaying a connection to ancestral lineage and eventual healing. The exhibition is presented in conjunction with MoAD’s 2024- 25 emerging artists series, which highlights local, emerging and lesser known artists who work with a variety of mediums. For more information, visit the museum’s website at www. moadsf.org or call 415.358.7200. MoAD is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. Artist Corrine Smith at work
articles.title: Corrine Smith exhibit continues through June 21 at MoAD

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, is on view through August 18. It showcases groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise features over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four largescale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, a Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibit are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.sfmoma. org.
articles.title: SF MOMA’s Art of Noise exhibition on view through August

articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s exhibition Phoenix Kingdoms, based on recent archaeological discoveries, is on view now through July 22. The exhibition highlights two kingdoms that flourished during China’s Bronze Age, the Zeng and Chu states, encompassing over 2,000 years of imperial history. Phoenix Kingdoms marries art and history while describing one of the most sophisticated, but forgotten, points of Chinese art and culture. The Zeng and Chu states reflect a shamanistic spirituality, rife with belief in human-animal communication, fascination with river and mountain deities, rituals filled with bell and drum music, and a proliferation of magical phoenix totems. “Drawing on the vibrant talent of its artisans and taking advantage of technological advances, the painting, sculpture, calligraphy, and music of this culturally fertile land were developed to an exceptionally high degree,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “It was in Chu that a distinctive religious and philosophical tradition evolved and matured into Daoism, a rival to Confucianism that emerged largely in northern China.” “We have no record that speaks of China’s unification from the perspective of the defeated Chu people,” said Jay Xu, Museum Director and CEO. “Because they were never told by the victor, the stories of Phoenix Kingdoms have remained hidden until now.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org. Museum patrons view artwork in the Phoenix Kingdoms exhibition at the San Francisco Asian Art Museum.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum opens Phoenix Kingdoms exhibit

articles.text: The Mendocino Music Festival, now in its 38th year, will feature a wide variety of music from classical to folk and opera to bluegrass. The music festival is held from July 13 through 27 at various locations throughout Mendocino. The festival was established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green. The festival features a blend of genres; evenings include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic town of Mendocino on the coast. Preview this year’s program at https://mendocinomusic.org. Tickets are on sale now.
articles.title: Mendocino Music Festival begins July 13

articles.text: Photo by San Francisco Symphony Four musicians take a bow following San Francisco Symphony’s performance of Schoenberg’s Erwartung. Paying a generous end-of-season dividend, the San Francisco Symphony provided the patrons with a triple bill: Orchestra, a colossal vocal drama and a modern dance troupe, all compressed into a single program. Additionally, the vocal part unleashed the most exciting operatic voice heard all year – Mary Elizabeth Williams acting out the Arnold Schoenberg monodrama Erwartung (Expectation) in passionate, semi-coherent detail. Music director Esa-Pekka Salonen carried off this budget-busting cornucopia of musical treats in the last month of his penultimate season, even as his musicians were leafletting the patrons on arrival about the deficit-plagued orchestra’s belt-tightening moves. These not only led to the announced departure of Salonen, but would also prevent such grand ventures in the future. Clearly, all caution was thrown to the winds with the brilliant modernist Peter Sellars stage-directing Erwartung for the volcanic opera singer Williams, complete with lighting effects and a stage space with a body bag probably containing the cadaver of her lover. She may have been responsible for the latter’s death in her wobbly state of consciousness. The overwrought singer acts out her torments, nebulous frustrations and fears over a searing half-hour span. Written more than a century ago, the halfhour work still packs a hysterical punch, bringing the whole Davies Hall audience to its knees in a unique way. For the most passionate of roles, Williams seems ideally suited, even though her name and her origins in Philadelphia and Iowa would suggest heading in other directions. As an actress, she projects all the dimensions of insecurity, angst, despair and semi-coherent madness, throwing herself about on stage, up and down. Vocally, her voice is a late-romantic volcano of fury, rendering the German poetry unerringly. Projections of English translations of the German were indispensable here. The orchestra was pushed upstage, with conductor Salonen half-turned to enable looking at both orchestra and theatrics. The performance was off the charts. This was a welcome broadening of the performance palette, as only the SFS can afford. It brought in other audiences by offering theater and dance, pairing the Schoenberg with the Alonzo King Ballet doing Ravel’s charming Mother Goose Suite of miniatures. King’s 11-member multi-racial modern ballet company never emulates Mother Goose’s Tom Thumb, Beauty and the Beast or Spinning Wheel. But King, a legend among Bay Area choreographers, finds the languid score a viable backdrop for his designs in movement, which blend ballet and toe shoes with modern dance via his robust, high-quality performers. Originally writing for concert settings, Ravel never introduced a fast-flying allegro segment showing off broader dimensions of dance. But no two works – composed at the same time before World War One – ever reflected better the sharply contrasting concurrent creativity in neighboring France and Germany. MUSIC NOTES Williams is a vocal rarity, singing roles in both the mezzo range (Erwartung) as well as soprano (Wagner’s Isolde). San Francisco Symphony staging both Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite with dancers of the Alonzo King Ballet, and the monodrama Erwartung, June 7-9. For SFS info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www.sfsymphony.org.
articles.title: French-German opposites at the Symphony

articles.text: Tickets still available for five performances San Francisco Opera’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas Mozart completed before his death, is being performed at the War Memorial Opera House now through June 30. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920s Berlin cabaret. Kim conducted The Magic Flute with several European companies as well as the Washington National Opera and will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation in nearly a decade. The cast includes New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, the opera company has scheduled nine performances: June 14 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (7:30 p.m.), 26 (7:30 p.m.), 30 (2 p.m.). To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. The Magic Flute will be performed by San Francisco Opera through June 30.
articles.title: SF Opera’s Magic Flute ends June 30

articles.text: SF Ballet’s “Starry Nights” takes place at Stanford’s outdoor Frost Amphitheatre. San Francisco Ballet’s fourth annual “Starry Nights” performances, presented in collaboration with the Stanford Live Arts Festival, will take place on Friday and Saturday, July 26-27 at at Frost Amphitheater. Starry Nights features Act II of SF Ballet Choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s Swan Lake, as well as the company premiere of Ben Stevenson’s Three Preludes, three mesmerizing ballets by the renowned choreographer Hans van Manen: Variations for Two Couples, Solo and the SF Ballet premiere of 5 Tango’s. Starry Nights includes two intermissions. Performances on both evenings begin at 7:30 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit www. sfballet.org. ®
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Starry Nights outdoor at Stanford July 26-27

articles.text: Beginning August 18, Filoli will offer live music with a rotating list of genres and performers at its Summer Stage outdoors. pages.text: Wednesday, June 12, 2024 17 French-German opposites at the Symphony Photo by San Francisco Symphony Four musicians take a bow following San Francisco Symphony’s performance of Schoenberg’s Erwartung. By Paul Hertelendy Paying a generous end-of-season dividend, the San Francisco Symphony provided the patrons with a triple bill: Orchestra, a colossal vocal drama and a modern dance troupe, all compressed into a single program. Additionally, the vocal part unleashed the most exciting operatic voice heard all year – Mary Elizabeth Williams acting out the Arnold Schoenberg monodrama Erwartung (Expectation) in passionate, semi-coherent detail. Music director Esa-Pekka Salonen carried off this budget-busting cornucopia of musical treats in the last month of his penultimate season, even as his musicians were leafletting the patrons on arrival about the deficit-plagued orchestra’s belt-tightening moves. These not only led to the announced departure of Salonen, but would also prevent such grand ventures in the future. Clearly, all caution was thrown to the winds with the brilliant modernist Peter Sellars stage-directing Erwartung for the volcanic opera singer Williams, complete with lighting effects and a stage space with a body bag probably containing the cadaver of her lover. She may have been responsible for the latter’s death in her wobbly state of consciousness. The overwrought singer acts out her torments, nebulous frustrations and fears over a searing half-hour span. Written more than a century ago, the halfhour work still packs a hysterical punch, bringing the whole Davies Hall audience to its knees in a unique way. For the most passionate of roles, Williams seems ideally suited, even though her name and her origins in Philadelphia and Iowa would suggest heading in other directions. As an actress, she projects all the dimensions of insecurity, angst, despair and semi-coherent madness, throwing herself about on stage, up and down. Vocally, her voice is a late-romantic volcano of fury, rendering the German poetry unerringly. Projections of English translations of the German were indispensable here. The orchestra was pushed upstage, with conductor Salonen half-turned to enable looking at both orchestra and theatrics. The performance was off the charts. This was a welcome broadening of the performance palette, as only the SFS can afford. It brought in other audiences by offering theater and dance, pairing the Schoenberg with the Alonzo King Ballet doing Ravel’s charming Mother Goose Suite of miniatures. King’s 11-member multi-racial modern ballet company never emulates Mother Goose’s Tom Thumb, Beauty and the Beast or Spinning Wheel. But King, a legend among Bay Area choreographers, finds the languid score a viable backdrop for his designs in movement, which blend ballet and toe shoes with modern dance via his robust, high-quality performers. Originally writing for concert settings, Ravel never introduced a fast-flying allegro segment showing off broader dimensions of dance. But no two works – composed at the same time before World War One – ever reflected better the sharply contrasting concurrent creativity in neighboring France and Germany. MUSIC NOTES Williams is a vocal rarity, singing roles in both the mezzo range (Erwartung) as well as soprano (Wagner’s Isolde). San Francisco Symphony staging both Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite with dancers of the Alonzo King Ballet, and the monodrama Erwartung, June 7-9. SF Opera’s Magic Flute ends June 30 Tickets still available for five performances By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Opera’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas Mozart completed before his death, is being performed at the War Memorial Opera House now through June 30. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920s Berlin cabaret. Kim conducted The Magic Flute with several European companies as well as the Washington National Opera and will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation in nearly a decade. The cast includes New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, the opera company has scheduled nine performances: June 14 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (7:30 p.m.), 26 (7:30 p.m.), 30 (2 p.m.). articles.text: Raphael Gold and Diluvian offer Strings & Serenades: A Summer Quartet Concert The community is invited to attend a special concert this summer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, June 29 when the Diluvian Quartet presents its Summer recital. The program will include Glazunov’s 5 Novelettes and Beethoven’s Quartet no.1 in F major, and other works by Price and Turina. Doors open at 6:45 p.m. and the program begins at 7 :00 p.m. with a dessert reception and drinks to follow. Free admission for children under 12. Tickets may be purchased at the door or in advance at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/915646050987. Diluvian comes from diluvium ‘deluge’ or ‘wash away’ – with reference to biblical rainfall and The Diluvian Quartet: Elizabeth Castro Greenberg, violin, Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello flooding. Diluvian musicians first met and played together during the historic rains of October 2021 when “an atmospheric river soaked the Bay Area with incredible amounts of rainfall… making it one of the biggest storms on record.” which Robbins described as a “miniature masterpiece.” He also pointed out that Beethoven took the opportunity to display his unique sense of humor. All of the best aspects of outstanding piano playing were on display. What was amazing was that the interpretation and style of Beethoven were completely different from the baroque style of Scarlatti. It was as if a different pianist had seated himself at the piano. The first and third movements of the Beethoven Sonata displayed Beethoven’s unique sense of humor. The slow movement brought tears to my eyes. I don’t think that I have ever heard a pianist play with such beauty of tone and such a seamless legato touch. The third section marked another complete change of mood. We were treated to ”Dumka” by Tchaikovsky. Once again, Gerald Robbins told us some important things about Tchaikovsky and his unique composition. Psychologically, Tchaikovsky had a bipolar personality. He used this to best advantage by drawing a musical picture of small-town Russian life. Life in a small Russian village is also bipolar. The composer was able to capture this ethos and the curiosity of Russian temperament to perfection. The fourth part of the program featured yet another change of temperament and style. We moved ahead musically to the French impressionistic period. Three of Debussy’s “Estompes” painted musical pictures which became the artistic impressionism as exemplified by famous impressionistic painters. Yet again, the musical personality changed. We found ourselves in the artistic studio of Monet or Manet… surrounded by canvassed impressionism. Perhaps by listening to interpretation such as this, the listener becomes the impressionistic artwork itself. As the concert progressed, I began to think that Gerald Robbins’ tone is quite like the tone of Arthur Rubinstein. Continuing the analogy, we were listening to a ruby, rich in color and having a sparkling finish. Gerald Robbins lets the music speak for itself. Whether you listen to the music with your eyes open or closed, you are transported to a very special musical world. Music lovers will have a chance to hear the artistry of Gerald Robbins in concert in our Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, June 15, at 7:30 p.m. Save some money by ordering tickets at: BPT.ME/6326316.

articles.text: Gerald Robbins was one of the most outstanding pianists of my youth. Many famous musicians thought the same. Talent like this is usually called prodigious. From the age of 18 he was the pianist to Jascha Heifetz, William Primrose and Gregor Piatigorsky. These three musicians were simply the most famous violinist, violist and cellist of their time and perhaps of all time. Not long after this, Gerry became pianist to almost any famous musician you can name. He is in town for about a week. The first concert was a birthday concert for his older sister at her retirement home. The rest of us will have the opportunity to hear him this Saturday evening in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7:30 p.m. It was my pleasure to hear him last week, and I look forward to hearing him in Piedmont. Here is a preview of what to expect: Gerald Robbins is a complete musician. By this, I mean that he is an outstanding pianist, as well as an accurate historian. His programs are a complete overview of the piano repertory. Pianists of the past always presented programs this way. Sadly, modern pianists have lost their way. They seem to like boring monochromatic programs. To make up for this, they have adopted ostentatious mannerisms rather than profound musicianship. Robbins began his program with a spoken introduction which was to the point and most gracious. The musical program began with three sonatas by Scarlatti. Seating himself at the piano, Robbins plays without muss or fuss. ence is put in the proper mood immediately. From the first salvo, we were assured that the piano knows how to sing. Another thing that was obvious is that the piano can play in many different registers and every register has a different volume and articulation. All of these things were accomplished without any extraneous movements. Every move is for the music. The result is beauty of tone and elegance. Next came a complete change of pace with a Beethoven Sonata, Two enthusiastic listeners congratulate Gerald Robbins (center) after a recent concert: Debbie Dare (left), board member of Piedmont Center for the Arts, and graphic artist and composer David Klein.
articles.title: The beauty of tone and elegance of pianist Gerald Robbins

articles.text: To suggest that Chloe is simply an erotic thriller is to diminish what is an intriguing film. It’s a character study and an examination of a woman’s attempt to bridge what seems an insurmountable distance between herself and her husband. At its center, this is a film not about seduction but about abiding loneliness. It is perhaps best captured by stark scenes where Catherine (Julianne Moore), a successful gynecologist in Toronto, stands looking through windows at the street below at her husband as he sits in his den working on his computer and at her patients in the waiting room. She is suffused with a feeling of disconnection, as if all she has known is now inaccessible and emotionally elusive. She has grown older. She feels less desirable. Her viewpoint has grown clinical. She and her husband, David (Liam Neeson), a professor of music, married some 20 years, have lost contact. She observes him being flirtatious with his students and with other women and suspects that he is having an affair. What she does at this moment, at this intersection in her life, is profoundly human and understandable, yet also immensely destructive. She hires a young prostitute, Chloe (Amanda Seyfried), to test her husband’s fidelity and sets in motion a series of events, in which she insists that Chloe report back the details of her time with David. Unexpectedly, Catherine finds herself in the position of a voyeur, more comfortable with hearing about and imagining the intimacy shared by Chloe and David than searching for a path toward intimacy herself. But then isn’t her voyeurism the handmaiden to pornography (however soft)? Ultimately she finds nothing satisfyingly personal about hearing about David and Chole, and yet she cannot stop herself. She might have hired a private detective, but then perhaps it’s not truth that she is looking for but something else, a fact that Chloe divines from the outset. It’s an interesting aspect of the Amanda Seyfried and Julianne Moore in Chloe

articles.text: Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill in Darkest Hour Gary Oldman is an essentially unrecognized treasure who represents perfection in his craft, a craft that requires the capacity to inhabit completely another persona. It is truly a remarkable ability. That gift reflects a certain genius. It often requires a disguise, studied mannerisms, facial tics as well as an intimate understanding of who/what one is portraying. And it is that moment when watching Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill that we realize that we are watching an actor in a role like no other. We also quickly come to understand that it is at this moment in the history of England, at the outset of WWII, which is like no other. England had sent the very core of its fighting force (some 300,000) to France to aid in its defense. The German juggernaut has swept across Europe, invading country after country, each falling, one after the other, like so many dominoes. This gesture of assistance to the French resulted in England’s army being pushed by the Nazis and their phalanx of panzers to Dunkirk, the English Chanel acting as a barrier, trapping the soldiers while the German Wehrmacht drew ever closer as their air force strafed the beaches. England was confronted with losing its entire army, leaving the island defenseless to what most assumed would be an imminent invasion. Churchill, newly named Prime Minister, was under immense pressure from members of his own party and his war cabinet who argued strenuously that England should sue for peace and hope that Hitler’s terms would leave them a shred of independence. Churchill deeply disagreed with this position and instinctively wanted to take what he knew would be a high risk/ high reward stand of resistance while knowing that the odds were against England. Oldman conveys beautifully and completely a man, who while he wavers, also struggles with his own powerful inclination to never yield. That steely determination is conveyed by a profound talent. He must convince the audience that he is deeply conflicted while consumed by certainty. Oldman’s portrayal is a stunning display of consummate acting. The Darkest Hour, reduced to its essence, is a deep character study of one man facing a moment that will impact not just him but all of history. Some may find the film “slow.” For others, it may seem a bit tedious (even the lighting of the film is dark to obscure). But, it is a film that’s about a crossroads. Dunkirk has since stood as an eloquent symbol, testimony to England’s unyielding stand against Fascism. And Churchill knew that to negotiate with Hitler would signal the end of the island’s autonomy. What he could not foresee was that his nation, and eventually its allies, would, at great cost in lives and effort, be judged heroic. The Darkest Hour. Directed by Joe Wright. Starring Gary Oldman, Kristi Scott, Ben Mendelsohn. 2 hrs., 5 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018.
articles.title: The Darkest Hour – the survival of England in WWII

articles.text: Mission Impossible: Dead Reckoning Part One is the seventh installment of this resilient franchise starring Tom Cruise as Ethan Hunt and his familiar IMF team consisting of Lither Stockwell (Ving Rhames), Benji Dunn (Simon Pegg) and the returning Isla Faust (Rebecca Ferguson). Their mission, should they choose to accept it, is to find a key that will disable an artificial intelligence weapon (referred to as the Entity), capable of destroying all life on the planet. The urgency is, of course, palpable. How this A.I. threat came into existence and who controls it is explained at the outset through long expository meetings between the IMF team. Even if you listen intently, trying to fully grasp the plot, well, it’s a challenge. But then, these frantic, frenetic missions are not about the narrative; rather, what is breathtakingly compelling are the extraordinary risks (stunts) that the M.I. Force takes in order to accomplish their mission, and each iteration proves to be supremely generous in such moments. For example, Ethan, riding a motorcycle drives off a cliff, falling into a 4,000-foot canyon. He is wearing, of course, a parachute. His objective is to land on a runaway train (was it the Orient Express?) racing out of control. Why not simply buy a ticket and board at the station? Well, that’s not entirely clear. But no matter. This stunt is one not to be missed. It’s pure wonder. As is a harrowing ride on the crowded Rome streets in a small yellow Fiat 500 with the Italian police giving chase close behind. This is all while Ethan is handcuffed to the newcomer, the lovely pickpocket (don’t ask) Grace (Haley Atwell). They take turns trying to drive, soon discovering they are also being pursued by what the audience learns later is the White Widow driving a huge, ominous black Hummer which she uses to destroy a remarkable amount of curb-side property while navigating the crowded streets. Outdoor café? Demolished, with people scattering for their lives. Grace, looking back, asks, “Who isn’t chasing us?” And there are more adrenalin-inducing set pieces. Not to forget the runaway train, which Ethan, of course, does land on. The train, absent the disposed of engineers, is approaching a bridge spanning a river far below, where dynamite has been planted at strategic points along its undergirding. The ending is spectacular, astonishing. Forget the plot, ignore the train’s urgent warning whistle. Just enjoy every moment of what is an overthe-top signature Mission Impossible story. The word on the street is that Part Two will arrive next summer. Perhaps. Maybe. The Writers’ strike slowed deadlines just a bit. Lastly, keep in mind that Cruise lobbies to do some of his running, leaping stunt work himself. Yes, he’s 61. When I see him do some of this remarkable stuff, I’m reminded of the movie where, in a diner, a woman watching Meg Ryan simulate an orgasm, says to the waitress, “I’ll have what she’s having.” Ditto, Tom Cruise. Mission Impossible: Dead Reckoning Part One. Directed by Christopher McQuarie. Starring Tom Cruise, Hayley Atwell, Ving Rhanes, Simon Pegg, Rebecca Ferguson. 2 hrs., 43 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2023. Streaming on VUDU/prime/Paramont+. Tom Cruise and Hayley Atwell in Mission: Impossible - Dead Reckoning Part One
