articles.text: Gerald Robbins, a distinguished international soloist, will perform a piano recital at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, June 15 at 7:30 p.m. Critically acclaimed for his recording artistry, a distinguished chamber musician, and an accomplished conductor, he is the winner of multiple major international awards and competitions. Artist Bio Pianist Gerald Robbins has distinguished himself internationally as a soloist, having performed throughout the world in virtually every major music center, including New York, London, Paris, Amsterdam, Bonn, Munich, Athens, Frankfurt, Belgrade, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Tel-Aviv, Jerusalem, and Tokyo. He has appeared with the London Philharmonic, Royal Philharmonic, BBC Symphony, London Mozart Players, Los Angeles Philharmonic, Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra, Moscow Philharmonic, and New York Virtuosi Chamber Orchestra, among many others, under such conductors as Sir Neville Marriner, Edouard van Remoortel, Harry Blech, Okko Kamu, Jorge Mester, Lawrence Foster, Ezra Rachlin, Kenneth Klein, Louis Frémaux, and Zubin Mehta. A champion of neglected Romantic repertoire, Gerald Robbins has received critical acclaim for his solo recordings for the London-Decca, Orion, and Genesis labels, as well as his world premiere recordings of concerti by Litolff and Reinecke, performed with the Monte Carlo Opera Pianist Gerald Robbins Orchestra conducted by Edouard van Remoortel, and re-released on CD for Genesis Records. Praising his “first-class, bravura performance” and “keyboard voice of true eloquence,” critics wrote that “Gerald Robbins’ technical prowess is phenomenal.” Mr. Robbins recorded the Leonard Bernstein and John Corigliano Sonatas for Violin and Piano with Glenn Dicterow and the Mendelssohn Complete Works for Cello and Piano with cellist James Kreger. Other recordings include a solo performance of Dvořák’s “Poetic Tone Pictures” and Goetz’s Complete Chamber Music for Piano and Strings; a collaboration with conductor Kenneth Klein and the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra of the Schumann Piano Concerto; a re-release on CD of piano works by Sjögren and Kjerulf; and an acclaimed CD of the Strauss and Turina Piano Quartets performed by the Lyric Piano Quartet. Mr. Robbins has also distinguished himself as a chamber musician. Whilst living in London, he was in close collaboration with Nathan Milstein, Mayumi Fujikawa, Richard Markson, Larry Adler, and Kyung-Wha Chung. He has worked closely with New York Philharmonic concertmaster Glenn Dicterow, co-founding the Lyric Piano Quartet, with which he regularly records and tours. He has also appeared as a frequent guest artist with solo members of the New York Philharmonic at Avery Fisher Hall, Weill Recital Hall at Carnegie Hall, and Merkin Hall. Also an accomplished conductor, Mr. Robbins co-founded with Kenneth Klein the Westside Symphony Orchestra of Los Angeles, presently called the Beverly Hills Symphony, and is a co-founder of the London Concertante, an ensemble that specializes in 18th and early 19th-century concerto repertoire. The recipient of important prizes in major international competitions such as the Van Cliburn and Tchaikovsky International Competitions, he received his Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees from the University of Southern California, where he assisted in the string master classes of Jascha Heifetz, William Primrose, and Gregor Piatigorsky. Mr. Robbins is a member of the chamber music faculty of Manhattan School of Music and Artist-in-Residence with the Lyric Piano Quartet at the Aaron Copland School of Music at Queens College, CUNY. He has developed a highly successful chamber music concert series at Queens College and is also affiliated with the Hoff-Barthelson School of Music in Westchester.

articles.text: The Glass Alliance of Northern California (GLANC) is pleased to present the Nor Cal Glass Festival, an inaugural exhibition of glass art in collaboration with Piedmont Center for the Arts. The festival will take place on Saturday and Sunday, June 22-23, from 10 am to 5 pm each day. Fifteen artists from northern California are featured in the gallery spaces at the Center. The artIncalmo Bowl Mosaic Pattern Cherry and Gold – Bruce Pizzichillo Pate de verre (glass) vessel – Andrea Ciak Chiisana Set – Christine Byrne works are executed using a broad range of methods for working with glass including blown, kiln fired, cold- and flame-worked techniques. pages.text: Wednesday, June 5, 2024 19 Pianist Gerald Robbins in concert June 15 at PCA Gerald Robbins, a distinguished international soloist, will perform a piano recital at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, June 15 at 7:30 p.m. Critically acclaimed for his recording artistry, a distinguished chamber musician, and an accomplished conductor, he is the winner of multiple major international awards and competitions. Artist Bio Pianist Gerald Robbins has distinguished himself internationally as a soloist, having performed throughout the world in virtually every major music center, including New York, London, Paris, Amsterdam, Bonn, Munich, Athens, Frankfurt, Belgrade, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Tel-Aviv, Jerusalem, and Tokyo. He has appeared with the London Philharmonic, Royal Philharmonic, BBC Symphony, London Mozart Players, Los Angeles Philharmonic, Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra, Moscow Philharmonic, and New York Virtuosi Chamber Orchestra, among many others, under such conductors as Sir Neville Marriner, Edouard van Remoortel, Harry Blech, Okko Kamu, Jorge Mester, Lawrence Foster, Ezra Rachlin, Kenneth Klein, Louis Frémaux, and Zubin Mehta. A champion of neglected Romantic repertoire, Gerald Robbins has received critical acclaim for his solo recordings for the London-Decca, Orion, and Genesis labels, as well as his world premiere recordings of concerti by Litolff and Reinecke, performed with the Monte Carlo Opera Pianist Gerald Robbins Orchestra conducted by Edouard van Remoortel, and re-released on CD for Genesis Records. Praising his “first-class, bravura performance” and “keyboard voice of true eloquence,” critics wrote that “Gerald Robbins’ technical prowess is phenomenal.” Mr. Robbins recorded the Leonard Bernstein and John Corigliano Sonatas for Violin and Piano with Glenn Dicterow and the Mendelssohn Complete Works for Cello and Piano with cellist James Kreger. Other recordings include a solo performance of Dvořák’s “Poetic Tone Pictures” and Goetz’s Complete Chamber Music for Piano and Strings; a collaboration with conductor Kenneth Klein and the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra of the Schumann Piano Concerto; a re-release on CD of piano works by Sjögren and Kjerulf; and an acclaimed CD of the Strauss and Turina Piano Quartets performed by the Lyric Piano Quartet. Mr. Robbins has also distinguished himself as a chamber musician. Whilst living in London, he was in close collaboration with Nathan Milstein, Mayumi Fujikawa, Richard Markson, Larry Adler, and Kyung-Wha Chung. He has worked closely with New York Philharmonic concertmaster Glenn Dicterow, co-founding the Lyric Piano Quartet, with which he regularly records and tours. He has also appeared as a frequent guest artist with solo members of the New York Philharmonic at Avery Fisher Hall, Weill Recital Hall at Carnegie Hall, and Merkin Hall. Also an accomplished conductor, Mr. Robbins co-founded with Kenneth Klein the Westside Symphony Orchestra of Los Angeles, presently called the Beverly Hills Symphony, and is a co-founder of the London Concertante, an ensemble that specializes in 18th and early 19th-century concerto repertoire. The recipient of important prizes in major international competitions such as the Van Cliburn and Tchaikovsky International Competitions, he received his Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees from the University of Southern California, where he assisted in the string master classes of Jascha Heifetz, William Primrose, and Gregor Piatigorsky. Mr. Robbins is a member of the chamber music faculty of Manhattan School of Music and Artist-in-Residence with the Lyric Piano Quartet at the Aaron Copland School of Music at Queens College, CUNY. He has developed a highly successful chamber music concert series at Queens College and is also affiliated with the Hoff-Barthelson School of Music in Westchester. articles.text: If time is a thin reed – or experienced as a Mobius strip allowing a traveler to leap forward and backward – think of the possibilities. Actually, Hollywood and literature have gone to this well often and sometimes with compelling results. Back to the Future comes to mind. The Time Traveler’s Wife takes all the inherent problems of time travel and embeds them in a tender, fragile love story. All things considered, it succeeds nicely. Based on Audrey Niffenegger’s bestseller, the film tells the story of Henry (Eric Bana) who, since boyhood, has against his will traveled in time, both into the past and into the future. All that he leaves behind is his clothing, arriving at his unknown destination naked. Time travel is one of the most difficult and interesting tropes in film and literature. From the outset the audience must suspend its disbelief and all but lend a hand filling in any illogical holes. Actually, The Time Traveler’s Wife manages quite well to deal with the multiple time traveling surprises without falling into the trap of being nonsensical. Henry’s unexpected traveling is never presented as a stunning achievement; rather, it is viewed as something that is deeply problematic for Henry and his new wife, Clare (Rachel McAdams). They are deeply in love (Clare has loved Henry since she was Eric Bana and Rachel McAdams in The Time Traveler’s Wife very young) and at the most inopportune moments, some scary to be sure, without warning Henry vanishes just moments before they are to be married. He returns as an older version of his younger self (you see the problem). But these moments are intriguing, not off-putting. Every romantic story – Titanic, Ghost Story, Love Story, Romeo and Juliet – has embedded in it the possibility of a tragic outcome. Hence, the filmmakers must search for the sweet spot, that elusive geography where the couple fashions a bond so strong that the audience invests in their relationship as well. Absent that connection, the film will merely seem a piece of shallow fiction or science fiction. With the sweet spot found, the film transcends and becomes deeply human. Despite a few jar ring moments, The Time Traveler’s Wife achieves that emotional connection. The Niffenegger book would be all but impossible to fully adapt. But director Robert Schwentke makes a fine effort and, with the fine performances of Bana and McAdams, manages to find the sweet spot. The Time Traveler’s Wife. Directed by Robert Schwentke. Starring Eric Bana, Rachel McAdams, Ron Livingston and Arliss Howard. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/prime/ apple tv.

articles.text: Solitary Man is an exceptional film. It is a not-always-pleasant snapshot of a deeply flawed 60-year-old man, Ben Kalmen (Michael Douglas), once famous and now infamous, who realizes to his chagrin and surprise that the center of his life will no longer hold. He’s charming and slippery and seemingly incapable of making choices that don’t have serious blowback. Once an affluent denizen of Manhattan, respected as a businessman, he has firmly hit the wall and his life is now imploding in slow motion. He cheated on his wife, Nancy (Susan Sarandon), they’re now divorced, he became a compulsive womanizer and he refuses to fully accept that the deeply lined face that peers back at him every morning in the mirror (after he takes his baby aspirin) is that of a grandfather, absent most, if not all, of the vestiges of his youth. Time has changed him externally. The internecine warfare he is experiencing is now all internal. Is the film dark? Yes, but in a good way. An interesting way. For though Ben has done just about everything in his power to isolate himself from those who care about him, this is a film about relationships. He is surrounded by people who still care about him, those who still remember the man who was and refuse to fully accept the man he has become: dissolute and self-indulgent and even a bit desperate. It is those people, meaning the actors who portray them, along with an exceptional performance by Douglas who lift this film into a different realm, from one potentially dreary, a tedious unravelMichael Douglas and Susan Sarandon in Solitary Man Advance tickets ($15/$35) at tix.com/ticket-sales/leftcoastensemble/5791/event/1344399 Tickets at the door will be slightly more ($18/student, $38/general)

articles.text: A scene from How to Train Your Dragon Kids are going to love How to Train Your Dragon. It’s one nifty movie. Let’s start not at the beginning but with an inspired scene: a young Viking named Hiccup, seated securely on the back of Toothless, an ebony dragon, soars through the clouds in a prolonged flight that is breathtaking The colors are lush and gorgeous, the sky a startlingly blue in contrast to the enormous cumulus clouds. Hiccup, eyes wide, is exhilarated – but terrified. This scene, like so many in this film, is testimony to the depth and breadth of the imagination of the filmmakers, and graphically illustrates how stateof-the-art animation, combined with the technology of 3-D, has made quantum strides in the last several years. Neither technology nor 3-D can save a film if the story lacks serious mojo. The good news is that How to Train Your Dragon has all the right stuff, It’s a sweet if recognizable story that will resonate with kids ages, say, nine and above. And to a person the characters are perfect. Briefly, there’s young Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), the son of Stoick the Vast (Gerard Butler), who lives on a small island, Berk, off the coast of Scotland. For 300 years dragons have been attacking their village, making off with their livestock. The Vikings have fought back and along the way developed an abiding hatred for and fear of dragons. Hiccup, a newbie adolescent, rebelling against his chieftain father and his community, resists learning to fight dragons. Stoic is both frustrated and angry with his son. Clearly Hiccup, lean in stature (the Vikings are all more than hefty), and not inclined to fight back when the dragons attack, is not cut out to be a dragon slayer. This becomes all too clear when, wandering in the forest, he comes across a fallen dragon, Toothless. Instead of killing the dragon he befriends him. And that budding friendship sets the story in motion. Hiccup not only helps Toothless regain his ability to fly (he designs and then makes him a prosthetic tail), but, with the assistance of Astrid (America Ferrera), a wonderful tween-teentomboy, they begin to work out a plan that will change the attitudes of the village toward dragons. Hiccup soon discovers that he and Astrid are not alone. With the help of his friends – Tuffnut, Fishlegs, Snotlout – they transform the future of Beck. What is also so much fun is that the dragons are marvelous and with captivating names – Hideous Zippleback, Monstrous Nightmare and the uber-dragon, Night Fog. As well, all the kids speak in hip teen vernacular (“Vikings have stubbornness issues”), absent the brogue of his father and Gobber the Belch, and they dress like they buy their clothes from the Gap’s Viking annex, to include Ugg boots. Very cool. Astrid has a nifty hairstyle, leggings, short skirt and tons of ‘tude. They’re a goofy but delightful group and youngsters will identify with them and their situation. So, if the gremlins are hanging out this weekend complaining there is nothing to do, sit them down to see How to Train Your Dragon. They will enjoy themselves… and possibly will thank you. How to Train Your Dragon. Animated. Directed by Dean DeBois and Chris Sanders. With voices of Gerard Butler, Jay Baruchel, America Ferrera, and Craig Ferguson. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG. Released in 2010. Streaming on VUDU/prime/ apple tv.

articles.text: The Cat Returns, directed by Hiroyuki Murita in his only feature for Studio Ghibli, is based on a manga story written by Aoi Hiragi. The narrative has at its center Haru (Anne Hathaway), a shy, insecure Tokyo schoolgirl who has a repressed affinity for cats (she can talk to them). One day, when she is out and about, she saves a cat from being run over by a truck. As it turns out, the cat, called Lune (Andrew Bevis), is the son of the Cat King (Tim Curry). Wanting to reward Haru’s heroism, the King insists that she come to the Cat Kingdom and there he creates a plan to have Haru marry Lune. But in order for this to take place, Haru must begin her transformation into a cat. Soon Haru grows ears, whiskers and a tail. Distressed by what is happening, she realizes that she must escape the Cat Kingdom before it is too late and she will never be able to return to her human world. It’s at this point in the story that, The Cat Returns drops down an Alice in Wonderland rabbit hole and becomes a mix of characters and silly plans all focused on Haru finding a portal that will return her to her previous life. She hears a soft feminine voice telling her to find a chunky cat named Muta (Peter Boyle). Muta leads her to the Baron (Gary Elwes), a statuette brought to life with the help of Toto (Elliot Gould), a stone raven. And so on. They plan and connive to rescue Haru, all while trying to avoid the King. When Lune discovers Haru’s wish to escape, he reveals he wants to marry another, Yuki (Judy Greer), a servant working in the kingdom. I would judge that The Cat Returns is best suited for young viewers. Unlike the work produced by Studio Ghibli, its story is slight, definitely cartoony, and just hectic fun. However, the quality of the animation, as always, is superb with a strong color palette with a cast of characters that will engage. The Cat Returns. Directed by Hiroyuki Murita. Animé by Studio Ghibili. With the voices of Anne Hathaway, Gary Elwes, Peter Boyle and Elliot Gould. 1 hr, 15 min. Rated G. Released 2019. Streaming on Fandango/ prime/MAX. articles.text: lated a 401(k), IRA and other investment accounts, along with insurance policies and physical properties. articles.text: Summer harvest season is just around the corner. Here are a few ways I keep my crops protected from bugs, slugs, squirrels, and rodents with pest control methods that work in harmony with nature. The most beautiful way to keep your garden pest-free is to grow companion plants to attract beneficial insects. Flowers like marigolds and nasturtium are not only edible and beautiful, they also attract beneficial ladybugs, lacewings, and hoverflies that will eat destructive bugs. In a similar fashion, crops in the allium family, such as garlic and onions, are also wonderful natural deterrents, warding off pests with their pungent smell. I like to plant a mixture of flowers and alliums in my vegetable garden to bring in the good bugs and keep out the bad bugs. For deliciously sweet fruit, like strawberries, I pull out my secret garden bags. They are just breathable, fabric gift bags, but they have been a game changer for my harvests. When I see unripe, green strawberries emerge, I place them in a bag, cinch it closed, and wait for them to ripen. No bugs can crawl in and no rodents can nibble on the fruit. When they’re finally ripe I open the bag and pull out perfect berries for my family to enjoy. When it comes to unruly slugs, I always save my eggshells, dry them out, and crumble them into small pieces. I’ll sprinkle these in the garden around leafy greens like kale, lettuce, and broccoli. To a slug, these eggshells are like walking on glass. It stops them from getting to your crops so you can harvest delicious, uneaten leaves. A simple shake of red chili Michelle Docter and Rita wrap strawberries in fabric bags as a pest prevention measure. flakes around my plants stops pesky rodents in the garden. Rats have a strong sense of smell so the hot pepper flakes can be too spicy for them to handle. It’s an easy and fun preventative method that has some success. If all else fails, get yourself a guardian of the garden dog, like Rita, to chase off the squirrels for good. articles.text: Photos by Will Adams There is a curious blend of influences behind the Ranch style. Self-taught architect Clifford May is credited as the originator which first appeared in southern California in the 1930’s. Strolling through Piedmont, walkers come across a fair number of Ranch style homes. This is no surprise. During the 1950s, even though best suited for the mild weather of places like California, this was by far the most popular style of new homes being constructed throughout the entire country. Although influenced to some degree by European architectural traditions, it is considered a uniquely American residential style attributed to the early work of architects Clifford May in southern California and William Wurster, the eponym of Wurster Hall at UC Berkeley. There were a number of reasons for the popularity. Primary was the informality of the architectural character. Simple building forms and detailing are its trademark, along with the resulting modest and affordable construction costs. Perhaps more importantly, the big change of open floor plans instead of divided rooms was a complete departure from virtually all traditional styles. This encouraged and suited the casual living of the era – easy livability was more important than impressive exteriors. A large part of the attraction also was the development of a very close connection between indoor and outdoor spaces. Slab on grade construction (as opposed to the traditional raised houses with crawl spaces) brought the interior rooms to the same level as the exterior patios, yards and terraces. Large picture windows and sliding glass doors joined, rather than separated exterior spaces from interior. This essentially enlarged the perceived and practical livable area of the house and also changed the focus of homes from the front to the backyard, a trend that continues to this day. Characterized by long, horizontal, one story construction (like a western working ranch building), this style “spreads out” the building and generally takes more lot area than multistoried buildings. As a result, it is less suited to more dense urban cities and found its place in more rural areas and suburban tract developments. And since the suburbs required cars, Ranch homes Long, low slopped hipped roofs on one-story buildings result in the characteristic horizontal feel of the Ranch style as illustrated in these nice Piedmont homes. The divided lights of windows here suggest a Craftsman influence as well.

articles.text: Mark Hsia is the Salutatorian of Piedmont High School’s Class of 2024. I would like to open with a quote from Homer – Homer Simpson. Homer Simpson once said, “no matter how good you are at something, there’s always about a million people better than you,” and Homer’s words carry some weight. It often feels like we’re overshadowed by the greatness of others, background characters in an episode of the Simpsons. Way back in 9th grade English, we all had to conduct an interview with a professional as part of our I-Search. It was scary. At first I didn’t even know who to talk to. There were so many people out there, different divisions of research in my topic, and then more subdivisions within those divisions. I felt like Bart Simpson when he accidentally ended up in a school for child prodigies. Every other person seemed to know so much more than me. After hearing Homer’s words, Bart replied, “Gotcha... can’t win, don’t try.” But my experience over the past four years has taught me otherwise because you can win, so you should try. Somewhere out there there’s at least one thing that you can win. There is something out there, whether you found it or not, that a million people will look up to you and think “that person’s the one.” A million people and a million spots, you just have to find your own. Easier said than done. It can be hard, but when you stand overshadowed by others, it’s even harder to see your way. And when you try to follow that person that you see as one in a million – you take the same classes and join the same clubs – then you’re still walking in shadow. The world outside of the shadows is full of opportunity. When Homer leaves his spiritless work at the nuclear power plant, and instead decides to follow his passions and desires by finding jobs as an astronaut, boxer, and food critic, it helps him discover what he really wants in life: for him, donuts, but it will be different for everyone. School forced me to step into the unknown for my I-Search. I cold called a researcher at MIT as my first interview attempt – a step towards an opportunity waiting in the untrodden path. To my surprise, he gladly accepted my interview request, although at age 15 I definitely felt thrown in the deep end, using words I barely understood. But I continued, and as time went on I felt more comfortable. After the interview, I digested his complex words into simple terms that another high school freshman could understand, intertwining his ideas with other aspects of my research. And now, I think it would be a safe bet to say that I know more about electrochemical carbon capture than at least a million people out there. Although for me, the researcher was the one in a million, unlike the complex scientific papers and research, I understood it in a way that other kids could understand as well, and so, I too became the one in a million among my peers. Through journalism, I’ve been able to see the others who’ve also started to find their ways. At the end of every semester of TPH, everyone in the class has to write a personality profile, an article about someone we think stands out. As we help each other brainstorm, we always end up with way more people than we can write about. So many of you have already gone out to find your ones in a million, whether that’s repairing semiconductors or using art to raise awareness and change the community. For those who’ve found your one in a million, we look to you as we try to find our own. Together, as a school, we are already one in a million, with our traditions like bird calling, and even things as small as saying thank you to teachers as we leave every class. This small gesture is something I’ve appreciated every day in my four years here. So as I leave PHS for the last time, I’d like to say, on behalf of the class of 2024, thank you. Thank you to all of our wonderful teachers and staff; each one of you has truly made a difference in our lives. Thank you to all the parents and other people who’ve supported us on our journeys and sacrificed to see us succeed. And finally, thank you to my fellow classmates who’ve persevered and made it here with me today. Thank you.

Students, already seated alphabetically, rose as a row and waited mercilessly for their names to be called, one by one, with high school soon to be in the rear-view mirror. One by one, to the cheers of the crowd and their colleagues, the 181 PHS students and 11 MHS students walked from Vice Principal Joseph Marik toward the podium, to trade a handshake for a diploma from Principal Goswami. Goswami then formally presented to the graduates to the audience. After a spirited cheer, students ran to the far side of the field with diploma, and cap in hand, to huddle as a class one last time. With a vigorous chant they tossed their caps skyward in a traditional jubilant release, one that celebrated not only their last four years of education but their first 18 years of life. articles.text: After losing nearly 30 trees in Dracena Park last year due to drought, the City of Piedmont is partnering with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) to plant trees in Dracena Park and further preserve the city’s urban forest. “Removing 30 trees from one park is a fairly big impact,” said Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent. “Especially in Dracena. It’s one of our parks that’s a bit more rustic and a little less developed.” The trees, which were a mix of cedars, firs, conifers, sequoias, cypresses and pines, were removed by the Public Works department in the winter of 2023. “It became apparent they were not going to recover,” said Kent. The trees were cut down and their stumps were left in place. The PBF is currently working with the City to raise funds for this project as part of their recently begun spring campaign, which this year is chiefly focused on reforestation efforts within Piedmont. The loss of the trees was not unexpected. “They were trees that we’ve had on the watch list for a number of years,” said Kent. “I think the stituation we saw was at the end of the drought years, and they just didn’t recover.” Despite the loss, Kent is optimistic that the replanting project could have a positive effect on Dracena. Instead of replanting the trees on a one-for-one basis, the City is holistically rethinking its planting strategy. “We’re not looking at a simple one-for-one tree replacement in one area, but maybe a situation where we’re replacing it with a specimen tree, and then an understory flower, a few more trees in the surrounding area, native shrubs on the ground [...] we’re hoping not just to replant trees, but to establish entire plant communities.” The City is also using projects like these to plan for the future of Piedmont’s urban forests by using California native plants that are used to warmer climates. “The focus on replanting will use climate-adaptive trees because these trees live for 50 years. So, we’re trying to plant trees that will thrive in a warmer climate, which is what all our best scientists say will happen in the next 50 years.” For more information about donating to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation or supporting your local parks, contact them via email at pbf.piedmont@ gmail.com. articles.text: Unknown person takes a hammer to Storyteller Bridge On Saturday, May 25, at 7:59 a.m., the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) reported signs of new damage to Storyteller Bridge in Dracena Park. According to police, the damage was likely caused by a hammer or other device that struck the horizontal hand railings of the bridge 19 times, chipping pieces out of the bridge with each swing. This is not the first time this has happened, with acts of vandalism to Storyteller Bridge dating back as far as three years, according to the Public Works Department. Currently, the bridge’s hand railings have a total of 69 damage marks. “I would say this is the third or fourth event of this type,” said Nancy Kent, Parks and Projects Manager with the City of Piedmont. “It’s relatively random. We don’t know when it’s going to occur.” According to Kent, when the first instances of vandalism occurred approximately three years ago, damage marks were found chopped into the vertical posts on the bridge. The Public Works Department installed metal caps on the vertical posts of the bridge to prevent further vandalism. “It’s just unfortunate because it is changing the appearance of the railing,” she lamented. Despite the history of vandalism at Storyteller Bridge, acts of vandalism can be notoriously hard to catch in the act. “We’ve increased our presence in the parks with the full-time Community Service Officers, but even with our small number of parks and one person, you’re not always going to be in the right place, necessarily at the right time,” explained Police Captain Chris Monahan. “We are aware of the damage, and we are working to create a greater presence in all of our parks with our new fulltime CSOs. So, we now have two full-time CSOs whose responsibilities include foot patrol in the parks. Hopefully, that will be a greater deterrent to vandalism activity.” Captain Monahan encouraged community members to report acts of vandalism. “When in doubt, make the call,” he advised. Public Works Director Daniel Staff photos 19 new damage marks were added to the Storyteller Bridge on Saturday, May 25, for a new total of 69 marks. Gonzales said that repairs for the bridge’s hand railing are being planned, although the department is still assessing its options when it comes to repair methods that preserve the unique style of the bridge. “We want to put something in that’s more resilient and resistant to damage, but we also want it be aesthetically appropriate for the bridge,” said Gonzales. “This stuff happens everywhere. I think what makes Piedmont unique, and perhaps exceptional, is that we take pride in trying to repair it as quickly as possible.” To report acts of vandalism, contact the Piedmont Police Department’s non-emergency dispatch at 420-3000. Storyteller Bridge replaces the original footbridge which spanned the ravine at Dracena Park from the 1920s until its demolition in the 1960s.

articles.text: American flags lined the walkways in Mountain View Cemetery on Monday, May 27, as a crowd of nearly 300 people from across the Bay Area attended its 100th Annual Memorial Day Ceremony. Audience members came to pay tribute to American servicemen who lost their lives in the line of duty. The morning’s program featured guest speakers, music, a color guard provided by Piedmont Scout Council Troop 6, as well as the placement of a ceremonial wreath on the cemetery’s Veterans’ Memorial Stone. Refreshments were served before and after the event. The ceremony began with opening remarks by Kristie Ly, the event’s organizer and Director of Family Services at Mountain View Cemetery. A short musical interlude from The Hardiman Trio followed. A variety of guest speakers lent their voices to the ceremony on Monday morning from cemeStructures all around Mountain View Cemetery were decorated in American flags, including this mausoleum. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Troop 15 held a Court of Honor on May 14 at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The highlight was the presentation of the Eagle Award, Scouting’s highest honor, to longtime Troop 15 Scout Nate Woodley. Families mingled in the Courtyard before the ceremony, enjoying a pot-luck supper. Fifteen new Scouts were recognized for attaining Scouting’s initial rank, including William Bleharski, Avery Chau, Joseph Corson, Yiyou Fang, Lucian Fedor, Muyan Hu, Alexander Lacker, Samuel Laubach, Adam Saxonov, Max Schultz, Owen Sukeforth, Leo Thakur, Theodore Thomas, Simone Tornatore, and Amos Yoon. “It felt rewarding to see all of the Scouts in our troop recognized for their efforts over the past few months”, said Daniel Lou, a Life Scout. articles.text: As part of their participation in the East Bay’s 30th annual Bike Day, the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division set up an energizer station at the corner of Highland and Vista Avenue for cyclists. It drew more than 30 visitors, the event’s highest turnout since the city began participating in Bike Day. “It was a fun and lively morning, and we were thrilled to see so many different types of cyclists – people commuting to work, to school, riding with children, riding for exercise. It was a fun and inspiring morning,” said Echa Schneider, the city’s Communications Manager. On Thursday, May 16, from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m., riders could stop by the energizer station to grab coffee and snacks provided by Mulberry’s Market as well as free reusable tote bags and reusable straw kits. Additionally, cyclists visiting the station were entered into a raffle to win a bike cleaning essentials kit from the Sustainability Division. The Energizer Station was hosted by the City’s sustainability staff with support from other departments. PPD Officer Tyler Petit was present to help participants sign up for the PPD’s free Safe Bike Program. Bike Day was founded in the East Bay in 1994 to celebrate bicycles as a fun and healthy way to get to work, as well as to give those who don’t normally use their bikes to commute an opportunity to try it out. With transportation accounting for almost half of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging more residents to use greener commute options is vital to meeting the city’s climate action targets. articles.text: Fourty-two Piedmont High School seniors were honored at the school’s annual Senior Awards Night on Monday evening, May 20, in Alan Harvey Theater. The soon to be garduating seniors walked across the stage to receive awards for their excellence throughout high school in a ceremony attended by faculty members, families, and friends. Six perpetual awards hold extra weight in the PHS halls of history. The winners of these six awards stand apart from the dozens of high achieving Piedmont High seniors were honored on the evening. Susan Kawaichi Diversity Plaque – VALENTINA PRIETO BLACK The perpetual award is named for Susan Kawaichi, a former school board member who co-founded the Appreciating Diversity Committee in Piedmont. The award honors students who promote diversity, tolerance, and progress in the school. “The work that she has done within the school district will have a lasting and meaningful impact,” said PHS counselor Ashley English. Prieto Black was a founding member of the DEIB Student Advisory Committee, and was appointed by the DEIB director directly. She was president of the PHS Diversity Club and the president and founder of the Mi Gente Club, the first-ever Latinx Student Union. “Vale leads weekly restorative justice circles to build community and amplify unheard student voices,” said English. “She has organized multiple district-wide events for both middle and high school students, developing grade-level workshops and lessons with enriching activities and reflective questions.” Valentina’s sister Sofia won the Diversity Plaque in 2023. Valentina will be attending Washington University in St. Louis in the fall. Gail Dryden Community Service Plaque – DANIEL BANIN The Gail Dryden Community Service Plaque is named for former School Board member Gail Dryden who displayed a strong commitment to community service. “Daniel not only has been thinking about our local community, but globally as well. He wanted to empower his peers with knowledge on how to take action on climate issues,” said counselor Amanda Carlson. Banin’s community service impacted the education of climate change, social justice, and the societal impact on technology. His selfless efforts started to make waves four years ago when he raised over $7,500 for COVID-related masks for local, low-income communities. Banin founded the Teens Around the World Club, Global Youth Pulse. and Educate for Change. Banin’s work was cited in the UN Climate Report. Banin brought to PHS opportunities to hear speakers in many fields, including science and social change. The topics range from how can climate modify our behavior to social power consumption, and the carbon cycle. Eric Rachesky Memorial Certificate – MIA LEGGETT Named after the late Eric Swart Rachesky, a Piedmont High School graduate, the memorial award is presented each year to a student who makes significant academic leaps while overcoming obstacles and hardships along the way. Rachesky died at age 21 by contracting an infection after receiving a tattoo. “You’re a quiet leader, but when you speak up and feel passionate, people really respond to you,” said counselor Chris Hartford. Along with the award, Leggett receives a $100 check. Leggett was named captain of the PHS flag football team in its inaugural year as a high school competitive sport. She was a member of the softball team and was a positive influence on players on both teams. The award is given to a student who exudes positivity and is a friend to all. articles.text: On January 15, Piedmont Key Club, a student-led club at PHS and a part of the larger Kiwanis nonprofit organization, started off the new year with a soccer equipment drive in collaboration with Soccer Without Borders. Soccer Without Borders is a nonprofit organization based in Oakland that fosters positive change in communities by giving refugee and immigrant youth a place to feel comfortable being themselves, allowing them to create connections in their community, and teaching them valuable life skills through their love for soccer. But to be able to make this opportunity available and affordable to underserved youth, the organization needs donations. Seeing an opportunity to support the organization by collecting used soccer equipment from students at Piedmont schools, Piedmont Key Club decided to host a soccer equipment drive with collection bins placed on school campuses. Students in the club spread the word about the drive by making posters. The drive was a major success, and resulted in collecting 37 pairs of cleats, 13 soccer balls, five bins of soccer clothes, one bin of shin guards, and one bin of soccer socks, as well as gear like pop-up goals, pennies, and soccer bags. Piedmont Key Club was able to make this drive possible because of the planning and coordination of the club’s leadership and the hard work of the students in the club to get the word out. The club, whose goal is to help PHS students give back to their community, gives students opportunities to perform small acts of community service during their Wednesday lunch meetings in room 302 of the PHS STEAM building. It also provides students with information about other volunteer opportunities outside of school and hosts its own events such as bake sales.

articles.text: The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California in Berkeley is a leader in the field of applied positive psychology. I was able to sit down with Jason Marsh, Executive Director of the GGSC, to discuss their work, positive psychology, and how Piedmonters can get involved. Through an online magazine, podcasts, videos, quizzes, and workshops, the GGSC reaches over a million people each month. Their website is particularly geared toward educators, ensuring that the latest insights into human happiness and social harmony are shared with those shaping future generations. The GGSC’s mission revolves around understanding and fostering positive emotions and social cohesion. This mission is underscored by the belief that personal wellbeing significantly contributes to the broader health of communities. As the center’s work shows, fostering compassion, curiosity, and kindness within individuals can weave these values into the fabric of society, promoting social peace and harmony. The journey of integrating GGSC’s principles into daily life begins with understanding the true nature of happiness. According to Marsh, “happiness encompasses two dimensions: momentary positive emotions like joy and hope, and a deeper sense of life satisfaction and purpose.” Marsh emphasizes that understanding the roots of sociological problems and addressing them paves the way for utilizing positive psychology effectively. This holistic approach acknowledges the necessity of meeting basic needs before personal development can flourish. Positive psychology’s focus on resilience and meaning offers tools for everyone, including those grappling with depression and negative thoughts, to achieve a more balanced and fulfilling life. Piedmont residents, many of whom have strong ties to UC Berkeley, are in a unique position to engage with GGSC’s resources. The center was founded by Berkeley alumni Tom and Ruth, who aimed to honor their daughter’s memory and give back to the university. The center’s initiatives are deeply integrated with UC Berkeley, involving university-funded staff, graduate fellows, and research assistants. Piedmonters can subscribe to the free newsletter, which provides regular updates on content and events, or listen to the “Science of Happiness” podcast. GGSC also offers various events, including free webinars and paid workshops, which are excellent opportunities for deeper engagement. Volunteering at these events is another way to contribute, especially as in-person activities ramp up post-COVID. For those interested in further exploring the field of wellbeing, Marsh recommends “Self-Compassion” by Kristen Neff and “The Myths of Happiness” by Sonja Lyubomirsky. These books provide valuable insights into personal growth and the science of happiness. Getting involved with the GGSC offers Piedmont residents a chance to enhance their own lives while contributing to a more compassionate society. positive psychology, you can help foster a culture of wellbeing that extends far beyond personal happiness to create a more interconnected community in Piedmont. To get involved with the GGSC see their website at https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/. To reach Erica Monical call or text 415- 689-8812 or email mindsglowing@gmail.com.

Great Good Science Center By Erica Monical The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California in Berkeley is a leader in the field of applied positive psychology. I was able to sit down with Jason Marsh, Executive Director of the GGSC, to discuss their work, positive psychology, and how Piedmonters can get involved. Through an online magazine, podcasts, videos, quizzes, and workshops, the GGSC reaches over a million people each month. Their website is particularly geared toward educators, ensuring that the latest insights into human happiness and social harmony are shared with those shaping future generations. The GGSC’s mission revolves around understanding and fostering positive emotions and social cohesion. This mission is underscored by the belief that personal wellbeing significantly contributes to the broader health of communities. As the center’s work shows, fostering compassion, curiosity, and kindness within individuals can weave these values into the fabric of society, promoting social peace and harmony. The journey of integrating GGSC’s principles into daily life begins with understanding the true nature of happiness. According to Marsh, “happiness encompasses two dimensions: momentary positive emotions like joy and hope, and a deeper sense of life satisfaction and purpose.” Marsh emphasizes that understanding the roots of sociological problems and addressing them paves the way for utilizing positive psychology effectively. This holistic approach acknowledges the necessity of meeting basic needs before personal development can flourish. Positive psychology’s focus on resilience and meaning offers tools for everyone, including those grappling with depression and negative thoughts, to achieve a more balanced and fulfilling life. Piedmont residents, many of whom have strong ties to UC Berkeley, are in a unique position to engage with GGSC’s resources. The center was founded by Berkeley alumni Tom and Ruth, who aimed to honor their daughter’s memory and give back to the university. The center’s initiatives are deeply integrated with UC Berkeley, involving university-funded staff, graduate fellows, and research assistants. Piedmonters can subscribe to the free newsletter, which provides regular updates on content and events, or listen to the “Science of Happiness” podcast. GGSC also offers various events, including free webinars and paid workshops, which are excellent opportunities for deeper engagement. Volunteering at these events is another way to contribute, especially as in-person activities ramp up post-COVID. For those interested in further exploring the field of wellbeing, Marsh recommends “Self-Compassion” by Kristen Neff and “The Myths of Happiness” by Sonja Lyubomirsky. These books provide valuable insights into personal growth and the science of happiness. Getting involved with the GGSC offers Piedmont residents a chance to enhance their own lives while contributing to a more compassionate society. By embracing the principles of positive psychology, you can help foster a culture of wellbeing that extends far beyond personal happiness to create a more interconnected community in Piedmont. To get involved with the GGSC see their website at https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/. To reach Erica Monical call or text 415- 689-8812 or email mindsglowing@gmail.com. articles.text: The Alan Harvey Theater hosted Piedmont High School’s Spring Concert on Tuesday, May 21, directed by 1st year band teacher Trevor Meseroll, with music by the Symphonic Band and Jazz Bands. The evening started off with the Symphonic Band performing Barry Manilow’s “Copacabana.” The ensemble then moved into pieces titled “Let’s Groove” by Wayne Vaugh and Maurice White and “Pirates of the Caribbean” by Hans Zimmer. PHS Senior Edwin Tang provided senior leadership for the ensemble on flute. He received accolades last week at the Senior Awards Night as “Outstanding Senior in Symphonic Band.” Photos by Sophie Hess Singer Claire Weiss The PHS Jazz Band presented four different combos of musicians during the show; music for the Jazz Band Combos were preLaurel Minor (left) on trombone, Kalyani Spieckerman on tenor sax, and Milo Bakshi on alto sax Edwin Tang (left), Henry Nielsen, Peter Stokes, Alden Meil, Ryan St. John, Will Kennedy, and Miles Antaya pared by Band Clinicians Claire Chaix and Natalie John. Senior Will Kennedy on Alto Sax, was announced as the winner of “Outstanding Senior in Jazz Band” as well. PHS junior Claire Weiss, a talented vocalist and trumpeter, handled vocals for The Jazz Combo II. She sang “I Know You Know” by Esperanza Spalding and “Lilac Wine” by James Shelton. The Jazz band played a number of songs including “Higher Ground” by Stevie Wonder and “Agua De Beber” by Antonio Carlos Jobim. The evening concluded with the recognition of Piedmont seniors who will soon be graduating. Senior Ryan St. John on drums Miles Antaya (left) and Will Kennedy on sax Dorothy Nemeth on cello Symphonic Band: (front row) Matt Steimle (left), Caitilin Boothby, and Shayna Chau. Back row: Toby Fleischer (left), Peter Stokes, and Alma Ruberto.

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s yearbook class distributed the 2024 yearbooks to students on Friday, May 24. This year’s yearbook, titled “Our Story, Our Voices,” was distributed by students in Anne Smith’s Yearbook-Broadcast class to 530 students in the Buzz Redford Gym. Production on the full-color 176-page yearbook started in August. Students and staff in all classes and activities are featured in the yearbook. In addition to producing the yearbook, this elective class also produces news broadcasts shown to the whole school during Academy periods. pages.text: Wednesday, May 29, 2024 9 Maker Faire Continued from page 1 way. Makers lined up all day to do their best Paul Bunyon impression while pumping the cart. Kinetic Steam also brought a steam-powered printing press that printed full color Piedmont Makers coasters for guests. New this year at the faire were interactive exhibits created by students. A bridge-building project let students make their own miniature SF Bay or Golden Gate Bridge out of balsa wood to then have its carrying capacity tested using a bucket full of sand. Popular among sweet tooths was a cotton candy maker allowing kids to spin their own candy. The fusion between Scouting and makers was on full display with the rope making station where students could test the strength of the newly spun rope. Piedmont became the first school district in the nation to host an official K-12 School Maker Faire 10 years ago – in 2014. Dave Ragones co-founded Piedmont Makers in 2014 with Piedmonter Vince Monical. articles.text: Photos by Michelle Luo of Foxtail Studio and Sasha Pryzbyla of From Stardust Photography Wildwood Principal Melissa Daymond celebrates the evening with parents. articles.text: Troop 4 Scouts gather for a discussion about police work with Chief Jeremy Bowers. Members of the Piedmont Police Department, led by Chief Jeremy Bowers, recently spoke to a group of Scouts in Piedmont’s Troop 4. Chief Bowers, Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo, and Officer Jehan Liles explained their roles, the gear they carry, and their rotating shifts. The Scouts were very engaged and asked many questions about what to do in different situations. They learned a lot about police work and how the department keeps their community safe. This interaction highlighted the dedication of Piedmont’s police force and helped the Scouts understand the importance of community policing in maintaining low crime rates. The officers also discussed the training required to become a police officer and the starting age for entering the force. This gave the Scouts insights into the preparation and commitment needed for a career in law enforcement. Thanks to Piedmont Police for teaching the Scouts about their jobs and experience. articles.text: Highlanders fall in NCS Championship to Justin-Siena Piedmont’s No. 2 seeded baseball team battled its way to the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship game, but fell short of claiming the top prize. After defeating No. 3 McKinleyville 4-1 in the semifinals at Humphries Diamond in Piedmont on Wednesday, May 22, the Highlanders hosted No. 4 Justin-Siena at Laney College but lost 11-1. But their season isn’t over. To the surprise of some, they were given the No. 1 seed in the Division 4 CIF NorCal playoffs and began play on Tuesday with a 13-1 victory over No. 8 Capuchino of San Bruno. It is the first time a Piedmont baseball team has competed in the CIF tourney since its creation three years ago. Saturday’s NCS final started well with Piedmont scoring the opening run and starting pitcher John Olsen looking strong on the mound. But as the cloudy sky turned to a bright and sunny afternoon, it was seemingly the baseball Gods shining down on Justin-Siena. The Braves began landing every bloop shot off weak contact and taking advantage of the wide outfield of Laney College, scoring seven runs in the top of the third inning and another four in the top of the fourth on their way to activating the 10-run rule following the bottom of the fifth. “I was telling the guys I’ve never seen anything go like that. We’d bring the infield in and they’d bloop it over their heads; we’d put the infield back and they’d get a swinging bunt down the line. It was an embarrassment of good fortune. It was just their day,” coach Eric Olson said. It marked the second time the two sides played this year with PHS winning their regular season meeting 1-0 on March 9. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School baseball team has etched its name in the annals of East Bay Middle School League history as the regular season and tournament champions. Their remarkable journey culminated in an undefeated season with a decisive 5-0 victory on Tuesday, May 21, over the reigning champions, the Cobras from Berkeley’s M.L. King Middle School,. Piedmont Middle School made its debut in the EBMSL this year, fielding its first-ever middle school baseball team. Comprising twelve 7th graders and 13 eighth graders, the team quickly established itself. Pitching and defense were the cornerstones of the Scots’ championship campaign. In the title game, Jimmy Lagios took the mound and gave up only two hits in six shutout innings. Henry Stein broke the scoreless deadlock in the third inning with an RBI groundout, driving in Dylan Toyama from third base. The fourth inning saw Aiden Bell and Orion Sachs deliver crucial singles, with Bell scoring on a fielder’s choice off Max Fujimoto’s bat. Fujimoto’s steal of home added another run to Piedmont’s tally. In the fifth inning, Mateo Long, Stein, and Toyama each contributed singles, scoring two more runs. Massimo Mittone, who had played flawlessly at shortstop, stepped in to relieve Lagios on the mound in the seventh inning. He threw just 10 pitches to close out the game. Jonah Cha-Foster, a stalwart behind the plate, transitioned to shortstop to replace Mittone after six innings of stellar play at catcher. Lagios boasted an impressive 0.276 ERA over 25 innings throughout the season, while Mittone’s ERA was an astounding 0.00 in 11 innings. Jonah Cha-Foster and Aaron Bennett also made significant contributions on the mound. Cha-Foster’s expertise behind the plate complemented Lagios’s pitching, while Sachs handled the bulk of the team’s innings behind the plate, while excelling also as a pitcher and second baseman. Sachs and Cha-Foster led the team in hitting, closely followed by Long, Toyama, and Sorenson. Max Fujimoto’s play in center field was a defensive highlight all season. Head coach Josh Campuzano, a former player in the league with Montera Hr. High in Montclair, summed up the team’s success: “We knew we had a talented group of middle schoolers, but playing in this highly competitive league against top-tier opponents was no small feat. The dominant pitching rotation of Lagios, Mittone, Bennett, Cha-Foster, and Sachs proved insurmountable.” The future looks promising for the Scots. The twelve 7th graders took on varsity squads from six schools and emerged unbeaten. With such talent and continued hard work, Piedmont Middle School baseball is poised for continued success. Saturday’s NCS final started well with Piedmont scoring the opening run and starting pitcher John Olsen looking strong on the mound. The Braves began landing every bloop shot off weak contact and taking advantage of the wide outfield of Laney College, scoring seven runs in the top of the third inning and another four in the top of the fourth on their way to activating the 10-run rule following the bottom of the fifth. “I was telling the guys I’ve never seen anything go like that. We’d bring the infield in and they’d bloop it over their heads; we’d put the infield back and they’d get a swinging bunt down the line. It was an embarrassment of good fortune. articles.text: Piedmont High named Peter Krumins and Hailey Marshburn as the school’s 2024 Outstanding Senior Athletes at the Seniors Awards event on May 20, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. Both athletes competed in two sports. PETER KRUMINS Water polo & Baseball Peter Krumins was a key leader on the water polo team in the fall and on the baseball team in the spring. He finishes his time at the school as a two-time Western Alameda County Conference champion on boys’ water polo and a member of the 2023 North Coast Section water polo title team, He also helped this year’s baseball team win the WACC’s regular season title, reach this year’s D4 NCS championship, and qualify for the first time for the CIF NorCal tournament. He was also a member of the 2022 WACC Shoreline championship team in baseball. In water polo, Krumins helped Piedmont win the D2 NCS title as a role player, finishing its season with a 19-10 overall record. The boys’ water polo team also won WACC titles in 2022 and 2021, which marked their first league title in school history. In baseball Krumins spent most of his time at shortstop but also appeared as a pitcher the last two seasons. This year’s team is currently 17-9 and placed second Staff Photos Peter Krumins was a two-sport athlete at Piedmont High with water polo and baseball. He’s pictured here with his family, Adrienne (left), Esme, and Rik. Hailey Marshburn was a two-sport athlete in soccer and lacrosse Peter Krumins helped this year’s water polo win the NCS title and the baseball team reach the NCS championship game. in the D4 NCS playoffs. He has a .268 batting average with 19 hits, seven doubles, one triple, one home run, 18 RBIs, 22 runs scored, and a team-leading 24 walks drawn. He was The Post’s pick as Sophomore of the Year in 2002. Krumins will continue playing baseball at next fall at Northern Kentucky. The soccer team went 12-2-4 (W-T-L) this year and reached the second round of the Division 3 NCS playoffs. Last year, she scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s dramatic sudden-death 2-1 win over No. 1 University to claim the D4 NCS title. She appeared as a fullback and midfielder. On the lacrosse team Marshburn was a midfielder and was often tasked to move the ball up field using her speed and elusiveness. The team finished their season with a 14-5 overall record and won the WACC title in an 8-7 battle against Bishop O’Dowd, with Marhsburn defending the Dragons’ best attacker. She received first-team AllLeague honors in soccer in 2024 and in lacrosse for the last three years. She got second-team honors in soccer in 2023. HAILEY MARSHBURN Soccer & Lacrosse Hailey Marshburn is a fouryear varsity starter on two teams who served as captain of the soccer lacrosse teams. She helped lead PHS to the North Coast Section championship in lacrosse as a junior and was a key player on this year’s team which won the WACC championship. Hailey Marshburn was a four-year starter in two sports. She helped the girls’ soccer team win the NCS title in 2023 and girls lacrosse win this year’s WACC title.

articles.text: Piedmont High School sailors who are part of the sailing team at Encinal Yacht Club in Alameda wrapped up a successful year with a celebration and awards dinner on Sunday evening, May 19. A total of 17 high school teams participated. Junior Sophie Hess presented awards to seniors Mica Jorcino and Peter Stokes, thanking them both for making it such a fun season filled with lots of improvement. Now in its 18th year, Encinal’s High School Sailing program has had 66 sailors move on to college level sailing at schools around the country with 22 serving as captains of their teams. Of those 66, 18 are currently active including PHS alumni Conor Kim who sails for UC Santa Cruz and Sara Govert who coaches for EYC. Peter Stokes will be sailing for UC Berkeley and Mica Jorcino for Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo in the fall. The Encinal Yacht Club (EYC) High School Sailing Program is for students in grades 8-12 with or without sailing experience. Participants attend weekly practices at EYC and weekend regattas in the Bay Area and Southern California from fall through spring. Regattas are organized by Pacific Coast Interscholastic Sailing Association. The EYC Junior Sailing Program works in partnership with high schools throughout the East Bay who have teams or clubs that participate in the Interscholastic Sailing Association (ISSA). Rising 8th -12th graders are welcome to join Piedmont’s sailing team. There are summer opportunities at EYC for kids of all ages and levels. For more information, contact Sophie Hess (shess@piedmont.k12.ca.us) or visit https://www.encinal.org/ youth-programs/high-school. Piedmont sailors show off their plaques from the Sailing Team: Sophie Hess (left, 11th grade), Mica Jorcino (12th grade), and Peter Stokes (12th grade).

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, May 29, 2024 Best moments from the spring season By Jonathan Comeaux The 2024 spring season wrapping up with most sports already finished its season and just baseball continues to play in the D4 CIF NorCal tournament. Here’s a quick look at some of the Post’s’ favorite sports moments from this spring. Baseball team in NCS Finals Piedmont’s baseball team made its way to the Division 4 North Coast Section Finals for the first time since 2018. They lost 11-1 to Justin-Siena on May 25 at Laney College, but received the No. 1 seed for the CIF NorCal playoffs. On its road to the NCS finals, PHS, the No. 2 seed, defeated No. 4 McKinleyville 4-1 in the semifinals and shut out No. 10 Hercules 5-0 in the quarterfinals. Baseball team plays game at Oracle Park March 23 was another fun day for PHS with the baseball team playing a game in the Dante Benedetti Classic at the San Francisco Giants’ Oracle Park. John Olsen was the winning pitcher with four innings and three strikeouts, while Seve Sanchez pitched three innings and struck out four. pages.text: Wednesday, May 29, 2024 15 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s sports calendar has officially come to a close for the 2023-24 school year. The spring wraps up with the baseball team bringing home the Western Alameda County Conference regular season title, and the girls’ lacrosse team capturing this year’s WACC title. The school earned 64 All-League selections through 10 different teams. 2024 All-League athletes Track and Field Piedmont’s track and field season came to an end with a record 21 students qualifying for the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin HS on May 17-18. The girls’ team earned six All-League selections, including Shayna Chau receiving first-team honors while Breah Bell, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, Jamie Schwarz and Ella Yasar received second-team honors. The boys’ team received two selections, including Xander Schulte-Sasse and Sebastien Swain getting second-team honors. Girls Lacrosse The girls team closed its season with a 14-5 overall record and won this year’s WACC Championship with an 8-7 victory over Bishop O’Dowd. They received a No. 5 seed in the D2 NCS Quarterfinals, and lost a narrow 9-7 match with No. 4 Acalanes. They earned nine All-League selections, including Hallie Burden, Chloe Graham, Ruby Guzdar, Hailey Marshburn and Friedie Schieckedanz receiving first-team honors, Laurel Bentley, Luisa Cole, Jane Hempeck, and Peyton Watson got second-team honors, while Henley Lorin and Jameson Sanford were honorable mentions. Swimming Piedmont’s boys’ swimming team won this year’s WACC Championship and the girls’ team placed second. The boys received seven selections including Owen Blanford, Cole Carnazzo, Nik Costello, Tom Rolefson, Dimitri Secor, and Asher Takazawa getting first- 64 Spring athletes named All-League recipients team honors, while Evan Byun received second-team honors. The girls’ earned four All-League selections with Taylor Rolefson, Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Abigail Jacoby, and Josie Oesterer. Boys Tennis The boys’ tennis team finished its season with a 13-10 overall record and battled its way to the NCS quarterfinals. Sophomore Lucas Smolko won this year’s WACC individual singles title and Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won the doubles crown. The team received six AllLeague selections, including Smolko, Imburg, Ben Breber and Arun Brahma receiving firstteam honors, while Nate Welch and Nick King were honorable mentions. Boys Lacrosse The boys’ lacrosse team went 8-6 and finished third in the Western Alameda County Conference. They qualified for the Division 1 NCS tournament with the No. 11 seed, falling to No. 6 San Ramon Valley in the first round. They earned eight All-League honors, including Keita Clear and Rylan Nelson receiving first-team selections, Connor Fredericks, Logan Huh, Oliver Shafroth, and Gus Von Metzsch were second-team selections, while Ethan Alering and Curtis Hohener were honorable mentions. Softball The softball team went 10-8 this season and qualified for the D4 NCS tournament, losing to No. 4 Fortuna in the quarterfinals as the No. 5 seeded team. Piedmont earned five AllLeague recipients, including Miya Fujimoto and Angelina Wu receiving first-team honors, Mia Leggett with a second-team selection, and Sa’Mara Levi and Samantha Ronen getting honorable mentions. Boys Volleyball Piedmont High’s boys’ volleyball team finished with a 6-10 overall record in the difficult WACC Foothill Division. They received three All-League selections, including John Champion with second-team honors and Shunji Higashi and Lukas Kim as honorable mentions. They laid down their life for us.’” Perhaps the most powerful speech of the morning was delivered by Air Force Lt. Col. Bradlee Seehawer. Currently stationed at Travis, Seehawer spoke of the sacrifices servicemen make even after they come home. “Although Memorial Day is typically thought to remember the ones we lost at war, I encourage you to think of today with a broader perspective. Whether they died fighting an enemy force, whether they are one of the 22 veterans per day who died by suicide, or whether they are part of the 41% of veterans who succumb to the effects of post-traumatic stress. We carry our military service with us long after we hang up the uniform.” Seehawer encouraged members of the audience to go home and talk to the veterans in their lives about their service. “These soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines, coast guardsmen, and guardians are never really gone as long as we have a way to remember them. As we stand here today in this beautiful space for the 100th time, we remember their sacrifice.” Following Seehawer’s speech, Dennis Valerio laid a ceremonial wreath on the Veterans’ Memorial Stone. articles.text: Show at de Young will draw florists and designers from across the Bay Area Next week, local florist J. Miller Flowers will participate in the de Young Museum’s annual Bouquets to Art event for its 25th consecutive year. Bouquets to Art, which itself is celebrating its 40th anniversary this year, is an event that allows museumgoers to engage with the de Young’s expansive collections in a novel way – through floral interpretations of some of its most classic works. Each year, the leading floral designers of the Bay Area draw inspiration from a particular work in the museum and create a floral arrangement inspired by the work, which is then displayed in front of the original art piece at the de Young for museumgoers to see. From sculptures to sketches, nothing remains off-limits as a source of inspiration. J. Miller Flowers reinterprets The Niagara River at the Cataract (left) and Horseshoe Falls from below the High Bank (c. 1832) by Gustav Grunewald for Bouquets to Art 2012. Designed by Valerie Lee, Maureen Owens and Robbin Lee. Photo by Valerie Lee J. Miller Flowers reinterprets Singing Beach, Manchester, MA (1863) by Martin Johnson Heade for Bouquets to Art 2022. Designed by Valerie Lee, Robbin Lee, Jacqueline McGillicuddy and Robby Ow. Staff photo Robbin Lee (left) and Valerie Lee, co-owners of J. Miller Flowers, will participate in the de Young’s Bouquets to Art event for their 25th year. The event lasts for six days, Tuesday to Sunday, June 4-9. “It’s one of my favorite weeks of the year because it brings together friends, art, and flowers while raising much-needed funds for the Fine Arts Museum in San Francisco, specifically the de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor,” said Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers on Piedmont Avenue. “And to be surrounded with flower-filled art galleries in June is just glorious to me.” In previous years, co-owners Valerie Lee and Robbin Lee have interpreted paintings of dresses, sunsets and swans as striking, vibrant flower arrangements. This year, the duo will be interpreting the de Young’s collection of New Guinean ceremonial shields. “I’m more intrigued with paintings or sculpture. However, this year I knew I wanted to perhaps do something with tropical flowers. So, the New Guinea wooden shields lent themselves well to that idea.” To suit her vision, Valerie Lee ordered her exhibit’s tropical flowers directly from Hilo, Hawaii, one of the largest tropical flower growers on the island. Her entry will be displayed in front of the de Young’s Shields of New Guinea in Gallery 20 on the second floor adjacent to the main staircase. Lee said that the most difficult part of the exhibition has always been keeping the flowers fresh between showings. “That’s the challenge of participating in this. You want to make sure every museumgoer has a chance to see the same, refreshing flowers.” The event will also feature a raffle of fresh arrangements from the museum’s flower cart, and eventgoers are encouraged to take part in engaging lectures with renowned designers and authors happening throughout the week. Opening night begins at 5:30 p.m. on Monday, June 4. Complimentary parking in the Music Concourse Parking Garage is provided for all Opening Night attendees. Food and drinks will be prepared by McCalls Catering & Events. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Dr in San Francisco. Tickets can be purchased online at www. famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Advance tickets are required for this event.
articles.title: J. Miller Flowers to participate in Bouquets to Art for 25th year

articles.text: Community members flocked to J. Miller Flowers last weekend for something more than a bouquet of flowers. It was the opening of a nature-themed pop art exhibit featuring the art of former Piedmont Middle School art teacher Kim Lipkin, a Piedmont resident, as well as others. The exhibition was held in a behind-the-scenes side room at J. Miller Flowers that is typically used for cutting and cleaning flowers, where visitors could enjoy glasses of lemonade and fresh rosemary shortbread while browsing and purchasing paintings from the gallery. The show was open Friday, May 24, to Sunday, May 26. Organizers estimate that it had nearly 100 attendees per day. “It’s all about building community. That’s what any business is about,” said Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers with her sister Robbin Lee. The show featured more than 125 pieces of artwork for sale by artists Kim Lipkin, Heather Piazza, Claire Finne, Hannah Avner, Robert Ow, Lorinne Lee, Jacqueline McGillicuddy, Andrew Ameral and Valerie Lee herself. Although the art at the show had a variety of subjects, Lipkin focused nearly her entire selection on paintings of bright, multicolored floral arrangements. “Flowers are very different from one another, and there are many different varieties to see. I think that’s how life is in a lot of ways,” said Lipkin. “Even the people who I surround myself with on a daily basis are all so different and yet still similar. I feel like that experience is simply part of being alive.” Lipkin describes her style as a mix of impressionism and surrealism accented with bright, swirling colors. Her paintings were prominently displayed on Staff photo Artist Kim Lipkin holds her painting “Floral 36,” while setting up her exhibit for the show. the back wall of the gallery room, making them visible to visitors as they entered. Lipkin said that she became involved in the exhibit entirely by chance. “I’ve known Valerie off and on for years, but my husband and all of his friends went to school with her,” she explained. A few weeks ago while she was in the flower shop, when Lee invited Lipkin to participate. “I’d heard of it before but never gotten to participate. So now, I’m just thrilled I get to do it this time.” Lipkin taught art at Piedmont Middle School for 20 years before retiring in 2016. She has lived in Piedmont for 38 years. J. Miller Flowers is a family-owned florist for 54 years and is located at 4416 Piedmont Avenue at the corner of Pleasant Valley. To learn more about their floral arrangements or upcoming pop-up art shows, call J. Miller Flowers at 658-0613. A pair of customers show off their newly purchased paintings from the art show.
