articles.text: Marking its historic 50th anniversary, Kronos Quartet will perform four concerts on consecutive days at SF Jazz’s Miner Auditorium in June. Founded in Seattle in 1973, Kronos Quartet has received more than 40 awards, including three Grammy Awards and the Polar Music, Avery Fisher, and Edison Klassiek Oeuvre Prizes. More than 1000 works have been written for the group, which has been praised for the inclusiveness of its repertoire. Kronos Quartet is the most well-known and nationally recognized string quartet based in San Francisco. The Quartet members are violinists David Harrington and John Sherba, violist Hank Dutt, and cellist Paul Wiancko, who performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a Piedmont Kronos Quartet includes David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello) Chamber Music Festival concert. This year’s Kronos Festival comes home to San Francisco in a four-day festival June 20-23. It will showcase Kronos musicians and a host of special guests, featuring world premieres and the final Kronos performances by violinist John Sherba and violist Hank Dutt. Miner Auditorium is located at 201 Franklin Street in San Francisco. For tickets and details of each concert, visit https:// kronosquartet.org/kronos-festival-2024/
articles.title: Kronos Festival at Miner Auditorium June 20-23

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s The Glass Menagerie is playing onstage now through June 15. Written by Tennessee Williams, The Glass Menagerie premiered in 1944. The play catapulted Williams to fame and tells the story of the dreamer Tom Wingfield, his mother Amanda, and his sister, Laura. With their father absent and the Great Depression underway, the siblings find comfort in alcohol, movies and writing. When a gentleman caller arrives for dinner, the Wingfield family’s lives are suddenly turned upside down. The cast includes San Francisco Playhouse founder Susi Damilano, Nicole Javier, William Thomas Hodgson, Jake Fong, Aleisha Lew and Kenna Tanaka. The show is on stage six days a week. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/2023- 2024-season/the-glass-menagerie/. Susi Damilano and Nicole Javier in The Glass Menagerie
articles.title: The Glass Menagerie at SF Playhouse through June 15

articles.text: Tickets for the symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley are on sale now. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. Now in its 18th season, the festival opens on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley, and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome locals and visitors to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the nonprofit Festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” For full programming and to purchase tickets. visit https://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/. Festival Napa Valley
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley to take place July 6-21

articles.text: Cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason will perform with the San Francisco Symphony in three performances led by Esa-Pekka Salonen June 13 through 15. Kanneh-Mason is a British cellist who, at age 17, won the 2016 BBC Young Musician award and was the first Black musician to win the competition since its creation in 1978. He played at the wedding of Prince Harry to Meghan Markle in 2018 under the direction of Christopher Warren-Green. Kanneh-Mason makes his orchestral series debut with the San Francisco Symphony on June 13, performing Dmitri Shostakovich’s Cello Concerto No. 1. All concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. Call the San Francisco Symphony box office at (415) 864- 6000, or visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2023-24/ SALONEN-KANNEH-MASON to purchase tickets. Cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason
articles.title: Sheku Kanneh-Mason to perform with SF Symphony June 13-15

articles.text: Summer outdoor performances Frost Amphitheatre San Francisco Ballet’s fourth annual “Starry Nights” performances, presented in collaboration with the Stanford Live Arts Festival, will take place at Frost Amphitheater, on Friday and Saturday, July 26-27. Starry Nights features Act II of SF Ballet Choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s Swan Lake, as well as the company premiere of Ben Stevenson’s Three Preludes, and three mesmerizing ballets by the renowned choreographer Hans van Manen: Variations for Two Couples, Solo, and the SF Ballet premiere of 5 Tango’s. Performances are at 7:30 p.m., with two intermissions. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit www. sfballet.org. SF Ballet’s “Starry Nights” takes place at Stanford’s outdoor Frost Amphitheatre
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Starry Nights at Stanford July 26 - 27

Kronos Quartet is the most well-known and nationally recognized string quartet based in San Francisco. The Quartet members are violinists David Harrington and John Sherba, violist Hank Dutt, and cellist Paul Wiancko, who performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a Piedmont Kronos Quartet includes David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello) Chamber Music Festival concert. This year’s Kronos Festival comes home to San Francisco in a four-day festival June 20-23. It will showcase Kronos musicians and a host of special guests, featuring world premieres and the final Kronos performances by violinist John Sherba and violist Hank Dutt. Miner Auditorium is located at 201 Franklin Street in San Francisco. For tickets and details of each concert, visit https:// kronosquartet.org/kronos-festival-2024/ Festival Napa Valley to take place July 6-21 By Allyson Aleksey Tickets for the symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley are on sale now. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. Now in its 18th season, the festival opens on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley, and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome locals and visitors to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the nonprofit Festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” For full programming and to purchase tickets. visit https://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/. Starry Nights features Act II of SF Ballet Choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s Swan Lake, as well as the company premiere of Ben Stevenson’s Three Preludes, and three mesmerizing ballets by the renowned choreographer Hans van Manen: Variations for Two Couples, Solo, and the SF Ballet premiere of 5 Tango’s. SF Ballet’s “Starry Nights” takes place at Stanford’s outdoor Frost Amphitheatre The Glass Menagerie at SF Playhouse through June 15 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse’s The Glass Menagerie is playing onstage now through June 15. Written by Tennessee Williams, The Glass Menagerie premiered in 1944. The play catapulted Williams to fame and tells the story of the dreamer Tom Wingfield, his mother Amanda, and his sister, Laura. With their father absent and the Great Depression underway, the siblings find comfort in alcohol, movies and writing. When a gentleman caller arrives for dinner, the Wingfield family’s lives are suddenly turned upside down. articles.text: Saturday, June 1, 6:30 p.m. Claudia Marseille Book Launch At age four, Claudia Marseille was diagnosed with a severe hearing loss. With determination and the help of powerful hearing aids, she learned to hear, speak and lipread. After earning master’s degrees in archaeology and in public policy, and finally an MFA, she developed a career in photography and painting. She ran a fine art portrait photography studio for 15 years before becoming a full-time painter, and has played classical piano much of her life. Marseille has written a memoir about her experiences growing up with her disability, called But You Look So Normal: Lost and Found in a Hearing World. She will read selections from it at the event. Admission is free, and refreshments will be available before and after her talk. Monday, June 3, 6:30 p.m. Piedmont Choir’s Ancora vocal recital Ancora, Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s chamber group, made up of high school-age treble voices who pass a rigorous vocal audition, will hold a recital at PCA. This end-of-year Ancora recital celebrates the vocal accomplishments of our most advanced treble singers, featuring performances of the full group’s repertoire alongside solos from individual singers. These singers explore the most advanced treble repertoire in up to eight parts. Please join us to watch them perform. This is not a ticketed event, and is open to all. Saturday, June 8, 7:30 p.m. Left Coast Chamber Ensemble In celebration of Black Music Month, Left Coast presents Florence Price’s romantic Piano Quintet alongside a duo by David Sanford and a world premiere by Chris Castro. Also featured are six world premieres by emerging Californian composers, each created since January under the guidance of one of four Mentor Composers. Performers include Allegra Chapman, piano; Anna Presler & guest artist Jory Fankuchen, violins; Phyllis Kamrin, viola; Leighton Fong, cello; Michel Taddei, double bass; Stacey Pelinka, flute; and guest artist Andrew Friedman, clarinet. Tickets are $5–$35, and are available at tix.com/ticket-sales/ leftcoastensemble/579/event/344399, or at the door. Saturday, June 15, 7:30 p.m. Gerald Robbins Solo Piano Recital PCA presents world-renowned concert pianist Gerald Robbins to perform an extensive selection of piano masterpieces from the 8th to 20th century, including compositions by Scarlatti, Beethoven, Schubert, Tchaikovsky, Debussy, Chopin, and George Gershwin. Robbins has distinguished himself internationally as a soloist, having performed throughout the world in virtually every major music center, from New York to Tokyo. A champion of neglected Romantic repertoire, Robbins has received critical acclaim for his important recordings. He is a distinguished chamber musician, an accomplished conductor, and the winner of multiple major international awards. Save $$ with advance tickets $20/student, $35/general, at www.bpt.me/632636. articles.text: Diversity is one of the spices of life. That’s the way it was on Friday and Saturday in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Friday’s spice was an out-of-the-ordinary string quartet concert and on Saturday a spicy chorus. Let’s start with the Circadian String Quartet concert on Friday. The repertoire was mostly modern – at least it had a very modern feel. While Debussy is not considered an avant-garde composer, the arrangements by second violinist David Ryther gave Debussy a modern feel. The quartet itself is very well-balanced tonally, and they present a very mature musical perspective to everything they play. Another thing they do very well is blend politics with music. This will be even more powerful if you buy into their political philosophy. I try to keep an open mind. Circadian’s outlook on the music is both thoughtful and disturbing. The results are never less than interesting. The second half of the concert featured the world premiere of David Ryther’s opera Euridice’s Defiance. The composer has a great gift for melody. This was obvious in all of his works for string quartet. His opera featured guest alto soloist Leslie Bonnet, a last-minute substitute. The results were excellent. There was one section which fell apart, but I think that if they had continued, no one would have known. The work was inspiring. After the concert, a splendid feast rewarded the audience and the performers. Circadian String Quartet: David Wishnia (left), Monika Gruber, David Ryther and Omid Assadi Cleresstory appeared at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Sunday, May 26.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 29, 2024 The Musical Gourmet Saturday at the PCA The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The concert the following evening, titled “Notes and letters: an evening of Brahms and the Schumanns,” was also out of the ordinary. It was a concert by Clerestory, a chorus I had never heard of prior to Saturday. Their concert formed a seamless program, completely unified musically and emotionally. The group is balanced musically and their diction is the best I have ever heard from a chorus. The language of the evening was entirely German. There was only one place where I heard a semblance of an American accent. Otherwise everything was absolutely idiomatic – and that is impressive. Another thing they do impressively is to change the formation of the chorus. They move with the precision of a championship marching band. I asked one of the singers why they do that and he explained that they all share the conducting responsibilities. While variety is one of the spices of life, the teamwork exemplified by the Circadian String Quartet and the Clerestory vocal ensemble was a beauty to behold. Writer/director Rebecca Miller has a remarkably well-tuned ear for conversation, especially that which is embedded in New York academia. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré It’s possible that Gran Torino will be Clint Eastwood’s last film as an actor, so it seems appropriate that his role in this film seems a solid reprise of his earlier, now iconic characters. Over the last 30 years Eastwood has cut a wide swath through Hollywood and our popular culture. Beginning with spaghetti westerns made in Italy, such as A Fistful of Dollars and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, he went on to create the character Dirty Harry, the rogue, jaw-clenching cop who grimaces, squints and asks the bank robber, “You feel lucky? Well, punk, doya?” And of course there were those five words that made their way into our language: “Go ahead, make my day.” In fact, watching Eastwood in Gran Torino portraying Walt Kowalski, a retired auto worker who has just lost his wife, his face deeply lined, his grizzled hair thinning, the rude, gruff mannerisms so familiar, it is clear that Eastwood has always played a variation of himself. Kowalski is Dirty Harry. But he’s also the Carmel DJ in Play Misty for Me, and Rowdy Yates in the television series Wagon Train, the righteous western homesteader in Unforgiven, or the G.I. hunting a German gold cache in Kelly’s Heroes. Fearless as an actor, Eastwood has never been averse to stepping away from the hard-shelled persona he perfected with Harry, He starred in the musical Paint Your Wagon, Anyway But Loose with an orangutan) as a supporting actor, and the romance, The Bridges of Madison County. What has surprised his audience the most, perhaps, s the fine work Eastwood has produced as a director, making such remarkable films as Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, The Changeling, and the two-film saga about Iwo Jima from the American and Japanese points of view. In Gran Torino, Eastwood inhabits the character of Kowalski and then some. The man is bigoted, narrow of mind, without patience or tolerance; yet, he is also decent, principled and courageous. When a family of Hmongs – people from the hills of Thailand, Laos and Vietnam – move in next-door, Kowalski regards them as “slopes” and “zipper heads.” His prejudice is undisClint Eastwood in Gran Torino

articles.text: Released in 1993, Free Willy is a family friendly drama that will undoubtedly appeal to a new generation of kids. At the center of this most engaging film are a 7,000 pound Orca whale, named Willy, and a 12-year-old boy, Jessie (Jason James Richter), who are both struggling to adjust to their situations. For Willy, captured while swimming with his pod (think family), it’s the confines of the Northwest Adventure theme park. Jesse, an orphan who was abandoned by his mother at a very early age, grew up in various foster homes, but prefers to hustles on the streets with his urchin buds, scrounging for spare change, and begging for food from the back door of local restaurants. Both Willy and Jesse have an attitude. Willy refuses to work with his trainer, Rae (Lori Petty), and Jesse is surly and filled with resentment at life in general. It’s obvious that if something doesn’t happen to turn Jesse around, he will slip through the cracks and be lost for good. One night, Jesse sneaks into a theme park with a can of spray paint, intent on leaving behind his signature graffiti. He begins with a window overlooking one of the large water tanks where the Orcas perform. He is interrupted by the police who give him three mandatory options: return the next day and clean the window, move in with a foster family, Glen and Annie Greenwood (Jane AtkinJason James Richter and Keiko in Free Willy son and Michel Madsen), who have agreed to give him a home, or take a hard pass and go to juvi. Not eager to go to jail, Jesse agrees to live with the Greenwoods, and returns to the park to scrub the observation window. Walking down by the tank, Jesse is warned by Rae to be careful, there’s an Orca just below the surface. Ignoring Rae, of course, he slips and falls in. But to the surprise of Rae and other park employees, to include the owners of Northwest, Willy gently lifts Jesse out of the water and places him gently onto the side of the pool. Now living with the Greenwoods, Jesse sneaks out at night, and returns to the tank and sits on the side, playing his harmonica. Willy hears him and swims over. And so the two begin to bond. Jesse, surprisingly, is hired by the owners, who have all but given up on Willy (he’s more valuable if sold or even euthanized), and given the job of assisting Rae as a neophyte trainer. With Jesse in the water, Willy becomes compliant and starts performing. Meanwhile, Jesse comes to realize that the Greenwoods are the family he has been hoping for, and they patiently make it clear that he is more than welcome. And so gradually Jesse, Willy, and the Greenwoods cohere. What is unresolved is the intent of the greedy, villainous owners. They are still considering Willy’s fate. Jesse gets wind of their indecision, and so begins acts three and a plan, which will delight the kids in the audience. Free Willy finds the sweet spot in the end. Free Willy. Directed by Simon Wincer. Starring Jason James Richter, Lori Petty, Michael Madsen, Jane Atkinson, and Keiko as Willy. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated PG. Released in 1993. Now Streaming on Netflix. articles.text: Based on the children’s book by John Nickle, The Ant Bully is a lively, animated film that focuses on 10-year-old Lucas (Zach Tyler Eisen). He’s not a big kid, wears specs, lives in the suburbs and is bullied by a small gang led by an older boy named Steve (Myles Jeffery). When the narrative begins, we learn that Lucas’ parents have gone on a special vacation leaving him with his grandmother (Lily Tomlin), who is a bit loud and overbearing. Feeling neglected, and pushed around by Steve, he discovers an anthill in the garden, gets the hose used for watering and proceeds to spray the ants. Of course, Lucas is oblivious to the damage he’s doing to the ant colony. But as it turns out the inhabitants of the hill are not simply defenseless ants. They possess an anthropomorphized intelligence, call Lucas The Destroyer, and vow to get the very huge bully to stop. There’s Hova (Julia Roberts), who volunteers to take on Lucas as a project and figure out a way to make the kid stop. She is supported by the Ant Queen (Meryl Streep), who is growing concerned for the survival of the colony. The initial response of the other worker ants is to get revenge. But their problem is one of size. Nova seeks out Zoc A scene from The Ant Bully Author, painter, photographer, world traveler, classical pianist — born with a severe hearing loss! At the center of this most engaging film are a 7,000 pound Orca whale, named Willy, and a 12-year-old boy, Jessie (Jason James Richter), who are both struggling to adjust to their situations. For Willy, captured while swimming with his pod (think family), it’s the confines of the Northwest Adventure theme park. Jesse, an orphan who was abandoned by his mother at a very early age, grew up in various foster homes, but prefers to hustles on the streets with his urchin buds, scrounging for spare change, and begging for food from the back door of local restaurants. Both Willy and Jesse have an attitude. Willy refuses to work with his trainer, Rae (Lori Petty), and Jesse is surly and filled with resentment at life in general. It’s obvious that if something doesn’t happen to turn Jesse around, he will slip through the cracks and be lost for good. One night, Jesse sneaks into a theme park with a can of spray paint, intent on leaving behind his signature graffiti. He begins with a window overlooking one of the large water tanks where the Orcas perform. He is interrupted by the police who give him three mandatory options: return the next day and clean the window, move in with a foster family, Glen and Annie Greenwood (Jane AtkinJason James Richter and Keiko in Free Willy son and Michel Madsen), who have agreed to give him a home, or take a hard pass and go to juvi. Not eager to go to jail, Jesse agrees to live with the Greenwoods, and returns to the park to scrub the observation window. Walking down by the tank, Jesse is warned by Rae to be careful, there’s an Orca just below the surface. Ignoring Rae, of course, he slips and falls in. But to the surprise of Rae and other park employees, to include the owners of Northwest, Willy gently lifts Jesse out of the water and places him gently onto the side of the pool. Now living with the Greenwoods, Jesse sneaks out at night, and returns to the tank and sits on the side, playing his harmonica. Willy hears him and swims over. And so the two begin to bond. Jesse, surprisingly, is hired by the owners, who have all but given up on Willy (he’s more valuable if sold or even euthanized), and given the job of assisting Rae as a neophyte trainer. With Jesse in the water, Willy becomes compliant and starts performing. Meanwhile, Jesse comes to realize that the Greenwoods are the family he has been hoping for, and they patiently make it clear that he is more than welcome. And so gradually Jesse, Willy, and the Greenwoods cohere. What is unresolved is the intent of the greedy, villainous owners. They are still considering Willy’s fate. Jesse gets wind of their indecision, and so begins acts three and a plan, which will delight the kids in the audience. Free Willy finds the sweet spot in the end. Free Willy. articles.text: It all starts with faction writer Amor Towles The long days of summer beckon, and for many it’s time to begin preparing an aspirational list of potential good reads. Indeed… so many books and so little time; however, bear in mind that a good summer read should: 1) Never require a grudging effort (it’s not homework) 2) Ideally be a page-turner, meaning a narrative that you know you will miss when the last paragraph concludes 3) Immune to sand, sun, water 4) Balance nicely on your midsection when lying prone. I should begin by saying that I love to read. I always have, starting with comic books and the backs of cereal boxes. I soon graduated to anything resembling The Hardy Boys, and soon discovered a small local library just a short block from my house. It’s long been my habit to carry a book with me if I expected to be sitting in an airport, a waiting room, or anything akin to a coffee shop, park bench or a stretch of grass. Of course, I read for information (praise be Wikipedia), and treasure my MacBook Pro. But my bias has always been ink on paper fiction, hardcover or soft, with a richly imagined plot as well as compelling characters. I like the feel of holding a book, turning the pages. I keep a variety of bookmarks nearby, many embossed with the names of bookstores. I never turn down the corner of a page to mark where I stopped. To do so seems a kind of violation of, well, the integrity of the book. And, then there’s the experience of reading, pausing to consider a sentence or paragraph, reflecting on meaning, or letting your mind drift as connections to other aspects of life are made. I’ve always regarded that latter process a kind of meditation, an adjunct benefit to reading. As mentioned, I prefer fiction hence the four books I’m suggesting below are all by the America author Amor Towels. Some years ago a friend recommended that I read Towels’ debut novel, Rules of Civility, published in 2011. Knowing little about Towels, and unaware that his book was listed as a New York Times bestseller, I found a paperback edition and began my Towels reading experience. Rules proved to be a captivating good read. Set mainly in New York City, the novel opens on the last night of 1937 and continues into 1938. It is told from the point of view of 25-year-old Katey Kontent, who possesses a keen intellect and sharp wit. She journeys from a Wall Street secretarial pool into the upper echelon of New York society. Coming to Towels late, and having enjoyed Towels’ Rules for its plot and characters, I searched for his second novel, A Gentleman in Moscow. The story opens in 1922. Russian Count Alexander Rostov has been arrested, and on the orders of a Bolshevik tribunal is expected to be executed. Instead, he is given a life sentence of confinement in the lavish Moscow Metropol Hotel, and is quartered in a stark attic room, once used by the hotel’s servants. He is allowed to move about the hotel at will, to include the dining room where other visiting guests, part of the new post-Tsar elite, take their meals. A Gentleman in Moscow is in so many ways a compelling read, and Towels’ characters and plotting are extraordinary. And so I then waited for the much-anticipated release of his third book, titled The Lincoln Highway. It is set in 1954 and focuses on three young men with very different backgrounds. It is a road trip of sorts across America. For reasons I can’t quite explain, this narrative didn’t pull me in. But as I’m sure readers know, there must be an inexplicable connection between the reader and the story – timing is everything. I did finish the novel, and I may give it a second chance later. After a long hiatus, and reading a variety of other fiction, to include the novels of Michael Connelly which feature the durable L.A. detective Harry Bosch, I noticed that Amor Towels had published his fourth book, A Table for Two. There’s a tag line on the cover that says, “A Work of Fictions.” And to my surprise, the book is a collection of six short stories, set in New York in the year 2000, and a novella based in the golden days of Hollywood. I am more than halfway through the book, and have just begun the promised novella titled Eve in Hollywood, featuring Eve Ross, a character lifted from the pages of Rules of Civility. A word that has been used to describe Towels’ work is “sophistication.” I would add the word “stylish,” pointing to the author’s masterful descriptions and subtle plots that captivate, no matter the length of the narrative. At this moment I’m reading with anticipation about Eve in the Hollywood of 1938. And once again I am marveling at the rich prose and extraordinary imagination of this gifted writer.
articles.title: A Summer Reading List

In these small, hands-on sessions, students will learn about key ingredients and techniques that make Asian cuisine so distinctive. articles.text: Kayakers are invited to join the UC Davis Tahoe Environmental Research Center (TERC) for the Fourth Annual Circumnavigate Lake Tahoe fundraiser supporting science around the lake and beyond. The event will take place over seven days, Monday through Sunday, June 17-23. Many people have paddled Lake Tahoe, but this event is unique. In addition to each day’s spectacular shoreline paddling, kayakers will see, share, and learn about Lake Tahoe’s ecology, geology and emerging challenges. TERC’s scientific experts will provide daily on-shore and on-water talks illustrating the science being used to restore and protect Lake Tahoe. Each day’s route is set near shore and extends 6-13 miles, with halfway rest stops on all but the shortest day. Experienced, professional kayak guides will lead the fleet. The odyssey starts at Sand Harbor, Nevada, and proceeds counterclockwise around the lake. (Daily details are provided after registration.) Paddlers will be shuttled by bus from takeout to put-in each day, to retrieve their cars. Multi-day paddlers will be also provided with onshore boat storage at each takeout. On the final day after paddling, there will be a gala party where paddlers can help to support TERC. The event is limited to 50 paddlers, and at the time of writing a few places remain. See https://tahoe.ucdavis.edu/events/ terc-circumnavigation-2024 for registration and more information. The backstory In the summer of 2020, longtime Piedmonter Scott Fitzgerrell, who now lives at Lake Tahoe, was building his fifth wooden sea kayak. Remarking to a friend, Dr. Geoff Schladow, then director of TERC, he said that once he “completed the doggone boat” he’d paddle it all the way around Lake Tahoe as a shakedown cruise. In that conversation was born the idea of inviting others to join the circumnavigation as a way of raising funds for TERC. Wildfire smoke put a halt to the event that summer, but in the clear skies of 2021, it was on with 35 paddlers eager to set forth. Now in its fourth year and UC Davis professor Dr. Alex Forrest delivers a talk at Whale Bay in Lake Tahoe. limited to only 50 paddlers, the event has become a must-do for kayakers as far away as Oregon Kayakers in the Tahoe Keys Scott Fitzgerrell in his new handmade wooden kayak and Illinois. Several have paddled all three years and are signed up for the fourth. It’s a unique event, especially given the on-beach and on-water lectures from UC Davis professors and TERC personnel. In addition to the learning opportunities, the route provides excellent wildlife viewing and wonderful views of every mile of the shoreline, including a stop in Emerald Bay. articles.text: Emily Anne Somers of Pasadena, a former Piedmont resident who attended Piedmont schools from kindergarten through 12th grade, passed away peacefully at age 38 on May 16, 2024 from a rare form of carcinoma. A graduate of Piedmont High School and UC Davis with Highest Honors, Emily also studied Drama at Oxford University. She enjoyed a much too brief but successful career in the Entertainment industry as an outstanding actor in film and television and as a film producer and playwright. At the time of her passing, Emily was an executive with Entertainment.net. Emily and husband Geordie are forever grateful to family members and friends who contributed to the GoFundMe effort. Emily will forever be remembered for her unending love, warmth, intelligence, creativity, energy, sense of humor and inclusiveness. A private family grave site service was held at East Lawn Cemetery in East Sacramento on May 19. In lieu of flowers, expressions of sympathy in memEmily Somers, a graduate of Piedmont High School, died on May 16 at age 38. ory of Emily may be made to the charity of your choice. Emily is survived by her beloved husband of 4-1/2 years, Geordie Robinson, her loving and beloved parents Diana (Christman) and Alvin Somers of Rancho, Murieta, CA, and parentsin-law Wendy McCue and Terry Robinson of Sydney, Australia.

articles.text: It had been a while since the group walked Crest Road just past Hampton Park. Crest is a long, slow climb and is a bit of a challenge, so members of Walking Wednesdays decided to go down rather than up. The group wend up Hampton Road, made their way to Estates Drive and then came down Somerset Road to Crest. The walkers continued to Hampton Road past Crocker Park to Hampton Park. The park was buzzing with students playing baseball and other games on a Wednesday morning. It was a group of fifth graders from Oakland’s Crocker Highlands School having their end-of-year field day. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the park’s history was shared with the walkers. This land is part of 50 acres that Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer purchased in 1911. Titus intended to build a mansion, but the new City of Piedmont raised property taxes dramatically in 1912, and he left town. In 1914, James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of the land for his home. He was a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, which began in 1910, and in 1921 Tyson made the land that is now Hampton Park available to the scouts for an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938, the Tysons also made the land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land, which was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 1950s and 60s, the space was a dusty, sometimes muddy little league baseball field. Later, youth soccer was played there often on a soggy field, as underground water was an ongoing problem. In 2000, the Piedmont Play School building was constructed at the back of the park. Dramatic improvements to the park were made during 2017 in a $2 million public/private partnership. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field much more serviceable. The climb went up Hampton to the lower portion of Inverleith Terrace to Estates Drive and crossed the Oakland/Piedmont city line to Somerset Road. At an elevation of 657 feet, there were views of Oakland and the Bay in the distance. Going on Somerset, the walkers crossed into and out of Piedmont three times. Somerset’s hillsides showed signs of recent slides with large, blue tarps trying to protect the soil. One very large home was high above the street with an outside elevator on the steep slope. The group finally came to Crest with its many beautiful Tudor style homes and made their long descent. When they got back to the Exedra, they had completed a 4-1/2 mile walk with great weather, some good exercise with friends, and lots to see. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among the 40 walkers and three K-9 best friends on last week’s walk were Irene Thompson, Chuck Oraftik, Jasmine Cai, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Tina Shum, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Stella Houston, Charlene Louie, Quincy Dong, Elizabeth Richter, Rick Eigenbrode, Edith Lee, Alicia Rivera, Peggy Shultz, Adrienne Hamlin, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Renee Goldhammer, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Alan Goldhammer, Matt Gerhardt, Jim Kuo, Ken Hubbert, Lori Austin, Lois Price, Jim Kellogg, Dottie Hutch, Helen Dong, Kat Lang, Albert Chen, Mark Davis, Melba Yee, Brenda Ferrero, Rob Smith, Priscilla Wanerus, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Avelina Buijs and Yolanda Jenkins who were walking with the group for the first time. A group photo was taken in front of Hampton Park.
articles.title: Wednesday walkers visit Hampton Park

articles.text: Mary Finley, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away peacefully on May 14, 2024 surrounded by her family. Born Mary Gaines on December 20, 1933 in San Diego, she was the second daughter of Captain Oliver and Phyllis Gaines. Mary had a unique childhood growing up with her sister, her mother and her grandmother in Vallejo. During the entirety of WWII, her father was a Prisoner of War after being captured on Guam following the bombing of Pearl Harbor. These were formative years for Mary, being raised by three generations of strong women. After the war, Mary’s family moved to the Elmwood district of Berkeley where she attended Berkeley High and UC Berkeley. She met her neighbor and future husband, Hugh Dozier Finley, on Christmas day in 1949. To be with Hugh on his deployment in Oahu, Hawaii, they agreed to forgo a traditional wedding and were married in a small ceremony on Whidbey Island in Washington in 1952. During Hugh’s Naval career, Mary had a chance to live in many parts of the country, making and re-making a home 19 times. Mary would often remark on these varied experiences with curiosity, humor and occasional disbelief. She didn’t understand why the washing machines in Florida laundromats were separated by “white” and “colored” until she realized that the segregation didn’t refer to the color of the clothes. Mary and Hugh had a son Bob in 1958, and in 1962 they welcomed their daughter Patty. In 1971, Hugh retired from the Navy and the family moved to Piedmont. Returning to the Bay Area, Mary reconnected with Long time Piedmont friend Mary Finley passed away on May 14, 2024. many friends and family, including the community at St. John’s Presbyterian Church in Berkeley where she was a lifelong member. She was active in her children’s schools, taking part in AFS, CHIME and parent boards (at the time, mothers’ clubs). Mary also volunteered at Children’s Hospital, Panhellenic/Sigma Kappa, and DAR. She was grateful to live in the family home, a backdrop for countless happy gatherings and celebrations, for 53 years until her death. Mary is survived by her son Bob Finley (Regina Hawkins), her daughter Patty (Carter Dunlap) and her three grandchildren: Taylor Brooke Naylor (Chris Naylor) Trevor Fleshman (Ana Szaky), and Morgan Finley. She is predeceased by her husband Hugh and her sister Pat. She missed seeing the arrival of two great-granddaughters by a matter of weeks. Leaving her family with grace and love, she will be greatly missed. A private memorial service is planned.
articles.title: Mary Finley dies at 90

The park was buzzing with students playing baseball and other games on a Wednesday morning. It was a group of fifth graders from Oakland’s Crocker Highlands School having their end-of-year field day. Drawing on Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, the park’s history was shared with the walkers. This land is part of 50 acres that Louis Titus, a Berkeley real estate developer purchased in 1911. Titus intended to build a mansion, but the new City of Piedmont raised property taxes dramatically in 1912, and he left town. In 1914, James Tyson, a lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of the land for his home. He was a strong supporter of Piedmont Boy Scouts, which began in 1910, and in 1921 Tyson made the land that is now Hampton Park available to the scouts for an outdoor camp. During the Great Depression in 1938, the Tysons also made the land available to the Piedmont schools. A WPA project leveled the land, which was intended to be the site of a future “East Piedmont” school. However, it was never built. In the 1950s and 60s, the space was a dusty, sometimes muddy little league baseball field. Later, youth soccer was played there often on a soggy field, as underground water was an ongoing problem. In 2000, the Piedmont Play School building was constructed at the back of the park. Dramatic improvements to the park were made during 2017 in a $2 million public/private partnership. Drainage and artificial turf were installed that made the field much more serviceable. The climb went up Hampton to the lower portion of Inverleith Terrace to Estates Drive and crossed the Oakland/Piedmont city line to Somerset Road. At an elevation of 657 feet, there were views of Oakland and the Bay in the distance. Going on Somerset, the walkers crossed into and out of Piedmont three times. Somerset’s hillsides showed signs of recent slides with large, blue tarps trying to protect the soil. One very large home was high above the street with an outside elevator on the steep slope. The group finally came to Crest with its many beautiful Tudor style homes and made their long descent. When they got back to the Exedra, they had completed a 4-1/2 mile walk with great weather, some good exercise with friends, and lots to see. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among the 40 walkers and three K-9 best friends on last week’s walk were Irene Thompson, Chuck Oraftik, Jasmine Cai, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Tina Shum, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Stella Houston, Charlene Louie, Quincy Dong, Elizabeth Richter, Rick Eigenbrode, Edith Lee, Alicia Rivera, Peggy Shultz, Adrienne Hamlin, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Renee Goldhammer, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Alan Goldhammer, Matt Gerhardt, Jim Kuo, Ken Hubbert, Lori Austin, Lois Price, Jim Kellogg, Dottie Hutch, Helen Dong, Kat Lang, Albert Chen, Mark Davis, Melba Yee, Brenda Ferrero, Rob Smith, Priscilla Wanerus, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Avelina Buijs and Yolanda Jenkins who were walking with the group for the first time. A group photo was taken in front of Hampton Park. Obituary PHS graduate Emily Somers dies at 38 Emily Anne Somers of Pasadena, a former Piedmont resident who attended Piedmont schools from kindergarten through 12th grade, passed away peacefully at age 38 on May 16, 2024 from a rare form of carcinoma. A graduate of Piedmont High School and UC Davis with Highest Honors, Emily also studied Drama at Oxford University. She enjoyed a much too brief but successful career in the Entertainment industry as an outstanding actor in film and television and as a film producer and playwright. At the time of her passing, Emily was an executive with Entertainment.net. Emily and husband Geordie are forever grateful to family members and friends who contributed to the GoFundMe effort. Emily will forever be remembered for her unending love, warmth, intelligence, creativity, energy, sense of humor and inclusiveness. A private family grave site service was held at East Lawn Cemetery in East Sacramento on May 19. In lieu of flowers, expressions of sympathy in memEmily Somers, a graduate of Piedmont High School, died on May 16 at age 38. ory of Emily may be made to the charity of your choice. Emily is survived by her beloved husband of 4-1/2 years, Geordie Robinson, her loving and beloved parents Diana (Christman) and Alvin Somers of Rancho, Murieta, CA, and parentsin-law Wendy McCue and Terry Robinson of Sydney, Australia. Mary Finley dies at 90 Mary Finley, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away peacefully on May 14, 2024 surrounded by her family. Born Mary Gaines on December 20, 1933 in San Diego, she was the second daughter of Captain Oliver and Phyllis Gaines. Mary had a unique childhood growing up with her sister, her mother and her grandmother in Vallejo. During the entirety of WWII, her father was a Prisoner of War after being captured on Guam following the bombing of Pearl Harbor. These were formative years for Mary, being raised by three generations of strong women. After the war, Mary’s family moved to the Elmwood district of Berkeley where she attended Berkeley High and UC Berkeley. She met her neighbor and future husband, Hugh Dozier Finley, on Christmas day in 1949. To be with Hugh on his deployment in Oahu, Hawaii, they agreed to forgo a traditional wedding and were married in a small ceremony on Whidbey Island in Washington in 1952. During Hugh’s Naval career, Mary had a chance to live in many parts of the country, making and re-making a home 19 times. Mary would often remark on these varied experiences with curiosity, humor and occasional disbelief. She didn’t understand why the washing machines in Florida laundromats were separated by “white” and “colored” until she realized that the segregation didn’t refer to the color of the clothes. Mary and Hugh had a son Bob in 1958, and in 1962 they welcomed their daughter Patty. In 1971, Hugh retired from the Navy and the family moved to Piedmont. Returning to the Bay Area, Mary reconnected with Long time Piedmont friend Mary Finley passed away on May 14, 2024. many friends and family, including the community at St. John’s Presbyterian Church in Berkeley where she was a lifelong member. She was active in her children’s schools, taking part in AFS, CHIME and parent boards (at the time, mothers’ clubs). Mary also volunteered at Children’s Hospital, Panhellenic/Sigma Kappa, and DAR. She was grateful to live in the family home, a backdrop for countless happy gatherings and celebrations, for 53 years until her death. Mary is survived by her son Bob Finley (Regina Hawkins), her daughter Patty (Carter Dunlap) and her three grandchildren: Taylor Brooke Naylor (Chris Naylor) Trevor Fleshman (Ana Szaky), and Morgan Finley. She is predeceased by her husband Hugh and her sister Pat. She missed seeing the arrival of two great-granddaughters by a matter of weeks. Leaving her family with grace and love, she will be greatly missed. A private memorial service is planned.

articles.text: Fourteen members of the Piedmont Seniors ventured to the South Bay where they learned about the two technology giants of the Bay Area, Google and Apple. Google recently opened its “Visitor Experience,” inside the company’s Gradient Canopy office building in Mountain View. This is the first Google brick and mortar retail outlet on the West Coast. The Seniors were a little tentative about exploring this “city within a city” as protestors had gathered there the day before. Fortunately, the campus was serene when the group arrived. The actual offices are not open to the public, but the Seniors still managed to explore the huge complex of buildings, open spaces and sculptured gardens. It was interesting to observe so many Google employees riding the company’s blue, yellow and A miniature bicycle offered by Google for its employees. Piedmont Seniors gather in front of Google’s Gradient Canopy office building. Members of the excursion included (front): Elizabeth Wierzbianska (left), Sue Getreuer, June Cohen, Lois Horwitz, Barbara Bigelow, Arlene Garfinkle (seated); (back) Mona Jamieson, Mary Buller, Carole Jones, Greg Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein and Edith Hereso. Not pictured: Jim Ayotte. Piedmont Seniors take a break at the Apple Visitors Center: Barbara Bigelow (left), Edith Hereso, Jane Cohen, Mona Jamieson, Lois Horwitz, Carole Jones, Janet Epstein and Mary Muller. The Apple Visitor Center in Cupertino red bicycles around the massive campus as they went from one office to another. The Google store even sells miniature versions of these iconic bicycles.The company retail store was built so that the public could experience some of the latest gadgets made by Google. The newest phones and other devices are tucked away in the store’s nooks and shelves, and there is a “high-tech” flavor to the store. The visitor center also includes the Huddle, where they offer free events and workshops for visitors. In fact, during this visit the Seniors witnessed a Google docent explaining some of the features of Google to the foreign press! After the tour, they had lunch at the newly opened Google Café. It was noted that each table in the café had outlets for laptop computers so they could work while eating. After lunch, the Seniors headed over to the Apple Visitor Center in Cupertino. Apple Park, the massive corporate headquarters of Apple, Inc., was opened to employees in 2017 at a cost of 5 billion dollars! It appears as a massive ring, almost a spacelike structure that houses 12,000 employees. The cantilevered carbon fiber roof appears to float and is only supported by stone clad cores. This Center is the world’s largest naturally ventilated building and one of the largest on-site solar installations in the world. iPad, visitors can lift the entire roof to reveal the collaborative office pod layout. The latest Apple products are on display, along with a large screen that offers various topics to get the best use out of their many products for sale. The Seniors also visited the roof terrace for beautiful views of the main building and surrounding areas. Though offices are off-limits to visitors, learning the basics of these tech giants on this visit was very worthwhile. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, including monthly meetings, or to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator, Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov or call 420-3070 for more information. He asks Maggie if she would mind reading the first chapters of his novel, something his wife, Georgette (Julianne Moore), a chilly, successful professor at Colombia, has little interest in doing. They do have two children, but John is perpetually discontent and feels neglected by Georgette. His solipsistic narcissism – nicely disguised behind his charm and impulse to write and create – is only gradually revealed as the narrative evolves. And so begins a satirical, funny, romantic comedy that results in a tilted, quirky triangle: John leaves Georgette for Maggie who finally has the baby she wanted. Three years pass. John is still writing his original novel, Maggie is working, raising their daughter, and playing backstop for his two kids. Suddenly she begins to wonder if perhaps John was a mistake and thus arrives the essence of Maggie’s Plan: she settles on a scheme to send the purloined John back to Georgette. Right child, wrong guy she concludes. It’s Shakespearean in a kind of screwy, comedic way. John observes at one point that in every relationship one person is the gardener and the other the rose. For a time he got to be the rose, but Maggie grows emotionally tired of weeding the garden. This is a delightful film, charming and idiosyncratic. It also has a superb ensemble cast with Bill Harder and Maya Rudolph portraying a New York married couple with compelling exchanges, making excellent use of every moment they are on screen. Gretta Gerwig is perfectly cast. She is the ideal third corner of an endlessly interesting triangle, the quintessential New York Millennial. And, of course, when it comes to love and initial passion, well the best laid plans, so to speak, ultimately end in a series of unintended consequences, no matter how urbane those involved may be. At no time does writer/director Rebecca Miller (daughter of playwright Arthur Miller), to her credit, try to explain in any kind of esoteric jargon exactly what “ficto-anthropology” is. Fetishes, neuroses and dysfunction unpacked? Almost certainly...and in a nice way. Maggie’s Plan. Directed by Rebecca Miller. Starring Greta Gerwig, Ethan Hawks, Julianne Moore. 1 hr., 38 min. We’re watching Eastwood doing Harry doing Kowalski. In one scene, Kowalski points a vintage M-16 rifle at a gang member and snarls, through clenched teeth, “Get off of my lawn.” Ah, yes. You feeling lucky, punk? Are you? Is Gran Torino worth an evening? Definitely. It’s a familiar but involving story, and all the performances are excellent. articles.text: The hotel quickly became a popular destination and drew visitors who passed a pleasant Sunday at Piedmont Springs, strolling the meandering paths to the mineral springs and enjoying an excellent lunch or dinner. The dining rooms served fresh meat from nearby ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fresh fruit and vegetables from its gardens. The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here. The hotel thrived until 1892 when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive from downtown Oakland. The site would not be empty for long... but that’s another story. The mineral springs are still in Piedmont Park, but they were capped in the 1950s because the sulfur fumes offended many residents. The historical marker at the Veterans’ Building gives the location of the springs. To learn more about Piedmont’s history, see the Piedmont Historical Society website: Piedmonthistorical.org. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on March 28, 2018. The invention of the telephone is delayed by a dropped call.

Papahadjopoulos had an RBI. Jack Meyjes threw two innings in relief for two innings, striking out two and allowing no runs. 4-1 win over McKinleyville Piedmont opened the NCS finals with a 4-1 win against McKinleyville. They scored three runs in the bottom of the first inning and added one more in the bottom of the sixth. Starting on the mound was Seve Sanchez, who threw a complete game with three strikeouts and allowing six hits and one run. PHS turned three double-plays on the afternoon. “The mentality every game is to always throw strikes. We know we have a top defense behind us and this game showcased that pretty well. We started a little rough but strikes started going in there and balls started going on the ground,” Sanchez said. Final stats: Lagios and Krumins went 1-for-2 with a double and drew walks. Parker scored a run. Papahadjopoulos went 1-for-3 with a run. Shafer Dando went 1-for-3 with an RBI and run scored. Brandon Dicke went 1-for-2 with an RBI and a run scored. The dining rooms served fresh meat from nearby ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fresh fruit and vegetables from its gardens. The hotel also offered fine wine and liquor for those who did not care for mineral water. Fashionable San Franciscans would come for a week to escape the summer fog. Many hotel guests enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to buy land and build their homes here. The hotel thrived until 1892 when a spark from a faulty chimney started a fire on the roof. Hotel guests watched helplessly as the hotel burned to the ground before firefighters could arrive from downtown Oakland. The site would not be empty for long... but that’s another story. The mineral springs are still in Piedmont Park, but they were capped in the 1950s because the sulfur fumes offended many residents. articles.text: On Monday, May 20 Piedmont High School honored dozens of its highest achieving students at the annual Senior Awards ceremony in Alan Harvey Theater. articles.text: During the May 8 Piedmont School Board meeting the board shined a spotlight on the progress of the racial equity board policy approved in September 2020. The racial equity policy, a piece of the larger educational equity policy, received a thorough review four years into the work in a city hall packed with enthusiastic supporters. Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen called the current moment in history ripe to assess the progress of the policy. Especially, “in the midst of hateful narratives that are calling for the end of [Diversity, Equity, Inclusive and Belonging] work,” she said. Jean Takazawa, in her first year as the Director of DEI at PUSD, spoke at length about progress made with the restorative justice circles. Takazawak reiterated that she is firm believer in restorative justice and thanked students for their work. Takazawa and Restorative Justice Consultant Ina Bendich spent time last year in Spring training 35 high school students to be community circle keepers. “It’s one thing to say it in practice, but then it’s another thing to actually be in the classroom and have 25 kids do a circle,” said Takazawa. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich also delineated vital information during the board presentation. “I want to take a moment to comment on what it means to adopt a curriculum with an anti-racist lens,” said Dolowich. “To be clear, there’s absolutely no intention to adopt a separate standalone curriculum. This is a lens in terms of how we review, pilot, and adopt curriculum moving forward.” Dolowich then specified what an anti-racist lens looks like for a teacher in the classroom and three things they are asked to do. “One, as educators, to have a level of self-awareness and training. Two, to understand our own biases and specifically, implicit, biases that we bring,” said Dolowich. Dolowich concluded with what he described as most critical and fundamental for students. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Jewish Community held an evening of visual and sensory experiences titled “Truth and Remembrance” at the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) on Wednesday, May 15. Titled an “evening of visual and musical creativity, remembrance and honor,” the art installation featured video presentations, photography exhibits, musical interludes and a candlelit memorial dedicated to the lives lost in the Israel-Hamas war. According to organizers, approximately 200 people attended the event which took place between 7:00 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. The greatest contribution of the evening was made by the 35-year-old Israeli singer-songwriter and music producer Orion Stone. “We need to focus on the living, not on revenge,” declared Stone. “Our grandparents fled the Holocaust to create a better future in Israel, not to plot their revenge.” Three of Stone’s family members were killed during the attacks on October 7, 2023. articles.text: Donors to receive T-shirts The American Red Cross will hold a blood drive in Piedmont at Veterans’ Memorial Hall (401 Highland Avenue) this Saturday, May 25 from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. Additionally, the Red Cross has teamed up with the creators of the videogame Tetris to celebrate the game’s 40th anniversary. People who make blood or Power RED donations before June 9 will receive an exclusive Tetris + Red Cross T-shirt while supplies last. Donors will also automatically be entered for a chance to win a trip for two to New York to meet Tetris creator Alexey Pajitnov. According to the Red Cross, every two seconds someone in the U.S. needs blood or platelets, but only about 3% of age-eligible people donate each year. Blood donations through the Red Cross are used for patients in need of surgery, cancer treatment and transfusions for blood loss from traumatic injuries. In addition to traditional blood donation, the Red Cross will also be soliciting “Power Red” donations. In this new process, a specialized machine allows donors to safely donate two units of red blood cells during one donation while also returning any plasma and platelets to the donor’s body. This way, donors can give nearly twice the amount of red cells at one time and help more patients. Power Red donations are an effective method for busy donors looking to maximize their impact on the community. Power red cell donation takes about 20-30 minutes longer than a whole blood donation and you can donate approximately every four months. Donors may select either blood donation or Power Red donation at the time of registration. To register for an appointment, visit http://RedCrossBlood.org and enter sponsor code PIEDMONT, or call 1-800-REDCROSS. This is a city-sponsored event. Attendees who donate blood before June 9 will receive an exclusive Tetris-themed T-shirt while supplies last. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS
articles.title: Red Cross Blood Drive this Saturday

articles.text: Mayor Jen Cavenaugh’s State of the City address on Tuesday, May 7, gathered both city officials and members of the public at the Community Hall for a recap of the year’s accomplishments and a glimpse at the projects the City currently has underway. “Tonight is about celebrating Piedmont, not just for what it has been, but for what we’re building here together,” said Cavenaugh. “You’re here because you care deeply for our city and its future, and that’s what we’re celebrating.” A State of the City address is a recent tradition, according to former Mayor Bob McBain. “It’s not a long-term tradition, but it’s an effort which I thought made a lot of sense,” said McBain, who served on the Piedmont City Council from 2012 to 2020 and as mayor from 2017 to 2020. “I suggested that people do it because it’s a useful tool that lets people know exactly what their city government’s been doing.” Former mayor Margaret Fujioka delivered her State of the City address in 2016. McBain planned on delivering his own speech but had to cancel it due to restrictions on in-person gatherings during the COVID-19 pandemic. Previous mayor Teddy King delivered her speech in 2022. During her presentation, Cavenaugh noted several milestones in the past year including the expansion of the public safety camera and Automated License Plate Reader programs by the police department, as well as the launch of multiple new digital services by the City, including tools for submitting online planning and building permits and the new real-time crime map implemented by the police via Citizen Connect. Cavenaugh addressed challenges facing Piedmont including regional issues like rising crime, housing costs, and the growing demands on Piedmont including the City’s aging infrastructure. “We possess all the necessary ingredients – the vision, the leadership, and most important, the partnership with … our incredible residents to not only overcome these hurdles but to thrive,” she said. “I think that what came across was how much she has appreciated being in Piedmont, and appreciated the opportunity to serve the community,” said McBain. Mayor Cavenaugh delivers her speech in Piedmont Community Hall.
articles.title: State of the City Address

This way, donors can give nearly twice the amount of red cells at one time and help more patients. Power Red donations are an effective method for busy donors looking to maximize their impact on the community. Power red cell donation takes about 20-30 minutes longer than a whole blood donation and you can donate approximately every four months. Donors may select either blood donation or Power Red donation at the time of registration. To register for an appointment, visit http://RedCrossBlood.org and enter sponsor code PIEDMONT, or call 1-800-REDCROSS. This is a city-sponsored event. State of the City Address By Matt Simons Mayor Jen Cavenaugh’s State of the City address on Tuesday, May 7, gathered both city officials and members of the public at the Community Hall for a recap of the year’s accomplishments and a glimpse at the projects the City currently has underway. “Tonight is about celebrating Piedmont, not just for what it has been, but for what we’re building here together,” said Cavenaugh. “You’re here because you care deeply for our city and its future, and that’s what we’re celebrating.” A State of the City address is a recent tradition, according to former Mayor Bob McBain. “It’s not a long-term tradition, but it’s an effort which I thought made a lot of sense,” said McBain, who served on the Piedmont City Council from 2012 to 2020 and as mayor from 2017 to 2020. “I suggested that people do it because it’s a useful tool that lets people know exactly what their city government’s been doing.” Former mayor Margaret Fujioka delivered her State of the City address in 2016. McBain planned on delivering his own speech but had to cancel it due to restrictions on in-person gatherings during the COVID-19 pandemic. Previous mayor Teddy King delivered her speech in 2022. During her presentation, Cavenaugh noted several milestones in the past year including the expansion of the public safety camera and Automated License Plate Reader programs by the police department, as well as the launch of multiple new digital services by the City, including tools for submitting online planning and building permits and the new real-time crime map implemented by the police via Citizen Connect. Cavenaugh addressed challenges facing Piedmont including regional issues like rising crime, housing costs, and the growing demands on Piedmont including the City’s aging infrastructure. “We possess all the necessary ingredients – the vision, the leadership, and most important, the partnership with … our incredible residents to not only overcome these hurdles but to thrive,” she said. “I think that what came across was how much she has appreciated being in Piedmont, and appreciated the opportunity to serve the community,” said McBain. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons, Lead reporter Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery will celebrate its 100th annual Memorial Day service at 10:00 a.m. this Monday, May 27, in a ceremony which welcomes the public. It will include guest speakers from the Armed Forces, a salute to fallen and music tributes. The event will take place in front of the Veterans’ Memorial Stone on the main drive. Refreshments – including donuts, hot dogs, and coffee – will be served before and after the service. This is a free event, and no tickets are required for entry. “It’s a time where we gather the community and remind everyone, all our community members and veterans, about how much we appreciate the sacrifices of our servicemen and servicewomen throughout for their sacrifice,” said Kristie Ly, the event organizer at Mountain View Cemetery. “Even if we don’t know them, we must be grateful for their sacrifices. They risked their lives so we can live ours.” Every year, people from all over the Bay Area attend Mountain View Cemetery’s Memorial Day ceremony because of the loved ones they have buried there. The ceremony includes an appearance by Piedmont Highlanders Drums and Pipes, Piedmont’s bagpipe band, and Piedmont Scout Troop 6 as color guard, which will conduct a flag ceremony. Singing group Tosca will perform patriotic songs, and brass musicians with The Hardiman Trio will play taps. This year’s guest speaker will be Lt. Col. Bradlee Seehawer, an active-duty airman stationed at Travis Air Force Base. The Master Florists Association has donated long-stem roses for audience members to lay on their loved mone’s graves. Small American flags also will be available for guests. Notably, this year’s Members of the Piedmont Highlanders Drums and Pipes at a Memorial Day service at Mountain View Cemetery Photos by Mountain View Cemetery Mountain View Cemetery’s Memorial Day ceremony will be held by the Veterans’ Memorial Stone, upon which a member of the Valerio family will place a wreath. event will not include the Valerio brothers, members of the Sons of the American who traditionally conduct the event’s gun salute, due to the passing of their brother Benjamin in 2022. A member of the Valerio family will attend the service to make a speech and place the ceremonial wreath on the Veterans’ Memorial Stone. Mountain View Cemetery established in 1863, is one of the oldest cemeteries in the U.S., and contains a plot for veterans of the Civil War. The cemetery has been the final resting place of many prominent local figures over the past generations including Josiah Stanford, Julia Morgan, Isaac Requa, Douglas Tilden, James A. Folger and Andre Hicks. For more information about the 100th annual Memorial Day service, contact Kristie Ly at Mountain View Cemetery by phone at 658-2588. Three of Stone’s family members were killed during the attacks on October 7, 2023, and nine of them were kidnapped. and taken hostage by Hamas militants, where they currently remain. Between songs in both English and Hebrew, Stone shared the experiences of his family in the wake of the October 7 attacks, as well as messages of music, hope and humanity. “Music has the magical power to make real change in the world,” he said. “Music not only touches our hearts, it inspires action. Don’t underestimate your own influence. I’ve witnessed the profound impact of individual voices creating an unstoppable ripple effect. Each of us must be the voice of those that cannot be heard, and desperately need us all to bring them home and end this horrific war.” Stone also encouraged members of the event to take to social media. “We’ve seen 100 hostages released already. Advocacy works.” The event was organized by Piedmont residents Donna Friedman Meir, Nicki Gilbert, Sari Kaplan, Melanie Marcus and Sharon Sagiv, as well as local Bay Area caterer and educator Aliza Grayevsky Somekh of Bishulim Caterers. The group, which calls itself the “Jewish Community of Piedmont,” has an active newsletter on Listserv that it uses to publicize its events. Their previous art installation in November 2023, an empty Shabbat table in the parking lot of the Community Hall with a seat representing each hostage taken in the Israel-Hamas war, brought out an estimated 700 attendees. “Our group is not a political group,” explained organizer Donna Friedman Meir. “Our mission is to help educate, support and create meaningful connections inside and outside the Jewish community.” The event also featured a fundraiser for Kfar Galim, an educational youth village in Israel’s Hof HaCarmel, which is a regional council in the country responsible for governing several rural settlements spread across its area. Since October 7, 2023, Kfar Galim has made efforts to support children ages 12-18 who were forced to leave their homes and those who have lost family members either during the war or as hostages. The event’s sponsors included the Jewish Community Federation, Temple Beth Abraham, Piedmont Center for the Arts and Piedmont Education Foundation. The event was free and open to the public. articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) will host a community picnic at Piedmont Park on Thursday, May 23 from 5:30 to 8 p.m. As the school year comes to a close, it’s an opportunity for Piedmont groups and the broader community to come together. It’s also a thank-you for engaging in PADC programming and showing up to support PADC’s work this year. Everyone is invited to bring a blanket and their family, and to enjoy a relaxing beautiful late spring gathering. Now in its 21st year, PADC continues to advocate for diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging in Piedmont. It hosted the annual Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. celebration in January featuring Dr. Amber Johnson, the assistant vice chancellor and chief of staff in the division for equity and inclusion at the University of California, Berkeley. PADC also awarded nearly $2,000 in grants this year to support and develop programs in Piedmont classrooms. PADC members continue to serve as thought partners and collaborators with Piedmont city leaders, school staff, and other community groups. To become involved, message contact@padc.info. Piedmont’s school board approved a Climate Literacy Resolution in the May 8 board of education meeting. Veteran Piedmont science teacher John White gave a presentation late in the evening with the help of Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich and PHS senior Max Rivera. Piedmont becomes the fifth district in California to do so. PUSD will use the definition of climate literacy developed recently by Fremont Unified School District (FUSD). Fremont’s work is based the model resolution put forth by the SF Bay chapter of the Sierra Club. White said the work Fremont has done shows that climate literacy doesn’t take away time from math, English or any other subject. “It’s a theme. articles.text: Have you ever wondered what skills you need to work with animals at the Zoo? Zookeepers and veterinarians are skilled in making careful observations. An observation is when we gather information through our senses, such as seeing, hearing, or smelling. Making observations is an important part of being a scientist. The animals who live at the Zoo can’t talk, so zookeepers and veterinarians carefully observe the animals’ behavior to ensure their happiness and health. When we observe animals engaging with fun things in their habitat, eating, and resting, we can tell they are healthy and comfortable. If we observe animals sleeping more than usual, not eating their food, or limping, we know they may need help. Zookeepers and veterinarians are scientists because they write down their observations. This allows them to learn how animal behavior changes over time, and detailed observations help us make the best decisions about what the animals need and want. Activity You can make observations like a zoo scientist, too. You’ll need a timer, a piece of paper, a pencil, and one animal to observe. This animal could be a pet in your home, a lizard in your yard, or a squirrel at a park. If you can’t find an animal, you can also watch live videos of animals at the Oakland Zoo (oaklandzoo. org/webcams). Pick one animal to watch, set a timer for 10 minutes and write down every behavior you observe (zoo scientists call this continuous sampling). Try to write down at least one behavior each minute, even if it’s the same behavior twice. You can also draw a picture. After 10 minutes review your notes. What did the animal do the most? What did they do the least? Do you notice any patterns? Congratulations! You’re now an animal behavior scientist! Do you have a burning question for an animal expert? articles.text: After spending their mornings working hard on CAASPP state testing, eighth graders in Shannon Fierro’s Spanish class at PMS got to decompress and be artistic while learning about how to make paper mâché piñatas. The process, which lasted several days and was funded by a grant from the Piedmont MakQuinn Wagener shows off the hard work she put in to make Peppa Pig. Nylah Kim took what started as a tiny piñata and made a beautiful pineapple. Period 5 students display their creations. Ben Fisher and Ari Lopez get messy using old copies of the Piedmont Post to cover their balloon. Olivia Bailey, Ava Casalaina, Carina Vora and Sharlize Sahagon display their creative takes on piñatas. Zayd Mahmood, Rylan Patty and Cazden Canada enjoy the decorating process together. Diego Branneria helps out with the daily task of moving the piñata around school to dry and store them. ers, involved covering balloons with strips of newspaper dipped in flour and water. There was no shortage of newspaper strips, thanks to a donation from the Piedmont Post. The second step was decorating with tissue paper and of course, the most fun was popping the balloon and filling the piñata with candy. “I was so glad to have this amazing opportunity,” said Rabia Mahmood. “I will forever appreciate the amount of hard work put into making piñatas. It is an experience I will never forget.” Students also learned about the origins of piñatas from China and how they were originally filled with seeds and later gold coins when the tradition moved to Europe. Lucia Dorsey, Sadie Hartman and Izara Dando agreed: “We are so glad we got this opportunity to learn about a fun tradition of many cultures.” Even though it was messy and delicate work, Ethan Hammond said, “It was one of the most fun school projects I’ve done. An experience I’ll remember.”
