articles.text: Ukranian Vlad Putrenkov now delivering for the neighborhood Piedmont Post paperboy Vlad Putrenkov delivers papers for the neighborhoods of Requa, Highland and Wildwood. Ever y Wednesday after school, third-grader Vlad Putrenkov walks to the Piedmont Center for the Arts to pick up a stack of papers and tucks them into his canvas delivery bag. After folding his supply of papers, he delivers the Piedmont Post to subscribers on his route, which includes Highland, Requa and Wildwood Avenue. “The hardest part is carrying the bag,” said Putrenkov. “It gets to be around 15 pounds, once a month for the All-City edition.” After nearly three months on the job, Putrenkov can now land his papers squarely at front doors with startling accuracy. “It’s just like baseball,” he said. And Vlad loves baseball. Vlad began delivering in February 2024 when he was put in touch with the Piedmont Post by his mother’s friend, Mary Ann Parachini, who thought it would be a good way for him to meet members of the community. The son of Ukrainian immigrants Alexander Putrenkov and Maryna Putrenkova, Vlad and his family came to the United States in April 2022 following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian War just two months earlier. “It was scary,” recalled Maryna. “They were shooting. The city immediately closed schools, hospitals, and grocery stores were left without food. There were armed soldiers and tanks on the streets. The police ceased to exist, and thefts became more frequent. People were kidnapped.” Since moving to Piedmont with the help of a sponsorship from Piedmont Community Church, the Putrenkov family has adjusted well to the town. Maryna said the greatest surprise was the kindness of the community. “The Miller family took us in for a while and helped get Vlad into Wildwood School. They also introduced us to the church in Piedmont where we made many friends. We are very grateful to the Miller family and our church members for helping us adapt to this country at such a difficult time for us.” She also thanked Piedmont resident Mary Ann Parachini for allowing her family to stay at her house for a short period. “We are also very grateful to her.” Vlad currently attends Wildwood Elementary, where his mother also works as a para-educator. Vlad’s friends know he delivers the Piedmont Post, which he loves to mention on occasion. “Sometimes they say, ‘Oh, I want to do that, too,’” he giggled. “You just have to ask.” When he isn’t delivering papers, Vlad likes to eat ice cream in Piedmont Park and play his favorite sports – basketball and soccer and do martial arts. “Soccer is my favorite,” he remarked proudly. “My favorite position is to play striker.” Vlad thinks that if anyone else should have a paper route with the Post, it should be his best friend, Maxim, who also attends Wildwood Elementary. “He would be good at it. I think he would like to earn money.” For more information about getting a paper route with the Piedmont Post, please contact our office via phone at 652-2051 or via email at news@piedmont-post.com. articles.text: Photos by Becky Spies Xander Schulte-Sasse closed his high school career at the NCS Meet of Champions. Piedmont’s track and field team concluded its season at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions at Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 17-18. The year’s team had a school-record 21 athletes qualify for the prestigious event. “When we started the season we weren’t sure what to expect, with 79 of our 109 athletes being freshmen and sophomores. Fast forward to the end of the championship run and we learned that we had the focus, will power, and character to push through,” noted PHS coach Pouyan Assadi “My final takeaway is that we’ll have giant shoes to fill with some very highly talented seniors graduating, but we have the depth and upside talent to take things to the next level over the next few year,” Assadi added. Closing a productive high school career in a big way was Xander Schulte-Sasse, who placed sixth of the 24 runners in the 3200 meters with a time of 9:21.90. It marks a strong close to his high school career and senior year after suffering an injury late in the cross-country season in the fall. “Xander missed three months of training from November to the start of track season, and he worked super hard to get here. Around lap-six, the field thinned out and we knew that as long as he held on tight he’d get on the podium,” Assadi said. It was also a strong performance from hurdler Ella Yasar. A junior, she reached the finals of the 300-meter hurdles on Saturday, finishing fifth of eight finalists with a time of 47.03. The previous day, Yasar was sixth of 22 athletes in the preliminary round, clocking a 47.22. “Simply put, Ella got it done. She capped off her monster season with back to back PRs and got on the podium to claim her first ever MOC medal. I can’t express enough what a privilege it is to be her coach. She deserves every moment and I loved seeing her smile ear to ear,” Assadi said. Girls Results Senior Breah Bell competed in two individual events. She placed 13th of 23 in the long jump with a distance of 16 feet, 8.25 inches, while she was 14th of 24 in the 100 meter dash preliminary round in 12.66. Bell also competed on the 4x100 relay team as the anchor leg. The team of Bell, sophomore Miranda Liu, Yasar, and freshman Claire Aubrecht had a time of 50.46. just .01 of a second away from the next best school, St. Mary’s. 4x400 relay team of freshman Daniela Lucaccini, sophomore Junior Ella Yasar was fifth of eight in the 300 hurdles finals and qualified by placing sixth of 22 in the preliminary round.

articles.text: Piedmont wins Spirit Award at Spaghetti Western Tournament Piedmont Middle School’s ultimate team, Purple Reign, wrapped up the competitive spring season with a second place finish in Bay Area Disc Association’s premier youth ultimate tournament, Spaghetti Western on May 4 in Stockton. Purple Reign’s Varsity squad (seeded 7th out of 10 teams) competed in the Middle School Division 1 of the tournament, when torrential rain and winds suspended the tournament midway through the day. This was only the second year that the team competed in Middle School Division 1 play. Purple Reign went 2-0 in pool play thanks to a stifling zone defense that created turnovers that the team was able to turn into goals. The team beat Baja Sunset (a team from Tijuana, Baja California) 8-7 and the Claremont Seawolves 6-3. The team featured superb handling by Aidan Stewart (7th grade), Ari Lopez (8th grade), and Drew DeVries (8th grade); strong defense by Ariel Grossberg (8th grade), Noah Hildebrand (8th grade), and Shane McNulty (8th grade); and leading scorer, Ben McMurtry (7th grade). articles.text: Staff Photos Coach Jordan Seiden (left) talks things over with the football team following a spring practice session. Spring is a time when many high school football programs begin training and installing systems to prepare for the fall season. Last year Piedmont players were not on the field until the summertime. They had no home field due to renovation of Witter Field and with a squad of only 13 players. This time around, there’s no shortage of optimism after PHS won the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division title. It resulted in a varsity group of around 30 athletes reporting to training camp thus year, “We didn’t have spring ball last year. We had a small spring practice my first year. We’re about up to 30 today and 5-6 significant players aren’t here yet. We have some new faces,” coach Jordan Seiden said following practice on Monday this week. Junior Sam Shelby, entering his third varsity year, has watched the development of the Sam Shelby reels in a reception during spring practice team under Seiden. “Last year, we learned a lot and improved as a team; it showed on the field, for sure. This year, we can take all that knowledge and apply it on the field. You can see the differences between this year and previous years in how much we’re learning as a team, I think it’ll make a big difference this year,” Shelby said. There is a different vibe around the Piedmont High football team. It’s no-longer a team looking to revitalize itself as when Seiden took over in 2022. Instead it is a team looking to continue building its culture and lift more championship banners next fall. “It’s crazy to see. It all happened so fast to me. All the guys show up every day and put in the work on and off the field. It comes naturally now,” Shelby said. Piedmont captured last year’s Shoreline title by defeating Newark Memorial in a heated 29-26 victory on the road. It was the team’s first league championship since 2015. Next season, PHS and Newark will compete in the more difficult WACC Mission Division. In 2023, the Highlanders were forced to play the entire season on the road due to continued delays of the renovations at Witter Field. PHS will be back under the Friday Night Lights of Witter in 2024. “It’s great to see. We were wondering all winter about how many kids would come back. The optimism was high based off of last year’s progress. It’s a real football culture now, we had great support from parents who really understood the vision we had,” Seiden said. Shelby, a receiver and defensive back, finished last year’s season with several honors. He was the SF Chronicle’s Player of the Year for the East Bay region, was named to the Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team, the Mercury News’ All-Bay Area second team, and was the Shoreline Division’s Player of the Year. Shelby competed on the track team this spring but suffered a season-ending injury. He’s back at full strength in football practice and is looking to move past the track season. “It’s tough because I’m a competitive guy and I still had that itch when I got hurt. Track is a big part of recruiting for football too, so that kind of slowed things down. But we’re back now and I just have to put it behind me,” Shelby said. The Highlanders look ahead

articles.text: Piedmont Mountain Bike Team finished its season at the NICA NorCal Championship. Pictured are assistant coach Jamie Howard (left), Miguel Rivera, Max Rivera, Team Director Heidi Sawicki, Schulyer Sawicki, Mark Sawicki, Mark Hsia, and Co-Head Coach Eric Hsia. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team, which includes high school club racing and a junior development middle school team, competed in its final races over two weekends at Six Sigma Winery, a private ranch in Lower Lake. They recently raced the NICA NorCal League Championship on Sunday, May 19, while they also raced at Six Sigma the previous week on Saturday, May 11. Six Sigma Winery includes rolling and rocky terrain through oak trees around a meadow where teams camped. The high school course lap for varsity riders was 16 miles with 2,000 feet of elevation gain, the JV 1 race was 12 miles with 1,500 feet of elevation gain, while the JV 2 event was eight miles with 1,000 feet of vertical gain. NICA NorCal Championship In the Varsity Boys race, graduating seniors Max Rivera was 38th of 63 riders with a time of 1:42:05. Matteo Scanu placed 40th in 1:43:14, Schuyler Sawicki was 43rd in 1:44:02, and Mark Hsia finished 47th in 1:45:33. Sophomore Jasper Schuetz had another strong run in the Division 1 JV1 race, finishing fourth of 69 racers in his three lap race with a time of 1:10:46.12. Also in the event was junior Cary Ward in 36th in 1:20:45. In the D1 JV 2 event, sophomore Caleb Canada placed 53rd Varsity riders Schulyer Sawicki (left), Mark Hsia, Max Rivera, and Matteo Scanu following their race. of 63 riders in 1:03:32. Sophomore Olive Reining raced the JV2 girls’ race, placing 37th of 41 in 1:34.37. Six Sigma Slinger In the varsity race, Hsia, Rivera, Scanu, and Sawicki completed in a close pack with respective finishes of 23rd in 1:13:40, 24th in 1:13:54, 26th in 1:14:22, and 28th in 1:14:24 out of 37 contestants. Schuetz was second of 30 racers in the three-lap D1 JV 1 race in 50:25.48. Jasper battled Casey Warren from Berkeley High School all season and swapped the lead multiple times in their race. Ultimately, the final sprint for the JV1 Boys D1 race ended with Warren in 1st (50:22) with Schuetz only 3 seconds behind in 2nd (50:25). This put Jasper Schuetz of Piedmont High School on the podium in second place with 530 points for the 2024 NiCa NorCal East Bay Central Region Season. Ward was eighth of 36 in the D1 JV 1 race with a time of 55:20. Canada placed 29th of 40 in the D1 JV2 race in 45:11.78. Reining placed 28th of 32 in the JV2 girls’ race in 1:01:40. The middle school Piedmont Devo team also raced at Six Jasper Schuetz (far right) was fourth of 69 riders in the NICA NorCal Championship on May 19.

articles.text: PBSF names “Livin’ The Dream” award winners The Dragons of the Piedmont Softball Foundation won the East Bay Pony Premier League on May 16. Pictured are (front) Robby Koch (left), Abe Mandel, John Arney, Drew DeVries, Ari Moskovitz, Russell Pan; (back) Coach Steve Long, Cyrus Emanuelson, Chase Knapp, Sean Heafey, Mateo Long, Alex Mikhailov, and Head Coach Danilo Juarez. The Piedmont Baseball Softball Foundation Dragons emerged triumphant as champions of the 2024 East Bay Pony Premier League (EBPPL). Comprising ten formidable 14U teams from the cities of Piedmont, Orinda, Moraga, and Lafayette, the EBPPL had d intense competition throughout the season. The Dragons, with an impressive regular-season record of 11-3-1, secured the top seed in the post-season tournament. Their dominance continued into the playoffs, where they swept four consecutive victories. In a high-stakes showdown on Thursday, May 16, the Dragons faced the third-seeded Lafayette Pink Bombers at Humphries Diamond. The Dragons executed near-perfection, shutting out their opponents with a resounding 9-0 victory. The pitching trio of Cyrus Emanuelson, Drew DeVries, and Robby Koch combined forces to no-hit the Bombers. Their stellar performance was complemented by outstanding defensive plays from Robby Koch, Abe Mandel, Mateo Long, and Russell Pan. Alex Mikhailov, behind the plate, thwarted base runners and allowed only one stolen base, while the Dragons swiped ten bases themselves. Offensively, Mateo Long, Cyrus Emanuelson, and Ari Moskovitz each notched two base hits. Long’s lead-off double in the fourth inning set the tone, and Emanuelson drove in three crucial runs. John Arney’s line-drive RBI single in the fifth inning ignited a five-run surge, breaking open the game. The championship clash on Sunday, May 19th, pitted the Dragons against the Piedmont Spartans. The Dragons wasted no time, erupting for six runs in the opening frame. Consecutive base hits by Long, Pan, Emanuelson, and Mikhailov fueled the offensive onslaught. Chase Knapp drove in a run and scored on Sean Heafy’s clutch two-out RBI double to add to the tally, securing a commanding lead. Heafey finished the day with three RBIs. Pan, Emanuelson, Mikhailov, and DeVries all contributed with two base hits. The combined efforts of Cyrus Emanuelson, Abe Mandel, and Drew Devries on the mound resulted in a four-hit shutout, sealing the Dragons’ championship triumph. The PBSF Dragons have etched their names in baseball lore, celebrating a well-deserved victory in the heart of East Bay baseball. PBSF “Livin’ the Dream” Award Winners The late Murray Davis, a former PBSF president, was instrumental in the development of the PBSF mission with his own youth baseball experience as his personal guide. Murray played youth baseball with Hall of Famer Robin Yount, and while Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. The award is not a MVP award, but rather it is given to a player who embodies positive, intangible contributions to the team, sportsmanship, perseverance, and a positive infectious attitude like Murray Davis. articles.text: Piedmont High golfer Bodhi Bloemker wrapped up his senior year in a big way. He placed second in the Division 2 North Coast Section Championship tournament on Monday, May 6 at Peacock Gap in San Rafael as an individual qualifier. As a result, he gained entry in the Division 1 NCS Championship on Monday, May 13 at Tilden Park in Berkeley, where he shot an 83. At the D2 NCS Championship, Bloemker finished with a round of 67, finishing one stroke behind first-place Will Chang from College Prep. “That was the best round of I’ve shot in a tournament, but I still feel like I left so much out there. I missed a lot of putts that were extremely makeable. On the last hole, I had one that lipped out which would’ve tied the leader,” Bloemker recalled. Peacock Gap is a Par-71 course, meaning Bodhi finished with a -4 under par. With a shotgun start, he began the day on Hole 13, a 190-yard par 3. It turned out to be an auspicious opening to the day. “It was a hard way to start on the first hole was a long par 3. I was nervous walking up to it, but it landed six-feet away from the hold and it turned out to be one of my best shots of the day. It got me started with a birdie and I was rolling after that. I went 2 over the next five holes, I just couldn’t miss,” Bloemker said of his day. Peacock Gap is a narrow course that Bodhi had never played before. To prepare, he participated in a tournament at Castro Valley’s Redwood Canyon. “Prior to D2 NCS, I played at a hard course in Castro Valley that was extremely narrow and I had to make adjustments. When. I got to Peacock Gap the course felt so much wider than I thought PHS senior Bodhi Bloemker finished second at the NCS with a Championship red-hot 67 in the Div. 2 tournament and an 83 in Div.1 it would be. Tilden Park, the hilly and treeladen course at Tilden is also a Par 71. Both NCS tournaments were 18 holes. Matches during the regular season are nine holes. “I had played individual tournaments before. A lot of the guys on the team haven’t played full 18s before, so I think people were getting used to that at the league championship,” Bloemker said. He was the only senior on Piedmont’s roster this season. His second-place finish was one of the best results in PHS golf history. Bloemker hopes to walk on to the college gold team at NYU in the fall. “It was a fun year. I didn’t expect that much from this golf season, to be honest. All of the college recruitment was pretty much off the table. But throughout the year, I just got better and better. It helped that I had such great teammates and it motivated me,” he said. Murray played youth baseball with Hall of Famer Robin Yount, and while Murray didn’t have the same skills of the future hall of famer, Murray was fond of telling anyone that his love of the game helped Yount fulfill his achievements in baseball. Former PBSF Board member Barry Barnes said, “Every time I asked, ‘how are you doing, Murray?’ His response was almost always, ‘I’m living the dream man, living the dream.’” Murray carried the positive attitude from youth baseball throughout his life. After his passing in late 2012, PBSF created the “Livin’ the Dream” award in his honor. The “Livin’ the Dream” award is given to one player on each team. The award is not a MVP award, but rather it is given to a player who embodies positive, intangible contributions to the team, sportsmanship, perseverance, and a positive infectious attitude like Murray Davis. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s summer season opens on May 30 with Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas the composer completed before his death in 1791. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920’s Berlin cabaret. Kim, who conducted The Magic Flute with multiple European companies as well as with the Washington National Opera, will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation of the opera in nearly a decade. The cast includes New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, nine performances of The Magic Flute are scheduled between May 30 and June 26. To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. articles.text: The American Conservatory Theater (ACT) closes its season with the five-time Tony Award winning production, The Lehman Trilogy, performing at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theater through June 23. Written by Stefano Massini, adapted by Ben Power, and directed by Sam Mendes, The Lehman Trilogy follows the rise and fall of the Lehman brothers and the largest financial crisis in U,S, history. “In the grand tapestry of human drama, The Lehman Trilogy unfurls as a magnificent saga,” said Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “Its epic scope, gorgeous stagecraft, and riveting narrative illuminate the rise and fall of a family empire – and leaves us thinking about its legacy and where we go from here. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s newest production, Head Over Heels, premieres this Saturday, May 25. Head Over Heels is based on a book of the same name by Jeff Whitty, and adapted for the stage by James Magruder. The play mixes pop punk and poetic prose as it explores a royal family’s narrative of love, friendship, gender, and sexuality to the tunes of the 1980’s all-female rock band The Go-Go’s. “I am really excited to delve into the theme of self-acceptance that Head Over Heels highlights,” said Director Mel Martinez. “To speak your truth is scary, but when you are truly yourself, everything looks better – even tastes better! It’s like being in love. I also love these characters to bits. This beautiful adventure they go on helps them break the molds society is comfortable with, and I find that inspiring.” Head Over Heels will be performed on the Berkeley Playhouse stage through June 30. To purchase tickets, visit https:// tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/. Berkeley Playhouse’s newest play, Head Over Heels, opens on Saturday.
articles.title: Head Over Heels premieres Sat. at Berkeley Playhouse

articles.text: An exhibition featuring the work of widely-recognized photographer Irving Penn is on view at the de Young Museum in San Francisco through July 21. Penn is Vogue Magazine’s longest-standing contributor, and he has become the most influential fashion photographer in the postwar era. Known for his use of neutral backgrounds, Penn emphasized models’ personalities through their gestures and expressions. The exhibition includes 175 photographs, spanning every period of Penn’s nearly 70-year career and ranging from early documentary scenes, celebrity portraits and workers with the tools of their trades to abstract nudes and fashion studies. This presentation also features a special section of photographs made during Penn’s 1967 trip to San Francisco, where he captured scenes from the iconic “Summer of Love.” Included are his portraits of hippies, members of the Hells Angels Motorcycle Club and local rock bands the Grateful Dead and Big Brother and the Holding Company. On Saturday, May 30, the exhibit’s co-curator Jeff Rosenheim will share various stories on pieces being shown and what transpired behind-the-scenes in making this exhibition. The lecture is free and begins at 2:30 p.m. in the museum’s Koret Auditorium To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ irving-penn?mc_cid=20ab0f- 52d7&mc_eid=573801a180. articles.text: Annual event has florists interpreting classic art with flowers Opening night during Bouquets to Art in 2023 at the de Young Museum. The de Young Museum will be holding its annual floral exhibition Bouquets to Art from June 4 to June 9. Celebrating its 40th anniversary this year, Bouquets to Art allows museumgoers to engage with the de Young’s expansive collections in a novel way – with floral interpretations of some of the museum’s classic art. For one week only, the leading floral designers of the Bay Area will return to the galleries this summer to showcase their creative botanical arrangements inspired by museum masterworks. From sculptures to sketches, nothing remains off-limits as a source of inspiration. Florists will then display their works in front of the various paintings, woodcarvings and other pieces for audiences to see. Photo by Drew Altizer Photo by Drew Altizer Kirk Wilder and Jeremiah Allen reinterpret Berkeley #3 (1953) by Richard Diebenkorn for Bouquets to Art 2023. Photo by Drew. Altizer Pico Soriano reinterprets A Taste of Gumbo (1990) by Robert Colescott for Bouquets to Art 2023. Photo by Valerie Lee Valerie Lee of J. Miller Flowers reinterpreted The Wild Swan (1900) by Alexander Pope for a previous year’s Bouquets to Art. This year’s exhibit marks the 25th year that Valerie Lee of J. Miller Flowers has participated. In previous years, Lee has interpreted paintings of dresses, sunsets and swans as striking, vibrant flower arrangements. This year, she will have a floral piece based upon the museum’s collection of New Guinean ceremonial shields. Lee said that the most difficult part of the exhibition has always been keeping the flower fresh between showings. “That’s the challenge of participating in this. You want to make sure every museumgoer has a chance to see the same, refreshing flowers,” she said. The exhibit will also feature a raffle of fresh arrangements from the museum’s flower cart, and eventgoers are encouraged to take part in engaging lectures with renowned designers and authors happening throughout the week. Opening night is Monday, June 4, at 5:30 p.m. Complimentary parking in the Music Concourse Parking Garage is provided for all guests. Food and drinks will be prepared and served by McCalls Catering & Events. The de Young Museum is located at 50 Hagawara Tea Garden Dr in San Francisco. Tickets can be purchased online at www. famsf.org or by phone at (888) 901-6645. Advance tickets are required for this event.
articles.title: Bouquets to Art arrives June 4 at de Young Museum

Friday, May 24, 7:30 p.m. Circadian String Quartet Concert Known for performing classical and contemporary repertoire with folkloric or cultural significance, Circadian String Quartet will present an exciting concert called Love and Chains, featuring the premiere of three acts of its newly composed chamber opera, Euridice’s Defiance. This opera, composed by David Ryther with a libretto by the novelist Kimiko Guthrie, reimagines the Orpheus and Eurydice myth as a modern-day detention story. The concert also includes works by Claude Debussy, Anton Webern, and Iranian-born Sahba Aminikia. The opera will feature soprano Lily Storm and the Circadian String Quartet, consisting of David Ryther & Monika Gruber, violins; Omid Assadi, viola; and David Wishnia, cello. Advance tickets $25 general, $15 Seniors/Students, available at www.eventbrite. com/e/894985956087. Saturday, May 25, 8:00 p.m. Clerestory A Cappella Vocal Concert Notes and Letters: Music of Brahms and the Schumanns. Clerestory takes a look into the complicated relationships between Clara Schumann, Robert Schumann, and Johannes Brahms, through their music and their correspondence. The music they wrote reveals themes of longing, love, loss, and redemption, expressed through the natural world. Pianist Kymry Esainko returns to collaborate with Clerestory for the first time since 2012. Clerestory is the Bay Area’s singer-led vocal chamber ensemble founded in 2006 with members from San Francisco’s finest professional vocal groups, including Chanticleer, Philharmonia Baroque, and American Bach Soloists. Advance tickets are available at www. eventbrite.com/e/881575886207! Saturday, June 1, 6:30 p.m. Claudia Marseille Book Launch At age four, Claudia Marseille was diagnosed with a severe hearing loss. With determination and the help of powerful hearing aids, she learned to hear, speak and lipread. After earning master’s degrees in archaeology and in public policy, and finally a Masters in Fine Arts, she developed a career in photography and painting, and a classical pianist. Marseille will read from her memoir, But You Look So Normal: Lost and Found in a Hearing World. Admission is free and the book will be available for purchase. Refreshments will be available before and after her talk, Doors open at 6 p.m. ********** Please note that during many weekend afternoons and evenings in May each year, PCA is used by music teachers to showcase their students’ progress and achievements to the parents of those students, providing the students the opportunity to perform in front of an audience, an essential element in learning to play a musical instrument. articles.text: Denzel Washington and Viola Davis have offered to filmgoers not only a master class in acting, but Washington, as director and actor, has created a startlingly fine film adaptation of August Wilson’s 1983 Pulitzer Prize-winning play, Fences. For the actors, it’s a tour de force bringing to bear their immense talent. They are remarkable in their ability to so completely inhabit the characters – Washington as Troy Maxson, a 53-year-old trash collector who carries with him a stone of embitterment, and Davis as his wife, Rose, who has invested 18 years of her life standing besides him, shoulder to shoulder, all while remaining undaunted. The place is Pittsburg. The year is 1957. The setting, in great part, is the backyard of the Maxon’s hard-used brick row house. It’s summer, and it’s there in that enclosed space, that Troy and his friend and fellow trash collector Bono (Stephen Henderson), return each day after work. While sipping gin, they reflect on life as they know it to be. Troy, once a gifted baseball player in the Negro league, laments the color barrier that kept him from breaking into the majors. He insists – reaching down into a well of anger and regret – that his color kept him from fulfilling a dream that was all but within his grasp. Jackie Robinson shattered that ceiling of bigotry in 1947, but it was too late for Troy. They are remarkable in their ability to so completely inhabit the characters – Washington as Troy Maxson, a 53-year-old trash collector who carries with him a stone of embitterment, and Davis as his wife, Rose, who has invested 18 years of her life standing besides him, shoulder to shoulder, all while remaining undaunted. He insists – reaching down into a well of anger and regret – that his color kept him from fulfilling a dream that was all but within his grasp. articles.text: a team of government assassins (to include anyone he has recently associated with, such as Danny) as well as two black op assignment associates. With his years of experience, Henry is not an easy kill and so he grabs Danny, calls a friend, and they fly south to Cartagena, Colombia, where it’s assumed they can vanish. For reasons still a mystery, the bad guys find them. And so begins act two, which is when the story falls off the rails and in just a few scenes goes from a solid enough plot to that familiar geography known as suspend your disbelief. Apparently, the three-letter agency this time sends not a team of paramilitary types, but just one exceptionally skilled killer who is Henry’s doppelganger, only a lot younger. A fact that Danny immediately notices. Who the killer is and why he is sent to take out Henry involves a Gemini black ops project director Clay Verris (Clive Owen), a previous mentor of Henry’s. Suddenly DNA and cloning are involved, taking the story into the realm of sci-fi/fantasy, which only slows down what was, until then, a pretty good story that didn’t need a surreal plot detour. There are two questions begged: what’s a multi Oscar winner like Ang Lee (Brokeback Mountain, Life of Pi) doing at the helm of a poorly written, pulpy B-movie like “Gemini Man”? Was it the new de-aging film technology when applied to Smith allows him to play both roles (aging retiree and young wannabe hit man)? Or was it the opportunity to shoot the film in an accelerated frame format (120 frames per second as opposed to the standard 24 frames per second), which allows the colors to really pop. Cartagena is shown in vivid pastels, the narrow street buildings all but glowing and gorgeous. There is one scene where a sky blue jeep drives along a raised highway and all but demands that the audience not take their eyes off what is less than an extraordinary car. It was the contextual color that created a can’t look away moment. In thinking back on the look of the film, I never found the 120 frames a distraction; rather there were moments that were incandescent. The thing is that it was Ang Lee’s rep as a superb filmmaker that caused me to watch Gemini Man and not to forget the proven charm of Will Smith whose characters are usually saturated with an insouciance style. But neither Lee, nor Smith, nor Winstead can save this film from its failure of imagination. Gemini Man. Directed by Ang Lee. Starring Will Smith, Mary Elizabeth Winstead, Clive Owen. 1 hr., 57 min. articles.text: Chris Honoré The BFG is a remarkable animated story, directed by Steven Spielberg, steeped in wondrous characters and gentle goodwill. With one exception, and it’s that exception that gives me pause when suggesting this feature film. All things considered, it may be best suited for youngsters on the cusp of tweenhood. But more about that later. The narrative, based on the popular Roald Dahl 1982 novel of the same name, begins with 8-year-old Sophie who lives in a Dickensian orphanage. Unable to sleep, she often roams the dark hallways, or often stands looking out her bedroom window, staring down at the shadowed streets of London. On one such night, during the witching hour, she sees an extraordinary sight: a giant, carrying a suitcase and a trumpet, walking on the sidewalk below. We come to understand that his mission is blowing dreams through the opened windows of children while they sleep. Sophie, mesmerized by this enormous figure, unexpectedly locks eyes with the giant. Frightened, she turns and runs back to the safety of her bed (or so she believes). However, the giant, worried that Sophie might disclose his presence, reaches through the window into her bedroom, and scoops her up, deciding to take her back to Giant Land. Sophie is breathtakingly afraid. Of course, she’s heard the A scene from The BFG tales about how giants not only capture children, but they regard them as tasty morsels. However this giant, when Sophie tells him why she is terrified, laughs. He explains that he is a BFG, a big friendly giant, and all he ever eats are snozzcumbers (like cucumbers) and only drinks frobscotties, a fizzy drink that causes loud flatulence, called whizzpoppers. Soon Sophie and BFG, despite their initial bickering, form a bond of mutual friendship. The neighborhood giants, much bigger than BFG, who is 24 feet tall, bully him, much to the consternation of Sophie. Naturally, when they come around she is told to hide. These massive, lumbering creatures are, after all, a rough crowd with strange, creepy names, like Fleshlumpeater and Bloodbottler. But then, as Sophie soon discovers, giants speak a very different language, a patois of sorts, mixed up but interesting. Sophie is precocious and therefore able to convince BFG that something must be done about these mean, rogue giants. She insists that they go to London and speak with Queen Elizabeth (Penelope Wilton) about the threat the giants pose to the children. And thus, Sophie’s adventure continues. Older kids will be captivated by this classic, wonderfully animated tale. But then there is something about giants that is impossibly compelling. The BFG. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Disney – stop-motion, animated. Voiced by Mark Ryance, Ruby Barnhill, Penelope Wilton. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Now streaming on prime/Disney+/Fandango. articles.text: Edited by Jay Russell Pick out your first summer read before May ends. The Indie Next List’s recommendations, curated by independent bookstore owners and staff, will help you find it. This list for May features fun Romance and Mysteries titles, and many other genres. The Indie Next List consists of only the newest releases, with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small bookstore culture. Real Americans Fiction “Rachel Khong’s latest tells the story of a first generation American’s adulthood and her teenage son looking for answers 20 years later. Real Americans grapples with racial identity, family inheritance, and becoming one’s true self.” —Rebekah Rine, Watermark Books & Cafe, Wichita, KS sip an aperol spritz. Mack’s perfect vacation read is packed with murder, mayhem, and the funniest footnotes.” —Katie Fransen, The Novel Neighbor, Webster Groves, MO Miss Morgan’s Book Brigade Books, Historical Fiction “As a female Army combat veteran, I know all too well how women’s contributions get forgotten. pages.text: Wednesday, May 22, 2024 21 Edited by Jay Russell Pick out your first summer read before May ends. The Indie Next List’s recommendations, curated by independent bookstore owners and staff, will help you find it. This list for May features fun Romance and Mysteries titles, and many other genres. The Indie Next List consists of only the newest releases, with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small bookstore culture. May’s #1 Pick Indie Next List of Best Reads of May Real Americans By Rachel Khong, Knopf, Fiction “Rachel Khong’s latest tells the story of a first generation American’s adulthood and her teenage son looking for answers 20 years later. Real Americans grapples with racial identity, family inheritance, and becoming one’s true self.” —Rebekah Rine, Watermark Books & Cafe, Wichita, KS sip an aperol spritz. Mack’s perfect vacation read is packed with murder, mayhem, and the funniest footnotes.” —Katie Fransen, The Novel Neighbor, Webster Groves, MO Miss Morgan’s Book Brigade By Janet Skeslien Charles, Atria Books, Historical Fiction “As a female Army combat veteran, I know all too well how women’s contributions get forgotten. Follow ‘Kit’ Carson as she and women from all walks of life bring hope and books to families devastated by the German occupation of France in WWI.” —Casey Luke, The Book Shoppe, Boone, IA May’s #1 pick of the month is The Ministry of Time by Kaliane Bradley. The Ministry of Time By Kaliane Bradley, Avid Reader Press/Simon & Schuster, Fiction “The Ministry of Time is a rare story that mashes up favorite time-worn tropes – from Star Trek to spy thrillers to Victorian romances — in a crucible of colonialism and the pitfalls of diversity in a near-future London. Oh, and it’s sexy as hell.” —Amanda Qassar, Warwick’s, La Jolla, CA Funny Story By Emily Henry, Berkley, Romance “If Emily Henry has thousands of fans, I am one of them. If Emily Henry has one fan, I am that one. If Emily Henry has no fans, I am dead. Daphne and Miles are the comfortable reliability of your dinnertime game show & the warmest quilt of eccentricities. A beautiful friends-to-lovers story.” —Nyawira Nyota, Page 158 Books, Wake Forest, NC All Fours By Miranda July, Riverhead Books, Fiction “A compulsively readable novel that follows a middle-aged artist as she undergoes a sexual and spiritual awakening. I loved this meditation on aging, restlessness, isolation, obsession, and the trials and triumphs of self-reinvention.” —Caitlyn Lyles, Hooked Community, Lansing, MI Long Island By Colm Tóibín, Scribner, Fiction “Eilis Lacey’s story continues in this superb follow-up to Brooklyn. Twenty years later, Eilis is stunned by her husband’s affair and the child he has fathered, and returns alone to her small Irish village. A beautiful, moving novel.” —Marilyn Negip, R.J. Julia Booksellers, Madison, CT The Paradise Problem By Christina Lauren, Gallery Books, Romance “A fake marriage trope with hints of Succession, all of the spice, and set on a beautiful private island? Sign me up! This had the predictability of a romance with enough intrigue to entertain. Christina Lauren just keep getting better!” —Amy Dickinson, Book Ends Winchester, Winchester, MA Sipsworth By Simon Van Booy, David R. Godine, Publisher, Fiction “Simon Van Booy performs a special type of alchemy by taking the simplest of tales — a woman approaching the end of her life discovering a small mouse in her house — and turning it into an astonishingly moving story of love and resilience.” —Luisa Smith, Book Passage, Corte Madera, CA Woodworm By Layla Martínez, Sophie Hughes (Transl.), Annie McDermott (Transl.), Two Lines Press, Horror “Martínez bends a haunting to her will. Woodworm is an offbeat tale about intergenerational trauma, classism, and the measures we take to grasp at anything resembling justice. I could taste its righteous malevolence; I savoured every word.” —Lauren Abesames, Wind City Books, Casper, WY Every Time I Go on Vacation, Someone Dies By Catherine Mack, Minotaur Books, April 30, Mystery “A mystery writer, a con man, and a ex-boyfriend walk into the Colosseum…in the perfect book to sit by the pool and read as you A Letter to the Luminous Deep By Sylvie Cathrall, Orbit, April 23, Fantasy “Sylvie Cathrall wraps cozy aquatic academia, strange abyssal mysteries, and deeply endearing characters into one delightful epistolary novel that is sure to reel you in! A fun and cozy science fiction/fantasy that pulls at your heartstrings!” —Oli Schmitz, Boswell Book Company, Milwaukee, WI Reading the Room: A Bookseller’s Tale By Paul Yamazaki, Ode Books, Memoir “Reading the Room is a precious artifact, a rare transmission from a truly great mind. If you’re a bookseller, pull up a chair and learn from a master; if you’re a reader, you’ll walk away with an entirely new appreciation for your local indie.” —Vanessa Martini, Green Apple Books & Music, San Francisco, CA 888 Love and the Divine Burden of Numbers By Abraham Chang, Flatiron Books, Fiction “Young recalls the first five loves of his life while making his way through his sophomore year of college with his sixth love, Erena. The book is warm and loving, peppered with ’80s and ’90s pop culture references and so many possibilities.” —Paul Swydan, The Silver Unicorn Bookstore, Acton, MA The Z Word By Lindsay King-Miller, Quirk Books, Horror “A gruesome, campy book that plays on the beautiful and messy dynamics of queer community, the seedy claws of rainbow capitalism, and every zombie killing method ever fantasized. The Z Word will leave you laughing between every shocked gasp!” —Skye Euryale, Literati Bookstore, Ann Arbor, MI Summers at the Saint By Mary Kay Andrews, St. Martin’s Press, Fiction “While the cover screams ‘beach read,’ Mary Kay Andrews fans know there’s more to the story. An emotional ride through grief, friendships, secrets, two murder mysteries, new love, and doing whatever it takes to protect home.” —Alecia Castro, Sweet Home Books, Wetumpka, AL Darling Girls By Sally Hepworth, St. Martin’s Press, Thriller “Sally Hepworth has masterfully crafted another suspense about families, secrets, lies, and love. Three foster sisters struggle to deal with their horrific past when a child’s bones are found under the foster home where they grew up.” —Sharon Davis, Book Bound Bookstore, Blairsville, GA The Paris Novel By Ruth Reichl, Random House, Fiction “I long to be a ‘tumbleweed’! Reading a book every day, helping customers, going on errands, enjoying a crepe, and living in the City of Lights! The Paris Novel is an escape into food, art, and couture with mystery and a cast you’ll adore!” —Sara Rishforth, Roundabout Books, Bend, OR A Magical Girl Retires By Park Seolyeon, Anton Hur (Transl.), HarperVia, Fiction “A quixotic blend of fantasy and reality. Magical girls are real, but so too are credit card debt, COVID-19, and mass unemployment. This strangely nostalgic, deceptively simple novel taps into both the dreams and anxieties of millenials.” —Shay Shortt, Brick & Mortar Books, Redmond, WA Colton Gentry’s Third Act By Jeff Zentner, Grand Central Publishing, Romance “I loved this second-chance romance about a high school football star turned Country singer who heads back to Kentucky after his marriage and career fall apart. Zentner captures Colton and Luann’s nostalgia and reconnection beautifully.” —Amy Traughber, pages: a bookstore, Manhattan Beach, CA Ocean’s Godori By Elaine U. Cho, Hillman Grad Books, Science Fiction “Elaine Cho articulates delicate, intergalactic celebrity politics and the nuances of queerness and racism in this incredible space opera, where we follow Ocean and her found-family crew setting off from a distant-future Korea.” —Devon Overley, Loganberry Books, Shaker Heights, OH Loneliness & Company By Charlee Dyroff, Bloomsbury Publishing, Fiction “Lee is an overachiever, but when she’s hired to teach an AI program the meaning of loneliness, her life skills are challenged. Dyroff draws an artful and memorable portrait of a woman trying to find answers in a world consumed by technology.” —Manda Riggs, Elm Street Books, New Canaan, CT Whale Fall By Elizabeth O’Connor, Pantheon, Fiction “A debut and a paean to the forgotten cultures on the British Isles. An intelligent yet innocent protagonist is confronted with ethnographers from the mainland, as class, gender, and education meet, while the prose mirrors island life.” —Richard Dixon, Politics and Prose Bookstore, Washington, DC The Demon of Unrest: A Saga of Hubris, Heartbreak, and Heroism at the Dawn of the Civil War By Erik Larson, Crown, History “Larson vividly depicts Fort Sumter’s untenable position, the ineptitude of the Buchanan administration, and the impossibility of a remedy from Lincoln, exposing Southern planters who linked slavery, secession, and war in a corrupted Code of Honor.” —Mike Hare, Northshire Saratoga, Saratoga Springs, NY Bite by Bite: Nourishments and Jamborees By Aimee Nezhukumatathil, Ecco, Essays “These essays are not just meditations on mouthwatering mastications of exotic fruits and savory favorites, but joyous and generous glimpses into the genius of a spirit that embraces the ascendance of the everyday into the sublime.” —Emily Liner, Friendly City Books, Columbus, MS How to Read a Book By Monica Wood, Mariner Books, Fiction “A charming novel about the power of books to heal, connect, and teach. A prison inmate, her reading group teacher, and the man damaged by the inmate’s crime are drawn together by their love of reading and their need for human connection.” —Susan Taylor, Book House of Stuyvesant Plaza, Albany, NY

articles.text: Dr. Kathy Hull, founder of George Mark Children’s House (GMCH) was recently honored with the Helping Heart Award from the Children’s Health Guild (CHG) for her extraordinary legacy of providing compassionate care for children with serious medical conditions. The presentation was made at the Children’s Health Guild annual Spring Gala at the Fairmont Hotel in San Francisco. “Receiving the Helping Heart Award was an uplifting honor, both for me and for the recognition of the positive impact that George Mark has had, and continues to have, on our community and beyond,” said Dr. Hull, a Piedmont resident. “From all of us at GMCH, enormous gratitude to the Children’s Health Guild for their unflagging support of the work that we do.” Established in 2004, George Mark is a model of compassionate care for children and young adults, and support for their families, provided in a beautiful home-like setting. As the pioneer in the United States for providing pediatric palliative care in a residential locale, George Mark has led the way for additional homes to adopt their comprehensive George Mark Children’s House’s Hummingbird Hill Garden was a specific source of inspiration for the Children’s Health Guild gala. “The Children’s Health Guild was honored to recognize Kathy and her legacy, George Mark Children’s House, with the 2024 Helping Heart Award,” said Christina Milne, CHG president. “She inspires us all to make the world a better place, and to lead with love and compassion and we are grateful as an organization to be a small part of her story, and to support the work for George Mark Children’s House.” Proceeds from the CHG gala are dedicated to support its two beneficiary organizations: George Mark Children’s House and UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, which provide children with much-needed healthcare services for a child’s full circle of life. George Mark has partnered with CHG since 2012. To mark the 20th anniversary of providing exceptional care to more than 1,100 children and support to their families, George Mark has planned a series of special events throughout the year, culminating with a celebratory gala on October 25, 2024. The House’s dedicated interdisciplinary team provides around the clock critical care including respite, transitional, end-of-life, and bereavement support. articles.text: Marilynn Hodgson, a longtime Piedmont resident, died peacefully the morning of May 11, 2024, just a few weeks shy of her 94th birthday, following several years battling dementia. Marilynn led a long, rich and fulfilling life. Born Marilynn Louise Davis in Grand Rapids, Michigan, she was the only daughter of Dr. David and Lilith Davis. She was raised in Grand Rapids until the outbreak of World War II. After Pearl Harbor, Dr. Davis enlisted and became the Chief of Psychiatry for the First Air Force, whose mission was the defense of the Northeast and Great Lakes regions of the United States. They moved about the East Coast until the end of the war, returning to East Grand Rapids, with Marilynn graduating from East Grand Rapids High School in 1948. Marilynn attended the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor (Go Blue) and graduated in 1952 with a BA in English and a minor in Art History. She was a member of Kappa Delta sorority and remained lifelong friends with sorority sister Peg Carter. In the Summer after her graduation, she traveled with three fellow Michigan alumni to Europe. From that point on, she was hooked on travel. Forever attracted to fashion and high society, in 1953 she attended the Tobé-Coburn School for Fashion Careers in New York City, aiming for a career in merchandising. She worked for a spell at J.L. Hudson (Hudson’s) department store in Detroit, Michigan. A visit to San Francisco to see her uncle, U.S. Army Colonel Carl Lundquist, the Commanding Officer at the Presidio of San Francisco his wife Thelma would forever change her life. She loved San Francisco and the Golden State on the spot. In 1956, she drove her dad’s 1955 Chevrolet west on what was then U.S. Route 40 (now Highway 80) and moved to California, where she remained for the rest of her life. She scored her first West Coast job as a merchandiser at the Joseph Magnin Company. She once dressed models for photo shoots, including future actress Tippi Hedren. Marilynn moved into the Lodge, a co-ed boarding house on Sutter Street (now the Queen Anne Hotel). She made many close friends and acquaintances. She also met at the Lodge her future husband of 54 years, Australian transplant David James Lambert Hodgson (1928-2011). David was an executive with P&O Lines who established the company’s first sales offices in North America. Marilynn and David married Longtime Piedmont resident Marilynn Hodgson died on May 11 at age 93. within a year and soon moved to Westwood then to South Pasadena and San Marino in Southern California to help establish the P&O Los Angeles office in downtown LA. There, they had two children, Suzanne and Mark. In 1967, David was transferred back to the Bay Area. So, the family moved north into their lovely home in Piedmont, where they resided for decades and made deep and lasting friendships in the community. Marilynn became an active member of numerous charitable and social organizations, among them C.H.I.M.E (Citizens Highly Interested In Music Education), Cedar Branch Auxiliary of Children’s Hospital, the Piedmont Garden Club, a Regent of the Piedmont chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR), the Book Club and the Piedmont Community Church. She was a huge supporter of the local arts and of her children, (both of whom were theatrically gifted) and of the sports efforts of her two grandchildren. David and Marilynn traveled the world, sailing on cruises and enjoying their many land trips throughout Europe. Marilynn spent her remaining years first as a resident at the Waterford at Rossmoor and finally at Aegis in Moraga. The family thanks the great memory care team that cared for her throughout the final two years of her life. Marilynn is survived by children Suzanne Kentris and Mark Hodgson, son-in-law James Kentris, son-in-law Tommy Hodgson, grandchildren Michael Kentris and Alison Nicholson, their spouses Amber Kentris and Jason Nicholson and six-month old great grandson James Nicholson, the little whippersnapper. A celebration of her life will be held at the Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue in Piedmont on Wednesday, July 31 at 10 a.m., with a reception to follow at the church.
articles.title: Marilynn Hodgson dies on May 11

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, May 22, 2024 Features The Wine Corner Robert Biale Winery – Master of Zinfandel By Pierre DuMont I have been writing about Zinfandel for 24 years. When I started this column in 2000, one of the largest wine tastings in America was the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP). Then held at Fort Mason in San Francisco, the event sprawled over two huge pavilions and involved hundreds of winery participants and thousands of tasters. It was a bacchanal for sure. I think it got too close to being out of hand and over the years the ZAP tasting has been moved around and scaled back. Wherever the venue, I have looked forward to the annual invitation to taste the new vintage of Zinfandels – and have not missed one. In the early days, there was much talk of the triumvirate of California’s great Zinfandel producers: the Three R’s – Ridge, Ravenswood and Rosenblum. Of those three, only Ridge remains at the top of its game. Ravenswood and Rosenbloom having been sold to giant corporate entities that have sucked the soul out of the wines. As I look back over the years of those tastings, there is one other winery that deserved a place in the Zinfandel pantheon. It has appeared in my top ten list year after year – Robert Biale. Robert Biale Winery remains what has it has always been – a small family owned and run winery that cares passionately about Zinfandel (and Petite Sirah). In 1937, four years after the repeal of prohibition, Pietro Biale, Robert’s grandfather, planted Zinfandel vines among all his other produce Robert Biale Winery 4038 Big Ranch Rd. Napa, CA 94558 (707) 257-7555 on his ranch in Napa Valley. The farm grew walnuts, prunes, other fruits and vegetables and also functioned as a chicken ranch. Pietro’s son Aldo expanded the production of Zinfandel which he sold “on the down low” to friends and neighbors to avoid government regulation. In 1991, Aldo’s son Robert Biale and a small group of friends established the Robert Biale Winery. The winery has now grown to produce about 15,000 cases annually and an amazing 30 different wines. I had the pleasure to visit Robert Biale Winery recently and winemaker David Natali poured some of the winery’s current releases. • 2023 Clementina Greco Bianco This is the only white wine Biale makes. An obscure Italian varietal, the Greco Bianco has a beautiful citrus nose with a touch of honeysuckle. On the palate, it is bursting with grapefruit and melon fruit flavors and has great acidity and balance. A perfect aperitif on a warm afternoon. • 2023 Rosato This rose is made from Sangiovese grapes. Aromas of strawberries jump from the glass. The body of the wine is light in the Provencal style with cherry fruit flavors and a clean dry finish. • 2021 Black Chicken Zinfandel This is sort of the flagship wine for Biale and is a blend of several different vineyards. It rolls effortlessly out of the glass with enticing scents of raspberries, raisins, and plums with nuances of cinnamon, cloves and earth. Medium-bodied and spicy in the mouth, it has soft tannins and refreshing acidity finishing on a lingering peppery note. • 2021 R.W. Moore Zinfandel This has often been my favorite of the Biale Zinfandels. It has dense aromas of blackberries, licorice, violets and leather, gaining more nuance with time in the glass. The palate is full-bodied and deeply fruited, with a firm and fresh frame and long, layered finish. It’s gorgeous and will have more to show with time in the bottle. • 2021 Grande Zinfandel The Grande has aromas of spice-laced red and black berries with accents of earth and Napa Valley’s Robert Biale Winery is home to many fine Zinfandels. tar. Medium-bodied, the palate is juicy with earth-laced fruits, pleasantly chewy tannins and a lifted finish. • 2022 Dickerson Zinfandel This iconic vineyard was made famous by Ravenswood Winery in the 1970s. The nose is delicate and pretty with scents of raspberry jam, apricots and citrus peel. The palate is medium to light-bodied, soft, bright and approachable with a floral character lingering on the finish. • 2021 Pagani Ranch Zinfandel This historic old vineyard is a field blend with lots of Alicante Bouchet, Carignan and who knows what else thrown into the mix. It opens with wild tones of earth, tar and graphite that give way to wild blackberries and currant hints. The palate is impressive, intensely fruited, silky and fresh. It finishes long with a flourish of floral perfume. • 2021 Palisades Petite Sirah In addition to their Zinfandel mastery, Biale has always had a In addition to Zinfandel Biale makes excellent Petite Sirah. great touch with one of California’s most underrated grapes – Petite Sirah. The Palisades Petite Sirah has pretty scents of cassis, violet, sagebrush and thyme. Full-bodied, its dark fruits are structured by firm, grainy tannins and just enough freshness to support the long finish. This wine is built to last decades in the cellar. articles.text: When you’re creating your estate plan, your biggest priority may be taking care of your family – your spouse, grown children, grandchildren, and other loved ones. And as you think of where you want your assets to go, you also may be thinking about how to be fair – but is that the same as treating everyone equally? In estate planning, “equal” doesn’t always mean “fair.” Let’s consider some factors that can help explain the difference: • Need – It’s highly unlikely that the individuals you want to include in your estate plan — especially your adult children – have the same family and financial situations. For example, you could have one child who is extremely successful and has no children of their own, while another child earns much less income and supports three children. Clearly, your two adult children have vastly different financial needs — so, you need to consider whether you want to treat them equally or fairly. If you decide you want to treat them fairly, you may want to divide your assets in a way that provides more help to the child who needs it most. • Abilities – You may well have some assets that you believe are more suitable for one child over another. This can be especially true if you are planning on passing on a family business. If you know that one child is the most capable of running the business or has been primarily involved in the business, then you may want to give that child control as a next-generation owner. Yet, this may not seem fair to another child, who might also express interest in the business, so you may want to look for ways to provide this child with enough assets to help make the overall inheritance more equal • Practicality – In some instances, you might think you can meet both the “fair” and “equal” criteria. Suppose, for instance, that you have a cabin or other vacation home that you think two of your children could share. In theory, this joint ownership might sound good, but in practical terms, it could cause problems. Are both children equally willing and capable of paying taxes and upkeep on the cabin or vacation home? What if one child wants to sell their share? And then, there’s the question of who gets to use the property at various times of the year. All these issues should be resolvable, but they can also cause great stress within the family. There’s no simple formula for solving the fair-versus-equal dilemma. But keep this in mind: Communicating your wishes to your loved ones while you are drawing up your estate plan can help reduce confusion — and hopefully lead to fewer hard feelings — when you are no longer around. By their nature, fairness and equality issues related to estate plans can trigger a range of emotions, and addressing these feelings beforehand can help provide a great service for your loved ones. You might also find that some objectivity can be valuable. That’s why, when creating your estate plan, you may benefit by working with a team of professionals, including your legal, financial and tax advisors. When developing your estate plan, you might well strive for equality and fairness but above all, you want to get things right. And careful planning, open communication and appropriate guidance can help go a long way toward this goal. articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson In my early 20s, less than a year out of college, I got addicted to berries. Until then I’d only eaten berries from the grocery store. But then I went to work at the Bainbridge Island Review, a twiceweekly community newspaper near Seattle, and was asked to profile a local strawberry farmer. He gave me a funny-looking, pinkish strawberry. I took a bite. Juice drizzled down the front of my shirt and ruined it forever. And the flavor! It was like having a Vosges truffle when all I’d known was Hershey’s kisses. You never find these local varieties in grocery stores. They can only last a day or two on the shelf before melting into goo. But the juiciness and sweetness hooked me forever. When the Pacific Northwest rains abated and I started riding my bicycle to work, I noticed an enormous blackberry bramble along the edge of a vacant lot. Every morning I’d stop, pick a half pint of berries, and eat them at my desk for breakfast. I plucked only those that were the softest, most sun-ripened, and most delicious. Years later, reading the book Jamberry to my young kids brought back memories of Bainbraidge Berryland and inspired me to re-create it at home. My taste buds were not the Once a staple of Native Americans, thimbleberries taste great but produce very little fruit. Raspberries fruit for most of the year, but the best season is spring. only motivators. I needed to grow something on my front yard’s split-rail fence to keep out loose dogs and kids. What could be better than a thorny berry bramble? After cultivating multiple varieties over the course of a decade, I strongly suggest you try the marionberry. Hailing from Marion County, Oregon, it’s the world’s most widely cultivated blackberry variety. Allowing the fruits to ripen on the vine before you harvest them will really set them apart from the ones you find in stores. Cultivating blackberries requires a lot of pruning. Left to their own devices, the vines will take over everything. I prune mine back severely in the fall, mostly give them free rein in the spring – lest I prune off a bunch of ripening berries – and then prune them regularly all summer. My raspberry patch has also fared quite well – perhaps too well. Lacking thorns and growing more upright than blackberries, raspberries share their cousins’ tendency to take over everything. I follow a similar pruning strategy as with blackberries, but raspberries can be harder to deal with as they will fruit almost year-round at the very tip of each shoot. My kids, who visit the raspberry patch almost daily, always complain when my pruning efforts lop off unripe berry clusters. Ripening loganberries Can’t decide between blackberries and raspberries? Try the loganberry. A cross between a North American blackberry and European raspberry, it makes plump fruits with a slightly reddish hue that taste amazing. This is hands-down my favorite berry. I haven’t had as much luck growing strawberries, though I’ve tried. They too often got eaten by squirrels or insects. If you want to cultivate something that you won’t find even at a farmer’s market, consider the native thimbleberry. Once a staple for Native Americans, thimbleberries grow across the West and Upper Midwest, though they are particularly dominant as an understory plant in the Pacific Northwest. Their delicious red fruits taste like stronger, less juicy versions of raspberries. Compared to most other berries, thimbleberries take well to shade but also produce much less fruit – typically only a handful of berries per plant. That’s probably why nobody sells them commercially. Not everything with value can turn a profit. That’s one thing that certain kinds of berries and certain forms of journalism have in common! Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. A split-rail fence is a great place for a berry bramble.
articles.title: In summer, it’s all about berries

articles.text: Dear Abby: We hope you can join us for a lot of sniffs and smiles on Saturday, June 1 between 2-5 pm at the 10th Anniversary of PINTS for PAWS, a benefit for the Berkeley Humane Society, 2700 Ninth Street in Berkeley. Voted the Best Fundraising Event in the East Bay, it’s one of the best ways to taste local craft beers, amazing ciders, and hand-crafted vodka while your dog stands by your side. There are yummy food bites too, which you can buy from a host of food trucks. Also on hand will be live music, crazy games, and even a live auction. All the while, you’ll meet hundreds of happy, friendly dogs as you support the Berkeley Humane Society’s mission to help unwanted puppies, dogs, kittens and cats. But note that PINTS for PAWS will sell out, so please buy your tickets soon. Our dear pets need your love and support. Drink Beer. Save Animals. That’s what we say. –Patches, a semi-doodle who was saved by a Piedmont family at BHS. Dear Patches: We won’t miss it. A couple of things: you must be at least 21 to attend this event (dogs can be younger), and IDs will be checked at the gate. Tickets are non-refundable but you can transfer them if you can’t make it. Tickets can be scanned from your phone or bring your printed copy. To learn more, call 510-845-7735 or buy tickets online at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/10th-anniversary-pints-for-paws-tickets-856420084527. articles.text: Members of the Walking on Wednesdays group are pictured last week on Bonita Avenue. Among those participating were: Bill Ahern, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Brenda Ferrero, Lois Price, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, Lee Hambrick, Priscilla Wanerus, Joyce Ahern, Jim Kellogg, Lori Austin, Alicia Rivera, Mark Davis, Bob Wong, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Linda Peacock, Peggy Schultz, Tina Shum, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Martin Levy, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Janet and Mark Laurent, Quincy Dong, Nava Shaham, Elizabeth Richter, Irene Thompson, Sherry Jacobs, Claudine Bach, Lisa Euphrat, Sarah Johnson, Ken Moy, Pat Nichols and Rick Eigenbrode, Alissa Quan, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Maci Negron, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Daksha Talati who was walking with them for the first time. There was big turnout of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays walk. Each year the Piedmont Planning Commission recognizes a small number of outstanding construction projects in Piedmont with Design Awards. They reflect the highest level of design excellence among all those that have come before the commission during the prior year. Three walkers, Eric Behrens, Mike Henn, and Jim Kellogg, are former planning commissioners. They said the selection process is for city staff to nominate their favorite projects and for the commissioners to pick the winners. This year the commission also introduced Sustainability Awards to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements like heat pumps, solar panels, and greywater systems into their homes. Seven projects were selected for 2024 Design Awards that span a range of project types. The walkers wanted to see the winners, and realized they could get to five of them in a 2.5-mile loop. The first was at 218 Bonita Avenue, Anna Putnam and Daniel Rampton’s winner of the Outstanding Integrated Addition award. Initially, the walkers couldn’t tell where the addition was due to a seamlessly-built extension to the original house. Only newer looking windows provided a clue. The next award winner was a bit of a hike, across town to Nace Avenue near Beach School. Stephen Selkowitz and Barbara O’Hare’s winner of the Excellence in Integrated Garage Design is at 22 Nace. The garage is a well-made, small replica of the home. Continuing on, they went to 11 Cambridge Way, the home of Peter Jaeschke and Supina Mapon, winner of the Excellence in Facade Composition Award. The new covered front porch with two white columns provide a dramatic new entrance. The walkers went over to 337 Magnolia Avenue, winner of the Outstanding Architectural Restoration award. Owners Lukas Bruggemann and Wendi Sue have done a great job creating a lovely “new” home, with one of only two magnolia trees on Magnolia Avenue. Then it was up to 319 El Cerrito, the home of Gina Song and David Woo and winner of the Excellence in Garage to ADU Conversion award with a new, large unit that complemented this beautiful home that was built in 1921. That did the morning’s tour. The group returned to Magnolia Avenue and finished their walk back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club (PGC) has proposed an ambitious new project to combat climate change. What if you could grow an entire native forest in your city in 20 years, rather than 200? This is the foundation of PGC’s latest initiative to establish an urban micro-forest within city limits. Aside from providing community members with the beauty of native plants, project chairs within the organization have stated that the project would reduce urban warming on the city’s streets, attract natural wildlife to the area, and maximize carbon sequestration. Project leaders went on to say that an urban micro-forest has the potential to be one of Piedmont’s most effective ways of combating climate change and that their goals could be met with spaces as small as ten square feet. “Climate change is a reality,” declared Cris Heins, co-chair of the PGC’s conservation committee and a lead organizer for its urban micro-forest initiative. “As part of the Garden Club of America’s directive in conservation we wanted to create a micro-forest Staff photo Indira Balkissoon (left) and Cris Heins, co-chairs of Piedmont Garden Club’s conservation committee, promoted awareness of micro-forests at the City’s annual Arbor Day celebration.
articles.title: Piedmont Garden Club lobbies for urban micro-forest

articles.text: Police Department to move some activities to Piedmont Center for the Arts Walk-in services at the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) will be temporarily limited beginning in June. During this time, services at the Police Station will be reconfigured to accommodate the construction of the department’s new dispatch center project. With the reception area under construction, visitor accommodations similar to those used during COVID-19, will be implemented. Commonly requested forms will be available outside the building, and a phone will be installed outside to connect visitors with police staff inside. During construction, the offices that were previously used for evidence processing, officer report writing, and briefings will be converted into an interim dispatch center. Police have been working with the Public Works Department and city IT staff for several months to rewire and retrofit the facility to ensure that service is uninterrupted during this transition period. With the Police Department’s floor space reduced by 32%, the department will relocate some of its functions to the “flex space” in the Center for the Arts building at 801 Magnolia Avenue. Police will use the space as a multi-purpose Photo by Piedmont Police Department The new interim dispatch center previously served as the Department’s space for evidence processing, report writing, and briefings.
articles.title: New dispatch center construction begins next month

articles.text: In the most recent school board meeting, May 8, teachers union President Elise Marks used the bulk of her allotted time to give an update on the contract negotiation impasse with the district. Marks cites progress with the district but a specific sticking point, that, as of May 13, the School Board has not agreed to publicly specify the point of disagreement. Marks and the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) informed Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and the school board that they really need to come to an agreement by Monday, May 20, in order to ratify it this school year. Classified CSEA workers of the district recently secured a contract with a similar raise structure to what Piedmont School District has offered teachers. Salary raises of 2.5 % this year, 4% next year and 3% for 2025-2026 were accepted in April. The district’s smallest labor group, the Association of Piedmont School Administrators (APSA), has around 20 employees, and includes Principals and Asst. Principals. APSA also came to an agreement with the school district with similar raise amounts during the May 8 board meeting, leaving only the teachers without new contracts. Classified CSEA workers of the district recently secured a contract with a similar raise structure to what Piedmont School District has offered teachers. Salary raises of 2.5 % this year, 4% next year and 3% for 2025-2026 were accepted in April. APSA also came to an agreement with the school district with similar raise amounts during the May 8 board meeting, leaving only the teachers without new contracts. articles.text: The writers of the Christian scriptures understood that their intended audience was likely to be very familiar with the stories, songs and admonitions of the Hebrew Bible. This is certainly true for the writer of the Gospel of Luke and its sequel, the Book of Acts. We see this in Acts chapter two as Luke tells the story of the Day of Pentecost. Pentecost originated as an agricultural festival, but by the time of Jesus it would also have been a covenant renewal ceremony celebrating the giving of Torah at Mount Sinai. Working with this background, Luke makes it clear that the gift of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost is akin to the gift of the Torah on the mountain as the people began their wilderness sojourn after escaping Egypt. On Mt. Sinai there was wind, fire and a voice, all representing God’s presence. On that Pentecost Sunday in Jerusalem, there was the rush of a mighty wind, tongues of fire descending on the heads of the disciples and voices of people of the many nations that had gathered in the Holy City, all representing the powerful manifestation of God’s Spirit. Fire was central to the theophany on Mt. Sinai. Fire was central to the theophany of Pentecost. I like what Baptist prophet Ken Sehested says about the fire of Pentecost. “The flame of the Spirit’s igniting presence does not scorch us. It makes us radiant.” Fire is both essential for life and a threat to life. Without the fire of the sun, we could not survive on planet earth. The coming of yet another fire season reminds us that fire is a clear and present danger. Fire can certainly scorch and scar us. On the pages of the Bible, God
