articles.text: Cyclists from Piedmont and across the Bay Area will mount their bicycles tomorrow and ride off to work and school in the Bay Area’s 30th annual Bike to Wherever Day on Thursday, May 16. An energizer station at Highland and Vista Avenues will dispense coffee and other refreshments to riders courtesy of Mulberry’s Market from 7 to 9 a.m. The station will be set up by the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Riders may also stop by for a free tote bag while supplies last, and a raffle entry to win a bicycle cleaning kit. Bike to Wherever Day was founded in 1994 to celebrate bicycles as a healthy way to get to work. Originally called “Bike to Work Day,” the event was renamed during the pandemic to encourage people to ride their bikes for other occasions as well, including running errands or meeting their friends. With transportation accounting for almost half of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging more residents to use greener commute options is vital to meeting the City’s Climate Action targets. The event is organized each year by Bike East Bay, a nonprofit organization based in Oakland. • Events for the public include: • Bike to School Day: Every year the Safe Routes to • • Schools Program in Alameda County joins the Bay Area region in celebrating May as Bike Month with the biggest celebration on Bike to School Day. Oakland Group Ride with Elected Officials: (7 a.m. - 8:30 a.m.) Join Mayor of Oakland Sheng Thao and members of Oakland City Council for a ride through the city. Riders will meet at various locations in the city before meeting at Frank Ogawa Plaza at 8:30 a.m. and then riding to Oakland City Hall. See website for details. Berkeley Group Ride with Elected Officials: (8:15 a.m.) Join members of Berkeley City Council for a ride through town. Riders will meet at the North Berkeley BART station and ride to Berkeley City Hall. Bike Happy Hour: (4 p.m. - 8 p.m.) Celebrate the Bike Day in the streets of l Old Oakland at Washington and 10th Street. Come together for Drake’s Beer and music by a DJ, To learn more about Bike Day, visit BikeEastBay.org/BTWD or contact Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun at 420-3058 (dergun@piedmont. ca.gov). A family prepares for their big ride at an energizer station near City Hall during Bike Day last year. from left to right.

PPD Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas stated that the space will be used “daily but for short periods” as needed until construction is complete. The impacts are significant for Piedmont Police who currently are working out of a space 40-50% smaller than those of similarly-sized agencies in the East Bay. “I’m not sure how comfortable [our officers] are going to be in a building that’s not the police department, but we just don’t have any other space here to do those types of things during construction,” Douglas explained. “I’m sure that as things move along in this construction process, we’ll learn what works and what doesn’t and we’ll adjust accordingly,” stated Douglas. Douglas also confirmed that the department has no plans to relocate any “heavy equipment” to 801 Magnolia Avenue and that the area will not be for dispatch use. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers has shared his appreciation to the community for their patience and support. “As the Police Department prepares for the Dispatch Center upgrade, we are mindful of the disruption the construction will cause to our working environment and to visitors. As we work to maintain uninterrupted high-quality public safety services, I am grateful to the community and especially to our valued partners at the Piedmont Center for the Arts for their support and understanding.” The Police Department will provide more information on procedures for walk-in visitors during construction in the coming weeks. Construction is expected to last 10 months. For more information on police services during the new construction, call the department at (510) 420-3000. Photo by Piedmont Police Department When construction is complete, the visitor reception window will be relocated to this wall. The new dispatch center will be in the space behind these doors, which currently serves as the City’s Emergency Operations Center as well as the Police Department’s conference and interview room.

articles.text: Organizers seek cars new and old for biggest city event of the year because people will remember these cars from their childhood.” Lazzarotto believes that this familiarity gives the event a nostalgic quality. Cars in the parade are usually arranged by decade. Cars from the 1950s typically ride together, as do those from the 1960s, 1970s, and so on will be welcomed. Every year in the parade these cars serve as spacers between musical acts and other similar entries, according to Lazzarotto. This ensures that no single act drowns out the others. “There was a time when we had three bagpipe bands in the parade and they really had to be separated,” he said. “You don’t want to hear During last year’s Parade, City Councilman Tom Ramsey and his wife, Ruth Ruark, drive Dan Erceg’s 1915 Pierce Arrow (right). Behind them in a red 1959 Triumph is Councilwoman Conna McCarthy and her Staff Photos Cory Smegal in the late Bob Ball’s legendary 1970 Pontiac during the Fourth of July Parade in 2021 three bagpipe bands at the same time.” And it’s not just the bagpipes. Every year, the Fourth of July Parade features marching bands, jazz bands, kazoo players, rock bands, and other noisemakers that would compete for loudness if it weren’t for the cars as spacers. In this way, the role of volunteer cars has evolved over the years from a nice-to-have spectacle to an absolutely necessary component of event planning. Furthermore, the parade committee goes to great lengths to ensure that the car owners are well-treated, given the amount of effort they put in to prepare for the parade. “It is not easy to enter a car in the parade and drive it. Many of these cars are very old. Sometimes they don’t start. They’ve got a bad battery. They overheat. They need to be detailed. Frankly, car owners go through a lot of work if they’re going to put their car in the parade,” he said. Community members who want their car to be in the parade should contact Roland Lazzarotto via email at r.lazzarotto@ sbcglobal.net. The Fourth of July Parade is the city’s largest public event of the year, drawing up to 6,000 spectators. The Fourth of July Parade Committee plans the event, which begins in February. In 2020, the parade was canceled because of COVID-19 concerns, only returning in 2022 with a mix of eagerness and cautious hesitancy. This will be the parade’s third year back since it was canceled, and the event is poised to be the parade’s first full-fledged return. 4th of July Parade

articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council’s annual Bike Rodeo drew a large number of kids to the playground at Beach School last Saturday, May 11. Beginning at 9:00 a.m. local youth gathered on their bikes to negotiate a detailed traffic course in multicolored chalk designed to teach children safe rules of the road. In addition to the traffic course, a variety of different stations had activities aimed at getting youth excited to use their bikes during the summer, including a trivia wheel, a station testing riders’ braking abilities, and a new crowd favorite. a pedal-powered, smoothie-making Bike Blender. “We had a lot more kids this year, which was great,” said Eris Turner, the Council’s Program Coordinator. “We’re always looking to get more word out and keep it going. The kids enjoy biking, and it’s a lot of fun to put on.” The obstacle course, the undisputed main event of the Bike Rodeo, has grown in complexity in comparison to previous years. The course had several roundabouts, four-way intersections with stop signs, and yield signs. Obstacles were color-coded for clarity, and signs were drawn on the ground in chalk. Police Explorers from Piedmont’s Post #911 also ran a station designed to test riders’ abilities to stop on a dime. The Explorers set up a strip where youth could build up speed and test how fast they could go, even using a radar gun. pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 5 By Matt Simons Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade Committee is looking for cars for the town’s annual parade on Thursday, July 4. Organizers say they could use about 20 more cars and are looking for enthusiastic volunteers throughout the community. Classic cars are preferred, but cars may be of any make or model as long as they have no obvious damage or blemishes. “A lot of this is because of the memories,” said Roland Lazzarotto, a parade committee member. “People will say, ‘oh, my dad had one of those’ or ‘oh, my grandfather had one of those,’ 4th of July Parade Committee needs cars Organizers seek cars new and old for biggest city event of the year because people will remember these cars from their childhood.” Lazzarotto believes that this familiarity gives the event a nostalgic quality. Cars in the parade are usually arranged by decade. Cars from the 1950s typically ride together, as do those from the 1960s, 1970s, and so on will be welcomed. Every year in the parade these cars serve as spacers between musical acts and other similar entries, according to Lazzarotto. This ensures that no single act drowns out the others. “There was a time when we had three bagpipe bands in the parade and they really had to be separated,” he said. “You don’t want to hear During last year’s Parade, City Councilman Tom Ramsey and his wife, Ruth Ruark, drive Dan Erceg’s 1915 Pierce Arrow (right). Behind them in a red 1959 Triumph is Councilwoman Conna McCarthy and her husband, Peter Craigie. Staff Photos Cory Smegal in the late Bob Ball’s legendary 1970 Pontiac during the Fourth of July Parade in 2021 three bagpipe bands at the same time.” And it’s not just the bagpipes. Every year, the Fourth of July Parade features marching bands, jazz bands, kazoo players, rock bands, and other noisemakers that would compete for loudness if it weren’t for the cars as spacers. In this way, the role of volunteer cars has evolved over the years from a nice-to-have spectacle to an absolutely necessary component of event planning. Furthermore, the parade committee goes to great lengths to ensure that the car owners are well-treated, given the amount of effort they put in to prepare for the parade. “It is not easy to enter a car in the parade and drive it. Many of these cars are very old. Sometimes they don’t start. They’ve got a bad battery. They overheat. They need to be detailed. Frankly, car owners go through a lot of work if they’re going to put their car in the parade,” he said. Community members who want their car to be in the parade should contact Roland Lazzarotto via email at r.lazzarotto@ sbcglobal.net. The Fourth of July Parade is the city’s largest public event of the year, drawing up to 6,000 spectators. The Fourth of July Parade Committee plans the event, which begins in February. In 2020, the parade was canceled because of COVID-19 concerns, only returning in 2022 with a mix of eagerness and cautious hesitancy. This will be the parade’s third year back since it was canceled, and the event is poised to be the parade’s first full-fledged return. Her smile brings out the sun on the darkest days. I wouldn’t have made it through this year without her. She truly is one of the most extraordinary people I’ve ever met. I am a junior in high school. I met Phoebe Soulis last summer at my friend’s birthday. She drove me home after because we had found out we live close to each other. We talked the whole way home from North Berkeley. I gave her some shoddy directions back to my house because I’m a horrible navigator. But even after we had made it to my house, I didn’t get out of the car for half an hour. I couldn’t, I was locked into a riveting conversation. I can’t remember what it was about, but I know that my dad had to call me to come inside. That was the last day without Phoebe being my friend. Granted, it took a couple months to really become friends, but I am grateful for every second. I know that I’m not the only person who is friends with a senior this year, and I know I’m not the only one who has to say goodbye. We are very, very close to resolution. Unfortunately, there is still a sticking point that we cannot get past. Under the rules of Impasse and Mediation, we can’t be specific in public about what the sticking point is, but I very much wish we could openly share what it is. This lack of resolution is, of course, exceedingly frustrating for all of us and for this community. The need to reach an acceptable deal is especially urgent given what’s happening behind the scenes with many Piedmont educators right now. I’ve stood here many times warning that if we don’t become more competitive with other local districts in terms of compensation that we won’t be able to attract or retain the best teachers for our students. In the last few weeks, we’re seeing the concrete results of the failure to get more competitive. As much as I’ve known this was coming, it’s still shocking to see. Piedmont has never been a district that teachers leave, certainly not to move to other districts within driving distance, but in the past couple of weeks, the who feels left behind in a way. My best friend is moving away, and I have one more year left. Of course, I will go to visit her like many others visiting their friends on different campuses. but it won’t be quite the same. I am happy knowing she will be starting a new life and getting closer to her dream of becoming a museum curator in Italy. Every senior leaving high school knows that they are leaving someone behind. But you only leave them behind if you forget them. The same is true when someone dies. The physical aspect of that person may be gone, but their spirit lives on in all those who loved them. That is why I implore every person who is saying goodbye to stay in touch. Call them, text them, visit them. Don’t forget. Don’t let the people you said goodbye to become distant memories of a happy time. This applies to the graduating class and the grades still there. I know that my life without my best friend would be one of monotony. Who would I quote Surf’s Up with? Who would I call when I had some inane errand to run and didn’t want to go alone? Who would come to my choir concerts other than my family? I don’t want to forget her or our experiences and adventures. I will have to adapt to a friendship that isn’t seven minutes away by car, but one that’s an eight-hour car ride or a two hour-plane trip. It will be different and difficult, but high school has taught me many things. Most importantly, no matter how cliché it is, good friendships are hard to find. I spent most of high school dealing with friendships that, truthfully, only brought me pain. It wasn’t until the end of last year that I started to find the people I am lucky to call friends. I have no idea what next year will look like. As a senior, I will be battling with the college application process like all the other seniors. My childhood will truly be coming to an end next year and I will be moving away. I will be my time to say goodbye – but that is next year. I am not done with this one yet. I will cling to every moment I get to spend with the graduating class of ‘24. I will cling to the last months the responsibility of college hasn’t set in. But most importantly I will spend each summer day that I can with my best friend, the wonderful Phoebe Soulis. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a student at The Bentley School. resignations have begun coming in, as teachers leave for Campolindo, Dublin, San Ramon, Walnut Creek, Berkeley, and more. These departures are in addition to the already unusually large number of resignations, leaves, and retirements we knew about in March. I know of six teachers so far … who have made their decisions final and have signed with other districts. I know many more who have offers in hand – sometimes multiple offers, with salaries $10,000, $20,000, $40,000 and even more above what the teacher currently earns in Piedmont. Often the health benefits are better. Every day, I learn of more teachers who are actively interviewing for jobs elsewhere. They include beloved veterans and dynamic young teachers, teachers in extremely hard-to-hire fields, people who’ve always said they planned to stay here until retirement, people who are the cornerstones of essential programs throughout the district. We cannot afford to lose them. Because our teachers are such strong candidates, they will surely receive offers from surrounding districts eager to snap them up. In the 24 years I’ve been here, I can think of maybe three or four teachers who have voluntarily left Piedmont to teach elsewhere locally. If we don’t arrive at a deal that makes staying here more economically viable, even larger numbers [of teachers] say they will be on the job market next spring. This is a disastrous situation. We know PUSD doesn’t have the means to match the compensation packages of those surrounding districts, but we need to close the gap to the greatest degree we can. Our teachers generally don’t want to leave. They love their students and colleagues and this community, and will make sacrifices to stay here if they can. But if the gap isn’t meaningfully narrowed, they’ll do what they have to do. We believe we are so close to agreement that waiting until late May or June for Fact-Finding – and therefore going into summer without a deal – will only cause more teachers with outside offers to make the choice to leave. To prevent any further loss of great educators, APT asks district leadership to agree with us mutually to formally end Impasse and make our most recent offers open to the public. Ending Impasse would also take the threat of a strike off the table, and lessen the anxiety the community has felt about that possibility. APT believes that if the community understands what’s holding us back from a deal, they will agree with APT’s position and see our path forward very clearly. APT is here and ready to talk at any time. We are asking the members of the School Board to please take that final step and reach an agreement.

articles.text: This month, observers in Nor ther n Califor nia were treated to a rare and dazzling display of colorful lights. These radiant lights, commonly known as the Northern Lights or aurora borealis, became visible in areas of the Bay Area due to a recent and intense geomagnetic storm. What triggered the geomagnetic storm? Multiple Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), which are large explosions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun’s atmosphere. At least four of these CMEs sent clouds of charged particles in the direction of Earth. As these particles interacted with the Earth’s magnetic field, they were deflected towards the magnetics poles, entering the atmosphere and producing auroras. Did you know? Due to the intensity of the storms, there was also a chance of disturbance in the Earth’s magnetic field, which may have resulted in communication disruptions and possibly power failures in the days that followed. A stellar sight to see Reflecting on this awe-inspiring weekend, we’re reminded of the beauty and power of Mother Nature. We’re not sure when we’ll have another chance to see the Northern Lights again in the Bay Area, but we invite you to join us for our free public telescope viewing events every Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., weather permitting. Visit chabotspace.org to learn more. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd. in the Oakland hills. Phone (510) 336-7300.

Northern Lights – Night sky lights up By Isabel Lopez This month, observers in Nor ther n Califor nia were treated to a rare and dazzling display of colorful lights. These radiant lights, commonly known as the Northern Lights or aurora borealis, became visible in areas of the Bay Area due to a recent and intense geomagnetic storm. What triggered the geomagnetic storm? Multiple Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), which are large explosions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun’s atmosphere. At least four of these CMEs sent clouds of charged particles in the direction of Earth. As these particles interacted with the Earth’s magnetic field, they were deflected towards the magnetics poles, entering the atmosphere and producing auroras. Did you know? Due to the intensity of the storms, there was also a chance of disturbance in the Earth’s magnetic field, which may have resulted in communication disruptions and possibly power failures in the days that followed. A stellar sight to see Reflecting on this awe-inspiring weekend, we’re reminded of the beauty and power of Mother Nature. We’re not sure when we’ll have another chance to see the Northern Lights again in the Bay Area, but we invite you to join us for our free public telescope viewing events every Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., weather permitting. Visit chabotspace.org to learn more. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd. in the Oakland hills. Phone (510) 336-7300. articles.text: Hana Thomas In the age of technology, social media and the Internet, and the proliferation of misinformation that surrounds us poses a threat to our country’s status as a democracy and its values. Misinformation is weaponized as a political tool, with both foreign and domestic sources. The spread of false narratives manipulates public opinion. In a political context, misinformation can take the form of false claims about electoral integrity, smearing political campaigns, and fabricated news stories to sway voters. While there are some obvious answers to this question, such as fake news being believed, there is some larger damage. The spread of misinformation poses a risk and undermines the democratic system that our society relies on. If people don’t know who or what to believe, they can vote based on false pretenses. The consequences of misinformation don’t stop in politics. With the use of misinformation, fake news, and AI, almost all media that we consume is at risk. These days with the surge of AI, determining real versus fake news has been more challenging than ever before. Using easily accessible AI, people can fabricate any image or audio recording they please. If people want to convince you of something, they now have the means to do so. Media literacy is one of the most crucial skills to learn in this age. Disinformation, misinformation and fake news are flooding the news we see every day. It can be easy for even educated people to see an outrageous news title and believe it without looking into it more. It is becoming more and more difficult to decipher real versus fake news. To raise the next generation in the current state of democracy, it is crucial to include media literacy education in schools. This type of education can easily be added into science, history, social studies, and English classes. Finland, a promising example, incorporates media literacy curriculum into their schools starting in preschool, with adult classes and resources for media literacy readily available. Finland leads the world in resilience against misinformation. of how to confirm real news, we can create more capable future members of society. articles.text: Fundraising concert held at Oakland Zoo in April Grateful Dead founding member Bob Weir is the latest celebrity to support one of Oakland’s hidden gems, Northern Light School, an independent progressive school in Oakland, dedicated to serving children from all socioeconomic backgrounds in grades pre-K to 8th. On April 19, Weir played an intimate benefit concert for Northern Light School. Past star supporters have included Bonnie Raitt, Peter Coyote, Jackson Browne, MC Hammer, and baseball star Vida Blue. At Northern Light School, 75 percent of students receive tuition assistance, compared to the national average for independent schools of less than 25 percent. 95 percent of NLS’ students are children of color, compared to the national average of 34 percent. Remaining steadfast to the school mission means a lot of fundraising for a small entity like Northern Light. Like other independent schools, NLS has experienced budgetary challenges coming out of the pandemic due to increased rent and salary costs to keep up with the ever-rising Bay Area cost of living. “We’re so grateful that Bobby did this for us,” said NLS Head of School Sanjev deSilva. “Times are tough and he totally came through.” The fundraiser was held in partnership with the Oakland Zoo, where Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia kicked off the evening with welcoming remarks, and guests got to walk through flamingo, tiger and giraffe exhibits on their way to the concert venue. A surprise moment of the evening was when one of Northern Light’s four founders, Michelle Lewis, announced that she would be donating her salary back to the school. “It’s for the children,” she said. “Anything for the children. When the founders and I opened the school in 1989, we wanted it to be for children from all walks of life, even if they couldn’t pay. It means so much to me that this same dream continues today.” Northern Light School prioritizes academic excellence as well as non-violence, acceptance of differences, respect for the environment and the moral advancement of humanity so that children develop an understanding that they have a responsibility to make a difference in the lives of others. The school boasts unique program offerings like an annual 8th grade trip to Washington, DC to learn about the importance of civic duty; and a biweekly Morning Circle to affirm the community’s values by discussing world events, celebrating important days, honoring cultural heritage, and hosting diverse speakers and performers. Over 90 percent of graduating 8th graders matriculate to private or parochial high schools and the same percentage attend and graduate from college. “Our annual benefit concert was a really big deal and affirmed all the love that Northern Light School supporters have at this time. Bobby Weir was a big part of that,” said deSilva. For more information contact the school by e-mail at: boardchair@nlsoakland.com

Misinformation is weaponized as a political tool, with both foreign and domestic sources. The spread of false narratives manipulates public opinion. In a political context, misinformation can take the form of false claims about electoral integrity, smearing political campaigns, and fabricated news stories to sway voters. While there are some obvious answers to this question, such as fake news being believed, there is some larger damage. The spread of misinformation poses a risk and undermines the democratic system that our society relies on. If people don’t know who or what to believe, they can vote based on false pretenses. The consequences of misinformation don’t stop in politics. With the use of misinformation, fake news, and AI, almost all media that we consume is at risk. These days with the surge of AI, determining real versus fake news has been more challenging than ever before. Using easily accessible AI, people can fabricate any image or audio recording they please. If people want to convince you of something, they now have the means to do so. Media literacy is one of the most crucial skills to learn in this age. Disinformation, misinformation and fake news are flooding the news we see every day. It can be easy for even educated people to see an outrageous news title and believe it without looking into it more. It is becoming more and more difficult to decipher real versus fake news. To raise the next generation in the current state of democracy, it is crucial to include media literacy education in schools. This type of education can easily be added into science, history, social studies, and English classes. Finland, a promising example, incorporates media literacy curriculum into their schools starting in preschool, with adult classes and resources for media literacy readily available. Finland leads the world in resilience against misinformation. By constantly reminding students of how to confirm real news, we can create more capable future members of society. Madeleine Mullin and Hana Thomas are students at Piedmont High School. articles.text: Tonight, May 15, the American Medical Women’s Association, Highlander Robotics FRC Team 8033 and Girl Scouts Service Unit 303 will present a special screening of the Paramount Plus award-winning film, Afghan Dreamers. Afghan Dreamers tells the incredible story of the Afghan Dreamers Girls’ Robotics Team, a group of Afghan schoolgirls who – led and inspired by Afghan tech entrepreneur Roya Mahboob – defied conservative gender roles to compete internationally in robotics. In doing so, they helped transform a people and nation. The team first gained international notice in 2017 when they were barred from attending FIRST Global in Washington, D.C., due to a travel ban against individuals from certain predominantly Muslim countries. Supported by international allies and with the intervention of members of Congress, the team was ultimately allowed to compete and went on to win several awards in the U.S. and internationally. Inspired by the Dreamers’ unlikely success, then-President Ashraf Ghani committed to building five STEM schools throughout Afghanistan. But the team’s journey came with many struggles, as the film poignantly demonstrates. The Dreamers then continued their international journey, transforming communities and bringing hope to women and girls along the way. But, as the film painfully shows, a tragic reversal of fortune came in August 2018 when the Taliban gained control of Afghanistan, and the girls, their coaches, and thousands of other Afghans were forced to flee their homeland. This film has special relevance to the Bay Area, as the Dreamers spent over a week in Piedmont hosted by a local family through the American Medical Women’s Association. During this time, the team had the opportunity to spend time with Piedmont robotics teams, Girl Scouts, and Boy Scouts. “Opening our home to the team was one of those unique moments in life that transforms the way you view and embrace the world and forges special friendships that last a lifetime,” said Douglas and Eliza Chin. Immediately following the screening on May 15, members of the production team will be joined by a former Afghan Dreamers team captain as well as an Afghan Girl Scout. They will share their perspectives on the film and the current status of women’s rights in Afghanistan, particularly with regard to education and work. The discussion will be moderated by an Afghan writer and human rights activist. The film has received critical acclaim internationally, awarded Best Human Rights Documentary at the Galway Film Fleadh, Runner-Up for Best Feature Length Documentary at Woodstock, Audience Choice Award at the Valladolid International Film Festival and Official Selection at the Heartland and Boulder International Film Festivals.
articles.title: Afghan Dreamers film at Driscoll Playhouse tonight

The morning started with opening assemblies and period 1 teachers leading discussions about the speakers they would hear and their areas of expertise or experience. Every student got to attend two of the 14 workshops, two concerts, a special lunch and participate in class discussions centered around diversity. This reporter first ventured to Diversity Day newcomer Sandi Hunt who was teaching a “foraging and wildcrafting” lesson on a little dirt hill bordering the school’s Magnolia Avenue side. Hunt brought various herbs and woodland discoveries to show students some of the many uses of plants with hopes of students becoming mindful stewards of the planet. Students first stripped pine needles from a branch before making an all-natural tea. Hunt procured and discussed a pine tree pollen said to slow aging and reduce fatigue. Hunt had made edible by cooking them in simple syrup. In Anjuna Lohnes’s 6th grade class next door, a jazz music workshop was conducted by Oluyemi “The Reedman” Thomas and wife, Ijeoma. With bass clarinet in hand he sprouted some of his jovial philosophy that keeps him jolly, and in good graces while generating joy wherever he goes. “It’s okay to be free with your expression,” he said. Thomas then challenged students in class to think about how they could decentralize themselves. Thomas’ wife, Ijeoma, teaches creative writing that meshes with her husband’s music. In the library, Piedmont parent Brij Kothari spoke about subtitling and literacy in India. Dr. Kothari and his innovated, researched, and nationalized the use of “Same Language Subtitling” (SLS) on entertainment content on TV, movie, and streaming platforms for mass literacy in India. Brij grew up in the Sri Aurobindo Ashram at Pondicherry and eventually achieved a Ph.D. in Education from Cornell University. He talked about his personal story and how a billion people in India are benefiting from same language subtitling on videos in Hindi. Another newcomer to the event was Mike Taylor, Executive Director of Bay Area Creative poetry collective. He used his past experience in teaching to lead a connected workshop on poetry and spoken word. Taylor worked with students to explore what makes up their personal identity and exemplified his ways of grasping the muse to create lyrics. Students used metaphor and simile and accepted See Diversity Day on page 31 Jairo Vargas of the Bayonics had middle schoolers Kidus Yalew and Gael Fierro come on stage to play the bongos and the tambourine, with student Logan Seto Nguyen (in back) on drums. Students Theo Mavrellis (left), Ruben Marangoly, and Mason Armstrong hang wish tags on a tree limb at the middle school to conclude Diversity Day. Diversity brunch for students was hosted by the PMS Parents Club. Committee leaders Dana Lung, Liz Cha, and Andy Tran coordinated 60 parent volunteers for pick up, set up, or serving food. Mike Taylor led Jessie Hare’s math class in a spirited lesson on the art of spoken word.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team had terrific results at this year’s North Coast Section Bayshore Championship on Saturday, May 11 at James Logan HS in Union City, resulting in 13 top-six finishes to automatically qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 17-18. The Highlanders also gained two more At-Large bids for the Meet of Champions, giving them 19 athletes spread across 15 events at next week’s prestigious meet. PHS athletes will now have a chance to qualify for the CIF State Championship on May Photos by Becky Spies Breah Bell qualified in two individual events for the NCS Meet of Champions and is also runs the anchor leg on the 4x100 relay team that qualified. Ella Yasar was third in the 300 hurdles and helped the 4x400 team qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions. Freshman Sebastien Swain will compete in the 1600 meters at the Meet of Champions. 24-25 at Buchanan High School in Clovis. The top three in each event will automatically qualify for State. “In the end every athlete we had hoped to get through to the NCS Meet of Champs got through, plus more. That’s about as good as it gets,” said coach Pouyan Assadi, “While we didn’t take 1st in any events this year our depth was on display as we’re sending the most athletes to MOC in school history.” It marked another stellar performance by senior Breah Bell, who qualified in two individual events plus the relays. Bell finished fourth of 23 sprinters in the 100-meter sprint with a personal record time of 12.55 seconds. She also claimed an At-Large bid in the long jump, finishing ninth of 22 with a distance of 16 feet, 7.5 inches. Bell ran the anchor leg of the 4x100 relay team, which included Miranda Liu, Ella Yasar, and Claire Aubrecht. Their team was fourth of 20 teams with a time of 50.03. According to school records on Athletic.net, Bell’s time in the 100 broke Toni Ali Daggao’s 100-meters record of 12.91 in 2017. “Our girls captains were the stars of the show, with Breah breaking the Piedmont 100m record. It’s nice having a group that’s so dependable,” Assadi said. Senior Jamie Schwarz qualified in the 800 meters, finishing fourth of 22 with a time of 2:23.24. She narrowly missed out on qualifying in the 1600, where she was seventh in 5:21.26. Schwarz also ran the third leg of the 4x400 relay team that was fourth with a time of 4:15.44. Schwarz ran with Daniela Lucaccini as first leg, Skylar Best as the second, and Yasar as anchor. Yasar had an impressive thirdplace run in the 300 meter hurdles in a field of 24 athletes, clocking a time of 48.47. Best also gained an At-Large big in the 1600 with a time of 5:26.81, finishing eighth of 22. The girls’ 4x800 team of Ryo Woltag, Caroline Taylor, Gladwin Horsely, and Nasreen Schulze had a big performance, finishing second of 13 with a time of 10:26.07.
articles.title: 19 athletes qualify for NCS Meet of Champions

articles.text: Both teams play this Saturday, May 18 Piedmont’s baseball and softball teams are set to embark on their Division 4 North Coast Section post-season journeys after both teams received firstround byes. The baseball team, seeded No. 2, will host the winner of No. 7 Fort Bragg vs. No. 10 Hercules on Saturday, May 18. The softball team with a No. 5 seed will play at No. 4 Fortuna on Saturday. BASEBALL Piedmont’s baseball team enters NCS with a 15-8 overall record and the Bo. 2 seed. After finishing the regular season in first-place of the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division, they faltered in an extra-inning battle to Alameda in the WACC Tournament semifinals, and lost 4-3. They are looking ahead to No. 7 Fort Bragg or No. 10 Hercules. PHS didn’t have any common opponents with Fort Bragg this year. As for Hercules, both Piedmont and the Titans faced Justin-Siena this season. PHS beat the Braves 1-0, but Hercules got demolished 17-0. The Highlanders enter post-season with one of its most complete lineups in coach Eric Olson’s career. Markos Lagios is hitting at a .372 clip, has a team-leading six home runs, 27 runs scored, 25 RBIs, 29 hits, and six stolen bases. He was recently named the Foothill Division’s Most Valuable Player. Piedmont also has options on the mound. John Olsen has been stellar with a 2.43 ERA over 40.1 innings of work with 40 strikeouts and two saves. Seve Sanchez has also been strong with a 1.34 ERA over 26 innings and 24 strikeouts. Peter Krumins, who slots in at shortstop, is also a force on the mound with 20.2 innings pitched with 25 strikeouts, and a 3.04 ERA. SOFTBALL The Highlanders walk into the NCS postseason with a 10-7 overall record and went 6-5 in the WACC’s Shoreline Division. They received a first-round bye in NCS as the No. 5 seed and are scheduled to face No. 4 Fortuna in the Quarterfinals on May 18. The NCS office elected to give the top six teams in the D4 playoffs a first-round bye, while the bottom four seeds play on May 15 to face No. 1 St. Helena and No. 2 Del Norte. Piedmont will travel five hours to Fortuna in Northern California for its Saturday meeting. The Huskies finished its regular season with a 16-7 overall record Staff Photos Markos Lagios has a .372 batting average and a team-leading six home runs. John Olsen has pitched 40 innings with 40 strikeouts and a 2.43 ERA.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s only diver, Nina Schwab, recently competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming & Diving Championship in the one-meter dive on Saturday, May 11 at Clovis West High School. She finished 16th of 28 athletes with a score of 429.55. To qualify for State she was fourth of 16 at the NCS Championships in Concord the previous week with a final score of 423.35. “The big thing is to just not get overwhelmed with how many great divers there are. I hit the board a couple times across a week, so going into States, I felt like I was starting to get some mental blocks. I feel like I did a good job. It wasn’t my absolute best, but I’m very happy with how it went,” Schwab said. Schwab’s venture into diving was a somewhat recent decision for her, making the decision to switch sports from gymnastics ahead of her junior year. Multiple fractures to her back, along with her uncle being a former diver, led Nina to make a decision about her athletic career. “I injured myself a lot in gymnastics and after fracturing my back a second time, I took some time recovering. Through the 6-7 month healing process, I realized I wasn’t getting recruited. I would’ve been trying to get back to a point where I was when I was 8-10 years old and I just didn’t want to do that,” Schwab said. “My uncle was a diver, so we talked about it and I decided I wanted to try. Two days later, I quit gymnastics,” she added. Schwab thinks her background in gymnastics helped with some aspects in diving, but noted the big changes were leaping off of a diving board compared to a spring board, as well as landing head-first. “It definitely helped, I wouldn’t be where I am without gymnastics. But I’m used to jumping off a spring instead of waiting for a diving board to carry you up. I also think landing on your head is pretty difficult. Letting the board do the work and learning to trust it was a big part of the learning process,” Schwab said. Two years later Nina has established herself as one of the best diving prospects in the East Bay. Her development has been faster than expected, admitting to still learning the sport and taking a few knocks along the way. “I’m still learning right now. I still feel like I’m getting used to the diving board and I still do little things that make me look like a gymnast. It was a quick transition,” Schwab said. Schwab competed with her club, Cal Diving Academy, in the U.S.A Diving Regional Championships in Chicago on May 4-5, where she placed sixth of 42 on PHS diver Nina Schwab finished 16th at the CIF State Championship. the one-meter dive. It was good enough to qualify for U.S.A Diving Zone Championships in Wisconsin on June 27. She will continue her diving career at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota. Nina Schwab became one of the best divers in the Bay Area after being a former gymnast. Nina Schwab describes her venture into the sport. She’ll continue competing at Carleton College.
articles.title: Diver Nina Schwab places 16th at State

articles.text: Piedmont High’s tennis team, seeded No. 7 in North Coast Section, saw its season come to an end on Thursday, May 9 in the NCS Team Tournament Quarterfinals, falling 7-0 to No. 2 Branson at the College of Marin in Kentfield. The Highlanders earlier defeated No. 10 Marin Catholic 4-3 at home on Tuesday, May 7. “We defeated Marin Catholic in the first round of the NCS team championships on Tuesday and then lost in the quarterfinals to Branson. There were some great matches both days,” coach Jim Landes said. Piedmont ends its season with a 13-10 overall record and will lose six players to graduation: Monte Imburg, Ben Breber, Graham Alban, Arun Brahma, Siddharth Bahtia, and Derek Chan. Imburg and Breber conclude their time at the school as fouryear starters in doubles and singles respectively. Imburg was the Post’s 2021 Freshman of the Year, and Breber was our honorable mention. Imburg graduates as the Western Alameda County Conference doubles champion. “The highlight for me was the end of Ben Breber’s and Monte Imburg’s great high school tennis careers, which was sad for both [assistant coach] Corey Reich and me. Ben gave me a hug after his match and it melted my heart, Corey and I loved coaching both of them. We will also dearly miss the four other seniors, Arun, Graham, Siddharth and Derek,” Landes said. 4-3 over No. 10 Marin Catholic Piedmont battled with Marin Catholic to a narrow victory, where No. 1 singles starter Lucas Smolko clinched the Highlanders’ fourth victory to claim the match day. He defeated Jack Millar in straight sets, including a heated second-set tiebreaker, winning by scores of 6-2, 7-6 (7-5). “The highlight of Tuesday was Lucas Smolko’s clinching win at #1 singles 6 -2 , 7 -6 (5) and the team lifting him up in victory,” Landes said. Also at singles was Breber winning in three sets, losing the first set but dominating the next two, 1-6, 6-1, 6-2. Nate Welch lost 6-0, 7-5 at No. 3 singles, while Alban lost a heated 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 match at No. 4. pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 13 Diver Nina Schwab places 16th at State By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s only diver, Nina Schwab, recently competed in the 2024 CIF State Swimming & Diving Championship in the one-meter dive on Saturday, May 11 at Clovis West High School. She finished 16th of 28 athletes with a score of 429.55. To qualify for State she was fourth of 16 at the NCS Championships in Concord the previous week with a final score of 423.35. “The big thing is to just not get overwhelmed with how many great divers there are. I hit the board a couple times across a week, so going into States, I felt like I was starting to get some mental blocks. I feel like I did a good job. It wasn’t my absolute best, but I’m very happy with how it went,” Schwab said. Schwab’s venture into diving was a somewhat recent decision for her, making the decision to switch sports from gymnastics ahead of her junior year. Multiple fractures to her back, along with her uncle being a former diver, led Nina to make a decision about her athletic career. “I injured myself a lot in gymnastics and after fracturing my back a second time, I took some time recovering. Through the 6-7 month healing process, I realized I wasn’t getting recruited. I would’ve been trying to get back to a point where I was when I was 8-10 years old and I just didn’t want to do that,” Schwab said. “My uncle was a diver, so we talked about it and I decided I wanted to try. Two days later, I quit gymnastics,” she added. Schwab thinks her background in gymnastics helped with some aspects in diving, but noted the big changes were leaping off of a diving board compared to a spring board, as well as landing head-first. “It definitely helped, I wouldn’t be where I am without gymnastics. But I’m used to jumping off a spring instead of waiting for a diving board to carry you up. I also think landing on your head is pretty difficult. Letting the board do the work and learning to trust it was a big part of the learning process,” Schwab said. Two years later Nina has established herself as one of the best diving prospects in the East Bay. Her development has been faster than expected, admitting to still learning the sport and taking a few knocks along the way. “I’m still learning right now. I still feel like I’m getting used to the diving board and I still do little things that make me look like a gymnast. It was a quick transition,” Schwab said. Schwab competed with her club, Cal Diving Academy, in the U.S.A Diving Regional Championships in Chicago on May 4-5, where she placed sixth of 42 on PHS diver Nina Schwab finished 16th at the CIF State Championship. the one-meter dive. It was good enough to qualify for U.S.A Diving Zone Championships in Wisconsin on June 27. She will continue her diving career at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota. Piedmont’s season ends in NCS Quarterfinals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s tennis team, seeded No. 7 in North Coast Section, saw its season come to an end on Thursday, May 9 in the NCS Team Tournament Quarterfinals, falling 7-0 to No. 2 Branson at the College of Marin in Kentfield. The Highlanders earlier defeated No. 10 Marin Catholic 4-3 at home on Tuesday, May 7. “We defeated Marin Catholic in the first round of the NCS team championships on Tuesday and then lost in the quarterfinals to Branson. There were some great matches both days,” coach Jim Landes said. Piedmont ends its season with a 13-10 overall record and will lose six players to graduation: Monte Imburg, Ben Breber, Graham Alban, Arun Brahma, Siddharth Bahtia, and Derek Chan. Imburg and Breber conclude their time at the school as fouryear starters in doubles and singles respectively. Imburg was the Post’s 2021 Freshman of the Year, and Breber was our honorable mention. Imburg graduates as the Western Alameda County Conference doubles champion. “The highlight for me was the end of Ben Breber’s and Monte Imburg’s great high school tennis careers, which was sad for both [assistant coach] Corey Reich and me. Ben gave me a hug after his match and it melted my heart, Corey and I loved coaching both of them. We will also dearly miss the four other seniors, Arun, Graham, Siddharth and Derek,” Landes said. 4-3 over No. 10 Marin Catholic Piedmont battled with Marin Catholic to a narrow victory, where No. 1 singles starter Lucas Smolko clinched the Highlanders’ fourth victory to claim the match day. He defeated Jack Millar in straight sets, including a heated second-set tiebreaker, winning by scores of 6-2, 7-6 (7-5). “The highlight of Tuesday was Lucas Smolko’s clinching win at #1 singles 6 -2 , 7 -6 (5) and the team lifting him up in victory,” Landes said. Also at singles was Breber winning in three sets, losing the first set but dominating the next two, 1-6, 6-1, 6-2. Nate Welch lost 6-0, 7-5 at No. 3 singles, while Alban lost a heated 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 match at No. 4. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Fencing Team wrapped up a busy month and recently competed in the Collegiate Cup RJCC in San Diego on Saturday and Sunday, May 11-12, including stalwarts Oliver Greenebaum and Sophie Choi. Choi also competed in the Rain City Super Youth Circuit in Bellevue, Washington on April 21 while Greenebaum entered The Fencing Center DIV2/Vet ROC on April 20 in San Jose. Multiple athletes were in the 5th Annual Precision RYC and RJC on April 12-13 in Torrance, and the ROC of the Rockies on April 5-7 in Denver, Colorado as well. Collegiate Cup RJCC Greenebaum, a junior at Piedmont High, finished 33rd of 82 contestants in the junior men’s foil category. He went 5-1 in pool play with one win against “very hard” competition and two wins against “hard” rated challengers—which impacts scoring for the final standings. He lost his one match in the direct elimination round. Choi, who attended Piedmont Middle School but now lives in Danville, competed in two events. She was 36th of 56 in the cadet women’s foil event, going 2-4 in pool play, including a win 13th place Audrey Yang. In the junior women’s foil category, Choi was 38th of 55, going 2-3 in pool play with a win over Yang, once again, who was 23rd. Oliver Greenebaum (middle, black shirt) recently competed in the Collegiate Cup with the Piedmont Fencing Team along with two other events. Rain City Super Youth Circuit Choi competed in the Y-14 women’s foil event, finishing 37th of 61. She went 3-3 in pool play, including a “hard” rated win over Sophie Choi (left), coach David Sinkkonen, Maya Dvoiris, and Myra Kulkarni of the Piedmont Fencing Team. Teresa McKay (right) had a successful run in the ROC of the Rockies. Eva Al-Battaineh, who finished eighth. The Fencing Center DIV2/Vet ROC In the Division 2 men’s foil category, Greenebaum finished 22nd of 34 after going 4-2 in pool play. Both of his losses came against “hard” rated opponents. 5th Annual Precision RYC and RJC Choi competed in two events in Torrance. She finished 12th of 38 in the junior women’s foil category, while she placed 37th of 67 in the Y-14 women’s foil event. She won four of five pool matches, including splitting matches against “very hard” rated competition. Her final two rounds included a win over 24th place Brielle Levesque and a loss to third-place Leila Do. Piedmont Middle School students also competed. Dario Banuelos was 49th of 54 in the junior men’s foil and finished 55th in the Y-14 men’s foil. Oliver Le was 47th of 51 in the Y-12 men’s foil. ROC of the Rockies Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Greenebaum represented their team. McKay had a strong showing with a second-place finish among eight competitors in the Division 2 women’s foil event. In the Division 1-A women’s foil, McKay placed seventh of 15 fencers. In her second-place finish, Teresa won all seven of her pool matches. In the final two rounds, she defeated seventh-place Mathilda Reiff but lost to firstplace Sylvie Troxel. Greenebaum competed in the Division 1-A men’s foil event, finishing seventh of 22. Greenebaum won four of six pool matches, including two wins and two losses against “very hard” rated competition. In the final two rounds, he beat 10th place Jayden Lee before losing to first-place Jeffery Miller.

articles.text: Piedmont High hosted their annual College Recognition ceremony on Tuesday, May 14 at the school’s outside amphitheater, where 14 Highlanders were honored prior to officially signing their collegiate letter of intent for their new schools. Players were honored by athletic director Bradley Smet and coaches in front of family and classmates. Baseball coach Eric Olson introduced two stalwarts, shortstop/pitcher Peter Krumins who will play at Northern Kentucky, and Dimitri Papahadjopoulos who has signed with Occidental. articles.text: Seniors at Piedmont High took a trip to San Francisco for their Prom Night on Saturday, April 27. The theme was Gotham City and the venue fit the bill – the 130-year old Hibernia Bank on Jones Street, where Piedmont High and Millennium High students danced and painted the town (purple of course). Piedmont teens reveled in the opportunity to get dolled up with their friends. Officially the evening began with a bus ride from Piedmont High at 5:30 p.m., although many pre-prom parties around Piedmont made Saturday morning and afternoon dedicated to the students a month away from commencement. Once at the Hibernia Bank venue, a disc jockey provided the sonic entertainment for prom, while Piedmont’s finest also enjoyed casino tables and two caricature artists. The photo booth was also a top attraction to help memorialize the day and was busy all evening. Food for the evening was catered by Piedmont resident Robert Dorsey and his catering company. articles.text: The Salvation Army of Alameda County, renowned for its dedication to providing essential services to thousands of children and adults annually, held its annual gala at Claremont Country Club on Sunday, March 24. The sold-out event with 150 guests raised an impressive $460,000. With a tradition of celebrating exceptional volunteers, this year’s honorees were retired neurologist, Thomas Wallace, MD, and the Order of Malta Clinic of Northern California, for their unwavering dedication to providing healthcare to those without health insurance. Dr. Wallace, a spirited 93-year-old, exemplifies the definition of volunteerism by volunteering daily at the clinic, located at the Cathedral of Christ in Oakland. His passion lies in removing barriers between medical providers and patients, ensuring seamless healthcare delivery without the complexities of billing or bureaucracy. articles.text: Stern Grove Festival audiences enjoy free concerts. Stern Grove Festival, the country’s oldest nonprofit and free music festival, kicks off on June 23. Headliners this year are electronic duo Sylvan Esso and iconic funk superstar Chaka Khan. The amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove in San Francisco will host ten weeks of admission-free concerts beginning June 23 and running through August 25. Reservation is required and is given on a first-come, first-serve basis. Last year’s festival drew 90,000 attendees over the course of two months. The festival, now in its 87th season, opens June 23 with performances by King Isis, a queer Oakland-based multi-genre artist, and sibling pop duo Tegan and Sara. San Francisco Symphony will perform a special concert on July 7 with Jessica Vosk, who performed as Elphaba in the Broadway musical Wicked. The SFJazz Collective, an all-star ensemble, will partner with jazz pianist Herbie Hancock for an August 11 performance. The Big Picnic Weekend, the festival’s annual fundraiser, is expanding this year to two days. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought to the public more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. mer performances. Visit https:// www.sterngrove.org to reserve tickets.

articles.text: Circadian String Quartet performs its first concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, May 24 at 7:30 pm. Titled Love and Chains, the concert includes special guests Leslie Bonnet and Nikolaus Hohmann. Tickets are $25 general/$15 seniors and students and are available at www.eventbrite. com/e/894985956087. The concert explores the deep bonds and binds that come with Love. Experience the world premiere of an original chamber opera, Euridice’s Defiance, composed by David Ryther. Inspired by the Greek myth of Orpheus and Euridice, this work in progress tells the story of a mother, Euridice, being detained at a border crossing and separated from her son, Orpheus, while she pleads with her guard to re-unite them. The ground-breaking libretto, written by novelist Kimiko Guthrie, is set to a haunting score by Ryther. The concert will also include Preludes by Claude Debussy, arranged for string quartet; Anton Webern’s romantic opus Langsamer Satz, and two works by Iranian-born composer Sahba Aminikia which are profound meditations on geopolitical struggles that are born from the love of our common humanity.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Berkeley Repertory Theatre The play chronicles maverick scientist Galileo Galilei’s life. Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s Galileo, by Tony Award winner Michael Mayer and Emmy winner Danny Strong, has been extended to June 23 due to popular demand. The play chronicles maverick scientist Galileo Galilei’s life, a man who makes celestial observations that challenge humanity’s understanding of its place in the universe. In this retelling, Galileo is summoned to Rome to defend his discoveries before the most powerful religious institution in the world. The play is accompanied with an original rock score with lyrics by Michael Weiner and Zoe Sarnak, and features fourtime Tony Award nominee Raúl Esparza. The cast includes Bradley Dean as Bishop Grasso, Jeremy Kushnier as Bishop Maffeo Barberini, Madalynn Mathews as Virginia Galilei and Christian Magby as Alessandro Tarantola. Post-show discussions will be held on May 24, May 30, and June 4 by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. The play ends June 23. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ galileo/.
articles.title: Galileo at Berkeley Rep extended to June 23

Less than an hour before the encore’s opening night performance on April 30, Osipova withdrew due to an injury. The news was delivered from the stage by Tamara Rojo herself. After collective sighs of disappointment, Ms. Rojo announced that the role of Odette-Odile would be performed by Jasmine Jimison, a newly promoted principal dancer who would be making her debut in the role. Unsure of what to expect, the audience clapped politely. The lights dimmed, guest conductor Martin West raised his baton, and soon the theatre resounded with Tchaikovsky’s haunting music. As the curtain lifted to reveal an evening lake, I braced myself for rewatching something I had tried to forget. But the moment Jasmine Jimison appeared on the stage, I was smitten. With her clean lines and impeccable undulation of her arms that instantly reminded me of Maya Plisetskaya, Jimison seemed born for the role. As the story unfolded – Odette falling in love, Odile tricking her lover, Odette suffering from his unwitting betrayal – Jimison handled transitions between innocence and seduction, hope and despair with technical prowess and dramatic flair. Judging from the solid ovations and loud “Bravos” her numbers received, including the famous “Black Swan Coda” featuring 32 consecutive fouettés, I wasn’t the only person in the audience impressed with Jimison’s performance. Her strong delivery was particularly striking given the short notice of the cast change and the intense pressure Jimison, a Bay Area native, must have felt to perform in an international superstar’s stead. Not only did she have to turn around the audience’s disappointment, she also had to make her own mark in one of the ballet’s most demanding character roles. Jimison succeeded in both. I felt drawn into Odette’s tragic story like never before. As I watched Jimison-Odette love, hope, suffer, and ultimately ascend with her beloved (Jimison has a natural ability to develop character), I at last perceived Swan Lake not as a prelude to something bad like I had in my childhood, but as an enduring love story, a triumph of the spirit over death – and a testimony of human capacity to push the boundaries of the possible. Impressing the audience with his clean, high, and effortless jumps, Hernández didn’t overpower the stage, achieving just the right balance between platonic love, passion, and sadness. pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 19 SF Ballet unveils new star in Swan Lake Jasmine Jimison enchants audience in debut role Review by Anastasia Edel From April 30 through May 5, the San Francisco Ballet presented encore performances of Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake. Originally premiered by the Bolshoi Theatre in 1877 to mixed reviews (Julius Reisinger’s choreography was considered dull and the score too complex for dancers), Swan Lake rapidly gained popularity thanks, in part, to orchestral revisions and updated choreography by Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov. Paris-based Ballets Russes popularized Tchaikovsky’s masterpiece in Europe. In 1940, San Francisco Ballet introduced Swan Lake to American audiences. Since then, the ballet has been a staple for the company, with the most recent adaptation done by Helgi Thomasson, the company’s former artistic director. Spectacular, passionate and technically complex, Swan Lake has long been considered the ultimate challenge for lead ballerinas, both technically and dramatically. Icons like Anna Pavlova, Galina Ulanova, Maya Plisetskaya and Margot Fonteyn delivered unforgettable performances in the dual roles of Odette, a girl turned into a swan by an evil sorcerer, and Odile, the sorcerer’s daughter, both traditionally portrayed by the same ballerina. On the contemporary stage, Natalia Osipova, formerly of the Bolshoi Theatre and now with the Royal Ballet, is widely believed to be the best interpreter of the role. Securing Osipova for the 2024 San Francisco Ballet encore performances as Odette-Odile was certainly a major win for the new artistic director Tamara Rojo, who recently completed her first season with the company. Osipova was certainly the reason I decided to see Swan Lake again. I have a complicated relationship with Swan Lake. Having grown up in the USSR, I dreaded turning on TV and seeing that specific Tchaikovsky’s ballet on every channel. It usually meant someone in the Politburo had died, or there was a coup. Using Swan Lake as a distraction in times of crises seemed appropriate to me: what could be a better metaphor for Soviet people than a giant flock of pliant ballerina-swans led through their doomed lives by an evil sorcerer? Long after the USSR had collapsed, Tchaikovsky’s score triggered my anxiety. Seeing Osipova as Odette-Odile, however, was not an opportunity to miss. It didn’t work as I had envisioned. Less than an hour before the encore’s opening night performance on April 30, Osipova withdrew due to an injury. The news was delivered from the stage by Tamara Rojo herself. After collective sighs of disappointment, Ms. Rojo announced that the role of Odette-Odile would be performed by Jasmine Jimison, a newly promoted principal dancer who would be making her debut in the role. Unsure of what to expect, the audience clapped politely. The lights dimmed, guest conductor Martin West raised his baton, and soon the theatre resounded with Tchaikovsky’s haunting music. As the curtain lifted to reveal an evening lake, I braced myself for rewatching something I had tried to forget. But the moment Jasmine Jimison appeared on the stage, I was smitten. With her clean lines and impeccable undulation of her arms that instantly reminded me of Maya Plisetskaya, Jimison seemed born for the role. As the story unfolded – Odette falling in love, Odile tricking her lover, Odette suffering from his unwitting betrayal – Jimison handled transitions between innocence and seduction, hope and despair with technical prowess and dramatic flair. Judging from the solid ovations and loud “Bravos” her numbers received, including the famous “Black Swan Coda” featuring 32 consecutive fouettés, I wasn’t the only person in the audience impressed with Jimison’s performance. Her strong delivery was particularly striking given the short notice of the cast change and the intense pressure Jimison, a Bay Area native, must have felt to perform in an international superstar’s stead. Not only did she have to turn around the audience’s disappointment, she also had to make her own mark in one of the ballet’s most demanding character roles. Jimison succeeded in both. I felt drawn into Odette’s tragic story like never before. As I watched Jimison-Odette love, hope, suffer, and ultimately ascend with her beloved (Jimison has a natural ability to develop character), I at last perceived Swan Lake not as a prelude to something bad like I had in my childhood, but as an enduring love story, a triumph of the spirit over death – and a testimony of human capacity to push the boundaries of the possible. Jimison didn’t do it alone, of course. Isaac Hernández as Prince Siegfried was a perfect match for Jimison’s Odette – poetic, ardent, and technically flawless. Impressing the audience with his clean, high, and effortless jumps, Hernández didn’t overpower the stage, achieving just the right balance between platonic love, passion, and sadness. Swan Lake is not an easy ballet for a male lead because of the built-in contradiction of the story: a hero who wows to save Odette, Siegfried fails to see the differences between her and Odile and professes his love to the wrong woman, forever ruining Odette’s chance to become human again. For Siegfried not to lose the audience’s sympathy, Rothbart and Odile must act subtly. Luckily, Alexander Reneff-Olson as Von Rothbart was the perfect evil genius, believably outplaying the idealistic prince – in mortal life at least. Swan Lake is also one of the best ballets to showcase corps de ballet. The iconic second act requires at least three dozen swans on stage, all moving in perfect unison. In the SF Ballet’s encore production, the swan dancers were superb. Their white tutus and matching sparking headdresses provided a remarkable moonlit frame to Odette and Siegfried’s developing romance. The ethnic dances (Spanish, Czardas, Neapolitan and Russian) during the Act III imperial ball were delightful and sported bright national costumes designed by Jonathan Fensom. On the opening night, Fensom faced some serious competition from the audience members. I saw at least one man in an elaborate tiered swan costume complete with a headdress. The standing ovation that Jimison and her dance partners received at the final curtain confirmed the old adage: Fortune favors the brave. While it’s a joy to watch a ballet veteran deliver her predictably magnificent performances, there’s an undeniable thrill in witnessing the birth of a new star. On April 30th, Jimison’s command of the renowned stage was undeniable. As a fan of San Francisco Ballet, I can’t wait to see what Jasmine Jimison does next. Anastasia Edel is a culture critic for Piedmont Post. Her writing has appeared in The Atlantic, The New York Review of Books, The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, and others. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian politics, history, and culture.

articles.text: Legion of Honor in San Francisco’s newest exhibition Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World is on view through August 18. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed publicly in a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks the time when Japan’s shogun was overthrown, marking the end of feudal military rule. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views of oceans and valleys dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked during both before and after the Meiji era. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World at Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

articles.text: San Francisco’s iconic fog, affectionately dubbed “Karl” by us locals, adds a mystical allure to our cityscape. Known as advection fog, it drifts horizontally, shrouding the Golden Gate Bridge and steep hills in a dreamy mist. Formed when warm, moist air meets the cooler Pacific waters, it blankets our city, providing a natural air conditioner while fostering a romantic ambiance. Despite being foggiest from June through August, global warming means fewer and shorter foggy days. Nevertheless, Karl continues to envelop our city at his whim, as evidenced by the remarkable display we witnessed on April 11 from Marin Headlands. We embrace Karl’s presence for its contribution to our city’s unique charm and the mesmerizing beauty it lends to our photographs, further cementing our city’s well-deserved reputation as the City of Fog. These images were captured on Bay Area hikes in recent years, showcasing the stunning landscapes and natural beauty accentuated by Karl. These photos serve as a testament to the remarkable beauty of the Bay Area and the reason why I’ve chosen to call this place home for over 40 years. From misty trails to panoramic vistas, each photograph encapsulates the Bay Area’s unparalleled charm and the profound connection it fosters with nature. These images not only capture moments in time but also evoke my sense of gratitude for the privilege of experiencing such breathtaking scenery firsthand.

Known as advection fog, it drifts horizontally, shrouding the Golden Gate Bridge and steep hills in a dreamy mist. Formed when warm, moist air meets the cooler Pacific waters, it blankets our city, providing a natural air conditioner while fostering a romantic ambiance. Despite being foggiest from June through August, global warming means fewer and shorter foggy days. Nevertheless, Karl continues to envelop our city at his whim, as evidenced by the remarkable display we witnessed on April 11 from Marin Headlands. We embrace Karl’s presence for its contribution to our city’s unique charm and the mesmerizing beauty it lends to our photographs, further cementing our city’s well-deserved reputation as the City of Fog. These images were captured on Bay Area hikes in recent years, showcasing the stunning landscapes and natural beauty accentuated by Karl. These photos serve as a testament to the remarkable beauty of the Bay Area and the reason why I’ve chosen to call this place home for over 40 years. From misty trails to panoramic vistas, each photograph encapsulates the Bay Area’s unparalleled charm and the profound connection it fosters with nature. These images not only capture moments in time but also evoke my sense of gratitude for the privilege of experiencing such breathtaking scenery firsthand. A student at Fontainebleau School of Fine Art in France, Gottlieb won many awards and excelled in both plein air and abstract work. She painted and traveled the world throughout her life. This opera, composed by David Ryther with a libretto by the novelist Kimiko Guthrie, reimagines the Orpheus and Eurydice myth as a modern-day detention story. The concert also includes works by Claude Debussy, Anton Webern, and Iranian-born Sahba Aminikia. The opera will feature soprano Lily Storm and the Circadian String Quartet, consisting of David Ryther & Monika Gruber, violins; Omid Assadi, viola; and David Wishnia, cello. After earning master’s degrees in archaeology and in public policy, and finally a Masters in Fine Arts, she developed a career in photography and painting, and a classical pianist. articles.text: Richard Gere and Ethan Hawke in Brooklyn’s Finest Cop movies are a time-tested genre. Some are referred to as police procedurals where an investigation is conducted in a rigorous, linear fashion. Others are, in essence, character studies, focusing on the exigencies of the job, the harshness of the environment, and the corruption of the human spirit. Many are hard-bitten morality plays, bringing into relief the universal struggle between good and evil. If done well, they can be superb entertainment. Examples are L.A. Confidential, Heat, To Live and Die in L.A., The French Connection, Se7en, Dirty Harry, Speed, Training Day, Die Hard, plus Roman Polanski’s Chinatown, one of the best. Brooklyn’s Finest focuses on three NYPD officers, Tango (Don Cheadle), Eddie (Richard Gere) and Sal (Ethan Hawke) who inhabit is the dark side of the city, riven with crime and drugs, where drugs and violence permeate. The film offers three snapshots of their lives as they move toward a fateful intersection. Each has made a Faustian bargain with some form of evil that will, in the end, spell ruin. Their journey makes for tense, gripping entertainment. There are moments in Brooklyn’s Finest when it seems all but necessary to suspend one’s disbelief so desperately raw and abysmal are the mean streets of Brooklyn. Is it possible that street cops are so deeply submerged in the inner city’s refuse that they begin to resemble the very people they are arresting? Friedrich Nietzche once wrote, “Whoever battles with monsters had better see that it does not turn him into a monster. And if you gaze long into the abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.” That is the admonition that haunts Brooklyn’s Finest. There’s Eddie, only seven days from retirement. He has long ago compromised himself and his oath to the point that he no longer cares. He is alone, his life so stark and sad that it has become devoid of purpose. In one scene he sits with the barrel of his revolver between his teeth. Tango, an undercover cop, lives each day with the violent exploitation of drug dealers and predators. People are disposable. All that matters is dope and money. Tango knows that he is lost, trapped in a labyrinth of destruction. His only wish is to get his life back and yet the universe conspires against him. Sal, a narcotics officer, is adrift, telling himself that the ends justify the means. His days are awash in druggies and drug money. Life is overwhelming him: he has children, a pregnant wife, a house that is moldy and hazardous and feels the pull of money as if it were an overwhelming gravity. Brooklyn’s Finest is a narrative that is intense and gritty. Some fans might call it pulp cinema, or a noirish tale that never flinches. This film will entertain and more. But be warned: it’s raw and violent and dark. Very dark. Brooklyn’s Finest. Directed by Antoine Fugua. Starring Richard Gere, Don Cheadle, Ethan Hawke, Wesley Snipes, Shannon Kane and Lili Taylor. 2 hrs., 5 min. Rated R. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/peacock/apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Skydance Studio’s Luck Older kids, tweens, and newbie teens will enjoy watching the adventures of Sam Greenfield (Eva Nobelzada) in the animated feature film Luck. First some backstory about Sam: she’s a teenager who has aged out of her foster care family, and is sad to leave her younger friend Hazel (Adelyn Spoon) who is also an orphan waiting to be adopted by a family. Meanwhile, Sam has found a small apartment of her own and a job at a flower shop. As we come to know Sam better, we begin to understand that she feels alone, and is struggling to find her place in the world. But we also soon learn that Sam is resilient and optimistic, vivacious and considerate. What is making her life difficult on a daily basis is that she is plagued by bad luck. Put another way, some might say that Sam is a klutz. This is revealed through a number of funny scenes showing how she loses things, creates a mess wherever she goes, locks herself out of her bathroom, is often late for work, and even drops her morning toast, jam covered, face down. And so we find Sam sitting on a curb eating a sandwich, when a black cat comes and sits next to her and she offers it some of her Panini bread. Later she finds a penny that seems to unexpectedly bring her good luck. She decides to give the lucky penny to her friend Hazel. Perhaps it just might help her find that much sought after family. But true to form, Sam drops the penny into the toilet and once again bemoans her bad luck. Sam returns to her familiar curb and once again the black cat returns; however, when Sam tells the critter named Bob (Simon Pegg) about the penny he admonishes her in a surprising Scottish brogue, and tells her to follow him. He leads her through a portal, which reveals a magical place called the Land of Luck. Maybe there she might find that penny. And so Sam’s adventure begins in this extraordinary place filled with leprechauns led by The Captain (Whoopi Goldberg), an enormous pink dragon (Jane Fonda), and a unicorn named Jeff (Flula Borg). Sam learns a life lesson about luck that comes with insights and new realizations. Kids will enjoy Sam’s journey and all the characters she meets along the way. Luck. Directed by Peggy Holmes. Animated by Skydance Studio. Voiced by Eva Nobelzada, Simon Pegg, Jane Fonda. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated G, Released in 2020. Streaming on apple tv. articles.text: Sixth giraffe is added to the herd A new male giraffe was recently added to Oakland Zoo’s herd after traveling from Louisiana’s Audubon Nature Institute. He traveled in a carrier specially designed for the nearly 10-foot tall giraffe to ride comfortably. The 13-month-old giraffe was brought to the Zoo upon recommendation by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums’ (AZA) Species Survival Plan (SSP). The Animal Care team at Oakland Zoo has been working hard to ensure the area is comfortable for the new arrival, keeping his overall wellbeing in mind. Providing different options of enrichment, bedding, and tree browse gives the keepers a better understanding of his preferences and allows the giraffe to choose how he would like to interact with his new environment. While exploring his space, he discovered a bamboo wind chime made by his keepers and has since become enamored. “He is a brave and bold giraffe who’s adjusting quite well. We’re thrilled to get to know him and watch him develop a bond with his new herd at the Zoo,” said Amy Phelps, Oakland Zoo’s Zoological Manager. While he adjusts to his new home, he will have the opportunity to start getting to know his herd mates through a fence.
