Care teams determine he is ready, he will move to the giraffe habitat at the Zoo’s African Savanna area. Giraffes are highly social animals and maintain relationships with many individuals in their natural habitats. The addition of another giraffe helps provide a more robust social structure to the herd at Oakland Zoo, bringing the total number of giraffes to six. It is common for giraffes to live in groups of varied ages. The Zoo has giraffes ages one to 12. Kendi, a female giraffe and the youngest was born just last year at the Zoo. The Zoo’s reticulated giraffes serve as ambassadors to their wild counterparts. Reticulated giraffe populations have experienced a 50% decline throughout the world in the past three and a half decades due to illegal wildlife trade and habitat loss. It has led to their endangered status on the IUCN Red List. Oakland Zoo supports The Reticulated Giraffe Project, which investigates reticulated giraffes’ behavioral ecology and population processes to inform conservation and management efforts. The Zoo supports the project by raising awareness, sending staff to Africa, and fundraising events like Brunch for the Wild Bunch. For more on supporting giraffes visit Oaklandzoo.org. The Zoo welcomes its fans online to help choose a name for the new male Giraffe. articles.text: Young and old alike embrace their inner “Zorba” on the dance floor at the Oakland Greek Festival. Celebrating its 52nd year, the Oakland Greek Festival kicks off the festivities Friday, May 17th at 4 p.m. and runs through Sunday at 9 p.m. Along with the breathtaking panoramic views, festival-goers can anticipate their delectable favorites such as gyros, souvlakia, lamb sandwiches, spanakopita, loukoumades, baklava, and much more! Ascension’s award-winning Greek Folk Dance troupes, historical festival photo displays, tours/ lectures, cooking demonstrations, Ascension Liturgical Choir concerts as well as live Greek music and dancing are featured throughout the weekend. A unique array of wares and take-home pastries are also available for purchase. For more details, please visit OaklandGreekFestival.com The festival is open Friday from 4:00p.m. to 10:00 p.m., Saturday 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., and Sunday 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Tickets are $5 at the door or availPanhellenic Dancers’ Chris Constantouros hangs Constitution Square street sign in Jack London Square, Oakland, CA. Festival-goers annually await loukoumades, a warm delicious treat, drizzled with honey. able in advance via EventBrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ oakland-greek-festival-2024-tickets-881518143497?aff=ebdshpsearchautocomplet). Children 12 and under are admitted free. Free parking is available at the cathedral and surrounding lots as well as Premium Parking for $20/day. Early History – Greek Week 1972 While there had been “food festivals” in Ascension Cathedral’s early history, there had never been anything that compared to the scale of “Greek Week” in May 1972. In honor of the 50th anniversary of the Ascension Church, scores of parishioners volunteered to present a month-long series of events leading up to the spirited weekend of its first Greek festival. At the time it was called “an ethnic celebration that made a resounding impact on the East Bay.” It was the first of its kind and was a citywide historic event. For one week, the city of Oakland embraced the Greeks as displays were created, Jack London Square was temporarily renamed Constitution Square and events highlighting the coming festival were held, all of which culminated in two days of food, dance and festivities! Six award-winning Greek folk dance troupes perform at the Windmill Plaza May 17-19 at the Oakland Festival of Greece. Pictured: Ascension’s Markos Lagios leads the Analypsis Dancers.

articles.text: This recipe has been on repeat lately at our house and will fit right in with your May menu close to Cinco de Mayo. Fortunately, Mexican grocers are nearby so sourcing Oaxacan string cheese and tomatillos is doable. It’s fine to use another mild, melty cheese, and any salsa you enjoy. Just be aware the star of the show is the mushroom, so select complimentary, not competing, flavors. Tan bueno! Hen of the Woods Quesadillas with Avocado Salsa Makes 6 small quesadillas plus about 1 cup of salsa a few minutes. Char the tomatillos, jalapeno pepper, wedge of white onion and clove of garlic on as many sides as possible to a deep mahogany color. Remove to a plate as needed. Peel the charred skin from the jalapeno pepper using the back of a knife, or with your fingers, wearing gloves to protect your skin. Slice in half lengthwise to remove the stem, seeds and any stringy membrane. Slice into thin, julienne strips. Chop the avocado, tomatillos and onion into half inch pieces and add to a small food processor or blender. Add the garlic, cilantro and lime juice, salt and pepper. Blitz to form a smooth consistency. (If you have a molcajete use it!) Taste and add jalapeno, salt and/or pepper as desired. Transfer to a serving bowl, cover and set aside. Quesadillas Unravel the ball of Oaxacan string cheese and break off in 2-inch long pieces. Pull into shreds about 1/ 4-inch thick. Heat a large skillet over medium heat. Add the tablespoon of oil, then the clumps of mushrooms and sauté until lightly browned. Add the chopped garlic and continue cooking until the garlic just softens. Remove from the skillet and set aside. Place three tortillas onto the heated skillet (or comal) in a single layer and warm one side of each until softened and pliable. Flip each tortilla over and place one-sixth of the mushrooms, about two tablespoons of shredded cheese and a few strips of jalapeno pepper onto each tortilla. Move the filling to cover half of the tortilla so you can fold the remaining half over the filling. Cook until the first side turns golden brown then turn over to brown the remaining side. This should be sufficient to melt the cheese. Remove the cooked quesadillas to a plate and repeat cooking the remaining three quesadillas. Serve immediately with avocado salsa. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.
articles.title: Hen of the Woods quesadillas with avocado salsa

articles.text: For the salsa • 1 medium avocado • 3 medium tomatillos, about 1/2 cup chopped after charring • 1 jalapeno pepper, fresh, divided; to taste • 1/4 small white onion, cut a wedge, about 2 tablespoons roughly chopped after charring • 1 medium clove garlic, about 1 teaspoon finely chopped after charring • 1/4 cup fresh cilantro, packed leaves and some stems • 2 tablespoons lime juice, freshly squeezed • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt plus a few grinds of black peppercorns For the quesadillas • 6 small corn tortillas, about 4” diameter • 8 ounces hen of the woods mushroom, about 2 medium “bouquets”, aka maitake mushrooms; separated into 1/2” clumps • 3-4 ounces Oaxacan string cheese, substitute any melty cheese such as Monterey jack • 1 medium garlic clove, about 1 teaspoon chopped • Remaining 1/2 of the charred jalapeno, sliced lengthwise in julienne strips • 1 tablespoon oil, neutral flavored

articles.text: Saul Dan Timens, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on May 6, 2024, at age 86. Saul was born and raised in Cleveland, Ohio and graduated from Cleveland Heights High School in 1954. Saul’s claim to fame was growing 10 inches during his freshman year. He loved to tell people that his friends used to visit him and “watch me grow.” In his youth, Saul worked during the summer as a driver for a Good Humor truck. Saul credits this job as the start of his lifelong love of ice cream. His favorite dessert for decades was the “Black and Tan” sundae at Fenton’s Creamery in Oakland. In 1958, Saul graduated Magna Cum Laude from Ohio University with a bachelor’s degree in business. He was president of Beta Gamma Sigma, the commerce honor fraternity, and a member of the Alpha Delta Chapter of Phi Sigma Delta. Saul served as an Officer in the Navy from 1958- 1961, assigned to USS Lookout, AGR2, a radar picket ship. He was proud of his service, saying it was instrumental in his growth as a person and a professional. Saul was a commercial property manager in the San Francisco Bay Area. He began his career at Coldwell Banker in Oakland before forming his own company, S D Timens and Company in 1981. He ran his own successful boutique firm until retiring in 2000. Saul lived most of his life in Oakland, Piedmont and Truckee. Saul enjoyed traveling in the Saul Timens passed away on May 6, 2024. He was 86. U.S. and abroad. He and Barbara enjoyed trips to Europe, Africa, Asia and Central America. In his later years, he took up oil painting, producing dozens and dozens of landscapes. Saul loved a good pun. He never failed to say, “I would relish some relish” every time the family had hot dogs instead of asking someone to pass along the condiment. Saul is predeceased by his parents Irving and Mildren Timens, and sister Annette Bedford. He is survived by his loving wife Barbara Bysiek Timens and daughter Laura Shipp, her husband Will Shipp and their children Claire and Olivia. He will also be missed by his stepchildren Paul and Beth Fischer and their children, Evie and Charlie. The family is planning a Celebration of Life on June 5th. In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to American Heart Association, or your favorite charity in Saul’s name. articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group enjoyed a large turnout of 17 readers at their May 6 meeting outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. The readers were there to discuss Perestroika in Paris, a 2020 fiction written by Jane Smiley. A review by the Wall Street Journal praised the novel as a successful combination of “the Parisian fairy tale and the equestrian novel.” The Journal also said, “Wholesomely timeless, full of good intentions and happy endings that feel far removed from the problems of the moment.” The New York Times called it a “feel-good escape.” Paras, short for Perestroika, is a spirited racehorse at a racetrack near Paris. Late one afternoon she finds the door of her stall open and the curious filly wanders off to see the city. She meets a German shorthaired pointer named Frida, and they live in the city’s green spaces. The two are nourished by the results from the dog’s trips to a vegetable market. Paras and Frida also become friends with two ducks and a raven, but Paras also meets a young boy, Etienne, and discovers a new world. Para takes up residence in the large house of Etienne and his nearly 100-yearold great-grandmother, who is blind. The boy and the horse live there without the woman and others knowing it. Things happen, nothing catastrophic and there is a happy ending for all. An initial question from the group was, is this supposed to be a book for young adults? They agreed that this book could be enjoyed by young people, but its audience is broader. Some readers definitely had issues. The writing was okay, but the story didn’t engage them. It might be a fable, but what is its moral? Nothing of consequence happened and it was tiresome and boring, some readers said. They had to force themselves to finish it. There are lots of small words. It was asked if Smiley hadn’t been a Pulitzer Prize winner for her other work, would Perestroika in Paris have been published? Karin Fetherston and Alicia Rivera had done some research and learned that Smiley’s publisher had initially not wanted to publish it. However, the times changed and something lighter was called for in 2020. It was reported that Smiley is an animal lover and actually has a horse named Perestroika. Smiley has written about serious subjects and some readers thought this was her “therapy book.” It was intended to be light and fun. Those on the positive side also found it to be an easy, enjoyable read. They liked the story’s different animals and could go with the unlikely events. The Paris setting was also a plus. Etienne’s mutually supportive relationship with his grandmother was an important part of the novel. Paras was restructuring her life. The diverse animals were a Prequel by Rachel Maddow is the reading group’s selection for June community. They were there for one another and pulling together. Readers could see the book being made into an animated movie that kids and adults would love. Some questions raised were: If you are part of a reading group, and aren’t enjoying the selected book, are you obligated to read it entirely? The book should be given a fair chance, but the group’s answer was no. One of the great things about the First Mondays Reading Group is that there are no obligations except to have fun. That was what they were doing, and what Jane Smiley had done with Perestroika in Paris. The book provided for good conversation and some laughs. The group had previously selected Prequel by Rachel Maddow for their meeting in June and The Dry by Jane Harper for July. Bob Hall presented three new non-fiction candidates and Country Girl by Edna O’Brien was picked for August. The next discussion will be on June 3 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee. To participate, click on https://bit. ly/3R86PP4 Participants in the First Mondays Reading Group on May 6 included Bob Hall, Sarah Johnson, Lois Price, Mike Henn, Karin Fetherston, Gerry Gregg, Phil Witte, Lois Price, Ken Young, Alicia Rivera, Darby Gregg, Adrienne Hamlin, Hilary Honore, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to welcome Claudine Bach who attended for the first time.
articles.title: Reading group discusses Jane Smiley’s Perestroika in Paris

articles.text: Last Wednesday, May 8, in advance of Mother’s Day was time for the Walking on Wednesdays group to make their annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden on Jean Street in Oakland at the Piedmont city border. A big turnout of 45 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up to see the garden. Meghan Bennett had created a website for the garden (https:// www.oaklandrose.com), so the walkers had lots of information. It is in a natural bowl on a 7.5- acre site that was purchased by the City of Oakland in 1911 and originally named Linda Vista Park. Local Oakland residents had petitioned and promised to contribute $8,000 for it. However, the best park entrance was through land in Piedmont. The Piedmont City Council joined the effort in June 1911 by acquiring Piedmont lots at the southern corner of Olive and Oakland Avenues to provide a “handsome entrance.” In 1913, it was proposed the park be converted into a zoological garden, but the park directors decided not to do it. The park’s conversion to a rose garden was a project of the Oakland Businessmen’s Garden Club in 1930 with the support of the city. It was originally known as the Municipal Rose Garden. Work began on the garden and the first first rose was planted on Jan. 27, 1933. The garden officially opened on May 28, 1933. The park’s name was changed in 1954 to honor former Oakland Mayor Fred Morcom, who served from 1931 to 1933. The park has been refurbished at least twice, in the 1950s and again in the 1990s, with many of the old roses, some going back to the 19th century, being regrafted on new rootstock. The group headed off down Magnolia to Wildwood Avenue and crossed Grand Avenue, which was originally called Pleasant Valley Road. A group photo was taken in front of the classical, curved colonnade entrance to the rose garden. A city employee said dogs on leashes were OK, so the group remained intact. The garden’s design was inspired by those of Italy and the park has over 2,400 rose bushes in three sections. There are winding walkways with a reflecting pool across from a 14-step cascade that goes down the hillside to the west and an octagonal wedding terrace above with more rose beds. The essential design has changed very little in the 90 years since it was created. What has changed is the City of Oakland’s ability to care for it. In the early 2000s, the hours of Oakland city workers to maintain the garden were reduced. A group of volunteers, the “Dedicated Deadheaders,” was organized to keep the garden beautiful, and they work there every Wednesday. In the early 2000s, “The Mother’s Walk” was created above the reflecting pool up to a Florentine oval garden at the north end of the park. There are brass plaques in the walkway with names of women honored each year in an annual ceremony on Mother’s Day. Walkers splintered off to see different sections of the garden. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, May 15, 2024 Scouts and adults from Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 15 recently prepared food to be served to the hungry at the weekly free meal at College Avenue Presbyterian Church (CAPC), located at 5951 College Avenue in Oakland. The team prepared 90 dinner servings on Thursday evening, April 25, then reheated it at the church in late afternoon Friday, April 26. Arranged by Montclair Rotary Club, this marked Troop 15’s first participation in the church’s Friday Feed program. The Scouts team baked at the Piedmont home of Kevin Ma and Liana Wu, co-chairs of Troop 15 Service Opportunities. “The Scouts did the work”, noted co-chair, Moira Chapman. “They prepared two types of lasagna – vegetarian, beef and spinach, as well as garlic bread and chocolate chip cookies for dessert.” On Friday in the church’s kitchen, Scouts placed portions onto serving plates. William Bleharski, a 7th-grade Scout, said, “I had a lot of fun helping. I can see now that it’s not easy for some people to get food, so I’m glad I could help.” The Coordinator for the Church’s Friday Dinner, Tim Hsu noted “These Scouts demonstrated all the best characteristics of volunteers. They were eager to work, focused, organized and efficient. And as one would Troop 15 Scouts pitch in to help feed the homeless expect from Scouts, they were respectful and courteous. It was a pleasure having them and I hope to see more of Troop 15 in the future.” The church has provided a hot meal once a week for homeless people for more than 40 years. Montclair Rotary Club is the chartering organization for Troop 15 and paid for the meal ingredients. “The Friday Dinner operation is grateful to have several amazing partners in the community – the regular cook teams include members of Piedmont Community Service Crew (a Venturing Scout unit of Piedmont Scouting Council) and cooking with ingredients provided by Montclair Rotary, Three Crosses Ministry, Montclair Presbyterian Church, and Trinity Fellowship of Berkeley. We also rely on regular donations of food from Safeway and Acme Bread.” Hsu added, “We need volunteers to set up, serve, and clean up on Friday night. Individual volunteers can sign up to help at https://www.capcoakland.org/friday-night-meal. pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 29 By Samantha Pell Piedmont Scouts eagerly anticipate the Camporee, an annual inter-troop campout once a year, often the first trip for new Scouts. This year they were met with 2024 Scout Camporee flushed out innumerable difficult circumstances, especially the weather, on the long-planned overnight campout. However, with true Scout spirit, they managed to make the best of it while learning some important life lessons. When Scouts piled into their carpools on the morning of May 4, many were brimming with excitement. Packs were stuffed with camping gear and no one had a clue about the theatrics that were to come. While they Scouts trudge through lush foliage. Scouts begin hiking up a hill, already wearing raincoats. Cold, wet Scouts warm up by a backpacking stove. were aware of the rain and low temperatures – overall inclement weather, the information did nothing to tone down the eager hope of the Scouts. As they neared Henry Coe State Park in Morgan Hill (Santa Clara County), rain began to seep through the clouds, slightly tarnishing their spirits. Luckily, the majority of Scouts had come prepared, protected by rain pants, windbreakers and the hope that the rain would let up soon. To the disappointment of many, the rain showed no signs of letting up and continued to pour down steadily, accompanied by sweeping gusts of wind. Troop 11 had decided to merely do a day hike and began hiking around 1 p.m. The other four troops persevered, holding onto hope. Members of the camporee staff held an emergency meeting and concluded that the safest option for all Scouts and adults was to hike out with the gear they could carry and effectively cancel camporee. While not the most popular choice, it was ultimately the most practical solution. After taking over the visitor center, Scouts climbed into vehicles with the heat on full blast and headed back to civilization. On Sunday, the “clean up crew” of Scouts on camp staff assembled at Piedmont Community Church – feeling rather refreshed from a good night’s sleep and comfortable mattresses – then returned to Henry Coe Park again. Due to the wet roads, Scouts had to hike in. Once at camp, the staff gorged themselves on the abandoned cold cuts and sandwich ingredients from the day before, savoring some belated sunshine. The next few hours were a flurry of activity as the staff gathered gear, aired out rain flies and even partook in a camporee activity - the team ski. In the long run – or rather, long hike – this rainsoaked, cancelled camporee held some of the most valuable lessons for young Scouts. One point of the Scout law that was incredibly useful for Scouts to hold on this trip was the eighth point: A Scout is cheerful. Quite frankly, while the trip was rather miserable at some points, when your umbrella had flipped out and rain is pelting on your cold head, being cheerful is difficult. Simply smiling and keeping calm put a positive spin on things for the Scouts, especially the younger Scouts. They remained upbeat for the majority of the hike. We can always keep smiling through freezing temperatures, through tough hikes, and through life. Just lift your head a little higher and remain...cheerful. READ IT IN THE POST Micro-Forest Continued from page 1 in Piedmont so that our city can reap all the benefits that come from building one.” Micro-forests are small dense woods grown in a relatively short time period using carefully selected plants that are best suited to the local environment. Micro-forests in cities can effectively provide noise buffers, restore ecosystems, absorb carbon, buffer against extreme heat, polluted air, flooding, and drought, provide an educational opportunity, connect people to nature, and contribute towards an effective global climate The modern concept of micro-forests stems from the work of Japanese ecologist Akira Miyawaki, who devised a method of planting native forests that mature in 20-30 years, as opposed to several hundred years required for conventional forests. “You plant them all at the same time in a specific way, pretty close together so that they sort of fight for the sun,” explained Indira Balkissoon, co-chair with Heins and lead organizer on the organization’s micro-forest project. The forests are typically self-sustaining within 2-3 years of planting. More than 21,000 micro-forests have been planted worldwide. Heins and Balkissoon have gone to bat for this project before and have made several public efforts to promote the project and awareness of micro-forests, including an appearance at the City of Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration this year. “We’ve met with Nancy Kent, and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation is also aware of the micro-forest ideas. I believe it’s a matter of priorities. The city has a lot going on,” Heins explained. She and Balkissoon are confident that they can gain the City’s support and eventually have a plot of land for starting their project. “Miyawaki was able to make it work with plots as small as 10 feet by 10 feet,” said Heins. “You can even get one started in your backyard.” Until they develop more traction with the project, Heins and Balkissoon are content to be heartened by the efforts of other local micro-forests. “Berkeley has planted approximately four or five good micro-forests around its schools. Berkeley Technology Academy is a great example. There are around 950 trees and 53 native species [there],” said Balkissoon. For more information on urban micro-forests and how you can help create one, contact the Piedmont Garden Club at piedmontgardenclub.ca@gmail.com. articles.text: 800 girls show up to try out different sports Nearly 800 girls from the Bay Area gathered at Witter Field on Sunday, May 5, to try different sports as part of the annual Play Like a Girl+ event. Now in its third year, Play Like a Girl+ invites girls between the ages of two and 18 to participate in a day of hands-on activities, live demonstrations, as well as Q&A sessions with former Olympians and female role models designed to promote interest in sports among young women. More than 25 sports stations were set up for youth to check out, including flag football, fencing, roller derby, track and field, boxing, rugby, golf, skateboarding, and volleyball. Stations were a mix of drop-in play and training sessions along with more structured demonstrations and classes given at regular intervals. A firefighter fitness station was also set up led by female firefighters Brittany Borges (Piedmont Fire Department) and Tamara Holmes (Oakland Fire DepartPhotos by Sophie Hess Juniors Lucy Barton and Alma Ruberto work through a play at the Flag Football station. This was the first year that PHS had a flag football team for girls.

articles.text: Classified CSEA workers, a group that includes paraeducators, custodians, and office staff have come to a new agreement with their employer, Piedmont Unified School District. The tentative contract was approved during the April 26 school board meeting; it settles upon salary raises retroactive to the current school year, and the next two years. The contract also includes a one-time payment of $800 for full-time CSEA employees, costing the district $111,000. The three years of cumulative additional salary that CSEA workers will receive is $1,667,000. “The negotiations team and the entire unit saw the wisdom in securing compensation increases and increases in the support for health benefits premiums,” said CSEA President Christine Petersen. The agreement also automatically reopens negotiations if another bargaining party (APT or APSA) gets a “higher percentage ongoing salary or benefit increase or one-time stipend than CSEA.” In this event, the reopening will be for the district to “apply said additional increases” to CSEA classified staff. “We haven’t done multi-year contracts in my entire time on the board,” said Cory Smegal in her 9th year as a member of the school board. “I think what this enables us to do is partner in a different way that will be better for the long-term health of the district.” Additional caveats in the contract will give the CSEA staffers small increases to salary in the event cost of living in the state goes up again. A 0.5% increase to salary would take place if COLA increases by more than 3% in 2024-25 and another 0.5% increase kicks in if COLA exceeds 5% in 2025-26. Increases to CSEA Classified Staff salaries 2.5% for 2023-24 4% for 2024-25 3% for 2025-26 CSEA classified staff packed city hall at a school board meeting in October 2022 to speak about increased healthcare costs.

articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School Board. Editor: The news and the web are inundated with information about climate change, the bad consequences for the future, and the actions needed. The problem is indeed very serious. Our students are well informed about the issues, some to the point of being traumatized by the fear of an upcoming apocalypse. Given the budget constraints that the District is facing, increasing staff to teach climate literacy could be done to the detriment of other academic subjects, in particular the STEM sciences essential to develop new technologies to decarbonize energy. I would also caution the Board on an approach where climate literacy would be incorporated in every academic subject based on the District previous experience (30?) years ago of mixing the math and physics curriculum: the end result was not much math or physics were taught because every class rehashed the same easy stuff: a unique innovative experiment made by the District that had to be stopped under the pressure from parents. If I remember correctly Martha Jones led the community in the transition and introduced for the first time Advanced Placement classes. Should you decide that such climate literacy education is needed, the best approach would be for the parents pushing the issue to create a group of students passionate about the subject oriented towards experimentation and field activities, such as the very successful and effective Piedmont Makers. Frugality should be part of that group mission statement. There is no easy answer to the warming planet. Our nation does not need more anxious activists, but rather well-educated optimist accountants, entrepreneurs, mathematiciens, engineers, chemists, biologists, ... to develop and implement effective solutions based on a deep understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. –Bernard Pech
articles.title: Climate literacy petition

articles.text: Climate literacy will be a “hot” topic at the Piedmont Unified School Board meeting on Wednesday, May 8, when a group of students, teachers and parents urges the Board to adopt a Climate Literacy Resolution. The Resolution calls for the District to commit to educating students “for a future with human-induced climate change” by integrating relevant lessons into the curriculum of all subjects at all grade levels, TK-12. According to Moira Chapman, the Piedmont parent who convened the Climate Literacy Working Group last year, “Young people today are concerned with what’s happening to our climate, but they don’t have enough information and skills to fully understand it and adequately prepare for the changes.” “Likewise, many teachers don’t have the training and materials they need to teach about it. The goal of this Resolution is to provide students with a broad knowledge of climate change science, issues, and solutions so they can succeed as the climate changes their future lives and careers.” If the Resolution passes, Piedmont schools will be in line with a new State law, AB 285, that requires science classes in first through 12th grades to “include an emphasis on the causes and effects of climate change and methods to mitigate and adapt to climate change.” The law stipulates that appropriate coursework be offered no later than the 2024– 25 school year. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, May 8, 2024 Opinion Climate literacy petition The following letter was sent to Piedmont School Board. Editor: The news and the web are inundated with information about climate change, the bad consequences for the future, and the actions needed. The problem is indeed very serious. Our students are well informed about the issues, some to the point of being traumatized by the fear of an upcoming apocalypse. Given the budget constraints that the District is facing, increasing staff to teach climate literacy could be done to the detriment of other academic subjects, in particular the STEM sciences essential to develop new technologies to decarbonize energy. I would also caution the Board on an approach where climate literacy would be incorporated in every academic subject based on the District previous experience (30?) years ago of mixing the math and physics curriculum: the end result was not much math or physics were taught because every class rehashed the same easy stuff: a unique innovative experiment made by the District that had to be stopped under the pressure from parents. If I remember correctly Martha Jones led the community in the transition and introduced for the first time Advanced Placement classes. Should you decide that such climate literacy education is needed, the best approach would be for the parents pushing the issue to create a group of students passionate about the subject oriented towards experimentation and field activities, such as the very successful and effective Piedmont Makers. Frugality should be part of that group mission statement. There is no easy answer to the warming planet. Our nation does not need more anxious activists, but rather well-educated optimist accountants, entrepreneurs, mathematiciens, engineers, chemists, biologists, ... to develop and implement effective solutions based on a deep understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. –Bernard Pech Piedmont Post news rack at Mulberry’s Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ Mulberry’s Market. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department won first place in several key categories at The Big Climb at Oracle Park marking the second consecutive year the department has won the competition overall. Despite being one of the smallest departments in the region, Piedmont Firefighters won several categories in the event’s First Responder Challenge on Saturday, May 4, including “Fastest Team,” “Top Fundraising Team,” and “Fastest Individual Climber.” The Big Climb is a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, a national organization dedicated to curing blood cancers and improving the quality of life for patients and their families. Conditions were rainy on the day of the competition, but despite the weather Firefighters Justin McNulty, Anthony Renteria, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, Christopher Kruger, Brittany Borges, and Brandon Clupny climbed the stadium steps of Oracle Park to a well-deserved, if wet, victory with a team time of 19:47. The Big Climb SF is a competitive stairs race at Oracle Park, where participants compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s second street entrance. On a national level, The Big Climb is hosted at several different stadiums and venues across the country, including Seattle, Dallas, Boston, and Philadelphia. Last year Piedmont won the “Fastest Team” award and its “Fastest Individual Climber” award as part of the First Responder Challenge. Fire Captain Justin McNulty, the department’s principal organizer, took home the “Fastest Individual Climber” award for Piedmont. Last year was the first time The Big Climb included a separate division for first responders, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. This year, Piedmont competed for the first-place title against other Bay Area fire departments like those of San Francisco and San Mateo. At the time of writing, the Piedmont Fire Department is the sixth-highest corporate donor to the event with $2,180. Overall, the event has raised a total of $175,754 in the LLS. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco and to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. Anthony Renteria (left), Justin McNulty, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, Christopher Kruger, Brittany Borges, and Brandon Clupny formed the winning team from Piedmont Fire Department at The Big Climb this year.
articles.title: Fire Dept. defends title as winner of The Big Climb at Oracle Park

articles.text: An auto accident near the corner of Park View Avenue and Magnolia Avenue left two vehicles damaged after a driver lost control of the vehicle and struck a parked car on Friday, May 3 around 3:00 p.m. The car flipped onto its side and trapped the driver inside their car, who was eventually rescued by nearby neighbors and responding police officers. No one was injured. Resident John Woodley was gazing out his front window, thinking about work, when he noticed a grey Subaru Forester quickly approaching a stop sign near his house. “It reared up like a horse,” as it entered his vision. The car flipped onto its side, trapping the driver inside. Police Captain Chris Monahan confirmed Woodley’s account. “A Subaru Forester struck a Mini Cooper on its side, which caused the Subaru to flip onto its driver’s side,” explained Monahan. Residents on Park View Avenue who heard the noise quickly gathered around the scene. “About eight neighbors showed up within 30 seconds to attend to the driver who was trapped inside the vehicle,” said Woodley. An airbag had been activated. The driver of the car was an older woman. Within three minutes of the accident, two police cars arrived. had the passenger door open and were using a ladder to help the driver escape. “When I went outside with my phone talking to PPD dispatch, neighbors were communicating with the trapped driver,” said Woodley, who provided his eye-witness account to Detective David Cutler. Overall, three police officers, one community service officer, and eight firefighters responded to the accident. Firefighters examined the driver at the scene for medical reasons, but she requested not to be transported to a hospital. articles.text: Spearheaded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF), a new flagpole and American flag will soon be installed to honor the late Presiding Justice Carl Anderson. PBF has teamed up with the Piedmont Scout Council and Piedmont Community Church to memorialize the legacy of one of Piedmont’s greatest volunteers who passed away last year. Even while carrying on a distinguished career, first with the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office, then as a Superior Court Judge, a Justice of the California Court of Appeal, and finally as its Presiding Justice, Carl found time to be one of Piedmont’s most important volunteers. Carl’s service on the Piedmont Scout Council was highlighted by his Herculean efforts in concert with Stephen Bechtel Jr. to preserve the Piedmont Council from absorption into a huge Bay Areawide council. Thanks to Carl’s efforts, the Piedmont Council still survives today and is the smallest Council in the national Scouting movement. Throughout his life, Carl was a member of Piedmont Community Church, where he served on many committees, including the Board of Trustees. In his later years, Carl became an Advisor to PBF, offering his wisdom and opening his home for meetings. Opening his home for charitable events was a hallmark of Carl’s approach to giving. Perhaps the greatest highlight in this regard was the unforgettable blessing bestowed upon the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). He and his wife Margo (who predeceased him) welcomed the PEF to operate from the entire bottom floor of their home for a time of four years. The new flagpole will be located on the Highland Way frontage of the church, near the Scout Office. Local Scouts will be responsible for the management of the American Flag and the location will afford easy access for Scouts working on flag-related requirements for their Tenderfoot and Second-Class ranks. Members of the community who have not yet had an opportunity to honor Carl’s memory are invited to send a contribution to Piedmont Beautification Foundation at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont 94611. Gifts may also be made via PBF’s website, www.piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. Gifts should be earmarked for the Flagpole Project. Carl’s family will be notified of all gifts made in his honor. articles.text: This week’s dog is fouryear-old Pritchard, an at-risk pittie mix at Oakland Animal Services. Pritchard was wellloved, but his family had to give him up when they moved to an apartment that does not allow dogs. Shelter staff note that Pritchard is sweet and enthusiastic. He loves toys, chasing balls and independent play. Despite finding himself at the shelter without his family, he is happy-go-lucky and finds pleasure in rolling around on the grass and sunning himself. At 75-pounds, he might be better suited for a home without small children. Pritchard is available to meet you this Thursday from 12-7 p.m., or Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. and is available for both adoption and foster. Potential adopters or fosters with a child younger than 12 Pritchard, a 4-year old pittie mix. or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Pritchard must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about Oakland Animal Services or fostering, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. articles.text: On the weekend of Sunday, April 21, the Recreation Department invited families to enjoy a free afternoon of homemade miniature golf courses at the first Pop-Up Putt Putt in Piedmont. Beginning at noon in the Community Hall parking lot, more than 260 community members played on 15 courses, 10 designed by Rec Dept. employees and another five by the public. Awards were given for “Best Overall Course,” “Most Creative Course,” “Most Clever Course,” “Best Use of Recycled Materials,” “Best Kid Theme,” and a category dubbed “Sooo Piedmont,” – for embodying the town’s spirit. Although the mini-golf activities were the main attraction, attendees also entertained themselves by enjoying picnic lunches on the lawn and listening to music. ACE Kids, an East Bay junior golf program, also brought a mobile golf simulator so participants could try their skills in a more controlled environment. And the winners are. . . • Best Overall: “House on the Green” by Akil Danjuma, Sports Coordinator at the PRD • Most Creative: “Sneaky Tiki” by Woody Miller Art & The Miller/Murphy Family • Most Clever: “Piedmont Pinball Putt-Putt” by Nicole Verhalen • Best Use of Recycled Materials: “Magnolia Avenue” by Piedmont Recreation Commissioners Jenny Feinberg and Dick Carter • Sooo Piedmont: “Piedmont is the G.O.A.T” by the Pike/Phillips Family • Best Kid Theme: “Pee-Wee Fairway” by Very Barry Labs Winners were recognized at the May 6 City Council meeting. “Overall, this was a wonderful and free family-friendly event,” said Rec Director Chelle Putzer. “PRD would like to thank all of the community members who created a hole for the course, ACE Golf, and PRD’s very own DJ Kev for spinnin’ tunes in the Park!” The “Magic is our Mojo” course created by the Piedmont Recreation Department for the event. Recreation Commissioners Jenny Feinberg and Dick Carter with their award-winning entry for Best Use of Recycled Materials, “Magnolia Avenue.” 4th of July Parade Photos by Jesse Rosenberg A family plays the course “PeeWee Fairway” in the parking lot of the Community Hall. Awards were given for “Best Overall Course,” “Most Creative Course,” “Most Clever Course,” “Best Use of Recycled Materials,” “Best Kid Theme,” and a category dubbed “Sooo Piedmont,” – for embodying the town’s spirit. Although the mini-golf activities were the main attraction, attendees also entertained themselves by enjoying picnic lunches on the lawn and listening to music. ACE Kids, an East Bay junior golf program, also brought a mobile golf simulator so participants could try their skills in a more controlled environment. Rec. Dept. holds Pop-Up Putt Putt event And the winners are. . . • Best Overall: “House on the Green” by Akil Danjuma, Sports Coordinator at the PRD • Most Creative: “Sneaky Tiki” by Woody Miller Art & The Miller/Murphy Family • Most Clever: “Piedmont Pinball Putt-Putt” by Nicole Verhalen • Best Use of Recycled Materials: “Magnolia Avenue” by Piedmont Recreation Commissioners Jenny Feinberg and Dick Carter • Sooo Piedmont: “Piedmont is the G.O.A.T” by the Pike/Phillips Family • Best Kid Theme: “Pee-Wee Fairway” by Very Barry Labs Winners were recognized at the May 6 City Council meeting. “Overall, this was a wonderful and free family-friendly event,” said Rec Director Chelle Putzer. “PRD would like to thank all of the community members who created a hole for the course, ACE Golf, and PRD’s very own DJ Kev for spinnin’ tunes in the Park!” The “Magic is our Mojo” course created by the Piedmont Recreation Department for the event. Recreation Commissioners Jenny Feinberg and Dick Carter with their award-winning entry for Best Use of Recycled Materials, “Magnolia Avenue.” PIEDMONT 57 th 4th of July Parade Photos by Jesse Rosenberg A family plays the course “PeeWee Fairway” in the parking lot of the Community Hall. 2024 PARADE ENTRY FORM We hope your group will be a part of this year’s 4th of July Parade in Piedmont. This year’s parade theme is small town. BIG SPIRIT. The parade will take place on Highland Avenue starting at 11 a.m. on Thursday, July 4. . As a reminder, candy may be handed out on the parade route but not thrown from vehicles. Send the completed form to: Kathy Kelleher, 9 Monte Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 email: kjkelleh@yahoo.com Phone: (510) 915-8842 Date: Group Name: Contact Name: Address: Phone: Day: Evening: Fax: Email: Group description: (# of people, vehicles, music, etc.) Special needs: (problems with hills, turning corners, parade placement, etc.) Akil Danjuma puts the final touches on his creation “House on the Green,” which won the award for “Best Overall Course” at the event.

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board meeting tonight, May 8, will be held in City Hall at 7:00 p.m., and will include important items for the future of Piedmont schools. To keep with a May 15 deadline, the district will approve the sending of final layoff notices to teachers and staff indicating impending terminations or reductions in employment for next year. Updates on the racial equity policies in the district, new contracts and raises for admins, and a pitch for a district-wide climate literacy resolution also appear on the agenda with anticipation. Addressing equity will be DEIB Director Jean Chen Takazawa, who will give a progress report on the Racial Equity Board Policies. She will be assisted in the presentation by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich. The board meeting will also include a presentation about adopting a Climate Literacy Resolution district-wide. Former school board member Sarah Pearson will be formally presented with the 2024 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year award at the meeting. Resignations The Personnel Action Report on the agenda, lists the following teachers who have tendered their resignations effective at the end of the school year. • Colin Chang, Science Teacher at PMS • Viviana Green, Spanish Teacher at PHS • Michele Sage, Special Education Teacher at Beach & Wildwood • Samantha Wilde, Music Teacher at PHS, PMS, Beach, Wildwood & Havens Another item of significance is the announced hiring of a new high school Athletic Director. Tyler Small. Access to the meeting can be done remotely via Zoom. us/j/81545337316.
articles.title: Preview of tonight’s vital school board meeting

articles.text: The busy Piedmont High School and Middle School instrumental music programs bring the school year to an end with three wonderful May concerts at the Alan Harvey Theater, beginning Tuesday, May 21st. Tuesday, May 21, 7:00 p.m. The PHS Symphonic Band & Jazz Band, directed by Band teacher Trevor Meseroll, will present a combined Spring Concert. The evening will include music by Stevie Wonder and Barry Manilow, selections from the movie Pirates of the Caribbean, “Agua De Beber” by Antonio Carlos Jobim, and the jazz standard “Unforgettable” with vocal soloist Nate McKenzie. Several small jazz combos will also be on the program. Wednesday, May 22, 7:00 p.m. The PMS 7th grade and 8th grade bands led by Meseroll and the 6th grade band led by Cathy DeVos (6th grade) take the stage. Included on the program is music by Freddie Mercury, Bruno Mars, and the rock band Chicago. A calypso piece, as well as a March and an Overture by Bruce Pearson, will appear on the program. Well-known musical standards such as “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” and “Saturday in the Park” will also be performed. Thursday, May 23, at 7:00 p.m. The PMS & PHS Orchestras, directed by Sam Wilde, take their turn on the Alan Harvey Theater stage. Music selections on the PMS program include “Viva la Vida” by Coldplay and music from the movie “The Hunger Games.” The PHS High School Orchestra repertoire includes the gorgeous Edward Elgar piece “Nimrod,” the first movement of Franz Schubert’s Symphony #5, and music from “Scheherazade” by Rimsky-Korsakov, which is based on the tales of the Arabian Nights. To help offset concert expenses at all concerts, a $5.00 suggested donation for adults will be requested at the door. All students are admitted free.
articles.title: Spring Instrumental Music Concerts begin May 21

articles.text: Deanna Johnson, Director of Highlands Preschool, has announced her plans to retire at the end of the school year after 25 years of teaching. Johnson began at Highlands in 1999 as a parttime classroom assistant and now, 750 students later, she retiring. Johnson has been involved with children in some capacity for over 40 years whether as a babysitter, nanny, camp counselor, reading coach, teacher or preschool director. “I have learned so much in my 25 years at Highlands. As teachers, we have the amazing, unique privilege of helping children discover who they are and develop a love of learning. It is a privilege to impact their lives in a positive way,” said Johnson. Johnson’s history in the Piedmont community goes back to Wildwood Elementary, where she attended school as a kid and then later graduated from Piedmont High. Some of her favorite memories growing up include exploring the creek and caves in Piedmont Park, and riding her bike around Witter Field. Johnson has had a significant Deanna Johnson playing dress up with a preschool student. impact on the community and can be spotted by her huge smile, infectious laugh, and unmistakable rapport with children. “[Children] are pure and genuine and are full of boundless energy and creativity. They help remind me to see things as they do: with wonder, excitement and awe,” she said. Johnson will stay on next year as advisor. Angela Livermore, who has been teaching at Highlands for 15 years, will become the school’s new director. “I have been so lucky to work for so long at a job that I love. There is truly a special feeling at Highlands. It’s magical, and I know that whatever I do in my life, I’ll take a little bit of that magic with me,” said Johnson. To share your Piedmont or Highlands memories with Deanna Johnson, email director. highlandspreschool@gmail.com Highlands teachers Danielle Biondi (left), Deanna Johnson, Angela Livermore, and Tracy Herrera at a retirement party for Johnson.
articles.title: Highlands Preschool director to retire

articles.text: Summer is just around the corner, and PUSD’s Summer Adventures program is gearing up for an unforgettable season of learning and fun. Two sessions of summer enrichment activities this June called Summer Adventure will be held at Havens Elementary this summer. The majority of classes are for elementary age kids; registration is now open. Summer Adventures Session 1: June 5-14 (8 days) Session 2: June 17-27 (8 days) Morning Only (9:00 a.m.-12:00 p.m.): $525 Full Day (9:00 a.m.-3:00 p.m.): $1050 Engaging Morning Classes Morning classes tailored to ignite your child’s imagination. From art to science to sports there’s something for every kids. Led by passionate instructors, these classes provide the perfect opportunity for children to explore new interests and develop valuable skills. Special Highlights The Welcome to Kindergarten/TK program is specially crafted to give young learners a head start before the school year begins. Led by dedicated PUSD teacher Claire Stephens, these programs offer a warm and welcoming environment where children can make new friends while learning and having fun. Welcome to Sixth Grade The Welcome to Sixth Grade program is aimed at helping students transition smoothly into middle school life. Taught by experienced sixth-grade teachers, Anjuna Lohnes and Hillary Voigt, this revamped program ensures that students are well-prepared for the academic challenges ahead. Afternoon Sessions For families in need of allday care, we’re excited to offer afternoon sessions from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. During these sessions, children will have the opportunity to rotate through a variety of exciting classes each day. Whether your child is passionate about art, science, sports, or cooking, they will be. Afternoon classes feature a dynamic mix of PUSD staff, coaches, players, and college students, guaranteeing a vibrant and energetic experience for all participants. Plus, lunch is provided every Friday. Piedmont Basketball Camp Led by Coach Jason Harris, players of all levels can enjoy 90 minutes of energetic activities daily. From fundamental drills to full-court workouts, the program offers insights into basketball concepts within a positive environment. Whether aspiring to a high school career or loving the game, everyone is welcome. Plus, morning session attendees receive transportation from Havens to Binks Rawlings Gym. Don’t miss a chance to make this summer unforgettable for your child. Visit www.piedmont. k12.ca.us/summer-school for more information and to register for the Summer Adventures program today.
articles.title: Summer Adventures at Piedmont summer school

articles.text: The Wildwood Parents Club will formally celebrate Wildwood’s 100th year in existence this Saturday, May 11, in the school’s auditorium. Current and former Wildwood students, parents, teachers and staff are invited to 301 Wildwood from 2-4 p.m. to honor the school with a birthday cake, live music, and fun activities for the whole There will be light snacks and beverages, plus an anniversary cake to share. Wildwood alumni bands will provide live music for parts of the celebration. During the event, Wildwood will be presented with a proclamation from the City of Piedmont. Artifacts from Wildwood’s beginning will be on display in the auditorium, bringing to life the school’s days of yore. A Wildwood Timeline showing events from all 10 decades of and a slideshow will satisfy the curiosity of any and all historians on hand. Guests in attendance on Saturday afternoon can participate in a scavenger hunt of Wildwood fun facts for a raffle ticket to win a basket of Wildwood Gear. A henna booth for guests will also be set up by Wildwood alum. During this event, the Parents Club will also honor a couple of teachers who will be leaving Wildwood after the year: P.E. teacher Brad Sullivan and 5th grade teacher Lydia Tang. Wildwood Parents Club President Carolyn Pan will again be spearheading this event, which is the culmination of a full year of celebration. It’s amazing how parents have been working with the school since the very beginning,” said Pan. articles.text: Tilden Steam Train Redwood-valley-railway.business.site 2481 Grizzly Peak Blvd, Orinda 548-6100 The Tilden Steam train has been in operation since 1952 and is open weekends from 11:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., weather permitting. Grab a $3.50 ticket for views of the Bay and even traverse through a dark tunnel while riding a reallife Thomas the Tank Engine. Put on the conductor hats and head to the hills. Kids will love riding the miniature steam train chugging along on 15-inch gauge tracks. Sit in an open-air cabin, ride in the caboose or have a snack in a miniature dining car. Alcatraz Tours Cityexperiences.com/san-francisco/city-cruises/alcatraz/ Pier 33, The Embarcadero, San Francisco “The Rock” is open for visitors. Take the kids on an unforgettable tour to Alcatraz Island. Steeped in local history, tours of the former penitentiary are also available at night and with a “behind the scenes” option. Now a historical site museum, Alcatraz is reached by the ferry from Pier 33 in San Francisco. Tours sell out quickly, especially in the summer months, so book a reservation in advance. Berkeley Marina - Walking Path Cityofberkeley.info/Marina_Home 11 Spinnaker Way, Berkeley 981-6740 The Berkeley Marina has over 100 acres of park space and 7 miles of trails. Grab the pooch and take advantage of the 17-acre off-leash dog area. The area lends itself to bird-watching, and has consistent wind for kite flying. Come for the fresh air, and feel the Bay’s majesty up close. Bring binoculars to check out the boats in the marina. Cal Academy of Sciences Calacademy.org Golden Gate Park, 55 Music Concourse Dr., S.F. (415) 379-8000 California Academy has a lot to engage the mind and changes on a daily basis. The four-story rainforest has everything from butterflies to the bioluminescent depths of the “twilight zone.” Kids will enjoy the feeding of the African penguins, and a tour of Steinhart Aquarium. Guests can glimpse the rich ecosystems of the California Coast, and the Philippine Coral Reef. Kids will want to stay for special programs at the planetarium so reserve in advance.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 8, 2024 9 Play Like a Girl Continued from page 1 ment) showing training exercises. In addition to an impressive selection of sports stations, many former Olympians were present to offer their experience and answer questions from youth on the event’s main stage. Five-time Olympic gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant (swimming), twotime Paralympic gold medalist Bethany Zummo (sitting volleyball), former professional boxer Dalia “La Pantera” Gomez, and former professional baseball player Tamara Holmes all spoke to theyoung women in attendance. articles.text: A Scout is many things (Trustworthy, Loyal, Helpful, Friendly, Courteous, Kind, Obedient, Cheerful, Thrifty, Brave, Clean, and Reverent); and Eagle Scouts work very hard over many years to earn their ranks. On Friday, May 10, five deserving young men and women from the Piedmont Scout Council Troop 11 were presented their Eagle Scout ranks in a ceremony at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens Elementary. The evening was filled with ceremony enough to inspire all the younger scouts towards the rank of Eagle. Earning the rank of Eagle takes years of devoted work and six ranks to qualify to start the Eagle requirements. Each rank has requirements that teach skills and leadership, until the Scouts are in active leadership roles for their unit. They participate as troop leaders for at least 16 months, and have seven boards of review, seven scoutmaster conferences, while volunteering time in the community and for the council. The goal is to teach them to be leaders in society with the award of Eagle, a rank widely being regarded by political, military, and business leaders to be a sign of special leadership skills. While earning ranks, each candidate must also earn at least 21 merit badges. Another requirement is to propose, get approved, then conduct an Eagle project that benefits their community. The current group of five have collectively contributed many hundreds of community hours from collecting food at Scouting for Food to their Eagle projects. They also have helped fund their council through their efforts supporting the annual Christmas tree lot. The Piedmont Scout Council is the smallest council in the United States, thriving in a small, tightknit community. Being small has its advantages. Nationally, only a very small percentage become Eagle, whereas the Piedmont Council’s program has a much higher percentage. Each year, about 100 scouts or more enter the program and about 20 Eagle ranks are awarded. Piedmont also benefits from a much higher percentage of saturation within our community. About 25% of available youth participate in Piedmont, as compared with the national average of 2%. Each of the five new Eagles has gone on many outings from ski trips, snow camping trips, rafting, and canoeing trips to competitive events that demonstrate and test their outdoor and leadership skills. They’ve spent time in rain-soaked tents and learning hard lessons about how to survive and thrive in all conditions. Each of them has cooked their meals over open fires and spent their nights among the wildlife that they try to respect and preserve. These individuals represent interests from Business to Aeronautical Engineering and the Arts, with instilled moral compasses that run true, leadership qualities that exemplify a future of greatness.

articles.text: Emily Thompson The end of the school year is fast approaching, and this time of year can be particularly stressful. On top of preparing for finals, many students are also taking AP exams, managing extracurricular activities, making college visits, and planning their summers. It is important to think about tangible ways students can navigate this stressful time. Below are three action items that we have found particularly useful in helping students manage their stress: • Take care of yourself When we feel stressed, selfcare is often the first thing we sacrifice. It is imperative that students prioritize sleep, healthy diet, and exercise. The brain’s ability to learn and store information improves when well-rested and well-fed. Exercise helps reduce stress hormones, like cortisol and adrenaline, which negatively impact our ability to concentrate. While staying up until 3 a.m. to cram for an exam might seem like a good idea at the time, it is likely counterproductive. • Make a plan Write out a thorough list that includes the dates of academic items (assignments and tests) as well as non-academic priorities (like an important track meet or a friend’s bat mitzvah). Creating a timeline of events makes it easier to understand what the top priorities are and what steps to take, which helps combat the feeling of overwhelm when it is unclear where to start. • Set realistic goals Have you heard of SMART goals? SMART goals are a game-changer for many students. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Rather than setting a vague goal to “study” for your biology final, here is an example of a SMART goal: “locate my biology study guide and organize my class notes by Tuesday; spend one hour reviewing my flashcards on Wednesday; complete the extra practice problems and review my misses on Thursday.” specific and manageable chunks, students have a better chance of holding themselves accountable and reaching their goals. Managing stress is about building better habits! While this time of year is particularly hectic, these tips can help mitigate stress for students (and adults!) any time the to-do list feels daunting. Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of College Counseling and Emily is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. For more information, please visit www.studysmarter. com, email info@studysmarter. com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: Samantha Huynh Need service hours? Want to give back to your community while having fun and meeting new people? Interested in exploring and developing leadership skills in a supportive environment? Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) might be the solution you are seeking. PCSC is a youth-led Venturing Crew, part of Scouts BSA, that strives to develop and instill leadership skills in local youth while helping out the community. Members of PCSC prepare meals for the hungry at local churches and charity facilities. They help renovate homes for the economically challenged, and they help clean up the environment. During the summer, Crew members attend service trips and Piedmont’s July 4th Pancake Breakfast. In addition to serving their community, Crew members can also run for various positions, allowing them to cultivate their leadership and teamwork skills in this youth-led program. “PCSC is a great way to give back and connect with the community,” said Shou Presley, a sophomore at Piedmont High School. “By joining PCSC, I have developed leadership skills through leading events that deal with large-scale problems like climate change and homelessness. Overall, the crew is really fun, and I would highly recommend joining,” said Presley. While PCSC is largely focused on youth leadership, another major goal of the organization is for teens to have fun while doing it. PCSC has a wide spectrum of events to cater to our members’ interests and the community’s needs. PHS sophomore Stephanie Lee and classmate Elena O’Connell are currently running for co-presidency. “PCSC has taught me skills like organization and has given me a platform to pitch my ideas. Elena and I are running for co-presidency and one of our goals is to create a community within PCSC that allows others to connect on a social level while doing service and gaining leadership experience.” To get involved, PCSC Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net or visit the PCSC website at www.pcservicecrew.org. Priyanka Seshan and Samantha Huynh are members of Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing program with Piedmont Scouts. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team gathers for one last photo following their NCS Quarterfinals match. The Highlanders’ girls’ lacrosse team had its season come to an end on Thursday, May 2 with a 9-7 loss to No. 4 Acalanes in Lafayette in the North Coast Section quarterfinals. PHS earlier defeated No. 12 Urban 20-5 in the first round on Tuesday, April 30 at Witter Field. Thursday’s game featured Piedmont responding to a fivegoal deficit in the third quarter when trailing 6-1. “At the end of the day, it was just landing our shots. We were getting our plays, we were getting shooting space chances, everything was coming together. Their goalie was amazing, so hat’s off to her. We just told them to make a slight adjustment in their shot to shoot it at her foot, or make the ball bounce about a foot in front of her, and it was beautiful to see the team execute that slight adjustment,” coach Carlton Chan said. Acalanes’ last line of defense ultimately made the difference with goalie Addie Martin recording 11 saves. Senior attacker Ruby Guzdar was a major part of the Highlanders’ turnaround, scoring four goals in the second half. “Their goalie was very good and was saving our usual shots. But we knew in the second quarter that if we falter this way and give in, this would be it and we’re going to go home feeling sad knowing we could’ve played better. We turned on the gas at the end,” Guzdar said. Winning face offs was a big factor in the Piedmont comeback rally, in which they scored five straight goals after winning draws in the third- and fourth-quarters. Senior midfielder Hailey Marshburn grabbed four draws while and Hallie Burden won six. “A big thing was the draws. We started winning those draws and it’s a big confidence boost because you have possession and it gives you an opportunity to make something of it on the offensive end,” said Marshburn. Piedmont concludes its season with a 14-5 overall record including going undefeated against Western Alameda County Conference opponents at 7-0, including winning this year’s league title. Seven players depart with the Class of 2024: Guzdar, Marshburn, Orla Cohen, Laurel Bentley, Jane Hempeck, Henley Lorin, and Kira Pan. Piedmont will potentially return key players in 2025: Friedie Schickedanz, Hallie Burden, Chloe Graham, Luisa Cole, Annika Hattan-Kutter, and Peyton Watson. 9-7 to Acalanes Acalanes opened the scoring near three minutes in, then won the next faceoff and turned it into a goal at the 8:04 mark, going up 3-0 with 5:48 to go. Acalanes’ Martin had five saves in the first quarter. In the second quarter, Luisa Cole got Piedmont’s first goal on a shooting space opportunity, launching in a low shot with 5:03 left. From there, Guzdar and Watson both had shots saved before the Dons scored with 44.6 seconds left, making it 4-1. Acalanes then scored two straight goals in the third quarter to jump up 6-1 with 9:53 on the clock, but the comeback was on from there. After a faceoff win by Burden, Marshburn gained a shooting space chance, scoring with 8:22 left. Marshburn then jumped on the following faceoff, but Acalanes forced a ground ball at midfield. Guzdar then fought to scoop the ground ball, sprinting up field to send in a shot, 6-3. After back and forth possessions, Burden scored from a shooting space chance with 1:52 on the clock. By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders’ girls’ lacrosse team had its season come to an end on Thursday, May 2 with a 9-7 loss to No. 4 Acalanes in Lafayette in the North Coast Section quarterfinals. PHS earlier defeated No. 12 Urban 20-5 in the first round on Tuesday, April 30 at Witter Field. Thursday’s game featured Piedmont responding to a fivegoal deficit in the third quarter when trailing 6-1. “At the end of the day, it was just landing our shots. We were getting our plays, we were getting shooting space chances, everything was coming together. Their goalie was amazing, so hat’s off to her. We just told them to make a slight adjustment in their shot to shoot it at her foot, or make the ball bounce about a foot in front of her, and it was beautiful to see the team execute that slight adjustment,” coach Carlton Chan said. Acalanes’ last line of defense ultimately made the difference with goalie Addie Martin recording 11 saves. Senior attacker Ruby Guzdar was a major part of the Highlanders’ turnaround, scoring four goals in the second half. “Their goalie was very good and was saving our usual shots. But we knew in the second quarter that if we falter this way and give in, this would be it and we’re going to go home feeling sad knowing we could’ve played better. We turned on the gas at the end,” Guzdar said. Winning face offs was a big factor in the Piedmont comeback rally, in which they scored five straight goals after winning draws in the third- and fourth-quarters. Senior midfielder Hailey Marshburn grabbed four draws while and Hallie Burden won six. “A big thing was the draws. We started winning those draws and it’s a big confidence boost because you have possession and it gives you an opportunity to make something of it on the offensive end,” said Marshburn. Piedmont concludes its season with a 14-5 overall record including going undefeated against Western Alameda County Conference opponents at 7-0, including winning this year’s league title. Seven players depart with the Class of 2024: Guzdar, Marshburn, Orla Cohen, Laurel Bentley, Jane Hempeck, Henley Lorin, and Kira Pan. Piedmont will potentially return key players in 2025: Friedie Schickedanz, Hallie Burden, Chloe Graham, Luisa Cole, Annika Hattan-Kutter, and Peyton Watson. 9-7 to Acalanes Acalanes opened the scoring near three minutes in, then won the next faceoff and turned it into a goal at the 8:04 mark, going up 3-0 with 5:48 to go. Acalanes’ Martin had five saves in the first quarter. In the second quarter, Luisa Cole got Piedmont’s first goal on a shooting space opportunity, launching in a low shot with 5:03 left. From there, Guzdar and Watson both had shots saved before the Dons scored with 44.6 seconds left, making it 4-1. Acalanes then scored two straight goals in the third quarter to jump up 6-1 with 9:53 on the clock, but the comeback was on from there. After a faceoff win by Burden, Marshburn gained a shooting space chance, scoring with 8:22 left. Marshburn then jumped on the following faceoff, but Acalanes forced a ground ball at midfield. Although the Highlanders finished the regular season in first place, they needed a championship victory in the WACC Tournament to secure an automatic home playoff bid for the firstround of the North Coast Section Piedmont opened scoring with two runs in the bottom of the second, but Alameda tacked on two runs in the top of the third. articles.text: Piedmont High sophomore Lucas Smolko battled his way to the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tennis Tournament at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco on Friday and Monday, May 3-6. Despite playing strong tennis on the opening day of the tournament, Smolko had to retire during the second set of his match against University’s eventual-champion Karam Dhawan due to illness. Smolko dropped the first set 6-3 and was down 4-0 in the second set. He earned fourth-place in singles. “Lucas was playing great on Friday and had two dominant wins. But on Monday, he was sick and had to retire in the second set of his match against Karam Dhawan,” explained coach Jim Landes. Karam went on to win the championship over Lick-Wilmerding’s Saahil Mishra,” Smolko defeated Mishra, the finalist from Lick, earlier this season 6-1, 7-6 (7-3) on March 13. On Friday, Smolko won his opening round match over Davis Walsh of Cardinal Newman in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1. He followed up with a dominant 6-0, 6-3 win over Rex Rutchik of Marin Academy in the quarterfinals. It’s an unfortunate turn for Lucas after entering the tournament with the No. 1 seed. He came to NCS after winning this year’s league championship singles title the previous week. Also competing in the singles ladder was Piedmont senior Ben Breber, falling to Mishra 6-1, 6-0 in the first round. The Highlanders also brought senior Monte Imburg and sophoStaff Photos Lucas Smolko reached the North Coast Section Individual Tournament semifinals but had to retire due to illness in a match with eventual champion from University. more Nate Welch to the D2 doubles tournament. They faced a difficult task in the first round, squaring up against top seed Cole Boake and Eli Linn of University, losing 6-3, 6-0. Boake and Linn went on to win the doubles title. Imburg and Welch were also coming off of a WACC doubles title the previous week. Piedmont now looks ahead to the Division 2 NCS Team Tournament. It enters as the No. 7 seed. Their first round match was on Tuesday, May 7 against No. 10 Marin Academy, hosting the Wildcats and the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Results were not complete by Post time. NEXT UP Piedmont will face the winner of No. 2 Branson or No. 15 Middletown on Thursday, May 9, likely traveling to the second-ranked school in Ross. With a quarterfinals victory, the semifinals and finals are both set for Saturday, May 11. Monte Imburg and Nate Welch (back) also competed in the doubles bracket.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse’s season came to an end on Tuesday, April 30 in the first-round of the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs. Seeded No. 11, they lost 15-7 loss at No. 6 San Ramon Valley in Danville. The loss concludes PHS’ season with an 8-6 overall record. Despite a productive start against SRV with five goals in the first quarter to trail 8-5 after a high-scoring opening 12 minutes, the Highlanders’ attack couldn’t find the same fluidity as the early going and managed to score just two goals in the remaining three quarters. It was a rough transition year for Piedmont High. They school didn’t secure a league title for the first time after six consecutive years as Western Alameda County Conference champions. PHS earned a promotion to NCS’ top division after reaching last year’s D2 NCS Finals, which they lost 9-8 in sudden-death overtime to Tamalpais. But shortly after last year’s Finals, coach Al Yu and assistant coaches David Hafner and Matt Palasek announced they were departing after the season. Palasek elected to stay closer to home to become Casa Grande’s head coach, which made it to the NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 8 seed before losing to No. 1 Marin Catholic. PHS freshman Connor Fredericks was a standout player in his debut year. Staff Photos Rylan Nelson scored three goals in his final Piedmont appearance. However, online records show Piedmont never prepared for Yu’s departure. The job opening was not posted on Edjoin.com until November. And with a lack of available lacrosse coaches in the area, Piedmont parents scrambled to find new coach Jeff Lamb through a personal connection just months before the season started. Despite Lamb’s lack of time in a coaching role, this year’s team was able to lean on the experience of Rylan Nelson, Curtis Hohener, Oliver Shafroth, Andrew Mclaughlin, Keita Clear, Logan Huh, and Gus Von Metzsch, while also identifying a standout freshman, Connor Fredericks. They established a sixgame winning streak in March to create a 6-2 record and even recorded their first shutout of a D1 opponent in a 7-0 win over Cal High on March 8. The last time Piedmont was in D1, they lost 21-7 to No. 4 Vista Del Lago in 2022 as the No. 13 seed. The next season, PHS returned to D2 to narrowly lose the Finals to No. 1 Tamalpais 9-8 as the No. 3 seed. It will be interesting to see if PHS will return to D2 in 2025. 15-7 to San Ramon Valley Piedmont trailed San Ramon Valley 8-5 after a high scoring first quarter, but the Wolves jumped out to an 11-5 lead in the second quarter by netting six and not allowing a single goal. PHS scored once in the third and once in the fourth. In the first quarter, San Ramon Valley won the opening face off and scored 30 seconds into the match. But Piedmont returned the favor on the next faceoff, with Fredericks winning the draw before Shafroth scored after just 12 seconds, 1-1 at 11:20. PHS then took a 2-1 lead with a shot by Nelson in transition after winning the faceoff for a goal just 13 seconds later. Shafroth then put PHS ahead 3-1 with 9:12 on the clock. But from there, SRV went on a three goal scoring run to lead 4-3 at the 4:07 mark. Timmy Kalamas tied it up for Piedmont at 2:35, but San Ramon Valley fired off another three goals in rapid fire succession to lead 7-4 with 44.5 seconds left. Nelson then drew it closed with a goal with 23 seconds left, but SRV won the following faceoff and scored right before halftime, 8-5. That was the closest things got for the Highlanders, going scoreless in the second quarter but allowing three. Nelson scored once in the third quarter, while Shafroth got one in the fourth. Final stats: Nelson had three goals and grabbed three ground balls. Shafroth also scored three, had one assist, and gathered three loose balls. Kalamas scored once. Fredericks grabbed four ground balls and won seven draws. Von Metszch had 14 saves. Senior Oliver Shafroth has a hat trick for Piedmont.
