articles.text: Nina Schwab qualifies for CIF State On May 3 Piedmont High’s swim team competed at the Concord Community Pool for the preliminary round of this year’s North Coast Section Championship. The top 40 swimmers in the section competed to determine which 16 would move on to the NCS finals on Friday May 4. Piedmont’s only diver, senior Nina Schwab, qualified for the CIF State Championship by finishing fourth out of 16 divers for the one-meter dive with a score of 423.75 after 11 dives. She’ll travel to Clovis West High School in Fresno for the State Diving Championship on May 9-11. The weather was a drastic change from Friday’s sunny and warm prelims, with temps all Saturday in the mid 50’s, and heavy rain. As a result, almost all swimmers had slower times than the previous day. In the NCS finals Owen Blanford placed ninth of 16 in the 200 Free with a time of 1:42.58. His time was fast enough to gain a CIF Consideration listing, making him an alternate at State. The boys’ 200 Free Relay of Blanford, Tom Rolefson, Nik Costello and Dima Secor placed 11th of 16 teams with a time of 1:28.23, gaining them a CIF Consideration time. To get there, the squad was 13th of 40 in the prelims in 1:27.79 which is a PHS record. PHS’ boys 400 Free Relay of Blanford, Rolefson, Costello, and Asher Takazawa were also 11th of 16 with a time of 3:11.66 to gain a CIF State Consideration as well. They reached the finals by finishing ninth of 40 in the prelims in 3:10.09. Both the 200 and 400 freestyle relay teams will be alternatives for State. According to team officials, both the 200 and 400 relay teams’ times are new school records, along with Blanford’s individual time in the 200 Photo by Kim Fisher Piedmont diver Nina Schwab automatically qualified for the CIF State Diving Championship by finishing fourth at the NCS Finals. freestyle. Asher Takazawa was 16th in the 100 backstroke with a time of 54.25. He qualified for the finals by finishing 17th of 40 in 53.03. For the girls, Taylor Rolefson placed 16th in the 100 butterfly in 59.73. She reached the finals by finishing 16th of 40 in the preliminaries, 58.44. She also narrowly missed out on the NCS Finals in the 200 freestyle, finishing 17th Photo by Kathy Rolefson Owen Blanford placed ninth of 16 in the 200 freestyle finals. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, May 8, 2024 Boys’ Lacrosse season ends in first-round of NCS By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse’s season came to an end on Tuesday, April 30 in the first-round of the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs. Seeded No. 11, they lost 15-7 loss at No. 6 San Ramon Valley in Danville. The loss concludes PHS’ season with an 8-6 overall record. Despite a productive start against SRV with five goals in the first quarter to trail 8-5 after a high-scoring opening 12 minutes, the Highlanders’ attack couldn’t find the same fluidity as the early going and managed to score just two goals in the remaining three quarters. It was a rough transition year for Piedmont High. They school didn’t secure a league title for the first time after six consecutive years as Western Alameda County Conference champions. PHS earned a promotion to NCS’ top division after reaching last year’s D2 NCS Finals, which they lost 9-8 in sudden-death overtime to Tamalpais. But shortly after last year’s Finals, coach Al Yu and assistant coaches David Hafner and Matt Palasek announced they were departing after the season. Palasek elected to stay closer to home to become Casa Grande’s head coach, which made it to the NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 8 seed before losing to No. 1 Marin Catholic. PHS freshman Connor Fredericks was a standout player in his debut year. Staff Photos Rylan Nelson scored three goals in his final Piedmont appearance. However, online records show Piedmont never prepared for Yu’s departure. The job opening was not posted on Edjoin.com until November. And with a lack of available lacrosse coaches in the area, Piedmont parents scrambled to find new coach Jeff Lamb through a personal connection just months before the season started. Despite Lamb’s lack of time in a coaching role, this year’s team was able to lean on the experience of Rylan Nelson, Curtis Hohener, Oliver Shafroth, Andrew Mclaughlin, Keita Clear, Logan Huh, and Gus Von Metzsch, while also identifying a standout freshman, Connor Fredericks. They established a sixgame winning streak in March to create a 6-2 record and even recorded their first shutout of a D1 opponent in a 7-0 win over Cal High on March 8. The last time Piedmont was in D1, they lost 21-7 to No. 4 Vista Del Lago in 2022 as the No. 13 seed. The next season, PHS returned to D2 to narrowly lose the Finals to No. 1 Tamalpais 9-8 as the No. 3 seed. It will be interesting to see if PHS will return to D2 in 2025. 15-7 to San Ramon Valley Piedmont trailed San Ramon Valley 8-5 after a high scoring first quarter, but the Wolves jumped out to an 11-5 lead in the second quarter by netting six and not allowing a single goal. PHS scored once in the third and once in the fourth. In the first quarter, San Ramon Valley won the opening face off and scored 30 seconds into the match. But Piedmont returned the favor on the next faceoff, with Fredericks winning the draw before Shafroth scored after just 12 seconds, 1-1 at 11:20. PHS then took a 2-1 lead with a shot by Nelson in transition after winning the faceoff for a goal just 13 seconds later. Shafroth then put PHS ahead 3-1 with 9:12 on the clock. But from there, SRV went on a three goal scoring run to lead 4-3 at the 4:07 mark. Timmy Kalamas tied it up for Piedmont at 2:35, but San Ramon Valley fired off another three goals in rapid fire succession to lead 7-4 with 44.5 seconds left. Nelson then drew it closed with a goal with 23 seconds left, but SRV won the following faceoff and scored right before halftime, 8-5. That was the closest things got for the Highlanders, going scoreless in the second quarter but allowing three. Nelson scored once in the third quarter, while Shafroth got one in the fourth. Final stats: Nelson had three goals and grabbed three ground balls. Shafroth also scored three, had one assist, and gathered three loose balls. Kalamas scored once. Fredericks grabbed four ground balls and won seven draws. Von Metszch had 14 saves. Senior Oliver Shafroth has a hat trick for Piedmont. PHS swim team competes at NCS Nina Schwab qualifies for CIF State On May 3 Piedmont High’s swim team competed at the Concord Community Pool for the preliminary round of this year’s North Coast Section Championship. The top 40 swimmers in the section competed to determine which 16 would move on to the NCS finals on Friday May 4. Piedmont’s only diver, senior Nina Schwab, qualified for the CIF State Championship by finishing fourth out of 16 divers for the one-meter dive with a score of 423.75 after 11 dives. She’ll travel to Clovis West High School in Fresno for the State Diving Championship on May 9-11. The weather was a drastic change from Friday’s sunny and warm prelims, with temps all Saturday in the mid 50’s, and heavy rain. As a result, almost all swimmers had slower times than the previous day. In the NCS finals Owen Blanford placed ninth of 16 in the 200 Free with a time of 1:42.58. His time was fast enough to gain a CIF Consideration listing, making him an alternate at State. The boys’ 200 Free Relay of Blanford, Tom Rolefson, Nik Costello and Dima Secor placed 11th of 16 teams with a time of 1:28.23, gaining them a CIF Consideration time. To get there, the squad was 13th of 40 in the prelims in 1:27.79 which is a PHS record. PHS’ boys 400 Free Relay of Blanford, Rolefson, Costello, and Asher Takazawa were also 11th of 16 with a time of 3:11.66 to gain a CIF State Consideration as well. They reached the finals by finishing ninth of 40 in the prelims in 3:10.09. Both the 200 and 400 freestyle relay teams will be alternatives for State. According to team officials, both the 200 and 400 relay teams’ times are new school records, along with Blanford’s individual time in the 200 Photo by Kim Fisher Piedmont diver Nina Schwab automatically qualified for the CIF State Diving Championship by finishing fourth at the NCS Finals. freestyle. Asher Takazawa was 16th in the 100 backstroke with a time of 54.25. He qualified for the finals by finishing 17th of 40 in 53.03. For the girls, Taylor Rolefson placed 16th in the 100 butterfly in 59.73. She reached the finals by finishing 16th of 40 in the preliminaries, 58.44. She also narrowly missed out on the NCS Finals in the 200 freestyle, finishing 17th See Swimming on page 31 Photo by Kathy Rolefson Owen Blanford placed ninth of 16 in the 200 freestyle finals. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks to regroup ahead of the NCS postseason playoffs. Piedmont’s softball team battled in the first-round of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Tournament as the No. 5 seed against No. 4 San Leandro on Monday, May 6 at Burrell Field. After trailing 2-1 through the first four innings, San Leandro piled on six runs in the bottom of the fourth and another three in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule and win 11-1. PHS was looking productive in its first four innings of work with Miya Fujimoto on the mound. Prior to exiting after three innings of pitching, Fujimoto had seven strikeouts. However, the junior leader twisted her ankle in the top of the fourth on first base after hitting a fielder’s choice groundball. Although Fujimoto is naturally an infielder and ideally plays shortstop as Piedmont’s best glove in the field, she’s pitched for the Highlanders over the past two years. Aside from her, PHS doesn’t have anyone with pitching experience. “Fuji got hurt and the momentum went downhill. She’s been the biggest part of the team all year, she’s thrown at least 100 innings for us in her two years as a pitcher. She’s been our ace and she’s not a pitcher, that’s the thing about it. But she’s pitching for the team and I appreciate that. These girls are giving it their all, and that’s all I can ask for,” coach Gene Denard said following the game. It was an inauspicious start for Piedmont High. Already short on players, the beginning of the game had to be halted with students late to the field due to ongoing testing around this time of the year. With just 11 players on the roster, Fujimoto’s injury exasperated an already depleted lineup. “Today just started bad, there was some miscommunication about testing and had to wait for players to come. It was a bad omen for the day, then Fuji gets hurt in an inning where it looks like we’re going to score about four runs,” Denard said. This year’s WACC Shoreline tournament was structured differently than other years, including the last time PHS won the division in 2022. articles.text: Postseason tournament starts May 9 Champions rise! In a thrilling culmination to their debut season, both of PBSF’s Middle School baseball teams – a dynamic group of 25 talented 7th and 8th graders from Piedmont Middle School – boasted an undefeated season in the East Bay Middle School Baseball League in their debut season in the league. Their skillful plays and unyielding spirit have rightfully earned them the League Championship and the coveted top seed in the upcoming tournament this weekend. As the Scots gear up for glory, they invite you to witness history in the making. Join them for the quarterfinal showdown at the iconic Witter Field Humphries Diamond. Come cheer on our young champions as they step onto the field this Thursday, May 9th, at 6:00 p.m. Piedmont Middle School’s eighth grade baseball team went undefeated through its league season. Pictured are (front row) Orion Sachs (left), Henry Stein, Jonah Cha-Foster, Max Fujimoto, Aaron Bennett, Mateo Long, (back row) Zachary Carter (left), Jimmy Lagios, Chase Knapp, John Bunje, Aiden Bell, and coach Josh Campuzano. The seventh grade team is also atop the league. Pictured are (front row) Benjamin McMurtry (left), Dylan Toyama, Abe Mandel, Robby Koch, Stein Mason, (back row) Clemens Conrad (left), Aidan Shartsis, Mason Gray, Ben Sorensen, Cyrus Emanuelson, and coach Josh Campuzano. articles.text: Visit the Oakland Museum of California this Saturday, May 11, for a curated gallery chat focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander history. Curated by longtime museum volunteer and former teacher Margaret Yee, this event presents an opportunity to share questions and reflections on key moments in California Asian American history and explore how the causes and consequences of these events still reverberate today. Yee has been volunteering at OMCA since 2017, first as a history gallery docent and now as a School Programs and Gallery Chats Facilitator. The event is free for museum members and begins at 12 p.m. To learn more, visit https://museumca.org/event/member-gallery-chats-california-aapi-history/.
articles.title: Oakland Museum celebrates AAPI history on Sat.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, entitled !!!!!, is on view now through September. The exhibition features artwork by British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones, known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. Jones studied at Glasgow School of Art and graduated in 2013. She then earned her Masters in Fine Art at the Royal Academy Schools, London, in 2019. Recent solo exhibitions include the Long Museum, Shanghai, China (2023) and the Chisenhale Gallery, London (2022). This is the first solo museum exhibition for Jones in the United States. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority Rachel Jones of Black bodies and their lived experience.” For more information, and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/rachel-jones.
articles.title: MoAD presents new exhibition

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will host a fundraising gala on Saturday, May 18 at 5 p.m. Guests are invited to immerse themselves in the vibrant beauty of South Africa’s dry garden landscape while enjoying a relaxed, outdoor affair with refreshments and live music. Curators will share insights into the drought-tolerant and climate-adaptive plants within Ruth’s collection. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake and founder, was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Gardens is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraising events like this. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ gala/. Gala guests are invited to enjoy live music and drinks in Ruth Bancroft Gardens. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Infinite Love, the highly anticipated and widely popular exhibition by artist Yayoi Kusama, will end May 28. Yayoi Kusama is one of the most iconic and globally celebrated artists working today, known for her use of mirrors and bright colors. The artist’s first solo presentation in Northern California encompasses two infinity mirror rooms in the museum, including her newest room, Dreaming of Earth’s Sphericity, I Would Offer My Love (2023), a kaleidoscope color and light. Love Is Calling (2013) is the second room in the presentation and one of Kusama’s largest and most immersive works. The exhibition features a darkened environment lit up by vividly colored inflatable forms that extend from the floor and ceiling, accompanied by the sound of the artist reciting a poem about love. All tickets for Kusama exhibitions are timed. Visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ yayoi-kusama-infinite-love/ to learn more. articles.text: Monika Gruber, Omid Assadi, David Wishnia and David Ryther of the Circadian String Quartet Circadian String Quartet performs its first concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 24 at 7:30 pm. Titled Love and Chains, the concert includes special guests Leslie Bonnet and Nikolaus Hohmann. Tickets are $25 general/$15 seniors and students and are available at www.eventbrite. com/e/894985956087. The concert explores the deep bonds and binds that come with Love. Experience the world premiere of an original chamber opera, Euridice’s Defiance, composed by David Ryther. Inspired by the Greek myth of Orpheus and Euridice, this work in progress tells the story of a mother, Euridice, being detained at a border crossing and separated from her son, Orpheus, while she pleads with her guard to re-unite them. The ground-breaking libretto, written by novelist Kimiko Guthrie, is set to a haunting score by Ryther. The concert will also include Preludes by Claude Debussy, arranged for string quartet; Anton Webern’s romantic opus Langsamer Satz, and two works by Iranian-born composer Sahba Aminikia which are profound meditations on geopolitical struggles that are born from the love of our common humanity.
articles.title: Circadian String Quartet in debut concert at PCA

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s 2024 Summer Season opens on May 30 with Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas the composer completed before his death in 1791. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920’s Berlin cabaret. Kim conducted The Magic Flute with multiple European companies as well as the Washington National Opera and will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation in nearly a decade. The performers include New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro, and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, the nine performances of The Magic Flute are scheduled for May 30 (7:30 p.m.); June 2 (2 p.m.), 4 (7:30 p.m.), 8 (7:30 p.m.), 14 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (7:30 p.m.), 26 (7:30 p.m.), 30 (2 p.m.). To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. Playbill cover for San Francisco Opera’s production of The Magic Flute.
articles.title: SF Opera’s The Magic Flute premieres May 30

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, May 8, 2024 The Musical Gourmet Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Speaking of many things By Joseph Gold Music and the arts continue apace – even this late in the season. “In the Tradition” jazz ensemble performs regularly in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Another concert of some interest was on Saturday, featuring pianist-composer Kadie Kelly and her ensemble of three flutes plus percussion. A worldly guitar concert by Leonardo Garcia concluded the weekend’s music. Leo Garcia is worldly in every sense of the word. He is a gentle spirit intellectually, personally, and musically. But more than anything else he is worldly. His concert on Sunday demonstrated all of these characteristics. There are many things to admire and to appreciate. The repertoire itself was a general overview of guitar music. Garcia is an excellent speaker, and he chose the most appropriate way to explain the pieces he performed. That, in itself, is extraordinary. When he performs, his tone is smooth, mellow and fluid. In my opinion, the guitar has the possibility to be dramatic. But, guitarists rarely venture into the The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet dramatic. That is the only thing that I missed in Garcia’s performance. He has a fluid technique at all times. At first I thought that his guitar was amplified. No, he does not use amplification. I spoke to him after the concert and asked him about his guitar. He told me that he plays a contemporary instrument of a unique design. I continue to wonder how his guitar would respond if he suddenly let loose with a display of virtuoso dynamics. But, all of his other musical attributes more than compensated for stentorian dynamics. And now for some food As good as these musical events were, the real treat was dinner at a friend’s house on Friday evening. Our friend, Doug, is very modest about his abilities in the kitchen. His main course of stuffed chicken breast served alongside a bulgur wheat pilaf would be the featured item in any fancy restaurant. What made it even more amazing was that it is very easy to prepare. Doug prefers to use skinless chicken breast with one large breast for two people. First, he pounds it to tenderize it and to reduce its thickness. Add a little salt and pepper to the outside and stuff it with red peppers from a jar and some mozzarella cheese. He uses mozzarella cheese because it will not run when heated. Stuff the chicken breast and tie it with some kitchen string. Brown the chicken breasts in a little bit of butter using a cast-iron skillet. Then place the entire cast-iron skillet into a preheated 400° oven. Cook for about 10 minutes. Take it out, and let it rest for a few minutes, then slice it. That’s it. Beautiful and tasty – and very simple to prepare. The sliced chicken breasts were served with a simple bulgur wheat pilaf. Doug is also very modest about his knowledge of wines. He served a simple, dry red wine: a Merlot. As if that were not enough, Doug then played a brief concert for us on the piano. The view of the San Francisco Bay, combined with the delicious food and the music, made for a very memorable evening. articles.text: The Dinner, set in a five-star, chic restaurant, where the many courses are presented with a monologue, is a film of humid At first it appears to be merely four people meeting for a meal – two brothers, Stan (Richard Gere), Paul (Steve Coogan) and their wives, Claire (Laura Linney) and Katelyn (Rebecca Hall). What quickly becomes obvious is that they arrive with more baggage than a hotel lobby, meaning unresolved issues that for Stan and Paul stretch back to their youth. It’s clear that Paul is dragging with him through life, like a wet sack of cement, anger and resentment and grievances that he insists were not of his He actually snarls to Stan, “Mom loved you more.” Stan is a successful congressman; Paul was once a high school history teacher now apparently unemployed. Katelyn is Stan’s second wife (previously a campaign aide). Claire is, beyond all understanding, a caring wife to Paul and not that long ago out of the hospital after recovering from Paul is a loose cannon on the dinner table deck, acerbically reactive, his language raw and vitriolic, perpetually skirting full-blown rage or on the verge of losing it altogether, contributing massively to the sustained tension. Through flashbacks, A scene from The Dinner with Richard Gere, Laura Linney, Steve Coogan, and Rebecca Hall which are used sparingly but to excellent effect, we’re told that he has suffered from a mental breakdown and clearly remains fragile and conflicted about all of his connections, especially to his brother. Contributing to the cognitive dissonance that grips the brittle dinner conversation is the arrival of their haute cuisine that remains, in great part, uneaten. What is really being served is Stan’s motivation for bringing them together. I am reluctant to explain in too much detail what has occurred, but suffice it to say that it involves the couples’ sons, both 16, who are involved in a horrific act. Stan insists that they, meaning all four of them, must confront what has occurred and make a decision as to how to proceed. He argues that if they fail to deal with this event, their lives will be ruined. He means all of their lives. Most especially the boys. What also becomes evident is that their inherent dysfunction is only intensified for there is nothing in any of their experiences that could prepare them for this crossroads moment. Of course they are flawed, haunted by their imperfections and therefore starkly ill-equipped to form any kind of a united front. The question to be asked is whether a movie such as this find an audience. It is a long and disjointed hothouse of conversation; however, it’s also a tour de force of acting by an ensemble that is remarkable. The Dinner. Directed by Oren Moverman. Starring Richard Gere, Laura Linney, Steve Coogan. 2 hrs., Rated R. Released in 2017. Streaming on Prime/Fandango/Hulu. tv

articles.text: The Edge of Seventeen is perhaps one of the best movies about adolescent angst and coming of age in the last 25 years. It’s that good. To write and direct a film that captures the essence of being 17, meaning that profound feeling that your life is unmoored and uncertain, feeling at a loss to explain the buffeting emotions that seem like a cascade of conflicting impulses that can rule one’s life; well, that is no small thing. Director Kelly Fremon Craig gets it just right, avoiding a minefield of clichés. At the center of Edge is Nadine (Hailee Steinfeld), suffering with a perfect storm of emotions. Several years ago she lost her father, to whom she was especially close. And now her best friend since childhood, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has fallen for Darian (Blake Jenner), her older, eternally perfect and popular brother. Nadine feels abruptly rejected and betrayed and so banishes Krista from her life. Suddenly rudderless, friendless, and convinced she is utterly alone, she decides to kill herself (or imagines she will.) During lunch hour she informs Mr. Bruner (a remarkably good Woody Harrelson), her history teacher, of her intention. While Nadine is a master of histrionics and self-absorbed drama, the laconic and dry Mr. Bruner Hailee Steinfeld stars in The Edge of Seventeen.
articles.title: The Edge of Seventeen a superb coming-of-age film

articles.text: The premise of Wreck-It Ralph is not only retro, but decidedly creative and fun. The story is set in a suburban arcade filled with games, a place where the neighborhood cool kids hangout during the day. But here’s the best part: when the arcade shuts down for the night, and the kids have all gone home, it’s transformed into an enchanting world where the game characters cross-over into each others platforms and, well, socialize. One of the video game meanies is Wreck-It-Ralph (John C. Reilly), a nemesis in a game called Fix-It-Felix Jr. Ralph is a big, hulking guy with oversized hands and feet who smashes up buildings while Felix (Jack Brayer) follows closely behind with his magic hammer, repairing the damage. Ralph has been wrecking the same building for years, day after day. Of course, he always faces the threat of the Newlanders, hostile residents who live in the building Ralph is wrecking. Meanwhile, Ralph sleeps in a garbage dump when he’s not wrecking stuff, using a tree stump for a pillow. For Ralph, it’s a lonely, sad life, and he wants out. So Ralph abandons his game to try out others. The problem is that when he doesn’t return the kids think Fix-It-Felix Jr. is broken. Felix is therefore desperate to find Ralph and get him to come back so he’ll have things to fix. Meanwhile, Ralph is wandering from game to game. As it turns out, he spends a lot of time in a game called Sugar Rush where he becomes friends with Vanellope von Schweetz (Sarah Silverman) who has been prevented by despot King Candy and a group of mean girls from competing in the go-cart races. Both Vanellope and Ralph are unhappy and want to break free of their games’ programs. The story has a nice finale, involving the gateway to the inner arcade, called Arcade Central, while introducing a bevy of characters. There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus, the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the kids’ pleasure. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. Directed by Rich Moore. Disney Animation. Voices of John C. Reilly, Sarah Silverman, Jack McBrayer. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG. Released in 2012. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+/Apple TV/ A scene from Disney Animation’s Wreck-It Ralph

articles.text: A scene from Raya and the Last Dragon Raya and the Last Dragon is a family friendly, action adventure tale that will resonate with young audiences. Its animation is extraordinary and has been judged to be some of Disney’s best work. The setting is a wonderfully imagined region of Southeast Asia called Kumandra, rich with color and cultural tropes. It’s a rainbow of blended areas from Thailand, to Myanmar to the Philippines. The story begins some 500 years ago when the denizens of Kumandra lived side by side with magnificent dragons. But, distressingly ominous black smoky orbs appear called the Druum and sweep through the five provinces turning to stone all they touch, including the dragons and humans. Only one dragon survives, Sisu (Awkwafina). Apparently all the dragons had transferred their power to one green gem, which defeated the Druum and was guarded by the province of Heart. Now, to the present: Heart still has the guardianship of the gem, though there exists a rivalry between the provinces for control of the sacred gem, now kept secure in a cellar vault. The Chief of Heart is Benji (Daniel Day Kim) who has trained Raya to be his warrior princess daughter. She has been given the task of acting as the protector of the magical gem. Benji, trying to unite the other four provinces, invites them to Heart for a feast. Unable to control the disagreement over who should keep the gem, a battle breaks out, and the gem is broken and Raya is betrayed by a close friend, Namari (Gamma Chan). Six years pass, and it’s at this point that the story takes hold. Raya sets off across Kumandra in search of the lone surviving dragon, Sisu, who could prove essential to restoring the gem and peace to her homeland. And on her journey she meets many interesting characters, finds Sisu, and tries to formulate (with the dragon’s help) a plan to restore the gem’s power and thereby protect all from the threat of the Druum. Raya and the Last Dragon is beautifully told and compellingly animated. Warrior princess Raya is a young, tenacious character, courageous and appealing. Girls and boys will enjoy her compelling adventure. Raya and the Last Dragon. Directed by Don Hall and Carlos Lopez Estrada. Disney animation studios. Voiced by Kelly Marie Tran, Awkwafina, Daniel Day Kim. 1 hr, 48 min. Rated PG. Released in 2021. Streaming on prime/Disney+/Apple TV. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus, the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the kids’ pleasure. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. This is what I call “the Great Divide.” Contemporary, or “modern”, is what we will touch upon today, and traditional is, well…everything else: from Spanish Revival to Tudor, to Craftsman to pretty much anything that appeared before the 1920s. In a nutshell, what happened is that in the early part of the 20th century, the development of new building materials and methods including structural steel, steel reinforced concrete, advanced roofing materials, and improved glazing (glass) production enabled engineers and architects to rapidly (over a few decades) develop and design buildings that were a complete departure from what the world had seen before. Interestingly, today, the way it is commonly used, “modern” is really a misnomer for a style type that is at least 100 years old now. Probably the most recognizable source of the “new” architecture, sometimes termed International Style, was the work of a number of famous modernists including Le Corbusier, Philip Johnson, and Mies van der Rohe. Their work was characterized by a rejection of the sentimentality of ornamented revivalist styles with instead the stated design goals of simplicity, clarity and “honesty” of structural expression. Close inspection of their work, however, often reveals ornamentation of a different kind as they sometimes employed unnecessary materials and detailing to make their buildings look more “machined” than they actually were. In any case, sharp clean lines, flat roofs, more use of metal materials, walls of large glass windows, exposed structural Just as in any traditional building, to be good architecture, contemporary styles must employ and enhance the same elements we have been discussing over the last months. Among these things are clarity and definition of a welcoming entry, proportion and harmony of the facades, well-detailed appropriate materials, and a strong relationship to the site and surrounding landscaping. steel and concrete were (and often continue to be) the result. In my opinion, one characteristic of this legitimate and sometimes beautiful style that inadvertently and ironically did itself a great disservice was precisely the unadorned, simple look. This evolved and proliferated into iterations and copies that were done minimally, were poorly crafted, and most of all, built cheaply—all justified by the structural “honesty” of the modern style. It is these compromised iterations on a large scale that people reject and react to as sterile and even ugly—often not a style at all, but the complete lack of any architectural style. Among a number of others, our friend Frank Lloyd Wright came to the rescue. He was apparently reluctant to venture into this world of modern architecture until demand required it, at which point he took it by storm. Unafraid of ornamentation and with his strong dedication to designing his buildings to harmonize with the land, he was instrumental in giving the “new” austere modern architecture another side: vitality, freshness, interest, character and soul. Although probably very functional and certainly fire resistant, this modernist concrete and masonry structure lacks the texture, personality and appeal of many other more crafted styles. One reason is, I think, that unfinished concrete seems to naturally belong as a foundation or lower level material. Once it is used extensively, especially overhead, there is generally an unnatural feel about it.

articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson Nothing is more controversial among California gardeners than the lawn. The cherished place to toss a baseball or roll out a picnic blanket, the lawn has also become a symbol of ecological callousness. According to a recent University of California study, lawns account for around 25 percent of residential water usage in California. With climate change predicted to increase the frequency and severity of droughts, we might not have that much water to spare in the future. But who wants to picnic on a bed of gravel or play croquet on bark mulch? Fortunately, there could be compromise: Native grasses have been growing in popularity for their beauty and ability to survive with little to no irrigation. I converted my lawn from traditional to native grass more than a decade ago. I felt very proud of myself at the time, but ten years later I’m still struggling with the transition. I’d suggest carefully considering the pros and cons before ripping up your sod. Among the many species of native and drought-tolerant grasses on the market, I know of only two that are tough and compact enough to walk on: festuca rubra (red fescue) and carex pansa (sand dune sedge). The fescue produces attractive clumps of thin, reddish-blue blades. It grows profusely in the East Bay hills – at least in places not taken over by invasive European grasses. of weeding to prevent invasive crab grass from swallowing up the natives, and a lot of water, so much that a neighbor reported me to EBMUD for wastage. (The agency declined to fine me after learning I was trying to establish drought-tolerant natives). After five years, 90 percent of the fescue had died. Although the carex pansa fared better, only half of it ended up surviving, mostly in the center of the yard where foot traffic was minimal. Over time, this critical mass gradually expanded. It now covers 70% of the yard and each year colonizes a few more square feet. It looks beautiful and stays green year-round with zero water. But maintaining it is tough. In the winter and spring, I yank out invasive crabgrass from the plot almost daily. It doesn’t tolerate foot traffic as well as a traditional lawn and needs sun for at least half the day. Though it can handle a picnic now and then, sitting on its inviting green clumps flattens them unattractively, so we mostly leave it to its own devices. At the end of the day, native grasses might be right for you if your lawn doesn’t get much footfall and you have the time or money to do a lot of weeding. But if you’re out there playing soccer or having lawn parties every weekend, you might consider holding on to your sod a bit longer. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. A close-up of carex pansa grass. Sand dune sedge, as its name suggests, grows in sand near to the ocean. It also doesn’t mind heavier soils. It spreads through rhizomes and puts up thick clumps of green, waxy leaves that extend a foot or more in length before falling into graceful tousles not unlike a surfer’s wavy hair. You can’t roll out a readymade lawn of native grasses as you can with traditional mats of sod. Their roots grow too deep. I purchased both varieties from the Bay Natives Nursery in San Francisco as plugs – big trays made up of hundreds of tiny pots each containing a miniscule blade of grass. Planting them, I felt like a hair replacement doctor as I spaced them out across the bare dirt and meticulously inserted a single plug at a time. Then I waited. . . for a very long time. To keep from crushing the fragile plugs, we couldn’t walk on the yard for one year. The first year required a lot My lawn, partially colonized by native grass.

articles.text: Piedmont Ladies Tennis Club members (front): Pam Kurtz (left), Ginny Wright, Charlotte Niel, Julie Braun, Bernardita Halili; (middle row) Emily Gorin, Anne Adams, Janet Nexon, Linda Wolfe, Lauren Eisele, Heidi Harris; (top) Diane Heinze, Atlantis Langowski, Julie Walsh, Randye West, Sharon Huff Robinson; Debra Aurora at side. Hearts beat a little faster in the chests of the Piedmont Ladies Tennis Club (PLTC) members who played in the annual Spring Tournament at the Corey Reich Tennis Center last week. Excitement and hope were in the air as the ladies took to the courts on a gorgeous Spring morning. PLTC President Julie Braun, Diane Heinze and Debra Aurora planned the annual event. Teams consisted of both A-players and B-players. Each team had seven matches. Whoever won the most games was the winner, followed by a runner-up team. The stakes included bragging rights and a gift bag of tennis paraphernalia. But, the real prize was a fun day of friendships and friendly competition. Heidi Harris and Lauren Eisele won with an impressive 28 games. Debra Aurora and Diane Heinze werem the runners up with 25 wins. After the tournament, the ladies adjourned to Heidi Harris’s beautiful home where PLTC members Wanda Rudsits, Elene Manolis and Dale Breen prepared a lovely celebratory lunch. The day ended on a sweet note with Heidi Harris’s delicious homemade chocolate chip cookies. PLTC welcomes new members to their friendly group, and players do not have to live in Piedmont to join. The A Ladder meets Tuesdays from 9:00–11:00 am, and the B Ladder meets Wednesdays from 9:00–10:30 am. Both groups play a doubles round-robin format at the at Corey Reich Tennis Center, located at the intersection of Vista and Bonita Avenues. Ladies interested in joining should contact Membership Chair Ginny Wright at ginny_wright@ sbcglobal.net.

articles.text: Innocence battles evil while tensions run high and passions conflict in The Third Man, one of movie history’s most gripping thrillers. It’s been called “a masterpiece,” “unmissable” and “the best British film ever made.” Lucky local moviegoers can see it next week as the May offering of Piedmont’t Second Thursday Flix Fest. No wonder it’s such a success.Winning packed audiences and many awards when it was released in 1949, the screenplay is by novelist Graham Green, the director is the great Carol Reed, and its star is the prodigiously-talented Orson Welles. The film also features striking black-and-white cinematography by Robert Krasker, and its theme music, the haunting “Third Man Theme,” even became the number one song in the U.S. for a time. As the tale begins, an out-ofwork pulp fiction novelist, Holly Martins (Joseph Cotton), arrives in an edgy post-war Vienna divided into sectors by the victorious allies, where a shortage of supplies has led to a flourishing black market. He arrives at the invitation of an ex-school friend, Harry Lime (Orson Welles), who has offered him a job, only to discover that Lime has recently died in a peculiar traffic accident. From talking to Lime’s friends and associates, Martins soon notices that some of the stories are inconsistent – who is the mysterious “third man” who was present at Lime’s death? – and determines to discover what really happened. In the course of his pursuit he falls for Lime’s beautiful, heartbroken girlfriend, Anna (Alida Valli). The movie concludes with the famous chase through the Vienna sewers. The Third Man will be screened on Thursday, May 9th at the Flix Fest’s new afternoon starting time of 1:00 p.m. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the event takes place at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The showing is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Registration at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP is encouraged. Viewers are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The Third Man will be screened on Thursday, May 9th at 1:00 p.m., at the Piedmont Center for the Arts

Teams consisted of both A-players and B-players. Each team had seven matches. Whoever won the most games was the winner, followed by a runner-up team. The stakes included bragging rights and a gift bag of tennis paraphernalia. But, the real prize was a fun day of friendships and friendly competition. Heidi Harris and Lauren Eisele won with an impressive 28 games. Debra Aurora and Diane Heinze werem the runners up with 25 wins. After the tournament, the ladies adjourned to Heidi Harris’s beautiful home where PLTC members Wanda Rudsits, Elene Manolis and Dale Breen prepared a lovely celebratory lunch. The day ended on a sweet note with Heidi Harris’s delicious homemade chocolate chip cookies. PLTC welcomes new members to their friendly group, and players do not have to live in Piedmont to join. The A Ladder meets Tuesdays from 9:00–11:00 am, and the B Ladder meets Wednesdays from 9:00–10:30 am. Both groups play a doubles round-robin format at the at Corey Reich Tennis Center, located at the intersection of Vista and Bonita Avenues. Ladies interested in joining should contact Membership Chair Ginny Wright at ginny_wright@ sbcglobal.net. On a perfect spring day last week the Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 53 walkers and four K-9 best friends. Many were there because architect and urban planner Will Adams was scheduled to lead the walk. Will is a 30-year Piedmonter and writes the Piedmont Post’s “Walking Piedmont” column. He took the walkers for a Mediterranean Style Architecture tour in February, and they wanted an encore. Will started the tour by providing an introduction to Craftsman style architecture. He told the group it is the most common architectural style in Piedmont. The Craftsman, or American Craftsman style, developed in tandem with the same style in England. Both are offshoots of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century, which idealized simplicity, harmony with nature and honesty in construction. It developed as an alternative to the ornate and opulent style of the Victorian age. Craftsman buildings were thoughtfully constructed by craftspeople who took pride in the quality of their work. The style is literally a blend of art and craft. Hand crafting of the building components both on the buildings’ exteriors and interiors is present and valued. Bernard Maybeck and his disciple Julia Morgan are among the famous architects who designed and worked closely with outstanding craftspeople to produce this type of buildings throughout the East Bay including Piedmont. Variations of this genre include the Craftsman Bungalow, the Prairie style and Mission Revival style. The large group went down Highland Avenue in what looked like an early 4th of July parade to Oakland Avenue and up to Hardwick Avenue. Will pointed to two Craftsman homes and pointed out similarities of natural colors, covered front porches, wide eaves and gables on lowsloped roofs, exposed rafters, double hung windows, brick chimneys and some stained glass windows. The tour resumed on Blair Avenue, crossing Oakland Avenue and then to two homes on Blair. One was a small bungalow, which Will said would have been inexpensive to build and very popular in California. Further down the street at Bonita Avenue was another Craftsman with its porch on the side. At Hillside Avenue was a larger Craftsman home with front steps that provided a setting for a group photo. The walkers continued to Dracena Avenue and to a lovely house where the architect has recreated a Craftsman style home with a porch at the front, and shingles, rocks and landscaping that complete the design. Will took the group into Dracena Park, emerging on Artuna and Ricardo Avenues where there are many Craftsman homes. The walkers expressed their thanks to Will for all the information he had shared. They are looking forward to another walk with Will later this year. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Dr. Joseph Yarris, a Piedmont resident for 60 years, passed away peacefully on Thanksgiving, November 23, 2023, with his family by his side. Born in Uniontown, Pennsylvania on February 24, 1932, to Joseph and Barbara Yarris, he was the youngest of three children. When he was in elementary school, his family moved to Vallejo, California, where he attended Vallejo College High School. He enrolled in the University of California at Berkeley as a freshman, with the intention of pursuing a career in medicine. After graduating from Cal, Joe continued his studies at McGill University Medical School in Montreal, Canada. There, he met the love of his life, Canadian Geraldine (Jere) O’Connell, at a party hosted by his fraternity. He was immediately captivated by Jere’s Irish wit, charm, and brilliant blue eyes. After dating for a year and a half, they became engaged, and, in 1957, exchanged wedding vows at the University Chapel on the McGill Campus. As newlyweds, the couple worked at the Royal Victoria Hospital, Joe as an intern and Jere as a receptionist in the Oncology/ Radiation Department. When Joe accepted a residency at Children’s Hospital in Oakland in 1960, they left Jere’s hometown of Montreal to begin a life in the San Francisco Bay Area. After the birth of two children and a few years as Oakland residents, they moved to Piedmont, where they would ultimately raise their five children. Upon completing his residency, Dr. Yarris began a private practice on “Pill Hill” in Oakland, partnered with mentors, Dr. Charles Dimmler and Dr. Bob Rappaport. He was a passionate pediatrician, and, with his reassuring bedside manner and a sense of humor, he easily earned the trust of his young patients and their parents. As a result, he affectionately became known as “Dr. Joe.” He spent many evenings on the phone with concerned mothers and fathers, made house calls, carrying his black bag, and was confident as Head of Pediatrics at Samuel Merritt Hospital (now Alta Bates Summit Medical Center). As his young patients matured, many were resistant to leaving their childhood physician, so Dr. Joe decided to expand his practice to include “Children and Young Adults”. Dr. Joe was a dedicated doctor with a hectic work schedule, but he was also a profoundly devoted husband and father, spending most of his free time with his children and wife. He was happiest in the outdoors with his family. He played with his children in the backyard, challenging them to games of football, ping-pong, basketball, and lively duels with water balloons and Nerf guns. He volunteered to coach his children’s sports teams, participated in weekend Scouting adventures and assisted in the construction of Pinewood Derby cars. Sundays often began with his smiley-faced pancakes and concluded with a bowl of Jiffy Pop popcorn and an evening episode of The Wonderful World of Disney. Family vacations usually involved a long station wagon ride to various California destinations – Tahoe, Palm Springs and Newport Beach among the favorites. Bikes, suitcases, and toys were stacked and tied to the rooftop of the car, while the inside was overcrowded with Yarris kids and their companions. Undeniably, Chambers Landing Beach, on the west shore of Lake Tahoe, was Dr. Joe’s most beloved location. He cherished time in the water, fishing for trout and crawdads from the pier with his kids and sharing a sunset cocktail on the Beach with Jere and their friends. Second to vacationing with his family, Joe loved being together for all holidays. The Christmas season was his favorite time of year. His lights and tree were always in place in time for the Piedmont Tree Lighting Ceremony. He was an enthusiastic shopper, a pro at assembling bikes and Barbie Dream Houses, and consistently overstuffed his kids’ and grandkids’ stockings. In 1998, when his third grandson was born at Summit Hospital, Dr. Joe performed his final newborn exam and retired from Pediatrics. In his newly acquired free time, he and Jere played tennis with friends, followed local sports teams, and discovered a love of cruising that took them to the Caribbean, Alaska, and Mexico. They took great pleasure relaxing at restaurants with water views: Sam’s in Sausalito, Quinn’s Lighthouse in Oakland, and Trader Vic’s in Emeryville for an “Old Way” Mai Tai as the sun was setting. They also spent time caring for their three young grandsons, who lived nearby in Piedmont. Just as with their own children, adventures with the boys were often outdoors: fishing from the Berkeley Pier and on the banks of Lake Temescal, and feeding the geese at Lake Merritt’s Lakeside Park. Dr. Joe’s appreciation of nature and outdoor activities cultivated his love of gardening. His patio was a sanctuary for squirrels and birds, as he enticed them daily with nuts and seeds. When he tended to his front garden, he was grateful when former patients and friends, who were walking or driving by his house, stopped to chat with him. He enjoyed reminiscing and hearing about family updates. In a quote from a 1975 article in an edition of the Piedmont High School newspaper, Dr. Yarris’ dedication to the well-being of children is undeniable. “Children are our most important investment in this world, and I feel that if we want them to grow up to be responsible citizens, we’ve just got to pass on every bit of knowledge we possibly can to make them strong and able to cope when we won’t be around to help them in their lives anymore,” he wrote. As a father, grandfather and Pediatrician, Dr. Joe undoubtedly helped generations of children become more confident and conscientious. Dr. Yarris is survived by his five children, Heather Yarris Price (Randy), Greg, Scott, Kevin, (Karyn), and Jennifer Mingham (Joe); seven grandchildren whom he adored: Brian, Matt and Nick Price, Cammi Yarris, and Andrew Dr. Joe Yarris toasting his 90th birthday with a Trader Vic’s Mai Tai. Joe and Jere Yarris on their wedding day. and Emily Mingham; his sister-inlaw, Wellner Gagnier; and many deeply loved nieces and nephews. Dr. Yarris was devoted to his Christian faith and profoundly believed in Heaven. In his happiest heaven, he would be surrounded by a garden, alongside his beloved Jere and others he’d missed, admiring a sunset. Donations in memory of Dr. Joseph Yarris may be made to: George Mark Children’s House, a local free-standing Pediatric respite care and hospice home (https://Georgemark.org) 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, Ca. 94578). Dr. Joe Yarris with his wife and kids. A photo of Dr. Joe Yarris on the cover of Children’s Hospital Oakland Newsletter.

He volunteered to coach his children’s sports teams, participated in weekend Scouting adventures and assisted in the construction of Pinewood Derby cars. Sundays often began with his smiley-faced pancakes and concluded with a bowl of Jiffy Pop popcorn and an evening episode of The Wonderful World of Disney. Family vacations usually involved a long station wagon ride to various California destinations – Tahoe, Palm Springs and Newport Beach among the favorites. Bikes, suitcases, and toys were stacked and tied to the rooftop of the car, while the inside was overcrowded with Yarris kids and their companions. Undeniably, Chambers Landing Beach, on the west shore of Lake Tahoe, was Dr. Joe’s most beloved location. He cherished time in the water, fishing for trout and crawdads from the pier with his kids and sharing a sunset cocktail on the Beach with Jere and their friends. Second to vacationing with his family, Joe loved being together for all holidays. The Christmas season was his favorite time of year. His lights and tree were always in place in time for the Piedmont Tree Lighting Ceremony. He was an enthusiastic shopper, a pro at assembling bikes and Barbie Dream Houses, and consistently overstuffed his kids’ and grandkids’ stockings. In 1998, when his third grandson was born at Summit Hospital, Dr. Joe performed his final newborn exam and retired from Pediatrics. In his newly acquired free time, he and Jere played tennis with friends, followed local sports teams, and discovered a love of cruising that took them to the Caribbean, Alaska, and Mexico. They took great pleasure relaxing at restaurants with water views: Sam’s in Sausalito, Quinn’s Lighthouse in Oakland, and Trader Vic’s in Emeryville for an “Old Way” Mai Tai as the sun was setting. They also spent time caring for their three young grandsons, who lived nearby in Piedmont. Just as with their own children, adventures with the boys were often outdoors: fishing from the Berkeley Pier and on the banks of Lake Temescal, and feeding the geese at Lake Merritt’s Lakeside Park. Dr. Joe’s appreciation of nature and outdoor activities cultivated his love of gardening. His patio was a sanctuary for squirrels and birds, as he enticed them daily with nuts and seeds. When he tended to his front garden, he was grateful when former patients and friends, who were walking or driving by his house, stopped to chat with him. He enjoyed reminiscing and hearing about family updates. In a quote from a 1975 article in an edition of the Piedmont High School newspaper, Dr. Yarris’ dedication to the well-being of children is undeniable. “Children are our most important investment in this world, and I feel that if we want them to grow up to be responsible citizens, we’ve just got to pass on every bit of knowledge we possibly can to make them strong and able to cope when we won’t be around to help them in their lives anymore,” he wrote. As a father, grandfather and Pediatrician, Dr. Joe undoubtedly helped generations of children become more confident and conscientious. Dr. Yarris is survived by his five children, Heather Yarris Price (Randy), Greg, Scott, Kevin, (Karyn), and Jennifer Mingham (Joe); seven grandchildren whom he adored: Brian, Matt and Nick Price, Cammi Yarris, and Andrew Dr. Joe Yarris toasting his 90th birthday with a Trader Vic’s Mai Tai. Joe and Jere Yarris on their wedding day. and Emily Mingham; his sister-inlaw, Wellner Gagnier; and many deeply loved nieces and nephews. Dr. Yarris was devoted to his Christian faith and profoundly believed in Heaven. In his happiest heaven, he would be surrounded by a garden, alongside his beloved Jere and others he’d missed, admiring a sunset. Donations in memory of Dr. Joseph Yarris may be made to: George Mark Children’s House, a local free-standing Pediatric respite care and hospice home (https://Georgemark.org) 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, Ca. 94578). articles.text: Scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 15 welcomed new members with an introductory campout on the weekend of April 20-21 at Camp Herms in the hills of El Cerrito. The purpose was to provide hands-on practice of basic scout skills for youth who joined Troop 15 following the Piedmont Scout Troop Open House during the week of February 26. The new scouts received guidance from seasoned scouts selected by Senior Patrol Leader Evan Friedman. The instructor group included four scouts who themselves were new scouts at the same event two years prior – Willow Thomas, Henry Ciriacruz, Eliza Hupp and Adelina Mbize. The new scouts reviewed outdoor etiquette and scouting values, practiced tying basic knots, setting up a tent, handling a pocket knife, helping to prepare a meal, and cleaning up after the meal. New scout Adam Saxonov said he liked learning about knots and the Outdoor Code. The instruction went until late Saturday afternoon for each patrol of about seven scouts, after which they prepared dinner on two-burner propane camp stoves. After dinner, the whole Troop gathered around the campfire where each patrol put on a skit. Following the entertainment, the scouts toasted marshmallows over an open fire to make s’mores. pages.text: Wednesday, May 8, 2024 29 Troop 15 Continued from page 28 Troop into a closing circle where individual scouts gave recognition to members who had been especially helpful. The scouts were in their tents and quiet by 9:15 p.m. A coyote puppy was heard yipping in the distance, and the air overnight was cool but calm. The Scouts were awake by 7 a.m. heating water for hot cocoa and oatmeal. Evie Luskin seemed pleasantly surprised that she slept through the night and Mai Levy complimented Adelina Mbise on her bacon. The new scouts helped with cooking and cleaning then attended some training for campfire safety, first aid, and handling hatchets and saws. The Troop packed up their gear and formed a line to sweep their camp for any trash. Seasoned scout Eliza Hupp said, “I learned to keep an extra layer within easy reach before settling into my sleeping bag. My favorite thing was instructing in knots, then also completing my own requirements for First Class rank. And I liked helping with toasting marshmallows.” New scout William Cain said, “I liked the good food, lashing poles to make a tripod, and the fun around the campfire.” Troop 15 will be camping along the American River on a white-water rafting trip on June 1-2. Then, from June 30 to July 6, the Troop will attend Wente Scout Reservation near Willits for a week of camping including horseback riding, archery, fishing, kayaking, canoeing, rifle shooting, small-boat sailing and swimming. If you are 11-16 years old and interested in Scouting with Troop 15, contact the Scoutmaster Maria Topete at maria. topete@gmail.com. Ever on guard from harmful bacteria, scouts follow their clean-up ritual. One of the two 746-foot Golden Gate Bridge towers is visible from Camp Herms in the El Cerrito hills, 840 feet above sea level. Scouts absorb a lesson in first aid from parent Jennifer Gregovich, a Physician’s Assistant. New scouts Jackson Chu, Henry Ciriacruz, William Cain and Leo Thakur trim the slack from their tent. At midday, Scouts hiked along the ridge, where Eagle scout Simon March-Cunningham gathered dry sage for the kitchen. The hike was a highlight for new scout Owen Sukeforth. The Troop converges around a campfire after dinner for skits and s’mores.

Meanwhile, Nadine fantasizes in a lustful way about Nick (Alexander Calvert), a bad boy, edgy, enigmatic, who works part-time at Pet Land. Nadine also finds herself drawn to a classmate, Erwin (Hayden Szeto), a budding filmmaker and gifted illustrator. Know that The Edge of Seventeen is not a collage of adolescent stereotypes; rather, it’s a film about fully-formed characters. Nadine is surrounded by a circle of caring friends and adults, to include her frazzled mom (Kyra Sedgwick). The narrative gradually morphs into is an attrition of Nadine’s anger and confusion, emotions that have turned her life into a roller coaster ride of hostility and all-consuming bewilderment. She loses her manic self-centeredness while she begins to gain small personal insights that come at her unexpectedly like small gifts. Who among us can forget what being 17 was like? What is there about being an adolescent that feels so real and involving? Will we ever live so intensely again, a time akin to walking on a high wire, framed by a sense of perpetual vertigo? Writer Craig gets all of that just right and so has made an achingly spot-on film that is to be embraced for what it manages to accomplish. The Edge of Seventeen. Directed by Kelly Fremon Craig. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, Haley Lu, Blake Jenner. 1 hr., 41 min. Released 2016. Steaming on Fandango/prime/hulu.

It freaked me out.” Four police officers entered the business and informed the man that he was under arrest and instructed him to raise his hands. The suspect was unresponsive and muttering incoherently. An officer grabbed his taser and ordered him to get on the ground. When the suspect refused to comply, the officer used his taser, which did not incapacitate him. The man ripped the taser barbs from his skin and began flailing his arms violently at the cops. Additionally, tasers and pepper spray proved ineffective. The suspect fled down Grand Avenue onto Sunnyslope Avenue, where he broke a window to gain entry to a nearby house. He threatened its owner, who fled her home without injury. From there, he hopped a nearby fence and eventually landed in the front yard of a home on Valle Vista Avenue, where he encountered Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, alone Chief Bowers had been monitoring the situation via radio and arrived at the scene in plainclothes. He stopped his car in the middle of the street and opened the door to approach the man on foot. Bowers identified himself as a police officer. When the suspect noticed Bowers’ car door open, he sprinted toward the driver’s seat. Bowers attempted to remove the man from his car, resulting in a struggle. The ensuing melee stained the interior of the car with blood from the suspect’s hand which was cut due to breaking a window. Moments earlier, security guard Angel Solis was on duty at the Safeway on Grand Avenue when a distraught customer asked him for help. He just received a phone call that someone had broken into his house and threatened his wife. “He saw the first form of authority, which I guess he assumed was me in a bulletproof vest, and asked me if I could help him. Without waiting for an answer, he just took off down the road, so I followed,” said Solis. Solis encountered PPD Officers Tyler Petit and David Cutler on the street and offered his assistance. The two officers made contact with the suspect first. The suspect man stepped out of the car, swinging at the officers and still refusing orders. Solis approached the man from behind, bear-hugged him and dragged him to the ground. From there, he and two officers restrained the suspect while another officer handcuffed him. Piedmont Police have identified the suspect as 42-yearold Willie Gomer. Gomer was arrested on suspicion of assault, elder abuse, battery of a police officer, carjacking and burglary. Gomer was also on parole for auto theft, robbery, kidnapping and multiple parole violations. He was taken to the hospital for injuries to his hand and then booked at Santa Rita Jail in Dublin. Piedmont police are still awaiting toxicology reports to identify any substances Gomer may have been using. The assault victim at Ace Hardware was taken to the hospital and is expected to recover. Solis said he was glad he could help and praised the professionalism of Piedmont’s police. “The Chief actually came into my job, which is Safeway on Grand Avenue, and he personally handed me a letter of appreciation that he wrote, which benefits me a lot, because I’m currently [having background checks] with the SFPD.” A random assault took place at Ace Hardware on Friday, April 26. articles.text: On Friday, April 26, the City of Piedmont celebrated Arbor Day outside the Community Hall with a variety of raffles, bulldozers, maintenance trucks, and an educational meet and greet with a live owl from Lindsay Wildlife Museum that was enjoyed by children and adults. At the event, the City announced its annual Heritage Tree selection, which strives to increase awareness and appreciation for Piedmont’s rich urban forest. The first selection was a Eucalyptus Tree in Piedmont Park near the top of Bushy Dell Creek. It was nominated by Dick Carter on behalf of the Walking on Wednesdays group. The second selection was a group of three live oaks that currently form an arc at the top of the path to Piedmont Park from Wildwood Avenue near Wildwood School. They were nominated by resident Robin Kettele in honor of her son, Augie Grahn, who passed away in February of 2020. “Our son August Robert Grahn was born and raised in Piedmont,” said Kettele. “He spent many happy hours at Wildwood School and in Piedmont Park, especially at this very western side. We would love to think of him in this process.” The Piedmont Garden Club and the City’s Sustainability Division rounded out the event by providing informational tables for participants to learn more about the city’s different programs for getting involved with the natural world around them. The Public Works Department helped educate the public on their role in maintaining the 9,000 trees that constitute Piedmont’s urban forest. With banner in tow, volunteers with the Piedmont Garden Club Staff Photos An owl provided by the Lindsay Wildlife Center allowed attendees to get close with wildlife at the event.
articles.title: City Celebrates Arbor Day on April 26

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has released its 2023 Annual Report, which provides a high-level overview of the department’s operations during one of the East Bay’s most significant crime waves in recent memory. Although the report acknowledges an increase in reported crime throughout the city, it claims that Piedmont still “experiences lower crime compared to much of the region.” The Annual Report typically includes information about crime data and trends but also offers a glimpse into other aspects of the Department’s work – from expanding technology investments to the launch of the popular Cop on the Block program last summer. “Cities throughout the region saw increases in reported crime during 2023, and Piedmont was not immune,” according to the report. “Reported crimes rose sharply through the summer and peaked in early fall. Multiple high-profile incidents, including several robberies, sparked heightened community concerns,” it continues. According to multiple sources, police departments in neighboring regions have reported increases in violent crime from the previous year, including Berkeley (+10.5%), Oakland (+21%), and Emeryville (+13%). articles.text: The City Council and the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee will discuss the City’s budget for the fiscal year 2024-2025 at a series of public meetings from April to June. These public meetings will result in the adoption of a new city budget by the City Council on Monday, June 17. Members of the public are encouraged to attend and provide feedback. Discussions about the FY 2024-2025 budget formally began on Monday, April 15, at a special workshop before the regularly scheduled City Council meeting, though the council’s study sessions on the subject began as early as March. The current schedule of remaining meetings is as follows: • Tuesday, May 14, 6 p.m.: Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee meeting • Monday, June 3, 6 p.m.: Budget Public Hearing – City Council meeting • Monday, June 17, 6 p.m.: Adoption of the FY 2024- 2025 City budget – City Council meeting The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee’s meeting on Tuesday, May 14 will be held in the city’s Emergency Operations Centere (EOC), as is normally the case. All other meetings will be held in City Hall. The proposed budget is expected to be published for review and feedback in early May. In previous years, public budget discussions began in May, following the release of the proposed budget. The earlier start to the process this year indicates the City’s move towards longer-term planning, a shift that has been underway for several years at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. Leading up to this workshop, the City Council held study sessions devoted to the budget as well as governance and goal-setting in March and early April. For questions about the City budget, contact Finance Director Michael Szczech at mszczech@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City budget public meetings underway

Police Chief Jeremy Bowers has detailed this response plan at multiple town halls and city council meetings since September, 2023. Overall, robberies, burglaries, vehicle thefts, and larcenies have all increased since the previous year. The department also declared its Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) system to be a success in the report. Since 2013, Piedmont Police have used ALPR cameras to alert dispatchers in real-time when stolen vehicles or vehicles associated with an alert enter Piedmont. Officers are then dispatched to locate the vehicles and take action. In 2023, officers responded to over 1,200 ALPR incidents, which resulted in 33 arrests, 37 recovered vehicles, and over 300 wanted vehicles fleeing Piedmont. The department now intends to add nine new ALPR cameras to its system at various locations throughout the city. The Annual Report encourages citizens to visit the police department’s Transparency page for more information on how camera data is used. The police department will also install five new public safety video cameras throughout the city in 2023. The decision to expand the program was made after cameras from their pilot program helped with the successful investigation and prosecution of several crimes, including one notable home invasion robbery. The report also highlighted the department’s community outreach efforts. In 2023, PPD launched Cop on the Block, a program in which officers meet with residents For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Photo by Kid Vicious PR Piedmonter Mike Rufo has released a new song in honor of Earth Day 2024. Mike Rufo, a Piedmont resident and singer-songwriter, has released a new song called “The Reckoning” in honor of Earth Day 2024. Rufo’s percussive acoustic guitar number, released independently on the singer’s website and on YouTube and Spotify, combines his twin passions for music and climate activism in this meditation on society’s relationship with the environment. The song and video were released on April 19, three days before Earth Day. “The Reckoning speaks to the poignancy and power of humanity facing itself, as well as the climate crisis,” according to a press release. “Part awakening, part confessional, part plea, the song conveys the layers of emotion underlying this moment in human history as we seek to re-understand and reshape our relationship to our fragile planetary home.” Brady Blade (Indigo Girls, Emmylou Harris, Steve Earle) plays drums on the track, and Sarah Larkin (The Real Sarahs) provides vocals. “The Reckoning” is the first single from Rufo’s new album, Living Is. The album, his fourth LP, will be released in late 2024 with a series of monthly singles preceding it. Other musicians have given Rufo’s previous album, Helsinki, positive reviews. “The part of my musical consciousness that was nurtured by the likes of Simon & Garfunkel [...] donned a warm smile while listening to Mike Rufo’s recent album, Helsinki,” said Gaelynn Lea, the American violinist who won NPR’s Tiny Desk Contest in 2016. “The melodies are lovely, the lyrics straightforward and honest, and the guitar rings true - beautiful, clear, and unpretentious.” In addition to his musical career, Rufo is an energy-climate policy consultant and a board member of Music Declares Emergency (MDE), an environmental advocacy organization. Mike has directed several sustainable energy consultancies and received a Lifetime Achievement Award for his contributions to sustainable energy programs and policies. For more information on “The Reckoning,” visit www.mikerufomusic.com.
articles.title: Singer-songwriter Mike Rufo releases song for Earth Day

articles.text: Piedmont firefighters led by Capt. Justin McNulty (left), Brittany Borges, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, and Anthony Renteria hold last year’s trophies from the 2003 Big Climb. Along with Firefighters Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, and Brian Protheroe, Piedmont Fire will attempt to defend their first-place title this year. The Piedmont Fire Department will compete against other Bay Area fire departments in this year’s Big Climb on Saturday, May 4, as part of the First Responder Challenge, a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The event is a competitive race up a series of stairs at Oracle Park, home of the San Francisco Giants. Participants will compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s entrance on Second Street. Last year, Piedmont won the first responder division in both the team and individual categories. They will have to defend their title this year as they go against the fire departments from San Francisco, San Mateo, and others. “We’ve done a lot of different fitness things over the years, whether it was CrossFit competitions or the Firefighter Challenge, which is an agility course,” explained Capt. Justin McNulty. “This competition came up last year for the first time when a local resident suggested it to us.” McNulty was the obvious choice to lead the Piedmont team. A self-described “fitness nut,” he regularly competes in physical competitions on his own time, including several running and CrossFit challenges each year. McNulty has also gained a reputation within his department for fitness running the annual 5K Piedmont Turkey Trot in full turnout gear at least half a dozen times. “I even had them change out my air bottle at the top of the hill on Sea View before I finished the course,” he told the Post. Last year marked the first time the Big Climb included a First Responders division, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. “I might be a little biased being with San Francisco Fire, but currently we’re the best at the stair climbs,” said San Francisco Fire Captain Jonathan Baxter in a promotional video. “I remember hearing that last year and thinking, ‘You don’t know what you’re doing, guys. You’re poking the bear,’” joked McNulty. The Piedmont team this year will include McNulty, Brittany Borges, Nikolas Christ, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Anthony Renteria, and Nadder Shehadeh. Erica Melgarejo, an event organizer with the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society explained that the First Responder Challenge is a great way for her organization to increase participation in its events, as well as inspire competition among departments for a good cause. “In the future, we hope to have even more departments join us at Big Climb in SF alongside other competitors to help take down blood cancer,” she explained. As of this week, Piedmont Fire Department ranks seventh in fundraising under the “corporate donor” category with $1,650. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco and to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. The Big Climb will take place this Saturday, May 4, at Oracle Park.
articles.title: Piedmont Fire Dept. to defend title in Big Climb at Oracle Park on Saturday

articles.text: On Wednesday, April 24, during the school board meeting, Piedmont High added Dr. David Yoshihara to the top of its faculty list, as the new principal. Yoshihara was selected for his nearly 30 year career in education taking him in and out of every kind of school, with an abundance of roles and titles. “Dr. Yoshihara has served in all types of schools and districts, including districts very similar in high achievement to PUSD,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. After receiving a thorough introduction from Hawn, Yoshihara, stepped to the podium in City Hall and made his first declarations in Piedmont. “I have no doubt that we will achieve great things together. Thank you once again for this incredible opportunity. Let’s make this next school year one to remember. Go Highlanders!” said Yoshihara. articles.text: Piedmont 10th grader Nikolas Kalamas won 3rd place in the Engineering Category at the Alameda County Science and Engineering Fair on March 16. The event was held at Chabot College in Hayward. His project involved creating a way to filter barbecue smoke which contains unhealthy (even carcinogenic) volatile organic compounds. Filtering the smoke without losing the sweet compounds (‘Syringol’) for cooking has never done before. However, a carbon scrubber (filter) was discovered that can do just that. This was demonstrated by Kalamas after he designed and engineered a barbecue grill to make barbecuing significantly safer than ever before.
