The Piedmont High School Dance Class will present its student choreography showcase on Friday night, May 3, at 7 p.m. in Alan Harvey Theater. Class members will perform The Red Shoes on Saturday night, May 4, at 7 p.m. Both performances of the Spring Dance Concert will be in the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus, 800 Magnolia Avenue. Saturday night’s concert features a short adaptation of The Red Shoes. It tells the story of a girl who falls in love with a pair of red shoes, which lead her to be torn between conflicting passions. Saturday night’s show also includes a student choreography showcase with pieces inspired by classic fairy tales. The concert will last approximately one hour. The show is choreographed by dance teacher Amy Moorhead, in her 30th year at PHS. Her son Andrew Moorhead (PHS ‘11) a playwright in New York City, has adapted The Red Shoes, for the show. It was originally told by Hans Christian Andersen. Tickets, available at the door, are Adults $10, Seniors $9, Youth (11-18) $5, and K-5 students free.

articles.text: Piedmont students take on another Mock Trial team during the 2024 Mock Trial California finals. Piedmont High’s Mock Trial team advanced to the State Finals in Los Angeles on March 22 as the representative for Alameda County. Piedmont finished in 12th place out of 32 County winners from across California. “I am incredibly proud of the team,” said team advisor Hillary Freeman. “It was so exciting to watch them compete at this level, place twelfth in the state and take home two outstanding witness awards. This achievement is a testament to their talent, dedication, hard work and exemplary teamwork throughout the season.” Round one action began in the Stanley Mosk Courthouse on Friday afternoon. Piedmont’s Defense team was in the courtroom first to compete against the prosecution team of Redwood High School. While nearly the entire Piedmont team made the trip south, some members were delayed in Piedmont to compete for their lacrosse team Friday afternoon. “Defense getting selected for the first round on Friday was definitely not ideal. Since we had a ton of athletes who were coming to Los Angles late, lots of people had to substitute, mostly alternates and members of the prosecution team.” explained PHS Mock Trial President Jane Hempeck. Although in unfamiliar roles, Piedmont students won their first match with Redwood High School of Tulare County. “We were definitely nervous, but the team did an amazing job, and beat our opponents even with little practice of the material,” said Hempeck. The scoring system used in the state finals is confusing, if not opaque. Scoring is based on power rankings and power matches and each trial has three judges who submit ballots in favor of the prosecution or defense. In the second round, now as a prosecution team, Piedmont won again by beating Yolo County’s Da Vinci Charter. In the third round, the Highlanders battled a familiar foe, Mt. Tamalpais. “We were really excited; we had scrimmaged them in the fall. Both teams were extremely well prepped,” said Freeman. In the state finals Piedmont lost to Tamalpais High on a split decision, 2-1. “We were nervous going against Tam. They’re a super impressive team and have won State the past few years. It definitely taught us a lot about performance, but we did awesome. I think the round was pretty close,” said Hempeck. Tamalpais went on to win all its matches and finished in 3rd place, narrowly missing the finals. Trinity Pacific Christian from Ventura County defeated Torrey Pines in the finals and will represent the state of California in the national competition, May 2-5 in Delaware. In Piedmont’s 4th match, they went against a top notch team, Menlo School from Atherton. They gained some points but ended up losing and Menlo finished in 10th place. “I don’t think Mock Trial is a widely known activity, and so seeing that there were so many others who also participate across the state was cool. Our team really rose to the challenge, and performed to the standard that we’ve been striving for since September,” said Piedmont senior and Mock Trial member Elena Stevens. PHS History teacher Hillary Freeman led the Mock Trial team to state in her first year as Mock Trial Faculty Advisor. Unlike in earlier years, the team did not have a parent attorney as advisor. PHS Mock Trial defeated Bishop O’Dowd on February 29 to secure the Alameda County title and earn them this trip to the state finals. Piedmont’s Mock Trial team competes in the state finals in Los Angeles’ Stanley Mosk Courthouse.
articles.title: PHS Mock Trial team finishes 12th in state

articles.text: Wildwood Elementary School second graders took a trip to the Cal Berkeley campus on Friday, April 5, to see a dance performance in Zellerbach Hall. Wildwood teacher Phong Ung took her class to see the legendary Alvin Ailey Dance Troupe put on a tremendous show. Piedmont students joined other local school children in the 2,000-seat auditorium to watch six powerful dances performed by NYC-based dance company. Accompanying the visual performance was recorded music. Of the six dances, three were choreographed by Alvin Ailey, founder of the world-famous troupe. “What impressed the second graders and parents alike was the warmth of the dances. The three by Ailey made even the most squiggly of second graders sit still,” said Katy Bradford, a parent chaperone. The entire day was a celebration of the arts, as the field trip took place following the school’s Spring concert for grades K-3 led by music teacher Adrian Behrendt. Students were all smiles after the fun day of performance art. The Wildwood Centennial Garden started off with a Lollipop pull game in which attendees could win vintage Wildwood School items. A time capsule table asked students to write down their predictions for the future. Other stations included book and game swaps and a photo booth. “It was so nice to see so many generations on hand,” said Pan. “It’s always fun to throw a party with other Wildwood parents. They really show up.” Along the back fence of the lower playground the Wildwood History Wall allowed everyone to walk through the ten decades of Wildwood history through newspaper clippings. The day of fun was fueled by a Top Dog truck and homemade lemonade. The lower playground was only recently reopened after nine months of work on Witter Field. The new garden on the lower playground will include input from students. More information on the history of Wildwood can be found at: Historyofpiedmont.com/wildwood. On Saturday, May 11, from 2:00-4:00 p.m. Wildwood’s Centennial will be celebrated in the auditorium with more artifacts of its 100-year history, a slide show and a birthday cake. Kids and parents painting Gratitude Rocks. Posters detailing each decade at Wildwood covered the back fence.

articles.text: As spring break began on April 6, ten Piedmont Middle School students and their families boarded an overnight flight to Havana, Cuba, loaded down with baseball gear and eager to experience legendary Cuban baseball. “We were just 90 miles from Florida,” said Carolyn Stewart, mother of seventh grader Aidan Stewart. “But as soon as we stepped off the plane, we felt like we were a world away.” The Piedmont families were in awe of the unfamiliar sights, streets full of classic cars, oncegrand mansions crumbling into the sea and endless images of Che Guevara. But it was at the baseball field at Santiago “Changa” Maderos stadium where the magic of the trip happened. The Piedmont team played four baseball games on successive days with competitive Cuban teams. While interpreters helped bridge the language barrier between umpires, coaches and players, the kids quickly realized that everyone spoke the universal language of baseball. Five Cuban 14-year-old players joined the Piedmont team and friendships formed quickly as everyone seamlessly became teammates. The opponents’ families displayed a taste of Latin American sports fandom with lively chants and cheering and a very distinct horn that blared loudly from their side of the stadium. The many curious onlookers peering through the fences at each game The Piedmont team at Estadio Santiago “Changa” Mederos baseball stadium. Pictured are: Clemens Conrad, Jack Dahling, Dylan Toyama, Ben McMurtry, Josh Campuzano, Ryan McMurtry, Zachary Cha-Foster, Orion Sachs, Aidan Stewart, Jonah Cha-Foster, and Mason Gray Charge d’Affaires Benjamin Ziff, who oversees the US Embassy in Havana, paid an official visit to meet the young American baseball players. Group photo with Cuban baseball team after the final game in Havana Piedmont players are taught some drills by Cuban baseball coaches and players. Piedmont players and families in front of the San Cristobal de La Habana Cathedral in Old Havana emphasized the importance of our presence and the cultural exchange to our hosts. On the third day of play, the Piedmont team took a break from competition to train with Cuban coaches. The boys engaged in a variety of drills for three hours of training. Even though the drills were familiar, being coached by former professional Cuban baseball players and hearing lessons offered in another language in a faraway place was a unique thrill. “We mostly already knew what they taught us, but it’s pretty cool that the baseball players in Cuba do the same drills that we do,” said seventh grader Ben McMurtry. Baseball Beyond Borders, a Bay Area youth sports non-profit founded by former Cuban professional baseball player Michel Rodriguez, organized cultural sightseeing trips that showcased the host country. The Piedmont players and families got to see a lot of Havana in six days and experience the hospitality of the Cuban people. The group walked the cobblestoned streets of Old Havana and learned about many historic plazas and sites while street vendors tempted the hot and tired kids with sugar coated churros and plantain chips. A lively rumba show at twilight on the rooftop of an old Colonial building offered picturesque views of the city and lessons of the quintessential Cuban music that is steeped in its African origins. articles.text: Smolko wins league singles title, Imburg-Welch win doubles Staff Photos Piedmont’s tennis league champions. Pictured are Monte Imburg and doubles partner Nate Welch (left), singles winner Lucas Smolko, assistant coach Corey Reich and coach Jim Landes. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team made a clean sweep of this year’s league championship match, winning both the singles at the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament at Chabot College in Hayward on Friday and Saturday, April 26-27. It was their first double win since 2017. Lucas Smolko took home the singles championship with a 6-2, 6-2 win over Bishop O’Dowd’s Neo Chai, while Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won 6-2, 7-6 (7-3) over O’Dowd’s Elias Cross and Max Hamilton for the doubles title. “I can’t remember the last time we won two championships, let alone be in both finals,” coach Jim Landes said on Saturday. Smolko appeared in last year’s finals as a freshman against San Leandro’s Elijah Cho, but lost in three sets. This year, he received a first-round bye with the top seed before shutting out Castro Valley’s Arik Hoffman 6-0, 6-0 in the second round. He then beat Berkeley’s Sze Ting Chen in the semifinals 6-3, 6-3. Smolko lost to Chen in straight sets on March 20, but defeated Chen 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 recently on April 18. In Saturday’s match, Smolko played with consistency and beat Chen with long rallies. “The first match, he really brought it to me with big serves and big forehands. The following match was insane and lasted like three hours. What I did differently was try to get into the match from the start and play longer rallies. From there, it was a grind to the last point,” Smolko said. In the finals, Smolko played even more consistently against Chai to a 6-2, 6-2 win. Smolko got the job done with more long rallies, consistent first-serves, and winning several games as the returner. Piedmont’s last WACC singles winner for the boys’ team was not available because the league recently cleared out its online archives. Makenna Thiel was the last to win a singles title for the girls’ team in 2021. In doubles, Imburg has appeared since his freshman year. He placed third in the doubles bracket in 2022 with Ben Breber, but did not compete in 2023. Going into this year’s tournament, Imburg had something to prove. “I’ve played with so many different people for four years, it’s kind of crazy. It’s strange adjusting to so many different partners. Playing with Nate, who has such a consistent serve and with me at the net worked; I think we played it well,” Imburg said. Pairing with Welch, a sophomore, the duo beat James Chea and Remi Banducci of Alameda 6-0, 6-4 in the first round before taking out three teams from Bishop O’Dowd. They beat Mateen LaClair and Lucas Tanaka in three sets, 4-6, 6-2, 10-7, in the second round, and then took out Lucas Smolko took home the WACC singles title as a sophomore.
articles.title: Tennis team sweeps league championships

articles.text: 8-7 win over rival O’Dowd; PHS gets No. 5 seed in NCS playoffs Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team got the job done in the 2024 Western Alameda County Conference tournament by beating league rival Bishop O’Dowd 8-7 on April 26. In a game played at Berkeley High, the win marked the team’s first league title since 2019 To get there, PHS defeated No. 4 Newark Memorial 19-2 in the semifinals. They have qualified for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs and will be the No. 5 seed. It was a fitting championship victory over O’Dowd, which won the last two league titles. Piedmont had to respond to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but the Highlanders quickly responded with goals by Friedie Schickedanz and Ruby Guzdar. “Part of it is we were getting very frustrated. I told them we have to clean up some things like dropped balls, turnovers, and making really good decisions. We kept the plays very simple; possession, possession, possession,” coach Carlton Chan said. PHS dominated O’Dowd 15-3 on March 22, but the Dragons were without star player Lucy Yu, a junior who gas already committed to Cornell, She is the daughter of former PHS championship-winning boys’ lacrosse coach Al Yu. A big part Ruby Guzdar scoring one of her four goals against Bishop O’Dowd. Friedie Schickedanz scored twice on Bishop O’Dowd. of the finals game on Friday was shutting down Yu with speedy defender Hailey Marshburn shadowing her for the entire game. PHS consistently pressed Yu to force her around the top of the 12-meter fan. “Basically, I had to apply pressure and make sure she didn’t get the ball. But it’s hard knowing she’s a Div. 1 commit as a junior,” said Marshburn “I just tried to get in front of her because we knew she’d try to drive to the right. It was all about communication,”. It was a big game for goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter, who had 12 saves. “Lucy is so fast. We had two or three people on her at a time,” Hattan-Kutter said. “I have to say, Annika had one of her best games of the entire season. She kept us in the game,” Chan said. With five minutes left in the game, Chan made a similar call to their 2019 North Coast Section title, which was an identical 8-7 win over San Marin. “Leep possession and kill the clock,” he told the team in the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s attack ate away the final five minutes of the game, largely with Guzdar and Schickedanz quickly changing possession, while Guzdar used her speed to evade multiple defenders. “We killed the clock in our Berkeley game. Against Miramonte, they scored late and won it in overtime, and that was heartbreaking. Friedie and I knew we weren’t going to give it up. It was so stressful, the main thing was to just keep the ball,” Guzdar said.
articles.title: Piedmont wins first WACC title since 2019

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team showcased exceptional talent and determination at the West Alameda County Conference championships on Friday, April 26 at Chabot College in Hayward. Piedmont’s athletes delivered outstanding performances, including the boys’ team winning the event and the girls’ team claiming second place. The boys achieved a remarkable milestone, winning the meet for the first time in 15 years. PHS emerged as the top medal earner among all 12 teams, amassing a total of 21 medals. They outdid Berkeley’s 19 medals and Castro Valley’s 15. Coach Colby Price commended the team’s performance, noting the challenges posed er teams with greater numbers. “Bigger teams gobbled up points in events where we just don’t have the numbers,” Price said of the girls placing second. ”Those teams are double our numbers in size, but the talent of our girls team always shines bright enough to stay in the mix, we just need more numbers to get all the way to the top.” Boys’ highlights Owen Blanford won two events on the day. He was first of 27 in the 500 freestyle in 4:40.98, while he won the 200 Free in 1:42.74 out of 35 swimmers. Cole Carnazzo also won a pair of events. He won the 100 Breast in 59.43 in a field of 45 swimmers and won the 100 Fly in 52.42 against a field of 26. Dima Secor won the 200 Individual Medley in 2:00.21 against 19 other swimmers. He won his event by 8.45 seconds over the next best swimmer. Asher Takazawa won his 100 backstroke in 54.22 against 33 swimmers. The 400 Free relay team of Blanford, Takazawa, Tom Rolefson and Nik Costello won against 24 other teams, clocking a time of 3:14.53. They beat the next best team by 6.7 seconds. Takazawa also placed second of 57 in the 100 Free with a time of 49.10. Byun also placed second of 18 in the 200 IM in 2:08.66. Girls’ highlights: Taylor Rolefson won two events. She won the 200 freestyle Cole Carnazo won the WACC’s 100 breaststroke and 100 butterfly championships. pages.text: Wednesday, May 1, 2024 13 PHS boys’ swim team wins league; girls’ second Piedmont High School’s swim team showcased exceptional talent and determination at the West Alameda County Conference championships on Friday, April 26 at Chabot College in Hayward. Piedmont’s athletes delivered outstanding performances, including the boys’ team winning the event and the girls’ team claiming second place. The boys achieved a remarkable milestone, winning the meet for the first time in 15 years. PHS emerged as the top medal earner among all 12 teams, amassing a total of 21 medals. They outdid Berkeley’s 19 medals and Castro Valley’s 15. Coach Colby Price commended the team’s performance, noting the challenges posed er teams with greater numbers. “Bigger teams gobbled up points in events where we just don’t have the numbers,” Price said of the girls placing second. ”Those teams are double our numbers in size, but the talent of our girls team always shines bright enough to stay in the mix, we just need more numbers to get all the way to the top.” Boys’ highlights Owen Blanford won two events on the day. He was first of 27 in the 500 freestyle in 4:40.98, while he won the 200 Free in 1:42.74 out of 35 swimmers. Cole Carnazzo also won a pair of events. He won the 100 Breast in 59.43 in a field of 45 swimmers and won the 100 Fly in 52.42 against a field of 26. Dima Secor won the 200 Individual Medley in 2:00.21 against 19 other swimmers. He won his event by 8.45 seconds over the next best swimmer. Asher Takazawa won his 100 backstroke in 54.22 against 33 swimmers. The 400 Free relay team of Blanford, Takazawa, Tom Rolefson and Nik Costello won against 24 other teams, clocking a time of 3:14.53. They beat the next best team by 6.7 seconds. Takazawa also placed second of 57 in the 100 Free with a time of 49.10. Byun also placed second of 18 in the 200 IM in 2:08.66. Girls’ highlights: Taylor Rolefson won two events. She won the 200 freestyle See Swimming on page 31 Cole Carnazo won the WACC’s 100 breaststroke and 100 butterfly championships. Piedmont’s girls’ 200 freestyle relay team won the WACC title with a time of 1:42.72 in a field of 38 teams. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team is still competing for the top seed heading into the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs. Over the past week, Piedmont lost 9-5 loss to league rival Bishop O’Dowd at home on Wednesday, April 24, but responded with a 4-2 win over the same team two days later. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 14-6 overall and 6-2 against WACC Foothill teams with just three games left in the regular season. PHS holds a 1.5 game lead over O’Dowd and Castro Valley with a 4-3-1 (W-L-T) record, and a two-game lead over Berkeley and Alameda at 4-4. PHS has a critical two-game series with Berkeley starting today, May 1, at the Yellowjackets field before returning to Humphries Diamond on Friday, May 3. With a top-four seed, Piedmont will qualify for the WACC Playoffs on May 7-9. Markos Lagios had an heroic performance in the 4-2 win over O’Dowd with two home runs, giving him six home runs this season as Piedmont’s leadoff hitter. His first of two shots marked his fourth home run of the season during his first at bat of the game. 4-2 over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont started the game with a run via Lagios’ solo blast to left field in the top of the first, then added two more runs in the top of th second. Bishop O’Dowd got on the board in the bottom of the fifth, but Piedmont tacked on one more in the top sixth. The Dragons scored once in the bottom of the seventh. In the top of the second, Jordan Vo drew a walk with one out. With two outs, Lagios stepped to the plate, and smashed another home run on the very first pitch of his at bat. This time, he went opposite field to right. PHS scored its last run in the top of the sixth when Jack Meyjes Staff Photos Markos Lagios slugged two home runs in the 4-2 win over Bishop O’Dowd. singled in Brandon Dicke, who led off with a walk. Final stats: Lagios was 2-for-4 with two home runs, three RBIs, and two runs scored. Will Parker was 2-for-3, Vo was 1-for-2 with a run scored, and Meyjes was 1-for-3 with an RBI. Pitching was Seve Sanchez, throwing a complete game with 10 strikeouts, allowing no earned runs and four hits. 9-5 loss to O’Dowd Bishop O’Dowd scored once in the top of the first and one more in the top of the third before piling on five runs in the top of the fourth. After runs in the top fifth and sixth, the Dragons led 9-0. PHS scored once in the bottom of the sixth and scored four more in the bottom of the seventh. Final stats: Diego Delventhal was 2-for-3 with two RBIs. Parker had an RBI. Sam Ragones went 1-for-1 with an RBI and run. Bo was 1-for-2 with an RBI and run. Meyjes was 1-for-2 with a run. articles.text: Piedmont’s golf team wrapped up its league season at the 2024 Western Alameda County Conference Championship tournament at Sequoyah Country Club on Monday, April 29. The previous week, PHS defeated Berkeley 222-225 at the same location. At the WACC Championship, Alameda won with a final score of 434 strokes. Bishop O’Dowd placed second at 429, Castro Valley was third with 435 strokes, and Piedmont was fourth with 441. Other schools included Berkeley (447), Encinal (487), and Arroyo and San Leandro, each with 499. Piedmont, senior Bodhi Bloemker tied for the third-best round of the day by shooting a 76, 6 over par, He was three strokes behind Kailer Stone of Alameda. Freshman Derek Lee finished with a round of 85, sophomore P.J. Brayer shot a 91, freshman Jackson Van Kleek had a 94, and Charlie Wright rounded out the team scoring with a 95. Bloemker individually qualified for the Division 2 North Coast Section Championship on Monday, May 6 at Peacock Gap in San Rafael. Piedmont’s golf team placed fourth at the WACC Championship at Sequoyah Country Club. 222-225 win vs. over Berkeley The previous week, Piedmont had a narrow three-stroke 222- 225 win over Berkeley at the Sequoyah Country Club, though the team was without Bloemker. Lee was the low medalist with a 9-hole round of 36 strokes, Wright shot a 43, sophomore Dillon Casey had a 44, Brayer show a 48, while Van Kleek rounded things out with a 51. “Dillon was a last-minute substitution and shot fantastic,” coach Gary Lorin said. Lee finished the day in strong fashion with a birdie on Sequoyah’s 385-yard par-4 eighth hole. NEXT UP Bloemker heads to Peacock Gap Golf Club in San Rafael on Monday, May 6 at 12:00 p.m.

In the finals, Imburg and Welch won the first set easily 6-3, including Imburg hitting a winner for the final point as the returning side. In the second set, both teams traded games until the net. O’Dowd held a 5-4 advantage, but won two straight games to go ahead 6-5 and hold match point. O’Dowd won its sixth game as the serving side to force a seven-game tiebreaker— to which Imburg and Welch dominated to a 7-2 win. articles.text: After rain rescheduled their third race, Piedmont High School and Piedmont Devo (junior development) mountain biking teams raced their third race of the season with the NorCal NiCA League in Granite Bay on the beach of Folsom Lake in Folsom, CA on Sunday April 28. Due to rescheduling, the race was set for the morning after Senior Prom, meaning Piedmont only brought a group of six high school riders. The course at Granite Bay was fast with a mixture of single track through meadows, forest, sandy beach terrain, and a few muddy puddles. Each lap is 6.2 miles with 576 feet of vertical gain. JV races two laps, while Varsity and JV1 race three laps. Varsity rider Max Rivera proved his dedication, finishing his 18 mile race with a time of 1:20:47, placing 31st and advancing in points. Olive Reining, a sophomore, racing on the JV2 Girls team, had her strongest race of the season by finishing in front of some familiar rivals with a time of 1:25:30. Caleb Canada and Asher Villareal, sophomores, raced next in the JV2 Boys race. Caleb came in with a very strong result of 1:04:23 finishing 21st out 34. Asher persevered through the rising heat and brought it in with a time of 1:21:59. Jasper Schuetz and Cary Ward raced for the JV1 boys team when the sun was at full blast. This exciting race was off to a quick start with Jasper leading a pack of six riders around the first lap in what was nicknamed the “Pain Train.” On the second lap he was third approaching the lap line but advanced in the sand on the beach to be right behind the lead, averaging 270 watts. The top three kept trading places throughout the third and final lap with Jasper putting in a final effort of 1200 watts for 15 seconds at the finish to beat Casey Warren of Berkeley High School by 0.5 seconds. His time was 1:12:57. This win brings Jasper into contention for winning the series, pending the results of his final race of the season on May 11th. Sunday was a redeeming win for Schuetz, responding strongly from placing 12th in his first race of the season due to a cold, while he placed second in his most recent race. The suffering continued with the rest of the field coming in as the sun pounded. Cary Ward felt the effects of dehydration and brought it in at 1:41:09 placing 31st. Middle School Development team The middle school Piedmont Devo team brought six strong young racers to Granite Bay. Four 8th grade girls, Josie Schuetz, Rose Reining, Olivia Bailey, and Gracey Ann Hatchell made up nearly a third of the category. They raced on a different course with 3.3 miles and 500 feet of climbing per lap along scenic trails full of wildflowers. 8th grade girls raced 3 laps. Josie Schuetz felt personal improvement by setting a time of 0:57:29 and placing ninth. Rose and Olivia came in close together at 1:05:23 and 1:05:53, and Gracey OaklandGreekFestival.com

The previous week, PHS defeated Berkeley 222-225 at the same location. At the WACC Championship, Alameda won with a final score of 434 strokes. articles.text: Free event includes kid-friendly museum-curated art activities de Youngsters Day Out invites Bay Area kids to engage with deYoung Museum’s permanent collections through hands-on activities. Visit the de Young Museum this Saturday, May 4, to experience de Youngsters Day Out, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s annual free community day for children. Family-friendly activities will be led by de Young’s teaching artists, allowing children to engage with the museum’s permanent collections through hands-on activities. The event also raises funds for arts education through the Equity School Partnership Project, an initiative with the San Francisco and Oakland Unified School Districts that provides art education to students in the Bay Area. “We are delighted to bring the de Youngsters Day Out to the families of the Bay Area,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Not only does this annual event provide crucial funding for our Equity School Partnership Project, but it also opens up museum doors to a new generation of visitors and connects them with art through a range of engaging activities. It’s a joy to see our galleries come alive with the creativity and excitement of children.” Activities include the San Francisco Public Library’s “Library on Wheels,” a mobile library program that gives out free reading materials for children and parents, as well as free eye exams by Zenni Eyewear. De Youngsters Day Out begins at 10 a.m. and will remain open until 5:15 p.m. with event activities wrapping up at 4 p.m. No registration is required. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more.
articles.title: Kids Day at de Young Museum this Saturday

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will exhibit Art of Noise, on view May 4 through August 18, to showcase groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise will feature over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” SFMOMA will host a free “Community Day” on Saturday, May 4, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. where everyone enjoys free admission to the entire museum, and a free “Family Day” on Sunday, June 9 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Up to four adults get in free when accompanied by a child 18 or younger. To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org.
articles.title: Art of Noise exhibit opens at SFMOMA May 4

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside will be open to the public on select evenings in May. Filoli is home to 16 acres of formal gardening grounds and a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. In 2021, a record 80,000 bulbs bloomed. In May, visitors will catch a glimpse of vibrant Tulips, Irises, Wisteria, Peonies, and wildflowers. Filoli is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Evening tickets allow guests to visit the house and gardens from 5 p.m. through closing at 8 p.m., an ideal time to witness the “golden hour.” Evening tickets are released weekly one week in advance. Food and drinks are available on-site at the Quail Cafe and Vegetable Garden Bar. To plan your visit, click https:// filoli.org/. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside; phone (650) 364-8300. Tulips bloom at Filoli House and Garden in May.
articles.title: Filoli House and Garden opens on select evenings in May

articles.text: Blue Door, Tanya Barfield’s new two-man play, premieres on the Aurora Theatre Company stage in Berkeley this Friday, April 19. Barfield’s play features Lewis, a high-achieving Black mathematics professor, in conversation with three generations of his ancestors during a sleepless night as he wrestles with his own sense of self and cultural identity. Lewis is estranged from his white wife, who accuses him of being out of touch with his heritage for refusing to attend the Million Man March, a grassroots demonstration of African-American men in Washington, D.C., on October 16, 1995. At that time, organizers united in self-help and self-defense against economic and social ills plaguing their communities. The ancestral visitations Lewis receives call upon joy and pain as well as music and song to situate him in a long lineage of Black men in America from enslavement and Jim Crow to Black Power. The cast is led by Michael J. Asberry and James Mercer II. Post-show discussions of Blue Door are hosted on Friday, May 3, Wednesday, May 8 and Thursday, May 16. The play ends May 19. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/blue-door. Michael J. Asberry (right) and James Mercer II appear in Blue Door at Aurora Theatre in Berkeley.
articles.title: Blue Door plays at Aurora Theatre through May 19

articles.text: Tickets for the symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley are now on sale. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. The festival, now in its 18th season, begins on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome everyone to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the nonprofit festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” Visit ht t ps://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/ for full programming and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley tickets now on sale for summer, July 6-21

articles.text: A scene from Mark Morris Dance Company’s production of Socrates Always count on the dean of US modern-dance choreographers, Mark Morris, 67, to pull rabbits out of the hat. The company director lost none of his mojo when he moved from dance toward theater pieces. The Mark Morris Dance Group performed a rarity at Zellerbach Hall. Not only was MM’s Via Dolorosa a world premiere, but it was the first time in memory that the veteran ever tackled a sacred-religious theme in dance with his troupe. His dancers – nine of them here, all stellar interchangeable parts – are exquisitely disciplined, with a unique lightness of foot, bobbing weightlessly about stage, playing out the Passion of Jesus Christ in rather abstract fashion. I’d even use that word taboo among dance reviewers, “graceful.” Christ was sometimes male, sometimes female. And various underplayed images caught the moment, whether crowds pointing fingers accusingly at prisoner Christ, or a dancer with arms outstretched portrayed Jesus crucified, or the whole group falling gently to the floor to portray his death. This was MM playing the supreme classicist, going way back to Biblical references subtly alluded to, with a deft, sprightly corps to show classical dance modes with a minimum of finery or décor, apart from Howard Hodgkin’s blazing/colorful abstract backdrops. This unusual 40-minute venture into sacred dance was backed by one mere solo harp (Parker Ramsay) rather than a Bach Passion or Verdi Requiem pounded out by an orchestra. To quote the architect Mies van der Rohe, “Less is more.” One resounding boo had pepPhoto by Chris Hardy pered the dance group’s opening night, possibly reacting to the Christ theater piece, with all the walking and stylized reenactments in place of, well, dance. But we still call it the MM Dance Group, no?? A companion piece on the program was Morris’ Socrates (2010). This work leaned heavily on painted images on ancient Greek vases, portrayed in two-dimensional fashion by the 15 dancers. Exquisite lightness of foot once again, but without the Satie music for solo piano and tenor (in incomprehensible French). You’d never know it had anything to do with the great ancient-Greek philosopher, his condemnation and his death scene. MARK MORRIS DANCE GROUP in two works by the director/choreographer Morris. Cal Performances, Zellerbach Hall, Berkeley, CA, April 19-20. For info: (510) 642-9988, or go online www.calperformances.org.
articles.title: Mark Morris, deserting dance?

articles.text: Premiere of award-winning show is this Sunday, May 5 Berkeley Repertory Theatre will premiere the award-winning play Galileo this Sunday, May 5. The play won a Tony Award for playwright Michael Mayer and an Emmy Award for Danny Strong. The play chronicles maverick scientist Galileo Galilei’s life, a man who makes celestial observations that challenge humanity’s understanding of its place in the universe. In this retelling, Galileo is summoned to Rome to defend his discoveries before the most powerful religious institution in the world. The play includes an original rock score with lyrics by Michael Weiner and Zoe Sarnak, and features four-time Tony Award nominee Raúl Esparza. Post-show discussions will be held May 24, May 30, and June 4 with members of Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s artistic team. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ galileo/. Berkeley Rep’s premiere of Galileo opens this Sunday, May 5. ®
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s newest play chronicles life of Galileo

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, May 1, 2024 Review by Anastasia Edel From April 11 to 13 San Francisco Symphony presented The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, performing Howard Shore’s Academy Award-winning score with a screening of the motion picture. Ludwig Wicki of Lucerne, Switzerland, conducted the orchestra, accompanied by the San Francisco Symphony Chorus and the Pacific Boychoir Academy. Few tales captivate like The Lord of the Rings, J.R.R. Tolkien’s three-part fantasy epic. Written during World War II, when the world was battling Hitler’s Nazis, Tolkien’s novel is centered around the quest to destroy the ring of power that “corrupts the hearts of men.” Wizards, hobbits, elves, dwarves, and men fight side by side to save Middle Earth, their home, from the forces of darkness. A clear parable of our own world despite its fantasy trappings, Tolkien’s tale delivered a powerful message of hope and enduring hero archetypes that have won millions of fans across countries and generations. One such fan was Hollywood film director Peter Jackson, who adapted the novel into three film installments in the late 1990s. Released between 2001-2003 to massive critical and popular success, The Lord of the Rings trilogy grossed $2.9 billion worldwide, sweeping Oscars and Grammys like a plow truck sweeps snow. It propelled a cast that included Orlando Bloom and Cate Blanchet into international stardom. The trilogy continues to command “most viewed” rankings on IMD today. British film magazine SF Symphony’s riveting Lord the Rings Live performance shines with Pacific Boychoir Empire ranks The Fellowship of the Ring, the first part of the trilogy, as the “Best movie of all time.” A key ingredient behind the movies’ success was the gripping music written by Canadian-born composer Howard Shore. Like Jackson, Shore worked from a place of deep appreciation for Tolkien’s tale, producing a score that is emotionally charged and musically complex. Its vast scope includes a symphony orchestra, mixed chorus, boys chorus, and instrumental and vocal soloists singing in the Tolkien-crafted languages, as well as English. So haunting and mesmerizing were those vocals, I used to anticipate their appearance no less than the enchantments of the elves or the epic battle scenes when I rewatched The Lord of the Rings at home. Last summer, when I learned that the San Francisco Symphony would be performing the music score live in April 2024, I knew I had to see it. Symphony performances typically don’t trigger traffic jams, but the 2 p.m. Saturday show on April 17 flooded Grove, Gough and Van Ness streets with music lovers who also were The Lord of the Rings fans and vice versa. Berkeley Pacific Boy choir conductor Andrew Brown It turned out to be a rare case when our already high expectations were exceeded. At 60 feet wide, the screen was large – though not as large as the center stage below that housed the full orchestra. At the upper terrace behind the screen, invisible to most of the audience, stood the San Francisco Symphony Chorus, flanked by the members of the Pacific Boychoir Academy. Overall, more than 200 musicians were engaged to perform the Grammy-winning score. As the epic’s famous opening words (“The world has changed”) emanated from the screen and Shore’s haunting score filled the vast space of the symphony hall, the line between reality and magic began to fade. Suddenly, we were in the movie – and in Tolkien’s Middle Earth. Performed live by one of the world’s premiere orchestras, the music added an exhilarating new dimension to our already intense journey, accompanying us to the Shire, the green hilly land of the hobbits; to the elegant castles of Riverdale, the realm of the elves; to Moria, the underground city of the gold-miner dwarves; and the ominous Mordor, where the Dark Lord and his orc army planned their takeover of Middle Earth. The vocals – both uplifting and menacing, and always otherworldly—deepened our emotional engagement. “Lothlórien,” the sorrowful lament performed by the Pacific Boychoir Academy, was particularly gripping. In the manner of classical Greek dramatists, Peter Jackson’s and Howard Shore’s collaboration was brought to life by the musicians, elevating the role of the chorus from a mere background to that of a conduit between the audience and the action. When the movie credits began to roll to “May It Be,” an acclaimed song written for the movie by the Irish singer Enya (and performed gorgeously by Kaitlyn Lusk and by Brenn Farrell of the Pacific Boychoir Academy Day School), it was hard to believe that the show was over. There was one more bit of magic though, this being The Lord of the Rings. As the audience broke into a standing ovation, I spotted a familiar face on the stage: Andrew Brown, the gregarious director of the Pacific Boychoir Academy (PBA) and the Concert Choir Director of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, was shaking hands with other artists. By all accounts he and his posse of young singers had just pulled off an impressive feat. The following week, I was sitting in the PBA’s homey rehearsal room off Piedmont Avenue in Oakland where the singers and maestro Brown shared their perspective on the exhilarating Lord of the Ring experience. I learned that it was PBA’s 30th collaboration with the San Francisco Symphony. I asked Brown if it was hard for them to learn to sing in Elvish, and the answer was a unanimous no. “Compared to Estonian and Finnish, in which we often sing, Elvish was easy,” Brown added with a laugh. There were plenty of challenges, of course. “Elvish phrases are long, like ‘ee-too-aw ee mah ke-e stahl dah – rawn mow-ree nye kwar’ – so we had to stagger our breathing,” said 7-year-old Emmett Stout, the youngest PBA member to ever perform on the symphony stage. Because the boys sang only seven times throughout the entire performance, they hummed during their downtime to keep their voices fresh. See SF Symphony on page 31

articles.text: Do you have a favorite cuisine? It might surprise many of you that every cuisine is fusion of some sort. Historically, Alexander the Great defeated the Persians, but he admired Persian culture big time. I am willing to bet that Alexander enjoyed ancient Persian cuisine. That premise started an adventure. Some cuisines offer consistency, some offer variety, and some offer value. I discovered that Persian cuisine offers some challenges. Some of the Persian restaurants I tried in the past are simply not very interesting. Alborz, in Berkeley is head and shoulders above the average. The food is beautiful in service and in preparation. Portions are large, and to top it off, the service is gracious and attentive. Finally, the prices are reasonable. Is this the result of 3,000 years of culture? As our group of four arrived at Alborz, we immediately noticed the lovely ambience. The staff is mostly Mexican though the owners are Persian. For the cuisine… Your server can advise you. The restaurant has all of the classic dishes. We began with a Persian soup called Aash Reshteh. At $9.50 it was a large portion. Then we got another classic Persian dish which was a combination of eggplant and lamb in a saffron broth. Once again, the portion was very large and reasonably priced at $21.95. The Persian tea was nothing special but the baklava à la mode at $9 was excellent. Two food discoveries this week Another very interesting discovery was a Laotian restaurant called Champa Garden, which is situated at 2102 8th Avenue, an obscure residential area of Oakland. Don’t be turned off by the tawdry area or the plain-looking front. This restaurant will surprise you in many ways. Once you enter, you’ll be surprised by the lively atmosphere. Champa Garden is family owned and family run. That just about guarantees good food, and the prices are very reasonable. A Sweet breads at Reve Bistro in Lafayette

articles.text: Babou Ceesay and Helen Mirren in Eye in the Sky In many ways the well-made and superbly acted Eye in the Sky is reassuring. But it can also be chillingly disconcerting. At the outset we see a straightforward surveillance of a militant group associated with the East Africa terrorist organization Al Shabab. It then unexpectedly morphs into something far more serious and morally hazardous. What is initially being watched from an altitude of 20,000 feet by an unseen, eerily quiet drone is a house in Nairobi, Kenya, where a meeting is taking place between highly placed Shabab leaders, to include a woman, a British citizen, who has aligned herself with the organization. The original plan is to raid the house and capture those inside. But using a cyborg beetle, an agent (Barkhad Abdi, who starred in the film Captain Phillips), is sitting outside on the street and using a control no larger than a cell phone. He positions the small beetle with a miniaturized camera inside the house where it reveals that in another room several suicide bombers are preparing to put on explosive vests. The stakes have suddenly changed for all concerned – Col. Katherine Powell (Helen Mirren), located in Surrey England, and Lt. General Frank Benson (Alan Rickman), who is in London with several British ministers and politicians. What was a “capture” is now suddenly reframed as a “kill.” The only question, both legal and moral, is what will be the collateral damage once the drone releases its hellfire missile. Complicating that question is the presence of a small girl, seated just outside the house at a table where she sells her mother’s homemade flatbread to passing locals. She is clearly within the kill zone. The pilot of the drone (Aaron Paul) remarkably is in Nevada. When he spots the girl he asks for a review of all facets of the operation, to include legal and ethical concerns. And so the tension is continually ratcheted up. Powell and Benson argue that to delay could mean that the suicide bombers will leave and ultimately appear in a shopping mall where perhaps hundreds of innocents will be maimed or killed. This reality is weighed against the life of that one little girl. Others argue for delay as the decision is “referred up.” No civilian in the room with the General Benson wants to take final responsibility. Across four continents, involving ministers and secretaries of state, the “kill” decision is incrementally postponed. The reality that confronts those involved, to include the pilot of the drone, is the proverbial rock and the hard place. The debate is both agonizing and complex and riveting. What is done is done in the name of the British and the American people. Collateral damage is a euphemism that is laden with horrible, unintended consequences. And to make the moment even more dreadful is that it has a video game quality to it – warfare at its most detached. This is an intense and rare military meditation on war that focuses not on the battle but on the choices that we ask our military personnel to make as they conduct this most lethal form of warfare. To its credit the film avoids becoming a melodrama, while still examining effectively the moral quandary that we can only hope our soldiers and officials confront with each “kill” order. articles.text: Winston Churchill once said, “Democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the others that have been tried.” And because democracy is collaboration, a process of advise and consent executed by human beings, it is deeply flawed. Too often democracy means governance by narrow, self-serving men and women who are ruled by the principles of careers, mendacity and venality. Many are also incompetent. And messy offers fertile ground for satire, as demonstrated in the British film In the Loop, a high energy, over-the-top send-up about the period leading up to the invasion of Iraq (though Iraq is never mentioned). Good satire can be difficult to achieve, often reliant on biting humor, ridicule, and irony. The air can often take leave of the satirical balloon and it can quickly fall into absurdity and silliness. In the Loop doesn’t, due to its staccato-like writing, with smart lines dropped like cluster bombs. It is both bitingly funny and scarily accurate. Britain ministers and directors of communication, in collusion with American undersecretaries and their sycophants, fashion a Baroque rationale for war, created out of whole cloth, based on unimpeachable intelligence, derived from a Middle East source, code name The Iceman. It’s a house of cards, pure fiction, reconstructed to resemble truth. No matter, apparently, that both British and American soldiers will be put in harm’s way and irrevocable actions will result in blood and treasure being expended. Recall the United Nations presentation by General Colin Powell, pointing to weapons of mass destruction on a split screen high above the Chamber of Nations, and the ubiquitous color-coded alerts perpetrated by an administration that was the purveyor of fear and catastrophe at every political turn. This is not to say that In the Loop has a light touch or is subtle. It’s a wonderfully blunt instrument, beginning with a bevy of Anglo-Saxon epithets, plumbed to great effect and delivered with practiced hostility by the Prime Minister’s communication director, Malcom Tucker (Peter Capaldi). Capaldi’s portrayal is but one example of a host of English and American actors who give nifty performances, each convincing. It’s hard not to think of the Kabuki dance being played out today in Washington around healthcare. Like war, the stakes are high, and yet the dissembling scenarios, the theatrical town hall meetings, complemented by wingnuts packing heat, all make In the Loop timeless and prescient. In the Loop is satire at its best: thought-provoking, exaggerated and delightfully humorous. In The Loop. Directed by Armando Iannucci. Starring Tom Hollander, Peter Capaldi, James Gandolfini, and Gina McKee. 1 hr., 46 min. Not rated. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, May 1, 2024 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Eye in the Sky a taut military ops story Babou Ceesay and Helen Mirren in Eye in the Sky By Chris Honoré In many ways the well-made and superbly acted Eye in the Sky is reassuring. But it can also be chillingly disconcerting. At the outset we see a straightforward surveillance of a militant group associated with the East Africa terrorist organization Al Shabab. It then unexpectedly morphs into something far more serious and morally hazardous. What is initially being watched from an altitude of 20,000 feet by an unseen, eerily quiet drone is a house in Nairobi, Kenya, where a meeting is taking place between highly placed Shabab leaders, to include a woman, a British citizen, who has aligned herself with the organization. The original plan is to raid the house and capture those inside. But using a cyborg beetle, an agent (Barkhad Abdi, who starred in the film Captain Phillips), is sitting outside on the street and using a control no larger than a cell phone. He positions the small beetle with a miniaturized camera inside the house where it reveals that in another room several suicide bombers are preparing to put on explosive vests. The stakes have suddenly changed for all concerned – Col. Katherine Powell (Helen Mirren), located in Surrey England, and Lt. General Frank Benson (Alan Rickman), who is in London with several British ministers and politicians. What was a “capture” is now suddenly reframed as a “kill.” The only question, both legal and moral, is what will be the collateral damage once the drone releases its hellfire missile. Complicating that question is the presence of a small girl, seated just outside the house at a table where she sells her mother’s homemade flatbread to passing locals. She is clearly within the kill zone. The pilot of the drone (Aaron Paul) remarkably is in Nevada. When he spots the girl he asks for a review of all facets of the operation, to include legal and ethical concerns. And so the tension is continually ratcheted up. Powell and Benson argue that to delay could mean that the suicide bombers will leave and ultimately appear in a shopping mall where perhaps hundreds of innocents will be maimed or killed. This reality is weighed against the life of that one little girl. Others argue for delay as the decision is “referred up.” No civilian in the room with the General Benson wants to take final responsibility. Across four continents, involving ministers and secretaries of state, the “kill” decision is incrementally postponed. The reality that confronts those involved, to include the pilot of the drone, is the proverbial rock and the hard place. The debate is both agonizing and complex and riveting. What is done is done in the name of the British and the American people. Collateral damage is a euphemism that is laden with horrible, unintended consequences. And to make the moment even more dreadful is that it has a video game quality to it – warfare at its most detached. This is an intense and rare military meditation on war that focuses not on the battle but on the choices that we ask our military personnel to make as they conduct this most lethal form of warfare. Eye in the Sky is taut and well constructed and highly recommended. Eye in the Sky. Directed by Gavin Hood. Starring Helen Mirren, Aaron Paul and Alan Rickman. 1 hr., 42 min. Rated R. Released in 2016, Streaming on prime/MAX/apple tv. articles.text: To begin with, kids are going to enjoy a Bug’s Life. It’s a superb, animated feature filled with a creepy-crawly menagerie of bugs, inspired by an Aesop’s Fable titled The Ant and the GrasshopThe story opens with a wonderfully natural-looking colony of ants that makes its home on a mound of dirt, near a creek bed. It’s known as Ant Island and is ruled by the Queen ant and her daughter, Princess Atta (Julia As we soon learn, every summer a gang of thuggish grasshoppers arrive, led by the swaggering Hopper (Kevin Spacey), and they demand to be given food collected by the hard-working colony. A nerdy ant named Flik (Dave Foley), a young tinkerer, has an accident while trying to invent a conveyor belt to move the seeds intended for the grasshoppers. When the gadget malfunctions, he knocks the gathered food into the water. Whoops. Hopper is furious, and he demands that the ants give him twice as much food as promised, to make up for the loss. Flik, rebelling, feeling bullied, insists that the demand for double the rations is wrong, and suggests to the Queen that he be allowed to leave and find bigger bugs, warrior types, to help the colony in a fight against the grasshoppers. Enough is enough. Princess Atta, apparently not a fan of Flik, encourages him, assuming it’s unlikely that he will return from his mission. Flik journeys to Bug City (a heap of trash piled under a trailer), and it’s there that he recruits a cohort of “warriors” who are actually a troupe of Circus Bugs that had recently been fired by ringmaster P.T. Flea (John Ratzenberger). The group agrees to return to Ant Hill with Flik, who they think is a talent scout, having no idea what they are getting into. When they arrive at the colony, they discover what is afoot and that they are not there to perform. Flik pleads with them to stay and pretend to be what they’re not: fightA STEINWAY Teaching Partner Superpower of the Song™ by Kadie Kelly Piano lessons + / Sound Healing experiences I was drawn to the piano, singing and composing music from an early age. Throughout my life, music has been a source of happiness, community, self-expression and healing. My background is rooted in classical music, but I also have experience with pop music, leadsheets, blues, song-writing, and singing. I have always sought out collaborations with people with diverse musical experiences to gain new perspectives and skills, and I pass that affinity and curiosity on to my students. I value self determination, and in supporting students in the needs that they have, where they are.

articles.text: Further adventures with Antonio Banderas Kids will thoroughly enjoy Dreamworks’ sequel Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. It’s been more than a decade since the release of the popular Puss in Boots, so perhaps it would be helpful to begin with the first animated feature as a good way to introduce the young ones to Puss, the swashbuckling, daring feline. The narrative begins when Puss (Antonio Banderas), never risk averse, realizes his escapades have used up eight of his allotted nine lives. Listening to his doc’s advice, he decides to retire and live a more domestic life. He hangs up his boots and sword, and tries to commit to simply hanging out with the old cat lady, Mama Luna (Da’Vine Joy Randolph). Of course he grows restless. When he finds himself standing in a long line to use the litter box, he knows there has to be a better alternative. Determined to find a way to get his lost eight lives back, Boots heads off into the ominous Black Forest in search of the Wishing Star, hence the title, The Last Wish. And thus begins his epic journey, hoping to not only find the Star, but recover his lives. As it turns out there’s a map involved, one that takes on greater and greater importance. Boots comes to the realization that if he is going to succeed in his quest he will need help. He hooks up with his former partner, Kitty Soft Paws (Salma Hayek). Reluctantly they agree to take along the annoying, endlessly talking Perrito (Harvey Guillén). We see a panoply of familiar fairytale characters such as the Three Bears, Little Jack Horner A scene from Puss in Boots: The Last Wish

articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s Planning & Building Department hosted its annual Design Awards on Wednesday, April 24, honoring seven of Piedmont’s most ambitious home projects. The event, which took place at the Community Hall, also hosted a separate category of Sustainability Awards this year for the first time, honoring homeowners in Piedmont who have dedicated their houses to zerowaste, carbon-neutral, electrification-based, and solar-heavy designs. Light appetizers and refreshments were served preceeding the awards presentation. “We’re excited to give some awards to some very deserving community members and contractors and architects this year,” said Kevin Jackson, City Planning Director. • Excellence in Indoor/ Outdoor Living Design The first award went to homeowner Vicki Smith of 974 Rose Avenue. Architect Kirk Peterson, and contractor Daryl Rush were also honored. “We used the deck for decades,” said Smith during her acceptance speech. “We loved Planning Commissioner Justin Zucker (left) with architect Kirk Peterson, owner Victoria Smith, and Planning Director Kevin Jackson Designers Vanessa Bell (left) and Eli Israel, with owners Daniel Rampton and Anna Putnam Planning Commissioner Aradhana Jajodia (left), owner Lukas Bruggemann, contractor Agustin Santos, owner and designer Wendi Sue Planning Commissioner Aradhana Jajodia (left), contractor Bill Worley, owner Gina Song, and architect Arleta Chang Owner Peter Jaeshke (left) with architect Rob Kelly, contractor Gabriel Zarate, Planning Commissioner Wayne Rowland, and Kevin Jackson Commissioner Chris Harvey (left) with owners Stephen Selkowitz and Barbara O’Hare Planning Commissioner Rani Batra (left) with owners Andy Hempeck and Cass Caulfield Planning Commissioner Rani Batra (left) and owner Russell Griffith Former Planning Commissioner Douglas Strout (left), with owners Larry and Hope Salzer Planning Commissioner Julie Ortiz (left), designer Jay Jeffords, landscape contractor Nick Ozier, and owners Steve and Karen Ellis it and we just wanted something a little bit better. My husband ordered the heaters from Australia. They came in three weeks…. The project took 14 months,” she joked to much laughter. • Excellence in Façade Composition Homeowners Peter Jaeshke and Supina Mapon of 11 Cambridge Way were honored along with Piedmont architect Rob Kelly and contractor Gabriel Zarate. • Outstanding Integrated Addition Homeowners Anna Putnam and Dan Rampton of 218 Bonita Avenue were honored, with designers from Integrity Modeling, Eli Israel and Vanessa Bell, and Tim Wooster Designs. “I think with Piedmont, the most important thing is to not over-modernize your space, because that will last for five years,” said Bell. “Don’t strip your houses, people.” She pleaded followed by much applause. • Outstanding Architectural Restoration This award went to homeowners Lukas Bruggemann and Wendi Sue of 337 Magnolia Avenue. Their architect WES Architecture and Interiors and contractor Agustin Santos were also honored. • Excellence in Garage to ADU Conversion Homeowners Gina Song and David Woo of 319 El Cerrito Avenue were honored. Song accepted the award in Woo’s absence. Architect Arleta Chang and contractor Bill Worley were also honored. • Excellence in Outdoor Living Area This award was presented to homeowners Steve and Karen Ellis of 100 Indian Road. Designer Mark Becker and contractor Nick Ozier were also honored. • Excellence in Integrated Garage Design This award was presented to homeowners Stephen Selkowitz and Barbara O’Hare of 22 Nace Avenue. Architect Ehsan “Sean” Majd and contractor Erik Ramirez were also honored. Fol low i ng t he D e sig n Awards, the Sustainability Awards were presented as a separate category. Because of the number contractors involved in each project, the homeowners were the main honorees.

articles.text: Part 2 Last week I shared the first part of my coverage of the wines of the Bandol region in France. It all started with Jim Harrison. One of my favorite writers and the author of the novella Legends of the Fall which was made into a movie with Brad Pitt. He is also author of several collections of books on food and wine that were collected from his years as food columnist for Esquire magazine. Time and again in his essays he would rhapsodize about the wines of Bandol particularly Domaine Tempier. After years of reading about his favorite wine I decided I needed to discover Bandol wines for myself. So along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey after four days exploring the wines of Burgundy we set off for the four hour drive south to sunny Bandol. France is world-renowned as a gastronomic center of excellence but has more McDonalds per capita than any other country. Bandol is world renowned for its complex age-worthy reds, but 80% of its production is rose. Count it up to the French paradox. The Bandol wine region is just east of Marseilles perched high on limestone cliffs that overlooks the cerulean blue waters of the Mediterranean and the fishing village of Bandol. The seaside resort district is filled with rocky beaches, seafood stands, patio brasseries and palm trees. There is no better place to drink rose – or make it – but our quest was for the mighty reds of Bandol. Crafted from up to 95% Mourvedre grapes, the region is the king of that grape and home to red wines that can compete with the greatest of the Rhone Valley in power and complexity. We settled into a comfortable Air B &B house in the charming seaside town of La Ciotat that we used as our base for four days of exploration. Chateau de Pibarnon is perched on the hilltop.

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, May 1, 2024 Features The Wine Corner The wines of Bandol Part 2 By Pierre DuMont Last week I shared the first part of my coverage of the wines of the Bandol region in France. It all started with Jim Harrison. One of my favorite writers and the author of the novella Legends of the Fall which was made into a movie with Brad Pitt. He is also author of several collections of books on food and wine that were collected from his years as food columnist for Esquire magazine. Time and again in his essays he would rhapsodize about the wines of Bandol particularly Domaine Tempier. After years of reading about his favorite wine I decided I needed to discover Bandol wines for myself. So along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey after four days exploring the wines of Burgundy we set off for the four hour drive south to sunny Bandol. Crafted from up to 95% Mourvedre grapes, the region is the king of that grape and home to red wines that can compete with the greatest of the Rhone Valley in power and complexity. We settled into a comfortable Air B &B house in the charming seaside town of La Ciotat that we used as our base for four days of exploration. Domaine Tempier – Plan du Castellet Due to Jim Harrison and impor ter Ker mit Ly nch’s unswerving devotion, Tempier is by far the most well-known Bandol producer in America. It doesn’t hurt that Lulu Peyraud, co-owner of the winery with her husband Lucien, also has written one of the greatest French cookbooks, Lulu’s Provencal Kitchen, and used to pal around with Julia Childs and Richard Olney. The winery was started in 1834 but really took off under the direction of Lucien and Lulu in the late 1940’s. They helped transform the entire Bandol appellation and brought their wines to the world’s attention. In 2000 Lucien and Lulu’s children retired and the baton was passed to Daniel Ravier who is head winemaker and overseer of the Domaine. We were pleased to be able to get a quick tour of the old house the Peyrauds lived in including the historic kitchen where Lulu dazzled visitors with her cuisine. Their regular red cuvee is now called Cuvee Lulu and Lucien and was medium bodied and fruity with nice balance. They also make three additional single vineyard cuvees that serve as their flagships – La Migoua, La Tourtine and Cabassaou. All three were excellent, desirable wines. The problem was the price – they were all over twice as expensive as other excelDomaine Tempier lent Bandols we had on the trip, and without being twice as good. So, to be truthful I must report that though the Tempier wines are excellent they are not excellent values. Available at Kermit Lynch Wine in Berkeley. FAVORITE WINE • 2020 Domaine Tempier La Tourtine Inky dark purple in the glass and marked by aromas of menthol clove, allspice, leather, blackberries and dried cherries, the full-bodied La Tourtine has many layers of dark fruit flavors. Complex, silky and long on the finish it will last for decades in the cellar. Chateau de Pibarnon – Cadiere d’Azur “Are you sure this is the right road?” Terry Hershey our driver kept asking as we made our way down the narrow one lane track. We had started at Cadiere d’Azur and punched the address into the GPS. We were climbing through vineyards and the beautiful soaring pines with views of the Mediterranean below. Then at the end of a long dirt track we finally arrived at the stately rose-colored mansion that is Chateau Pibarnon. The house overlooks the most magnificent vista of meticulously crafted vineyards with row after row of stone terraces. The most magnificent vineyard is in the shape of a semicircle like a classic Greek amphitheater. Pibarnon was founded in the mid-1950’s by Modesto Ramognino who began planting vines in the dry. desolate site. In 1977 the property was taken over by Catherine and Henri Saint Victor after tasting a bottle of the wine in a restaurant in Bandol. They have greatly expanded and improved the vineyards, but the house is still primitive and the location makes farming difficult. The high elevation – more than 300 meters above the Mediterranean – gives the wines a great freshness and structure. We tried two roses, the better being Rose Nuances, which was made in an amphora and showed a dark pink color similar to Tavel. Like Tavel it was powerful and full in the mouth and strong enough to accompany any meat dish. The entry level red is called Restanques de Pibarnon and was made with 70% Mourvedre and 30% Grenache. It imedium bodied and fruity and totally ready to drink now. We tried three vintages of the Pibarnon red and all three were outstanding but will benefit from time in the cellar. Available at North Berkeley Wine on Shattuck Blvd. FAVORITE WINE • 2018 Pibarnon Bandol Rouge This delicious wine jumps out of the glass with aromas of asphalt, black olive, plums and earth. It is medium to full-bodied, richly tannic and sturdy on the Pibarnon is one of Bandol’s great red wines. palate, with a long dusty finish. Complex and layered is should easily improve and last for two decades in the cellar. When Reynald’s father bought Domaine de Terrebrune in the early 60’s he struck gold. He found a property that is located on fossilized bedrock of Triassic limestone. articles.text: The four flagship wines of Domaine Tempier. his white wine, a mix of Clairette, Ugni Blanc and Bourboulenc. It was citric and refreshing with a strong sense of minerality. Perfect aperitif for a warm afternoon. His rose was big and meaty in the typical Bandol way and is nothing like the light bodied ephemeral Cote de Provence roses. articles.text: A Film About the Robotics Team that Visited Piedmont in 2018 2018 Afghan Dreamers Girls’ Robotics Team On May 15, the American Medical Women’s Association, Highlander Robotics FRC Team 8033, and Girl Scouts Service Unit 303 will present a special screening of the Paramount Plus award-winning film, Afghan Dreamers. Afghan Dreamers tells the incredible story of the A fg h a n D re a me r s G i rls’ Robotics Team, a group of Afghan schoolgirls who – led and inspired by Afghan tech entrepreneur Roya Mahboob – defied conservative gender roles to compete internationally in robotics. In doing so, they helped transform a people and nation. The team first gained international notice in 2017 when they were barred from attending FIRST Global in Washington, D.C., due to a travel ban against individuals from certain predominantly Muslim countries. Supported by international allies and with the intervention of members of Congress, the team was ultimately allowed to compete and went on to win several awards in the U.S. and internationally. Inspired by the Dreamers’ unlikely success, then-President Ashraf Ghani committed to building five STEM schools throughout Afghanistan. But the team’s journey came with many struggles, as the film poignantly demonstrates. The Dreamers then continued their international journey, transforming communities and

articles.text: May 15, 2024, 7-9 pm Ellen Driscoll Playhouse 325 Highland Avenue, Piedmont Register to attend at: bit.ly/amwamay15 Producers: David Cowan, Sheila, Nevins, Ellen Goosenberg-Kent Creator & Associate Producer: Dr. Douglas Chin Directors: David Greenwald & Beth Murphy Trailer: https://bit.ly/Dreamers-Trailer Paramount: http://afghandreamers.movie bringing hope to women and girls along the way. But, as the film painfully shows, a tragic reversal of fortune came in August 2018 when the Taliban gained control of Afghanistan, and the girls, their coaches, and thousands of other Afghans were forced to flee their homeland. This film has special relevance to the Bay Area, as the Dreamers spent over a week in Piedmont hosted by a local family through the American Medical Women’s Association. During this time, the team had the opportunity to spend time with Piedmont robotics teams, Girl Scouts, and Boy Scouts. “Opening our home to the team was one of those unique moments in life that transforms the way you view and embrace the world and forges special friendships that last a lifetime,” said Douglas and Eliza Chin. Immediately following the screening on May 15, members of the production team will be joined by a former Afghan Dreamers team captain as well as an Afghan Girl Scout. They will share their perspectives on the film and the current status of women’s rights in Afghanistan, particularly with regard to education and work. The discussion will be moderated by an Afghan writer and human rights activist. The film has received critical acclaim internationally, awarded Best Human Rights Documentary at the Galway Film Fleadh, Runner-Up for Best Feature Length Documentary at Woodstock, Audience Choice Award at the Valladolid International Film Festival, and Official Selection at the Heartland and Boulder International Film Festivals.
