articles.text: Member of 2004 World Series champion Boston Red Sox A loving husband and father, former MLB first baseman and outfielder David Andrew McCarty, 54, passed away suddenly and unexpectedly on April 19, 2024. Known for his versatility, fielding, and power threat off the bench, Dave had an 11-year major league career with seven teams, including the 2004 Red Sox during their historic championship season that would break the infamous “Curse of the Bambino.” Born in Houston, Texas on November 23, 1969, Dave excelled both athletically and academically at Sharpstown High School. Recruited in baseball and basketball, he decided to focus on baseball and picked “the farm” at Stanford University in California (BA ‘92), where he would meet Piedmont native Monica Canty (PHS ’85), his wife of 32 years, who was attending Stanford Law School. The two were married on January 11, 1992. While at Stanford, Dave put up record numbers that would eventually land him in the Stanford Hall of Fame, including a 1991 season with a .420 batting average, 24 homers, 66 RBI, and an incredible .828 slugging percentage. Over his college summer months, he played in the Cape Cod Baseball League (1989 Cotuit Kettleers) and for Team USA in the 1990 Baseball World Cup. An All-American and Baseball America’s College Player of the Year, Dave was the third pick in the 1991 draft by the Minnesota Twins. That marked the beginning of a 14-year journey filled with many ups and downs that would see him play for nine different baseball organizations and seven major league teams over 11 seasons. The once top prospect would become a journeyman utility player who could come off the bench to play defense, provide a power-threat, and – a few times – pitch. The 6’5” right-handed batting, left-handed throwing (an unusual combination in baseball) first baseman, nicknamed “Big Mac” by his teammates, lightened the clubhouse with his sharp humor and enjoyed razzing the pitchers about his 2.45 ERA (3.2 IP, 4 SO, 1 BB). Over his career, Dave played in 630 major league games with the Minnesota Twins (1993– 1995), Cincinnati Reds (1995), Dave McCarty with World Series trophy at Fenway Park on April 9, 2024, at a celebration of the 20th anniversary of the Red Sox World Championship Family Day at Fenway Park during the 2004 Championship season The McCarty family (Reid, Monica, Maxine and Dave) at Royal Ascot in England, June 2023 San Francisco Giants (1995– 1997), Seattle Mariners (1998), Detroit Tigers (1999), Kansas City Royals (2000–2002), Tampa Bay Devil Rays (2002), Oakland Athletics (2003), and Boston Red Sox (2003–2005), posting a career average of .242 with 36 home runs, and 175 RBIs. With a Stanford degree to fall back on, Dave was tempted to hang up his spikes many times over the years. But he stuck with it and was rewarded when he was signed by Billy Beane of the Oakland A’s in 2000 during the “Moneyball” era. It rejuvenated his career. After an exceptional Spring Training with the A’s, Dave was traded to the Royals where he had his most productive season with career highs in batting average (.278), home runs (12), RBI (68), and games played (103). But the highlight of Dave’s baseball career was being part of the 2004 Red Sox, who were dubbed “The Idiots” due to their infamously loose clubhouse and inventive facial hair. Down three games to none in the ALCS, the Sox mounted a historic comeback against the Yankees. They would go on to defeat the Cardinals in four games in the World Series, winning eight in a row and breaking the Red Sox’s 86-year championship drought. Dave retired from baseball in 2005 but continued to work for the Red Sox as an analyst on NESN until the 2008 season. Dave adjusted to life after baseball with surprising ease. He joined Lee & Associates as one of the founding members of the commercial real estate firm’s Oakland office in 2006. There he found the camaraderie that he’d missed from the clubhouse and a job that he loved. While baseball was a large part of his life, the most important thing to Dave was family. With the demanding life on the road behind him, he was able to turn his four months of being a devoted, hands-on dad into twelve. Dave and Monica moved to Piedmont, CA in 2000 to raise their two children, Reid (PHS ’15) and Maxine (PHS ’17). The same big personality, sharp wit, and easy smile that made Dave a popular figure in the clubhouse continued after he retired; he was a well-known figure around town, walking the kids to school and taking them to various activities or sport practices. The family shared a love of sports – and competition – from the ski slopes, to the swimming pool, to the golf course, to the hiking trail. Staying active was a big part of Dave’s life. The former journeymen never stopped traveling. The family explored the globe together, traveling to Russia, China, Japan, Iceland, the Baltics, Europe, Greece, Mexico, Canada, and spending many weeks a year in London. Closer to home favorite spots were Tahoe, Hawaii, and frequent trips to the Disney parks. Dave’s passing comes just weeks after he and other members of the 2004 team were honored at Fenway Park as part of the 20-year anniversary of their championship season, a fitting sendoff to a man who was a champion in both sport and life. Dave was preceded in death by his father, Dennis. He is survived by his wife, Monica, his children, Reid and Maxine, his mother, Joan, his sister, Kelly, and a large much-loved extended family. A celebration of Dave’s wonderful life will be held on Thursday May 9, 2024. More information can be found at https:// rb.gy/xr9i93. In lieu of flowers, please consider donations to Sunflower Hill in Pleasanton, CA (a special needs housing and programs community) or the Special Olympics of Northern California, where Dave and his son Reid recently won a gold medal in a local golf competition. Over his career, Dave played in 630 major league games with the Minnesota Twins (1993– 1995), Cincinnati Reds (1995), Dave McCarty with World Series trophy at Fenway Park on April 9, 2024, at a celebration of the 20th anniversary of the Red Sox World Championship Family Day at Fenway Park during the 2004 Championship season The McCarty family (Reid, Monica, Maxine and Dave) at Royal Ascot in England, June 2023 San Francisco Giants (1995– 1997), Seattle Mariners (1998), Detroit Tigers (1999), Kansas City Royals (2000–2002), Tampa Bay Devil Rays (2002), Oakland Athletics (2003), and Boston Red Sox (2003–2005), posting a career average of .242 with 36 home runs, and 175 RBIs. With a Stanford degree to fall back on, Dave was tempted to hang up his spikes many times over the years. But he stuck with it and was rewarded when he was signed by Billy Beane of the Oakland A’s in 2000 during the “Moneyball” era. It rejuvenated his career. After an exceptional Spring Training with the A’s, Dave was traded to the Royals where he had his most productive season with career highs in batting average (.278), home runs (12), RBI (68), and games played (103). But the highlight of Dave’s baseball career was being part of the 2004 Red Sox, who were dubbed “The Idiots” due to their infamously loose clubhouse and inventive facial hair. Down three games to none in the ALCS, the Sox mounted a historic comeback against the Yankees. They would go on to defeat the Cardinals in four games in the World Series, winning eight in a row and breaking the Red Sox’s 86-year championship drought. Dave retired from baseball in 2005 but continued to work for the Red Sox as an analyst on NESN until the 2008 season. Dave adjusted to life after baseball with surprising ease. He joined Lee & Associates as one of the founding members of the commercial real estate firm’s Oakland office in 2006. There he found the camaraderie that he’d missed from the clubhouse and a job that he loved. While baseball was a large part of his life, the most important thing to Dave was family. With the demanding life on the road behind him, he was able to turn his four months of being a devoted, hands-on dad into twelve. Dave and Monica moved to Piedmont, CA in 2000 to raise their two children, Reid (PHS ’15) and Maxine (PHS ’17). The same big personality, sharp wit, and easy smile that made Dave a popular figure in the clubhouse continued after he retired; he was a well-known figure around town, walking the kids to school and taking them to various activities or sport practices. The family shared a love of sports – and competition – from the ski slopes, to the swimming pool, to the golf course, to the hiking trail. Staying active was a big part of Dave’s life. The former journeymen never stopped traveling. The family explored the globe together, traveling to Russia, China, Japan, Iceland, the Baltics, Europe, Greece, Mexico, Canada, and spending many weeks a year in London. Closer to home favorite spots were Tahoe, Hawaii, and frequent trips to the Disney parks. Dave’s passing comes just weeks after he and other members of the 2004 team were honored at Fenway Park as part of the 20-year anniversary of their championship season, a fitting sendoff to a man who was a champion in both sport and life. Dave was preceded in death by his father, Dennis. He is survived by his wife, Monica, his children, Reid and Maxine, his mother, Joan, his sister, Kelly, and a large much-loved extended family. A celebration of Dave’s wonderful life will be held on Thursday May 9, 2024. More information can be found at https:// rb.gy/xr9i93. In lieu of flowers, please consider donations to Sunflower Hill in Pleasanton, CA (a special needs housing and programs community) or the Special Olympics of Northern California, where Dave and his son Reid recently won a gold medal in a local golf competition. News clipping from Piedmont Post on November 3, 2004

articles.text: Piedmont School Board is expected to announce at its meeting tonight, April 24, at 7:00 p.m., the appointment of David Yoshihara as Piedmont High School’s new principal. The board will also announce that Jean Fagin will become the new Director of Special Education. Yoshihara, currently the Assistant Principal of Frick United Academy of Language in Oakland, will succeed PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami. During tonight’s meeting, the school board will also provide a report on a successful collective bargaining agreement between the district and CSEA Classified Employees. The district will grant them raises of 2.5% for this year, 3.82% for ‘24-’25 and 2.87% for ‘25-’26; a total of 9.19% over three years. The cumulative salary of CSEA Classified employees, prior to the agreement was $5,558,869 and will increase by $140,000 this year. Full-time CSEA employees will also receive one-time payments of $800. Details of increases to district contributions to benefits for these employees can be viewed in the background document Simbli. eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/ Attachment.aspx?S=36030373& AID=770120&MID=29502 The meeting will include a presentation by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich on the next Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP) for 2024-27. Piedmont is currently in the final year of their current LCAP plan which outlines the goals, actions, and expenditures of the school. Tonight’s meeting may be attended at City Hall at 7:00 p.m. or it available remotely via Zoom. us/j/86876332241. articles.text: The following letter was emailed to Piedmont Unified School District families and community members on April 19, after a meeting between PUSD and the teachers union on April 17. The statement was signed by Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) Elise Marks and school board president Veronica Anderson Thigpen. “On Wednesday, the Superintendent, two Board members and several APT union leaders met for a clarifying discussion. This meeting was productive and both sides learned more about the other’s perspective in ways that we believe will facilitate moving forward to a settlement. Board members and the Superintendent learned that for teachers, the impact of the April 16 community statement was very different from what was intended. articles.text: The Piedmont Scouting community gathered at Piedmont Community Church’s Guild Hall on Thursday, April 18 for Piedmont Scout Council’s 103rd annual Awards Dinner and Recognition ceremony. The event has been held every year since the council was officially chartered with the national organization in 1921 and recognizes outstanding service by local scouts and volunteers. In addition to the many awards and recognitions received that night, Lisa Gros, a longtime leader of Troop 6 at Corpus Christi Catholic Church and a former President of the Piedmont Council Executive Board, was presented with the highest award for adult volunteers, the Silver Beaver Award. The event began with drinks and light appetizers served in the church’s courtyard. A Wood Badge court of honor was held in the courtyard at 6:30 p.m. before the proceedings were moved We are thrilled to recognize them this evening.” Key volunteers were then recognized: • Erin Ashton – Program Director for the one-week summer day camp in Dracena Park • David Cole and Greg Wolff – Pinewood Derby • Anne Hauss-Davies – Chair of the annual food drive, Scouting for Food. Paul Jahn presented the President’s Award to former Eagle Scout Tom Smegal III for his continued contributions to Piedmont scouting as Chair of the annual Christmas Tree Lot. “Let’s be honest. Two words describe Tom’s involvement: they are ‘tree’ and ‘lot,’” joked Jahn. As Smegal turned to leave, Jahn renewed his speech. “Tom, however, made one rookie mistake. He told me his favorite tree.” At this moment, a Scout emerged from a nearby closet holding a California Buckeye which was given to a smiling Smegal. Next, Arun Brahma and Sara Staff Photos Lisa Gros, the newest recipient of Piedmont Scout Council’s Silver Beaver Award inside Guild Hall for dinner. A blessing over the food was said by Father Leo Edgerly of Corpus Christi Catholic Church, and the ceremony started around 7:30 p.m. with opening remarks by Executive Board President Paul Jahn. “This past year has been memorable to say the least,” began Jahn. “Many of our volunteers have continued to step up, lead, and serve our community through the Scouting program.

articles.text: The City Council and the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee will discuss the City’s budget for the fiscal year 2024-2025 at a series of public meetings from April to June. These public meetings will result in the adoption of a new city budget by the City Council on Monday, June 17. Members of the public are encouraged to attend and provide feedback. Discussions of next year’s budget began on April 15 at a special workshop before the regularly scheduled City Council meeting. The current schedule of meetings is as follows: • Monday, April 29, 6 p.m.: City Council Budget Workshop • Tuesday, May 14, 6 p.m.: Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee meeting • Monday, June 3, 6 p.m.: Budget Public Hearing – City Council meeting • Monday, June 17, 6 p.m.: Adoption of the FY 2024-2025 City budget – City Council meeting The location of the workshops on Monday, April 29, and May 14 will be in the city’s Emergency Operations Center at the Police Station. 403 Highland Avenue. All other meetings will be held in City Hall. The proposed budget is expected to be published for review and feedback in early May. In previous years, public budget discussions began in May, following the release of the proposed budget. The earlier start this year indicates the City’s move towards longer-term planning, a shift that has been underway for several years at the recommendation of the City’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. Leading up to this workshop, the City Council held study sessions devoted to the budget as well as governance and goal-setting in March and early April. For questions about the City budget, contact Finance Director Michael Szczech at mszczech@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: The first Revised Common Lectionary reading for the first Sunday of November is Joshua 3:7-17. We need to be careful in reading Joshua, for it is a violent book. It describes violence. It countenances violence. It depicts God commanding violence. Further, Joshua describes one group of people taking the land of another. Even though God is given credit for this conquest we need to be careful. We need to interpret wisely. In human history, including the history that is unfolding even now, such narratives have given rise to tragedies of epic proportion. I would assert that rather than reading Joshua as literal history, we read it as metaphor, as an examination of the challenges we face as we move into the unknown, as we face challenges to our dreams, as we face threats to the common good. As the book of Joshua begins, the great leader Moses has died. Joshua is named as his successor with these stirring words from on High, “Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.” Joshua’s chief work will be to lead the people into the promised land, their intended destination when they left Egypt 40 years earlier. The first challenge they face as they come west out of the eastern wilderness will be to cross the Jordan River. It is the spring of the year and the river is at flood stage. There are no boats, there are no bridges. As so often is true in life, high hopes and great expectations are met with significant difficulty. God instructs Joshua to prepare the leaders and organize the people. The priests, carrying the Ark of the Covenant will lead the people across the raging river. Plans and preparations are made. Prayers are offered. Rites of purification are completed. The time to move forward arrives. The priests step foot into the river and then, and only then, the river waters stop their flow. The people cross the riverbed on dry ground. There are likely many lessons in this account. The one I would like to make is that while faith involves planning, preparing, purifying and praying, sooner or later it involves taking action. It involves moving from thinking about the water, analyzing the water, singing about the water, preaching about the water, to actually wading in the water. It is when our actions mirror and match God’s intent that the challenges before us can be met. Don’t get me wrong. There is a time for planning and a time for praying. Yet, there is also a time, even when we do not know what will happen next, for us to step into the surging river. God of all, give us the wisdom to know when that time has come. Amen. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue & Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. articles.text: You’re right: to be happy. To be healthy is #2. “Happy” here doesn’t mean ephemeral pleasures, such as a tasty meal, a good cup of coffee, a ‘frivolous’ book, a movie, getting a nice car, gambling, or watching sports. Last pop quiz: If you could only ask one question to figure out if someone will be happy today, what would it be? Okay, a few possibilities popped into your mind this time right? Let’s come back to that and offer the answer. In a Gallup World survey of 1,551,362 adults collected from 164 nations, the largest, most representative sample of the world’s population, the best predictor of the amount of positive emotions felt today was: “Did you learn something new yesterday?” Interesting, right? But, so what? Learning something is meaningful, and meaning is what creates a life of joy, which is truly what parents wish for their children, above all. In exploring how individuals find meaning in life – essentially, how they discover sustained fulfillment and joy – it is apparent that there are four cornerstones central to this pursuit: 1. Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained t h r o u g h self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing ou r i n ner s elve s t o the world. This can be through art, communication, or any for m that allows one to convey their p e r s o n a l essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult m ay fo c u s more intensely on discovery and express i o n . T h e cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which c or ne r s t o ne predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful – similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections – the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for more than 20 years and is excited to share AMeaningOfLife.org with the world.

Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained t h r o u g h self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing ou r i n ner s elve s t o the world. This can be through art, communication, or any for m that allows one to convey their p e r s o n a l essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult m ay fo c u s more intensely on discovery and express i o n . T h e cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which c or ne r s t o ne predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful – similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections – the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. By choosing to engage with these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for more than 20 years and is excited to share AMeaningOfLife.org with the world. articles.text: Highlander Robotics, FIRST Robotics Competition Team 8033, just returned from their finals appearance at the World Championship, and will be co-hosting an Open House at the Piedmont High Student Center on Thursday, May 2 at 7 p.m. Families with rising 7th to 12th graders are invited to attend. Presenters will share their experiences with the FIRST Robotics Competition and FIRST Tech Challenge, demonstrate their robots, give a tour of the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab, and recommend pathways for students looking to progress from FIRST Lego League to FTC or FRC. Highlander Robotics welcomes all students regardless of experience. “Our program expects to train students from scratch. The Highlanders provide training in programming, CAD (computer aided design), and general building. Outside of technical work, the Highlanders also seek members interested in community outreach, visual and industrial design, marketing, branding, and video production. To learn more, please join the team May 2nd at the PHS Student Center or visit frc8033.com.

articles.text: Students get to choose from studios ranging from Animation to Jewelry Making & Metal Arts, Illustration & Drawing to Film & Photography, Comics & Visual Storytelling to Architecture & Interior Design. With summer approaching, parents are starting to plan how to keep their middle school students engaged, focused, and with a certain level of structure when For parents of creative students or students who want to learn art, there is one easy choice: the Young Artist Studio Program (YASP) at California College of the Arts in San Francisco. YASP is a summer art program, where over the course of one week, sixth, seventh, and eighth grade students of all skill levels gain hands-on experience in art-making within a chosen medium from a wide selection of offerings, from animation or graphic design to illustration or fashion design, jewelry making and painting, “Trying to decide what to have your kids do each summer is tricky as it has to fit both the kids’ interest and the parents’ schedule, which sometimes is impossible to align,” said Ryan Parham, associate director of Studio Operations at CCA. “Our approach has been to find those summer camps and activities kids don’t have access to within their typical school year – surf camp, circus camp, and skateboard camp. These YASP weeks fit right in.” Reasons why the program is a favorite among Bay Area students. #1 A wide variety of individual studios to match student interests. Students have many options to explore art making. And with such studio offerings as Animation, Ceramics & Drawing, Illustration & Drawing, Jewelry Making & Metal Arts, and Fashion Design & Illustration, it can be difficult to choose just one. (This summer, YASP offerings have expanded to two sessions: one in June and one in August.) #2 Opportunities to learn something brand new or deepen artistic skills. Although YASP students select just one topic to focus on for the duration of the program, tailored instruction with practicing professionals allows students to try something completely new or build on what they already know. The studios are also praised for their depth and instruction of both the fundamentals and development of artistic techniques. #3 New friendships and a taste of professionalism. The Young Artist Studio Program’s week of activities culminates in a special exhibition of student work on campus. It gives students a preview at professional practices as well as a fun celebration of their achievements. When they reflect on the experience, YASP parents say a favorite for their students is the friends they make and the community they build. “They have a wonderful opportunity to meet and interact with other intro/extrovert kids outside of their typical friend group which has really reduced their fear in meeting new people,” says Ryan Parham, associate director of Studio Operations at CCA.. “They come back each day energized from what they have learned, who they have met, and what they plan to do the next day.” We’ve got summer covered for middle schoolers. YASP registration is now open for June 10–14 and August 5–9 programs. articles.text: Things are gearing up for local scouting as the Piedmont Council prepares for its annual Bike Rodeo on Saturday, May 11, at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. Cub Scouts, as well as all other youth, are welcome to attend the event where they will learn the rules of the road and put their skills to the test on an obstacle course that simulates being on the road. As with previous years, the Bike Rodeo will continue its partnership with the Piedmont Police Department and Police Explorer Post 911 as well as with new partner Alameda County Safe Routes to Schools. Organizers have provided several improvements this year, including a newly enhanced obstacle course, a trivia wheel, and a “bike blender” where kids can make smoothies by pedaling a bicycle wheel. Interested youth may join the Bike Fest at the start of each hour at 9 a.m., 10 a.m., or 11 a.m. Participants will go through a 15-minute introduction before riding on the course. Activities include a “who can go the slowest” race and a test to see if riders can brake on a dime. A representative from Westside Joe’s Bicycle Shop of Alameda will be on hand to help with safety checks. Get more information at www. piedmontbsa.org/events/hh-bikefest. Youth interested in joining Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing Units, or Exploring are encouraged to contact the Piedmont Scout Council for more information by phone at 547-4493 or via email at contact@piedmontbsa.org. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont still holds first place in the WACC as it enters a final stretch of the regular season. After splitting games with Western Alameda County Conference foe Castro Valley last week, Piedmont remained in first place in the league. They defeated the Trojans on the road 6-2 on Wednesday, April 17, but lost 6-4 at home after going two extra innings on Friday, April 19. They also lost 8-1 to non-league opponent Oakland Tech the following day. Piedmont is still in first place of the WACC with a 5-1 record, but Alameda and Berkeley are creeping back into the picture at 3-2. Bishop O’Dowd, meanwhile, is 3-2-1 (W-L-T) and Castro Valley is 2-3-1. “I love coaching these games where things can go either way… With everyone in the league, you have to bring your best game to get a W. The message is to just play the best baseball we can play. We don’t want to look ahead to rankings or seeding and just want to play the best game we can,” said coach Eric Olson. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team finished up its regular season by winning two of their last three games in as many days. They recently defeated league foe Newark Memorial 17-1 on Thursday, April 18 at Witter Field, beat Granada 9-4 at home the previous day, and lost a 14-13 heartbreaker to Miramonte at Witter Field on April 16. PHS celebrated its six seniors on Senior Night prior to their game against Newark: Hailey Marshburn, Ruby Guzdar, Orla Cohen, Jane Hempeck, Laurel Bentley, and Henley Lorin. “Just walking up and looking at all the seniors, I got all teary eyed. It’s a moment where everyone comes together to celebrate you and it’s really special,” Marshburn reflected. “After watching other seniors graduate in the years before us and seeing how emotional it was for them, tonight hit close to my heart,” Lorin added. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team concluded its regular season with a dominant 9-3 win over Terra Linda at Witter Field on Monday, April 23. Significantly, they beat North Coast Section foe Acalanes 9-7 on the road in Lafayette on Wednesday, April 17. “Like all of these teams, I think the beginning of the season versus end of the season form matters. Teams get better throughout the year. That’s a good team we just played, They had some guys that could shoot and a couple good defenders, so I’m proud of our guys for staying mentally strong. That was the challenge we threw out after we lost to Berkeley,” coach Jeff Lamb said after the win over Terra Linda. The Highlanders enter the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with a game tonight, April 24. A win over No. 2 Berkeley puts Piedmont into the final on April 26. PHS is eager to avenge its 10-4 loss to No. 1 Bishop O’Dowd on March 22 and 11-4 loss to Berkeley on March 28. Terra Linda, notably, beat Berkeley 5-2 on March 5. “We’re on a good run now and could end up playing both Berkeley and O’Dowd in playoffs. It’s just sticking together as a team and staying focused. I think the biggest thing we want to do is hold the ball on offense and make sure to stay calm,” said senior leader Oliver Shafroth. In the earlier losses to Berkeley and O’Dowd, Piedmont had a difficult time maintaining possession in the attacking area and finding shooting lanes. “We want to focus on mental and physical toughness, and just keep the intensity up. We switched up some offensive tactics. In the O’Dowd game, they played a zone and it countered us well,” freshman Connor Fredericks said. 9-3 over Terra Linda Piedmont ended the first quarter with a close 1-0 lead and tacked on two goals prior to halftime, 3-1. PHS then scored four unanswered goals in the third quarter to jump ahead 7-1, adding two more goals in the fourth. After a string of shot attempts, Shafroth broke through for his first goal with 4:18 left in the first quarter. In the second, Terra Linda tied 48 seconds into the quarter to tie it at 1-1, but that is the closest things got. One minute later, Rylan Nelson scored on an underhand laser shot into the net to retake the lead. After back and forth possessions, Fredericks scored with 52.6 seconds left, 3-1. Piedmont started the third quarter with a man advantage after Terra Linda committed a slashing penalty prior to halftime. It led to Shafroth scoring after receiving a pass from Nelson just 13 seconds into the third. Shafroth then scored again with 7:45 on the clock, 5-1. articles.text: Members of Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in a pair of events on Saturday, April 20. Seven athletes traveled to the Sacramento Meet of Champions at American River College, and the rest of the varsity team went Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa for the Viking Invitational. The Meet of Champions has runners from across the state and is a good precursor to the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on May 18. “I was really impressed by how calm and collected all of our athletes were,” said coach Pouyan Assadi..”They worked through their pre-race process and were in control while also learning about how to get better.” Meet of Champion results Breah Bell competed in two events in Sacramento. She finished fourth in the long jump with a distance of 16 feet, 7.25 inches, and was 15th in the 100 meter dash with a time of 12.72. “Breah’s inching her way down towards the school record and I’ll admit my heart pounds with excitement every time she gets into the blocks,” Assadi said. She’s been ultra consistent and now has a couple last things to work on for her final leap [in long jump]. She’ll have at least a couple more cracks at it so we’ll see what happens,” Assadi said. Jamie Schwarz finishing 16th of 32 half milers in the 800, clocking a time of 2:24.03. Ella Yasar competed in the 300 meter hurdles with a time of 48.30 seconds. Sebastien Swain continued a strong freshman year, placing ninth of 33 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:58.07. “Seb continues his prolific freshman season. Athletic.net has him ranked as one of the top freshmen in the state,” confirmed Assadi. Photos by Becky Spies Breah Bell was fourth in the long jump at the Sacramento Meet of Champions. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club successfully hosted the second year of its charity golf-tournament on April 19, celebrating another year of fund raising for Wildwood School. A total of 20 dads took Friday off from work to play a round of golf at Oakmoore Golf Course in Stockton, a par-3 course designed for small tournaments. The day started with an 8:00 a.m. pickup at the Community Center. With breakfast burritos in hand the dads enjoyed one another’s company on the one-hour trip to the first tee. “It was a great opportunity to build community with other Piedmont dads while raising muchneeded funds for our schools,” said Havens dad Vipul Kumar. “Reed Johnson and the rest of the Wildwood Dads’ Club did a great job planning. Everyone had a blast.” “It has become the culmination of a year of Dad’s Club events that strengthen the bonds of the community and friendship we all love here in Piedmont,” said Johnson. “The day was filled with sunshine and good times by Wildwood dads and a Havens dad. Hopefully, we can continue to build the Wildwood dad community and also inter-school dads’ club relationships,” said Rohit Giri. Trophies were awarded for longest drive, longest putt, and best golf outfit. Following the golf. they had a barbeque with ribs and hot dogs. Johnson said the golf event will be an annual outing and will be held at a new golf course next year. Wildwood Dads hosted a golf tournament on Friday, April 19.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School swim team dominated a meet against rival Bishop O’Dowd in the final dual meet of the season on Friday, April 19. The boys’ team won decisively, 186-61, and the girls’ team won comfortably, 148-108. Coach Colby Price expressed pride in the team’s performance, especially after facing challenges in previous years: “We absolutely crushed our rival after a couple of years hindered by injury,” said Price. “It was exciting to have the team at full strength and to be able to perform when we needed to.” Coach Price pointed to several standout performances, including Cole Carnazzo’s thrilling 500 against two of Bishop O’Dowd’s best swimmers. Additionally, the 200 free swimmers, Samantha White, Taylor Rolefson, and Dima Secor, dominated their event. The meet also marked senior night, a special occasion to celebrate the team’s seniors and their contributions: Samantha Smith, Yessica Cruz, Josie Oesterer, Anne Reardon, Lauren Ashton, Evan Dickason, Micah Temple, Tom Rolefson, and Taylor Rolefson. Price expressed gratitude to the parents who organized the celebration, ensuring that the seniors were honored in a meaningful way: “We were happy to celebrate all the seniors and their accomplishments. We got to announce Taylor Rolefson during her 200 free event against O’Dowd. their post-PHS plans, and they went home with a small gift to remind them of their days at PHS.” Three of the seniors have committed to continue their swimming careers in college. Taylor Rolefson will be attending Bates College, Tom Rolefson will be attending Hamilton College, and Nina Schwab will be diving at Carleton College in Minnesota. Looking ahead, both the boys’ and girls’ teams are poised for success in the upcoming WACC league championships. With the team currently seeded first in overall power points and nine of the top 20 swimmers signed up for the event, the team is gearing up for another impressive showing as they strive for league championship titles. articles.text: Although the 3rd Annual Food Fest in Piedmont Park was brimming with a smorgasbord of exciting eats, food wasn’t the only attraction at the event. The Food Fest also served as a celebration of the Bay Area’s diverse culture. “Three years ago, we set out to do something that celebrated the diversity of the Bay,” said founder Roger Tsai to the audience. “Today, we get to do just that.” The day’s entertainment started on a stage in Piedmont Park with a performance by the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, a youth group from Oakland specializing in traditional Chinese music and opera played on authentic Chinese instruments. The Oh Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance School from Brisbane gave an exciting display of traditional Tahitian dances by their youth classes, beginner classes, and professional soloists. Oakland Taiko brought an energetic fervor to the stage as the third act of the day. The East Bay community dojo pounded drums with such passion that it brought out residents from houses surrounding the park. “I live nearby and I was pretty tired from my day, but I heard the drums and I had to come out. They just called to me”, joked Celeste Boyd, who lives near the park. In a brief reprieve from the high-energy acts of the morning, professional chef James Yeun Leong Parry took the stage for a Q&A session about what it is like to work in the culinary world. Parry is the creator of Happy Crane, a critically acclaimed Cantonese pop-up restaurant in San Francisco. The Devendra Sharma Folk Ensemble performed a series of Nautanki, a form of North Indian musical theater passed down through oral tradition. After receiving funding for a full-scale production in 2021, the company will be performing their production of Princess Nautanki next month in San Francisco along with musicians from India as well as local singers and dancers from the Bay Area. Nonprofit organization No Immigrants No Spice, founded by Staff Photos Oakland Taiko performs at the Piedmont Food Fest. The East Bay community dojo has been teaching classes and performing since 1998. Since 1946 Lic# 792463 Sabrina Cezar, a lead dancer from the Oh Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance School, performs a solo dance on the stage. Singer and musician August Lee Stevens performed as part of the “HiiWav Presents” portion of the afternoon backed by a rock band. The Great Wall Youth Orchestra opened the day’s festivities with a performance of traditional Chinese music.

In a different section of the event, adults mingled in the beer and wine zone, where eventgoers over 21 could purchase a wristband for unlimited tastings from 10 of the Bay Area’s most robust independent wineries and breweries. “I never thought I could win awards for this. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will present a concert titled Pictures at an Exhibition on Sunday, June 2 at 4 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. The final Symphonic Series concert of the 2023-24 season, led by Music Director Joseph Young, seeks to bring color and light together in a program of mesmerizing symphonic works by Jimmy López Bellido, Duke Ellington, and Modest Mussorgsky. “Throughout our 52nd season, we’ve explored musical colors and styles, welcomed a diversity of artists, and created orchestral experiences that are powerful, joyful, and inclusive,” said Young. “I dedicate this final program to all who went on this musical journey with us, especially the musicians of the Berkeley Symphony and the audiences who turned out to support us all season long.” Leticia Moreno, a Spanish-born violinist, will perform in the West Coast premiere of Jimmy López Bellido’s violin concerto, Aurora, following its successful world premiere performance and GRAMMY-nominated recording with the Houston Symphony. López Bellido’s previous work, Rise, was commissioned by Berkeley Symphony and premiered in 2022. López Bellido said he was inspired to write Aurora after seeing the Northern Lights, which he described as “one of Nature’s most spectacular displays.” The program also includes Duke Ellington’s wistful “Solitude,” a 1934 jazz standard Spanish-born violinist Leticia Moreno will perform with Berkeley Symphony. recorded numerous times by Ellington, that will return to Zellerbach Hall via Morton Gould’s string orchestra arrangement. Ellington famously wrote this brief yet poignant work in only 20 minutes, but the piece has left a lasting legacy in the music world. The program’s final piece, Mussorgsky’s Pictures at an Exhibition, began as a romantic suite for solo piano but was expanded by Maurice Ravel’s magnificent orchestration to depict scenes by Mussorgsky’s contemporary, Russian architect and painter Viktor Hartmann. Audiences are invited to a 3 p.m. pre-concert chat, moderated by Berkeleyside journalist Andrew Gilbert. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet has announced its 2024-25 season, which includes modern works by today’s celebrated choreographers and an expansion of the company’s own classical lexicon. Curated and led by Artistic Director Tamara Rojo, this season will feature works by Dutch choreographer Hans van Manen, and contemporary choreographers Christopher Wheeldon, Akram Khan, Wayne McGregor, and Annabelle Lopez Ochoa. The season will begin in December with the holiday favorite Nutcracker, set in San Francisco and honoring the company’s legacy as the first to present a full-length production of the show. “Across an extraordinary 2024 season, I have been deeply inspired by the incredibly talented artists of our world-renowned company and our audiences in San Francisco. In 2025, SF Ballet will explore a range of choreographic and artistic styles and deliver profound human connections through dance—from seduction to heartbreak, and from stories of conflict to gothic science-fiction,” Rojo said. The season includes the return of Liam Scarlett’s Frankenstein and Manon, Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s most widely celebrated works performed for the first time by the San Francisco Ballet, as well as Rojo’s own Raymonda. “I am thrilled to expand the classical repertoire for SF Ballet with works that showcase the brilliance of our dancers, while continuing to engage fresh perspectives and uplift the artistry of leading creatives from around the world,” said Rojo. To learn more about the 2024- 25 season, visit https://www. sfballet.org/24-25-season/. articles.text: South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata In celebration of South African Freedom Day, SF Jazz welcomes South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata to the Miner Auditorium stage for two performances this Sunday, April 28. Mrubata hails from Cape Town’s historic Langa township and grew up with the sounds of African music, including the soulful hymns of the Zion Church, the chants and rhythms of traditional healers and the music of the Merry Macs band. In the aftermath of the 1976 uprising, McCoy studied informally under Langa greats including Madoda Gxabeka, Winston Ngozi, the Ngcukanas, Ezra and Duke, Blackie Tempi and Robert Sithole. By the early 1980s, he was playing in cover bands Fever, Touch, Airborne, and Vukani. He gained inter national fame in 1992 when he toured the world with Hugh Masekela’s Lerapo band and has collaborated with Brazilian artists Airto and Flora Purim. Mrubata’s albums have won numerous awards, including the South African Music Award for best traditional jazz release. Concerts at SF Jazz this Sunday will be at 6 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/23-24/mccoymrubata/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: McCoy Mrubata performs at SF Jazz this Sunday

articles.text: Award-winning classical guitarist Leonardo Garcia, an Oakland resident, returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, May 5th at 5:00 p.m. for a solo concert highlighting the music of Spain. The program will feature the music of composers Domenico Scarlatti, Enrique Granados, Isaac Albéniz, Francisco Tárrega, and others. As a performer, Garcia has performed across North America, South America, and Europe as both a soloist and as a chamber musician. As an educator, he has worked with hundreds of children and families for over 20 years through KinderGuitar. He has authored over 10 curriculum books for KinderGuitar, multiple editions and arrangements of music by Bach, Albéniz, Barrios, and Narváez, and numerous books on guitar technique. His writings have appeared in Guitar Review, Tonebase, the KinderAward-winning classical guitarist Leonardo Garcia Guitar blog (kinderguitar.com), and Six String Journal (sixstringjournal.com). He has acted as a jury member, performer, and lecturer at musical festivals such as the Bay Area’s Junior Bach Festival, the Boston Guitar Festival, the Yale Guitar Extravaganza, the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, and the Guitar Foundation of America’s International Festival. Tickets are $40 for adults, $10 for students, and are available at the door and at brownpapertickets.com. 6287265.
articles.title: Guitarist Leo Garcia at Center for the Arts May 5

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes former artist-in-residence Angelique Kidjo back to Zellerbach Hall for an evening concert on Friday, April 26. Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and has earned recognition over the years for projects like Yemandja, the artist’s first major foray into stage acting, and a reboot of the Talking Heads’ classic 1980 album Remain in Light, both part of the Cal Performances 2021–22 season. The Benin-born singer was also named one of Time magazine’s “100 Most Influential People of 2021” for her work as a performer, teacher, and cultural ambassador. Her latest recordings incorporate West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. “Having been a presenter, collaborator and fan of her work for years, I know firsthand of her passion, conviction, and boundless curiosity,” said Jeremy Geffen, Cal Performances’ artistic director. “Angélique draws from her personal experiences a deep sense of conviction as well as profound passion for exploring the breadth and depth of the human experience.” To purchase tickets, visit https://calperformances.org/ events/2023-24/vocal-celebration/angelique-kidjo-2324/. The concert begins at 8 p.m. Angelique Kidjo

articles.text: The debate rages. What were the greatest musical performances of all time? Those were the recordings on the famous program radio program, The Hit Parade. Fortunately, the public had a chance to voice its opinion. But what about the bottom of the list? How about the worst recordings ever made? You guessed it… the debate rages. And along with this debate, there is a lot of misinformation. Many composers have had a chance to tickle the musical funnybone. Mozart knew how to do it, perhaps better than any other composer. He had a lusty sense of humor bordering on the vulgar. Listen to his composition “The Musical Joke” where his bawdy sense of humor is shown to best advantage. Hardly any other composer knew how to parody wayward amateur musicians at their worst. The musicians get lost and wander around trying to find the exit. Somewhere along the way they have musical indigestion, resulting in flatulence. No one can listen to this music without bursting out in laughter. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, April 24, 2024 The Musical Gourmet Welcome to the Piedmont Center for the Arts Myths and misconceptions By Joseph Gold The debate rages. What were the greatest musical performances of all time? Those were the recordings on the famous program radio program, The Hit Parade. Fortunately, the public had a chance to voice its opinion. But what about the bottom of the list? How about the worst recordings ever made? You guessed it… the debate rages. And along with this debate, there is a lot of misinformation. Many composers have had a chance to tickle the musical funnybone. Mozart knew how to do it, perhaps better than any other composer. He had a lusty sense of humor bordering on the vulgar. Listen to his composition “The Musical Joke” where his bawdy sense of humor is shown to best advantage. Hardly any other composer knew how to parody wayward amateur musicians at their worst. The musicians get lost and wander around trying to find the exit. Somewhere along the way they have musical indigestion, resulting in flatulence. No one can listen to this music without bursting out in laughter. The same can be said for the infamous singer Florence Foster Jenkins. Did she know how terrible she was or was this a ruse to gain publicity? Either way, her fame persists. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Other famous singers have made silly recordings. Some of them were great opera singers. Some of them were pop singers, imitating other pop singers. Of these, my favorite is Johnny Cash imitating Elvis Presley. Many people consider Jascha Heifetz to be the greatest violinist of all time. He also had a perfectly timed sense of humor. And herein the debate also rages. He frequently used the initials JH to create a pseudonym. For example he wrote some pop songs using the pseudonym Jim Hoyle. There is also a violinist by the name of Joseph Hague. Once again, the initials JH. Joseph Hague was a terrible violinist. In fact, his inability to play was “perfectly” awful. Some people have made a case that Joseph Hague was a real person. The truth is that Hague was “perfectly” horrible and the violinist was actually Jascha Heifetz making a comedy recording. I know this for a fact. Part of the proof is on YouTube in a video entitled “Jascha Heifetz… The audition.” Heifetz pulled this routine on very rare occasions, and was always a surprise to his students. I remember witnessing one of these events. The playing was awful. In fact, it was perfectly awful. There are other recordings in the same vein played by Jascha Heifetz. The names of the violinists are Victor Belmont and Victor Belmor. All of these violinists are played by the same performer. The names of the piano accompanists are also ridiculous. Floyd E. Sharp for example. Look at the photo on the cover of the record. It is a photo of Jascha Heifetz with an innocuous head glued atop. The violin is Heifetz Guarnerius. He never let anyone touch it. In fact, he never let anyone even look at it for any length of time. I bought one of these records in a Salvation Army store in the 1960s for $.25. It’s worth a lot more now. Heifetz is enjoying a good laugh. pages.text: Wednesday, April 24, 2024 27 Features By Josh Harkinson I dug and planted my first vegetable garden when I was 10. I can’t remember why. My mother says I wanted to sell vegetables on the driveway. The tomatoes – giant beefsteaks that were more than we could eat – ripened around the same time that the neighbor had a garage sale. I put up a table nearby to capitalize on the footfall and sold out much faster than our neighbor did. Years later after starting my own family, I always planted a vegetable garden. My two toddlers quickly learned to appreciate where food came from. They would spend hours each week foraging. A bean teepee built from bamboo poles doubled as a fort. The kids learned to be mindful of fragile stems. Waiting to pick things until they were perfectly ripe taught them patience. Now that I have a preteen and teenager, the vegetable garden continues to play a central role in our lives. The kids help me amend the soil and plant the seedlings. When they get home from school on their razor scooters, they usually pause in the yard to nibble a few raspberries or pick an orange and eat it on the bench overlooking the creek. My daughter has become our resident salad expert, adding spicy and peppery greens from the yard to our store-bought lettuces. Planting vegetables in your yard does not necessarily require turning it into Green Acres. There are advantages to farmlike raised beds with uniform rows of plantings (more on that in a minute), but personally I like to integrate my edibles with my flowering decorative plants. For example, my tomatoes grow in a front-yard bed along the sidewalk, but the street-facing side of it has ceanothus, salvia, and butterfly bush that provide color, attract pollinators, and prevent passersby from swiping the juicy red fruits come August. In the cold season, I replace the tomatoes with winter greens. April and May are the perfect months to plant your summer vegetables. Make sure you give yourself time to prepare. Many root vegetables and certainly tomatoes require very rich, welldrained, loosely tilled soil. To create my tomato patch, I dug down about 18 inches and took out all large rocks. I removed about a third of the soil and added enough manure (for nitrogen), peat moss (for water retention and acidity), and sand (for drainage) to more than replace it. It was hard, sweaty work. Too bad my kids weren’t teenagers back then or else I could have used them as free labor. The ideal soil amendment will depend upon your initial conditions. The more clay you have, the more you will need to amend it. In general, you want the soil to look dark brown and crumbly and to smell like a ripe cow pasture. If you are using raised beds, you won’t need to dig as deep, but you’ll need to add a lot more soil. Don’t forget to run irrigation. Vegetables require more water than most ornamentals. I don’t like soaker hoses because they constantly spring leaks. Consider using a system with adjustable spray nozzles. Your first tomato harvest will be amazing. Your third or fourth, not so much. Tomatoes rapidly suck nutrients from the ground. Later, you can use nitrogen-fixing plants to revive your soil. In my garden, I’ve also had great success with summer squash and cucumbers. Just be aware that these plants can take up a lot of space. One solution is to trellis them. You can even use a bamboo teepee as with pole Photos by Josh Harkinson A massive heirloom tomato from our garden. My daughter with her tomato harvest. A front-yard tomato patch. You know he’s a stickler for a clean house, orange juice with no pulp, and the thermostat at 67°. We’ll know that, too. A bounty of cherry tomatoes. beans. Be sure to leave an opening in the teepee to get inside and harvest everything. Kids love this stuff, but watch out: If they’re like mine, they might eat it all before you do. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. articles.text: This is the granddaddy of all Bandol wineries. Situated on the outskirts of Saint Cyr-sur-Mer the estate has been in the hands of the Portalis family since before the French Revolution. The estate was devastated during the French Revolution and suffered the effects of the phylloxera epidemic in the 19th century. The estate is currently under the direction of Cyrille Portalis assisted by his wife Magali and his two sons Etienne and Edouard. We were greeted by Etienne and led into the tasting room next to the old house. He gently reminded his American guests that the table we were standing in front of was older than our country. They started with a wine called Bienfait des Pradeaux made from young vines. It was light and fruity and would make a good picnic wine and at 10 euros was a good bargain. Then on to the main show. The red Bandols of Chateaux Pradeaux were some of the biggest most massive and tannic wines we had on our whole trip. They were highly concentrated and build to withstand decades in the cellar which made them slightly challenging to drink at such a young age. Patience however will be rewarded with these Nicola at La Bastide Blanche. The ancient Mourvèdre vines of La Bastide Blanche.

articles.text: This estate is run by Alain Pascal and named after his father Honore who was indeed Gros (big). He farms sixteen hectares of vineyards on the hillsides of La Cadiere d’Azur. The vineyards are composed of both clay and limestone, imparting a pronounced structure of earthy splintered rock. This microclimate near the Mediterranean brings warm weather and full sun tempered by the Mistral winds. His red wines use 80% Mourvedre for additional strength and boldness. It is medium to full-bodied, concentrated and supple, framed by tannins that grow in intensity on the long finish, culminating in a potent but ripe savoriness. It’s a great effort that should age two decades or more.

articles.text: Alma Lowell Dittmer, a professor and writer who worked at UC Berkeley for 40 years and specialized in Chinese politics, died at age 82 on April 15 in Oakland. He was named after his father Alma, but throughout his life went by his middle name, Lowell. His parents Alma and Veda met when they were teachers at a junior high school in Utah. They would spend much of their life teaching; Alma as a university professor of music; his wife as a K-12 teacher with specialties in Home Economics and Remedial Reading. Lowell was the eldest of their six children, and they instilled in him the sense that he ought to be an example for his younger siblings. He went on his Mormon mission to German-speaking Switzerland, an experience that he would credit as being one of the most challenging of his life. He would later speak of being proud of having completed his mission; however, when he returned to Utah, he found he had lost his faith in God, and would describe himself throughout the rest of his life as an atheist or agnostic. He sought out his next challenge in academia, where, after a brief flirtation with journalism, he dove into the field of political science, earning his bachelor’s degree from Utah State in 1965. He then moved to Chicago, where he would begin his career of more than 50 years as a China scholar. He learned to speak Chinese; went to basic training with the U.S. Army reserves; and met Helen Roth, the woman he would marry. He earned his master’s degree in 1967 and his PhD in 1971. His dissertation was published as his first book in 1974: Liu Shao-Ch’i and the Chinese Cultural Revolution. He and Helen were married on August 14 of that year. In 1978, he came to UC Berkeley, where he would become a leading scholar in his field. He wrote, edited, or co-edited over Lowell Dittmer, a University of California professor of Chinese politics, died on April 15, 2024. He was 82. 16 books, as well as probably over 100 articles in scholarly journals. In addition to writing, he also took on interesting responsibilities near and far. He was the head of the UC Center for Chinese Studies from 1979-1983; and then editor-inchief of the Asian Survey from 2001-2019. He was a research fellow at the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, D.C. from 1986- 1987, and later a director for the UC’s Education Abroad Program in Beijing from 1997-1999. His love of work-related travel would never leave him; in the last decade of his life he spent semesters abroad in Singapore, Malaysia, Korea, and Taiwan. He also enjoyed traveling on family trips. He often visited with his wife’s family in Chicago, and to various spots in the U.S. for semi-annual Dittmer family reunions. In his spare time he enjoyed exercise, healthy eating, bargain hunting, listening to music of all kinds, collecting odds and ends (‘one man’s trash is another man’s treasure’), and consuming art and literature – especially foreign-language movies. He is survived by his sisters Ruth Ellen, Kaye, and Debbie; his brothers Kent and Phil; his son Mark, and his wife Helen. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: Last Wednesday, April 17, marked the 6th anniversary of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. To celebrate, they had a special tour of historic Mountain View Cemetery. It was a lovely spring morning and there was a strong turnout of 50 walkers. The tour was conducted by historian, author, and newspaper man Dennis Evanosky. A longtime docent at Mountain View. He has written two books on the cemetery, as well as books about Alameda and Oakland’s Laurel District. His knowledge of the Mountain View Cemetery is encyclopedic. Before the walk began, Piedmont Post cartoonist Phil Witte surprised Walking on Wednesday founder Dick Carter with a drawing that recognized his six years with the group. Dennis first pointed out his “three girlfriends” in front of the “main mausoleum” that was built in 1928. They are statues of ancient Greek women that represent life, and how well and long it is lived. Dennis noted one is holding cissors. The group was led up a hill to the mausoleum of David Douty Colton. He was an associate of the “Big Four” railroad men who bankrolled the construction of the transcontinental railroad and became very wealthy. Dennis said “Big Five” might be a more accurate name. Colton’s mausoleum is a classical revival building with Corinthian columns and an Egyptian sphinx in front. A statue depiction of a cloth was also noted. It represents a pall that covers a casket. Depending on the deceased’s wealth, it could be buried with the person, or just Sketch of Dick Carter by Phil Witte. rented, leading to the term “pallbearers.” Dennis pointed to the many obelisks around the cemetery. They mark graves from the late 19th Century at the time when the Washington Monument was built – a time when the cemetery was being created, and Egyptian archeological discoveries were being made by the western world. Everything Egyptian was the rage. There is a large pyramid built for William Gwin, California’s first senator, and his family. Up the hill is a tall statue of an elk on a monument, marking the section of the cemetery for Elks Club members. The story of renowned landscape architect Fredrick Law Olmsted, who designed the cemetery in 1863 and also designed New York’s Central Park, as well as much of the UC Berkeley and Stanford University campuses. Olmsted was managing gold mines in Bear Valley, California, when he was asked to design the cemetery. There were 197 acres to work with, and 23 more were bought later – now totaling 220 acres. Dennis said the number of people buried in the cemetery is unknown because in the past some people were buried in unendowed areas and not recorded. He estimated there are about 180,000 graves. The group made their up the cemetery’s south boundary and saw Moraga Avenue homes with backyards facing the cemetery. This was the area of Walter Blair’s late 19th and early 20th Century “Blair Park” attraction. Workers were cutting down huge eucalyptus trees. Dennis said the trees were a fall danger and needed to be removed. Further on was a small lake that provides water for the cemetery. Turkeys, deer, fish, and other wildlife also make use of it. Next stop was a small, worn obelisk with a plaque that reads, “Jane Waer 1822–1865 1st Burial in Mountain View Cemetery.” The last stop was the family plot of George Pardee, mayor of Oakland from 1893 to 1895 and California governor from 1903 to 1907. The walkers thanked Dennis Evanosky for a most enjoyable, information-packed tour of a beautiful place on a beautiful morning with a wonderful storyteller. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Members of Walking on Wednesdays at Mountain View Cemetery on April 17 included Alicia Rivera, Joyce Ahern, Lisa Euphrat, Sharona Fischrup, Oden Deacon, Martin Levy, Jack Fischrup, Mark Laurent, Janet Laurent, Sarah Johnson, Ken Moy, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Pat Keller, Chuck Oraftik, Karin Fetherston, Helen Dong, Pat McMahon, Greg Keller, Claudine Bach, Nadine Guffanti, Joanne Larson, Dana Shultz, Peggy Shultz, Quincy Dong, Priscilla Wanerus, Mark Davis, Kat Lang, Irene Thompson, Sarah Johnson, Bob Wong, Bill Ahern, Phil Witte, Alissa Quan, Kay Kewley, David Haecker, Shirley Nakao, and Dick Carter.

APT wants to affirm that the Board and the Superintendent have been transparent about the state of the district budget and that they recognize the real financial need of teachers and have been exploring productive solutions to raise compensation. Thanks to our conversation on Wednesday, both sides were also able to gain clarity on some key non-monetary issues that are still to be resolved, and we were able to gain a better understanding of why these issues matter to each team. As we await the formation of a Fact-Finding panel, the process allows us to continue talking and working on a deal. At our meeting on Wednesday, we agreed that both sides would very much like to resume bargaining face-to-face as soon as possible in hopes of reaching agreement more quickly than Fact-Finding would allow. And the Board has scheduled a closed session meeting this Saturday to discuss negotiations to ensure these face-to-face meetings with APT can resume as early as [this] week. Building Electrification Champions: Cass Caulfield and Andy Hempeck Caulfield and Hempeck have electrified their 1936 home on Blair Avenue with a 26-panel 10.4 kW solar photovoltaic system, heat pump water heater, and ducted mini split heat pump system. Their new systems are currently saving them hundreds per month in PG&E bills. At its peak, their solar system generates 7.6 kW/hour, which allows them to fully power their home while exporting any extra energy back to the grid. Caulfield and Hempeck’s solar photovoltaic system was installed by NRG Clean Power. Their split pump heating system was installed by Element Home Solutions Inc., and their heat pump water heater was installed by Cerulean Construction. Building Electrification Champions: Russell and Amy Griffith The Griffiths’ home electrification journey began in 2017 with a solar photovoltaic system. Today, the couple has gone fully electric – their home now includes a Level 2 EV charger, HVAC heat pump, heat pump water heater, and induction cooktop. The Griffiths’ induction cooktop was installed by Madrone Builders. Their HVAC heat pump was installed by Altas Heating and Air Conditioning. Their heat pump water heater was installed by Hassler Heating and Air Conditioning. For questions about the Sustainability Awards program or how you can add new heat pumps, solar panels, or greywater systems to your home, please contact Sustainability Program Manager Deniz Ergun via email at dergun@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3058. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew spend many hours each month planning and cooking meals for the food insecure. articles.text: Photos by Piedmont Fire Department A house fire on Tuesday, April 9, at 660 Blair Avenue consumed the interior of the home and threatened to spread to other houses. The Piedmont Fire Department responded to a “high stakes” house fire at 660 Blair Avenue on Tuesday night, April 9 at 11:10 p.m. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan stated that when his crew arrived, the fire was “hazardous” and “devastating” due to the severity of the damage sustained and the fact that the fire had begun to spread to a neighboring home. Because the homeowner was unable to be located at the time, firefighters had to assume that she was still inside and took heightened risks to ensure her safety. Luckily, a thorough search of the house revealed that no one was inside. The owner was later discovered to be on vacation out of the country. Officials are still investigating the cause of Piedmont’s second major house fire in as many months. station at 11:11 a.m., Fire Captain Justin McNulty knew the house fire would be a problem. “As soon as we turned out of the station, we could already see a glow on the hill coming from the house on fire and a column of black smoke above it,” McNulty said. When firefighters arrived, Piedmont police had already closed off the area. The entire bottom story and left side of the house was on fire, and a second-story window was sending fire toward a neighboring house that was smoking and smoldering. Fire Lieutenant Zach Heliker took over as Incident Commander, and two teams were formed – one to fight the initial fire and another to prevent it from spreading to neighboring homes. Firefighter Brian Protheroe led the exterior team in protecting neighboring homes from the spread of the fire. Fire Captain McNulty led the interior team through the front door. “When I forced the front door open, I was immediately knocked to the ground by the heat from inside the house,” he said. At that moment a heavy metal porch light fell to the ground next to him, narrowly missing him. Because the smoke obscured their vision, the interior team used thermal imaging cameras to navigate through the house and find the source of the fire, which was discovered in the kitchen. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 3 is coming to Piedmont Park this Saturday, April 20 and the feeling of excitement and anticipation I hear around town belies the uncertainty surrounding this experiment as it first got started just three years ago. In late 2021 as we emerged bleary-eyed from the pandemic, our feeling of community, connectedness, and overall appreciation for differences had not only been tested but strained. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, April 18 at the Piedmont Community Church Guild Hall. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now- such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impacts also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver award – the highest honor for volunteers – will be presented to Lisa Gros, a mainstay of Troop 6 and former President of the Piedmont Council. The selection committee was chaired by Chris Lee and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. Gros was chosen for her depth and breadth of service- she served as council president during her board tenure; has served as a dedicated assistant scoutmaster that includes leading a trek through the boundary waters of Minnesota and Canada; and has served as a Webelos den leader to help younger scouts make the transition to a troop. She has provided outstanding support to the Order of the Arrow (honor society for Scouts BSA), and also volunteered with the High Adventure Crew. She has consistently demonstrated cheerful service through irksome tasks and weighty responsibilities. “Working with youth, not only your own child, is one of the most meaningful legacies you can leave,” said Gros. “It’s also a great way to meet other really cool adults.” The council will also recognize many other volunteers who have served in some cases for many, many years. The dinner is open to community members and tickets are available online at www.piedmontbsa.org. For more information contact Kate Benson, Executive Director, at 547-4493. REVIEWERS

articles.text: “The Lord is my shepherd: I shall not want. He has me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside still waters.” In his delightful book The Psalms: A Guide for the Heart and Soul, my friend Rabbi Allan Berkowitz begins his reflection on the 23rd Psalm with these words. “Is there a Psalm with greater brand recognition than Psalm 23? Its opening verse, The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want, is universally familiar. Psalm 23 evokes pathos, thus it is recited at funerals and is borne deeply in many hearts as a comforting mantra for God’s personal protection. It is a poetic blanket that wraps us in warmth and comfort. One of the enduring images of this warm and comforting poetic blanket is that of being led to rest in green pastures. This portrait is consistent with the poet’s experience. It is also a vision that is familiar to residents of the East Bay in the spring as we look toward the verdant hills dotted with orange poppies. It is an image of serenity, abundance, protection and provision. On Earth Sunday 2024, I invite us all to contemplate green pastures. To call to mind a mental image of the psalmist’s words. Green pastures represent the earth as it is, beautiful yet oh so vulnerable. They represent the earth as it can be, a safe home for all living things, a garden in which all things bright and beautiful grow, a paradise in which all creatures great and small thrive. They all represent the peril before us. The green pastures of our planet are not doing very well. It is important to note that green pastures are an ecological imperative. In addition to beauty, they provide oxygen, food for many species, protection to organisms seen and unseen, stability to the soil, connections for watersheds and cover for the aquifers below. It is important to note that green pastures are vulnerable. They are disappearing at alarming rates. Many species are endangered because of the loss of habitat. If green pastures disappear, can thriving human communities be far behind?
articles.title: Reflection on Earth Sunday – Green Pastures
