articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest Founder Piedmont Food Fest 3 is taking place this Saturday from 11am-4pm. The Piedmont Food Fest team spent six months curating this year’s multicultural showcase of culinary, musical, and changemaking talents from Since its debut in April 2022, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees and pushed the envelope on how many different experiences can fit into a single day. From gourmet food and drink to exciting cultural performances, Food-Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something new when they come Attendees are encouraged to come early to get a good view of this year’s performances. Piedmont Food Fest will feature three Food Zones spanning Magnolia and Highland Avenue with more than 20 vendors, including new joiners Lola’s Spanish Cuisine (paella), Doc Bones BBQ (brisket), and Momolicious (Nepalese dumplings recently posted about by Steph Curry!), as well as Food Fest returners such as Piedmont’s own Robert Dorsey Catering (fried chicken sandwiches) and Arthur Mac’s (pizza), as well as Bay Area favorites like The Chairman (baos) and Satay By the Bay. Attendees can also visit the new Sweet Zone located in the Community Circle for handmade gelato from Hila Gelato, Japanese crepes from BB Tea, Southern-style banana bread pudding from O.G. Desserts, and Taiwanese mooncakes from Annie’s T Cakes while meeting with community groups such as Oakland Roots, Soccer Without Borders, No Immigrants No Spice, Piedmont Language School, League of Women Voters, Immedium Books, and Shared Cultures. The Beer & Wine Zone will offer all-day tastings from Oakland United Beerworks, Alameda Island Brewery, Del Cielo Brewery, Altamont Beer Works, Dokkabier, Headlands Brewing, Maker Wines, Deer Hill Vineyards, Blindwood Cider, and Mount Diablo Cider Company. For younger Food Festers, the first (and often, only) stop will be at the KidZone, which features 12 carnival games, the always-popular sno-cone station, and a hosted cultural crafts table to create their own foodie butterflies using colored rice. This year’s Piedmont Food Fest is made possible by the support of generous sponsors led by the Compass team of Stacey Isaacs, Anna Bahnson, Sarah Abel and Julie Gardner, Piedmont Grocery, Body Fit Training, HDR Remodeling, Xantrion, EVOQUE Home Studio by Erika Vexler, Alameda Pediatric Dentistry & Orthodontics, Burke, Williams, & Sorensen LLP, Bernard Hale Optometry, Piedmont Asian American Club, Arthur Mac’s, Mulberry’s Market, Piedmont Post, Piedmont Exedra, and Pizzeria Violetta. articles.text: In its 45th year, the annual Betty C. Howard Award was presented by the Recreation Department to Carolyn Yang Stewart and Madison Mills. The Award is given to staff and community members who exemplify outstanding volunteer achievement. In addition to her duties at the Recreation Department, Stewart serves as the ultimate frisbee coach for the Piedmont Middle School team. Madison, a former Piedmont High varsity player, serves as the basketball coach for Piedmont Middle School. The ceremony took place in City Hall on April 1. Many members of the PMS ultimate frisbee team, Purple Reign, were there to show support. The two awardees were introduced by Sports Coordinator Akil Danjuma. “The Betty C. Howard Award symbolizes more than just recognition of service. It is a celebration of individuals who have profoundly impacted their communities through their dedication and spirit,” said Danjuma. The Betty C. Howard Award was established in 1979 by Recreation Director Mark Delventhal to honor a longtime key member of the staff. Originally a parttime worker, Howard eventually worked in the department for nearly 30 years, cultivating a reputation for kindness and commitment to the department. “Betty Howard was iconic within the Recreation Department,“ said Delventhal, who created the award. “She was sort of like a mother figure to a lot of people in the department, including the directors.” He explained that the award was meant to honor Howard’s dual legacy of dedication to the department and volunteering in the community. “Once a year we gave an award for an outstanding staff member, almost always a partPhotos by Jesse Rosenberg Carolyn Yang Stewart wins Betty C. Howard Award. time staff member who was the backbone of the department in a lot of ways, and then a volunteer in the community, particularly in the sports area,” he said. Danjuma described the basis for selecting Stewart and Mills for the Award. “Since 2016, Carolyn Yang-Stewart has led the Piedmont Middle School ultimate Frisbee team, Purple Rain, with unparalleled dedication and skill, Coach Mills exemplifies what it means to be a beacon of commitment, passion, and energy in the community of Piedmont. Her passion for basketball as a tool to give back to her community embodies the very essence of this award,” he said. Stewart assumed head coaching responsibilities of the PMS team in 2016 following the departure of Kevin Lee, a friend and Piedmont resident. Since then, the team has gone on to play in Bay Area Disc Association tournaments all over California. Madison Mills, a basketball coach at Piedmont Middle School.

articles.text: Photos by City of Piedmont Contractors with the company OneSource clear vegetation above the Corporation yard. Last week, contractors began clearing vegetation on the hills above the Corporation Yard for fire safety reasons, according to the Public Works Department. Laborers are currently working their way up the hill to remove vegetation that could pose a fire risk in the hotter summer months. This work has been requested by members of the Maxwelton neighborhood in recent years and is part of a larger initiative by the Public Works Department and Piedmont Fire Department to reduce fire risk in “the highest priority locations” across the city. “Our goal is to prevent fire from being able to spread from point A to point B around the City,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “In this case, we don’t want the uphill travel of fire from a lower area in this topography up to the higher levels where there are residents and houses.” Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works, agreed with Brannigan about the project’s importance. “The topography makes it particularly onerous because it is so steep. Fire could spread very quickly, and we have a neighborhood above it,” said Gonzales. He also mentioned that the 1991 East Bay Hills Fire ended only a few hundred yards from the area, which was a close call for the entire city of Piedmont. According to Gonzales, the work is especially dangerous for the contractors due to the steep slopes and the difficulty of using equipment such as chainsaws, industrial vehicles, and other power tools. To keep workers from losing balance and injuring themselves, contractors are frequently required to anchor to a stable piece of the landscape using a harness or other methods. The city awarded the contract for the vegetation management project to a private company, OneSource, in January but only started clearing the dense vegetation last week due to the risk of soil erosion posed by the recent rains. “We don’t want to start removing vegetation when there’s a high probability of rain and erosion that can occur. So, we’ve been looking to time it for after the rain but before the fire season, if that makes sense,” said Gonzales. The goats, however, will still return. Officials hope that this effort will make the annual vegetation clearing done by goats in the summer more effective, as well as provide a critical buffer for homes on the hill in the event of a fire. Heavy machinery is being used to clear away vegetation that poses a fire risk to the Maxwelton neighborhood.

articles.text: Earlier this month, the last total solar eclipse visible from the United States until 2044 took place. Observers near or within the path of the eclipse celebrated the celestial event, each experiencing the phenomenon from their own unique perspective. Depending on where they were, people had the chance to see either a total solar eclipse or a partial solar eclipse, and both were a stellar sight to see. What’s the difference? A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, fully blocking the face of the Sun. During a partial solar eclipse, only part of the Sun is blocked by the Moon. Did you know the Sun is about 400 times bigger than the Moon? It’s also about 400 times farther from Earth than the Moon. That is why, when we observe a total solar eclipse, the Moon appears to be the same size as the Sun from our view on Earth. What is the path of totality? During a total solar eclipse, the Moon’s shadow is projected onto the Earth’s surface. Every time there is an eclipse, the shadow lands in a different place. This is also known as the path of totality. The path of totality is where the Sun appears completely blocked by the Moon. The path of totality for the solar eclipse that took place earlier this month on April 8, 2024, had a 115-mile-wide path. The path extended across Mexico and the middle and northern part of the United States, where it crossed 15 states from Texas to Maine. Observing from the Bay Area This explains why Bay Area observers witnessed a partial solar eclipse instead of a total solar eclipse. California was outside the path of totality, and although we did not observe a total solar eclipse, we did have the chance to witness about 45% totality in the Bay Area. There are plenty more astronomical events in store this year for Bay Area observers. Stay tuned for more upcoming viewing events at Chabot Space & Science Center. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

They will be held at Havens Elementary this summer and the majity of classes are for elementary age kids; registration is now open. These summer classes will be taught by dedicated PUSD staff and offer a range of subjects including Spanish, Mandarin, science, reading, math, art, and writing for students. articles.text: The top Spanish, Chinese, and French students at Piedmont High will sing in the finals of the World Language Department’s Singing Competition on Thursday, April 18, at 7:30 p.m. The public is invited to attend the free event, known as “All Champs” in the Alan Harvey Theater, which coincides with the PHS Art Show in the foyer. Twenty-nine foreign language classes from Piedmont and Millennium High and Piedmont Middle School sang and danced in the amphitheater on Monday in the first round of competition. After the first round the competition was whittled down to eight classes. The second round concludes today, Wednesday, with the semifinals and finals scheduled for Thursday night. This interdisciplinary competition combines foreign language with performing arts, two subjects that recently have been threatened with staff reductions. The public is encouraged to come support foreign language in Piedmont, and all the arts.

articles.text: PFD to defend their title against other First Responder units The Piedmont Fire Department (PFD) will compete against other Bay Area fire departments in this year’s Big Climb on Saturday, May 4, as part of the First Responder Challenge, a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The event is a competitive race up a series of stairs at Oracle Park. Participants will compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s entrance on Second Street. Last year, Piedmont won the first responder division in both the team and individual categories. They will have to defend their title this year as they go against the fire departments from San Francisco, San Mateo, and others. “We’ve done a lot of different fitness things over the years, whether it was CrossFit competitions or the Firefighter Challenge, which is an agility course,” explained Fire Captain Justin McNulty. “This competition came up last year for the first time when a local resident suggested it to us,” McNulty added. McNulty was the obvious choice to be part of a team from Piedmont. A self-described “fitness nut,” he regularly competes in physical competitions on his own time, including several running and CrossFit challenges each year. McNulty has also gained a reputation within his department for fitness running the annual 5K Piedmont Turkey Trot in full turnout gear at least half a dozen times. “I even had them change out my air bottle at the top of the hill on Sea View before I finished the course,” he told the Post. Last year marked the first time the Big Climb included a First Responders division, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. “I might be a little biased being with San Francisco Fire, but currently we’re the best at the stair climbs,” said San Francisco Fire Captain Jonathan Baxter. “I remember hearing that last year and thinking, ‘You don’t know what you’re doing, guys. You’re poking the bear,’” joked McNulty. The Piedmont Fire Department’s team this year includes Justin McNulty, Brittany Borges, Nikolas Christ, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Anthony Renteria, and Nadder Shehadeh. Erica Melgarejo, an event organizer with the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society explained that the First Responder Challenge is a great way for her organization to increase participation in its events, as well as inspire competition among departments for a good cause. “In the future, we hope to have even more departments join us at Big Climb in SF alongside other competitors to help take down blood cancer,” she explained. At the time of writing, the Piedmont Fire Department ranks fourth in fundraising under the “corporate donor” catagory with $1,159.47. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco or to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. Staff Photo Capt. Justin McNulty (left), Brittany Borges, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, and Anthony Renteria hold last year’s trophies from the Big Climb 2023. Along with Firefighters Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, and Brian Protheroe, the Piedmont Fire Dept. will attempt to defend their first-place title this year. articles.text: MARKOS LAGIOS Baseball Junior Markos Lagios is the baseball squad’s leadoff hitter and currently leads the team in hitting with a stellar .500 batting average in 46 at bats. He’s the team-leader in home runs with three, while his 20 RBIs also lead the team despite being the leadoff hitter. His 23 runs scored and 10 stolen bases also leads all players. He was critical in a recent 2-0 win over Alameda on April 2, where he went 3-for-3 with a solo home run and scored both of Piedmont’s runs. He also went 2-for-3 with three RBIs and three runs scored in a 13-6 win over Encinal on March 30. Baseball is currently carrying a 12-2 overall record and are a perfect 4-0 against WACC teams. Staff Photos Markos Lagios leads the baseball team with a .500 batting average and three home runs. MIYA FUJIMOTO Softball Miya Fujimoto is another junior at Piedmont High and is captain of the softball team as an infielder and pitcher. With the bat, Fujimoto is swinging for a .522 average in 23 at bats, including one double and a triple. She has a team-leading 14 RBIs and her 17 runs scored is second to Angelina Wu’s 20. On the mound, Fujimoto leads the team with 31.2 inning of work for 52 strikeouts and an ERA of 3.53. Miya Fujimoto leads the softball team with a .522 batting average, while also recording 52 strikeouts as their pitcher. Some of her best performances was a 3-for-5 hitting display with three RBIs in a 17-6 win over De Anza to open the season on March 7. She also had a triple in a big 5-4 win over Oakland Tech on March 25, where she had two RBIs in the victory. Softball is currently 6-4 overall and are 2-2 in league. JOHN CHAMPION Volleyball John Champion is a senior leader on the volleyball team as an outside hitter and at the forefront of Piedmont’s offense. He set a school record for kills in a single game with 19 against San Lorenzo in a 3-0 win on February 29. He also put up 18 kills in a 3-0 win over Mt. Eden two days earlier on February 27. Champion matched his 19 kills in a 3-2 loss to Head-Royce recently on April 4. The volleyball team is currently 5-8 overall. John Champion notched school records of 19 kills in volleyball victories over San Lorenzo and Head-Royce. RUBY GUZDAR Lacrosse Ruby Guzdar is a leading scorer for the lacrosse team, which is a favorite to win the WACC. Senior Ruby Guzdar leads Piedmont’s offense on the lacrosse team, and has helped make them contenders in the Western Alameda County Conference and North Coast Section. She has scored multiple goals in nearly every game this season. Some of her top performances include seven goals in a 15-3 win over Bishop O’Dowd on March 22, five goals in a 15-5 win over College Park on March 25, and another five goals in a 12-5 win over Dublin on February 28. The lacrosse team currently has a 9-3 overall record and in undefeated in league with a 4-0 record.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team had a strong return from spring break, defeating Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division foe Arroyo 8-6 in San Lorenzo o on Monday, April 15. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 12-2 overall and 4-0 against league competition. PHS continued its hitting against Arroyo with a nine-hit performance. “We have a lot of depth in our batting order. When you have guys who can hit from one through nine, you can stay in games,” coach Eric Olson wryly. It marked the start of a critical nine-game stretch to end the regular season, including six games against league competitors. 8-6 win over Arroyo Piedmont scored to open the game in the top of the first, but went behind after Arroyo scored twice in the bottom of the second and once in the top of the third. But PHS came alive in the top of the fourth, scoring three runs to take the lead and tacked on another four in the top fifth. Arroyo added individual runs in the fifth, sixth, and bottom seventh. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team returned from their spring break on Monday, April 15 with a game against Acalanes in Lafayette, losing by 7-6 after a rally in late innings by the Dons. The Dons entered the seventh inning trailing 6-5 but scored the game-winner in walk-off fashion. It marked a strong performance by first-year varsity player Samantha Ronen with two RBIs and a double. Pitcher Miya Fujimoto, struck out 10 batters and allowed just three hits and one earned run. “We’d rather have Miya in the field where she’s best, but she’s carrying our pitching staff. We have to rely on her,” coach Gene Denard said. 7-6 loss to Acalanes Piedmont scored twice in the top of the first, but allowed three in the bottom half. PHS then got back to the lead with a two-run top of the second before Acalanes tied at 4-4 in the latter half. The Highlanders then took a 6-4 lead with a two-run top of the fourth, while the Dons added one run in the bottom of the fifth. Then in the bottom of the seventh, Acalanes scored two runs to win the game. With two outs in the top of the first, PHS got both of its runs by drawing walks with the bases loaded when Caitlin Boothby brought in Cyntiche Kouadio, while Sophena Tuli walking scored Miya Fujimoto. In the top of the second, PHS scored twice in a two-out rally, where Mia Leggett drew a walk followed by Fujimoto smacking a single to right field. Then Samantha Ronen then drove a single to right field to score Kouadio, who was pinch running for Leggett. Sa’Mara Levi then his a hard ground ball to force an error, allowing Fujimoto to score—4-3. With the game tied at 4-4, Ronen cracked a one-out double to bring in Fujimoto and Angelina Wu, who both drew walks to start the inning. But Ronen was stranded at second with two straight outs. Holing a narrow 6-5 lead in the final inning, Acalanes’ leadoff hitter reached on an error, who then stole second and third base. The Dons tied on a fielder’s choice, beating the throw home. Acalanes then hit the game-winning single with a runner on third. Staff Photos Miya Fujimoto went 1-for-3 and scored three runs, while also throwing 10 strikeouts as the starting pitcher. Angelina Wu went 1-for-3 and scored a run. Final stats: Ronen went 2-for-4 with a double and two RBIs. Wu went 1-for-3 with a run scored and a walk. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with three runs scored and a walk. Boothby and Tuli had RBIs. Kouadio scored twice. Fujimoto pitched the entire game, striking out 10 and only allowed one earned run and three hits. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-4 overall, 2-2 league) hosts Hayward for a league game today, April 17, at 4:00 p.m. They also host Tennyson two days later on Friday, April 19 for another 4:00 p.m. league game and bring in nonleague El Cerrito on Monday, April 22 at the same time. Samantha Ronen went 2-for-4 with a double and two RBIs against Acalanes.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Fencing Team competed in multiple events in recent weeks, including the 5th Annual Precision RYC and RJC in Torrance on April 12-14 and the ROC of the Rockies in Denver on April 5-7. The event in Torrance proved to be productive for Sophie Choi in two events. She finished 12th of 38 in the junior women’s foil category and placed 37th of 67 in Sophie Choi had a strong showing at the 5th Annual Precision RYC and RJC in Torrance last week. the Under-14 women’s foil event. Sophie won four of five pool matches, including splitting matches against difficult competition. Her final two rounds included a win over 24th place Brielle Levesque and a loss to third-place Leila Do. Piedmont Middle School fencers also competed. Dario Banuelos was 49th in the junior men’s foil and finished 55th in the Y-14 men’s foil. Oliver Le was 47th in the Y-12 men’s foil. At the ROB of the Rockies in Denver, Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Oliver Greenebaum represented their team. McKay had a strong showing with a second-place finish out of eight competitors in the Division 2 women’s foil event. In the Division 1-A women’s foil, McKay placed seventh of 15 fencers. For her second-place finish, Teresa won all seven of her pool matches. In the final two rounds, she defeated seventh-place Mathilda Reiff but lost to firstplace Sylvie Troxel. Greenebaum competed in the Division 1-A men’s foil event, finishing seventh of 22. Greenebaum won four of six pool matches, including two wins and two losses against “very hard” rated competition. In the final two rounds, he beat 10th place Jayden Lee before losing to firstplace Jeffery Miller. Teresa McKay (right) competed in two events at the ROC of the Rockies on April 5-7. Oliver Greenebaum also competed in the ROC of the Rockies.

articles.text: When covering accomplishments of current student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can get easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers after graduating. This week we take a look at Simon Lins on Virginia’s swim team, Parker Terrill on California’s track and field team, and Michael Aikawa on Lewis & Clark’s baseball team. MICHAEL AIKAWA SIMON LINS Virginia Simon Lins, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman season at the University of Virginia. He was our 2022 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. Lins concluded his debut season in a big way, helping the Cavaliers’ 200 meter freestyle relay team finish 13th of 25 teams with a time of 1:16.13 on March 30. He competed in three individual events in the 2024 Atlanta Coast Conference championship on February 20-24. He was 27th of 57 swimmers in the 50 freestyle with a time of 19.76, was 34th of 49 in the 100 freestyle in 43.92, and was 34th of 46 in the inches), 60 meter hurdles (9.12 seconds), and the 1000 meter run (2:53.33). Staff Photos Simon Lins, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his freshman season on the University of Virginia’s swim team. 100 butterfly in 47.52. PARKER TERRILL Lewis & Clark Michael Aikawa is embarking on his freshman season on Lewis & Clark’s baseball team and earned a starting role. We named him The Posts’ 2021 Sophomore of the Year and was an influential four-year starter. So far this season, Aikawa has 26 appearances with Lewis & Clark, recording a .239 batting average with 22 hits, eight doubles, 21 runs scored, and 13 RBIs. His best performances include recently going 3-for-4 with a run scored on Puget Sound on April 13, went 2-for-3 with two doubles and three runs scored against Pacific Lutheran on April 6, and he went 4-for-5 with two RBIs and a run scored versus George Fox on March 30. Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is a sophomore on the California Golden Bears’ track and field team. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. California Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is a sophomore on the University of California’s track and field team. He was our 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year as a record-setting pole vaulter at Piedmont High and continued his focus as a decathlete in the college ranks. He recently competed in the Brutus Hamilton Invitational at Cal on April 6, recording a height of 16 feet, 3.5 inches. He came less than two inches shy of matching his personal best of 16 feet, 5.25 inches set in April of last year. At the 2024 Ken Shannon Last Chance in Seattle on February 23-24, Terrill competed in the seven-event heptathlon to finish 14th. He recorded personal bests in the javelin toss (21 feet, 11.75 inches), shot put (38 feet, 5 inches), high jump (5 feet, 10.75 Michael Aikawa, PHS Class of 2023, is a freshman starter on the baseball team at Lewis & Clark College.

articles.text: From January 2021 We return to one of our hikes in 2021 where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than most others found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. Aside from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it Hikers can still spot the char marks from fires from previous decades among the redwoods in Portola Redwoods State Park. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent for nearly two miles with 550 feet in elevation gain until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail. Turn left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. Turning right starts a 1.5 mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than six-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turn left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until reaching Upper Escape Road. Turn right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car, making it a four-mile day. Aside from towering redwoods in every direction, you can often hear chickadees chirping about, see an occasional banana slug wriggling by the trail, and hear the knocking of woodpeckers in the distance. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. Watch out for banana slugs, a common sight in coastal parks. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. articles.text: Blue Door, Tanya Barfield’s new two-person play, premieres on the Aurora Theatre Company stage in Berkeley this Friday, April 19. Barfield’s play features Lewis, a high-achieving Black mathematics professor, in conversation with three generations of his ancestors during a sleepless night as he wrestles with his own sense of self and cultural identity. Lewis is estranged from his white wife, who accuses him of being out of touch with his heritage for refusing to attend the Million Man March, a grassroots demonstration of African-American men in Washington, D.C., on October 16, 1995. Organizers united in self-help and self-defense against economic and social ills plaguing their community. The ancestral visitations Lewis receives call upon joy and pain as well as music and song to situate him in a long lineage of Black men in America from enslavement and Jim Crow to Black Power. Post-show discussions will be held on Friday, April 26; Tuesday, April 30; Friday, May 3; Wednesday, May 8; and Thursday, May 16. The play ends May 19. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/blue-door. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s popular Bohème Out of the Box returns to the East Bay this spring. Free outdoor performances of an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème will be held at Alameda’s Radium Runway at 2 p.m. this Saturday, April 20 and Sunday, April 21. Puccini’s classic and beloved opera about love and loss among a group of bohemian artists will be performed in a 75-minute version on a converted shipping-container-turned-mobile opera stage. Directed by Jose Maria Condemi, Bohème Out of the Box is sung in Italian with English narration and features a cast of San Francisco Opera’s Adler Fellows and guest artists accompanied by piano. Radium Runway is at 2151 Ferry Point in Alameda, a short walk from the Seaplane Ferry Terminal. The converted stage uses the San Francisco skyline and Bay Bridge as backdrops, with seating available on the concrete taxiway covered with an artificial lawn. These free events are family-friendly. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets and the whole family. Registration for Bohème Out of the Box is encouraged but not required. Visit sfopera.com/ box to register now. Admission and seating is on a first-come, first-served basis. Food and beverages will be available for purchase at many of the locations or nearby, and audiences are welcome to bring their own food and beverages to enjoy during the shows. A scene from Bohème Out of the Box in last year’s production Photo by Kristen Loken
articles.title: SF Opera hosts Bohème Out of the Box this weekend in Alameda

articles.text: Ballet Company pays homage to its artistic director Oakland Ballet Company’s current season will conclude May 3 - 4 with Lustig Live!, a celebration of the choreography of the company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig. The performance will be inspired by the life and career of Russian ballet dancer and choreographer Vaslav Nijinsky. The program of four works will feature live music throughout with guest artists Leor Beary, Hank Maninger, Hadley McCarroll, Arturo Rodrigues, William Skeen and Shawnette Sulker. Lustig Live! will be performed at the Odell Johnson Performing Arts Center at Laney College with performances at 7:30 p.m. on Friday, May 3, and Saturday, May 4. Tickets, starting at $20, are now on sale at oakland-ballet-company.ticketleap.com/lustig-live. The program will include Faun, Uncertain Steps, Dialogues, and Heartbreak Hotel. In the world premiere of Faun, we meet the 60-year-old Vaslav Nijinsky, on April 8, 1950, his final afternoon. A spirit of his former self leads him on this final journey where the former Ballet Russes star relives his life through the roles he danced. Woven through the work are quotations from Nijinsky’s original Skeen will join Oakland Ballet on stage for the production next month. Dialogues features guest dancer Stephanie Powell in a role about a woman looking back at her life and past lovers. Set to a score by composer Pat Rasile, with text from several of Michelagelo’s love poems, the ballet features soprano Shawnette Sulker and pianist Hadley McCarroll. Finally, Heartbreak Hotel draws inspiration from the Californian invention of speed-dating and is set to a suite of songs popularized by Elvis Presley. The score is accompanied by spoken candid dating advice. Hank Maninger performs vocals and guitar, and Leor Beary on percussion and vocals. Lustig joined the Oakland Ballet in 2010 following the retirement of Artistic Director Ronn Guidi in 2008. Lustig has trained at the Royal Ballet School in London, danced with the Dutch National Ballet and Birmingham Royal Ballet, and has developed a wide freelance choreographic career that has included operas, ballets, and musicals. Lustig Live! will be held at the Odell Johnson Performing Arts Center at Laney College at 900 Fallon Street. Tickets are available online at oakland-ballet-company.ticketleap.com/lustig-live or by phone at 893-3132. articles.text: Myths and misconceptions often go hand-in-hand. Those fables in music are especially good. In fact, a number of popular books perpetuate these amusing tales. Let’s see if you can separate the truth from fiction. Let’s start with one that is told frequently. The famous Czech violinist Jan Kubelik (1880–1940) enjoyed fabulous success early in his career. On one of his concert tours in the United States in the early 1900s, he earned at least a half million dollars. He had matinee idol good looks. Kubelik had one of the greatest and most disciplined practice schedules of all time. We know that he practiced many hours every day. A man who was a waiter at the Bohemian Grove at the time told me that he remembers hearing Kubelik practicing scales for hours at a time. One story that has been popularized is that Kubelik practiced until his fingers were bleeding, yet on the same day he was able to play a successful concert. I think you will agree with me that this story is ridiculous. Rafael Kubelik, the son of Jan, told me as much. Our second story involves two of the great singers of the 20th century, tenor Enrico Caruso and bass Andres de Segurola. They were singing La Boheme at the Metropolitan Opera. Just before Segurola was to sing his famous aria, he lost his voice. In terror, he went close to Caruso and whispered: “Enrico save me!” The story goes that Caruso said: “No problem. You go to the front of the stage and mouth the words and I will sing the aria for you.” This story is absolutely true. It is corroborated in the autobiography of Segurola. In addition, there is a recording of Caruso singing this aria. Next is the story about the immortal violinist Nicolo Paganini and the prominent soprano of the era, Maria Malibran. articles.text: In celebration of South African Freedom Day, SF JAZZ welcomes South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata to the Miner Auditorium stage for two performances on Sunday, April 28. Mrubata hails from Cape Town’s historic Langa township and grew up with the sounds of African music, including the soulful hymns of the Zion Church, the chants and rhythms of traditional healers and the music of the Merry Macs band. In the aftermath of the 1976 uprising in South Africa, Mrubata studied informally under Langa greats like Madoda Gxabeka, Winston Ngozi, the Ngcukanas, Ezra and Duke, Blackie Tempi and Robert Sithole. By the early 1980s he was playing in cover bands like Fever, Touch, Airborne and Vukani. He gained international fame in 1992 when he toured the world with Hugh Masekela’s Lerapo band. He has collaborated with Brazilian artists Airto and Flora Purim. McCoy’s albums have won numerous awards, including McCoy Mrubata the South African Music Award for best traditional jazz release. Concerts are held at 6 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/mccoy-mrubata/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata at SF Jazz April 28

articles.text: Tickets are still available for San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Art Bash, the museum’s biggest annual fundraiser. The event helps fund SFMOMA’s education, family programs and community engagement events, benefiting over 150,000 people every year. The fundraiser begins at 5 p.m. with cocktail reception and immersive dinner experience designed by iconic filmmaker and installation artist Isaac Julien. Julien’s filmmaking career began with his celebrated 1989 drama-documentary Looking for Langston, an exploration of the poet Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2017 Birthday Honors for services to the arts and was knighted in the 2022 Birthday Honors for services to diversity and inclusion in art. Art Bash 2024 will feature photography and large-scale images from the artist’s series Ten Thousand Waves. The dinner program will be followed by a lounge experience for dinner guests opening at 8 p.m., including Solo to Symphony, a multidisciplinary installation conceived by Bay Area– based artist Richard Misrach, an American photographer known for his portrayal of deserts of the American West. articles.text: Selected pieces from SFMOMA’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, will be on view May 4 through August 18. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will exhibit Art of Noise, on view May 4 through August 18, to showcase groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise will feature over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” SFMOMA will host a free “Community Day” on Saturday, May 4, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. where everyone enjoys free admission to the entire museum, and a free “Family Day” on Sunday, June 9 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Up to four adults get in free when accompanied by a child 18 or younger. To learn more, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ®

pages.text: Wednesday, April 17, 2024 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Everybody Knows a stunning film from Spain By Chris Honoré Everybody Knows was written and directed by two-time Iranian Oscar winner Asghar Farhad (Separation and The Salesman). The setting is Spain, in a small village near Madrid. Laura (Penelope Cruz), the oldest daughter in a large extended family, has arrived with her two children from Argentina for the wedding of Laura’s sister, Ana (Inma Cuesta). Her husband, Alejandro (Richard Darin), has not come along, remaining behind, she explains, for business reasons. Initially, the audience is left to try and sort out the many members of this large affectionate and voluble family – Laura’s father and mother, her cousins, nephews, the bride and groom, uncles and aunts. With Laura on the visit is her 16-year-old daughter, Irene (Carla Campra). A bit wild, brimming with life and energy, she instantly begins to flirt with a teenage cousin, Felipe (Sergio Castell Anos), As the arriving family members and guests settle in, Laura’s long ago adolescent crush, Paco (Javier Bardem), a local vintner, arrives to warmly welcome Laura and kids home. All is deliciously wonderful and quickly transitions to the wedding filled with Catholic liturgy, ringing bells, followed by a celebratory party. During a long night of dancing, drinking, and eating, Irene is taken sick, and with Laura in tow goes to her room to rest. She A scene from Asghar Mailet-Guy’s Everybody Knows is left alone to nap and Laura returns to the party. Later, going upstairs to check on Irene, she discovers that her daughter is not in her room. Finding Paco, the two search the estate, inside and out, as rain turns from misty sprinkles to a downpour. Irene is nowhere to be found and Laura’s concern has morphed into fear, verging on panic. She receives a text that states that Irene has been taken and the kidnappers demand $300,000 euros as ransom and warning to not contact the police or Irene will be harmed. At this point the narrative dramatically changes from a light, interesting look at a Spanish family gathering for a wedding to something sinister. It is a mystery that initially focused on where Irene is, and how, absent the police, to possibly get her back. Surprisingly, the crime soon becomes almost secondary to a granular examination of individual family members. What is of apparent interest to writer/director Farhadi is how old grievances, latent animosities and unresolved grudges suddenly emerge as the tensions swirl around the hunt for Irene. The focus turns to the family’s interactions. They don’t coalesce around the need to find Irene (who is asthmatic) but spend time on unresolved familial issues causing Laura, now looking haunted and in full despair, to often remark to family members, “This is not the time.” And yet this is the geography of human behavior that most interests Farhadi, not the whodunit aspects nut drifting toward understanding relationships that, under stress, begin to crumble. The kidnapping becomes a crucible that is decidedly unflattering. To his credit, Farhadi doesn’t allow the years-ago romance between Paco and Laura to rekindle, even when she feels turning to him to help recover Irene is her only option. What makes Everyone Knows exceptional are the fine performances by a very strong ensemble, led by Penelope Cruz’s powerful portrayal of a fragmenting mother. Complementing Cruz is Javier Bardem, who convincingly inhabits the deeply conflicted Paco, suddenly overwhelmed by a secret told to him by Laura that he never saw coming. During the denouement, there are many opportunities for the family to question Irene about her captors, or simply question her for details and clues. For reasons that are consistent with their involvement from the outset, the family asks nothing of Irene, and so Laura, Alejandro and their children leave to return to Argentina. If there was family complicity in the kidnapping, no one is especially interested. Not even Paco, who loses a great deal, asks that essential question: Who? Everybody Knows. Directed by Asghar Mailet-Guy, Spanish with English subtitles. Starring Penelope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Ricardo Darin. 2 hrs, 13 min, Rated R. Released 2019. Whatever the answer, Hollywood continues to be in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel Comics. Captain America: The First Avenger is a perfect example of the genre. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans a la CGI), is desperate to join the army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), but he can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. It is a compelling fairytale adventure that will captivate its young audience. The narrative opens with Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), a young girl, 10, sitting in the backseat of the family car. Her arms are crossed, her attitude is petulant; she’s clearly not happy. The family – mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) – have decided to move to the countryside. Chihiro is already missing her friends. As it turns out they take a wrong turn, enter a tunnel, and discover they are in what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. Spotting a restaurant, they go in and the parents begin to eat. Chihiro wanders away and soon runs into a boy her own age, Haku (Jason Marsden), who takes her on a tour of the park. When she returns to the restaurant she discovers that her parents have been transformed into pigs. She learns that this shocking change was brought about by a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette) who runs a bathhouse for tired spirits. articles.text: Review and essay by Anastasia Edel As an ex-Soviet myself, I am baffled by the renewed global fascination with autocracy. According to Freedom House, 8 out of 10 people now live in a partly free or not free country. In the United States, surveys show that a substantial number of people would support authoritarian rule and do not consider the decline of democratic institutions a mortal threat. In China, Russia, and elsewhere, the winds of change seem to be blowing in the wrong direction. Given this shift, HBO’s miniseries The Regime, whose finale aired on April 7, could not have been timelier. All this chaotic politicking unfolds against Elena’s droning on about love, which she constantly either bestows on or demands from her people. Ever the shrewd economist, Elena proclaims, “The American beast and its client states try to strangle us, but petty sanctions will always fail because our love cannot be sanctioned.” Having shipped her subservient, poetry-loving French husband, Nicky (Guillaume Gallienne), to Swiss exile, Elena, who has regained her sex drive, passionately makes up for lost time with Herbert—and fails to notice the unrest growing among her populace over the country’s economic downturn and crude handling of protests. ers ahead—it seems that Elena’s ruling model is no match for revolution. She is chased out of the palace and must run for her life through a land it’s clear she knows nothing about, despite the “special connection” she often claims to have with its people. For once, someone in this world other than Herbert has managed to outmaneuver her delusions. But soon enough, Elena bends the knee to the very oligarchs she once vilified. One could also see it as a love story, in which two broken individuals find a semblance of happiness by tormenting each other in their own make-believe reality. Armando Iannucci’s The Death of Stalin poked fun at the brutality and hypocrisy of Joseph Stalin’s flunkies in the postwar Soviet Union. Instead of real people, The Regime offers us walking cliches: a delusional woman with hot flashes and daddy issues; cowering and corrupt ministers; greedy Americans pining for other nations’ resources; the dull, kerchiefed masses who look like props recycled from last century’s movie sets. It’s not that we can’t care for bad people. We did for the Roys in Succession because they were nuanced characters, at once tragic and funny, with clear agendas that drove the plot. But The Regime’s characters feel generic, simply dropped into the set, stirring no feelings from the viewer, sympathetic or otherwise. The only character with an identifiable interest is the U.S. senator, Judith Holt (Martha Plimpton), who just wants the country’s cobalt. The rest merely float through the episodes, as though searching for a good scene to act out but coming up blank. This is a shame because the show has no lack of talent. Winslet does her best with the material she is given, but there isn’t much she can do with lines such as, “I like a bit of spice. Spice is nice,” in reference to Herbert’s “spicy” dreams. She has no real antagonists, no articulated desires, and no emotions. Viewers are left to blink at the screen, admiring her outfits and waiting for something substantive to happen. Schoenaerts, who plays Herbert, is more plausible, if cliched: a tortured warrior prepared to kill—and die—for love. Andrea Riseborough, playing Agnes, the palace manager, is less lucky. Having shined as Stalin’s daughter in The Death of Stalin, here she is reduced to a brittle, peacoat-wearing loyalist who has an unexplained co-parenting arrangement with Elena and yields her maternal rights the moment Elena demands it. Her epileptic son doesn’t seem to mind, as long as he gets new toys. Hugh Grant as Edward Keplinger, the country’s imprisoned opposition leader, is charming, but his cameo feels like a checkmark on the celebrity cast list. With his carpeted cell, steady supply of sausages, and access to the prison’s keys, Grant’s performance lacks the gravitas that the suffering of real imprisoned political figures, including the late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, deserves. And then there is Mr. Laskin (Danny Webb), the head of Elena’s security service. In real dictatorships, the requirements of this job are gruesome and attract rather monstrous personalities—think Lavrentiy Beria

articles.text: Don’t search for your next novel on your own, utilize the Indie Next List’s list of recommendations curated by independent bookstore owners and staff. This list for April can help you find your next book and is a good way to support the careers of writers. This list consists of only the newest releases with rave reviews. The American Booksellers Association fights to keep independently owned bookstores alive and thriving. At the start of each month ABA publishes a list of 25 inspired recommendations from independent booksellers called the “Indie Next List.” The titles below received praise from independent bookstore owners from across the country. Go to Indiebound.org/indienext-list for archives of recommendations, more information and ways to order that will support the small book store culture. Fiction “ A Short Walk Through a Wide World is an epic novel charting the adventurous journey of one woman trying to outrun a mysterious curse. Douglas Westerbeke’s debut captures the imagination. A dazzling read!” —Linda Kass, Gramercy Books, Bexley, OH The Emperor and the Endless Palace Books, Fantasy “The Emperor and the Endless Palace is a hard novel to sum up, but let me try: an erotic love story, three eras, loyalty, betrayal, intrigue, mythology. The story is gloriously addictive and will keep you turning page after page!” —Kathy Baum, Tattered Cover Book Store, Denver, CO lic, the allure of ‘home’, and of ‘up North’, and the craft of writing itself.” —Melanie Fleishman, Arcadia Books, Spring Green, WI Clear Fiction “Insightful and memorable, Clear is an elemental portrayal of loneliness, language, and unlikely companionship. Set on a harsh and unforgiving isle in northern Scotland, Davies elegantly shares how regular daily moments can be profound.” —Miriam Roskam, Mountain Shire: Books & Gifts, Winter Park, CO The Prospects Trade Paperback, Romance “A joyful, heartfelt debut! Gene loves baseball and his team, even in the minors. It’s enough to be the first openly trans player. When a face from the past joins his team, it upsets the life Gene’s made for himself. Can he restore the balance?” The Familiar —Jennifer Jones, Bookmiser, Marietta, GA Books, Fantasy “Luzia and Santángel, a duo for the ages! A scullion and an immortal familiar team up to win the king’s competition in the Spanish Golden Age as the Inquisition looms. The Familiar will lead you down new paths you won’t ever forget.” —Coco Zephir, Phoenix Books, Essex Junction, VT Worry Fiction “Insidious millennial malaise and the exhaustion of performative activism are contrasted through the story of two sisters who overstay their welcome in one another’s orbit. The dialogue will split you, gut you, and stitch you back up again.” —Kyle Rea, Greenlight Bookstore, Brooklyn, NY The Woods All Black Fantasy “A visceral queer revenge story wrapped in the mists of Post-WWI Appalachia. Mandelo’s rabid, religious community unsettles with its modern parallels. But it’s his eerie, possibly unhealthy forest that will drag you in and refuse to let go.” —Christy Peterson, Vintage Books, Vancouver, WA The Wives Scout Press, Memoir “With courage and raw truth, Simone Gorrindo conveys the stress, anxiety, and pain of military marriage. She illustrates the importance of the friendships that are formed among those left behind and the camaraderie of those in the Unit.” —Laura Edwards, The Little Bookshop, Midlothian, VA Like Happiness Celadon Books, Fiction “With fantastic prose and a compelling story and protagonist, Like Happiness grabbed my attention from page one and never let go. I cannot wait to follow Ursula Villarreal-Moura’s career; I know I will eagerly read anything she writes!” —Christine Bollow, Loyalty Bookstores, Washington, DC Memory Piece Fiction “I finished Memory Piece on a family trip, and found myself thinking of it when I woke up and itching to get back to it. I’ll remember Giselle, Ellen, and Jackie — their friendships, art and community making, and survival — for a long time!” —Jhoanna Belfer, Bel Canto Books, Long Beach, CA There’s Always This Year: On Basketball and Ascension House, $32, Mar. 26, Social Science “Using basketball as a vehicle for reflection of East Columbus history and personal memoir, There’s Always This Year is a triumph of contemplative, emotionally-rich writing that will have you wiping tears and on the edge of your seat.” —Gary Lovely, Prologue Bookshop, Columbus, OH Table for Two Stories “This collection of stories and a novella is the perfect thing to tide over Amor Towles’ legion of fans till the next novel. There’s even an Evelyn Ross appearance, from The Rules of Civility, which is worth the price of admission alone.” —Cody Morrison, Square Books, Oxford, MS Rainbow Black Perennial, Fiction “The setting: 1980s New Hampshire, a society roiled by suppressed memories. The characters: two young teens, parents convicted of child abuse arising from these memories. Maggie Thrash does not shy away in this compelling story.” —Willard Williams, Balin Books, Nashua, NH Annie Bot Fiction “Annie is an AI-enabled sex doll that learns from her mistakes to please humans. What happens when her intelligence turns inward? A novel about power, intimacy, artificial intelligence, and an imperfect relationship under patriarchy.” —Jennifer Carney, Sidetrack Bookshop, Royal Oak, MI Just for the Summer Romance “Justin and Emma share the same curse: everyone they date goes on to meet and marry their soulmate. They decide to date just for the summer to break the curse. Abby Jimenez writes characters working through their traumas with humor and joy.” —Chantalle Carles, East City Bookshop, Washington, DC I Cheerfully Refuse Press, Fiction “Haunting yet hopeful, this futuristic tale will hit close to home with its honesty and pertinent observation of what it is to be human. I Cheerfully Refuse is proof of the power of a well-told story to ask the reader to live and feel deeply.” —Katrina Mendrey, Chapter One Book Store, Hamilton, MT The Age of Magical Overthinking: Notes on Modern Irrationality Signal Publishers, Memoirs “Exploring our current culture of overthinking and the language surrounding it, these essays are fascinating and enlightening. Peppered with anecdotes and self-evaluation, this is the book Montell was meant to write.” —Mallory Melton, BookPeople, Austin, TX The Cemetery of Untold Stories Books, Fiction “Alvarez’s beautiful new novel synthesizes her familiar themes: storytelling, sisters, family differences, the violent legacy of the Dominican RepubWomen! In! Peril! Bloomsbury Publishing, Short Stories “Women! In! Peril! is a sharply written, eclectically bizarre collection that starts with a bang and ends in tender tears, and everything in-between. A fantastic debut from an author to watch out for!” —Jessie Wright, Copper Dog Books, Beverly, MA Secrets of the Octopus Geographic, Nature “If you’re not already in love with octopuses, Montgomery’s new book will seduce you. For those in love, you’ll be filled with more. Perhaps most interesting are the funny, weird, and intense emotional human-octopus relationships.” —Kay Wosewick, Boswell Book Company, Milwaukee, WI The Tree Doctor Graywolf Press, Fiction “Verdant, potent, real, The Tree Doctor explores so much about relationships as one woman lives through the isolation — the unexpected wintering of one pandemic year along the California coast. This book is the spring that arrives at last.” —Melinda Powers, Bookshop Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz, CA A Good Happy Girl Fiction “Higgins’ debut is a pull on the cigarette you shouldn’t be having, the shot of adrenaline you get when you wake up through the daze of a hangover and remember your bad dreams. A Good Happy Girl is a pitch-perfect entry into the lesbian canon.” —Gaby Iori, Epilogue: Books Chocolate Brews, Chapel Hill, NC
articles.title: Indie Next List’s 25 Best Reads of April

articles.text: April’s pick of the month is James, by Percival Everett, an actionpacked reimagining of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn told from the enslaved Jim’s point of view. James Fiction “Percival Everett, deep into his brilliant career, adds another indelible novel into his vast canon. James reimagines an emblematic — and yes, problematic — American classic and asks about life, history, and our cultural psyche.” —Stephen Sparks, Point Reyes Books, Point Reyes Station, CA Expiration Dates Fiction “I came for Rebecca Serle’s signature magical realism and romance, and stayed for the free will vs. determinism conversation. A quick, enjoyable read that I cried during. Love is a net. articles.text: Wonderful food will be served at the Montclair Village Restaurant Walk, including cheese and wine from Farmstead Cheeses and Wine. For over a decade the annual Montclair Village Restaurant Walk fundraiser was passionately led by dedicated volunteers from the Montclair Lions Club. In 2022 the baton was passed to Montclair Village Association (MVA) so this festive community gathering could continue supporting local service projects (including Safety Ambassadors) that benefit everyone who works in or lives near the Village. The ’24 Montclair Village Restaurant Walk will return on Tuesday, April 23 from 5-8 p.m. and will feature more than 20 “Passport” stops where a growing list of local businesses will offer samples of delicious bites & libations. In addition, patrons are invited to gather on Village Plaza while enjoying seating and two sets of live music entertainment provided by Jazz Education Ensemble, a nonprofit that recruits professional musicians who provide enriching experiences for students through shared performances and one-on-one instruction. Community leaders from Montclair Presbyterian Church and Oakland Center for Spiritual Living have partnered with the MVA to promote patronage of the Restaurant Walk fundraiser by purchasing Passports (tickets) through Eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/ e/2024-montclair-village-restaurant-walk-tickets-859603496197): • Adult Passport ~ $50 ($55.20 w/ processing fee) • Under 15 Passport ~ $20 ($23.18 w/ processing fee) • Package of 4 Adult Passports ~ $200 (processing fees waived, savings of $20.80) Restaurant Walk patrons who become new supporters of the Montclair Cares Club (MCC) will receive a $20 discount. The combined total will be $150. Passports will be available for pickup beginning on April 23at CRUfit Collective, 6125 Medau Place. Standard street parking will be available, as well as paid parking in the Montclair Parking Garage on La Salle Ave. Festively strolling patrons will be able to identify participating businesses by balloons placed out front. articles.text: Charming Montclair Village is the perfect spot to take a break from the bustle of the Bay during the Montclair Village Art Walk. This sidewalk art show celebrates art in the outdoors with more than 40 artists from the Bay Area displaying their handcrafted works. Support the artists the weekend of April 20-21 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. each day. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this free open air art gallery offers a chance to get to know the participating artists and learn the stories behind each piece they make. Among the artisans this year’s event are: Brad Berkheimer Abstract Art Brad Berkheimer has been a full-time professional decorative painter in the Monterey and Pebble Beach areas for over 40 years, specialized in many types of faux finishes, decorative painting of home interior spaces, and custom automotive painting and graphics. He transitioned those skills and experiences to find renewed joy and inspiration in the painting of original abstract artwork on canvas. “My art is guided by the forms, textures, colors and movement I find in Nature,” says Brad. “I look to create unique organic images that attempt to mimic a full spectrum of tones, dynamics and harmonic corrosion found in the natural world.” David Bowman Metal Art Consisting of David Mills Bowman and his son, Reed Christopher Bowman, David M Bowman Studio produces a range of functional and decorative metal artwork. These talented artists collaborate on the design and creation of a wide range of pieces including wall art, vases and candle holders. They construct all of the pieces by hand, with hand tools and simple machines. All the work is produced from brass and copper sheet and rod, formed into shape with shears, hammers, sanders and grinders, and brazed together using an oxyacetylene welding torch. The two do not cast work or use cast parts and they mix patina chemicals from scratch and apply them by hand. Jacque Price Paintings Jacque Price paints in oil using brush and knife, and she often incorporates oil sticks to create meandering lines that silhouette forms or ridge lines. Her process of toning the canvas in a myriad of colors when she first starts a painting sets the groundwork for creating a workable composition that then leads to inspired contextual forms in the final layers. Jacque’s current body of work is curious in nature - amorphous shapes encompass figures in contemplation, ambiguous compositions disperse focus, emotion and stillness meet along lines of vivid color. Her work reveals skill in rendering, an understanding of design, and a proclivity for nature and its influence on the human experience. Doug Rubenstein Ceramics Doug Rubenstein is a potter who uses clay as his primary medium. His work spans a range of creations and sizes. On the small side, he sells dishes, jewelry holders, salt cellars, breakfast bowls, mugs, and tumblers. The medium items include ramen bowls, side plates, dinner plates, jars and pasta bowls. Larger items are vases and serving bowls. “I like to think of my artwork as part of a fifth season - or a season of feeling - honoring, digesting and fathoming that which the world unfolds for us each year,” says Doug. “I design with aesthetics and textures that respect, pay homage and connect to nature while exploring the marriage between natural materials and man-made tools.” Visit these and other talented artists at the Montclair Village Art Walk which takes place on Mountain Boulevard at LaSalle Avenue. For more information, contact the Montclair Village Association at (510) 339-1000 or Pacific Fine Arts Festivals at (209) 267-4394, www. pacificfinearts.com. Presented by

articles.text: It was sunny and warm for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday on April 10, and there was a big turnout of 45 walkers and two K-9 best friends to enjoy it. The group went to the Davie Tennis Stadium last September, but it was “temporarily closed” in February by the City of Oakland after storms knocked down a eucalyptus tree near the courts. After some local news coverage, the stadium was finally reopened. The walkers hadn’t been inside since June 2022, so it was time for a revisit. An eastern dogwood behind the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park was in peak bloom and provided a good start. The group made their way up the hill to Guilford Road and took an almost hidden path to Hazel Lane and then Requa Road with clear views of San Francisco and Wildwood Avenue. At the steps above Witter Field, they saw a Heritage Tree, an eastern redbud, which the group hadn’t seen before. The group continued on to Prospect Road, Oakmont Avenue, and down Oak Road to the entrance of the stadium. The smell of eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium welcomed them. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research reported that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area, established a nursery near Mountain View Cemetery in the second half of the 19th Century and sold eucalyptus seedlings. Frank C. Havens also brought eucalyptus to the area from Australia thinking their wood would be a fast-growing building material replacement for the redwoods that were cut down during the late 19th and early 20th-century for home building. Unfortunately, the eucalyptus wood was generally not suitable for lumber as it is heavy and shrinks when dry, which can cause splitting and cracking. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development. In the city’s earliest days, construction materials like stone blocks and paving stones were imported as sailing-ship ballast around Cape Horn. Oakland’s geologic variability, because it is near the edge of a continental plate, provided a variety of construction materials from surface deposits and outcroppings. Since much of Oakland’s period of most rapid growth occurred prior to the adoption of asphalt in the 1920s, macadam was used extensively in road building. This led to many quarries throughout the area. A quarry at what is now the Davie Stadium was opened in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie. The facility was built in 1936-1937 as a WPA project. The land is primarily in Piedmont, but Davie giving it to Oakland probably explains why the stadium is managed by the City of Oakland. The walkers were impressed by the steep cliffs from the old quarry that surround the courts, but erosion and fallen eucalyptus are evident. Unfortunately, the vintage 1920s clubhouse was locked and the walkers couldn’t go inside to see its pictures and memorabilia. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register with the Recreation Department at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers last week included Bill Ahern, Noemi Alvarado, David Haecker, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Chuck Oraftik, Tina Shum, Stella Houston, Quincy Dong, Sherry Jacobs, Rick Eigenbrode, Helen Dong, Lisa Euphrat, Martin Levy, Janet Laurent, Nava Shaham, Alicia Rivera, Nancy DeRoche and K-9 best friend Pepper, Adrienne Hamlin, Sarah Johnson, Kat Lang, Priscilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Dottie Hutch, Matt Gerhardt, Elizabeth Richter, Lori Austin, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Peggy Shultz, Phil Witte, Joyce Ahern, Eric Behrens and K-9 best friend Mocha, Charlene Louie, Claudine Bach, Mark Davis, Jasmine Cai, Jim Kellogg, Karen Glasser, Brenda Ferrero, Irene Thompson, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased Sharona and Jack Fischrup brought their grandson, Oden Deacon, who was visiting from England.

articles.text: Julia Stokes, a Piedmont Post newspaper carrier, recently ended her paper route after four years of service, capping off an 11-year family tradition of having a weekly paper route in their neighborhood. The Stokes family began delivering papers in 2013, when Julia’s eldest brother Ryan started his paper route for the Post. The route has been passed down through the three Stokes siblings over the years – first from Ryan to his brother, Peter, and then from Peter to Julia – and has served as the backdrop for numerous family memories. “Next year I’ll be in ninth grade, and I started to do volleyball this year, which has practice every Wednesday. So, balancing that with delivering the paper was getting to be a lot,” she said. This decision has been in the works for a while, as both of her siblings stopped delivering the paper when they started high school. “It was just time for me to let it go, but I really enjoyed it.” The Stokes’ paper route began in 2013, when eldest sibling Ryan Stokes sent a handwritten letter to the Piedmont Post requesting a paper route. “I think it was written in crayon,” Ryan recalled. “Every Wednesday, I saw the kids walking around my neighborhood, and I thought it would be a cool job. Aside from that, there Julia Stokes, the youngest of three, recently retired as a newspaper carrier with the Piedmont Post, ending an 11-year tradition within her family. The Stokes family: 11 years of delivering the Piedmont Post: Peter (left), Ryan, and Julia Stokes aren’t many job opportunities for third-graders.” Ryan delivered his route with diligence until 2017, in seventh grade, when he broke his leg . At this point, his younger brother Peter Stokes began filling in for him, and by the following year, Peter took over the route. “It was a good first-job experience,” said Peter. ”Just delivering papers once a week, so building that consistency was fairly low stakes. But having that source of commitment definitely helped me later on when I got my next job.” Peter, now a senior at Piedmont High School works at Mr. Greenbubble, a boba tea café located on Piedmont Avenue. Julia Stokes inherited the paper route from Peter in 2020, and established her own routine. Every Wednesday after school, she would walk to the Piedmont Center for the Arts to pick up her bag of papers. Before delivery she would take her papers home, put on her favorite headphones, and fold the papers while listening to music. After that, she would get her dog, Ollie, from the backyard to keep her company while she delivered the papers. Unlike her two brothers, who preferred to ride scooters, Julia Stokes made her deliveries on foot However, all good things must come to an end. The siblings agreed that while it would be strange to see their beloved paper route leave the family, they would remember it fondly. “Even though Gray explicitly said never to throw the papers and always to place them at the front door, I definitely got good enough at throwing the papers that I could land them at front doors every time,” said veteran paperboy Ryan Stokes, who now attends the College of Wooster in Ohio. “I think it’s just a good way for people who are in school to have some money and get some experience,” said Peter, also retired. “I have cousins from out of town, and when they visit, they love delivering it with me,” said Julia. “It’s fun and a good way to get to know your community.” Since her retirement last month, Julia has handed the Stokes family paper route over to Ronan Price, the younger sibling of her best friend. articles.text: As the families of elderly parents celebrate Mother’s Day on Sunday, May 12, there are many options for activities and gifts that can bring joy to all involved. As people age, the ultimate expression of love is the way they care for others. This could be an elderly wife caring for her ailing husband, or an adult daughter providing care for her ill mother. This makes celebrating Mother’s Day more difficult than it used to be. One option for a Mother’s Day gift comes in the form of respite care. By finding a temporary stand-in caregiver for a loved one, it gives the adult daughter or older wife a much-needed break. Sometimes a few hours of refreshing separation can be the most help. There are also several other ideas for possible gifts and activities families can try that can make for an enjoyable experience. Activities: • Go for a scenic drive or tour old neighborhoods. These trips to beautiful locations or down memory lane can lead to meaningful discussions and stories. • Create a scrapbook. Going through old photos and recipes and putting them into a book is a fun activity and it creates a treasured item along the way. • Go to church or temple. This may be something that is difficult to do on a regular basis, so going on Mother’s Day is rewarding spiritually and it allows your elderly mother to connect with friends. • Spend a day working on the yard or in the garden. While your mother may not physically be able to do yard work anymore, she will appreciate spending time outside with you as you work to make the view out her window more beautiful. • Play games or put together puzzles. These group activities are full of fun. They keep your mother’s mind active, but do not tax her physically. • Ask for help. By involving your elderly mother in any activity, she feels needed. Depending on her physical abilities, you can cook together or work in the garden. Start by asking what she would like to do. Gifts: • Give your elderly mother the latest large-print book by their favorite author or enroll them in a large-print book club. If that is not an option, a magnifying glass can go a long way. • Buy clothes that are easy to get on and off. Using these items helps your elderly mother retain independence because it is something she can do easily herself. If the mock-buttons or snaps are hidden by panels, these clothes can still look fashionable and don’t let others know about your mother’s struggle with dressing herself. • Get a foot massager or portable foot bath with whirlpool. This can help if your mother complains of tired or aching feet. • Sign up your mother for a Netflix subscription or for another movie service. If your mom loves the Hollywood classics, this can give her the opportunity to once again enjoy the films she loved during her youth. The whole family can watch the films together and it becomes a gift that keeps on giving. • Get your mother a subscription to a magazine. There are many magazines devoted to senior health and travel. These can provide a sense of empathy and valuable information. Ask your mother what sort of magazines she would enjoy reading regularly. • Get your mom a spa package that can include a massage, a facial, a manicure and/or a pedicure. Check to see if the spa caters to elderly clients. This sort of rejuvenation could be just what your mother needs. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.
