Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I will be traveling a lot this summer, and I want to make sure I have the right settings to make my iPhone safer. I will be in several countries and don’t plan to take my computer. Also, is there a way to have access to files on my computer? Gerry, Piedmont Dear Gerry: More and more people are leaving their larger laptops and even iPads at home when they travel and just using their phones. Luckily you can do most everything you need on your phone these days. Let’s take your last question first. If you have iCloud Desktop and Documents enabled, which means that your data that is stored on your desktop and in your documents folder is also backed up onto iCloud, you can access these files through your phone app called, “Files.” It looks like a little blue folder and if you open that app, you can browse through items in your document folder as well as in your desktop. This is handy in case you are away from home and unexpectedly need a file that is stored on your computer. Once you find that file, you can email it, send it via a message and even edited it. If you use Microsoft Office, you can install the iPhone version and that would allow you to edit a Microsoft Word or Excel file. There are also other apps that more and more can make your iPhone like a mini computer. One of them is called Genius Scan. This allows you to scan documents with your phone, and then share them via email or text message. I have this app and find myself using this much more than my fancy document scanner. One of the features that I like is this. If you need to scan a document that has been folded, so it doesn’t like quite flat, this application actually flattens it out in the scan. If you must sign a document that you have scanned with your phone, you can use an app like Signeasy or Acrobat mobile. Now for your first question about making sure your iPhone is secure when you travel. There are a few settings that can help your phone be secure. Of course you must be vigilant, don’t do banking on local Wi-Fi if possible, and if you’re in a country that has a lot of theft, keep your phone out of view. If you are riding in a cab, don’t keep your phone next to you on the seat with the window open. Now for some good security settings. 1 If you haven’t already set a passcode, do so. And if you have a four digit passcode, set a six digit one. And make sure it is a secure one, not something like 000000, or 123456. 2. Use Face ID or Touch ID if you have an older phone. 3. Make sure that you have Find My iPhone enabled. This helps to prevent anyone else from activating your phone or using it. You can sign into your iCloud account from another device, even another phone that has “find my iPhone,” with your Apple ID, and disable, your missing iPhone. You can even create a message that will display on the screen with a phone number to reach you. 4. Turn on Stolen Device Protection. This is a security feature that has been added and is a no-brainer when you’re traveling and even when you’re not. This protects your phone in case someone who has stolen it can figure out or knows your passcode. With this feature activated many actions require you to use Face ID or Touch ID. And even more sensitive operations require a security delay. For iPhones with Face ID, go to Settings/ Face ID & Passcode and enter your passcode/ scroll down to Stolen Device Protection. Tap to turn it on. There are a couple of options with this. If you only want it activated when you are away, tap “Away from Familiar Locations.” And if you want to just have this on all the time, tap “Always.” 5. Use “Safety Check.” This allows you to review the information that you share with people and apps. You can go here to immediately stop sharing information. 6. Control app tracking. This is where you can go to stop all apps from requesting permission to share or access your data. 7. There are also ways to protect you when you’re using Mail. If you subscribe to iCloud+, Hide My Email allows you to generate random email addresses that will forward to your personal account. For example, if you want to sign up for a newsletter on the web or fill out a form, you don’t have to expose your personal email address. 8. If you are using your phone and are in a business or that requires you to protect yourself from sophisticated remote attacks, you can use Lockdown Mode. Although most of us are not in this category, if you find it necessary to put an extra level of security on your phone, you can use feature. This automatically protects Safari, Messages, and many other Apple services and apps. It will reduce usability and performance, but it is available if necessary. pages.text: Wednesday, April 17, 2024 29 AMERICANS IN PARIS Continued from page 28 Louis XV reigned from 1715 to his death in 1774. Oil painting by Maurice Quentin de la Tour (French). and statuary; and the several dozen monuments dedicated to the glory of the king himself. No other French king in history had been more self-celebratory. However, his achievements were monumental, including expansive upgrades to Versailles and Louvre palaces – contributions of permanence and extraordinary beauty, and singularly French. Toward the end of his reign, the Sun King’s shine lost some of its glow: critics gained traction about cost overages and extravagant expenditures; depleted royal coffers; and taxes that fell too heavily on an exhausted populace. Sometime in the 1690s the war gods abandoned Louis, and he ultimately suffered a series of defeats at the hands of England’s greatest general, John Churchill, who Queen Anne rewarded by naming him the First Duke of Marlborough. His greatest victory over the French was the Battle of Blenheim. As the end of Louis’s life, three of his heir-apparent successors – his son, grandson, and elder great-grandson – were all struck down with fatal illnesses within one year. On his deathbed in 1715, Louis advised his remaining great-grandson, the future Louis XV, then five years old, to “lighten the burden on the people and avoid going to war as much as possible,” declaring that war was “the ruin of the peoples.” Aware of his own mistakes and many futile battles, he asked his grandson to be “a peaceful prince.” The boy became king under the regency of his cousin Philippe II, Duke of Orléans. Louis XV reigned for the next 59 years, a span second only to that of Louis XIV, but he did not take his great-grandfather’s advice on war. He began waging war in 1756 on two continents: The Seven Years’ War in Europe where France fought Great Britain and Prussia; and in North America, where France was engaged in the French and Indian War and allied with American natives against the British. France lost in both theaters. In North America, Louis’s empire lost their eastern holdings of Quebec, the Great Lakes and the Ohio Valley to England, and substantial territories overrun by the Brits in the West Indies and India. In Europe, France was forced to cede the Austrian Netherlands to Prussia, all costly and humiliating losses. History has judged Louis XV as a gentle person, an excellent Louis XV’s mistress Madame de Pompadour was his most trusted and beloved lover whose death was a great tragedy for the king. father, but lacking in confidence and generally weak as a national leader. He had poor financial skills and was not a good war strategist. He did some building, most notably the Ecole Militaire, Place Louis XV (now Place de la Concorde), the Petit Trianon at Versailles and opera theater of the Palace of Versailles; and the Pantheon of Paris. But with hereditary rulers you get what you get. Socially, Louis was shy and inordinately modest, indecisive and hesitant to speak his mind. He was honest, but a penchant for secrecy hobbled him as a negotiator. His most trusted advisor in his later years was Madame de Pompadour, one of his many mistresses, most of them from a much lower societal caste. His reign is not regarded as a particularly successful one. He died of smallpox at age 64 in 1774. Louis had one son, his heir-apparent, or Dauphin, as the French call their “Prince of Wales,” but he preceded his father in death, Three of the Dauphin’s sons would become kings: Louis XVI in 1774, during whose reign the French Revolution broke out in 1789 and then lost his head in 1793; Louis XVIII, the Bourbon restored to the throne after Emperor Napoléon abdicated in 1814; and Charles X, who reigned until the July Revolution of 1830 when he was forcibly deposed. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris in September 2019 and now await the promise of normalcy someday post- pandemic. In-house historian Michael Mathews contributed to this column. The complexity and size of the fire required mutual aid from neighboring agencies. With all Piedmont’s firefighters working the fire, Berkeley Fire Department sent an engine to help and to handle additional emergency calls throughout the night. Oakland Fire Department provided on-site support. Crews remained for several hours afterward to prevent any smoking or smoldering areas from reigniting. “Piedmont’s firefighters are always ready to put themselves in harm’s way to protect our community,” said Fire Chief Brannigan. “This fire was intense and spread quickly. We train daily for situations like this, and it’s a testament to that work that this challenging operation went off without a hitch. I’m grateful we saved both structures and no one was injured.” “There are simple things everyone should do to reduce the risk of a fire at home,” he added. “Ensure your smoke detectors are installed and working, unplug any non-essential electronics and appliances when not in use, and make sure your neighbors are looking out for each other when you’re away.” This was the second major house fire in Piedmont this year, the most recent of which occurred on March 6 on Sea View Avenue. articles.text: On April 1, the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) union announced that mediated discussions with the school district had failed. APT has elected to apply for a fact-finding panel with the Public Employment Relations Board (PERB). The fact-finding panel will have three members, one member chosen by APT, one member chosen by PUSD, and a member from PERB who is considered neutral. Once the neutral party is assigned, a report must be completed within 30 days. The fact-finding panel will conduct a hearing in which each team makes their best arguments and makes their case. A date for the hearing has not been set. “It’s important for the public to understand that fact-finding is not an audit, and no new ‘facts’ will be found, so it’s incumbent upon district leadership to find a solution so great teachers can stay in Piedmont with their students,” said APT President Elise Marks. The fact-finding panel will try to get the two parties to settle upon and make an agreement on the day of the hearing. If an agreement cannot be reached, the panel of three will have until the end of the 30 days to write a report suggesting a reasonable compromise. Once the report is complete it will be made Pied. articles.text: I am a long time Piedmont resident who went through Piedmont schools more than 50 years ago. As good as it was then, it is way better now – for the most part. I walk this city extensively; I hate all the uphills and love the downs. My favorite downhill is Wildwood, as it takes me by one of my favorite views in all of Piedmont, looking over the ramps and through the trees to Witter Field and its beautiful track & field At least some of it is beautiful. But the unfinished work has been an eyesore for more than three months for those of us who pay for these facilities with our taxes. We do that so our children can be taught how to run, hurdle, jump, and throw and in their own I ran track on the late sixties and early seventies, I know what a horrible facility we had to train on and play on, but at least we were doing it in our own community at our own facility. The big question is: What is further delaying the replacement of the track? Please do not tell us it is because of the weather. There was a long period of time with no rain when the sub surface was If weather is cited as a reason, why were there so many delays on the job during all those dry days? And why were the neighbors on the streets below the field inconvenienced for so long? Perhaps more importantly, why has there been no regular public information by the school district, to include why all the Spring sports athletes don’t have their long promised new track? Why are so many people having to waste so much of their time having to travel to other locations, in order to train to compete for their own school? Why has all of this not been explained to the students, coaches, parents and Piedmont taxpayers. Please tell me – someone, anyone – that our kids will be able to finish out the 2024 Track & Field season at home on the promised freshly minted track. Just confirm also that the long-delayed projects is officially done. Please...no more excuses and no more silence. Manny Myers is a longtime Piedmont resident, a Piedmont High School graduate and a retired Track & Cross-Country coach at Acalanes High School and Piedmont High. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, April 10, 2024 Opinion EDITORIAL Are You Serious??? By Manny Myers I am a long time Piedmont resident who went through Piedmont schools more than 50 years ago. As good as it was then, it is way better now – for the most part. I walk this city extensively; I hate all the uphills and love the downs. My favorite downhill is Wildwood, as it takes me by one of my favorite views in all of Piedmont, looking over the ramps and through the trees to Witter Field and its beautiful track & field facility. At least some of it is beautiful. But the unfinished work has been an eyesore for more than three months for those of us who pay for these facilities with our taxes. We do that so our children can be taught how to run, hurdle, jump, and throw and in their own backyard. I ran track on the late sixties and early seventies, I know what a horrible facility we had to train on and play on, but at least we were doing it in our own community at our own facility. The big question is: What is further delaying the replacement of the track? Please do not tell us it is because of the weather. There was a long period of time with no rain when the sub surface was finished. If weather is cited as a reason, why were there so many delays on the job during all those dry days? And why were the neighbors on the streets below the field inconvenienced for so long? Perhaps more importantly, why has there been no regular public information by the school district, to include why all the Spring sports athletes don’t have their long promised new track? Why are so many people having to waste so much of their time having to travel to other locations, in order to train to compete for their own school? Why has all of this not been explained to the students, coaches, parents and Piedmont taxpayers. Please tell me – someone, anyone – that our kids will be able to finish out the 2024 Track & Field season at home on the promised freshly minted track. Just confirm also that the long-delayed projects is officially done. Please...no more excuses and no more silence. Manny Myers is a longtime Piedmont resident, a Piedmont High School graduate and a retired Track & Cross-Country coach at Acalanes High School and Piedmont High. As a student at PHS he competed on the football and track teams. articles.text: Residents urged to complete an important survey What would you do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the genuine possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. Please help us help you. Complete the survey today, then send it to five friends and neighbors to take as well. Your city thanks you. For more information, call the fire department at 420-3030.

articles.text: City council needs to avoid giving developer carte blanche Piedmont’s city council will soon choose between two options for locating 63 rent-controlled apartments and 133 market-rate homes on parkland in Moraga Canyon. One option would put all 199 units in Blair Park while the other would distribute them around Coaches Field. The city will provide parkland for the rent-controlled units at essentially no cost to developers. Builders of the market rate homes will compensate the city with a negotiated fraction of the value of the parkland. The council has stated that it plans to use the compensation to enhance Coaches Field. Consultants have told the council that building around Coaches Field would provide higher compensation to the city. Parcels there have excellent views and avoid Blair Park’s impediments to constructing market rate homes. Those impediments include the costs of moving sewer lines, building high retaining walls to protect new and existing homes from landslides, and protecting new homes from subsidence of the un-engineered landfill that underlies much of Blair Park. Developers of rent-controlled apartments in Blair Park would, of course, expect the city to pay all these costs. Other characteristics of Blair Park also make it the less attractive option for market rate builders. Proposals over the last two decades to add recreational facilities in Moraga Canyon were abandoned, at least in part, because three independent traffic studies found that the volume and speed of vehicles on Moraga Avenue were so great that no westerly entrance to Blair Park could meet Caltrans safety standards for corner sight distance. The proposed 199 homes in Blair Park would generate at least 800 “turns” a day through a flow of 15,000 vehicles expected to travel, without safe sightlines, on Moraga Avenue. Experience predicts that children living in Blair Park will cross Moraga Avenue to use the enhanced playfields. Driver sightlines in either direction on Moraga Avenue are dangerously short for protecting pedestrians. Reducing this risk would require that a Blair Park neighborhood be fenced along Moraga Avenue to “funnel” pedestrians to a crosswalk at Red Rock. So, residents of Piedmont’s new neighborhood would appear isolated not only by impassable terrain, retaining walls, and funneling fences, but also by dangerous access to Moraga Avenue – their only physical connection to the remainder of the community. Given the above circumstances, why would the Council even entertain the option of building an economically marginal, demonstrably unsafe, isolated enclave in Blair Park when an economically advantageous, safe neighborhood could be built across Moraga Avenue? Advocates for the Blair Park option argue that the city must maximize the economic return to prospective builders of 63 low-income housing units. Council members have stated, for example, that the City of Piedmont should approve a project that can take advantage of an Alameda County program that would give $2.3 million to any developer who can build low-income housing in Piedmont. That project, however, must be approved by January 2025. A project in Blair Park would supposedly take less time and cost to design than one on the northern side of Moraga where the issue of how to physically accommodate the expansion of Coaches Field remains unresolved. Councilmembers’ commitment to a $2.3 million subsidy for developers has, in effect, entitled the builders of 63 low-income apartments to dictate the character of an entire neighborhood of 199 homes. Advocates for the Blair Park option will, of course, object to my characterization of the current state of affairs. They will claim that Moraga Avenue can be made safer by “traffic calming” schemes such as narrowing the roadway or adding more stop lights. But such schemes were suggested a decade ago and judged infeasible for at least two reasons. First, congestion at rush hour would make Moraga Avenue virtually inaccessible for existing and new residents of the Canyon. Second, these schemes would cause vehicles to “stack” on Route 13 at the Moraga Avenue exit during rush hours. Sightlines for easterly traveling vehicles on Route 13 are too short to allow for safe “stacking.” Those advocating for the Blair Park option will also argue that building housing on the north side of Moraga will require the city to incur the unanticipated and otherwise unnecessary cost of shrinking or moving the “corporation yard” where public safety equipment is stored, staged, and repaired. This argument defies both history and logic. Several years ago, the city had a choice between building a regional aquatics center or restoring city buildings that were either or both seismically unsafe or reaching the end of useful life. The city council chose the aquatics center. Arguments for that choice included that rebuilding essential infrastructure was premature and should, when required, trigger a bond campaign that would likely succeed because Piedmonters would understand the need to upgrade police, fire, and corporation yard facilities. Members of the current council have publicly noted that the time for such a campaign is nearing because public safety facilities will continue to degrade while demand for safety services expands to serve the more than 600 recently approved new homes. The argument that building 199 homes around Coaches Field would force the city to modernize Piedmont’s safety facilities but building those same homes in Blair Park would not is absurd. Piedmont’s approval of 600 or more new homes requires modernizing police and corporation yard facilities regardless of where those homes are built. Modern police and corporation yard facilities should be consolidated in Blair Park so that a safe, economically viable, and vital neighborhood can be built around an enhanced Coaches Field.
articles.title: Piedmont should plan safe, welcoming neighborhood in Moraga Canyon

Zip through the trees, climb to the top of Skyscraper, tie dye a shirt, shoot some arrows on the archery range, or simply relax in a hammock with a glass of wine and your favorite book. It’s all part of a Women’s Mid-Week Retreat at Camp Augusta May 1-3. For more information and to register, visit: campaugusta.org/womens-mid-week or email office@campaugusta.org. Come and unplug, unwind, and reconnect with nature and yourself. This event gives women the opportunity to connect with one another and experience the joys of summer camp. Many of the same activities summer campers experience will be offered with a structure similar to family camps. Additionally, Women’s Mid-Week has a few extra special offerings of its own. Among the best offerings are the meals which are definitely not your typical summer camp food. Come for two days and two nights for a chance to reset and relax before heading into the summer. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, April 18, at the Piedmont Community Church Guild Hall. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now — such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impact also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver award – the highest honor for volunteers – will be presented to Lisa Gros, a mainstay of Troop 6 and former President of the Piedmont Council. The selection committee was chaired by Chris Lee and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. Gros was chosen for her depth and breadth of service- she served as council president during her board tenure; has served as a dedicated assistant Scoutmaster that includes leading a trek through the boundary waters of Minnesota and Canada; and has served as a Webelos den leader to help younger Scouts make the transition to a troop. She has provided outstanding support to the Order of the Arrow (an honor society for Scouts BSA), and also volunteered with the High Adventure Crew. She has consistently demonstrated cheerful service through irksome tasks and weighty responsibilities. “Working with youth, not only your own child, is one of the most meaningful legacies you can leave,” said Gros. “It’s also Lisa Gros a great way to meet other really cool adults.” The council will also recognize many other volunteers who have served in some cases for many, many years. The dinner is open to community members and tickets are available online at www.piedmontbsa.org. For more information contact Kate Benson, Executive Director, at 547-4493. articles.text: As parents, we all want what’s best for our children – to see them grow, thrive, and reach their full potential. But what if you notice that your child is struggling with certain developmental milestones? This is where early intervention comes into play, offering support and resources to help your child overcome challenges and flourish. Early intervention has the power to make a profound difference in the lives of children and families. Early intervention refers to a range of services and support systems designed to identify and address developmental delays, and other challenges in young children from birth to age three. These services aim to provide targeted interventions that promote healthy development and enhance a child’s overall well-being. One of the key principles underlying early intervention is the concept of brain plasticity – the brain’s ability to reorganize and form new connections in response to experiences and stimuli. Research has shown that the early years of life are a critical period for brain development, and early intervention can capitalize on this plasticity to promote optimal development and learning in the first three years of childhood. Research has shown that early intervention can have powerful immediate benefits, leading to significant improvements in a child’s outcomes across various Toddlers who struggle with developmental milestones can benefit from early intervention. domains, including language and communication, social skills, cognitive development, and motor skills. Numerous studies have demonstrated that children who receive early intervention services show significant improvements in various areas of development compared to those who do not receive such services. Early intervention has also been linked to long-term benefits that extend beyond childhood. A study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) Pediatrics found that children who received early intervention services were more likely to graduate from high school, attend college, and secure employment as adults compared to those who did not receive such services. If you have concerns about your child’s development, the first step is to reach out for help. Start by talking to your child’s pediatrician and sharing your concerns. Your pediatrician can provide guidance and referrals for further evaluation if needed. Early intervention services can be coordinated through your state or local government, or can be obtained privately. During the evaluation process, a professionals will assess your child’s development and identify any areas of concern. Be open and honest about your observations and experiences with your child

articles.text: Piedmont’s youngest vocal music students hosted Spring Concerts last week at each elementary school. The 45-minute shows featured well-rehearsed performances by students in kindergarten through third grade, The theme of this year’s concerts was “Broadway,” and for vocal music teacher Adrian Behrendt, the concerts marked a big step for the young musicians. The shows kicked off bright and early, at 8:45 a.m. giving the 5-9 year olds a chance to sing like morning doves. The kids have been working with Behrendt since January on songs taken from Broadway musicals, including “Peter Pan” and “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown.” “When we began learning these Broadway selections, students became aware of their role as singers, listeners, and storytellers,” explained Behrendt. “They may look cute but producing a nice sound requires many skills that have been learned along the way. Performing in concert requires a student to focus on diction, expression, and choreography, all while following the conductor’s cues. Even getting onto and singing on the risers involves some learning, patience, and practice,” said Behrendt. Havens School singers held their concert in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on Tuesday, April 2. Beach School kids performed on Thursday, April 4, and the concert at Wildwood was on Friday, April 5. Behrendts said he feels the community appreciates the effort the students have put into their performances. “Certainly, the human voice is the most personal instrument, and when shared with others, whether sung alone or as a choir, there is something in that shared human experience we can discover and appreciate,” he said. Vocal Music teacher Adrian Behrendt in front of Wildwood 3rd graders participating in the school’s Spring Concert on Friday, April 5. JOIN US FOR OUR FINAL WAREHOUSE SALES IN BERKELEY

articles.text: City adds Sustainability as award category The City of Piedmont has announced the winners of the annual Design Awards which will be presented publicly at an event on Wednesday, April 24, at 5:30 p.m. in the Community Hall. The Excellence in Indoor/Outdoor Living Design award, 974 Rose Avenue Excellence in Facade Composition award, 11 Cambridge Way Planning Commission selected seven home improvement projects this year that demonstrate a high level of excellence. The City has added a sustainability category to this year’s event to celebrate property owners who have incorporated green elements into their homes. To be eligible for the annual awards a project must conform to Piedmont’s design and planning guidelines and the project must have been completed in the previous calendar year. The seven projects selected for 2024 Design Awards are: • • • • • • Excellence in Indoor/Outdoor Living Design owner Victoria Smith of 974 Rose Avenue, architect Kirk Peterson, contractor Daryl Rush. Excellence in Facade Composition owners Peter Jaeshke and Supina Moon of 11 Cambridge Way, architect Rob Kelly, contractor Gabriel Zarate. articles.text: Charming Montclair Village is the perfect spot to take a break from the bustle of the Bay during the Montclair Village Art Walk. This sidewalk art show celebrates art in the outdoors with more than 40 artists from the Bay Area displaying their handcrafted works. Support the artists the weekend of April 20-21 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. each day. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this free open air art gallery offers a chance to get to know the participating artists and learn the stories behind each piece they make. Among the artisans this year’s event are: Brad Berkheimer Abstract Art Brad Berkheimer has been a full-time professional decorative painter in the Monterey and Pebble Beach areas for over 40 years, specialized in many types of faux finishes, decorative painting of home interior spaces, and custom automotive painting and graphics. He transitioned those skills and experiences to find renewed joy and inspiration in the painting of original abstract artwork on canvas. “My art is guided by the forms, textures, colors and movement I find in Nature,” says Brad. “I look to create unique organic images that attempt to mimic a full spectrum of tones, dynamics and harmonic corrosion found in the natural world.” David Bowman Metal Art Consisting of David Mills Bowman and his son, Reed Christopher Bowman, David M Bowman Studio produces a range of functional and decorative metal artwork. These talented artists collaborate on the design and creation of a wide range of pieces including wall art, vases and candle holders. They construct all of the pieces by hand, with hand tools and simple machines. All the work is produced from brass and copper sheet and rod, formed into shape with shears, hammers, sanders and grinders, and brazed together using an oxyacetylene welding torch. The two do not cast work or use cast parts and they mix patina chemicals from scratch and apply them by hand. Jacque Price Paintings Jacque Price paints in oil using brush and knife, and she often incorporates oil sticks to create meandering lines that silhouette forms or ridge lines. Her process of toning the canvas in a myriad of colors when she first starts a painting sets the groundwork for creating a workable composition that then leads to inspired contextual forms in the final layers. Jacque’s current body of work is curious in nature - amorphous shapes encompass figures in contemplation, ambiguous compositions disperse focus, emotion and stillness meet along lines of vivid color. Her work reveals skill in rendering, an understanding of design, and a proclivity for nature and its influence on the human experience. Doug Rubenstein Ceramics Doug Rubenstein is a potter who uses clay as his primary medium. His work spans a range of creations and sizes. On the small side, he sells dishes, jewelry holders, salt cellars, breakfast bowls, mugs, and tumblers. The medium items include ramen bowls, side plates, dinner plates, jars and pasta bowls. Larger items are vases and serving bowls. “I like to think of my artwork as part of a fifth season - or a season of feeling - honoring, digesting and fathoming that which the world unfolds for us each year,” says Doug. “I design with aesthetics and textures that respect, pay homage and connect to nature while exploring the marriage between natural materials and man-made tools.” Visit these and other talented artists at the Montclair Village Art Walk which takes place on Mountain Boulevard at LaSalle Avenue. For more information, contact the Montclair Village Association at (510) 339-1000 or Pacific Fine Arts Festivals at (209) 267-4394, www. pacificfinearts.com. Presented by

articles.text: Wonderful food will be served at the Montclair Village Restaurant Walk, including cheese and wine from Farmstead Cheeses and Wine. For over a decade the annual Montclair Village Restaurant Walk fundraiser was passionately led by dedicated volunteers from the Montclair Lions Club. In 2022 the baton was passed to Montclair Village Association (MVA) so this festive community gathering could continue supporting local service projects (including Safety Ambassadors) that benefit everyone who works in or lives near the Village. The ‘24 Montclair Village Restaurant Walk will return on Tuesday, April 23 from 5-8 p.m. and will feature more than 20 “Passport” stops where a growing list of local businesses will offer samples of delicious bites & libations. In addition, patrons are invited to gather on Village Plaza while enjoying seating and two sets of live music entertainment provided by Jazz Education Ensemble, a nonprofit that recruits professional musicians who provide enriching experiences for students through shared performances and one-on-one instruction. Community leaders from Montclair Presbyterian Church and Oakland Center for Spiritual Living have partnered with the MVA to promote patronage of the Restaurant Walk fundraiser by purchasing Passports (tickets) through Eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/ e/2024-montclair-village-restaurant-walk-tickets-859603496197): • Adult Passport ~ $50 ($55.20 w/ processing fee) • Under 15 Passport ~ $20 ($23.18 w/ processing fee) • Package of 4 Adult Passports ~ $200 (processing fees waived, savings of $20.80) Restaurant Walk patrons who become new supporters of the Montclair Cares Club (MCC) will receive a $20 discount. The combined total will be $150. Passports will be available for pickup beginning on April 23at CRUfit Collective, 6125 Medau Place. Standard street parking will be available, as well as paid parking in the Montclair Parking Garage on La Salle Ave. Festively strolling patrons will be able to identify participating businesses by balloons placed out front. Those listed below will be hosting delicious bites and libations and / or activities such as discount promotions, giveaways and introductions to owners and staff. Standard street parking will be available as well as ample paid parking in the Montclair Parking Garage (6235 La Salle Ave.) Enjoy the entertainment by the Jazz Education Ensemble at this year’s ’24 Montclair Village Restaurant Walk.

articles.text: Police Sergeant David Cutler (middle) with his friends and family at a pinning ceremony on April 1. Piedmont Police Officer David Cutler was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in a pinning ceremony at the April 1 City Council meeting. In attendance were his wife Shannon and daughters Cassidy and Madison, as well as co-workers and members of his extended family. Cutler was honored for his promotion alongside Officer Jehan Liles, who was being recognized for his achievement in the department. In a speech to the city council, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers praised Cutler’s leadership in the department and congratulated him on the new role of being one of four sergeants in the department. “In addition to developing into a very dependable police officer over the years since I’ve been here, it’s been a pleasure watching you develop and grow and mature into the leader that you are today,” said Bowers. Cutler joined the police department in 2012 after a career in the Marine Corps. In his 12 years in Piedmont, Cutler has served as an acting watch commander, firearms instructor, police explorer advisor, and most recently as a police detective before his promotion. In addition to his law enforcement work, Cutler is also pursuing a master’s degree in criminal justice through an online program. “Oftentimes in policing, you get people who are one-trick ponies,” continued Bowers. “They’re either all tactics and high-speed stuff or community-oriented. David does both, which is so impressive to us.” When it came time to present the badge, Chief Bowers looked toward the other officers present with confusion. “Where’s the badge?” he asked. A beat followed. “Just kidding, April Fool’s,” he proclaimed, and the audience laughed. “I couldn’t help myself.” Cutler was pinned by recently retired Police Sergeant Robert Jaime, a mentor whose guidance Cutler said was instrumental in his career progression. “You know, you get a little emotional, but in a good way,” said Cutler. “To be pinned by someone who I respect greatly, to have it all come full circle is something I’ve worked really hard to achieve. And I didn’t do it alone.” In his new role, Cutler said he was most excited about the increased responsibility and opportunities for leadership. “I’m huge into leadership and giving back to those who have given to me. I’ve had some really good mentors throughout my career, and as a sergeant, it allows me to do that much more for the mentorships in my life.” Officer Cutler is pinned by his longtime mentor, retired PPD Sergeant Robert Jaime. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team continues to play red-hot ball, positioning itself among the top teams in the Western Alameda County Conference and Division 4 of North Coast Section. Last week it posted two strong wins over league opponent Alameda. The Highlanders beat the Hornets 2-0 at home on Humphries Diamond on Tuesday, April 2, and defeated Alameda the following day in a two game series, 7-2. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 11-2 overall and 3-0 against league competition with 10 games left in the regular season. Junior Markos Lagios led the hit parade, smacking a leadoff home run at the start of the 2-0 victory, and went 3-for-4 with three stolen bases in the 7-2 win. Cleanup hitter Dimiti Papahadjopoulos was highly productive in the second game, going 3-for-4 with two triples and a double. Outfielder Shafer Dando was also 3-for-4 in the away-win, and drove in 3 runs. Starting pitcher John Olsen threw a one-hit shutout for the 2-0 victory. 7-2 win over Alameda Piedmont opened the top of the first with one run, then carried a 4-0 lead in the top of the fourth until Alameda scored two in the bottom half. PHS added three more runs in the top half of Staff Photos John Olsen pitched complete game, a one-hit shutout in a 2-0 win over Alameda. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos had two triples and a double in a 7-2 win over Alameda. Markos Lagios hit a leadoff home run in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Alameda. He also stole three bases in a 7-2 victory. the fifth inning. Lagios opened the game with a single, stole second, and then stole third with two outs. With Papahadjopoulos up, Lagios took home on a wild pitch for the first run. Dimitri went opposite field with a triple to right, but was stranded on third. In the three-run fourth inning, PHS’ Will Parker reached first after a fly ball was botched by Alameda’s left fielder. Papahadjopoulos then cracked his second triple of the afternoon on a firstpitch smash to right field, once again, scoring Parker. With one out, Dando smacked a double to center field to bring in Papahadjopoulos, and then Jack Meyjes hit a single and a throwing error allowed Dando to score. With a 4-2 lead entering the top of the fifth, PHS got its rally started with a leadoff single by Lagios. With one out, Lagios stole second, then Will Parker knocked a ground ball single over second base to score Markos from second. Papahadjopoulos then hit a double to left field, followed by Dando hitting a two-out single to score both Parker and Dimitri. Final stats: Lagios went 3-for-4 with three stolen bases and two runs scored. Parker went 1-for-4 with an RBI and two runs scored. Papahadjopoulos was 3-for-4 with two triples, a double, two runs scored and an RBI. Dando was 3-for-4 with three RBIs and a run scored. Peter Krumins was the winning pitcher with 4.1 innings, six strikeouts, and allowed just one hit. articles.text: Saturday, April 6 marked a monumental day for Piedmont High sophomore Layth Haddawy. He set four different state powerlifting records in the age 14-15 category at 132 pounds. At a U.S. Powerlifting Association meet in Oakland, he hit 280 pounds in the squat, 206 pounds on the bench press, a 371 pound dead lift, and the combined total record at 857 pounds. It’s a day Haddawy never expected when the school year started. He played on Piedmont’s JV football team in the fall and felt like he wasn’t making a big impact. But there was one place Haddawy always stood out with his peers – the weight room. “I began working out towards the end of 8th grade and into freshman year. Following the football season this year, I started looking into lifting and wound up meeting my coach. He said we’d need to train for a while before entering a meet,”Haddawy said. “I’ve been lifting for a while, but I began taking powerlifting very seriously in November when the football season ended. Throughout my life I’ve played all the team sports you can think of, but I never was great at any of them. I realized, especially in football, I wasn’t the best guy Layth Haddawy stands proudly after setting four California powerlifting records for age 14-15. on the field but I was always the strongest player on the team. I thought, if I’m too undersized for football, I should find something that fits me,” Haddawy said. Once the football season was over, Layth began training at Get Bent gym in Oakland under Layth Haddawy has qualified for the National Championships in powerlifting in Las Vegas in June. owner Jason Romero and coach James Cunningham. He began making big jumps over the following months. “When I first got there, my deadlift was about 310 and two months later, I was already around 360. I realized I had a lot of potential. My squat went from sub-200 to now around 280 pounds,” Haddawy described. The USPA 2024 Spring Break meet last weekend marked Haddawy’s first official competition. At the meet, lifters are allowed three reps to achieve their maximum weight and are permitted a fourth attempt if they are going for a State or National record. He eclipsed the one-year old squat record by 4.4 pounds, the two-year old bench record by 3.1 pounds, the one-year old deadlift record by 1.8 pounds, and the two-year old combined total record by 25 pounds. “I was really excited but nervous on the day of the meet. My coaches had me lower my attempts heavily to make sure I was nailing them and reaching my goals… On my third squat attempt, it warranted me taking a fourth try. It went well and I managed to break the State record for squat. Then came the bench, my second attempt was about eight points away from the State record. On the third attempt, I tweaked my form and I was able to do a slow, grind-it-out lift by about two points over the record.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team split its last two matches, defeating Western Alameda County Conference opponent Encinal in five sets in Alameda on Thursday, April 4 with scores of 26-24, 25-16, 16-25, 22-25, 15-11. They lost in five sets to non-league opponent Head-Royce the previous day. The loss to the Jayhawks came after the Highlanders won the opening two sets, but dropped the next three sets , 25-11, 25-18, 22-25, 25-27, 7-15 “I got cocky and switched up the lineup after the second set, I’m telling the team it’s my fault and it won’t happen again,” said a disappointed coach Mariah Cardenas. With a 5-6 league record, Piedmont must finish with an even .500 record to qualify for the North Coast Section playoffs. They’ll return from Spring Break to play five tough matches: Berkeley on April 15, Arroyo the next day, San Leandro on April 19, Castro Valley on April 23, and Bishop O’Dowd for the season-finale on April 26. The match with Head-Royce marked the debut season of Olivia Theut as the Jayhwks head coach. She graduated from Piedmont High in 2019. “There’s definitely a lot of pressure returning to your former high school. After the first game, we just talked about staying positive. It was such a competitive game and was a lot of fun to play against them,” Theut said. 3-2 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont dominated the first set with a 25-11 win, including five kills from John Champion, two from Spencer SorensenWald, and two by Mateo Devries. PHS also had a seven-point 25-18 win in the second set. There were five lead changes during the second set, but PHS took the lead at 18-17, leading to a 7-1 scoring run to close things with a 25-18 win. In an attempt by Cardenas to get players more time in different positions, the Jayhawks were able to storm back from then on. They John Champion had 19 kills against Head-Royce. articles.text: It’s springtime in the Bay Area and wildflowers are bursting with color throughout the entire state. Following the rains, Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve is the perfect place to take in the array of colorful plants in the Oakland Hills. Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but the sun has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Lupine provide a sharp contrast to the orange of poppies. Yellow French Broom has also bloomed as far as the eye can see. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles long and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths and other geological features. The park is a popular area for dog walkers and is also child friendly. Once the loop trail connects to the Volcanic Trail, veer to the right to find the first quarry pit. It will be trail marker No. 2 on the park information pamphlet’s selfguided tour. Old quar r y operations removed massive basalt lava and exposed the interior of the Round Top volcano. The base of the pit consists of bedded tuff-breccias, which is volcanic ash and sediStaff Photos Thousands of California Poppies cover the hills of Sibley Regional Park in the Oakland hills. Poppies are profuse at Sibley Regional.

Sibley is most known for its stone labyrinths, but the sun has allowed vegetation to grow and keep the hills green. Throughout Sibley Regional, the sharp contrasting orange of California Poppies and purple of Lupine provide a sharp contrast to the orange of poppies. Yellow French Broom has also bloomed as far as the eye can see. Sibley’s Round Top Loop trail is about 2.5 miles long and connects to the Quarry and Volcanic trails, where you can find the labyrinths and other geological features. The park is a popular area for dog walkers and is also child friendly. Once the loop trail connects to the Volcanic Trail, veer to the right to find the first quarry pit. It will be trail marker No. 2 on the park information pamphlet’s selfguided tour. Old quar r y operations removed massive basalt lava and exposed the interior of the Round Top volcano. articles.text: The exhibit Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style is now on view at the deYoung Museum in San Francisco. It features iconic collections of 20th and 21st-century women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture, and is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.The exhibit is on display through August. Visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more.
articles.title: Fashioning San Francisco on view at de Young through August

articles.text: Entries due Monday Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside’s annual haiku contest is currently underway. All entries are due by Monday, April 15. Submit up to three original haiku poems before April 15. The poems should be in the traditional haiku format of three short lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Submissions in languages other than English are strongly encouraged as long as they follow haiku poem-structure. This year’s contest theme is migration and belonging. Filoli is looking for poems that muse on how beings create a sense of home in gardens and the natural world, and encourages content based on its spring blooms. The winner will receive the Ecopoetry Award, which recognizes a haiku that celebrates this theme while touching on the connection between humans and the environment, as well as family membership and gift basket. The second-place winner will receive a Filoli Individual Membership. The poetry will be judged by former San Mateo Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto. A total of 10 semi-finalist poems will be announced on Filoli’s website on Earth Day, April 22. Prize winners will be announced May 1. For more information, visit https://filoli.org/haiku/.
articles.title: Last chance to enter Filoli’s annual spring haiku contest

articles.text: The final Chamber Series concert of the season, Play on Words, will be performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, April 14, at 4 p.m. With former Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director René Mandel on violin, soprano Lisa Delan, cellist Evan Kahn, and pianist Kevin Korth, the audience will be taken on a literary journey from 19th-century Austria to the Golden Age of Hollywood to the present-day Bay Area. The Berkeley Symphony & Friends chamber music series, now in its 11th year, was founded by Mandel. Completed the year before his death, Franz Schubert’s monumental Piano Trio in E-flat Major, Op. 100 was among the last of his compositions he heard. It’s a dramatic work dappled with light: a Swedish folk song inspired the famous melody of the slow movement, which has appeared in films such as Barry Lyndon and The Piano Teacher. Erich Wolfgang Korngold’s Much Ado About Nothing Suite for Violin and Piano originated in 1918 as a commission of incidental music for the Shakespeare play. The young composer’s score made the production such a hit that the run was extended – but the orchestra’s musicians had already booked other gigs. Korngold thus created a more intimate arrangement, which has since become popular around the globe. Gordon Getty’s Four Dickinson Songs, which includes the arresting poem “Because I Could Not Stop for Death,” is a testament to the expressive power of Emily Dickinson. Getty has long admired Dickinson’s poetry: some of this music, for soprano and piano, dates back to his college days, and The White Election, another of his Dickinson cycles, comprises a staggering 32 songs. Jake Heggie’s Shed No Tear for soprano and piano evokes the natural world as illuminated by the poetry of John Keats: “Shed no tear! oh, shed no tear! The flower will bloom another year.” The music will be brought to life with soprano Lisa Delan and pianist Kevin Korth. Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the Berkeley Symphony ticket office at (510) 841-2800. René Mandel, violin Soprano Lila Delan Kevin Korth, piano

articles.text: Berkeley Choro Ensemble will perform a concert with the great Douglas Lora at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 19 at 7:00 p.m. Tickets are $30 for General Admission and are available at https://www.bpt. me/6251519. Three-time Grammy nominee guitarist and composer Douglas Lora has established himself as one of the most prominent artists of his generation. He has collaborated with renowned artists YoYo Ma, Paquito d’Rivera, Assad Brothers, Anat Cohen, Marco Pereira, Jovino Santos Neto, Ney Rosauro, Marina Piccinini, and Paulo Bellinati. A member of the Brasil Guitar Duo, Trio Brasileiro and Caraivana, Lora has performed at major concert halls in the U.S., Europe, Asia and Latin America. He is the newest member of the awarded Los Angeles Guitar Quartet. His has taught at the University of Miami and Miami Conservatory of Music, and is the guitar instructor at Cal State Fullerton. The Berkeley Choro Ensemble is a group of world-class musicians from the SF Bay Area that debuted in 2010. The group celebrates the music, culture and history of Brazil, with a special Guitarist and composer Douglas Lora emphasis on the Choro genre, a style of music which emerged in the 1800s in Brazil, fusing the music of Brazil’s European immigrants and the native music of Brazil’s indigenous and African-Brazilian population. The choro sound is somewhat akin to a combination of European classical music, ragtime, and blues. Historically, the choro style influenced Brazil’s most famous classical composer, Heitor Villa Lobos, to compose some of the world’s most beautiful music, the Bachianas Brasileiras.
articles.title: Berkeley Choro, Douglas Lora coming to Center for the Arts

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet is now performing Dos Mujeres, the company’s first double bill of dances by Latina choreographers Arielle Smith and Annabelle Lopez Ochoa. Performances feature the world premiere of Smith’s Carmen and company premiere of Ochoa’s Broken Wings. Smith, a Cuban-born choreographer, reimagines the original opera San Francisco Ballet Dos Mujeres is the company’s first double bill of works by Latina choreographers. by Bizet with the first same-sex love story between two women to unfold on the San Francisco Ballet stage. Escamillo is recast as a female dancer played by principal Dancer Jennifer Stahl and soloist Sasha Mukhamedov. The role of titular character Carmen is played by principal dancers Jasmine Jimison and Sasha De Sola. The ballet is accompanied by a score from Grammy Award–winning Arturo O’Farrill. Ochoa’s Broken Wings bring audiences into the world of celebrated Mexican painter Frida Kahlo. The ballet stage is adorned with bright art installations, including giant Frida and Diego statues in Mexican folk art style, and an all-female Mariachi group Mariachi Bonitas in the lobby after every show. Dos Mujeres performances end this Sunday, April 14. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. sfballet.org/productions/dos-mujeres/.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Dos Mujeres onstage now through Sunday

articles.text: Blue Door, Tanya Barfield’s new two-person play, premieres on the Aurora Theatre Company stage in Berkeley on Friday, April 19. Barf ield’s play features Lewis, a high-achieving Black mathematics professor, in conversation with three generations of his ancestors during a sleepless night as he wrestles with his own sense of self and cultural identity. Lewis is estranged from his white wife, who accuses him of being out of touch with his heritage for refusing to attend the Million Man March, a grassroots demonstration of African-American men in Washington, D.C., on October 16, 1995; organizers united in self-help and self-defense against economic and social ills plaguing their community. The ancestral visitations Lewis receives call upon joy and pain, as well as music and song to situate him in a long lineage of Black men in America from enslavement and Jim Crow to Black Power. Discussions of Blue Door will be held after the show on Friday, April 26; Tuesday, April 30; Friday, May 3; Wednesday, May 8; and Thursday, May 16. The play ends May 19. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/blue-door. Playwright Tanya Barfield
articles.title: Blue Door premieres on Aurora Theatre stage April 19

articles.text: World-renowned musical theater vocalist Patti LuPone performs at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco this Sunday, April 14. LuPone gained acclaim for her leading stage performances on Broadway and in London’s West End theater stage. She received three Laurence Olivier Awards, presented annually by the Society of London Theatre to recognize excellence in professional theater in London. In particular, for her performances as Fantine in the original London cast of Les Misérables, Moll in The Cradle Will Rock in 1985, and for Best Actress in a Supporting Role in a Musical for Company in 2019. LuPone is joined at Davies Symphony Hall by music director Joseph Thalken, director Scott Wittman and string instrumentalist Brad Phillips for a brandnew show she calls her “personal musical memoir.” The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2023-24/Patti-LuPone. Patti LuPone

articles.text: 29-year-old Kedrick Armstrong takes the helm after two-year search Oakland Symphony has announced the appointment of 29-year-old Kedrick Armstrong as its new music director. Armstrong, originally from Georgetown, South Carolina, previously served as Principal Conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Galesburg, Illinois. Armstrong will also actively participate in Oakland Symphony’s many education and community engagement programs, designed to inspire a love of music in people of all ages throughout the Oakland and greater Bay Area. Armstrong is the successor to the late Michael Morgan, who passed away in 2021 after a 30-year tenure leading the symphony. Armstrong’s next appearance with the Oakland Symphony will take place on October 18, 2024, when he will help the company open its 2024-2025 season. “I am deeply honored and grateful for the opportunity to serve as the new music director of the Oakland Symphony,” Armstrong said in a statement. “As a Black conductor, I find it humbling to stand on the shoulders of both Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons [the most recent and the first African-American Music Directors of the Symphony, respectively]. The Oakland Symphony community has embraced member Jim Bell, was impressed by Armstrong’s demonstrated leadership and community-building abilities, as well as his passion for and command of a wide range of music genres. “The committee was overwhelmed by Kedrick’s scholarship and curiosity about all kinds of music, from classical and jazz to gospel and hip-hop,” said Mieko Hatano, Executive Director of the Oakland Symphony and a member of the search committee. “His programming is innovative and reflects his commitment to including underrepresented composers, works, and artists, which speaks directly to the Symphony’s mission [...] We are thrilled to have him join us at the Oakland Symphony.” Armstrong is an alum of Chicago Sinfonietta’s Conducting Fellow program, where he served as Assistant Conductor during the 2018-2019 season. He holds a B.M. in History and Literature from Wheaton College and an M.M. in Orchestral Conducting from the University of Colorado. Armstrong was also named one of The Washington Post’s “22 for ’22: Composers and Performers to Watch in 2022.” For almost 100 years, the Oakland Symphony has presented classical and symphonic music in the Bay Area. For more information about their 2024-2025 season, visit www.oaklandsymphony.org. Photo by Scott Chernis Kedrick Armstrong, previously Principal Conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Galesburg, Illinois, will serve as the new Music Director of Oakland Symphony. me with open arms since my first visit in 2022. It felt like a place I wanted to call home.” “The board, administration, and I are already building a relationship guided by trust, collaboration, and innovation, deeply rooted in the transformative work that has been a part of the Oakland Symphony’s legacy for many decades,” he said. After an extensive two-year search, Armstrong was selected unanimously by Oakland Symphony’s Board of Directors and musicians. The search committee, chaired by longtime Board

Lord is best known for her watercolors with sophisticated color and bold compositions, influenced by the California Watercolor Style of artists. Most recently she has been a full-time student at the Golden Gate Atelier. This show is open for viewing Saturdays and Sundays, April 6-21, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. Sunday, April 14, 4:00 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert In this season’s final Chamber Series, Berkeley Symphony presents Play on Words, a program including music by Erich Korngold, Gordon Getty, Jake Heggie, and Franz Schubert, performed by Evan Kahn, cello; Kevin Korth, piano; and guest artists Lisa Delan, soprano; René Mandel, violin; and Jake Heggie, piano. Please be sure to buy advance tickets at https://bit.ly/3OjC0XR, as these concerts usually sell out. For more information please see the Berkeley Symphony website. There will be refreshments served after the concert. Friday, April 19, 7:00 p.m. Berkeley Choro Ensemble Concert Members of Berkeley Choro Ensemble will perform a concert with the three-time Grammy nominee guitarist and composer Douglas Lora of the LA Guitar Quartet. He tours with the Brasil Guitar Duo and Trio Brasileiro. The group celebrates the music, culture and history of Brazil, with a special emphasis on the Choro genre. The choro sound is akin to a combination of European classical music, ragtime, and blues. Purchase advance tickets at https://www.bpt. me/6251519. Sunday, April 21, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Spring Concert Almost thirty active members of the hometown Piedmont Chamber Orchestra present a free concert to celebrate Spring, called “Suite Antiques” and including three stunning pieces of music composed in the 1880s. The music will be Edvard Grieg’s Holberg Suite for Strings; Émile Bernard’s Divertissement for Winds, Op. 36; and Albéric Magnard’s Suite for Orchestra in the Ancient Style, Op. 2. Donations will be gratefully accepted, and refreshments will be served after the concert. Saturday, April 27, 7:30 p.m. Insight Chamber Players Concert For their first East Bay concert, members of Insight Chamber Players and Van Ness Piano Quartet will perform an exploration into J.S. Bach’s Goldberg Variations. Insight’s composer in residence, Cooper Grosscup, will guide the audience through the entire work, sampling and discussing details with help from Cuna Kim, violin; Isabel Tannenbaum, viola; and Kyle Stachnik, cello. Audience questions and open discussion will be included. Doors will open at 7 p.m. for appetizers and beverages. The performers request a $30 donation at the door. The music begins at 7:30 sharp For more information see https://www.insightchamber.com. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations. articles.text: A rousing celebration of Hispanic culture came off with the S.F. Ballet’s “Dos mujeres” program, continuing offstage well into the night before the large and wildly enthusiastic crowd. The entire Opera House was decorated high and low with multi-color South-of-the-Border images, including oversize flowers enhancing the box seats. The new Artistic Director Tamara Rojo hit the nail on the cabeza with her unique pairing, one celebrating the Mexican artist Frida Kahlo in the US-premiere gala spectacle Broken Wings, the other Carmen. Broken Wings is a glorious fantasy piece by Annabelle Lopez Ochoa, as if intended for the joyful Mexican Day of the Dead complete with amiable and ambulatory cadavers. If you were baffled by the gender mishmash, you were not alone. In the latter, dominant tall males with headdresses played female roles, much as in the Harvard Hasty Pudding comedy shows of old. And in Ariella Smith’s ballet, only distantly related to Carmen, the leading US-premiere of Lopez Ochoa’s Broken Wings at the San Francisco Ballet lady (Sasha de Sola on April 4) passionately kisses the bullfighter Escamillo, played by another woman (Jennifer Stahl). If the Smith Carmen had little to do with bullfights, gypsies, tabernas, the opera or Prosper Mérimée’s original novel, it allowed the tempestuous Carmen to ping-pong back and forth between a devoted father figure (Wei Wang) and the despised husband José in black (Joseph Walsh). It was as though the whole far-ranging drama of Carmen were transported to a spartan drawing room, with passions running wild, and Carmen literally sprinting all with them all over. A few measures of the Bizet opera are quoted in the opening of the helter-skelter Arturo O’Farrill’s score, which overall lacked the high drama required. But whatever Carmen lacked was made up for in the pageantry of Broken Wings, which deserves a rerun next season. This drama of the real-life Frida Kahlo wandering through the real world, a fantasy domain and ultimately a beautiful death was powered by the ballerina Isabella DeVivo, plucked from the ranks of mere soloists to take on Frida. On pointe, DeVivo appears to become airborne in scene after scene, unawed by the imaginary figures that encroach all about her. Playing a minor role as Frida’s (renowned) husband Diego was the robust guest artist from the Oregon Ballet Theatre, JohnPaul Simoens – a surprise loaner, given the raft of leading males in the 83-member S.F. Ballet roster who were untapped. No answer is forthcoming, so far. The wispy story line deals with Frida’s husband, her entering the underworld, then turning into a butterfly and fortified by a spirit headed heavenward. The music by Peter Salem included everything from the song-lament “La Llorona” to a mariachi bringing down the house. Overall, SFB director Rojo made her point several times over: These works were created by teams of women for the most part; and in this region we need some central, focal Latino cultural input, first on stage and extending to lavish Opera House Mexican décor. After the show comes a thunderous all-female mariachi (Mariachi Bonitas de Dinorah) in an unprecedented nightly lobby postlude. BALLET NOTES – Ochoa’s choreography had been featured here previously in her 2018 Guernica. Casts for this run change nightly. This program marked the company’s first-ever double bill of works by Latina choreographers. “DOS MUJERES” (Two Women), a program of Carmen and the US-premiere of Broken Wings, through April 14, by San Francisco Ballet. Opera House, S.F. For SFB info: (415) 865-2000, or go online www.sfballet.org.

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, April 10, 2024 Oakland Symphony hires new Music Director 29-year-old Kedrick Armstrong takes the helm after two-year search By Matt Simons Oakland Symphony has announced the appointment of 29-year-old Kedrick Armstrong as its new music director. Armstrong, originally from Georgetown, South Carolina, previously served as Principal Conductor of the Knox-Galesburg Symphony in Galesburg, Illinois. Armstrong will also actively participate in Oakland Symphony’s many education and community engagement programs, designed to inspire a love of music in people of all ages throughout the Oakland and greater Bay Area. Armstrong is the successor to the late Michael Morgan, who passed away in 2021 after a 30-year tenure leading the symphony. Armstrong’s next appearance with the Oakland Symphony will take place on October 18, 2024, when he will help the company open its 2024-2025 season. “I am deeply honored and grateful for the opportunity to serve as the new music director of the Oakland Symphony,” Armstrong said in a statement. “As a Black conductor, I find it humbling to stand on the shoulders of both Michael Morgan and Calvin Simmons [the most recent and the first African-American Music Directors of the Symphony, respectively]. The Oakland Symphony community has embraced member Jim Bell, was impressed by Armstrong’s demonstrated leadership and community-building abilities, as well as his passion for and command of a wide range of music genres. “The committee was overwhelmed by Kedrick’s scholarship and curiosity about all kinds of music, from classical and jazz to gospel and hip-hop,” said Mieko Hatano, Executive Director of the Oakland Symphony and a member of the search committee. “His programming is innovative and reflects his commitment to including underrepresented composers, works, and artists, which speaks directly to the Symphony’s mission [...] We are thrilled to have him join us at the Oakland Symphony.” Armstrong is an alum of Chicago Sinfonietta’s Conducting Fellow program, where he served as Assistant Conductor during the 2018-2019 season. articles.text: The professional wing of Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC), will present the Tony Award-winning musical Fun Home by Jeanine Tesori and Lisa Kron, based on the graphic novel of the same name by Alison Bechdel. Fun Home runs Apri 26–May 12 at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts in Oakland. This YMTC+ production will feature YMTC alumni, current students, teaching artists, and guest performers. Winner of seven Tony Awards, the original musical Fun Home tells the story of cartoonist Alison Bechdel as she prepares to write her first graphic memoir. The memories of her youth overwhelm her. Exploring her past to write about the sudden death of her father, the adult Alison conjures two younger versions of herself to help her make sense of the volatile, brilliant, one-of-akind man she knew. The show features a cast of 9 actors, including 2 YMTC alumni and teaching artists, 4 current YMTC students, and 3 guest artists. Nine current YMTC students understudy the main cast. The production features a 7-piece chamber orchestra playing John Clancy’s original orchestrations. Fun Home opens Friday, April 26. Performances run for three weekends, Fridays and Saturdays at 7:30 pm and Sundays at 2 pm, closing on Sunday May 12. All performances will be held at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts, 1428 Alice Street in downtown Oakland. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $19–$52, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. YMTC will close out its 2023-24 season with The Sound of Music in July at El Cerrito High School’s Performing Arts Theater. Learn more about the company or buy a season pass at www.ymtcbayarea.org. The Berkeley C C h h o o r r o o Ensemble (pronounced "shoro" ), is a group of world-class musicians from the SF Bay Area that made its debut in January, 2010. In particular, the choro sound is somewhat akin to a combination of European classical music, ragtime, and blues. pages.text: Wednesday, April 10, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The guitar in the twilight zone By Joseph Gold Remember the television program “The Twilight Zone”? If all goes well, you’ll be transported to another dimension. Out of nowhere comes mysterious music. The narrator arrives on the set smoking a cigarette. “Good evening,“ he says. “Our story today is out of the ordinary. You might even call it a musical allegory. Our star is the guitar, an artistic masterpiece. Does any musical instrument have such sensual lines? Let’s just say that it has an inanimate sex appeal. Its history begins even before history was recorded. Musically, it appeals to every aspect of humanity. Does this sound like the Picture of Dorian Gray? It does. Let’s let Oscar Wilde tell the story of… The guitar in the twilight zone.” A huge crowd lines up to see an exhibition of the guitar. There are many on display, and the crowd expresses its admiration. Everyone wants to play it. The very first one is Noah’s grandfather. They say he invented the guitar. Leonardo da Vinci is next. Then come Bach and Vivaldi. They talk to each other a little bit and decide to write some guitar music. Not much time passes and Paganini sees his own guitar resting on plush velvet in all of its glory. He signs it with a flourish and gives it to his friend Berlioz who adds his signature. The crowd whispers: “It’s so beautiful.” Each, in turn, wants to try a tune. Andres Segovia wows the crowd with his playing. He uses a variety of foot stools. To change keys, he uses a capo. All of the classical guitarists copy this style of playing. But the unanimous decision is that the guitar needs more punch. They discover artificial amplification and loudspeakers. Problem solved! Guitar players from every country in the world discover that the guitar expresses world music. For convenience, they might use a pick and a neck strap. Someone comes up with the idea that the guitar needs a stronger tone. Let’s make an electric guitar, they decide. They do, and it becomes even more popular. The guitar adapts its personality to jazz, rock ‘n’ roll, heavy metal, yet remains as beautiful as ever. A few rock ‘n rollers find that smashing their guitars on stage is what they want to do. People pay Classical guitarist Andres Segovia millions of dollars for an instrument, whether in good condition or smashed condition. The admiring crowd departs… not through the front entrance, but through the back door. Guitars on display in the museum are as beautiful as ever. But this is the twilight zone. There is always an allegory…a surprise knock-out punch. After all, Oscar Wilde wrote the screenplay. As the admiring crowd leaves the museum by the back door, they see a large pile of gear; footstools, capos, microphones and cables, amplification devices of all kinds, loud speakers and ear plugs, neck traps, tuners, slides, audio interface, looper pedals, ground lift, reverb devices, and costumes of all kind. On the very top is a smashed guitar. Wilde concludes his allegory with a group of lemmings playfully encircling the scene. The narrator returns to tell us he hopes we enjoyed the program. He smiles as he says: “Did you know that a group of lemmings is called a ‘suicide’?” Sic transit la gloria dei musica. (Thus is the glory of music.) articles.text: Thomas Hardy wrote Far From the Madding Crowd in 1874 during the height of the Victorian era. It was a time when women deferred to the wishes of men and were considered property to be acquired and then ignored. Men, in contrast, offered women safe harbor and financial security. Hardy’s story has proved timeless and prescient in great part because Hardy created in the character of Bathsheba Everdene ­ — an atypical woman who is independent, desiring to live on her own terms and not those dictated by a husband. She declares to a suitor that she wishes to be no man’s property. The film, starring Carey Mulligan as Bathsheba, is not only beautifully photographed, but Mulligan shines as she conveys the emotions of a woman who inherits a large farm and the title of mistress of all she surveys. She is determined to “astonish” all who now work for her and make a success of the farm, for she is no dilettante, but a woman who wishes to live on her own terms in a society where women are cloistered by custom and social mores. However, for all of her sturdy values and willingness to work hard in a man’s world, she is also a woman of emotions and passions. Bathsheba finds herself desired by three men, each vastly different. One is the farm’s shepherd, Gabriel Oak (Matthias Schoenaerts), a quiet man who has no station in life but is ever willing to step into the breach when needed.
