articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. Parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, begin there before heading on to Lightyear. Here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. He loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz Lightyear. What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. So far so good? The question then begged is, “what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination?” First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Lightyear a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic Enterprise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission; all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, they decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however, the ship is damaged on landing. Plus, there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (voiced by Pixar director Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear — a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk. Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min. Released in 2022.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, April 10, 2024 MOVIE FOR ADULTS MOVIE FOR KIDS Far From the Madding Crowd still resonates since 1874 By Chris Honoré Thomas Hardy wrote Far From the Madding Crowd in 1874 during the height of the Victorian era. It was a time when women deferred to the wishes of men and were considered property to be acquired and then ignored. Men, in contrast, offered women safe harbor and financial security. Hardy’s story has proved timeless and prescient in great part because Hardy created in the character of Bathsheba Everdene ­ — an atypical woman who is independent, desiring to live on her own terms and not those dictated by a husband. She declares to a suitor that she wishes to be no man’s property. The film, starring Carey Mulligan as Bathsheba, is not only beautifully photographed, but Mulligan shines as she conveys the emotions of a woman who inherits a large farm and the title of mistress of all she surveys. She is determined to “astonish” all who now work for her and make a success of the farm, for she is no dilettante, but a woman who wishes to live on her own terms in a society where women are cloistered by custom and social mores. However, for all of her sturdy values and willingness to work hard in a man’s world, she is also a woman of emotions and passions. Bathsheba finds herself desired by three men, each vastly different. One is the farm’s shepherd, Gabriel Oak (Matthias Schoenaerts), a quiet man who has no station in life but is ever willing to step into the breach when needed. The second is a wealthy gentleman farmer, William BoldSee Madding Crowd on page 27 Lightyear a wonderful adventure from Pixar Matthias Schoenaerts and Carey Mulligan in Far from the Madding Crowd By Chris Honoré Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. Parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, begin there before heading on to Lightyear. Here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. He loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz Lightyear. What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. So far so good? The question then begged is, “what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination?” First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Lightyear a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic Enterprise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission; all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, they decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however, the ship is damaged on landing. Plus, there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (voiced by Pixar director Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear — a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk. Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min. Released in 2022. pages.text: Wednesday, April 10, 2024 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers view more Heritage Trees By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar t ment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a strong turnout of 43 walkers and five K-9 best friends last week, April 3. The previous week the walkers had gone to see 14 of the Park Commission’s 28 Piedmont Heritage Trees. There were eight more trees still to be seen in the lower sections of Piedmont, so it was off to Dracena Park to see a coast live oak, which is native to California. The group went down the park’s central trail looking for another Heritage Tree, the bigleaf maple, or Oregon maple, but the walkers weren’t sure which tree it was. The walkers made their way to the tot lot and in the distance could see the six Dawn redwoods, where they took a group photo. It is a genus of fast-growing coniferous trees known as redwoods. The other two are coast redwoods and giant sequoias. Since their rediscovery in 1944, they have become popular ornamental trees in parks in many countries. The walkers emerged on Ricardo Avenue and went up Howard Avenue to see a tree at 46 Nace Avenue, a Northern Catalpa believed to have been planted by residents in the early 1900s. Then it was over to Linda Avenue to see the Ceanothus in the Linda Kingston Triangle. Ceanothus is a genus of about species of nitrogen-fixing shrubs and small trees in the buckthorn family. The group retraced their steps on Linda to a set of Tea Trees adjacent to the Beach Playfield. They may be the only ones in Piedmont planted as street trees. They form a dense evergreen canopy and when in bloom have dense white bottle brush like flowers. Just below the playfield is a grove of Coast redwoods. On their way back, the walkers went up to another grove of Coast redwoods in the Jerome Triangle. Then it was up Oakland to El Cerrito and Magnolia Avenues back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu Wednesday Walkers viewed more of the city’s Heritage Trees last week. Be careful when naming beneficiaries You might not have thought much about beneficiary designations, but they can play a big role in your estate planning. When you purchase insurance policies and open investment accounts, such as your IRA, you’ll be asked to name a beneficiary, and, in some cases, more than one. This might seem easy, especially if you have a spouse and children, but if you experience a major life event, such as a divorce or a death in the family, you may need to make some changes because beneficiary designations carry a lot of weight under the law. In fact, these designations can supersede the instructions you may have written in your will or living trust, so everyone in your family should know who is expected to get which assets. One significant benefit of having proper beneficiary designations in place is that they may enable beneficiaries to avoid the time-consuming — and possibly expensive — probate process. The beneficiary issue can become complex because not everyone reacts the same way to events such as divorce — some people want their ex-spouses to still receive assets while others don’t. Furthermore, not all the states have the same rules about how beneficiary designations are treated after a divorce. And some financial assets are treated differently than others. Here’s the big picture: If you’ve named your spouse as a beneficiary of an IRA, bank or brokerage account, insurance policy, will or trust, this beneficiary designation will automatically be revoked upon divorce in about half the states. So, if you still want your ex-spouse to get these assets, you will need to name them as a non-spouse beneficiary after the divorce. But if you’ve named your spouse as beneficiary for a 401(k) plan or pension, the designation will remain intact until and unless you change it, regardless of where you live. However, in community property states, couples are generally required to split equally all assets they acquired during their marriage. When couples divorce, the community property laws require they split their assets 50/50, but only those assets they obtained while they lived in that state. If you were to stay in the same community property state throughout your marriage and divorce, the ownership issue is generally straightforward, but if you were to move to or from one of these states, it might change the joint ownership picture. Thus far, we’ve only talked about beneficiary designation issues surrounding divorce. But if an ex-spouse — or any beneficiary — passes away, the assets will generally pass to a contingent beneficiary — which is why it’s important that you name one at the same time you designate the primary beneficiary. Also, it may be appropriate to name a special needs trust as beneficiary for a family member who has special needs or becomes disabled. If this individual were to be the direct beneficiary, any assets passing directly into their hands could affect their eligibility for certain programs. You may need to work with a legal professional to sort out beneficiary designation issues and the rules that apply in your state. But you may also want to do a beneficiary review with your financial advisor whenever you experience a major life event, such as a marriage, divorce or the addition of a new child. Your investments, retirement accounts and life insurance proceeds are valuable assets — and you want them to go where you intended. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Advisor in the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue. articles.text: Do you need a break from the stresses of daily life? Piedmont Adult School is offering a new class, Introduction to Mindfulness and Compassion, on Tuesdays, April 16-May 21, from 7:00-8:30 p.m. Mindfulness is the practice of focusing attention on the present moment. Practicing mindfulness has been shown to reduce anxiety and stress, improve emotional and physical health, and even improve relationships. Enrolled students will learn and practice basic mindfulness techniques and loving kindness practices. Instructor Nani Vohryzek has been a psychotherapist for more than 26 years, specializing in somatic therapy. She enjoys facilitating groups that support people in being mindful, aware and friendly towards their experiences. To enroll, visit Piedmontadultschool.org or call 594-2655. Introduction to Mindfulness and Compassion Tuesdays, April 16-May 21 7:00-8:30 p.m. $175

articles.text: Twenty-one members of the First Monday Reading group met at the Japanese Tea House. In Piedmont Park on April 1 to discuss Maya Angelou’s 1969 autobiography, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. The book was on The New York Times paperback bestseller list for two years. It has been required reading in some schools, including Piedmont High. However the book’s depiction of childhood rape, racism, and sexuality has caused it to be banned in other schools and libraries. The book begins when threeyear-old Maya and her older brother are sent to Stamps, Arkansas to live with their grandmother and ends with Maya becoming a mother at the age of 16. Many of the problems Maya encounters come from the overt racism of her white neighbors. Everything changes in her life when Maya’s father unexpectedly appears. He takes the two children with him, and leaves them with their mother in St. Louis. There, eight-year-old Maya is sexually abused and raped by her mother’s boyfriend. Maya feels guilty and withdraws from everyone except her brother. Maya and her brother are sent back to Stamps. Later, Maya’s grandmother wants to protect the children from the dangers that Stamps’ racism poses, and sends the children to their mother who is now in San Francisco. Maya attends school in San Francisco, but during her final year of high school she worries she might be a lesbian and has intercourse with a teenage boy. She becomes pregnant and gives birth. The group was almost unanimous in their enjoyment of I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. They admired Angelou’s writing style and the honest storytelling of her situation, family, and herself. She doesn’t blame anyone; this was simply her life. The readers also liked the book’s ending with the birth of her son. Readers appreciated Angelou’s descriptions of the racist environments and situations she grew up in, as well as her use of language that created reader emotion and empathy. She was a poet too, and this is reflected in her prose. For some readers, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings qualified as “one of the best books ever” for them. The book’s title generated some discussion. It is a metaphor taken from a poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar, an African American poet who wrote in the late 1800s and early 1900s. His poem “Sympathy” speaks of the feelings of a bird in a cage. It bloodies its wings because its cage is smaller than the spread of its wings and abilities. It sings not because it is happy, but because it wants freedom to fly, sing, and achieve its potential. The book also sparked personal stories of racism that readers had experienced. Racism in the 1930s was onerous for Maya and African Americans, but other Book cover: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings people were and have been subjected to racism too. The readers said they fell this type of hatred has diminished in our country, but unfortunately is still a part of our lives. So, to some degree Angelou reminds us we are all caged birds. The group had previously selected Perestroika in Paris by Jane Smiley for May and Prequel by Rachel Maddow for June. Laura Goldman presented three new fiction candidates and The Dry by Jane Harper was chosen for July. The next discussion will be on May 6 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, Register at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. articles.text: Lester Ellis, a longtime Piedmont resident, will give a presentation on his experience living in Richmond’s Harbor Gate Project after World War II. “Growing up in Richmond’s WWII Housing. A Personal Story” uses images from his childhood to describe what life was like in this unique part of the Bay Area during the 1940s. In 1940 the Census reported that Richmond had a population of 23,672. In two years Richmond’s population would quadruple, to over 100,000, due to the WWII Kaiser shipyards. To put this in modern day terms, this would be equivalent to Piedmont’s population of 11,000 suddenly exploding to 40,000. To meet the need for housing for people working at the shipyards, 23,000 apartments were rapidly built to accommodate 70,000 workers and their families. Immediately after the War, all housing units became low-income rentals. The Ellis family moved into the Harbor Gate Project in 1946. Come to Piedmont Center for the Arts on Wednesday, April 17, when Lester Ellis tells his family’s story about living in Harbor Gate while Richmond’s leaders laid the plans to demolish all 23,000 homes, including theirs. Growing Up in Richmond’s WWII Housing. A Personal Story Illustrated lecture Wednesday, April 17, 6:30 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Lester Ellis as a boy living in Richmond’s Harbor Gate Project

articles.text: One of the highlights of Ridge’s Spring releases is the unveiling of the new vintage of Ridge Montebello. This wine is simply one of the most iconic wines in the history of California winemaking. It was selected to be a part of the tasting of 1976 in Paris where the California wines showed that they were as good or better than the famous wines of France. Then, when the competition was conducted again 20 years later, Ridge again showed what a world class wine it is. The Montebello Vineyard was planted in 1886, but the vineyard fell into near ruin during the prohibition era. Over the years, it has been replanted and the elevation ranges from 1300 to 2700 feet. Its elevation and exposure to cool Pacific breezes always gives the wine an amazing freshness. The success of the Montebello wine along with an incredible range of Zinfandels and an iconic Chardonnay have caused many to call Ridge a member of the “First Growths” of American wine. articles.text: While I was tending to my new hydrangea patch last week, a passerby stopped to remark upon my garden. “I walk past your yard every day,” he said, “and I’m always impressed at how cottagecore it is.” “Thanks,” I said, not exactly sure if this was a compliment. (Turns out it’s an Instagram hashtag referencing dreamy pastoral scenes.) Pointing past my split-rail fence to the massive clusters of purple flowers rising out of the broad-leaved foliage along the creek, the young man asked. “What are those?” I get this question a lot this time of year. Even in the showiest of gardens these flowers stand out. But nobody ever believes me when I tell them that they are geraniums. The geraniums that you probably have in mind – the sun loving, (usually) red ones with slightly fuzzy leaves, the ones growing out of Parisian planter boxes in oil paintings – are not actually geraniums. At least, not anymore. When so-called geraniums were introduced to the gardening public back in the 1700s, they had been categorized into an eponymous genus by Carl Linneaus, the father of modern taxonomy. Some 80 years later, however, a French botanist reclassified that group of species into a different genus, Pelargonium. Botanists accepted the change, but the gardening public didn’t—so “geranium” is what the common man has been calling these plants ever since. My geraniums are, in fact, the real deal. Which is a funny thing to say given that they look and act like something out of science fiction. The Geramium maderense, as it’s known, grows three to four feet tall and wide and puts out dinner-plate sized, jagged-edged leaves that seem almost tropical. It blooms in the second year by pushing up an enormous bouquet Geramium maderense in bloom in early spring Photo by Josh Harskinson of flowers from a central stalk. And then it dies. You won’t mind, however. They prolifically reseed themselves. I think I started with two or three plants and this year I must have at least 30. While most geraniums hail from the Mediterranean region, these unique plants are endemic to the island of Madeira, a Portuguese territory located in the Atlantic Ocean some 280 nautical miles from the coast of North Africa. It has a foggy and temperate climate like that of San Francisco and was once covered with a forest of evergreen laurel trees. The Geranium maderense grows in the understory, though it is now seldom seen in the wild. In the Bay Area, you can see Madeira geraniums growing in Golden Gate Park near the Queen Wilhemina garden. I have planted mine on a slope beneath oak trees. They require little sunlight and can survive through the summer with minimal water. They prefer acidic soil of the sort that comes naturally from abundant tree leaf litter. Give them plenty of space – this is not a planter box geranium! The older leaves will bend towards the ground to become supports for the plant before it pushes up its flower stalk. Trust me, the spectacular blooms are worth the two-year wait. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. Sanen directed questions to Gonzales, and Mamuyac directed questions to the City Communications Manager, Echa Schneider. “We continue to be grateful for the community’s strong and generous support for the pool project,” said Schneider. “Piedmont residents have repeatedly demonstrated their desire for a full-service, all-ages aquatics facility – first by passing Measure UU in November 2020, then by stepping up to privately raise over $2 million last year to fund the pool as designed rather than further scale back the project’s scope to reduce costs. We are committed to building a facility that will fully meet Piedmont’s athletic and recreational needs.” Construction on the pool began in February 2023. Upon completion, the facility will include a 27-meter competition pool with a diving well, an activity pool with three 25-yard lap lanes, a one-story building with locker rooms, an indoor multi-purpose room, two changing rooms, and a rooftop pavilion. The community pool project has had a history of delays. In December 2022, Stuart Isaac, who the city retained as the financial manager of the project, stated that he was “looking for the pool to launch [open] in Spring [2024], ahead of heavy summer-season demand.” In August 2023, Sanen claimed the project was still on schedule to finish in Summer 2024. In September 2023 Gonzales stated that a summer 2024 completion date was “no longer possible,” and that the pool should be finished in September 2024. The community pool is now scheduled to be completed by Winter 2024, and the project budget is currently $29,967,550. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Guidelines for BPXpress Online Bidding Instructions are provided in Appendix B. Proposals will be timestamped by the website upon receipt and placed in a secure location by BPXpress to be accessed only by a representative from the City of Piedmont. Bids will be publicly opened via an online Zoom meeting at 2:15 p.m. on May 2, 2024. The Zoom meeting information can be found in the bid documents. Please note that bidders must be logged-in as a registered user in order to see the “Submit Bid Docs” tab. The “Submit Bid Docs” tab will only be available until the bid deadline, and all submitted bids are “sealed” and inaccessible until that time. After the bid deadline, the “Submit Bid Docs” tab will be unavailable on the Planroom platform to prospective bidders. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1770 et seq. of the California Labor Code, the Director of Industrial Relations for the State of California has ascertained the current general prevailing rate of wages for employer purposes, in Alameda County, State of California. Not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for work of a similar character in Alameda County and not less than the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for holiday work fixed as provided in the California Labor Code shall be paid to all workers engaged in performing the project. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 1771.1 of the California Labor Code, A contractor or subcontractor shall not be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any contract for public work, as defined in Chapter 1 of Part 7 of Division 2 of the California Labor Code, unless currently registered and qualified to perform public work pursuant to Civil Code Section 1725.5. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. articles.text: At 3:06 in the morning on Thursday, April 4, three suspects burglarized the Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue in Piedmont by backing a tow truck into a plate glass window. The suspects stole merchandize valued at approximately $1,000, and caused $20,000 of damage. One broken window measured 8’ x 16’. Suspects fled in the tow truck on Grand Avenue into Oakland after seeing the police arrive. Less than a year ago, on July 9, 2023, the hardware store was burglarized overnight after the alarm had been deactivated. That theft, which took place for more than one hour, resulted in over $100,000 worth of merchandise and cash stolen. After the robbery, the store owner hired a security guard. The alarms did go off on this occasion. One of the suspects was described as wearing a black hoodie with beige pants; a silver sedan may also have been associated. The Public Works helped secure the opening to the store. This is an ongoing investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective John Lagios at 420-3015. “We’re filing as married, sleeping separately.”

articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 3 is coming to town in two weeks and the organizers are eager to unveil a completely reimagined community experience that’s been in the works for six months. Building on the success of the first two years, the Piedmont Food Fest team has re-examined every dimension of the festival to find new ways to inspire and delight attendees. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year, organizers will turn Magnolia Avenue into a veritable food boulevard helping hungry attendees easily stroll by the many options, making it easy to go back for seconds and even thirds. The Food Zone will feature 22 food vendors, including new additions Tea on Piedmont, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Doc Bones BBQ as well as the Nepalese food truck Momolicious of recent Steph Curry-inspired internet fame. Food Festers will also discover the Sweet Zone, located by the Community Circle, where they can indulge in handmade gelato from Hila, Japanese crepes from BB Tea Station, banana bread pudding from OG Desserts, Taiwanese pineapple cakes from Annie’s T Cakes while getting to know local non-profits, retailers, and community groups such as Oakland Roots, Soccer Without Borders, No Immigrants No Spice, Piedmont Language School, and Immedium Books. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. For more information see: www. piedmontfoodfest.org.
articles.title: Piedmont’s third annual multicultural festival comes to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 20

Navigating the early intervention process can feel overwhelming, but remember that you’re not alone. Early intervention professionals are there to support you every step of the way, providing guidance, resources, and encouragement to help your child succeed. Early intervention not only supports the child’s development but also empowers families to play an active role in their child’s growth and well-being. Studies have emphasized the importance of a family-centered approach in early intervention, which involves actively involving parents and caregivers in the intervention process. Research has shown that when parents are actively engaged in their child’s intervention, children are more likely to make progress and achieve better outcomes. Pearson was a school board member for two terms and has volunteered her time for over 22 years in Piedmont and the East Bay. Pearson, a pediatrician, served on the school board from 2012 to 2020. articles.text: Avian af icionados and bird-calling buffs flocked to the Alan Harvey Theater in Piedmont last week for the 55th Annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest. Fourteen acts featuring more than 80 contestants competed to be crowned the greatest bird callers in town on Friday, March 29, at 7 p.m. A judging panel included a trio of former bird-calling competitors – 1991 winner Joe Fendel, former student and current Piedmont High School math teacher Auban Willits, and celebrity guest judge Alex Hirsch, writer-animator and creator of the award-winning Disney TV show Gravity Falls. The night began with a welcome from School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, attending her first bird calling contest, and PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami, who departs the school in June. First-place winners Cat Pasion (left), Clio Salzer, Charlotte Mascola, and Carmen Gaylord hold the coveted Bird Calling Contest trophy after the contest. Daniel Banin joins the photo in the background. “It’s great to have this program back again,” said Goswami. “Last year we brought it back after four years, and this year we are back with a roar.” PHS senior Daniel Banin, the Master of Ceremonies, introduced each act and provided audience banter between performances. The bird calling competition Students from Beth Black’s Period 4 English Class won third place for the call of the Ross Goose (anser rosii) and their accompanying sketch where the goose squares off with a three-year-old kid at Lake Merritt.
articles.title: 55th Annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest is a hoot at Alan Harvey Theater

articles.text: As we enter April, now designated as Earth Month, there is much to grieve and much to celebrate. On one hand, our planet just experienced its warmest February on record. This was our ninth month in a row with record-breaking temperatures worldwide. On the other hand, we are making unprecedented progress on the long journey away from greenhouse gases. Last year, solar power made up most of the country’s added grid capacity for the first time since World War II. We don’t have to go far to see the shift. Piedmont alone has hundreds of properties with finished solar projects. The origins of Earth Month can be traced to California when Santa Barbara experienced the biggest oil spill in U.S. history in 1969. As the nation watched oil spread over 35 miles of water and witnessed dead animals wash in with the tide, Wisconsin Senator Gaylord Nelson was inspired to take action. Drawing inspiration from student-led anti-war protests, he began planning a nationwide teach-in on college campuses for spring 1970. April 22, the day we still celebrate as Earth Day, was selected to maximize student participation. Over 20 million Americans took part. American environmental consciousness was already growing because of events like the 1962 publication of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, one of the seminal works on modern environmental science. The first Earth Day unified the fragmented efforts of the nation’s conservationists. In the next few years, the U.S. would not only create the Environmental Protection Agency, but also pass landmark legislation such as the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. This year, I invite everyone to celebrate Earth Month by attending one of these local events: • Earth Day at Chabot Space and Science Center This family-friendly event on April 21 from 10 a.m. - 4 p.m. showcases the many ways local organizations are tackling climate change right here in the Bay, with hands-on activities, guest speakers, and more. Highlights include a field diary hike with Chabot educators, climate storytelling workshops, pollinator-friendly crafts, and an eco-trivia game show. articles.text: Piedmont’s third annual Food Fest is less than three weeks away and the reimagined experience will make good on its promise to offer something for everyone. This year, the multicultural festival will turn Magnolia Avenue into a veritable food boulevard, helping hungry attendees to easily stroll by the many options, making it easy to go back for seconds and even thirds. Additionally, the Food Fest will introduce the Sweet Zone located by the Community Circle, where visitors can sample delicious treats such as gelato, Japanese crepes, and tea cakes while chatting with local non-profits, retailers, and community groups. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year’s lineup of food vendors will include fan favorites such as Robert Dorsey Catering, The Chairman, La Santa Torta, Arthur Mac’s, Satay by the Bay, and Tea on Piedmont, as well as newcomers MOMOlicious, Lahore Di Khushboo, Sunrise Deli, Hila Gelato, and Annie’s T Cakes. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org for more information on this can’t-miss community experience. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont resident Bruce Joffe was presented with the Urban and Regional Information Systems Association’s (URISA) Horwood Distinguished Service Award on March 19. URISA is a multi-disciplinary geospatial organization that provides professional education and training, community and advocacy for geospatial issues. The award, named for Edgar Horwood, an early pioneer in the field of information systems for local government, is URISA’s highest award, given occasionally for service, leadership and significant contributions to URISA and to the geospatial technologies industry. Bruce Joffe (right) is presented with the Horwood Distinguished Service Award by URISA Board Member Tim Nolan on March 19.

articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter If you own real property in California, you must pay property taxes twice a year. The second installment of property taxes is due on April 10, next Wednesday. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since you will incur a penalty of 10% plus a $10 fee. If you don’t pay by June 30th, things start to get worse very quickly. You can send a check, along with your 2nd payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s secure URL for making payments is: https:// www.acgov.org/propertytax/ index.htm. If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you will pay a 2.5% processing fee, money that does not go to the county. A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges. Although there are several electronic payment services in common use (PayPal and Venmo, to name a few), the Tax Collector has a specific warning about PayPal on its website: NOTICE TO TAXPAYERS USING PAYPAL A message from the Alameda County Tax office reads: “At this time we are strongly discouraging the use of PayPal for your property tax payments. Using this method of payment may result in late fees and costs. With our current technology, we can only accept full payments for property taxes; partial payments are not allowed.”
articles.title: Property taxes due April 10

articles.text: Fire Chief Dave Brannigan urges residents to share perspectives on disaster readiness Do you know what you would do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting Fire Chief Dave Brannigan much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the very real possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. Please help us help you. Complete the survey today, then send it to five friends and neighbors to take as well. Your city thanks you. For more information, call the Fire Department at 420-3030.
articles.title: Help Piedmont deliver preparedness programs

articles.text: The Recreation Department is inviting community groups and individuals to participate in a new event, the Piedmont Pop-up Putt-Putt in the Park, on Sunday, April 21. Design entries are already rolling in from community groups that plan to install a novelty hole for the course in the Community Center parking lot from 12:00-4:00 p.m. “The idea is that groups will design and test their installation at home, then bring it to the parking lot in pieces in the morning to install it,” said Supervisor Eva Phalen. pages.text: Wednesday, April 3, 2024 5 Help Piedmont deliver preparedness programs Fire Chief Dave Brannigan urges residents to share perspectives on disaster readiness By Dave Brannigan Do you know what you would do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting DISASTER PREPAREDNESS SURVEY IN AN EARTHQUAKE, WILDFIRE, OR OTHER EMERGENCY, DO YOU HAVE A PLAN FOR YOURSELF? YOUR KIDS? YOUR PETS? The Piedmont Fire Department wants to understand how we can help you become more ready for disasters. Please help by taking a brief survey. Your answers will help inform future education and programming around preparedness. PIEDMONT.CA.GOV/DISASTERSURVEY Fire Chief Dave Brannigan much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the very real possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. Please help us help you. Complete the survey today, then send it to five friends and neighbors to take as well. Your city thanks you. For more information, call the Fire Department at 420-3030. articles.text: Last month’s exam on March 9 was the first national administration of the redesigned SAT: an adaptive exam administered on a laptop or tablet. While the core content of the digital SAT is very similar to its predecessor, there are a few major changes: • The digital SAT is now 2 hours and 14 minutes long compared to the old test, which was 3 hours. • The test is adaptive, which means a student’s performance on the first module of each section determines the level of difficulty of the second module of the section. • The reading and writing section has been completely redesigned, and there are no more multi-page passages. • Students can now use a calculator for the entirety of the math section. For students who have been approved for accommodations, the digital SAT can be adapted in a variety of ways. Unlike the SAT, the ACT is not currently going through a major redesign; however, it is piloting the option for computer testing in select locations. ACT scores are accepted at all colleges that accept SAT scores. The new digital SAT comes at a time when colleges are reconsidering their test optional policies. Dartmouth, Yale, and Brown recently announced that they will require standardized test scores for the class of 2029 (current high school juniors) and beyond. After conducting a research study, Dartmouth found that standardized test scores are predictive of academic success at its institution. SAT/ACT scores are also particularly helpful in identifying high-achieving students from under-resourced schools and less advantaged backgrounds. Dartmouth concluded that standardized tests allow them to admit a more diverse and broader range of students, something that is at the forefront of many schools’ minds. Most private universities are committed to a holistic review process. Standardized test scores are a potential opportunity to share more information with a college about a student. As schools gather more information and conduct their own research, it is important to make sure students and families stay informed about testing and other admission requirements as they will surely continue to evolve and can vary school by school. Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of College Counseling at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: Benicio Perez (left), Emilio Perez and Owen Cain with their collection of signatures in support of their P.E. Teacher Brad Sullivan Piedmont School District’s plan to downsize its staff due to budget concerns is affecting many people. The situation has some students at Wildwood Elementary School unsure of who will teach a favorite class, Physical Education, next year. When a few Wildwood students heard a rumor that their Physical Education teacher, Brad Sullivan, would be leaving, they became upset. When students directly confronted Sullivan about it, he confirmed he likely would not be teaching at Wildwood next year. A pair of brothers, second grader Benicio Perez and fourth grader Emilio Perez, then decided to do something about it. They teamed up with friends, including 4th grader Owen Cain, to collect signatures at recess in support of Mr. Sullivan. With the proposed budget cuts, Wildwood students stand to lose Sullivan, their P.E. teacher, and Louisa Cheung, their veteran Tech teacher next year. The students, along with kindergartener Salvador Perez, recently walked into the office of the Piedmont Post to tell their story about how they acquired the signatures of 111 Wildwood students. Emilio and Owen were inspired by a friend who first made a poster in support of Mr. Sullivan. The poster got left at a friend’s house, but the initiative did not stay at home, the fourth graders brought their concern to the Wildwood blacktop during recess with a student petition. Emilio and Owen received some surprise support for their petition. Unexpectedly a few girls in their class campaigned and they even got some fifth graders to sign. “Pretty much the whole grade likes Mr. Sullivan,” said Emilio. “He makes sure everyone has fun. The previous teachers were nice but didn’t make you try hard, like Mr. Sullivan does.” Younger brother Benicio joined in as well and acquired the signatures of 44 of his classmates – nearly the entire Wildwood 2nd grade – to sign his “Save Mr. Sullivan petition.” Benicio actually performed the task twice, The first petition was done with a yellow marker at recess. When the ink appeared too light to be seen, he got a black pen and got his friends and classmates to sign again. “We were happily surprised. Usually signatures are hard to get,” said Cain. An early version of the kids’ signature sheets was titled “Don’t Fire Mr. Sullivan,” and while that may be what it feels like to the kids, the reality is complex. The district has responded by saying that Sullivan has chosen to resign. Sullivan explained that since he is not tenured, he is still in a probationary period and the district can elect not to bring him back without giving a reason. After two years with the district, a teacher becomes tenured and gains more rights. Sullivan was a long-term substitute with Piedmont Middle School during 2021- 22. Afterwards, his colleagues recommended him for the Wildwood P.E. position, where he is in his second year. “At this point, we’re looking at reducing the number of [P.E.] sections at the high school if we do not have the enrollment,” said Superintendent Hawn. But kids aren’t familiar with compromise, tough decisions and stark realities. One may ask “what’s so special about an elementary P.E. teacher? Can’t anyone teach P.E.?” Sullivan’s students not only acknowledge his charisma and ways of making everyone participate. They also get excited when asked to explain the rules of games Sullivan invented and taught to them. One game is called bucket tag, which combines elements of tag with capture the flag, While recounting the rules of pickle-square and drawing up the field boundary of mat-ball, Sullivan’s students became animated. Sullivan told the Post he loves working in Piedmont and hopes the district will reconsider the planned cut. As it currently stands, the district is likely to move staff around and have multiple P.E. teachers splitting the role with other teaching obligations.
articles.title: Wildwood kids rally to save P.E. teacher from budget cuts

articles.text: Students in kindergarten through 3rd grade will be singing their hearts out this week as each elementary school hosts a Vocal Music Spring concert. The young singers at Beach, Havens and Wildwood have been working hard with vocal music teacher Adrian Behrendt and will celebrate music with a theme of Broadway musicals. Each concert starts at 8:45 a.m. and lasts about 50 minutes. Havens held its concert in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse yesterday morning, Tuesday, April 2. The students in the Beach auditorium will shine brightly tomorrow, Thursday, April 4, and Wildwood students will perform Friday, April 5. “The kids have been working hard with me since January on songs from musicals such as Oliver!, Peter Pan, the King and I, and You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown,” said Behrendt The vocal music spring concerts allow young musicians to step into the role of performer. Although Behrendt expects a lot of his students, he teaches the K-3 graders for only one 40-minute period per week, a significant reduction from the district’s earlier years with a robust music program. “I want them to have fun in concert while striving for their personal best as a musician. I think the community as a whole appreciates the effort the students have put into their performance,” Behrendt said.
articles.title: Vocal Music Spring Concerts take place this week

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, April 3, 2024 Bird Calling Continued from page 1 began in 1963 when legend has it that a student asked PHS Science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck if there was anything they could do to “liven things up around here.” It began in his classroom, but soon the halls were crowded with students eager to see and hear the commotion. Its instant popularity required moving the event to the school theater, where it has remained ever since. In its early years, the competition was a black-tie event with celebrity judges and a related Miss Bird Calling contest. The event has evolved over the years to resemble a more vaudevillian tradition, allowing both casually dressed audiences as well as group performances, elaborate costumes, and sketch comedy. This year’s contest theme was “A rose by any other name would sound just as sweet,” a reference to recent efforts in the ornithology world to change the naming conventions of birds to fit their habitats or physical qualities rather than the people who discovered them. The rules of the contest are simple. articles.text: Staff Photos Gravity Falls TV show creator and PHS alum Alex Hirsch returned to his alma mater last week to serve as a judge at the 55th Annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest. After the competition, Hirsch stayed behind to talk with locals in the lobby of the Alan Harvey Theater. Pictured are Sophie Wagganer (left), Alex Hirsch, and Anthony Simons Contestants of the Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest had something extra to be excited about this year. Writer, voice actor, and Piedmont High School (PHS) alum Alex Hirsch agreed to be a celebrity judge for the competition. Hirsch is the creator of the critically-acclaimed Disney TV show Gravity Falls, which besides winning two Emmy Awards, three Annie Awards, and a BAFTA Children’s Award, is also beloved among the student body at Piedmont High School. “We’ve asked him a bunch of times over the years, but there was always a scheduling conflict” said Kathryn Levenson, producer for this year’s contest. “But this year, one of the students, Chaz Amit-Guite, really wanted him to come [...] so I drafted an official-looking email, contacted him, and he said ‘Oh, well, I think I could do that.’” A member of the PHS Class of 2003, Alex Hirsch grew up in Piedmont with his twin sister Ariel. As a junior, he won the Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest in 2002 and earned a chance to perform his bird call on the Tonight Show with David Letterman. Of his call, the Little Blue Heron (Egretta caerulea), Hirsch said the most important parts of his performance were “volume and shamelessness.” During his senior year, Hirsch learned that one of his heroes, Pete Docter of Pixar Animation, would be a judge for the 2003 Bird Calling Contest. Docter, at the time, had just completed Monsters Inc. (2001) to popular and critical success. “I didn’t enter the bird calling contest that second year,” recalled Hirsch. “I really wanted to go to film school for animation and I didn’t know if I was going to get in or not. I was very stressed out, so I coped with that stress by realizing, ‘we’ve got a captive audience here.’” Thus, Hirsch conspired with his classmates Elliot Grossman and Zack Keller to create an animation that would impress Docter. The result was a nine-minute animated short film, Alfred Hitchcluck Presents: Schoolhouse Flock, a story about birds attacking the high school along with a cast of caricatures based on PHS staff, including then vice principal Dennis Creek. The video was shown while the judges decided that year’s winners and received a standing ovation from the audience as well as a mention in the San Francisco Chronicle via its website, SFGate.com. Completing the technically ambitious short by the time of the contest required several all-nighters. A frame from Alex Hirsch’s locally famous short film, “Alfred Hitchcluck Presents,” which debuted during the 2003 Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest.

At the end of their sketch, an example bird call for their chosen species plays over the theater’s PA system to refresh contestants’ memories, and then they perform their bird call for the audience. Acts are judged on the authenticity and beauty of the birdcall, information communicated about the bird, and poise of delivery. After all the performances were finished on Friday night, Ben Ferguson (left), Oliver Amen, and Ben Perez prepare to sacrifice their classmate Grant Schaefer (below) in a skit involving the Monteczuma Quail (cyrtonyx montezumae). Will Kennedy (left) and Marlowe Nelson created owl costumes for their performance, complete with masks meticulously crafted using pipe cleaners. judges went backstage where they had 10 minutes to select three winning acts. In the meantime, audiences were treated to a mini-concert by the Piedmont High School Troubadours, who sang a selection of songs from their Valentine’s Day show. Out of the many talented contenders, three acts stood a cut above the competition. First place (and two-handled, time-honored Bird Calling trophy) was won by Carmen Gaylord, Charlotte Mascola, Cat Pasion, and Clio Salzer for their performance of the Ruddy Duck, oxyura jamaicensis. In their act, Mascola and Salzer played the role of two English hunters while Pasion and Gaylord played their prey, a pair of Ruddy Ducks. Second place went to Chaz Amit-Guite and Theodore Ferguson for their performance of the Canadian Goose, branta canadensis. The duo re-enacted a brawl between two members of the typically ornery species, complete with their signature guttural, nasal honks. Members of the audience physically jumped in their seats when Amit-Guite uttered his first lines, a proud, accusatory “hey!” aimed at his foe. Third place went to students in Beth Black’s Period 4 Junior English Honors Class for their performance of the Ross Goose, anser rossii. It featured Luisa Cole, Clara Murray, Zenn Donatiello, Dorothy Nemeth, Dylan Hickman, Jacob Rodriguez, Ella Hughes, Jacques Saldanha, Leo Hurwitz, Jacob Shusteff, Kasper Jansson, Sophena Tuli, Olive Litwin, August von Metzsch, Jackson Lommen, Clare Weiss, Simon March-Cunningham, and Ryo Woltag. Overall, the winners of the competition expressed great joy at being able to demonstrate their calls for the community. “It’s just such a rush,” said first-place winner Charlotte Mascola. “It’s so much fun preparing a call and coming up with something creative and then getting to share that with people. It’s a wonderful tradition we have here.” Students from Beth Black’s Period 1 Junior English honors class imitate peregrine falcons about to prey on unsuspecting students on the Cal campus. articles.text: Piedmont’s team and robot Banshee win top award Banshee (8033) climbs a chain alongside alliance partners in the last seconds of a match. Thirty five members of Highlander Robotics attended the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Orange County Regional last weekend with their robot ‘Banshee’ and won the top judged award, earning their third consecutive qualification to the World Championship to be held in Houston in two weeks. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots built by students in 9th to 12th grade. The competition takes place in in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot, which operates both on its own and with a driver, must be built for each season and local and regional competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. Teams can win awards based on the performance of their robots, on the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs and the impact they make on their communities. Bids to the World Championship are earned by the captain and first pick of the winning alliance and the winners of the two most prestigious awards, the Impact Award and Engineering Inspiration Award, which the Highlanders received in 2022. The team, attending their second regional of the season and ranked 12th in the state, entered the 48-team event as the favorite. However, after struggling through three different matches where partner robots, which are randomly selected during qualifications, failed to move for some or all of the time they found themselves with a record of five wins and four losses and in 16th place. Even so, they averaged the highest points in the tournament and in the draft preceding the double-elimination playoffs were the first selection of the tournament by the first seed captain “Robot Dolphins from Outer Space” from Dana Point. The three-team alliance was completed with 16th pick, Team Sprocket from Diamond Bar. In the first round of playoffs the alliance won, setting a tournament high score of 137-61. In their second match however, Banshee malfunctioned during the self-driving period, moving at full speed into a steel truss and afterwards had difficulty picking up game pieces. The alliance lost to the fourth seed captained by Nomad from Escondido. In the lower bracket, despite a rapid set of repairs performed by the Highlanders pit crew, Banshee continued to behave erratically and struggled through two more wins 97-79 and 95-58 largely due to the strength of the Dolphin’s robot, Siren. Finally, in the semi-finals, the Highlanders’ alliance lost a second time to Nomad and finished third overall. In the awards ceremony the Highlanders were awarded Scouting Lead Cassie Colby works with her counterpart to choose a third alliance Partner before playoffs. Mechanical Lead Ayaan Jajodia repairs the robot Banshee between matches.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics qualifies for Worlds for 3rd time

articles.text: Vaughn Khouri, Vice Captain of Highlander Robotics, has been selected as a FIRST Dean’s List Finalist and will represent California at the World Championship in Houston later this month. FIRST founder Dean Kamen sponsors The Dean’s List award to highlight outstanding 10th and 11th grade student leaders involved in FIRST’s international robotics competitions. Nominees have demonstrated a commitment to promoting STEM in their communities and shown personal technical expertise and accomplishment. Khouri’s nomination cited his volunteer work mentoring other robotics teams, building STEM curriculum through a non-profit he founded for that purpose, and growing training programs within Highlander Robotics. “FIRST has become a huge part of my life and a lot of what I do within it is beyond our team” said Khouri. “The award seems to recognize that alongside my leadership on 8033 and it feels incredible to receive it.” Similar to the National Merit Scholarship Award, there are three levels of FIRST Dean’s List Award students. Semi-Finalists Vaughn Khouri and Lewy Seiden, both juniors at Piedmont High School, were nominated by the Highlander Robotics team 8033. After interviews, two Finalists are selected across all teams in a regional robotics competition. Khouri was named at the Orange County Regional out of semi-finalists from 48 teams. His nomination will now advance to Houston where 10 Dean’s List Winners will be selected from roughly 100 Finalists on April 19. “Vaughn is the real deal,” said Highlanders Lead Mentor Natalia Feretti. “He has the vision, the skills and the leadership to be a strong advocate for quality STEM education in our community. We are all so proud of him and can’t wait to see what he’ll do with that transformative power.” FIRST’s most prestigious award, the Impact Award, which honors the team that best represents a model for other teams to emulate and embodies the mission of FIRST. The judges cited the use of their skills to support Oakland School District’s Special Education department, their free release of a scouting application used by hundreds of other teams to track robot performance at competitions, and the number of communities they touched with teammates in 17 schools over 11 districts. Banshee was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Max Seiden and supported by drive coach Justin Green, technician Alex Gish, and human player Chloe Kessinger. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is composed of 62 students from 17 high schools around the area. They work from the Mary G Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information, visit the team on its website: frc8033.com. ®

articles.text: Former Piedmonter Denise Bostrom, who teaches a writing course at Piedmont Adult School titled “Family Stories and Memoir Writing,” celebrated her most recent student authors by hosting a Spring Reading for them. Some 40 guests warmed the Piedmont Center for the Arts on March 20 to hear the authors take a firm step towards publishing their works. The special event was the cherry on top of Bostrom’s four-session course, which she has adapted from a 16-week Screenwriting course she taught at San Francisco State. Attendance at the informal Wednesday night event blew Bostrom away, who was expecting possibly 10 guests to the reading, but ended up with a full room “What was just so wonderful was many writers had their parents come, some were in their 80s and 90s. Other writers had their kids attending and we had some grandkids hearing their grandparents too,” said Bostrom. Bostrom helps foster author’s skills in a course taught on Saturdays, with lessons on setting, character development, structure and developing a writer’s voice. “[With] the memoir writers, it’s almost like, all you have to do is add water and they just grow,” she said. Literary topics ranging from the humorous to the deeply personal, were shared with the captive audience. “It was a lovely evening, and a great chance to showcase the work of these talented writers,” Bostrom said. “Hearing one’s stories, art, or work publicly is just so important. I think it is kind of what makes us human. I think we need that to make community,” she said. The course was capped at 10 students and Bostrom teaches another course in the fall. As many of Bostrom’s students have discovered, this particular kind of writing and recording family Piedmont Adult School teacher Denise Bostrom has found a teaching home at Piedmont Adult School after a career as a screenwriter and teacher. and personal stories goes beyond merely writing. “We are all looking at our watches saying, how many more years before we forget our names? If we are not doing it [write a memoir] now, when are we ever going to?” said Bostrom. Adult School students in Denise Bostrom’s writing class are shown at their Literary Evening at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on March 20. Bostrom helps foster author’s skills in a course taught on Saturdays, with lessons on setting, character development, structure and developing a writer’s voice. “[With] the memoir writers, it’s almost like, all you have to do is add water and they just grow,” she said. Literary topics ranging from the humorous to the deeply personal, were shared with the captive audience. “It was a lovely evening, and a great chance to showcase the work of these talented writers,” Bostrom said. “Hearing one’s stories, art, or work publicly is just so important. I think it is kind of what makes us human. I think we need that to make community,” she said. The course was capped at 10 students and Bostrom teaches another course in the fall. As many of Bostrom’s students have discovered, this particular kind of writing and recording family Piedmont Adult School teacher Denise Bostrom has found a teaching home at Piedmont Adult School after a career as a screenwriter and teacher. and personal stories goes beyond merely writing. “We are all looking at our watches saying, how many more years before we forget our names? If we are not doing it [write a memoir] now, when are we ever going to?” said Bostrom. articles.text: Highlanders beat Yellowjackets 12-10 in Berkeley Ruby Guzdar scored four goals in a big win over Berkeley. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team is rolling on a four-game winning streak following a narrow 12-10 victory over Berkeley, a Western Alameda County Conference foe, on Thursday, March 28. With a 9-2 overall record and undefeated at 4-0 against league teams, the Highlanders are firmly in first-place with four games left in the regular season. Ruby Guzdar continued to lead the team with four goals. She earlier scored seven goals against Bishop O’Dowd and five in a victory over College Park. Chloe Graham notched a hat trick with three goals, and Laurel Bentley helped put the game away with w critical goal with five minutes left. Piedmont has one match before spring break at San Marin this Thursday. They return on April 16 for the start of three games in three days starting with Miramonte at home, followed by Granada at home the next day, and will close the regular season at Newark Memorial. The Highlanders are set to enter the WACC Tournament on Wednesday, April 26 with as the No. 1 seed with the championship round being hosted at Berkeley two days later. 12-10 win at Berkeley Piedmont carried a 4-3 lead through the first quarter and went up 7-5 at halftime. But Berkeley went on a wild five-goal scoring run in the third quarter to capture the lead at 10-9 entering the fourth. However, the Highlander defense kept Berkeley scoreless in the final quarter and scored three goals to secure the win. In the first quarter, Piedmont’s Friedie Schickedanz scored the game’s opening goal after 45 seconds, but Berkeley tied on their next possession and went ahead with 7:33 on the clock. The matched waged on scoreless until Guzdar got her first goal with 2:28 remaining. Chloe Graham then put PHS up with around 1:20 on the clock, then Hallie Burden made it 4-2 on the very next possession just 20 seconds later. But Berkeley got one back with eight seconds left, 4-3. Guzdar scored again quickly in the second quarter on a run from the left side on Piedmont’s opening possession, but Berkeley quickly answered less than a minute later and then tied 5-5 with around seven minutes on the Staff Photos clock. Guzdar, once again, put PHS ahead with around 3:30 left, then Schickedanz made a play to score a couple of minutes later to make it 7-5 going into half. In the third, Graham made it 8-5 after around four minutes of action, then Burden quickly added their ninth goal. But from there, Berkeley went on a five goal scoring run to end the quarter leading 10-9. Guzdar tied things up at 10-10 with 9:55 left in the game on another rocket into the net. Slightly over a minute later, Graham put Piedmont ahead 11-10. Then with around five minutes left, Laurel Bentley scored to clinch the victory. Final stats: Guzdar had four goals, one assist, one ground ball and won one draw control. Graham had three goals while Schickedanz had two. Burden had two goals, three ground balls, and won four draw controls. Bentley scored once. Hailey Marshbrun won five draw controls and scooped one ground ball. Goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter had five saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (9-2 overall, 4-0 league) heads to San Marin in Novato on Thursday, April 4. Chloe Graham scored three goals against Berkeley. Laurel Bentley scored the final goal to help clinch the win over Berkeley.

articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ tennis team claimed two Western Alameda County Conference victories last week, defeating Castro Valley 6-1 on Thursday, March 28 at home, and Arroyo 5-2 on the road in San Lorenzo two days earlier, Tuesday, March 26. “We defeated Castro Valley 6-1, but four of the matches were close and went to a third set,” explained coach Jim Landes. :Arroyo is the best team in the Shoreline Division and took two doubles matches, albeit we didn’t play our usual duos. All of our singles players won in straight sets against Arroyo,” Against Castro Valley, Lucas Smolko got back in the win column with a dominant 6-0, 6-1 win over the Trojans’ top singles player, Arik Hoffman. Smolko, the Post’s 2023 Freshman of the Year, has faced some tough competition this season, having recently lost to Bishop O’Dowd and Berkeley. “It’s been an interesting season, a little bit up and down. I’ve been without a coach for a while so my game has felt streaky at times. High school matches are great practice,” said Smolko, who plays in outside NCTA tournaments. “The main thing is I’m taking opportunities to work on my game, I haven’t gotten many matches outside of high school, so I’m just trying to practice and improve my strategy,” he added. Piedmont plays a double-header against Encinal and Alameda today, April 3, and has two weeks with no matches during Spring Break. It returns for a match at Head-Royce on Wednesday, April 17. Following Wednesday’s matches, PHS will have just four regular season appearances left on the schedule before the WACC Tournament on April 26-27. 6-1 over Castro Valley Arun Brahma and Monte Imburg brought in the first win of the day at No. 1 doubles in straight sets, 6-0, 6-2. Soon after, Smolko beat his opponent at No. 1 singles, 6-0, 6-1. Appearing at No. 3 singles was Nick King winning the third match of the day in three sets, 6-1, 4-6, 6-1. Winning the clinching fourth victory of the match day was Will Tenney at No. 4 singles, 6-2, 6-2. At No. 2 doubles, Kasper Jansson and Torsten Olsen won in three sets, 6-7 (7-2), 6-2, 10-5. Derek Chan and Hunter Fasteau also won in three sets at No. 3 doubles, 7-6 (7-1), 5-7, 10-5. The only loss of the day was Graham Alban at No. 2 singles, 6-4, 0-6, 7-5. 5-2 win vs. Arroyo At singles, Nate Welch appeared at the No. 1 spot, winning 6-3, 6-2. At No. 2 was King, winning handily 6-1, 6-1. Tenney played at No. 3 singles to a double-bagel, 6-0, 6-0 win. Siddharth Bhatia won 6-0, 6-1 at No. 4 singles. At doubles, Jansson and Olsen Staff Photos Lucas Smolko brought home an easy win at No. 1 singles against Castro Valley. lost 7-5, 1-6, 6-3 at No. 1. Fasteau and Maximo Miller also lost 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2. Winning at No. 3 doubles was William Richardson and Elias Reed-Miguel, 3-6, 6-1, 10-7. NEXT UP Piedmont has a double-header today, April 3, against Encinal and Alameda. PHS will host Encinal at 3:30 p.m., and then travel to Alameda HS for an evening match. Will Tenney won the clinching fourth match against Castro Valley. Nate Welch won at No. 1 singles against Arroyo.
