articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team looks strong in its first eight games of the season, building a 6-2 record thus far. Over their last three games, Piedmont has scored 45 runs and allowed five. They recently defeated Healdsburg 19-1 at Witter softball field on Monday, April 1. They beat San Lorenzo on the road 15-3 on Thursday, March 28, and bashed Tennyson 11-1 in Hayward on Tuesday, March 26. “We’re trying to put together some wins. We’re a young team, we have only six girls returning from last year and have five new players,” said coach Gene Denard, “Learning the game of softball is tough and sometimes and it shows. We’re just going day by day.” It’s been a big start to the season for several returners from last year’s team. Leading the team in hitting is junior Angelina Wu with a sterling .632 batting average with 12 hits in 19 at bats, including 19 runs out of the leadoff position, 13 stolen bases, and 11 walks. Junior Miya Fujimoto is also swinging the bat with a big .526 average with 10 hits in 19 at bats, a double, triple, 13 runs scored and 13 RBIs in the three-spot. She’s also drawn eight walks. Both Wu and Fujimoto carry the innings for PHS’ pitching staff. Fujimoto, who usually lines up at shortstop as the team’s best infielder, is 2-1 and has thrown 21.1 innings with 2.625 ERA, 39 strikeouts. Wu is 3-1 in 18.2 innings pitched with an identical 2.625 ERA and 21 strikeouts. “A lot of things fall on Fuji and Angelina. We’re trying not to give them too many innings just yet. I don’t even think Miya is really getting into her groove yet,” Denard said. Emerging in the starting lineup is junior Samantha Ronin, hitting .350 with seven hits and the team’s only home run, including nine RBIs, nine runs scored, and seven stolen bases. She can also contribute on the mound with three innings pitched. 19-1 over Healdsburg PHS opened with a bang, scoring 11 runs in the bottom of the first inning, scored twice in the second, once in the third, and another five in the bottom of the fourth—activating the 10-run rule after the top of the fifth. Final stats: Wu went 2-for-2 with four runs scored, two walks, and a stolen base. Mia Leggett was 2-for-2 with two runs scored, two RBIs, two walks, and hit a triple. Fujimoto was 2-for-2 with four RBIs, three runs scored, drew two walks, and hit a double. Ronen had an RBI and run scored. Sa’Mara Levi had an RBI, walk, and two runs scored. Sophena Tuli was 2-for-3 for three RBIs, two Staff Photos Angelina Wu is hitting a remarkable .632 in eight games. runs scored, and stole two bases. Fujimoto started as pitcher, throwing three innings and allowed no hits, striking out six and walked one. Wu threw two innings, striking out three and allowed two hits and one walk. 15-3 over San Lorenzo As the visiting team, Piedmont scored six runs in the top of the first, two in the second, three in the third, and another four in the fourth inning. Final stats: Wu went 1-for-1 with one RBI, three runs scored, drew three walks, and stole two bases. Leggett was 1-for-3 with a run, RBI, walk and two stolen bags. Fujimoto scored three runs, one RBI, and drew two walks. Ronen was 1-for-1 with two runs scored, two RBIs, and drew two walks. 11-1 over Tennyson Piedmont scored three runs in the top of the first, tacked on four in the third inning and another four in the fourth inning. Final stats: Wu went 3-for-3 with three runs scored, an RBI, and three stolen bases. Leggett was 1-for-3 with two runs scored and an RBI. Fujimoto was 3-for-3, three runs scored, and an RBI. Ronen was 1-for-3 with an RBI. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-2 overall, 2-0 league) heads to Encinal in Alameda today, April 3, for a 4:00 p.m. game. Miya Fujimoto is hitting .526 and leads the team with 21 innings pitched. Samantha Ronen is emerging as a new varsity starter, hitting .350.

articles.text: Highlanders have back-to-back WACC losses for first time Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team suffered a rare loss to Berkeley on Thursday, March 28 at Witter Field, spoiling their Senior Night with an 11-4 loss. It was Piedmont’s first loss to Berkeley since 2012. PHS is the six-time Western Alameda County Conference champion. It is their first two-game league losing streak since joining the WACC in 2017. Thursday’s loss to the Yellowjackets had similar tones to their 10-4 loss at Bishop O’Dowd the previous week, March 22. PHS struggled to maintain possession in the attacking area, often losing ground balls before being able to find a shot attempt. Berkeley had a similar defensive approach to the Dragons, where Piedmont’s isolated attacker was crashed on by defenders as he approached net to force turnovers. Piedmont hopes to regroup after suffering its first loss to Berkeley in 12 years. articles.text: Samantha White swims the breaststroke against Berkeley. Despite facing a challenging meet against Berkeley High School on Friday, March 22, the Piedmont High School Swim Team showcased their resilience and determination. Piedmont, with a smaller group than usual due to multiple meets occurring simultaneously, found themselves outnumbered by Berkeley. Berkeley had 63 swimmers and Piedmont had 25. However, this did not deter the swimmers. Several swimmers, including Simon March-Cunningham, Zach Dupree, Sam Smith, and Sam White, rose to the occasion, stepping into new roles on varsity and the A relays. Coach Colby Price said a highlight for him was seeing a lot of improvement in certain swimmers. “Zach Dupree’s remarkable improvement in the 100 fly, shaving off 1.5 seconds after a 5-second improvement the week before, and Sam White’s impressive performance in the 500 free, finishing with a time of 5:49 and pushing the field, were particularly commendable,” Price said. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team suffered a rough 3-0 loss to Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponent Alameda on Thursday, March 28 by scores of 25-20, 25-14, 25-15 at Binks Rawlings Gym. It’s been a tough start for the squad this year after losing all but two starters from last year’s roster – Shunji Higashi and John Champion. Last year’s team was a big part of redeveloping boys’ volleyball at PHS after the sports’ 20-year absence at the school. PHS is still about middle of the pack at 4-6 in the WACC and must take four of its final six matches in order to qualify for North Coast Section for a third consecutive year. “We’re just trying to have fun and make sure the kids keep coming back. It’s been sad to see the drop off from last year. We’re 4-6 in league and have beaten the teams I think we needed to. When we go against those bigger schools, those teams have a lot of players who do club. We only have a few kids playing club, so players are learning this game for the first time,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Still, Cardenas sees bright spots, including senior Spencer Sorensen-Wald. He just started playing volleyball competitively for the first time after being a pole vaulter on the track and field team last year. He’s Piedmont’s primary outside hitter opposite of Champion. “It’s a great community; I love all the guys, but it hurts when we lose. I just started playing this year. I did a couple of open gyms, but not much after that. It’s a lot of technique and mine may not be the best, but I’m learning as I go,” Sorensen-Wald said. Piedmont will have a chance to rebound at Encinal on Thursday, April 4 for its final match before spring break, then they’ll return on April 15 against Berkeley. 3-0 loss to Alameda Piedmont lost in three straights sets by scores of 25-20, 25-14, 25-15. In the first set, Champion finished with six kills, while Sorensen-Wald had three spikes to his credit, but it wasn’t enough to outlast an aggressive Hornets’ group. articles.text: Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture in San Francisco will host the 21st Annual International Ocean Film Festival (IOFF) showing more than 50 films from around the world from Friday through Sunday, April 12-14. The IOFF has become internationally recognized as specializing in ocean-themed independent film screenings, question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers, and free panel discussions. Films focus on ocean animals and marine environments and range from shorts to feature-length works. Many films shown this year will be world premieres. The International Ocean Film Festival kicks off this year on Friday, April 12 with two films at 4 p.m. and 7 p.m., concluding with an opening night party at 9 p.m. A ticket for the opening night party includes appetizers, beer, and wine and costs $150 per person, which includes both film screenings. Individual film screenings are $10 to $30 per person. Screenings are shown in the Cowell Theater and free panel discussions take place in the Tidepool in Landmark Building D at Fort Mason. Admission to panel discussions must be reserved in advance. For a full list of films, and to learn more, visit https://fortmason.org/event/international-ocean-film-festival-2024/. Fort Mason in San Francisco will host the International Ocean Film Festival.
articles.title: Fort Mason hosts International Ocean Film Festival next week

articles.text: Museum member previews this Thursday & Friday The Legion of Honor museum in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of feudal military rule in the Asian country. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked in both pre-and postMeiji era. A museum member preview takes place Thursday, April 4 and Friday, April 5. A Japanese Prints in Transition donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at Legion of Honor through August 18. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints.

articles.text: The Jewish Folk Chorus of San Francisco will perform at the Pardee Home Museum in Oakland on Sunday, April 21 at 4:00 p.m. as part of the Carriage House Salon series, The cost is $30 per person, and will be held at 672 11th Street, Oakland, with entry through white gate on Castro Street. The Zingeray ensemble of the Jewish Folk Chorus of San Francisco, now in its 97th year, will perform an afternoon program of songs with selections in Yiddish, Ladino, Russian, and Hebrew. Singing and participation will be encouraged for everyone. The Chorus has been spreading Yiddish music and culture since the 1920’s and is delighted to entertain with songs reflecting the tapestry of Jewish life – joy, struggle, justice, and peace. In existence since 1926, the Jewish Folk Chorus stays true to its roots in the labor movement by preserving and performing works from its library of Yiddish labor songs. A champagne reception with savories and sweets will be served following the performance. Purchase tickets on Eventbrite (https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ the-carriage-house-salon-returns-jewish-folk-chorus-of-sanfrancisco-tickets-845027669507) or call Richelle Lieberman 510- 381-1973. The Jewish Folk Chorus of San Francisco will perform at the Pardee Home Museum on Sunday, April 21.

pages.text: 16 Wednesday, April 3, 2024 Arts & Entertainment Fort Mason hosts International Ocean Film Festival next week By Allyson Aleksey Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture in San Francisco will host the 21st Annual International Ocean Film Festival (IOFF) showing more than 50 films from around the world from Friday through Sunday, April 12-14. The IOFF has become internationally recognized as specializing in ocean-themed independent film screenings, question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers, and free panel discussions. Films focus on ocean animals and marine environments and range from shorts to feature-length works. Many films shown this year will be world premieres. The International Ocean Film Festival kicks off this year on Friday, April 12 with two films at 4 p.m. and 7 p.m., concluding with an opening night party at 9 p.m. A ticket for the opening night party includes appetizers, beer, and wine and costs $150 per person, which includes both film screenings. Individual film screenings are $10 to $30 per person. Screenings are shown in the Cowell Theater and free panel discussions take place in the Tidepool in Landmark Building D at Fort Mason. Admission to panel discussions must be reserved in advance. For a full list of films, and to learn more, visit https://fortmason.org/event/international-ocean-film-festival-2024/. One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, a series of 119 ukiyo-e prints begun and largely completed by the Japanese artist Hiroshige (1797–1858) Japanese Prints exhibit opens at Legion of Honor this Saturday Museum member previews this Thursday & Friday By Allyson Aleksey The Legion of Honor museum in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of feudal military rule in the Asian country. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked in both pre-and postMeiji era. A museum member preview takes place Thursday, April 4 and Friday, April 5. A Japanese Prints in Transition donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at Legion of Honor through August 18. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints. articles.text: Berkeley Rep play ends April 14 Photo by Kevin Berne Tommy Bo, Sharon Shao and Feodor Chin appear in Berkeley Rep’s production of The Far Country. Pulitzer Prize finalist Lloyd Suh’s critically acclaimed new play The Far Country is performing at Berkeley Repertory Theatre now through April 14. The Far Country follows Moon Gyet as he arrives at San Francisco’s Angel Island Immigration Station in the wake of the Chinese Exclusion Act with an invented biography and a new name. Moon, played by Tommy Bo, soon finds that passage to San Francisco, and the dream of a better life, comes with a price. “I’m incredibly proud to bring Lloyd’s beautiful play home to the Bay Area,” said Berkeley Rep Artistic Director Johanna Pfaelzer. “It is an honor to share this story with our community, in this magical, complicated place that has inspired and compelled people from all over the world to leave their countries of origin to seek opportunity, safety, and home.” The cast includes Bo, Feodor Chin, John Keabler, Whit K. Lee, Tess Lina, Sharon Shao, and Aaron Wilton. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (510) 647-2949 or by visiting www.berkeleyrep.org. Performances are Berkeley Rep’s Peet’s Theatre at 2025 Addison Street.

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra will perform its Spring Concert on Saturday, April 27; at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The program of music includes Gershwin’s An American In Paris (1928), Stravinsky’s’ Firebird Suite (1945), and select chamber music pieces. Tickets are $20 General, and free for students who register at the ticket site. For advance tickets see http://data.ypsomusic.org/ tickets. This year, YPSO celebrates its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director/Conductor. He will be conducting approximately 100 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from Bay Area cities from Napa to Pleasanton. Starting this season, YPSO offers free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and to high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. Program The Spring Concert will feature two iconic pieces, George Gershwin’s An American in Paris and Igor Stravinsky’s The Firebird Suite. In addition, the concert will showcase select chamber music pieces performed by YPSO chamber ensembles. American in Paris is a symphonic tone poem that captures the spirit of Paris in the 1920s. Known for its jazzy rhythms and colorful orchestration, the piece is a vibrant portrayal of the bustling streets, Parisian nightlife, and the joie de vivre of the city. The performance will feature the percussion section with taxi horns, the woodwind section with bluesy saxophones, as well as the brass section with a spotlight on trumpets. Stravinsky’s 1945 version of The Firebird Suite is a ballet suite derived from his larger work, “The Firebird.” Composed for the 1910 Paris season of Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russe, the suite includes some of the most memorable music from the ballet. The Spring Concert will serve as the kickoff for YPSO’s annual Spring Silent Auction, a virtual fundraiser that runs for two weeks from the Spring Concert until Mother’s Day. (April 27- May 12). Visit the online auction website at ypso2024.ggo.bid. The auction will feature a variety of goods and services donated by YPSO families and local businesses. They include wine tastings, outdoor adventures, and homemade meals, Proceeds support YPSO’s orchestra education program, scholarships for students in need, and the upcoming tour to Japan this summer. This annual fundraiser is a vital part of supporting YPSO’s music education program - ensuring that no student is left behind. It provides crucial funding for their annual programs and is especially important this year as they work to ensure that every student who needs it has the opportunity to go on the oncein-a-lifetime cultural and musical experience to Japan and nurture their growth as global citizens. For more information and to donate items to the auction contact ypso@ypsomusic.org. In its active calendar, in addition to their Fall and Winter Concerts, they played at Davies Symphony Hall for the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival. Later this season, they will embark on a 9-day, 3-concert summer tour to Japan in June 2024, performing in Sakai (Sister city to Berkeley), and Tokyo. The students will play

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s popular Bohème Out of the Box returns to the Bay Area this spring, with free outdoor performances of an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème at Alameda’s Radium Runway at 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, April 20-21. Puccini’s classic and beloved opera about love and loss among a group of Bohemian artists will be performed in a 75-minute version on a converted shipping-container-turned-mobile opera stage. Directed by Jose Maria Condemi, Bohème Out of the Box is sung in Italian with English narration and features a cast of San Francisco Opera’s Adler Fellows and guest artists with piano accompaniment. The performances will take place at Radium Runway, 2151 Ferry Point in Alameda, a short walk from the Seaplane Ferry Terminal. The converted stage uses the San Francisco skyline and Bay Bridge as backdrops, with seating available on the taxiway covered with artificial turf. The free performances are designed for families. Guests are encouraged to bring blankets. Registration is encouraged but not required. Visit sfopera.com/ box to register now. Admission and seating is on a first-come, first-served basis. Food and beverages will be available for purchase and audiences are welcome to bring their own food and beverages to enjoy during the shows. Boheme Out of the Box opera comes to Alameda on April 20 and 21.
articles.title: SF Opera’s free Bohème Out of the Box comes to Alameda April 20-21

articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, likely the best-known and most successful Spanish filmmaker of the last three decades. His most memorable film in the U.S. was Volver (Return), and starred Penelope Cruz, considered Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. As she is gradually pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity the film takes on a noirish tone, moving from 2008 to 1994 The film is completely taken with the transformative face of Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like we are lookmatic westerns. Penélope Cruz and José Luis Gómez in Broken Embraces ing at a Vogue fashion layout, so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance. Perhaps it is because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices; the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the audience is not interested in knowing about the motivations of the characters. From this reviewer’s perspective, it is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience. And so, though all is revealed, little is revealed. Even when the film is set briefly on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. If you love movies and have followed the remarkable career of Almodovar, Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. Broken Embraces. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. articles.text: The term B movie has long been used to refer to second tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 1940s and 50s. To make sure audiences felt they were receiving sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel, a cartoon and two feature films. That was the norm. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, small budgets, and were the equivalent to the widely popular dime magazines during the same time known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subjects ranging from gritty detective mysteries, wildly imagined tales of science fiction, and melodraInstead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B movie, it might be more accurate to call it pulp cinema. This is not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plots and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. If it’s a truism that not all films have to be analyzed, then B movies are a good fit. They are rarely ambiguous, or enigmatic. Edge of Darkness uses the familiar and satisfying trope of revenge to move the plot along at an intense clip. Boston Detective Tommy Craven (Mel Gibson) and his only child, daughter Emma Craven (Bojana Novakovic), are leaving his home when a shotgun blast kills Emma. Initially Tommy thinks the shot was aimed at him and wonders who from his past (an ex-con seeking long contemplated revenge?) might have tried to kill him. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s new animated movie Soul Soul is an animated fantasy/ comedy produced by Pixar-Disney Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter and Kemp Powers. The filmography of Pixar-Disney is extraordinary and has demonstrated a remarkable consistency in its ability to create magical entertainment for youngsters, examples being the Toy Story franchise, Inside Out, Up, Coco, Lightyear, and Wall-E. Soul opens with the sounds of off-key, discordant band music and quickly cuts to a New York City middle school cluster of kids all playing a variety of instruments, led by their tall, lanky music teacher, Joe Gardner (Jamie Foxx). The look on his face tells all. He’s cringing while the kids are doing their best to play a marching song that is unrecognizable. Finally, class is over and as Joe prepares to leave he is stopped by the principal and told that he has been hired permanently. Unexpectedly, Joe’s reaction is ambivalent. We soon learn that his passion is to play gigs at jazz clubs rather than teach. Shortly after leaving school he gets a phone call from a former student, Lamont “Curley” Baker (Quesrlove), who remembers Joe’s love of playing jazz. He’s heard of an opportunity to audition as a pianist with the iconic saxophonist Dorothea Williams (Angela Bassett). He goes and lets ‘er rip. Dorothea is impressed and hires him on the spot. His longedfor opportunity has arrived. Joe leaves the audition with his head in the clouds, oblivious to the crowded streets of New York. Paying no attention to where he is walking, he falls into an open manhole. Before continuing with the journey of Joe Gardner, it’s impossible not to comment on the animation created by Pixar in acts one and three. It’s astonishingly good – as close to photography as can be imagined and so good it’s almost surreal. NYC comes alive, people, cars, buses, all viewed through the lens of the animators’ talented imagination. Pixar has a long history of knowing its audience, those youngsters who stand ready to suspend their disbelief. But then there’s Joe at the bottom of the manhole. And thus begins act two. The narrative cuts to a disembodied Joe (the soul of Joe) on a crowded moving walkway, surrounded by tiny blue blobs headed to the “Great Beyond.” Wait. Joe died as a result of the fall? Do important characters ever die in cartoons? In Soul, apparently the answer is yes. And rather abruptly the story shifts to a place in which Joe is not a hip jazz musician or a music teacher; instead, he’s a fuzzy, blue image of his former self with only his familiar hat and glasses. He really doesn’t want to go to any beyond, and definitely not to a place called the “Great Before.” While possible to barely track the story from this point on, it loses its mojo. Heaven (a word never mentioned in the story) is not a gig that Joe wants any part of. There are strange denizens and other wordly counselors all named Jerry. Keep in mind that in the world of Pixar’s audience, death and what’s beyond is way out of their wheelhouse. Why include the metaphysical scenes at all? You might ask if Joe find his way back to NYC? Or wake up in a hospital? Yes and no. Will he make his way back to the piano? I don’t want to be a spoiler, so I’ll stop here. But I did miss the Joe who was introduced at the outset. He’s a sweet character with a dream, a guy in search of a different life, who ultimately learns the lesson that he should follow his passion, which is to play jazz. He will thereby find that life can be remarkable. Soul. Directed by Pete Docter and Kemp Powers. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Jamie Foxx, Phylicia Rashad, Angela Bassett. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2020. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/Disney+.

articles.text: The official launch of Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America, the most recent book by Piedmont author and journalist, William Gee Wong drew an audience of 200 at the Oakland Asian Cultural Center in Chinatown on March 24, It started at 1 p.m. and didn’t finish until about 4 p.m., even though it was advertised to go for an hour with book signings to follow. Harvey Dong of Eastwind Books sold almost all 100 books he brought. Wong read excerpts from his most recent book, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America, and answer questions posed by Dong and audience members, many of whom patiently waited in a long line for Wong to sign. “I felt so uplifted by their presence and support,” Wong said. “A classmate from elementary school whom I hadn’t seen in many decades showed up and bought 4 books. We exchanged warm, if brief, greetings, then Bill Wong signs copies of his newest book, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America. we texted one another. He called me yesterday from his home in Vacaville and told me how he learned of my event. His sister lives in Piedmont and she saw the articles [in the Post] which she sent to her brother, my old friend. He drove down from Vacaville just to see me and buy my books.” Wong said. Copies of the book are available at www.williamgeewong. com for access to Temple University Press. Author Bill Wong (left) with Harvey Dong of Eastwind Books at Wong’s book launch in Oakland Chinatown on March 24.

articles.text: Where is the best place to hear a concert? Some people like large auditoriums and big name stars who frequently “phone in“ their performances. Do you think that Frederick Chopin would sound good under these circumstances? I don’t think so. He was always at his best performing for an intimate crowd. I think Frederick Chopin would have loved our Piedmont Center for the Arts. You can be sure that private concerts in Chopin’s time included delicious refreshments as well as lively conversation. These are some of the benefits we get at the concerts at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. That’s the way it was last Saturday evening, March 30, when the members of the Temescal Quartet were joined by pianistCarl Blake. To make matters even better, the concert was free, and there was an excellent catered reception after the concert. I arrived early and heard the musicians in lively discussion. All five of them are longtime friends. Part of the conversation was where to set up. At the Piedmont Center for the Arts, it really doesn’t matter because every seat is a good seat. Another good thing is that the acoustics are lively. As the audience assembled, it was quite clear that they were part of the performance. It is always gratifying to see young people at concerts. What a joy to see so many young kids enjoying the music. All aspects for the concert were a combination of formal and informal. The concert was entitled “Taking flight – a fugal adventure.” Every aspect of the programming showed great intelligence. The entire first half contained pieces which somehow flew under the guise of the word “Fugue” (meaning to pursue). Most of the selections were short, but they formed an impressive unity. “Contrapunctus 1” from the Art of the Fugue by Bach and the finale from Haydn’s String Quartet Op. 20, No. 6 served as warm-ups. delssohn’s Scherzo Fugue, the quartet’s emotional energy really sprang to life. The world premiere of Jane O’Leary’s Taking Flight proTemescal Quartet members Barbara Riccardi and Dana Myers violins; Jonna Hervig, viola; Nancy Bien, cello, with guest pianist Carl Blake, who played a musically persuasive performance of Brahms’ Piano Quintet and F minor.

articles.text: A solo show of paintings by Carolyn Lord will open at Piedmont Center of the Arts on April 6 and will feature paintings inspired by Googie architecture, flower gardens, and the California landscape. There will also be a group of landscapes inspired by a trip to Colorado. Lord is best known for her watercolors with sophisticated color and bold compositions, influenced by the California Watercolor Style of artists such as Millard Sheets and George Post. She has been active in the Oakland arts community for many years, recently as a full-time student at the Golden Gate Atelier. She has participated in plein air events in Sonoma and Crested Butte, Colorado and has had paintings in juried shows at the Triton Salon, De Young Open, and Greater Bay Area Open. For detailed information about galleries that represent her work, in Santa Rosa, San Francisco, and Carmel; and upcoming watercolor workshops in Denver, Berkeley, and Whidbey Island, see: www.carolynlord.com Open Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays on April 6-7, 13-14, and April 20-21. articles.text: What would the world be like if President John F. Kennedy hadn’t revealed how much he enjoyed Ian Fleming’s James Bond novels? Can we imagine a world in which Sean Connery doesn’t purr, “Bond…James Bond,” to the dangerous lady spy who has just inquired the identity of the provocative hunk at the baccarat table next to her? Well, JFK spilled the beans about his literary taste, and worldwide audiences have reaped the benefits for more than 50 years in a series of 25 James Bond films that have earned nearly 8 billion dollars. One of those films is coming to Piedmont as the next offering in the Second Thursday Flix Fest. It’s From Russia with Love, number two in the franchise, following Dr. No and just before Goldfinger cemented Bond’s continuing presence in the hearts of lovers of witty adventure. Released in 1963 and directed by Terence Young, From Russia with Love saw Sean Connery’s second outing in the role he would play seven times. In this adventure he battles SMERSH, the evil multinational organization bent on sowing disruption and seizing power, headed by the slyly malevolent Ernst Stavro Blofeld, who strokes a purring cat while he plans mayhem. Connery is abetted by Danielle Bianchi as the “Bond girl,” Bernard Lee as M, and Robert Shaw, Pedro Armanderiz, and Lotte Lenya as the assassin with a knife in her shoe. The movie will be presented on Thursday, April 11 at the Flix Fest’s new afternoon starting time of 1:00 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The film is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is encouraged at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 3, 2024 21 Features Girl and her Dog Farm By Michelle Docter The sweet fragrance of neighborhood magnolia trees always reminds me that spring is here. If you’re anything like me, a ray of sunshine in the garden has me pulling out my collection of seed packets, ready to get sowing. There are so many ways to start seeds and I’ve tested a lot of them. After my fair share of fruitful and failed attempts, here are a few tricks I’ve learned. First, start with seeds that are no more than three years old for the strongest germination. Starting seeds is an act of patience, so I don’t want to take my chances with seeds that may be past their prime and fail to germinate. Head online or to the local nursery to gather your favorite 2024 seed varieties. Buying seed packets rather than seed starts offers much more choice of unique varieties - like Barry’s Crazy cherry tomatoes or Dragon’s Tongue bush beans! Second, choose a high-quality potting soil to create the ideal growing conditions for your seeds. You can purchase E.B. Stone’s 420 Potting Mix which is stocked at the Grand Lake Ace Garden Center and most local nurseries. Ideally, you’re looking for a mix that provides moisture retention, like coconut coir or peat moss. Try earthworm castings as a source of organic matter to provide beneficial microbes and bacteria. As I prepare my seed trays, I like to mix in just enough water so it feels like a wrung out sponge. This will help achieve a uniform level of moisture for seeding. Third, to account for poor germination, sow two seeds per Michelle Docter and Rita sow spring seeds. seed cell. Murphy’s Law is all too present in the gardening world: if something can go wrong it will. That’s why I tend to over-sow. You will have to thin out all but one of the seedlings that sprouts, but this allows you to pick the stronger seedling, resulting in stronger plants in your garden. When sowing seeds, a good rule of thumb is to make a hole two times as deep as the seed is wide. For example, a big bean seed should be sown much deeper than a tiny chive seed. You’ll know it’s time to plant out your seedlings when its true leaves emerge. These are the ones that resemble the mature plant’s leaves. Trust your gut if you’re unsure. I only plant out my seedlings once they look like they can fend on their own in the wild. Crops you can start now Here is a list of just some of the crops you can start from seed right now: tomatoes peppers lettuce parsley cilantro Swiss chard peas arugula spinach green onion beets kale broccoli carrots For cut flowers you can start the following: Lisianthus Statice Feverfew Forget-Me-Nots Sweet Peas Violas Sunflowers Zinnias Happy seed starting. Please reach out if you have any garden questions. I’d love to help. Girl And Her Dog Farm is run by backyard farmer Michelle Docter in Albany. It offers backyard CSA produce, home-baked breads, and kitchen garden designs. Find us on Instagram & Youtube @girlandherdogfarm, or email girlandherdogfarm@ gmail.com. James Bond to pay visit to Piedmont By Bob Hall What would the world be like if President John F. Kennedy hadn’t revealed how much he enjoyed Ian Fleming’s James Bond novels? Can we imagine a world in which Sean Connery doesn’t purr, “Bond…James Bond,” to the dangerous lady spy who has just inquired the identity of the provocative hunk at the baccarat table next to her? Well, JFK spilled the beans about his literary taste, and worldwide audiences have reaped the benefits for more than 50 years in a series of 25 James Bond films that have earned nearly 8 billion dollars. One of those films is coming to Piedmont as the next offering in the Second Thursday Flix Fest. It’s From Russia with Love, number two in the franchise, following Dr. No and just before Goldfinger cemented Bond’s continuing presence in the hearts of lovers of witty adventure. Released in 1963 and directed by Terence Young, From Russia with Love saw Sean Connery’s second outing in the role he would play seven times. In this adventure he battles SMERSH, the evil multinational organization bent on sowing disruption and seizing power, headed by the slyly malevolent Ernst Stavro Blofeld, who strokes a purring cat while he plans mayhem. Connery is abetted by Danielle Bianchi as the “Bond girl,” Bernard Lee as M, and Robert Shaw, Pedro Armanderiz, and Lotte Lenya as the assassin with a knife in her shoe. The movie will be presented on Thursday, April 11 at the Flix Fest’s new afternoon starting time of 1:00 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors open at 12:45 p.m. The film is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is encouraged at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. articles.text: A good turnout of 33 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays stroll. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. It has designated 28 Piedmont trees as “Heritage Trees.” The intent of the program is to recognize noteworthy, distinctive trees in Piedmont city parks or open spaces, encourage residents to visit City parks and open spaces, and promote the study of nature. Last spring, the walkers nominated the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Park as Heritage Trees, and with the help of the tots at the school who also proposed it, they won. The walkers have proposed another tree this year, and the winners will be announced by Arbor Day, April 26. The walkers decided last week to see some past winners. Getting started was easy as they looked up at the trees that surround the Exedra Plaza. This grove of 10 Highland poplars are Heritage Trees. They are a hybrid of two North American plain poplars that are native to the Northern Hemisphere. The walkers then made their way to City Hall to see a group of Evergreen dogwoods at its entrance. These trees are native to Bhutan, China, on the Himalayas’ eastern edge. Then it was down Vista Avenue to Hillside to see the stately palm trees at the Recreation Center. These trees are known as Canary Island date palms or pineapple palms. They are native to the Canary Islands off the coast of Northwestern Africa. Jim Kellogg said this is a popular palm species because its trunk doesn’t grow large and the canopy of palms at its top have a uniform shape. The group then went to the tot lot behind the Exedra to see a Coast live oak grouping, and continuing on, Coast live oaks on the path to Bushy Dell Creek. A large, twisting Coast live oak that has been used for family photos is a Heritage Tree too. These oaks are native to California’s central valleys, as far north as Mendocino County, and as far south as Baja California in Mexico. In front of the Community Hall is a Yulan magnolia, native to central and eastern China. It and produces stunning white flowers in the spring. Other Heritage Trees nearby are Japanese maples, native to Japan, Korea, China, eastern Mongolia, and southeast Russia, and a group of Akebono cherry trees from Japan. Near the Community Hall is the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree in December. The walkers continued to Guilford Road and Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa Road the walkers saw another large Coast redwood Heritage Tree. This specific tree once marked the entrance to the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls, Piedmont’s first school, which opened in 1913. The walkers went up Requa, down Highland, and up Wildwood Avenue. This two block section of Wildwood was originally lined with large, stately and colorful American elms, but they died from Dutch elm disease. Thy were replaced with colorful but smaller trees, Autumn Blaze maples. The ones on Wildwood are Heritage Trees. Wild Autumn Blaze maples are found in eastern North America where the parent species overlap. Just off Wildwood is the Hall Fenway and a grove of European white birches that are native to Europe and parts of Asia. The walkers went on to Crocker Park looking for a Copper beech. It is deep purple in the spring and turns to a coppery hue in the autumn. Not all trees in the park had their leaves, and the group wasn’t sure which one was the Heritage Tree. The walkers continued to Hampton Park so see the mulberry trees at Piedmont Play School. These trees are known as white mulberry, common mulberry and silkworm mulberry. The species is native to China and India and is widely cultivated elsewhere including in the United States, Mexico, Australia, Kyrgyzstan, Argentina, Turkey, and Iran. Mulberry trees were brought to Piedmont in the early 1880s as silkworm food for the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society’s Silk Farm which was on what is now Littlewood Drive. on the walkers and they needed to return to the Exedra via LaSalle Avenue and St. James Drive. Other Heritage trees would have to wait for a future walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register with the Recreation Department at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Part 2 Last week’s Part One of my two-part report on a recent trip to Burgundy covered the 2022 vintage. I went with my intrepid colleagues Terry Hershey and Richard Wing, who have shared many wine exploration trips with me. Burgundy battles Bordeaux for the title of France’s greatest wine region, but the two could not be more different. Bordeaux is the land of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and huge, impressive chateaus and estates. Burgundy is the land of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay grown by hundreds of small producers making tiny amounts of wine. The Cote d’Or, which stretches from just south of Dijon to 10 miles south of Beaune, is a small region divided into thousands of tiny vineyard plots called climats. International demand for the wines and the small amounts produced have caused the price of Burgundy wine to skyrocket. The world’s most expensive wine, Domaine Romanee-Conti Romanee-Conti, now sells for $16,000 a bottle for the current vintage and it is said the land it grows on is the most expensive real estate property in the world. On our trip, we had the pleasure of visiting eight different Burgundy wine estates from large negociants to small family farmers. Here is part two of my report. parts of the city of Beaune and in fact the wines are aged not in an underground cellar but within the 11-foot-thick fortified walls of the city. The thickness of the walls creates an ideal dark, damp, and humid home for the barrels of wine to age. We were met by Vincent Avenal General Manager of the estate, a convivial chap who spoke perfect English and clearly had a love for his job. After the tour of the city wall cellars, we were escorted into an elaborate parlor with 12-foot ceilings and baroque paintings abounding. On the coffee table lay a 300-year-old handwritten manuscript recording the business dealings of the winery. The place was steeped in the deep history that you experience so often when you are touring the wine estates of Burgundy. Vincent poured five reds and five whites ranging from basic Bourgogne to Premier Cru Clos des Mouches from 25 to 120 euros per bottle. All the wines were well made and worth exploring but my favorite was… FAVORITE WINE • 2022 Domaine Chanson Beaune Premier Cru Clos des Marconnets A big, powerful Burgundy with firm tannins good acidity and solid structure with great flavors of cherry plum, red currant and earth. The nose has hints of cherry, herbs, leather and tobacco. The finish is long and satisfying. Great job.

Located between the Cote de Nuits and the Cote de Beaune, the Pernand-Vergelesses vineyard, buried in the greenery of a peaceful valley, originates at the foot of Corton hill. Production seems to be split evenly between red and white wines. They served a lovely fresh Aligote that would make a great aperitif and costs only 13 euro. In fact, most of the wines they produce (except the Grand Cru Corton Charlemagne) were very reasonably priced and represent great value. Robin Rapet was a wonderful and gracious host. The wines of Domaine Rapet are imported by Weygandt-Metzler and are available at Weygandtwines.com. Vincent Avenal, General Manager of Domaine Chanson Isabelle Collotte of Domaine Collotte Isle de Vergelesses was the top wine at Domaine Rapet. Domaine Evenstad and Domaine de la Cree – Santenay Like Domaine Drouhin last week, this is another winery with an Oregon backstory. Last year on a tour of Oregon wineries. I visited Domaine Serene in the Willamette Valley and they proudly announced that they had purchased a winery in Burgundy which they were renovating. They invited me to visit should I ever be in Burgundy. We were warmly greeted by Mark Magnet the General Manager of both estates. After starting Domaine Serene, Ken and Grace Evenstad decided to follow their love for French wine and pulled off the unthinkable – they purchased a prime Burgundy wine estate. These properties hardly ever go on the market and when they do they are almost never sold to foreigners. But the Evenstads ended up with a magnificent 15th century estate Domaine de la Cree located in Santenay. The estate comprises seven Premier Cru blocks located entirely along the renowned Cote d’Or escarpment, home to some of the world’s most storied Pinot Noir and Chardonnay wines. Holdings include Pommard, Volnay, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet, Santenay and Maranges. Biodynamic farming practices are employed to drive optimal terroir expression and ensure soil and plant health. Squeeze the lime to obtain two tablespoons of juice. 2. Transfer the zest to a small bowl, then add the lime juice, vinegar, honey, mustard, chile powder, salt and pepper. Stir to combine, then slowly whisk in the olive oil. Stir in the sliced red onion and set aside. For the salad 1. Cut or peel the rinds from the grapefruit and orange, making sure to remove the white pith, which is bitter. Slice crosswise into 1/4-inch rounds. Cut each round into large bite-sized pieces. Transfer to a large salad bowl. 2. Cut the avocadoes in half lengthwise and remove the pit - carefully. Cut into lengthwise quarters then slice across each quarter into 1/2-inch pieces. articles.text: Shelagh (Phibbs) Udovch, an active member of the Piedmont community for 47 years, passed away on March 21, 2024, from complications related to dementia. She was 84 years old. Shelagh was born in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 1939, and graduated from Potchefstroom High School for Girls in 1957. She worked as a bookkeeper at Rustenberg Farm in Stellenbosch before sailing from Cape Town to Southampton, England, in 1960. Getting her first taste of travel, she decided to keep going. She sailed to Canada with friends, and then drove across the country during the depths of winter in a Volkswagen Beetle. She settled temporarily in Vancouver, where she worked as a Secretary to the Vice President of Engineering at the B.C. Telephone company. Upon visiting San Francisco in 1963, she was offered employment as a receptionist at the South African Consulate and eventually became Secretary to the Consul-General. While working at the Consulate, she met her husband, Frank Udovch, on the tennis courts of San Francisco. Playing tennis was to become one of their favorite pastimes. Shelagh enjoyed not only the competitive and social aspects of tennis, but also the obligatory cold beer after a tough match. When her sons were born, tennis remained a central part of her life, and the Udovch family could often be seen playing family doubles on the Piedmont tennis courts or at the Berkeley Tennis Club. Shelagh Udovch passed away on March 21, 2024. She was 84. Shelagh became the first locally hired staff member to join the Scottish Development Agency. Over the next 22 years, she helped multiple directors from Scotland transition to life in the local office and in the Bay Area. Her networking skills were legendary; she continually had to reorder her business cards, which she would distribute to any interested riders that she picked up from the Casual Carpool line on Oakland Avenue on her daily commute to San Mateo. Mere days after she and Frank moved to Piedmont in 1977, two Piedmont moms rang the Udovch doorbell, and recruited Shelagh for the Beach School mother’s Club (now the BPO) treasurer position. She happily obliged. As time went by, she continued her volunteerism and community involvement with the Piedmont Community Church, Dress Best for Less, the Red Cross, and League of Women Voters. When the Piedmont Post first started, Shelagh agreed to spearhead advertising sales, selling ad space to local businesses. Shelagh’s picture was often found in the early Post editions’ “Where in the World” section, featuring shots of her many travels around the world. Shelagh was fun-loving and spontaneous. Whether driving her youngest son Justin down to Mexico on a surfing trip or traveling solo to Turkey, she was always game for a new adventure. When her husband died suddenly in 1999, she began recruiting new travel companions. She loved to host parties and share a glass of Chardonnay with anyone who was available. All who knew her would not soon forget her unabashed physical affection and her trademark move of beginning a dinner-party conversation with a potentially shocking opening line. Shelagh is survived by her sons Peter (Leila Hebshi) Udovch of Piedmont and Justin (Joy) Udovch of South Kona, Hawaii; and four grandchildren. She is also survived by sisters Sandra Rickwood and Evelynne Gunn of Surrey, UK. She was preceded in death by her sister Karin Cockroft, and her brother Owen Phibbs, both of South Africa. A memorial service for Shelagh will be held on Friday, April 26, at 11 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. 5649 COUNTRY CLUB DRIVE, OAKLAND ⊲ JUST SOLD IN 8 DAYS ⊳ Exemplifying mastery in the art of real estate representation, Pamela navigated the sale of Claremont Pines’ distinguished crown jewel with unparalleled sophistication. articles.text: Wayne Batavia, a lifelong Bay Area resident and longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on March 27, 2024. Born Wayne Ellis Batavia on August 31, 1954, he was the youngest child of George and Katherine Batavia. He attended Skyline High School where he was Student Body President, then University of California in Berkeley where he majored in Business with a concentration in Real Estate. He spent one year away from the Golden State to earn a Masters of Science degree in Real Estate at the University of Wisconsin in Madison. He soon returned with his beloved dog, Shade and began a career spanning 30 years as a Real Estate Developer and Consultant. It brought him a great sense of accomplishment and joy. Wayne met his wife Melissa “Missy” Kane on a blind date and they were married in 1981. They have two children, Julia and Margaret (Colleen), with whom Wayne enjoyed spending as much time as possible: whether walking the dog, playing sports, watching movies, going camping, or eating dinner together every night after he got home from work. Wayne loved his family, and spending time with them was his greatest passion. Over the years, Wayne enjoyed being an active member at Temple Sinai in Oakland, and with the greater Jewish community. He was a member of two wine tasting groups, a softball player as well as coach, an avid skier Wayne Batavia died on March 27. He was 69. and cyclist, and a proud Porsche driver. Above all he was a steadfast friend to the many people who loved him, and whom he loved in return. He is survived by Melissa, his wife of 42 years, and daughters Julia and Margaret (Colleen). He is also survived by older siblings Leslie (Stan) DeLugach and Clyde (Gail) Batavia. To honor Wayne and with a nod to his untimely death brought on by a long battle with Lewy Body Dementia, the family requests that memorial donations be made to the Brain Support Network for the advancement of research in brain diseases. The website is www.brainsupportnetwork.org.

In 1852, Walter purchased 600 acres from the U.S. government at $1.25 per acre of what is now central Piedmont, with property that extended from Scenic Avenue west to Grand Avenue. The brothers selected a level site just south of Moraga Avenue near a freshwater spring and built a modest one-room cabin. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, April 3, 2024 The History of Piedmont The first house in Piedmont was built by brothers William and Walter Blair and was on Highland Avenue (then called Vernal) between Blair Avenue and Park Way. By Gail G. Lombardi Introduction During the City of Piedmont’s Centennial in 2007, the Piedmont Post, in cooperation with the Piedmont Historical Society, began printing stories and photos of the earliest history of the city from its founding in 1907, its growth resulting in part from the earthquake and fire in San Francisco in 1906, and the city’s earliest settlers. For families who have moved to Piedmont since 2007, when the city’s Centennial was widely celebrated and publicized, the series of history pieces by historian and researcher Gail Lombardi, may prove insightful, providing a look at the earliest settlers, and why people have chosen to move to Piedmont for more than a century. Walter Blair, Piedmont’s first pioneer Walter Blair was Piedmont’s enterprising first settler who played an important part in the early development of today’s city. He built the first house in the Piedmont hills (see photo) and established a dairy and rock quarry. In the 1860s, long before bridges spanned the Bay, he developed the first horse car line bringing visitors and picnickers into the Piedmont hills. Many of these visitors enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to build their homes here. Raised on a dairy farm in Vermont with 11 siblings., Walter was born In 1851. He and his brother William sailed around Cape Horn to get to San Francisco. Within months, they rowed across the Bay and discovered the fertile lands in the Piedmont hills. The brothers selected a level site just south of Moraga Avenue near a freshwater spring and built a modest one-room cabin. They named the pathway from Moraga to their home “Vernal” for the abundant ferns and shrubs that grew around that nearby spring. Vernal Avenue was renamed Highland Avenue in 1911. The dairy quickly became known for its high quality milk, cream and butter, and soon the Blairs were delivering their milk and butter to residents in Oakland and even across the Bay to a few wealthy San Francisco customers. It was difficult for the horses hauling those wagons filled with ten-gallon milk cans. The roads were filled with muddy ruts in the winter and covered in thick dust in the summer. Blair realized that a hard surface was needed for these roads. Always the entrepreneur, Blair hired Chinese laborers to quarry rock from a basalt outcropping near his dairy and sold crushed rock to lay over the muddy/dusty streets in Oakland. The walls of the quarry are still visible in lower Dracena Park. Walter Blair went on to develop the first horsecar line to Piedmont and Blair’s Park. (More on that in a later column.) William Blair established a nursery near Mountain View Cemetery and sold eucalyptus seedlings. Today, the eucalyptus trees he planted still grow along the cemetery border on Moraga and in Dracena Park. As a successful businessman, Blair rebuilt his cabin in 1862 into the large gabled house with gardens as seen in the photo. Walter Blair married and soon moved to downtown Oakland. He leased the house to the Arthur Bowman family. The Bowman children Walter Blair was Piedmont’s first settler and entrepreneur. and staff are shown in the photo above, with a fresh water spring in the foreground. Later, Blair’s daughter, Florence, lived in the house from the 1890s until her death in 1924. The Blair homestead was demolished in 1926, and Waldo Avenue was created. articles.text: At its March meeting the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) joined the bandwagon gaining steam to reforest Piedmont with native plants, neighborhood by neighborhood. Among the reasons for this ambitious effort is climate change, which seems to be more concerning with each passing month. Many trees and other plants which thrived in a moderate climate with plenty of rain every winter are suffering and dying in our increasingly hot, windy weather. Two recent examples of this new effort include: 1) the Park Commission spent a day at Bushy Dell Creek planting riparian native plants donated by Watershed Nursery thanks to Tom and Jane Kelly of Greens at Work. 2) Piedmont Garden Club commemorated it’s 100th Birthday with a $10,000 donation to the City. The funds will be used to install native plants near the Firehouse at City Hall. Next is the much-anticipated decision as to what to plant to replace the iconic Sequoia gigantea in the traffic circle at the Mountain and Bellevue intersection. This redwood tree stood tall in this intersection for generations, even serving as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 1920s and 1930s (stopped by the onset of WWII). Showing grave danger of toppling, this tree was removed last fall. At its March meeting the Park Commission approved the recommendation of the City staff and supported by PBF to replace that tree with an Island Oak (Quercus tomontella), a tree indigenous to California (especially the Channel Islands) and regarded as likely to thrive in a small traffic island that has no regular source of water. PBF will undertake a campaign to raise funds to select a good specimen of Island Oak. Campaign proceeds will help refurbish the traffic circle with suitable landscaping, install a plaque commemorating the Sequoia, contribute to the cost of hand watering through the City’s landscape maintenance contract, and provide care for the Island Oak for its first two years. After that time the tree should thrive on its own. Representatives of PBF plan to visit nearby neighbors to solicit funds for the project. PBF’s main Spring project will be on a much larger scale: a campaign to reforest Piedmont neighborhoods. A map of the City will be marked with areas where reforestation is needed. This will include parks, civic areas, traffic circles, tree-lined streets, and other appropriate spots. The emphasis will be to replace trees that are no longer surviving in our increasingly harsh climate with trees indigenous to California that are likely to thrive going forward. PBF’s Spring Brochure (to be mailed in early May) will show various neighborhoods to which gifts may be targeted. PBF and the City will first aim to reforest Dracena Park, where the need for new trees is most urgent. Donors who wish to contribute to an alternative area where reforestation is needed will be able to do so. This exciting new campaign will be known as “Reforesting Piedmont Neighborhood by Neighborhood.” The community is encouraged to look for PBF’s Spring brochure which will include details on how to give our City a beautiful, new and greener look. Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s mission, in partnership with the City, is to provide a safe, sustainable and beautiful community. The foundation is comprised of eight trustees from the City and Piedmont Garden Club, and 26 advisors from the community at large. To learn more about Piedmont Beautification Foundation, please visit https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/.

articles.text: White Elephant Sale volunteers reveal the amount of money raised at last year’s Sale – $2,650,000 – the largest in the history of Oakland Museum. This year’s annual White Elephant Sale, a major fundraiser for Oakland Museum of California, raised more than $2.652,000 – a record high in the museum’s history. The sale was held five weeks in February and March. Organized and presented by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, it is the largest annual fundraising event benefiting the museum. A substantial portion of the proceeds supports exhibitions, programming, and operations each year. An army of volunteers staff the different departments in the WES warehouse, a large building on Lancaster Street in East Oakland. At an event where the total amount raised was revealed, each department recited a little bit about the items they sold, then the volunteers turned over their cards to show the total dollar amount. In a skit, volunteers on the right side of a lineup of seven people shoed the number 2, so that the total amount was revealed in reverse order. “We were so excited to welcome shoppers back to the warehouse for our 65th White Elephant Sale, and continue our mission to support OMCA,” said Marge Harvey, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. “I’m so proud of our Board and our dedicated volunteers for their commitment to this Oakland tradition.” “We are extremely grateful for the extraordinary commitment of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board to OMCA throughout the past 65 years,” said Museum Director and CEO Lori Fogarty. “As the single largest donor to OMCA, the Women’s Board and their White Elephant Sale are absolutely essential to the success of the Museum. We extend our heartfelt thanks to the leadership of the Women’s Board and the hard work of hundreds of volunteers who make the White Elephant Sale possible each year.”
articles.title: White Elephant Sale raises record amount

pages.text: Wednesday, April 3, 2024 31 Alex Hirsch Continued from page 9 “I may have missed a few days of school,” Hirsch said wryly. “I closed the blinds. I forgot to eat. I put everything I had into trying to finish this cartoon. There was no YouTube back then, there was no Instagram, there was no way of getting your cartoon in front of your hero except for commandeering the local bird calling contest and forcing them to put it on the screen. So, I had to shoot my shot.” It paid off. To bring things full circle, Hirsch was recently invited to speak at Pixar on March 8. When questioned by an interviewer at his talk, “would you ever make a movie at Pixar?” Hirsch hesitated a moment before slyly asking, “are you offering?” A f ter h is compet it ive bird-calling career, Hirsch attended California Institute of the Arts (Cal Arts) in Santa Clarita. He would go on to work on shows like Cartoon Network’s Marvelous Misadventures of Flapjack, and the Disney Channel series Fish Hooks before creating Gravity Falls in 2012. Students at this year’s bird calling contest were aware of Hirsch’s presence. After one performance, a student on the way off the stage flashed a triangle gesture around his eye toward the judges table, a reference to a fan-favorite character on Gravity Falls, Bill Cipher. Others whispered excitedly to one another in the audience about his presence between acts. After the contest, Hirsch set up a small table in the lobby of the Alan Harvey Theater where adults and children alike came to talk with him and get items signed—a mixture of contest programs and Gravity Falls memorabilia. The atmosphere was warm and informal as Hirsch answered questions from fans and doled out life advice to young animation hopefuls. Hirsch said that he doesn’t regret skipping class to work on “Alfred Hitchcluck Presents...,” because it led to a fruitful animation career that he loves dearly. “So remember that, kids. Drop out of school and you’ll be a big success!” laughed Hirsch. It turns out that she worked for a major defense contractor, Northmoor, located in Northhampton, and that she was thinking of becoming a whistleblower. Since this is pulp cinema, there has to be pulp dialogue, (here spoken with a Boston accent) an example being the Chief of Detectives saying to Tommy, “These guys are armed and dangerous.” Tommy replies, “What do you think I am?” Note the lack of ambiguity. Or when Tommy looks at a corporation CEO, who he senses is somehow involved in Emma’s death, and says, “You had better decide whether you’re hanging on the cross or banging in the nails.” The pulp imagery is spot on, sounding hard-edged and threatening, mirroring Tommy Craven’s persona throughout the film. Is Edge of Darkness violent? Definitely. In the Craven world you can have conversations, brief and to the point, and then the moment is quickly reached when the best response is simply to hit or shoot the bad guy. Sometimes these moments of carnage and gunplay, or the threat of carnage and gunplay, are connected to the plot by the slightest of threads. No worries, though, they’re a rush. This is, after all, a take-no-prisoners pulpy revenge movie. Edge of Darkness. Directed by Martin Campbell. Starring Mel Gibson, Ray Winstone, Danny Huston and Bojana Novakovic. 1 hr., 57 min.
